I honestly cannot see where the negative reviews are coming from with this game.  While there is a lack of content, the game plays extremely well.
Character animations aren't flashy, but truly, they don't really need to be.  They look fine in my opinion.  The control of the game is rather good, playing with a controller for once in a moba besides Smite is a GODSEND.  It is amazing.
I will admit, there isn't truly much to the game, the music truly is kind of dull and sometimes I question if there is music at all, but all things aside, most people play their own music anyway when playing such games, though a soundtrack would have been appreciated.
The characters are rather interesting to look at, though the diversity is well appreciated.  I have to say, they are fun for what they have.
All in all, it's a good game, not fantastic, but certainly not terrible.
Would I recommend it?  Most likely, it's not for EVERYONE, but if you enjoy Smite, and LoL, this is certainly a game you should in the very least, play once or twice.

This is a review of Fight the Dragon by 3 Sprockets games, an early access arpg on Steam.
It is currently available for PC, OSX and Linux.
The developers are planning on making it available on other platforms at some point.

Fight the Dragon is a Arpg-style game that takes elements from games in the Diablo or Torchlight series, and mixes them up with a bit of Little Big Planet as well as Minecraft.
I've been playing arpg's of one sort or the other for many years-since the debut of the first Diablo game back in 1996 in fact. I've played almost every single game in the arpg genre. While Fight the Dragon isn't exactly like a traditional arpg due to its incorporation of things like puzzles and its lack of a main storyline I feel it more than makes up for it in its replay value as well as its customisability.
It all starts with their Adventure Creation Kit. This is a simple to learn editor that allows players to create and share their own adventures.
Players can also share their adventures or campaigns online. The game has Steam workshop integration. You can subscribe to custom character modifications that let you change your characters look OR you can share your own creations with others. Adventures (as well as gameplay) are also cross-platform.
This game has a ton of replay value. There are over 3k player-made adventures, and more are added all the time. There's also four player co-op via internet OR LAN, and two player local co-op! Between single player content and multiplayer it means way more than your moneys worth. There  are features that haven't been implemented yet. Money has no use aside from the games 'loot sacrifice' system. Every player gets a loot shrine. They can add excess loot to get donation tiers.
When you've donated enough items to reach the next tier you get to choose a random item of rare or better quality. It means your chances of getting something decent are good whether you accomplish an adventure or not. This game is challenging! It has easy maps but the real fun starts on medium. Maps aren't just about killing monsters. There are puzzles to solve as well. It means that no matter how many times you play the game there's always a new problem to solve which means less chance of losing interest.
I think this game is worth the low price they're charging for it ($14.99, currently on sale (as of 12-10-14) for $11.99), and the developers are constantly adding great new features to it. I think this is a solid buy for any arpg fan or for anyone who loves a good hack and slash dungeon crawling adventure.

It would be understanable if the game was in alpha or beta, or even freshly released, but it's over 2 years old at this point. Retro City Rampage is fantastic. The gameplay is simple and addictive, with high replay value.
The game is nearly 100% a reference/parody of the 80's (including Back to the Future, Ghostbusters and TMNT) or popular NES games at any time (including Mario, Mega Man, and Rad Racer). It's very charming and doesn't take itself too seriously.
One of the coolest features is the graphical options. You can change your "television" to several different sets, including an arcade cabinet or a Gameboy. You can also change the color settings to look like an NES, Super NES, Sega Genesis, Atari 2600, Gameboy, and many more. You can even turn on scan-lines for an authentic 80's CRT TV experience.
My only gripes with this game are particular levels. The underwater levels are overly difficult and frustrating.
Another level pits you against several rocket launcher-wielding goons with little to fight back with; defeating them is pure dumb luck.
The final boss fight is initially interesting and stylish, but quickly becomes overly difficult and unfair.
Other than these few issues, the game is incredibly fun and I would reccomend it to anyone.

Fine! i was thinking about doing a review from another game, but then i saw this and my ADD for roguelikes kicked in..
So what's TinyKeep? It says it is a roguelike and it is, to an extent. I'm now debating the way to aproach explaining the amount of valid critique i have for the game, for both i find it doing things right and at the same time having some features in it that also spoil some of those said good parts..
Let's list all the things that i found valid critigue for:
The game has a physics-engine, which to me feels a bit out of place in a roguelike. Although i can somewhat see the reason for it being there, giving more ways of trying to strategize your way through it. But i also found it.. Very annoying. Reason being, that gold usually gets buried under corpses or some of the fallen rubble and trying to get them from under the piles of death and crockery is really frustrating.
The Altars and the buffs they give is also something that i found.. Well, broken would be the best term. If you have the gold and just spam the cheapest altar, you can easily get enough buffs to become totally overpowered, which i did mind you. (About 2 dozen[12] buffs.) And with all of those, the game immediately turned from roguelike to Hack&Slash. This might be just a bug or something that the devs will correct at some point, but it really makes the game, (keep in mind, ROGUELIKE.) just way too damned easy.
And while i'm on the subject of mechanics, i must voice my disappointment towards the games option-screen. It is pretty non-existant, which cold be argued against with the games simplistic visual-design. However if the game does not have all the options visible on the main menu, (Most of the "resolution" and audio-options are only visible when the game has been started.) Will turn people of it. With the obvious quote of "mobile-port", which i kind of felt like using, but because i'm a nice guy i wont. It would be nice to set individual levels of detail, the game seems to have just presets and resolution options. Which is very bareboned..
Now, for a roguelike. Some people, like me. would welcome the option of saving the game, it seems to be totally absent from the game. It is annoying and kind of selfish from a game to, ask for complete interest for its duration. Even if the game is about 2h in length... Hang on, 2 hours.. Uhm..
With that i could also make a note of the price, 13€*. (Currently -34%, about 8,60€)*. It might seem a bit too much for most people, even if it's a roguelike with obvious re-playability value. It is still asking 13€* for, what i can see, only 2-3h of content.
And with all that. The game is very easy, if you use the "ÜberBuff" tactic. It is just way too simple, which is both its charm and curse at the same time..
Geez, this is hard.. I guess, there is an enjoyable roguelike game here to enjoy. However, the problems it has, need some massive correction work. Broken buff-system and the somewhat obnoxious physics with the corpses and the few bugs that i also managed to find during my short playtime. During which i got to the end boss-fight, which killed me instantly. Because my laptop hyperventilated, from all the crazy amount of stuff on screen just before that..
Anyway..
TinyKeep is a somewhat simplistic, but enjoyable roguelike. It has some features and issues that need repairing, badly.
But in its current state, i could recommend it. But not for 13€*, only when its on sale and the issues with it have been fixed.

TinyKeep is a permadeath style roguelike dungeon crawler, you're utimate aim is to escape.
Along your journey you pick up an assortment of weapons, you rescue other unfortunate prisoners, you find keys and unlock doors. Mysterious and strange objects grant you buffs and other unpleasent surprises. The key here is to use your wits, your skills and your environment to your advantage.

Basic premise: You’ve been locked in a dungeon and your cellmate found a way out while you were sleeping. It’s up to you to find your own way out – but watch out, there’s no extra lives, no saved games. Are you up to the challenge?
This is an amusing game that can be a bit confusing at first. Things to find: weapon, shield, food, other prisoners? … explore to find out. The graphics are cartoony but fun. This is not a massively complex game (no classes, no skill tree ... just you and whatever you find) but it’s not simple to beat either.
Pros:
Great physics: Almost anything can be pushed or moved (this can be very useful).
Amusing  quotes & many nice atmospheric touches.
Good voice acting.
Random generation means different dungeons every time.
You can tell that a lot of care has gone into making this. (this was also seen during the KickStarter fulfilment process)
Cons:
Currently keys can’t be remapped (as a lefty I really hope this is changed in a future update) (hit [H] to see player controls- arrow keys work too.)
No tutorial (This can be quite frustrating at the start - no you can’t pick up the club the guard dropped when you tipped the fire brazier in his path - but once you’ve played a bit you should have it figured out).
Limited config. options (hit [esc] while in game for more)
Saved games? (would be nice but would this spoil the perma-death  experience?)
A fun little challenge the isn't as near as "tiny" as you might think, and might "keep" you occupied for longer than you expect.

I want to recommend this game! The visuals and art design are awesome and the fluid mechanics are grounds for an amazing game, but I can't help feeling like it falls short. I think it lacks depth. You'll get a few hours of enjoyment out of it but after getting really far and having to start all over with nothing to show for it, multiple times, you'll probably put it down. Of course some will find perma-death exactly why the game is so good and I have to agree to an extent that the challenge is definitely there, however, it becomes repetetive the more times you have to start over. Random Power-Ups add a bit of flair to each try but I think adding weapons, armor, and other random inventory items would make it even better and make each playthrough that much more unique.
TL:DR: you'll probably get bored of this game very quickly unless you're familiar with the Perma-Death roguelike challenge and love it.

I think it's underrated.
It is not the greatest game of all time, but it certainly has its qualities.
It has its flaws and it is over all not the most polished game. The story's pretty dull. Things like the questionable driving mechanics reveal the game's console origin. However, I haven't encountered any major problems, such as regular crashes (it crashed maybe once or twice), preformance issues or bugs... I guess some of the issues discribed in earlier reviews had already been fixed by the time I bought the game.
The open world, while not offering a whole lot of depth and interaction, makes sense for this game. It offers freedom of approach during and in between missions, which is kind of the point in a sniper game -- sneaking around, scouting and finding a good sniping position. There are also a few side missions, a most-wanted list (a list of high value targets who hide somewhere on the map), outpost you can clear, and quite a few "points of interest" (although they're usually not that much "of interest") to discover.
The game focuses very much on its core mechanics, which are sniping, stealth and gunfights, and it does all that really well. Sniping and fighting feels rewarding and even spectacular at times. The game tries to be a bit more serious... a little more simulation and a little less over-the-top arcade shooter than other FPS games like, say, Far Cry 4 (not saying it's better than Far Cry, because it isn't). Sniping is supposed to take some patience. Taking on several enemies at the same time in gun fights can be brutal. You can play it different styles, but using a bit of care and tactics usually pays out. Now, it may not be for everyone, but if you're into that type of game, I think you're going to be satisfied.

You're likely here looking at reviews due to the game currently (at the time of this review) being in "Early Access." If you're curious about the game and its stability, read part 1. For the actual review - read part 2. Enjoy!
1) I'd like to immediately shut down those fears by saying this game has very few bugs or issues that will deter you from enjoying the game wholeheartedly. I recently 100%'d the game (excluding all achievements - but that's another beast) and only faced two 'big" glitches throughout the entire playthrough (which admittedly weren't all that troublesome).
Without spoilers - the first was being stuck on a rock on a certain level where you ride a familiar-looking "friend" the entire level. I simply did the "charge" attack and ended up being stuck on top of a rock, but that was easily fixed by just reloading the level. The second one was a bit of a bummer, but not a big deal either. While watching the ending cutscene, my game crashed. Upon loading in, i spawned underneath the main hub only to fall for eternity (until exiting the level and going back in again). To me, these weren't very impactful to how much i enjoyed the game. Now for the review.
2) This game is fan-f***ing-tastic! I bought this due to nostalgia, as I'm sure most did - but even IF you never had a chance to play this game as a kid - I'd highly reccomend it. It has fun, rewarding gameplay that's not too difficult - but also adds in a challenge to each level by hiding collectables very cleverly. Sure, there are a few repeated tropes here and there (TY HELP ME I LOST MY 12 CHILDREN A >SECOND< TIME!), but nonetheless it's an amazing game to just sit down and relax with. Keep in mind that it has full controller support, which, in my opinion, is the best way to revisit this classic - but keyboard and mouse should do just fine as well if you aren't able to snag a reasonable gamepad. As for the graphics the devs are trying to improve upon - don't expect Battlefield 4 style'd graphics or anything - but in my experience they've been a nice touch. If you don't particularly enjoy them - there's always the option to switch them back to the good ol' pixels included in the original PS2 release (it's really not bad looking, if I had to be honest).
All in all, this game is DEFINITELY worth a purchase if you're looking for something fun and relaxing to play, and can also satisfy those looking for a bit of a challenge (completionists who want to get ALL the things!). I would wholeheartedly reccomend it to just about everyone, and have already happily purchased this game for a friend or two already.

While this game seems fun enough what lies beanith is a game filled with problems.

But one I got down to actually playing I was sorely dissapointed.  The combat is basically win or die, with no health upgrades or body armor in the game you basically can only take a few hits before you die, and you will die a LOT!  Your character can't even swim!
The aiming system with the guns...confuses me to say the least, I really don't get the lock-on system.  The game features like, 10 melee weapons...all of which do as much damage as your first does, with the exception of the sword, and except for dying you can't get rid of a weapon you don't want.

Having said that, there is one underlying thing that Bad Company 2 has that the others do not. Heroes. It's game play rewards heroic and bold play styles. Meaning the entire outcome of the round can sometimes come down to that one person, that one play, that turns the tide of the battle. With every new Battlefield released, the numbers in multiplayer drop... But they always. Always, come back to Bad Company 2

Update 10/30/14:
A recent patch introduced a temporary save feature, rebindable keys, an unlockable level select, and some other goodies.  It's important to note that the temporary save feature will only kick in when you finish a level, so my advice is not to stop halfway on a level if you can help it.
As such, I'm changing my recommendation from "No" to "Yes" due to the temporary save feature alone.  I've praised Indie devs in the past for listening to consumer feedback and the like (not all do, but most) and its nice to see that this particular Indie dev reinforces my position.
---
Written 9/29/14:
TinyKeep isn't a bad game, but the lack of a savegame feature is a deal-breaker due to my busy schedule.  There's also no inventory system, no way to rebind keys, and only one difficulty level that could be described as "challenging".  The in-game map is too small for my liking and the enemy types are fairly limited.  I do like the fact that levels procedurally generate and that combat is pretty fluid to boot.  There's also a bit of strategy involved as you'll need to lure tougher enemies into traps while staying on the move.  While I didn't see any other weapons besides my starting sword and shield, you can gain random buffs by spending coins at wells you come across.  While it's a fairly decent game, I couldn't recommend it to those who have to address family obligations on a whim like I do.  If you're not tied down by such things and enjoy roguelikes, then I'd say give "TinyKeep" a shot.

This game falls on the spectrum somewhere between a classic roguelike and a fast-paced FPS game like Serious Sam. The core game is very solid, with attractive graphics, fast-paced gameplay that's just challenging enough to keep it interesting, traps and monster AI just complex enough to be both dangerous and useful, a pleasant soundtrack and engaging voice acting.
What it isn't is a traditional RPG roguelike with levels and armor and gear and so forth. Instead, as befits a dungeon-escape storyline, it's basically a speed run challenge -- how far can you run before one of the Dungeon's terrors catches and kills you.
As such, therefore, and in keeping with classic roguelikes, the game is fairly challenging, there is permadeath, and there is *not* a save feature.There are some limited loot mechanics (kill monsters, get coins, dump coins in shrines for randomized bonuses) but character advancement is a relatively small part of the game compared to other roguelikes. If you're looking for a more traditional RPG experience, this game probably won't satisfy you. If you're the sort of person who liked Hardcore mode speed runs in Diablo, though, this might be right up your alley.
I've had a lot more fun with this than I thought I would. At first it was *very* frustrating to play -- it took me a while to wrap my head around the permadeath -- but the random elements keep the gameplay fresh and overall it's just really engaging. It probably isn't for everyone, but it's great at being what it is.

So this is my first review of any game and I've played a lot of steam games. This particular gem was one I started long ago on the console but never got to finish it due to time constraints. I came across this during a steam sale of a collection of star wars games. That being said as soon as I discovered that I possessed this, I immediately started playing this. After beating it, it left such a good impression on me that I couldn't help but write a detailed review over it. I'll try to break things down into different categories and give my final two cents.
Graphics: Considering that the game is dated back to 2005 on the XBox (literally 11 years and 2 days at the time of this review), the graphics aren't the best when you compare it to today's hi tech stuff. Once you get over that and appreciate the visuals for what it is during that time period, it is quiet a beautiful environment. All the enemies are detailed to scale, the settings you traverse look gorgeous, and the weaponry look pretty good too. I had no problems at all coursing through this game.
Controls: They are somewhat clunky in certain areas. Playing off of mouse and keyboard the reaction is spot on as well is the movement. A couple times clicking the melee button on the keyboard didin't respond fast enough. My only real complaint was that the zooming feature of sniping was bit cumbersome to cycle through. Besides that tidbit the controls served me quite nicely.
Audio: The musical score and scripts were fantastic. From creepy like scenes to the traditional star wars trumpeting to the more militaristic theme song of the clone troopers, the game didn't fail to bring you into the enviroment. During fights did I tune it out but it served well as ambiance. The dialog in the game is by far the shining point of this game. As the main character Delta 38 your character is voiced by Temuera Morrison aka Jango Fett. From issuing orders to commenting on the story to talking to his squadmates, one doesn't get tired of hearing his voice. Ontop of the other 3 troopers and the advisor, you really feel like you're a leader issuing orders and expanding the story. The inner dialogue between each trooper is quite appreciative. It would have made the game a bit dull if each trooper didn't have their own personality.
Story: The story of a commando unit is pretty immersive. You get a quick setup of your origins and meet your team. After the brief prologue you go through stage after stage uncovering a bigger plot involved for the level as you complete each objective. From my perspective I never really gave much thought about the over arching story. I think that was the point of the game. You're a soldier and the information you're given is a need to know basis or stumbling across it as events unfold. The only true negative in all of this is that you are left on a cliff hanger and that the supposed sequel for this game is on hiatus.
Gamplay: I played this game on hard so I used QuickSave a LOT to get through the game. There were moments that you felt overwhelmed as you have pretty stacked odds of tough AI against you followed by pride when you accomplished it. The real difficulty wasn't the tough enemies or type of enemies or amount of enemies but how flimsy your main character was. I didn't play normal so I have no idea what the differences are. The AI could hit harder and last longer. My character could have shorter life. Maybe there are more enemies. Either way it was pretty apparent that your comrades could tank quite a bit whereas that same punishment applied to you would floor you in less than a second. It was the number one negative in the game. I get that on hard you're a bit weaker life wise but make it consistent with your squadmates. I went through the game issuing orders to kill certain enemies or reviving me while I would run and gun around cover when I was up. Besides that, completing the game on hard felt pretty rewarding. The hardest moment in the game is to accomplish an objective within 5 minutes else you lose. Oh yeah don't forget the hoards of enemies that are between you and your object. Nearing the end of each level meant that the punches were no longer pulled as you faced wave after wave of super enemies instead of scrubs. You felt a sense of accomplisment finishing that level.
Overall thought: This game is worth getting. Full price? Probably not. I'd wait for a sale but when you get it, I highly recommed to play through the game on hard. There are no achievements just you, some grit, and your 3 commandos against the Separatists. Just make sure you have the patience for it. I finished this game in 17 hours. No doubt the amount of times to restart a certain section over and over to perfection probably contributed to that length of time. Lastly you see a side of the star wars universe through the eyes of a soldier. A badass one at that. That alone makes the game worth getting and beating. It is simply sad that the sequel may never come to life and simply leaving you on a cliffhanger.
Rating: 9/10

This game had potential, but unfortunately, while the general concept is good - it just doesn't live up to what it COULD be.
Went into this game thinking "Oh hey, it's based on tabletop RPGs - I've played those before and they can be entertaining, going through dungeons in a group, questing, etc. Sure, I'll give it a shot!" but alas, it wasn't meant to be...
There is absolutely nothing in this game that "sucks you in" in terms of gameplay. The ENTIRE time you're playing, you're staring at a tiny little map broken up into hexes, with giant figures featuring you, the three opponent "player" AI, and various other AI representing the King's guards, Rot enemies, etc. all moving around....but that's it in terms of gameplay. Want to quest in a dungeon - just step on a dungeon hex! But that's all you end up doing - after that your reward is randomly generated or you could trigger one of the Rot NPCs....you don't get to go through an actual dungeon, quest, deal with monsters, find treasure, etc. like you would in a tabletop RPG. Nope, you just step on a tile and the system randomly rewards (or penalizes) you.
Want to explore a town, maybe do a quest? Yeaaah....no. Not gonna happen. Once again, step on a tile, a quest pops up - you gotta roll dice or burn cards with symbols on them (seriously?) to somehow "win" the quest. Fail - penalized, win - oh boy, you get a few coins or maybe a card...
Want to buy equipment or upgrade your pre-existing? Nope - you gotta somehow hope that you pick an item card (when that finally happens in the game) that fits what your need, if not, you're stuck with a card for a piece of equipment you don't want.
No, the entire time you're playing this game, you're staring at a hex map. Want to start a party - maybe quest some? Nope, not here. A "party" are basically npcs you win through questing - and we've already talked about questing. They're basically cards that hardly ever interact (if at all) with you and just provide a modicum of points/benefits (if any) for you.
This entire game is nothing more than numbers chasing - you're trying to become the Prestige leader for every turn, trying to acquire 4 soul stones to MAYBE heal the Lion King, trying to gain enough corruption/hit points to take ON the King in combat, etc. Meantime, the other npc players are trying to handicap you at every turn, laying traps, stealing your money, attacking you, etc.
Needless to say, this got boring FAST.
Listen, this game is basically eye-candy and even then - not much else. Plotwise - it's got about as much depth as a kiddie pool with a half-inch of water in it. The storyline is the barest boned I've seen in a LONG time. You never really explore this world - you just wander through it, trying to get your character high enough before the game times out or is won by someone else. Game mechanics are pretty much luck based, and if there's something along the lines of actual strategy involved - I've yet to see that.
This game had the potential to be SO much more. Given the types of similar "anthropomorphized animals in a medieval/magic-based setting" content out there - such as the Autumnlands and Mouse Guard comics, plus pre-existing RPG games that follow D&D mechanics, such as Might & Magic, this game could've been more immersive, more plot driven, so much more INTERESTING than it currently is! Where are the quests to try and find out more about "The Rot"? Where are the quests to explore the history of this land? Where are the quests to explore the land, PERIOD!?!? I'd have loved to be able to put together a party of npc characters or even multiplayer friends, and just QUEST in a dungeon or explore the wilds of this kingdom, fighting monsters, doing quests, etc. instead of running around like crazy people, from one end of the map to the other, trying to perform what comes down to as MEANINGLESS quests, all in an effort to numberchase against AI opponents...
This isn't entertainment, it's very pretty annoyance and monotony. And yes, much like everybody else, I find it appalling that there's FURTHER in-game purchases for what is nothing more than variations of the same eyecandy skins that already comes with the game, and very little of anything else. i only have a couple of hours playing with this so far, but as a gamer, and as a programmer, the brilliance of this whole system just jumps out at you.
first, the game engine seems awesome. the art style and level "building blocks" are pleasant, fun and well ... RPG'ish.
the mechanics of melee attacks, mana/rage attacks, and movement seem like that perfect balance, so that you've got options and growth in what your character can do, but you don't have an overwhelming number of things that you can do that clutter controls and make gameplay fiddly.
the comparisons are to Torchlight II, and that is a great comparison, a fair comparison, and a compliment to both games.
once you start playing, if you have a mind and disposition for these things, you instantly recognize how the engine and the level editor are truly going to be best friends, and how creating levels for the engine is going to be intuitve and awesome for a fan with that creative bent.
the browsing of fan content, and integrating that content into a given users play experience (the workshop/level browser) looks and feels like it could be awesome and literally a game changer for games using distributions systems like steam.
it'll be interesting to see if the community driven content mechanic is able to seperate the wheat from the chaff so that players can get access to "good" levels, and robust, connected experiences.
the content browser supports a number of filters that give some pretty good control to the consumer for finding the content from the community that meets good criteria, such as 'popular' and 'by a given author'.
the engine and level development tools are designed to favor small experiences, which will make it interesting to see how larger experiences are serialized by level developers.
with my limited gameplay experience so far, i have nothing bad to say about the engine ... i _really_ like how it plays, and i like the "art" and look and feel so far.
the developer is taking a huge chance that the "community" is going to create good quality content that is going to make their game worth playing, vs. bad content making the game "suck".
i'm a little worried about that part, but a) it's too early to tell, and b) i would imagine, if the developers are smart, that they might curate or produce enough of the content at some point, that the game could be played with _just_ that curated content and be complete and good.

I started writing a pretty long review for this, because I actually quite like this hidden gem, but I decided to keep it simple since the description and other reviews already give you an idea of the kind of things you can do in this game.
If, like me, your biggest concern about the game is/was the bugs, I'd suggest just getting the game on a sale (it goes on sale fairly frequently actually) and seeing for yourself how buggy it is, because I personally have had minimal problems. Cover works as intended, guards act realistically, and I've only had one instance of glitching into terrain that I was able to promptly fix anyway by ordering the guy into a different spot of cover that he could clip himself back into.
The isometric camera view combined with real time gameplay is quite novel too, and between that, the aesthetics, the wide-open areas with few loading screens, and the mechanics you have access to makes for a very immersive game in my opinion. Which, in a cyberpunk setting, feels awesome.
With the real time gameplay, you're often not going to have time to come up with convoluted solutions. You'll have to take risks and will probably get a bit reckless at times, holding onto a small hope it'll work (and sometimes you're right, even). The good news is, the punishments for failure really aren't that harsh. Harsh enough to want to avoid it, obviously, but not so harsh that it just feels crushing to fail. And so failure becomes fun.
So get creative with your solutions. Try going totally silent, or try making a lot of noise. Try making a lot of noise so your other agent(s) can go totally silent. Though you won't be able to take on guards for long early in the game (you can still lead them on a goose chase), later on your agents can really tie up security for a long time. It's quite a nice game, well worth more than the $5 I bought it for, and I'd love to see a sequel that irons out some of the quirks and also has better modding support. Being able to make districts or even entire campaigns would add a ton of additional playtime, but that's not to say there isn't replay value in the current game already given the different approaches you can take.

I've never had such irreconcilable feelings for a game.
As an actual game, to play, it's mostly pretty fun. The puzzles are well-designed, but there's a few very annoying bits. There's a lot of obnoxious stipulations to puzzles to artificially make them harder than they are, such as not being able to see the whole screen, trial-and-error time limits, missiles that come out of nowhere and kill you...but I can forgive it. I can't remember the last time an adventure game was this long and varied.
The much vaunted, award-winning story felt very strange to me, though...I don't know what this game really wanted to be. It is trying to be a tragic, heartfelt war memoir, but also the characters communicate in cartoonish mumbles, there's boss fights with a stereotypical Evil German General who utilizes ridiculous contraptions, there's very Rayman Legends-esque rhythmic car chase segments. There's one point where a character, in typical adventure game fashion, speaks a speech bubble with a picture of a saw cutting off a human arm, because he needs medical attention. It felt absolutely surreal and tonedeaf, to jarringly gameify something so serious, that the game itself WANTS me to take seriously. Very, uh..."Press F to Pay Respects."
The villain, Baron Von Dorf, who I can't believe is named Baron Von Dorf, is the most cartoonish, Dr. Robotnik type villain. He felt like something out of a wartime propaganda cartoon. There are other minor characters--mostly those in leadership positions--who felt like absolutely stereotypical. That isn't necessarily a problem in itself, especially in a game set in a war hat was heavily influenced BY the caricaturization of its enemies. But in a game that is intending to humanize the war, show that people on both sides of the battle were unique, real humans going through something unimaginably difficult, it is cancelling out its own moral, the point the writers and developers seem to genuinely want you to believe, to have such unbelievable stock characters juxtaposed against the tragic, human element of the game is almost uncomfortable.
As I stated, the game simply doesn't know what it wants to be. It's a funny cartoon. It's a sad memoir. It's a platformer, it's a puzzle game, it's a stealth game. It's a game about the harsh realities of war. It's a game where someone chases you down in an unreal mechanical zeppelin. It's an upbeat story about three unlikely wartime buddies chasing a common enemy. The mood shifts so much and so frequently, and the game doesn't really seem to understand how off-putting its vaccilating tone is.
I can think of no better way to describe the game's uncomfortable tone shifts than the ending. Truth be told, it got me feeling choked up! Genuinely! I was very misty-eyed as the credits began to roll. I was expecting the typical Ubisoft 2-hour credits...but then halfway through, like a Marvel film, the game cuts to a sequel hook; one of the surviving characters watches on as America joins World War I, with the narration stating that war's hunger is insatiable. A sequel hook for a game about finality and the tragedy of war. That's Ubisoft!
When the game was announced, I was surprised--it seemed so far out of Ubisoft's wheelhouse, it didn't seem like something they could do. After playing it...I guess I was right, unfortunately. Playing the game was a complicated emotional roller coaster and I felt like I was being split in two--ultimately I realized it was because while I was feeling very sad emotions contemplating the actual reality of World War I, I was simultaneously off-put by the game's tone, its inherent goofiness that in spite of appearances to the contrary, it seems to revel in.
I'm putting "no" for if I recommend the game or not, but it still feels harsh. Ultimately I didn't like it, but my feelings were more neutral. If they added a "I'm confused about how I feel about this game" button between "yes" and "no" I'd be ticking that one off. For as discomfortingly unaware the game's overall vibe was, I think there was merit to it.
Also, the dog is really good, and he doesn't die.

As others have no doubt mentioned, TinyKeep is a Rogue-
with a number of distinguishing features.  Like previous and upcoming titles that fuse elements of the original Rogue formula with other genres, TinyKeep's primary offerings are randomly-constructed levels and permadeth wrapped in tactical, hack'n'slash gameplay.  Fans of The Binding of Isaac and its derivatives should feel right at home, despite this game boasting some significant differences.
Room-to-room exploration is similar enough to competing titles, though TinyKeep frequently surprises the player with the myriad split-second decisions that each area offers.  A robust if masochistic physics implementation provides constant obstruction and destruction opportunities. Barrels, crates, columns, spike traps and highly-flammable (and more importantly
) braziers are strewn throughout the dungeon, providing neverending frustrations and delights.
Combat is a mixture of swinging and blocking and, despite being simplistic, is extremely satisfying.  The game seems aware of this and frequently offers a slow-mo death cam for the player's viewing pleasure.
I've not yet beaten the game as I'm terrible at it, but I've enjoyed myself the entire time.
PRO(S)
Graphics (highly-stylized, borderline
and quite beautiful, really)
Sounds effects
Music (wonderfully appropriate music for 'adventuring')
Gameplay (frenetic yet thoughtful, despite the improbability of anyone ever typing those two adjectives together)
Random dungeon layouts (keeps the challenges fresh and forestalls boredom)
CON(S)
Occasional physics quirks (can cause irritation, though they also frequently benefit the player)
HIGHLY SUBJECTIVE CON
Camera movement (the entire level swings around your character as you rotate with the mouse, which may dizzy and even induce nausea in those easily-susceptible to spinning motions)
I think most will find TinyKeep to be an enjoyable dungeon romp that will elicit numerous attempts to escape. The success-to-failure ratio displayed on the title screen won't be the only reason why.

TinyKeep is a (very) casual roguelike based, in part, around speed-running a scripted sequence of dungeon levels.
After completing the game you unlock an enhanced difficulty mode. Hardcore Steam achievements presumably add some additional, longer term play value.
 
The fact that this plays better as a speed-running game rather than a more traditional roguelike is obscured by the campaign scripting, which is written in a way that implies more story than is actually the case. Ultimately, the dialog is simply an excuse to provide some light direction to point the player towards what they need to do next.
 
Room layouts within a level are procedurally generated. The rest of the game is fully scripted, including the sequence of levels (including dungeon graphics and type of monster), event triggers and (very light) mini-puzzles.
 
There's no direct character leveling or stats, however there are altars scattered around which give you random, permanent boosts which accumulate, and therefore have the effect of making your character more powerful over time. As you might expect, some boosts are more powerful than others, meaning that the luck of the draw can play a part in the success of your run.
 
There is no inventory system and no loot, other than picking up a sword and shield on the first level. The sword and shield are not in your starting room and the game can be a bit confusing here as you can't damage the guards until you get the sword, and it turns out that you need to do a crazy sprint to find these while dodging the guards, setting the tone for the rest of the game, although this is not explained.
 
It is not possible to save your game
. (As of patch v1.2 you can, however, quit the game in the middle of a run and pick up from the start of your most recent level next time you play. Your save is still wiped, however, if you die.)
 
The game plays best when you sprint around the levels as it can feel quite slow if you're just wandering. Playing the game as a speed-run, however, creates a nice flow and manageable craziness that does effectively get the adrenalin flowing.
 
Combat is simple - attack with sword or block with the shield. The dev has suggested that timing hits is worthwhile, but I've not had any trouble just whacking away. Blocking seems kind of useless as successfully landing a hit creates a knock back that gives you enough time to launch the next attack. When mobbed there's even less incentive to block.
To add complexity to play, there are a number of ways to use the environment to your advantage, for example traps effect both you and the monsters, meaning you can kite monsters to their deaths, and fire pits can be tipped over to set adversaries on fire. Monster types will also sometimes fight each other.
 
The foundation of the game is incredibly solid. The graphics are evocative, gameplay is smooth, and I've found no noticeable bugs.
 
To my mind, unfortunately, the game suffers from a noticeable lack of variety. Each run the levels are basically the same, and the lack of inventory, drops or emergent events leaves no great incentive to explore.
 
This is a shame, as a ton of additional unscripted content would give the game a lot of potential staying power, particularly as a quick diversion.
As things stand, however, I've bounced off the game in less than three hours, and I suspect most others will find the same. There's simply not enough here to justify the investment.
Considering an alternative? I can highly recommend
instead.

Wake up, prisoner! It's time to undertake a swashbuckling, breakneck escape and free yourself of this fetid dungeon at last! But be warned - your prison isn't home to just lumbering guards and your malnourished and chap-fallen fellow prisoners. Dark things lurk around every corner, and they brought friends.
TinyKeep brings a new whimsy to the oft-dark and foreboding PDL subgenre; this is Dark Souls meets Disney, with the tactical attack/defend combat of the former, and the cute and quirky art and music of the latter. The physics-based combat in TinyKeep requires skillful timing and execution, the mastery of which will only strengthen your chance of survival--not guarantee it.
Equipped at the outset with nought but the tattered rags on his back, your macrocephalic would-be escapist must sneak about the keep until he can arm himself, and even then, he will only be
safer. TinyKeep features a custom dungeon generator dubbed
, which ensures a fresh and exciting run every time.
The enemies in TinyKeep are not brainless drones that wander about drooling all over themselves; they are aware of you, their surroundings, and other enemies! With good planning and maneuvering, you can sometimes clear a level without swinging your sword!
8/10 - An easy recommendation for PDL fans

TinyKeep is a third person dungeon crawler with procedurally generated maps and roguelike elements. You play as a prisoner trying to escape from a dungeon, fighting off guards, skeletons, orcs, demons and all manner of other things along the way.
The game is a roguelike in that permadeath is a thing - when you die (not if - when), you're starting over from the beginning. No 'rogue-lite' elements here. This may or may not be a plus depending on your personal preferences.
The maps follow the same series of tilesets and themes each time you play through the game (in the same vein as Spelunky, for instance) - you always start in a dungeon tileset for the first 3 floors, the next 3 are in a jungle-ruin-esque tileset, etc., and each level within the set has a set theme and a boss, but the randomization of each floor is very thorough, and the room layouts are interesting and varied. There's occasionally some weirdness with the layouts like traps at the end of dead-end hallways or rooms that clip into corridors slightly, but I found this sort of thing to add to the game, rather than detract - all of these little architectural quirks can be used to your advantage, and that's really an important factor in surviving the game.
There's numerous traps and environmental hazards which you can use to help you kill the enemies there (and the game actually recommends that you do so via loading screen tips occasionally). Additionally, enemies take friendly fire damage from each other, which creates some opportunities for tactical positioning or 'baiting' of attacks to eliminate other enemies - overall, the combat system, while simple, feels engaging and fluid, and the controls are quite tight.
The game supports an Xbox gamepad (probably others, too, though I can't personally verify that) out of the box with no configuration required, and plays very well with one, though it's not required to enjoy the game.
You become more powerful as you progress by way of randomized powerups that you buy for gold (looted from slain enemies and the environment), and these can be pretty major factors in how you play on any given run. For instance, on one run, I got a number of movement-enhancing effects, and on another I got a selection of damage-reducing / blocking effects, and the tactics needed in each case were vastly different. You'll need to adapt your playstyle to the bonuses you receive, creating a pretty dynamic feeling game.
The graphics are cute, and the models are fairly simple, but the lighting and textures fit perfectly - the graphical style fits the gameplay very well, in my opinion.
There are a few minor issues - environmental objects (boxes, vases, corpses, etc.) have volume in the world and inhibit movement (which in itself isn't bad - it's just something to take into consideration when navigating rooms), but occasionally through physics weirdness this can have undesireable effects - if you get boxed in by such objects, it's difficult to get out. Additionally, coins can occasionally fall in locations that are difficult or impossible to reach due to environmental obstructions, but neither of these issues really detract from the core gameplay.
In summary, Tinykeep is a fun dungeon crawler roguelike with action-oriented combat and a cute graphical style. If you enjoy games like Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, this is probably up your alley.

"Mostly Negative"
I know when I see that, I just have to try the game out so I can revel in its mediocrity.
But that wasn't the case with this game so let me explain why it has mostly negative reviews first and then if this game is for you.
The game controls (with a keyboard and/or mouse) like♥♥♥♥♥♥ There is no getting around it, it was designed with touch screens and controllers in mind, not for keyboard and mouse and CERTAINLY not for solo mouse!
If you dont have (or are unwilling to use) an xbox controller (or similar) then you can stop reading now and walk away from this game. You will not enjoy it
Its shocking really to have a PC port that wasn't designed for PC in the slightest, but look a little deeper and you can figure out why. Cross platform? yup, you know what that means. Mobile-port, the bane of Steam users everywhere.
Not helping is the fact that the game is a chinese development team so communication with the dev team is just not going to happen.
That aside however the game is designed from the bottom up to be casual friendly and in doing so it accidently solved many of the flaws that the more hardcore MOBA games have. I have put years into MOBA type games and by design they are meant to obsfucate new players. This means they
to ask others for help or they have to play with friends. That is the design philosophy behind League of Legends and don't take my word for it as a google search shows many people feel the same way and Riot Games themselves have gone on record to say that is how they intended the game to be.
Defense of the Ancients* was a huge success and League of Legends is a huge commercial success and so every other MOBA just copied what they did and like Flappy Birds, we now have a saturated market. Heroes of Soulcraft is just another MOBA in that ocean of MOBA games however if you have never played a MOBA before this one does everything for you. Well, it doesn't explain what it is doing or why but, well, neither does League of Legends.
Now, to the point, because I could talk about LoL all day but you are curious if this game is for you and the answer is, do you like arcade games? Completely by accident and by virtue of doing everything for you, Heroes has boiled down the MOBA experience to its simplist form and believe it or not, its actually quite fun! Well, with a controller.
Based on the negative reviews I'm not going to lie, I expected an absolute train wreck and if you are looking for flaws then trust me, the game has lots of them! The interface is a mess, a few things that are important to us MOBA players IE how much +speed does this item give? vs that item? are just completely missing, leading you to just guess and if you were wondering, buying from the shop is automatic. Before you flip your desk and walk away however this goes back to my earlier comment "its simplist form" because if you can navigate the bizaare in game menus you can actually pre-define what you buy from the shop and what order you buy it in, per hero! There is also nothing stopping you from turning the option off and manually buying items as well or from buying, during a match, by visiting the shop like most MOBA games.
They had some fantastic ideas, going into this game and I really think a lot of them were accidental and I wish, I really wish, that LoL will look at some of the things Heroes~ is doing.
If you want to get into MOBA games but LoL was too complicated for you then this is THE game for you bar none, although I hear Heroes of the Storm is casual friendly too*.
If you like the other MOBA offerings then there is nothing to see here apart from controller support.
If you don't know what a MOBA is then give this game a try and see if the genre is for you, although I recommend picking up DOTA or LoL if you do infact like the genre.
*Thanks to Nebulous & Tibbers for corrections.

I am posting this "review" after investing almost 8 hours of gameplay over two weeks. I don't think that's enough time to call this a propper review, so let's call it a first impressions. If I make it past 16 hours within the next two weeks, I'll review my review and fix anything I may have gotten wrong.
This is a game that feels like it should be in early access instead of full release. I do hope that it improves, but I cannot reccomend this game in its current state.
But before I put in a wall of text about how it sucks, first I'll go over what this game does right:
1) Map Editor. Any game with an in-buillt map editor gets brownie points from me, I love creating custom content (even though I suck at it). This editor is clunky and un-intuitive (you can tell it was designed with controllers in mind), but it exists so I'm happy.
2) Community created content. You mean there's constantly new stuff and I don't have to wait on the devs to make it? sweet.
3) It's pretty. The aesthetic is simplistic, but nice. The cartoonish feel works well with high-res textures on low-poly models.
4) It hasn't crashed yet, nor have I experienced any noticable frame-drops (running a AMD FX-4170 / GTX550ti if that helps anyone).
That's about it. Now to complaining!
1) Controls are extremely clunky. The delay between pressing the attack buttons, performing the animation, and being able to do something else (such as move) is waaaaaaaaay too long and has resulted in many bulshit deahts. I can tell that the issue is a lack of animation cancelling (look at Diablo3, which this game claims to partially inspiried by, it feels great because everything responds immediatly).
2) You can't change attack directions between strikes. This could just be part of 1, but it's aggrivating enough to warrent it's own spot)
3) Hitboxes don't match up with attack animations. Need I say more?
4) The auto-targetting system frequently can't find on-screen targets. Prime example is The Dragon, which makes wands (hitscan projectile weapon) completely useless because it relies entirely on the auto-targetting system to automaticcly hit things then the attack button is pressed. Speaking of auto-targetting, you can't aim things yourself, it just goes in the direction you're facing (unless the auto-target finds something, which as I said is unreliable).
5) This might just be a problem with inexperienced map makers, but several of the levels can be "broken" by getting on top of the outside wall (which I'm certain you're not supposed to be able to do) to find the exit in seconds in a level that should take half an hour.
6) Lack of variety in class builds. So I a basic attack that varies on weapon, a secondary attack that varies whether that weapon is one handed or two handed, and four class abilities that never change (you just unlock them as you progress). Come on. Diablo 2 had 30 class skills PER CLASS (granted several were passives), and it came out in what year? I know comparing an indie dev to blizzard isn't fair, but they brought it upon themselves when the description said it's like diablo meets little big planet. That set some high expectations.
I'm still playing it though so I guess it's fun.

Great game, great premise, but one very huge flaw in its design.  The game is based around player created adventures but lacks a fair implementation of advertising any new adventures.
Searching for adventures at first glaces seems to be very complex but after a while you you notice a poor design choice.  Only the top 24 adventures will ever be displayed in a search, no matter how many tags you select.  What does this mean?  Only adventures with a high rating will ever be visible to other players to play, meaning, your new maps will never get a chance to be played unless someone searches for it by name.  You can search for Easy, Medium, Hard, or Extreme adventures, but you will never see any adventures that are 25th+ place.  Yeah there is a search for newly created adventures, but that category only shows adventures that haven't been played once.  Once someone plays it, your adventure is now unsearchable.  There is a category for weekly, monthly, and featured adventures but those will always display the same 24 adventures in the category, most of which are the same adventures.  Since I have been playing, no new maps were added to featured (about 2 months).  There is an option to play a random adventure, but that only selects an adventure you haven't played yet in one of the top 24 adventure categories, only playing a truly random map after those have been exhausted.

World War 1 games are rare. Those with a compelling and touching story are even rarer.
'Valiant Hearts: The Great War' is a 2D puzzle adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier. Set in France during WWI it tells the story of four characters (and a dog), a French, a German, an American, and a Belgian Nurse and how the war affects their lives, dependencies they build and friendships that are made in the process.
From a gameplay point of view, Valiant Hearts is less of a game and more of an interactive animated movie/comic. Gameplay mechanics are restricted to solving a few easy puzzles in the form of tossing objects, pulling levers, issuing orders and executing QTE sequences. There are absolutely no hair-pulling moments or frustrating puzzles which is a positive because, in games belonging to the same genre, narrative often gets buried underneath tough gameplay and extremely difficult riddles.
Art is one of the two areas (music being the other one) where this game truly shines. The art-style is, simply put, phenomenal. The story events are set in France and the areas include trenches, underground tunnels, field hospitals, prisoner of war camps, towns and farms.
Now coming to the soundtrack.............it was brilliant! Easily the best in-game music I've listened to in some time. Really captures the mood and reminds you of war-themed movies like Schindler's List and Saving Private Ryan.
The game touches the themes of war including conscription, desertions and mutiny. The characters are very close to life and it's easy to empathize with their condition. The story is touching and, suffice to say, I almost shed a tear when it ended. Not to mention it was fun and very informative reading the diary and historical facts related to WWI that were included in-game.
Valiant Hearts: The Great War is the best six bucks I've ever spent. Who says Ubisoft only makes rubbish games?

A+ Platformer: This is what alot of platformers should aspire to be what with how much fun it is, with its open world type enviroments and wide variety of enemies.
Hours of fun: This game is a pretty big collect-a-thon, which can leave alot to do if you want to reach 100% progress and get all the acheivements.

: Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a platform adventure game where the goal of each level is to find all the collectibles. This includes Opals, Golden Cogs(Which unlock boomerangs),Bilbies, and the lesser known portraits which if all are collected unlock a movie. If you 100% the game you will unlock a secret level. The game is easy as it's meant for kids but it still has many fun mechanics such as how the boomerangs interact with the enviroment. The combat consists of throwing 'rangs or biting your foes.
: The game is old but it has an artistic charm and the new fancy effects of this remastered edition help bring it up to speed. What more can you expect? It's an old game meant to run on Xbox, Ps2, and Gamecube. As for as graphic fidelity, the devs are doing a splendid job updating it regularly with little tweaks here and there. Although they could replace textures to enhance it even more but it is fine.
: Best soundtrack for a kid's game I have ever heard. This game nails the Australian theme by adding tunes that use authentic Australian instruments(or emulates them) that make each level a joy to play on. Plus the Australian accents on the characters is cheesy in a good way.
: You will 100% this game and be done with it maybe only returning for funsies or to compete in the leaderboards to see who can complete each level the fastest.
: The nostalgia goggles are off. Ty is a kid's game that succeeds by giving an experience that is not totally braindead but charming and memorable. It is my favorite game from my own childhood near Crash,Ratchet,Spyro and Jak. It deserves to be listed there. The port is damned good too. Ty 2 and 3 will be an insta-buy for me.

If you spot the game on sale, without a doubt give it a try.
At first I was very unsure about how I feel around this game as it has many pros and con's and depending on what type of gameplay you enjoy, these directly influence the experience you will have.
I found that in the first hour or two of play the game was about a 6/10 for me, this is due to the strange filter applied to the environment and the fairly predictable and wooden characters. I had a huge freeze up in the opening tutorial and also a few graphical/audio issues, these actually made me strongly consider refunding the game.
I decided however to stick with the game and play on as the sole reason I acquired the game was for the very enjoyable and challenging sniping that is semi-realistic. After 4 hours of play it was almost as if I had been playing a new game, the world and characters opened up and the many immersive and attractive mechanics and features implemented in the game were shown to me. It is important to note that the game has many very tasteful features that work very well to create a high quality stealth and sniping experience such as, dragging and hiding bodies, frequent hiding places, sneaky and stealthy ways into levels, an indicator of how much noise you are generating and also the noise made by the sniper rifle you have is also shown on the map, this means you are able to pick prime distances for engagement. These features are not in any way new or ground-breaking but they do work well and as they have all been implemented into the same game they complement each other greatly.
I have just hit 10 hours of play and I am on chapter 3/4 and I would say that this game takes some time to adjust too and some patience to deal with some pretty serious bugs however if you keep at it despite all of these it is  a very enjoyable game and a gem. I would also like to mention I haven't experienced these glitches awfully often and they haven't impacted my experience very greatly at all, maybe I am more tolerant than the average player or just lucky.
To summarise I would give SG3 a solid and sure 7.9/10, this is taking into account is a " B game " made with a smaller budget than some games we have seen and by a smaller team however it can hold its own against these reasonably well and provides the authentic sniper feel. I would say the story is better than many people have said and deserves an 8/10 as it interested me and kept me wanting to progress it which is more than I can say for some games.
I hope this review helped some of you guys to get an insight into the game from a person who has played and enjoyed all games in the franchise and has attempted to write a truthful review from my findings of the game that hasn't been influenced by anyone else.

Ok, so I'm more than halfway through Chapter 3 and I've seen enough to give an intelligent review. In short, this game is good almost great. I read all of the negative "professional" reviews and I feel like I've been playing an entirely different game then they did. A couple things that keep kicking around in my head that I've heard them say is that the game does not respect your time. I have found my experience to be the opposite of that.
The main missions can be played one after the other, without pointless fetch quests or some random "?" you must go discover. The driving does take time, but what open world game doesn’t make you traverse parts of it's land? At least the fast travel works and only pushes a small amount of exploration onto the player. If you love exploration however, there are plenty of places to go and see across all 3 maps. You'll be rewarded one way or the other for taking the time to explore, but by no means is it necessary to progress the story. The side quests I really enjoyed were the HVT (High Value Targets), it's a simple most wanted list that rewards you in currency for the kill.
The graphics are nice and the lighting from CryEngine 4 really does the scenery some justice. The characters could have been done better, but when your staring at them from over 200M they do their job of portraying a soldier. After playing The Witcher 3, I'm not sure we will see facial animations of that like until Cyberpunk 2077, so I simply just got over that short coming it did not impact my experience one bit.
Gunplay is solid and the guns feel responsive and require more skill than your COD guns. They went for realism and as someone who has experience with firearms I can tell you they did great. The sniping is the most engaging aspect and at higher difficulties (which I strongly recommend you to play at) is as real of a sniper experience as you can have.
Besides the sniping, I was almost even more impressed by the enemy AI. They flanked and intelligently moved around structures and rarely ever came directly at me. This again was at the higher difficulties, but nonetheless I've played plenty of shooters and nothing for me has compared to the level of intelligence this AI brings to the game.
In closure, the story is good enough, nothing that will blow you away, but I found it entertaining enough to want to keep progress and seeing how it would play out. It does a solid job of setting up each mission and the mission variety is great! It almost reminded me of Goldeneye 007 in its mission structure, don't ask me why lol. I Haven’t really experienced any devastating bugs or glitches, but I am playing after the large patch that was issued recently. The worst I've seen is that a few frags never exploded or the button to throw them bugged out. If that's the worst then I'm fine with it, this is a sniper game after all and that part they nailed!
If you like sniping sims then this is a game you have to check out. Play it on at least Hard as the pure nature of this game benefits from that level of realism/challenge. I hope this was helpful and good hunting!

This game is for people who are fans of arcade and NES games, and people who are soft enough to wanna have a good laugh. Every mission is different in it's own way, and there's always a reference or parody that gets you to laugh. As you progress through the game, it obviously gets harder. This game isn't impossible, but it gets difficult, that's for sure. At first you just kill dudes with pistols, but then you're gonna run into dudes with bazookas.
The story is obviously not supposed to make sense, I mean this game is a parody, just look at the title. Despite how senseless it may be, it surely is entertaining. It was fun for me to walk down the street and randomly run into some batman parody, and then having to impersonate him. At least the game actually had a story, and it's been a while since I've enjoyed one this hilarious.
I do recommend this game, and trust me, it is worth the 10 bucks.

It's like a well-designed (e.g. modern conveniences like just-in-time help/tutorial reminders) GTA2 chock full (this is an understatement) of video game related references. I mean they poured their heart and soul into this thing. Less common references include the "history of IBM", "Commodore 64 load flags", "Game Genie noises", and tons of musical parodies that will be nostalgic of particular games/tunes without actually stealing the audio. This game screams "polish polish polish" and everyone who has been gaming for a while or likes/is intrigued by 2D open-world games should give it a try.

You can't go wrong with this one.

This game is one of my favorite games I have ever played. It starts out as a third person crafting game, and ends as the most complex RTS building sim you've ever played.
It starts out fairly similar to Minecraft in 2D: mining minerals, crafting things, punching trees. Then, you build automated mines, conveyer belts to take those to your furnaces. You would think you would sit back satisfied at the materials your machines are making for you. But that's not how this game works. There's a hunger to keep building. Curiosity at all the fantastic machines in the massive tech tree. Desire to destroy the biters who come in the night that you have to run from while firing wildly. So you keep building, blanketing minerals with electric mines, building rows and rows of furnaces to hopefully supply your city sized factory that is constantly producing weapons, building components, and research. But it isn't enough. Your pathetic organizational scheme of routing belts wherever you need them is only hindering your progress. So you research what other people have done, designing layouts on a massive scale, dreaming of new ways to expand and automate even more, more, more. Luckily there is a way to beat this game, or I might still be expanding my factory to this day.
It is very fun and addicting (the good kind of addiction, not the bad throwing birds or popping balloons addiction) it keeps you engaged for long periods of time and provides lots of challenges

I finished the main campaign of State of Decay and I enjoyed it.  Being an indie title published by Microsoft, there is a lot of room for polish that I hope they put in to State of Decay 2.  Specifically, actual animated cutscenes would be nice, and a better story.  Also, the combat was a little odd being focused on a per-zombie system; it'd be nice to be able to swing a big weapon and take out all the zombies around me instead of use it for one zombie at a time, with the zombie directly behind sometimes getting hit when the game decides to damage them.  It's wonky, it's tough, it's fun.  Just don't go in expecting a ton of polish.
Also, the ending was very abrupt and unsatusfying.  So, as I said, hopefully a better story next time.  The DLC hasn't really grabbed my attention either.  The first is just endless sandbox mode which is pretty much the main game but it doesn't end and has no overarching story, although arguably the main game's overarching story didn't feel very well connected anyway so, it's essentially just more of the same but endless.  The second DLC has story and a new map but it didn't really grip me.  This was mainly because I loved the wilderness-style environment of the main game, while the "Lifeline" DLC takes it to the big city.  Something about big cities in games like this just don't click well with me.  But who knows, others might love it.

WFWL does still work with GTA IV however you may need to do several things to get it working.
Try loading the game first to see if you can connect to GFWL, If you can then you won't need to do any of the following.
Here are the instructions on how to get Multiplayer working, do them in order.
"To start we need to remove any programs that use, conflict or depend on the GFWL system or services so un-install:
* the Microsoft Games for Windows - LIVE redistributable and Marketplace
* the Bing bar
* Windows Live Essentials (including Windows Live Messenger)
* Microsoft Silverlight
* the Windows Live ID sign-in assistant (this may be missing from the add/remove programs list)
* any Microsoft .NET frameworks
Then restart your computer.
Now we need to re-install everything (You must do it in the order posted below).
1st - Install Microsoft .NET framework depending on your version of windows.
After it installs, run windows update to update your computer with any important updates. Then restart your computer and run windows update again.
2nd - Install the Windows Live ID Sign-in Assistant.
3rd - Install Microsoft Silverlight.
4th - Install the Games for Windows Marketplace.
After this installs, try to sign into the GFWL on GTA IV, if it doesn't work then message me and I'll see if I can help.

Too often I died (or rather, my agents died) because they wouldn't obey my simple command "go hide there" and instead wander around, getting shot at, slowly dying.
They don't really shoot back - you have to microcontrol them, tell them every move.
Whoever thought that CTRL-A is a good hotkey to select all agents: it's not. While I applaud the idea of using an almost universal standard key that just screams "I select everything", it's not something that can be pressed quickly in a panic.

I don't usually play war games because they tend to be tactical and strategy based, but this caught my eye. The graphics, the stories, the characters. By some sheer luck, a friend had a copy of the game and gifted it to me. While some have complained about Uplay, it's just one small hitch. Putting that aside, I immensely enjoyed this game, and cried buckets as I played.
The game mechanics and puzzles seem easy, but actually take a few tries at certain parts. It all adds up to the urgency of the game. There have been times when I've to replay a scene a few times because either my timing was wrong, or just to get a feel of the pattern. Then there is the characters and stories behind it. I like that it has proper history behind it and you can read about them as it goes on. It makes so much sense when a specific character does certain actions or why that route is taken. As all the four characters (and the dog)'s story unfolds, they crush my heart. At times nail-biting, other times heart-wrenching. You begin to feel for them, and in a way, they represent the many facets of all those involved during the Great War.
Valiant Hearts really echoes with me, and I highly recommend this game to everyone. It's also educational and engaging. I find myself playing it just to unveil the events, and in the end find it a satisfying, yet entirely bittersweet. This game really throws you into the horrors of war, but also the bravery and self-sacrifice of it all: Emile, Freddie, Karl, Anna, Walt, and even the side characters. They all play an important part. Perhaps I should have expected that ending (I knew not all endings are happy), but it still made me shed tears.
The only thing I wish this game has is a DLC of the soundtrack. Because honestly, I'll buy it if there's one. All in all, get this game! I promise you won't regret it.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a gaming treasure. This game falls in line with other platforming greats of the era, such as Spyro the Dragon, Crash Bandicoot, Super Mario 64, and others. Ty is special, just like those games are special. Ty has really fun controls, and neat abilities, which is key to an enjoyable platforming game. The characters are well voiced, the graphics are beautiful, the levels are very well designed, and I have to play a level through multiple times to find everything because of how well they are made. The story is interesting enough, and the music is just a joy to listen to. Do yourself a favor and experience this gem. Most of the reviews I read here are through a lens of nostalgia "I played this as a kid and enjoyed it then, so its good now."  I did NOT play Ty as a kid, so my review is unbiased from a nostalgia perspective, and is purely based on the game I see now in 2016. I have no idea why the devs are calling this early access. This game is more complete than most AAA titles, and its certainly more complete than its original console release, with better graphics, tighter controls, and more feature. -PR0XIDIAN

Love this game!  Always been a big board gamer, and have played a lot of Talisman with friends.  Armello is the perfect balance between RNG and strategy.  Sure there is dice rolling (beautifully rendered dice rolling), but you DO have to weigh the chances of success over those of failure, and then go for it if feasible.  Sometimes you win, sometimes not.   So much charm in the characters, and different strats for each one.  You move, play cards, equip items on your own turn, but you can also strategize on your off turn, look at other players, and play cards to thwart them.  I also love the chat lines for each character, keeps the multiplayer civil and adds a delightful flavor to the game.  The endgame is fantastic, sometimes you've cleared all your quest to gain automatic entry into castle, other times you have to knock out another player, and still other times you sit with that banish card in hand to protect your prestige lead, a lot of paths to victory to contemplate, always tense!  To top this off, the developers challenge you to play them each week on Twitch, and they are such a fun group of people!  Join me in multiplayer!

Pros:
- An old-schoolish real time strategy rpg in the same vein as Syndicate and Total Mayhem.
- There's a lot of visual polish in the game, great world design.
- When everything works as intended it *is* a fun game.
Cons:
- Mechanics such as Wayfindingfor your characters is frustrating, the AI is not fantastic often shooting into walls and corners when they were being shot back.  For effectiveness you will want to micro manage everything but the UI makes it more difficult.
- Visual cues aren't fantastic, you can't really tell if where an enemies line of sight and what the range is and whether you can be spotted which is frustrating if you want to take a stealth option.
- The game can be buggy and inconsistent (and I don't know whether the inconsistency is due to bugs).  Sometimes I will load a game and it will force me to go through the Tutorial steps despite me not being in the tutorial, as a result I needed to reload the save again which is slow.  I ended up being stuck behind some card boxes and was unable to get unstuck. Another time I destroyed a power unit and upon reloading the game a minute later it was undestroyed.
- Explanations of abilities were lacking, for instance there is no explanation if hardwiring things were permenant changes or if they were temporary like hacking.
- You needed to be able to do more with the world and interact with things outside of the objectives.

This is a brilliant game inspired by Syndicate and Syndicate wars.  It even has music inspired by the original with a 80s techno funk vibe added. If you played the original you will hear it right away.  Although the user interface is a little different to the original syndicate it still feels like the same game only more modern.
Great catchy sound you will find yourself randomly humming at the strangest of times.  You can zoom right in on your dudes to almosts first person.  Totally useless but looks cool.    Hacking and tampering.. almost all doors, gates and security have ways for you to tamper with them, some more than one. Addictive gameplay. You get really attached to your little dudes.  Lots of customisation options for your little soldiers too.
Destructive world..  takes a lot of fire, but given enough time most walls, vehicles etc can be shot to bits.
Eases you nicely into gameplay too.. what I thought was a tutorial dropped me right into the first part of the city.. and i was into the game before i realized.
Cant seem to see a way to drive cars around like in the original.. but I may be missing something there.. and fast travel compensates for it.
Some irritations tho -
1: Every now and again 1 of your guys will get unselected.. either by resurrection or someone was still in a door. Then he will just stand there like an idiot getting shot to death while all the other guys run away.. like he was meant to be doing.
2: Although they will pull a gun automatically on someone shooting them enough.. making the threat level go up and resulting in more someone's shooting at you - they wont shoot back unless you tell them. Really annoying if you are off screen with another guy but convenient if you are in the normal city playing dumb and tell him to put it away fast enough.
3: Sometimes they just stop following orders for no reason whatsoever and do the most stupid things.
4: That camera view.. you cant rotate it all the way around.. so there is always something in the way of your view when sneaking around. Doesn't hurt gamplay much just irritating.
Irritations aside.. I want to keep playing.  You should buy this! Its pretty damn fun.
