Episodes from Liberty City é um pacote com as duas expansões de GTA 4, inicialmente lançadas separadamente, sendo que podem ser jogadas mesmo sem possuir o jogo de base. Ambas trazem pequenas variações no mapa em relação ao original e algumas pequenas novidades.
O primeiro episódio, The Lost and Damned, diz respeito a uma gangue de motoqueiros que teve seu líder (Billy Grey) capturado pela polícia. Até que ele pudesse retornar, a gangue passou a ser comandada por Johnny Klebitz que guiou seus companheiros à prosperidade.
No entanto, anos se passaram e com o retorno de Billy, ele estava totalmente transformado de forma que sua liderança estava destruindo tudo que havia sido construído e pondo em risco seus membros. Esta situação faz com que alguns dos membros se revoltem.
Nesta expansão, o jogador controla Johnny, que por sinal se movimenta muito devagar, bem mais devagar que Nicko. Como há um maior foco em motocicletas, foram acrescentados alguns modelos novos e tornou-se praticamente impossível cair delas.
Uma coisa ruim é que as vozes dos motoqueiros não combinam com os personagens e nos faz ter dificuldade de saber quem é quem está falando, o que prejudica um pouco o entendimento dos diálogos.
Já o segundo episódio, The Ballad of Gay Tony, assumimos o papel de Luis Lopez, braço direito de Tony Prince, um viadinho dono das melhores boates em Liberty City. Luis é sócio de Tony e eles são apenas amigos, sendo que não há nenhuma outra relação entre eles.
Diferente dos outros personagens, Luis vive na vida boa, tem um bom apartamento e várias mulheres. O problema é que o negócio das boates já não está tão lucrativo como antes, e seu mentor Tony se meteu em algumas enrascadas tentando diversificar os investimentos.
The Ballad of Gay Tony tem as melhores músicas tocando nas rádios contando todos os GTA’s já lançados, pelo menos na minha opinião, além de missões frenéticas e um sistema de pontuação por missão que premia o jogador em realiza-las usando métodos específicos.
Há nas duas expansões algumas adições muito bem vindas, como um sistema de checkpoints nas missões em que, no caso de falha, o jogador não precisa repetir a missão desde o começo, mas sim do último checkpoint.
Também foram adicionados novos mini games, como queda de braço e competição de bebida, corridas com bastões e habilidade para dançar. Foi retirada (felizmente) a necessidade de ficar ligando para as pessoas para manter relacionamentos.
O interessante é que as tramas das expansões ocorrem paralelamente a do jogo principal, sendo que por várias vezes passamos pelo mesmo local onde ocorreu algum evento e podemos ver os personagens dos outros jogos realizando as ações que fizemos, quando estávamos jogando com eles.
Além disso, as histórias são interligadas, com várias referencias cruzadas, e há situações em que realizaremos missões  com a participação dos personagens dos outros jogos, o que nos ajuda a entender melhor qual o que ocorreu em cada evento.
Algo que já acontecia no GTA 4 original, mas agora é muito frequente é o recebimento de alguma ligação que faz iniciar uma missão qualquer... Isso é muito chato porque não há como não aceitar e você deverá fazer aquela missão compulsoriamente naquele momento, mesmo que tivesse em mente fazer outra coisa.
Não se pode deixar de mencionar que também foram herdados alguns bugs do título principal, mas pelo menos são bem menos numerosos, e não atrapalham tanto jogar como eram naquele, de forma que não há quase nada para reclamar do jogo.
No fim das contas, se você jogou GTA 4, é praticamente obrigatório que você jogue suas expansões também, pois são bastante sólidas e talvez até mais divertidas que o título principal. EXCELENTE (9/10).

I don't usually play war games because they tend to be tactical and strategy based, but this caught my eye. The graphics, the stories, the characters. By some sheer luck, a friend had a copy of the game and gifted it to me. While some have complained about Uplay, it's just one small hitch. Putting that aside, I immensely enjoyed this game, and cried buckets as I played.
The game mechanics and puzzles seem easy, but actually take a few tries at certain parts. It all adds up to the urgency of the game. There have been times when I've to replay a scene a few times because either my timing was wrong, or just to get a feel of the pattern. Then there is the characters and stories behind it. I like that it has proper history behind it and you can read about them as it goes on. It makes so much sense when a specific character does certain actions or why that route is taken. As all the four characters (and the dog)'s story unfolds, they crush my heart. At times nail-biting, other times heart-wrenching. You begin to feel for them, and in a way, they represent the many facets of all those involved during the Great War.
Valiant Hearts really echoes with me, and I highly recommend this game to everyone. It's also educational and engaging. I find myself playing it just to unveil the events, and in the end find it a satisfying, yet entirely bittersweet. This game really throws you into the horrors of war, but also the bravery and self-sacrifice of it all: Emile, Freddie, Karl, Anna, Walt, and even the side characters. They all play an important part. Perhaps I should have expected that ending (I knew not all endings are happy), but it still made me shed tears.
The only thing I wish this game has is a DLC of the soundtrack. Because honestly, I'll buy it if there's one. All in all, get this game! I promise you won't regret it.

Love this game!  Always been a big board gamer, and have played a lot of Talisman with friends.  Armello is the perfect balance between RNG and strategy.  Sure there is dice rolling (beautifully rendered dice rolling), but you DO have to weigh the chances of success over those of failure, and then go for it if feasible.  Sometimes you win, sometimes not.   So much charm in the characters, and different strats for each one.  You move, play cards, equip items on your own turn, but you can also strategize on your off turn, look at other players, and play cards to thwart them.  I also love the chat lines for each character, keeps the multiplayer civil and adds a delightful flavor to the game.  The endgame is fantastic, sometimes you've cleared all your quest to gain automatic entry into castle, other times you have to knock out another player, and still other times you sit with that banish card in hand to protect your prestige lead, a lot of paths to victory to contemplate, always tense!  To top this off, the developers challenge you to play them each week on Twitch, and they are such a fun group of people!  Join me in multiplayer!

Again a game which was somewhere in my "Library void" for many month now. I actually "found" it again as i was playing "This War of Mine" - but thats another game and another review.
So.
VH begins with really lovely and fitting music, telling you the story of a Family (or "lovers" or how ever you wana call that now) which is thrown appart by the WW1.
You mainly play 4 Characters wile the story holds on, without spoiler to much, i explain them shortly.
Emile (I would call him the "Frontman" or "Main character")
A French farmer, who begins to seach his Son-In-Law, Karl. He sadly had to go to war at the side from france.
Freddie
An American volunteer fighting in the war to avenge his fallen wife whos also getting Emiles "brother in arms".
Anna
A Belgian nurse searching for her father kidnapped by Baron Von Dorf, meeting Emile, Freddie & Walt later on the story.
Karl
A German, married to Emileʻs Daughter Marie and had to fight in the war for the german side.
As you might read, i also called the name Walt next to the 4 main characters. Walt is a dog, a doberman pinscher. He is kinda the "side-kick" next to each character and a very good one. along the way (with each character) he is there, somehow helping and working together with all the other characters, giving small hints and helping out at riddles.
The story tells the destiny along those Characters, beginning with Karl who is forced to leave france and his mate Marie and had to fight for the german forces. Shortly after, Emile is also "forced" to join the forces of france to fight against the german army. Wile the story has twists and turns, it still is easy to follow since its nicely told, i would call it "book-like". Wile every Level is a part of the story, the story goes on with the game which fits perfectly and it gives nothing which is "useless told" somehow...well, nearly nothing.
It gives 2 parts in the game which i, for myself, dont really like or where i thought the game tries now to make fun of itself.
- the first part are the cardriving levels which are played after known musics. which means bombs and like drops in a rhythm of a special music which plays and you have to take care where it drops. those parts are actually not so bad but they anyhow dont fit into the game from my side at least (i mean i was sitting and listen to the music there wile playing those levels and was like "are you kidding me now?"; they might tried to be funny here but...well...)
- the other parts i didnt enjoy, mostly later on, are the Quicktime events. Im honest, I never "HATED" to play a nurse/medic in a game, which is in this game Anna. As the role of the nurse...let me call her FIELD-DOC (srs, it fits better), she has to make a "minigame" wile healing people. And what are those minigames? Youre right! Push the RIGHT BUTTON in the RIGHT MOMENT - in short Quicktime events. At the beginning, it might be easy but it quickly gets faster and harder. A Spoiler (ONLY READ IT IF YOU REALLY REALLY WANT!!!)
The Gameplay is a classic-like adventure but more in levels sections insteed a open-world like one.
Get X to do Y with Z, open part A to go forward and playing with D character wile character F is waiting for item H - Just to keep it short.
So you have a lot riddles to do and solve on the way. Even if this game is "about" war, you nearly never use a gun or like and if you do its very short and more minigame like. So is that game a action game? Sure not. Its a pur adventure game and a very nice one. The riddles and puzzles are not "to hard" and even if you need help, if you wait a bit, a soldier-dove (yea, you read it right...) gives you hints how you can solve the puzzles.
Even if it is a nice story and has a great OST, Graficstyle and co, the game is kinda short. For the normal price of 15€, the playtime is around 4-6 hours (maybe longer if you really want to collect everything).
Valiant Hearts is a great Puzzle Adventure with a great story told like a good book. It might be a short game for the price tag but it sure is worth playing. It is not a action game even if its a "War game" and even if you have (sometimes) a weapon or like, its more a minigame using it. The actual minigames like a lot quicktime events might need practise to get "better" in those but i guess those are not to hard, like the riddles. The game plays pretty smooth, has a fitting soundtrack and a great storyteller and graficstyle.
I can only recommend this game, mostly for people who like puzzle games or adventures with a very deep story.

I don't know what to write, so here's the recipe for chocolate chip cookies:
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar
Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

One of the most well layed out afterthoughts of a game you'll ever experience. Created out of the Half Life 2 Source engine as a bit of an experiment in third person, it works awesomelly for a game nearly 8 years old now. A squad based shooter with the option of just going nuts in easy mode, or really challenging yourself tactically with higher skill levels.
This is the 2017 update of the Original Alien Swarm, with many cool updates including all the things you had to do with the console to make the game work in single player, now simply a menu option! The real fun is group play of course, but perfectly playable now in Single mode either if you dont like multiplayer or to hone your skills.
The isometric view can now be morphed into first person if you really would like a challenge, but the real fun lies in destroying the near endless waves of alien beasties with your selection of death dealing weapons, along with your medic and tactical sergeant you have a hacker and potential sniper any of whom can carry welding torches to seal off access temporarily or throw down auto-turrets or tesla mines.
The graphically superb environment can be complemented by the now rather varied Steam Workshop possibilities including Warhammer Space/Choas Marines skins and further maps and mods. None of which are needed at all, but are nice to play with!
The sound is quite destructively incredible with very satisfying gun fire and when you hit certain keypoints or a squad member deploys the adrenalin perk and the world slows while the eerie backround music speeds up...well...its gone and reached new levels of cool that need defining.
Community maps integrated as actual game maps, with voice overs etc stuffed in, a wonderful reboot to a game that has already stood the test of time and continues to be one of the most enjoyable Steam experiences to date! Get in here!

The gameplay in Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is really where it's at. Initially, during the beta, and even into the earliest stages of its release, Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 was plagued with many issues, from extreme framerate drops to stuttering, crashes, and other sometimes hilarious bugs. However, CI Games promised to work those issues out before moving on to the season pass stuff and whatever else they had planned, and they were true to their word. As of a couple weeks ago, almost all those issues were sorted out via at least one substantial patch and a couple minor tweaks, and although I still experienced minor glitches from time to time, not one was even remotely game breaking or even immersion killing.
With the latest patch in place, I was able to really dive into this game and the gameplay was tight and spot on. First of all, this is a sniper game, so you really have to nail the stealth aspects and especially the actual gunplay, especially when looking through a scope at your target. These aspects were as good as it gets, and when I say as good as it gets, I mean better than Sniper Elite, better than any Ghost Recon, better than really any other game that relies at least partially on sniper mechanics. You could creep around and snipe the hell out of anybody you pleased in this game with enough planning. I quite liked the stability mechanics, which took into account not only your physical position and positioning, but also wind and elevation as it pertained to bullet velocity. A huge amount of work went into making this a peerless experience.
However, you don't HAVE to strictly snipe your way through the game, and there will be plenty of moments where you didn't tag an enemy or simply had no space available to plot out a long range execution. As such, in addition to your sniper rifle of choice, you also carry a secondary rifle (or shotgun), a pistol, and a knife. All found copious usage during my playthrough. Creeping up and using a knife on somebody to gain proper position to switch to sniping was pretty awesome. Blasting a fool with a shotgun was incredible. However, for my secondary weapon, I generally settled on a scoped LMG. It had a nice medium range and was also powerful enough to knock out even armored opponents. I did find silenced pistols to be especially effective when indoors or in very tight places, and a headshot with one guarantees results.
You are also kitted out with a variety of tools and explosives which will come in handy often. Eventually, you will find body armor and upgraded versions of said armor to help absorb some bullets. Most important however is your scout drone. This thing will allow you to get the lay of the land, plot out your trajectories and paths of ingress and egress, and tag both enemies as well as important geographical or building features. The drone can also be fit with luring devices to distract opponents. The most useful upgrade to the drone was the hacking mechanism that allows the drone in close proximity to camera panels and other electronic devices to hack into them and allow you to control them (such as shutting down electric grids or hacking cameras to further scout areas and tag opponents).
I alluded to this above, but in addition to sniping, you can in fact choose to run and gun, and sometimes, this will become necessary once enemies are on alert and have a reasonable idea as to where you have been hiding. Related to this, a lot of enemy encampments have mortars, and they will lock onto your last known position. So, as in real life, you want to change position here and there to avoid enemies getting a solid bead on where you are sniping them from.
There are a lot of different way to approach almost every mission. Secret access points and hidden sniping spots will change the dynamic of quite a few missions. Some missions are straight forward though. For example, there are a couple missions where you provide cover for other operatives. There are search and rescue missions. Missions where you have to destroy oil tanks or weapons caches, and so on. You will also have a vehicle, and driving is quite easy in this game. Vehicles are responsive. However, with unlocked checkpoints, your driving time will be more limited as you progress, most likely, unless you are simply taking in the local scenery.
It is also worth mentioning that Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is in fact an open world experience, and one that you can enjoy at your leisure. There are a lot of secret areas and unlockables, which might be artwork or might be actual usable weapons and equipment. There are also bounty missions on each map area (of which there are three map area). You have a safe house on each map, where you can reset, recharge, craft disposable equipment, and accept quests.
Oh...and I almost forgot: CI Games does pay homage to some of their own favorite games within Sniper Ghost Warrior 3. Most notable for me was the Witcher series style tracking available while using your heightened senses. You will see footprints or tracks glowing on the ground and can follow them to solve a few mysteries or help with certain campaign quests.
I could easily keep going with gameplay, but I will stop here.
9.5 out of 10
CryEngine was used for this iteration of the Ghost Warrior series. As such, you get a completely beautiful and amazingly well rendered world. When you really look closely, you can see the rough edges, but taken as a whole, Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is a stunning looking game. The world is quite vibrant and alive, with different geographical areas featuring distinct scenery, towns and villages looking lived in, and so on.
However, the actual character animations, while definitely solid, do in fact look dated. I would expect these character models mid Gen 7, not fully invested in Gen 8 where we sit today. That doesn’t mean they look bad. However, I think quite a bit more could have been pulled from CryEngine to make the characters look at least close to as great as the rest of the game. The same can be said of the death animations, which, although really cool looking, lack quite a bit of variety and also carry that dated look.
All told though, this is still a stunning looking game that simply features some rough edges and at times palette bleeding. 8 out of 10.
Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is a gem in the stealthy sniper-y sub genre where the Sniper Elites, Ghost Recons, and Ghost Warriors of the world reside. There is no better actual sniping mechanics in all of gaming (and I include MGS 5, the pinnacle of control mastery, in this assessment of Sniper Ghost Warrior 3’s mastery of this genre’s marquis gameplay aspect). The actual campaign was fairly engaging, characters reasonably approachable, and the world vibrant and lived in. It is very easy for me to recommend this game to pretty much anybody, despite its rough release, which is now a thing of the past. Even after you finish the campaign (which took me about 34 hours), there is easily another 10-15 hours of random stuff such as side quests, places of interests, bounties, and collectibles you can wrap up. The release day version featured the inclusion of the season pass which was a nice bonus, and the first DLC was available upon release. I will be playing and reviewing that separately.

If you are a board game junky, and like P v P/ P v E, and games like "Risk"; then you're probably an Armello fan and just don't know it.
Armello is a turn based, table-top video game. The objective: Become the king of Armello. Armello is currently ruled by a tyrannical king simply known as "The King." He is consumed by "Rot," and no longer acts on the behalf of his fellow country men (animals?). Take control of members of the Bear, Wolf, Rabbit, and Rat clan and seek to overturn his rule. You can win via four paths: Collecting 4 spirit stones and breaching the castle walls to banish the King, gathering so much rot of your own that you can kill the King at his own game (players roll several die to attack and defend, and if you have more rot than an opponent you get their rot number in additional dice), simply retain the King's favour via "prestiege" (Prestiege is earned by completing your own personal quests, claiming burning settlements as your own, and of course killing enemy players. This is where the P v P comes into play full-force), and lastly you can win by simply breaching the kingdom walls and just killing the King the old fashioned way in head-to-head combat.
I typed this out and it still doesn't explain the game well enough. The strategy nerd in me can't even convey this properly. Just buy it, man. If you are even thinking about it; do it. Quests, items, badass animal characters, a whole Kingdom to explore, and a fun way to mess with your buddies. You won't know the sensation of breaking an alliance in the very last minute of a game by killing your friend with a spell card and taking their place in the throne room as the new king of Armello. Not if you don't buy it.

To be honest, I have mixed feelings about this game. This is one of those games for which "neutral" opinion is perfect. So, what Armello is all about?
It's a mixture of a board game, card game and strategy wrapped in gorgeous graphics and very nice soundtrack. Audio-visuals are very good and immersive. It feels like a fairy tale, every character is unique, likeable, and has a very cool design. Atmosphere is warm, nice, and calm... under one condition, and that is, if You have luck on Your side. Because this game can turn from a family friendly game to a table flipping rage fest. Why? Answer is simple, and to many people it's a turning point in buying a game or not. RNG! This game is so filled with randomness that sometimes You will feel You have no control over what's happening on the board.
-Card picking at the beginning of each turn? Kinda random, except in one case if You have Usurpers DLC. One character can see what cards he's choosing.
-Quests locations? Random. And the game is programmed that every time You complete one quest, next quest starts at the opposite side of the map/board.
-Villages, main source of income for Your equipment? Random. So, it can happen that one person can have two villages nearby his clan grounds while another player has none and has to walk further to intercept it.
-Exploring dungeons? Random. While exploring You can get many different outcomes, like finding gold/treasures, recruiting companions or The Stranger, spawning a wraith or even being teleported to another dungeon. The annoying part is that it isn't being determined by any factor at all, You just have to be lucky to get what You want.
-And now the worst part. Battles with another players or npc's (knights and the king) are based on throwing dices, and although it's understandable it is random (since in real life throwing a dice is also random obviously) it presents a very, very nasty problem. The outcome of the fight isn't determined by Your playing skills but by sheer luck and the amount of dices You hold. The amount of dices depends on Your battle stat but even so there will be times when You're overpowered, having 7 or more dices and You still lose because RNG "decided" that You will roll 6 Rots and 1 Sword while Your opponents will roll 3 Wylds which gives them 3 additional rolls... and that can lead to another Wylds, and so on until You end up getting rekt. This can be very frustrating, to the point where You just quit the game. I would rather see some other mechanic that involves You as an active player more. You can burn Your cards to force symbols to appear, but that doesn't help much. At least not in my case.
But despite all these flaws and rage inducing moments, I still enjoy this game for the most part. It may be because I am a calm person in general, but I can see how some other players will hate this type of gameplay. I wouldn't give this game a negative review, but positive one is also a little bit of a stretch, because that depends heavily on what kind of a player You are. If You are a rage quitter, You won't like this. But, if You're chill and aren't taking games that seriously, You can definitely enjoy Armello.

A solid decendent of Syndicate, complete with vaguely-communicated mechanics that you figure out inconsistently through random accidents, with awesome Blade Runner graphics and lots of ways to spec out your team.  Mostly bug-free (sometimes, rarely, your character will get stuck in geometry; it is possible to get weird or missing mission log text).  No hand-holding.  People get confused by this game, but if anyone thinks the game is too hard, read my guide at the end here.  The combat and infiltration mechanics are pretty awesome when you figure them out, and the game is pretty imbalanced if you wanna min-max your team.  Being able to see the electrical grid and use it to disable things was cool. Figuring out how to overcome or bypass infinitely-spawning mechs and hoards of elite mobs with shields and heavy weapons was satisfying even if it's OP.  Despite what some reviewers say, stealth is absolutely viable and even OP.. once you develop your team to use it.  The weapons you choose don't really matter but I give strong preference for ones that are silenced, which is most of them if you acquire the right gun mods.
Here is a simple OP guide for building your team to handle any situation by giving you multiple ways to escape or defeat any combat roadblock.  This is legitimately imbalanced so also definitely SPOILERS.  Note that each of these requires you to level up your characters to support it, or to spend the time to research and deploy the appropriate supporting mods, items, and weapons.
1) ALWAYS research and carry Grenades and deployable Ammo Packs.  Do this as soon as possible.  Ammo Packs replenish Grenades.  Two people with Ammo Packs replenish eachother's Ammo Packs.  Infinite Grenades makes you into an artillery squad.  Enemies are infinitely respawning, so there are diminishing returns to engaging in war, so make sure you at least can win.  Infinite grenades blow up infinitely respawning enemies forever until you get bored of it.  They also are absurdly effective against every door and turret and sentry gun and mech and generator in the game.  Brokely OP.
Secondary Good Ideas:
2) ALWAYS research and install character mods to support moving through vents.  No enemy in the game can use vents.  It is OP and guarantees disengagement from the current combat.
3) ALWAYS research and carry cloaking items.  You can walk right through any enemy in the game and it usually guarantees escape.
4) ALWAYS buff your character's energy regeneration.  Most of the special abilities in the game rely on it.
5) ALWAYS research and carry silenced weapons.  Taking out cameras will still trigger a suspicious investigation, but it makes it substantially easier to dissect your way through any fortification.
6) ALWAYS research and carry at least one Smoke Grenade.  Enemies shooting you at point blank range cannot target you in a cloud and guarantees disengagement from combat, at least for a few seconds.  Pop a Smoke and press Cloak and walk away from giant mechs and dozens of assorted assailants.
7) ALWAYS buff the class ability that slows down time.  Only one of your characters gets it, but it is the most useful character ability in the game.  Buffing energy regeneration is critical to supporting this ability.
8) If you want to level up your characters faster, unlock grenades and ammo packs as soon as possible.  Go stand near any enemy spawn point and mortar the crap out of them for an hour or so.  Character XP is specific to who gets a kill, so give whichever characters you want to level up a Grenade so they can rack them up.'

This game was recommended to me by a friend, and although I am not much for either puzzle games or side-scrollers, I figured, why not. After I installed and started to play the game, I got to a spot where I couldn't continue due to some sort of bug: the first taxi ride in which you evade the bombs and machine guns of the Zep, during Chapter 1.
Eventually I came back to the game and the bug had been fixed. So I played it through almost to completion. But I will probably never finish the game, sadly.
As the game progresses, the puzzles get trickier, which is OK, I guess. But the problem for me is that the game also keeps turning up the gain on the hand-eye coordination puzzles: I was particularly frustrated by the final assault where you have to dig your way past all those unexploded bombs, and God forbid you should hesitate or the roof will literally fall in.
But I did get past that, only to be ultimately denied an ending by the last "Heal Karl" episode. I'm sorry, but at the age of 57--and as one who was never that gifted in the hand-eye department anyhow--I'm just not good enough to make it through the "hit-the-right-button-at-the-right-instant" part. I got close a couple times, but by then I was so annoyed, frustrated, and exhausted that I wasn't able to do it and in fact just got worse.
You would think that since there were three separate bits, they'd give you credit for each one as you complete it, but no...if you fail at any point, it's back to zero for you. I don't quite understand this, especially as the game is much more forgiving in most of the other parts.
And this, finally, brings me to why, after all is weighed in the balance, the game doesn't work for me. It's advertised as this great emotional experience, and that part is entirely correct...just as long as you don't hit the wall. The minute you find yourself stymied by a puzzle, or unable to make it past a hand-eye moment...the emotional content drains away as if you'd pulled the stopper in your sink.
The artwork is charming, the characters tolerably endearing...though it tells you something that the most attaching one is the dog. The plot makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, but I'll let that one go. And I'm not altogether happy with the narrative having to be carried by a voice-over in the style of Ken Burns' Civil War series: the first rule of a visual medium is, after all, show, don't tell. If I had the skills to do the transitions, I could do pretty much every voiceover in graphical form, and surely they would be more powerful that way.
The game may be more appealing if you really, really like puzzle-game side-scrollers that require substantial amounts of hand-eye coordination. I am not that person. So it is with some reluctance, but no hesitation, that I conclude "Not Recommended."

The orignal blow everything up simulator, BFBC2 really took the old battlefield formula and cranked it up to 11. Buildings exploded. They fell down. People were horribly crushed to death in the collapse. Entire maps were levelled, reduced to ruin and despair, and we loved it.
Downsides? The unlock/progression system ground to a standstill after you reached a certain level and every little thing became a grind. It could be rage inducingly difficult, and especially brutal on your nerves if you dared take a week or two away from the game. If you wanted to be consistently good it demanded constant use, constant refinement of your skills.
Ultimately, BFBC2 remains my second favourite BF game after BF1942 (I'll be shot down by 2142 players, but I skipped that installment), a great source of happy gaming memories, and a formula I can compare other similar games to.

Fight the Dragon is a user-generated action RPG, which can be good or bad based on the community involved in making the content. If you're looking for good content, I recommend NOT looking at the highest rated content because they happen to be the most bland and generic of them all. It makes me wonder how exactly they became the top rated in the first place, while unique and creative maps go completely unnoticed. This is because of how the game streamlines new content; it does it very poorly. There is a "new content" tab but its clearly filled with "not new content" because of the amount of ratings each map has, as if they haven't updated the new content tab since alpha. You just have to hope that your map falls under the "local unplayed map" pool that seems to be randomly generated for each user, since that is the actual "new content" tab, but this tab seems to only have like 5-7 maps at a time. I published my map yesterday, and as of right now, only one person other than me has played it. This game prides itself for over-saturation of content, when in reality, it's the main downfall of this game. You really have to sift through a lot of crap to find a few gems, or just give up and make your own gems that only you will end up playing anyway.
Which brings me to why im recommending this game: The level editor.
If you like creating your own levels, but are completely stupid and impatient when it comes to using editors (like me), then I highly recommend this game, because not only is the editor extremely easy to use, its also very intricate. You can do practically anything with this level editor. Every interactable item or prop you can place has its own programmable event tab, which you can use to trigger events throughout your level. Events such as "When this monster dies, break down breakable wall" or "When player opens this chest, close X doors and spawn Y monsters in vicinity". There are so many things you can do with this level editor, that you will spend so many hours messing with it and thinking of creative ways to use it. The only problem I have with it is that there's not a huge selection of props, textures, and enemies.
Now you may be saying to yourself "That's great and all, but hows the gameplay?"
Well, the combat is a bit clunky and needs improvement... But LOOK AT HOW SHINY THIS LEVEL EDITOR IS!
In all seriousness though, if you like to create your own levels, but don't have the knowledge or patience to use a professional editor, then it is well worth the money. The game itself ain't half bad either, if you can deal with a few bad eggs.

This free game is surprisingly well-developed and fun for many hours.  I love the 1st ed. AD&D aesthetic (done tongue-in-cheek), combined with turn-based party RPG and card-game mechanics.  It's a fun throwback to old Dungeons & Dragons play, but lovingly mocked for its geekiness throughout, and updated for simple but deep tactical gameplay.
It's funny without sacrificing any of the actual nerd enjoyment of card-driven fantasy RPG battle tactics.  The perfect audience for this game is someone who loves these sorts of games yet also laughs at the dorks (always dorkier than ourselves, naturally) who played these games in the 1980s.
Beautiful graphics, extremely smooth lag-free play, clear user interface. In-game purchases available but totally non-invasive and inessential to success.  Worth $20, but the developers seem to be banking on the in-game purchases to make up for the excellent development.  No skimping here!

Card Hunter is basically a tactical-board game where you have three characters who each have their own deck composed of items that you equip to them and the character's race (of Human, Elf, Dwarf, I would be happy to see more, but I have played this game since before it was on Steam and it has only ever had the three).
I am unaware of any pay to win aspects in the game. There are microtransactions, but they are cosmetic, or for expansion packs, which I am okay with. Most of the stuff you can buy seems reasonably priced to me, your mileage may vary.
The game itself can be frustrating at times, as there is a lot of rng-madness going on. Some games you'll draw non-combat card after non-combat card despite having a deck on the character that consists of a great many combat cards. Other games you'll get a plethora of combat cards, but not enough ways to actually move to opponents, which leads to having to discard all of your lovely cards.
Most matches run fairly well though, I have had many good runs where I felt everything went well, but when playing with rng, you are going to come up to points that are frustrating.
The art style of the game is clear and enjoyable. The campaign story isn't terrible, though the meat of the game is the tactical combat, so the story isn't a major focus.
I recommend the game, it is a good pick-up-and-play game, lightly casual, but with enough depth to sink into.

TLDR:
It's Cyberpunk meets Baldur's Gate. Gameplay is different from Syndicate Wars. More like Baldur's Gate. It’s like Syndicate Wars in game content e.g. persuading enemies & citizens, agent augmentations weapons. The game was made with a lot of love but glitches in the Matrix let it down. Tactical depth is enormous. Bigger guns not always better. You can (and have to) mix many different character types, skills and weapons get through missions, and past different enemy types. If you can’t problem solve and figure out the different combinations of skills, weapons and paths needed to win, you won’t find it fun.
PROS
- Enormous tactical depth
- Immersive world. Beautiful artwork. Akin to Bladerunner.
- True to Cyberpunk Lore from Neuromancer to Deux Ex HR.
- Awesome soundtrack
- Character designs are cool (sometimes OTT)
- Movement/animations have realistic inertia and weight, unlike most strategy games. (it can feel slow if you’re not used to it)
- Things aren’t as predictable without being procedurally generated because you can’t save during danger moments.
- Different districts have very different look and feel. Nice variety of the same night-time neon cyberpunk city.
- Slight RPG element, but without needing to grinding
CONS
- Characters can get lodged into the wall/objects. A long mission can end due glitch. Very annoying.
- Poor pathfinding. (But battles and mission coordination doesn’t need good pathfinding)
- Ending sucks (but you have to apparently read the ebook to understand it)
- Story could’ve been better.
WHAT MAKES IT FUN
- You can pull off the same mission in multiple ways.
- Fun little easter eggs e.g. upgrades that reference energon and transformers and other tongue in cheek sarcasm and humour.
- Taking over a whole city. Gives you a sense of conquest.
- Getting new skills and upgrades.
- Figuring out the enemy and punking them.
EXAMPLE OF TACTICAL FUN
There’s multiple enemies, and a drone. The infiltrator can do stealth gun kills on the guards but not the drone. The guards are facing each other so you can’t sneak up on them one by one, so you go into bullet time, and kill the guards from behind with all agents simultaneously, then use the infiltrator to do blade kill on the final drone in one hit just before it sounds the alarm, but then he has to cool down. But another drone is coming around the corner, so you immediately use the hacker to hack the drone. Then you can use the drone as your “key” to get you through the doors because hacking the doors takes too long. Then you can use the infiltrator to go invisible and get to the terminal, and use the hacker to hack through the infiltrator…. then you accidentally make a wrong move and all the guards rush to you so you have to blast your way out and get to a safe point and try again with a slightly different strategy. You can’t just save and reload (like in Deus Ex) during danger moments, and you want to not have to let an agent with good set of skills die otherwise you lose those innate skills which can only be acquired by capturing and cloning good quality enemies/citizens.
You may have figured out that you can stand near a beacon, to get ammo replenished, and then launch unlimited grenades at the enemy or into their base. Not that it achieves the mission, but fun to watch and racks up “kills” easily and experience points.
PERSONALLY
I love Satellite Reign to death. I can’t believe I’ve played more than 100hours! I’ve played it twice. It’s addicting and fun for me because its cyberpunk, tactically deep, slight RPG element, but not the grinding type. The glitches happen about 5-10% of the time. Once you figure out how to pop the character out from being stuck, it’s ok (not great). It’s a bummer, but its forgivable because you’re very prone to the “stuff up, try again” cycle anyway. And there wasn’t so much that I couldn’t get to the end. I hated the ending more than the glitches.

I loved the game. It was a great World War one game, actually the only one Ive seen. It was interesting to view WWI through the eyes of the soldiers. I liked the game all the way up to the heartbreaking ending.

Don't be discouraged by the
requirement or that it is published by
. This game is nothing like you're used to in the mainstream market.
In
you play as several different characters during the First World War.
You'll be encountering puzzles of varying, but similar difficulty, fight and sneak your way through different places, all while seeing how the stories of the different characters interact and play out.
Additionally the game provides quite a bit of factual information regarding the First World War, if you're interested.
Graphically the game is very beautiful, despite its setting and comic-like art style. By placing 2d elements in an actual 3d world and also using 3d objects, that look 2d, coupled with its art style, the games has a very distinctive look, that fits it very well.
And while the trenches of the battlefields do depict a gruesome and terrible part of history, I found them to be the second-most beautiful elements for the amount of detail the game shows in such scenes and how all of them have their own color composition.
Similar to its comic art style, the game's characters never fully talk in a certain language, instead often mumbling only certain words in English, German or French, depending on their nationality, which I found quite charming and very fitting.
The same goes for the soundtrack and background music. The orchestral songs really support what happens on the screen and for when things aren't as hectic or cheerful, the game provides a few quieter songs.
Control-wise I played the game through with an Xbox 360 gamepad, but I'd say that it would work fine on a keyboard as well.
It took me around five hours to complete the game, which I think is more than fine.
The game's biggest selling point to me is, however how it tells its story, themes and overall message: How terrible war is, what it does to people, all while being not too serious throughout.
There were quite a few scenes in the game that made me somewhat stop and think about that time period one hundred years ago.
I'd call that mission accomplished.
If you didn't find my review helpful, let me know with a comment, so I can improve it and any upcoming reviews! It would be much appreciated!

So I've had a passing interest in games that emulate board games lately. At the top of my list for this interest was Armello, and when I was finally able to get my hands on it, it lived up the hype people I'd listened to built up around it. Imagine for a moment... You're a character in a fantastical fantasy world. Your lands King has grown ill from a dark disease that your people simply call "The Rot". This disease is not only slowly killing your king, but has also driven him completely insane to the point that he's passing laws that undermine the people and sending his guards out into the kingdom to terrorise the innocent!
That's where you come in! Playing the role of one of the lands intrepid heroes that would stand against the King and his new found madness in the hopes that you can overthrow the current crown, and restore peace to the land! The only catch being, there are other heroes that have the same goal as you, and they aren't too keen on working together for the greater good, turning your epic quest into a race against time to see who will win the right to wear the crown!
That, in a nutshell, is Armello's story. Given the nature of the game, I really don't have any issue telling you guys all of that. It's a glorified board game after all. A single play through (or session if you'd rather) lasts maybe an hour, and the mechanics and gameplay have so many things happening in it, that it would take me forever to explain that here. Simply put. I think Armello is "super neat" and all of you out there reading this should go buy it and play the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the game! It even has an online mode so you can strongarm your friends into playing with you! And the tutorial does a fairly good job of explaining the game as well. So seriously. Go buy this one. You can thank me later.

This is due to how some of the cards are balance.
There are "Spells" card that put some players at a disadvantage. Some of them that  hinders movement on the board.
If you are first, you will NEVER be hindered. The day and night cycle will always give you the advantage to be reset your status. You will always go the maximum distance and no one can do anything about that.
You will also have the advantage of casting these spell to hinder the players as well.
Most of the game is played online for a better experience.
However, that can be turn against you when this game is suppose to be a free for all.
You will find games where it is 2v1 or 3v1! It is not a enjoyable experience to be bullied.
There is no Soloqueue.
And also not to mention the AFK botter who are farming the keys and chest of this game.

It is the tale of a bullying victim taking her revenge on those who bullied her years ago. The cute nerdy girl working in the library is not a killer, but she gives back what she received. The movie is pretty short, but it had potential to go on further.

There is no limit to which one can praise this game. While not as action filled as its counterparts, it fills the player with a sense of roleplay that makes one envision themselves in the spot of Emile in this conflict that rocked the world. It demonstrates that there is no good or evil on either side. It is all but gray as the dirt below you as you make way passed the countless bodies of the fallen. Whether German, English, French, Indian, Australian, American, and ect, it does not matter to bullets.

Cardhunter is the crazy love child of the 80s boardgame Heroquest and a simple card game.  The name is slightly misleading as there is no card collecting.  Cards are made available through many hundreds of items.  Deck building is done by equipping items to characters like any other D&D inspired game.  But unlike other D&D inspired games, the effectiveness of each item depends on how it synergises with other items.  An item with powerful cards will be balanced by also containing a number of weak cards.  All items are available for free and will drop randomly just by playing the game.
Many of the Steam reviews suggest this game is pay to win.  This is simple not true.  I became a top 10 player without spending a cent*.  I have seen some rich players dropping hundreds of dollars to fast track their item collection.  But you cannot buy any specific items.  So money gives them very little advantage.  Any seasoned player in the world chat will tell you the same.  You must grind your way to the top and this is a good thing.  The match making system makes use of Elo ranking, and will prevent you from playing against an experienced player that will definitely win.
Ignore the negative Steam reviews.  Instead go read the positive reviews on Kongregate -
*After a thousand hours of gameplay I did purchase content, but only to support the developers.  So should you.

I've tried about three times to like Satellite Reign. In theory, it should be right up my alley - the cyberpunk setting is really neat, the idea of building the team members different ways appeals to me, and all of the subterfuge to get new items and upgrades and should be really fun, right? And, yes, I understand the throwback this game is making to Syndicate.
I think the reason I can never even bring myself to play past the first area boils down to A) some fairly clunky controls and B) the incredible amount of micromanagement you're supposed to do with them. Mostly the latter.
Don't get me wrong, trying to select your agents one at a time on a screen with that zoom-out cap is already pretty annoying on levels as massive as this game's scale (oh, another should-be positive: the districts are huge and offer lots of exploration). I could get past the zoom limit making it nearly impossible to direct all of my agents with ease... if I could give them some passive directions. If only I could put my infiltrator on overwatch from their vantage point against hostiles targeting my agents instead of needing to break up the flow of whatever other plan I was putting into motion to manually select the infiltrator, tell them to shoot a specific target, and then going back to command everyone else - repeat every time she gets a kill. If only I could set the soldier to automatically engage the closest enemy that's shooting him in his dumb face, instead of needing to also manually set the soldier to a new target every time they take one down.
It leads to this really awkward feeling about each engagement where you second guess doing -anything-. Do I go into an enemy base one at a time? Maybe not, because if an enemy wandering around on random patrols happens upon that character while you're trying to get the rest in position, they'll probably be dead before you realize they're in trouble, since they'll just take whatever is done to them. Do you bring everyone in? Nnnno, because trying to path for four characters will cause someone to inevitably stand somewhere obvious instead of hiding properly. So what do you do? Probably sit at the entrance and wait for one enemy at a time to randomly wander by so you can get a stealth kill until they're thin enough that you can keep going. Or try to wipe out the entire enemy force from a defensive position, using command all agents to have them focus fire the enemy of your choosing one at a time.
Honestly, it feels like I'm just missing something, but every time I leave someone by themselves with their gun out and expect them to maybe protect themselves, they just take it on the chin. A little bit of friendly AI management could have gone a long way toward making this game really good - without it, it's barely playable.
Honestly, I want so badly to like this game and recommend it to someone, fans of cyberpunk settings or something... but for a $30 price tag, with controls that make it so unenjoyable to play, it's honestly difficult for me to suggest it to anyone.

What could be a great game let down by atrocious bugs, performance and interface. I enjoyed this game a lot when starting but eventually the bugs got too irritating to continue with it.
Pros:
- Great concept, real time open world Syndicate style tactics
- Great story with lots of background and good writing
- Lots of choices in how you go about tasks (bribes, stealth, shoot everyone, smash and grab and run etc)
- Many missions affect later activity (e.g. a strike on the police communications system will cause police to be slower to respond to alarms in the future)
- Great art/map design of a cyberpunky city
- Can be played as real-time or real-time-with-pause tactics
Cons:
- Horribly flaky and buggy, frequently crashes
- Horribly slow, long loading times, terrible performance even with graphics at minimum. Just switching to the menu and back takes eons.
- Many terrible interface decisions, e.g. your most recent save is not preselected or highlighted so you have to search for the latest save yourself; generally awkward menus; no system to compare weapon stats easily, etc
- Developer has not updated in years and seems to have no intention of fixing any of the above.
- World isn't as interactive as it first seems, gets shallow quickly.
- Jagged progress curve, often things are too hard until your squad gains another level and then they're too easy

I really got into this game for the first couple of hours, but then it really started to annoy me, and here's why:
1) The game acts, for whatever reason, as though it's an online tablet game running on a server, even when you're not playing. That means that stuff will happen even when you're not in game. Which means that neighbors die, survivors use supplies, and you basically get punished if you don't sit on your *** for days binge-playing this.
What makes this worse is that most of the "random events" that the survivors tend to engage in all seem to be deliberately negative.
Frank shot a gun inside! He could have killed someone! Morale decrease.
Shelby is scared! She's a total bummer who brings everyone down! Morale decrease.
Jack doesn't like zombies and he's grossed out so now he's mad at you for not talking to him about it. Morale decrease.
So-and-so got food poisoning from canned food somehow! Morale decrease.
The way to boost morale is to actively work for it (or by outpost defenses against hordes, it seems, but the increase is tiny), by engaging in missions or other positive events. This is a total PITA, because a bunch of negative crap can be waiting for you when you get back on the game, and you have to go out and get your morale back. Why do I even want it back at this point? My survivors are just going to act like jerks again when I'm gone and my neighbors are going to die.
These survivors seem to need a lot of babysitting. You'd think people who survived this far into a zombie apocalypse would have bigger stones than this. They just act like a bunch of whiners. Suddenly the currently played character is their only hope despite surviving through this until now.
2) I'm okay with the perma-death (kind of...), but what I don't like is how I died for the first time: basically getting stuck in a doorway while a zombie standing halfway through a floor kept knocking me down into another two zombies behind me, who grabbed me from behind. The combat controls don't help, either, as they're a little clunky. So the game basically gave me the middle finger in this instance, and I couldn't go back unless I started the game over, but I was already about four hours into it and didn't feel like starting the entire game over again.
3) all the different types of ammo and variations of medications. I like the realism, but this makes it more frustrating to arrange your inventory properly and clogs up your storage lockers. It'd be fine if there was one type of weak medication and one type of powerful medication, and one of each ammo type/gun type to make inventory more manageable, because some ammo, despite being totally different, have very similar images applied to them. So you'll go to pick them up, only to find that they aren't the same that you're already carrying. You feel a little cheated, because you're missing out on extra meds that you just can't carry because you're carrying another type. If they're worried about you being over-supplied with meds, they can easily remedy this by slimming down the chances of you finding any while also omitting all the unnecessary different types.
4) I'm confused by some of the directions the missions give me when it relates to morale issues (such as someone being "freaked out" or whatever). They imply that I need to go talk to that survivor to calm them down. I go inside the base to talk to them, but it only gives me the opportunity to ask them to accompany me outdoors. Maybe I'm an idiot, but I can't seem to figure out exactly how I'm supposed to help these people. Maybe I don't have to at all?
5) The driving controls make me want to hang myself. I don't know if it's any better when using a controller, but on the keyboard, it's a nightmare.
6) I asked one of the survivors to come fight with me. While in the middle of a mission, he said it was time for him to go home now, and he ran straight into a horde of zombies within a minute and nearly died. If I hadn't had the mind to chase after him and "escort" the idiot home, he would have been guts on the pavement. So now I feel like I have to go out alone, because my followers are too stupid to survive in a high-stakes environment by themselves.
There are good things about the game. I like the immersion (although the story seems very meh), and I like getting to know various characters (even in the most bare-bones sense of the word), and I do greatly enjoy some of the survival aspects (going into abandoned homes and rummaging through stuff to find supplies). But the positives don't outweight the negatives for me right now.  I really, really want to enjoy this game, I really do. I was pumped for it, and I was getting into it at first. I might actually be more okay with it if there was a way to turn off activity happening when I'm not playing. If there was ever a mod or add-on or something for this, I'd continue playing it.
Seriously, someone get on turning that crap off.

I had an eye on this game for quite a while.  I thought the concept of creating your own community and switching characters within that community was interesting.  But after reading reviews, I saw many people found this game to be dissapointing, pointing out glitches, bugs etc. and mostly complaining about the price mainly because they were forced to rebuy the game for minor upgrades.  I was very skeptical, but after waiting until yesterday, one day before the end of the steam summer sale, I decided to roll the dice and give the game a chance.
And by all means THIS GAME IS NOT BAD AT ALL
Sure, it has glitches, but they're very minor and not gamebreaking.  All games are like that.  No crashes so far, no graphical glitching.  Overall this game is very stable.  The only glitches that are encountered are the animations, which most games have problems with, so no biggy there.  (I did see another review posted before mine saying that it's so buggy that it takes away from the game....it does not at all.)
This game provides alot of content, not even including the DLC.  The only problem that I find somewhat dissapointing with this game is that you can't have enemies or rival communities, so no survivor vs. survivor ordeals.  Although this threw me for a loop, it's still quite enjoyable since you're not worrying too much about being shot at.  The Zombie A.I. is pretty nice.  They react to sound as they should, and they're not too tough and not too easy.  You mainly need to worry about the special zombies (I've been ripped in half by a feral twice on breakdown.)
Now for the price of the game...is a big downside.  I paid $9.81 USD for this game, and I'd say it's well worth it for that much.  $30.00 USD for this game seems alittle much if you're like me and have to limit what you can buy.  However, if you're able to catch this game during a sale or can just throw out $30 like nothing, then by all means, buy this game.  If worse comes to worse, give it an hour and a half and see how you like it.  If you hate it, refund it.
Overall, this game may seem a bit pricey, but for a good sale I'd say this game is well worth a try.

While the game was not as good as I have expected, I had loads of fun playing SGW 3. It offers good graphics, decent story, challenging stealth and amazing sniper gunplay.
Open world exploration does not offer much variety - you can collect loot, rescue hostages, unlock weapon modules and camos and clear the outposts.
Side-ops are great, as they shed more light on the events in Georgia and let you delve into the main story and local conflicts even more. And you get an amazing sniper rifle for completing them all.
Main story missions are wonderful, althought the plot itself is not that good. Most of all, I enjoyed the missions where you need to provide cover with your sniper rifle - that's where the game truly shines in all its glory. Unfortunately, there are very few of them.
Key locations are designed quite well, offering you an abundance of infiltration methods and elimination strategies. Drone is a big addition to the game as well, since it allows you to scout the area, figure out enemy positions and patterns, hack into surveillance, plan and strategize your moves.
All in all, I'd recommend the game for those who truly enjoy sniping gunplay and stealth.

I'm a  late-comer to this game.  It's not my STYLE of game.  It's not my TYPE of game.  It's not even my preferred means of gaming --- I like open world fantasy role playing, solo adventuring.  No MMoRPG's in my library.  Don't care for them.
That said, I was looking for something that a specific friend and I could but heads in, something simple enough to learn in a day or two, but complex enough that my friend wouldn't constantly be beating the crap out of me.  Armello went on sale, and I decided to give it a shot.   Now, I'm glad I did.
This game, it seems, has a long history.  From book-case style board game (I still have a few of those around the house) to a GoFundMe pitch to Early Access to final product.   Each step along the digital path has given it broader appeal and as a reward to it's fans, they've given us back treasures that actually make the game more fun to play..... but I am getting ahead of myself.
A Kingdom in the throws of anarchy.   The King --- poisoned.... growing weaker every passing day.   The clans each send forth one hero in the hopes of courting favor from the people...... or finding a cure.... or, depending on the malevolence of the "Hero", maybe even to take the throne by force.  Assassinate the king and claim his throne your prize.
Winning the game is not so simple as piling up treasures and honor.   Prestige can be gained along the path of your adventure here, but in a single move some other hero might swoop in and claim a Rot victory or a Spirit Stone victory.  There are many paths to the throne, and that is what makes the game really worth investing in.
A single turn consists of choosing game cards (Trickery, Spells or Equipment) wisely based on your desired strategy FOR JUST THAT TURN.  Do you hope to battle?  Grab some spells and equipment.   Do you want to wreak havoc among the other players?  Grab some trickery and spell cards.   The balance of game play is amazingly fun.
From choosing your cards, you move.  The game board consists of various TERRAIN types (Swamps, forrests, mountains, dungeons, Spirit Cirlces, etc.) some of which help you, some hurt you and others.... protect you.   Move carefully, and choose your end point wisely.
During your turn (and after, if you are smart about it) there are opportunities to play your cards and enhance your game. Each card changes the way you might want to win the game.   Extra ROT cards in your hand, maybe a ROT victory (EARLY ON) might be worth going for.  Each turn brings added changes which make the game far more interesting to play.
I've played this game for 12 days now.   I've won a few, I've lost a few.   I've learned what works --- but more importantly I've learned to think on my feet because persuing one course of action may not be the way you win in the end.   My friend and I have really grown to love gaming together.  It's been a blast.....
and I really, honestly recommend that everyone should try this.
That said by a FRPG / First Person Shooter style PC Gamer.
....  I think I may have branched into a new direction with this one.... and I'm really loving expanding my territory on this one.

I amost never write reviews, but this game is such a gem I feel compelled to spread the word.
So far, I've played 623 hours and am still not tired of the game. The multiplayer is the best aspect, since there is now a ranking system and prizes. After every game, players receive either a chest or key. Once you have both, you open the chest to receive a set of dice (ranked white, green, blue, purple and orange--like MMO loot). The dice can sell for a good chunk of change on the marketplace, and I was able to pay for the expansion with nothing but my profits from selling extra dice.
I feel this game isn't that well known, but there is a committed player base so finding a multiplayer match usually never takes more than a few minutes. It's a slower paced game that stresses strategy over twitch reflexes, which I enjoy. While there are random elements, a good player knows how to mitigate losses and be flexable enough to win. I would compare it to poker--randomness is an element, but good players find ways to win consistently.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys strategy or board games. Hope to see you in game!

Before i start my review , lett me point out this game plays way better with a gamepad or controller. It works fine with a keyboard but the game is more difficult and less enjoyable to me.
This game is a game full of suprises and yet so much cliché, where you go wtf and say "ahaha now i get the reference".
The game is kind of a parody of the old gta games, talking about gta 1-3, where you run around in an open world and do quests and sidequests (or ♥♥♥♥ around and do what you want). When you start the game however you instantly notice this is a throwback to the past with references for movies, news and games from the 90's and early 2000's. The basic gameplay is you running, stomping and killing enemies and getting from point a to b. Unlike the old gta games you can get a highscore for killing and stealing stuff which makes free roaming more enjoyable, but the main part of the game are the quests. So far being 5 hours into the campaign i found it extremely enjoyable to find the references in these missions. The missions often contain new power-ups, minigames, new characters and items to keep the game interesting for longer playthoughs. Retro city rampage also has a good sence of humor and made me laugh several times. The animations are quite good as well altough they are pretty simple sprites. Something i have to mention, i like to play the game for around 30 min.-1 hour everytime i play. I think that the game might start to bore you after playing it for more than 2 hours in one playthrough.
Overall i love the stylized graphics and great music a lott, altough if the references can't interest you or if you are to young to get them the game loses some of it's potential. If you like getting highscores, have a good laugh and do quests where you get struk by references at every corner this game is something for you! If you would would like a game with some good mechanics, lotts of minigames and some hours of gameplay you might also like retro city rampage. This game does not have multiplayer for people looking to play with friends!
Overall i would give the game a 83/100
Retro city rampage is surely worth the 9€ or regional equivalent. If you think this is to expensive or are doubting that you would like it, then i advise to wait for a sale

Star Wars Republic Commando is a squad based tactical fps from LucasArts released in 2005 for PC and Xbox (And it had a mobile version, apparently) that's really good. How good? Well here's the review:
Story: Star Wars Republic Commando takes place during the clone wars. You play as delta squad (Original name, right?) and they do various missions for the Republic. While the story is fairly nonexistant, the characters breath alot of life into the game. The dialogue is consistantly witty , and you can truly sense the comradery between the members of the squad. Also the story doesn't get in the way of the action much. At most, after you beat a level you might get a 30 second piece of dialogue with your advisor explaining what the mission is. In short, the characters are likable, and the story doesn't get in the way of the gameplay.
Graphics: It's 11 years old, and many of it's textures and animations look better then most Call of Duty games...Wow...In all seriousness, it looks great for it's time, and sounds amazing. One thing I would like to note is the visor effects. When you stab an enemy, blood (Or oil) gets on the visor, and a laser...thing wipes it off after a second, looks pretty badass. Not to mention the raindrops on your visor...immersive stuff.
Gameplay: It's alot like Rainbow 6 with a bit of Halo thrown in. The fps gameplay is well done, if not amazingly innovative. You got your various guns that you can carry all at once (Blaster Rifle, Pistol, Sniper Rifle, anti armor, and one weapon dropped by an enemy) you got your grenades that each vary in effectiveness on different enemy types, and you got your shields and health. Unlike Halo, however, your health in this is a lot larger than your shields, which are pretty weak in this game. So for those of you who don't like regenerating health, don't worry, because the shields are the only thing that regenerates, and they aren't very much help in the first place (Especially if you are playing on hard like myself, which I would recommend seeing as the game isn't very hard, also difficulty can be changed at anytime) Then the Rainbow 6 influence enters, and it truly elevates the game. You can command your squadmates to do a variety of things, from slicing doors to targeting certain enemies, which is useful seeing as many enemies in this game are way too much for you to handle alone. Also you can give them a formation to follow, which changes how they act. This leads to brilliant moments where you order a teammate to hack a terminal, command another to take up a sniper position, and order your final teamate to follow you as you go scrounging for ammo while waves of enemies slowly and methodically force your team back. Also, while the game is linear, battles are up to you. I only remember two times where you had objectives that you could fail, forcing you to reload a checkpoint. The game doesn't hold your hand, which is appreciated. Another plus is the enemy variety, it's great. Certain enemies will rush you with knives, pikes, or shotguns, while others act as slow moving walking tanks. (Super Battle Droids are vicious) You can shoot the backback on a trandoshan and force him to take an impromptu flying class, limbs can be blasted off droids, and a certain enemy can attach themselves to your head and drain health. Ai is great as well, your teammates obey orders, and unlike some games actually revive you when ordered! Enemies have patterns you can exploit to your benefit (Like Halo). Overall the gameplay is beautiful, you don't feel like a solo alien slaughtering machine, but a team perfectly in tune with each other, it's a wonderful feeling to actually need your allies to win battles and the spirit of jolly cooperation is strong with this game.
Length, replay, and multiplayer: The game is about 10 hours long to complete, and besides the sheer fun it provides, doesn't have much replay value. I didn't try the multiplayer, but from some guides I've read I think people still play it, even though servers were shut down. One plus is you unlock some cool, "Making of", videos when you beat chapters of the game. Also this game does not feature co-op campaign, which I was fine with seeing as the ai is so good, but some of you may be disappointed.
Do I recommend this game? Yes. It's an amazing ten hour fps for ten bucks, that's worth it to me. Also if you so desire you can get it on xbox, which has four player deathmatch. Having played both the xbox and pc version I would say they both look great, with the graphical edge going to the pc version. Whichever way you play it, I hope you enjoy it!
Thanks for reading my review! My friend and I also have a youtube channel called CultGamerAlliance. Check it out if you get a chance!

I've had this game for a while, and I've now decided to write my own review for it.
Over the past week a friend and I have been doing our own multiplayer game and let me tell you, this game takes on a whole new level of enjoyment and complexity. A solo game is a lot of fun, but having a friend to split the work has made things much more enjoyable.
This game is unique in my opinion. I have yet to find another game with the perfect blend of managing resources, and complex logistics. Nearly every aspect of this game is refined to a degree that doesn't cause annoyance, and almost all in-game problems come down to you either messing something up.
The only area this game falls down really is combat. If you've enemies turned to passive, then it's little more than just waiting until you've gotten tanks and then just mowing them down. However having enemies on default adds a whole new level of challenge which, in my opinion, isn't worth it if you're struggling with resource managements. All in all I reccomend this game, especially if you can get a friend or two to join you.

This is a prime example of Early Access as it should be done. The developers are very communicative and effective. As for the game, you have to try it out if you have any interest in "system design". It is very polished for an early access game. With the latest 0.15 stable release, I play single player without autosaving (I save manually) and the game did not crash or bug out after more than two hundreds hours of play time. Not a single time! Some Triple-A title don't even manage to do that!
The game puts you as a (futuristic?) engineer stranded on an habitable yet hostile planet. You have to mine resources, develop weapons (to protect you from the hostile fauna) and build automated machines to eventually be able to assemble a rocket and get out of this forsaken place.
The game is presented in a very stylized 2D top down view. Lots and I do mean a lot of events occur in realtime: Belts that moves stuffs around are filled with thousands of items, dozens and dozens of "bitters" nests are continually expanding around your defensive perimeter, trains moves from station to stations... All that without any hiccups or slowdown (providing you do have decent hardware). Very impressive the amount of optimization done on this game.
Ah, and there is also a multiplayer mode! Coop or PvP. You can customize rules and host games where other players can join you and partake in the fun.
A real bright star in a galaxy of otherwise rather mediocre early access games. The 98% review score tells everything about the quality of this "yet to be finished" title...
Utterly addictive time-sink.
