An incredible, charming, and unforgettable experience. Distinct from other games by its characters and their struggles, showing that not every one involved in war is just a generic soldier, and that everyone is a unique person with their own set of morals and history and their own way of life. A definate way its set apart from games like Wolfenstein and Call of Duty. Its a game about people, more loyal to eachother than their respective nations who struggle in a world covered in blood where the sound of clashing steel overtakes all.
For those of you who dislike Ubisoft (I do too) i didn't even realize it was an Ubisoft game (I didn't realize U play is ubisofts ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of steam) until I came to write this review. It is really not the type of crap (cough cough♥♥♥♥♥creed) Ubisoft normally puts out. Only downside is you have to go through Uplay to play the game.
While it may be a war game its not action packed in the sense of running through the battlefields and shooting everyone you see, if you want that buy Verdun (WW1 shooter game available on steam) or Battlefield 1 when it comes out. The gameplay aspects of Valiant Hearts is that it is a puzzle game, of course with the World War 1 theme, which if your a history fan (like me) you'll enjoy quite it a bit more than say Portal 2. Instead of escaping a facility like Portal your turning switches and pushing minecarts around to turn off Mustard Gas switches so the soldiers can advance.
In correlation to earlier where I said about the characters being people with their own morals, at one point you find an enemy soldier hanging by the ankle from a rope in an underground tunnel (he got caught in his own trap or was hanging something up and got himself instead). Instead of picking up his rifle on the floor next to Emile (one of the main four characters you play) and shooting the guy to leave his body hanging there, Emile cuts the rope and gets the German soldier back on his feet. While you may think its a poor decision the soldier then thanks Emile and you two go towards the German line, (something that would never happen in nearly all other games around) and once you get the the end of the tunnel you run into three armed German soldiers. They point their rifles at Emile (Him being French), and could either take him captive or shoot him dead on the spot, though the guy you just rescued convinces them to let you go. And they agree, showing you the way out.
It also has many historical aspects, it has an amount of trinkets and other memerabilia you can collect each stage of the game, each has a description of what it is and its use and relevence. You can find dog tags, letters, helmets, gas masks, rations, medals, personal items, and other stuff. It also gives out loads of facts and information about all this stuff and World War One in general, making Valiant Hearts very educative. The characters are also put into historical events you probably didn't even know happened, like at one point your fixing then driving a taxi to bring soldiers to the front line. Wait. What? This made little sense when i was doing it though the game explains that during the Initial push to Paris the French government hired out a bunch of taxis to drive out soldiers from the city to the frontline to stop the Germans from taking it. I sure as hell didn't know that. It also features the old trapezoid models of tanks seen during the war, along with biplanes and older models of artillery. One of the main antagonists of the game is a german baron, who infamously has a pretty large and impressive Prussian zeppelin. It occasionally will show you a map as well of where each character is towards each stage of the game, showing the trench lines and fronts in the Western Theater.
The game is also brilliantly atmosphere depending on how far you are in the game, there are four main stages that definately show this. Towards the start of the game you play as Emile, a french farmer turned soldier, and you go through basic training. During this you see all these soldiers in this bright, sunny, and colorful training area, flags and insignia are easy to spot and you get this proud, nationalistic sense of the area, that the French are confidant in victory. Shortly after that you are at a train station, soldiers about to be loaded onto the train, headed for war. The colors are bright, happy, and lively. Their uniforms are bright and clean, you can clearly see the blue shirts and red pants of the French Uniform. The soldiers are talking and their is even a little band there by the train, You get this overall feeling that the French are optimstic in the war, ready to see combat, and that they will kick the German army's♥♥♥♥♥all the way back to Berlin, That the war will be over in weeks with little loss or devastation.
Later in the game its winter, and everyone feels it, though doesn't pause the war from it. The people and in general the entire stage is greyer, more war battered and combat experienced. You can tell that the Morale is lower, soldiers complain about not having shoes or socks and the bad meals, when they get food at all. You can still see that both sides are still willing to fight for victory. It gets far worse as mustard gas gets used.
Towards the end of the game it is pure hell. The entire war is grey and blood stained. Both sides are so invested in victory after leaving millions dead the men rarely sleep as they are constantly fighting, and you can see the desperation in the officers and the rise of tension between the soldiers and command. Emile runs with a group of French soldiers, its obvious they have had their limit tested through war and suffering. They are grey, dirty, demoralized, injured, and covered in bandages. As you run with this group of frenchies you run into a French Officer, I felt♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by this guy. All around him were these wounded, tired, dirty soldiers and this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is standing there, fit as a fiddle, wearing a clean uniform and looking like he just had a hot meal and a nap. He yells at the men you ran with to run into an onslaught of German machine gun fire. They are hesistant for a momment, but after more order yelling they run into the open area, only to be cut down in a swarm of flying lead. The officer, so desperate to get results, so out of touch with the soldiers and proper strategy, so wasteful of human life, so impatiant, using backwards♥♥♥♥♥tactics in modern warfare, gets the french soldiers killed. Its makes you upset inside. What happens next is pretty important so I won't spoil it here.
There are a few minigames in it as well where at one point your amputating someones leg and if i recall giving cpr. There is also a part where you get a paper saying locations to destroy, and find yourself in front of a piece of artillery. Not gonna lie pretty fun shooting at things with it. Also has a fun though somewhat long minigame where you drive a taxi out of the way from bombs the previously mentioned Prussian Baron is dropping on you from his zeppelin, and you dodge various debris and garbadge in the road. The puzzles also are pretty interesting and complex yet simple enough that you don't need to look up a guide online.
In conclusion Valiant Hearts: The Great War is an unforgettable and educative experience not matched by many if any games as narrative games go, a game about people and their struggles and history, national and personal. A game I highly recommend that shows the true horrors and struggles of Modern Warfare.

The game play is pretty fluent and so are the animations.
Some might call this a typical hack n' slash, and maybe I would agree...
And that's not a bad thing at all. The whole game feel like a big love letter to the genre.
You start out in your hub area, in which you create a new character and customize him/her
(yes..there is a female avatar too).
You can also use the ACK (the in game level editor) which will let you make small to medium
stories - Standalone adventures or whole campaigns, consisting of more adventures.
This opens up a large community of player created content.
Two adventures in, the game opens up for the loot shrine, and man is that good!!
Besides the chest functionality we all know and love, the shrine offers something more...
You go on the adventures and pick up loot, then sell all your junk loot to the shrine, which
will fill up a bar. This will earn you four different tiers - Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum.
Pick a tier and fill the shrine till you're there. Then chose one of three items or perks.
The better the tier, the better the reward.
Three adventures in, the game opens up the dragon mentioned in the title.
This dragon has a ton of HP and it is going to take you a lot of tries to kill.
Luckily, the dragon's HP is persistent, so you are going to shave it down little after little.

I don't do reviews, but I feel a bit compelled to do one here because this game really could use more press. This is probably one of the best independent developments I've played, with (as far as I know) an almost entirely novel premise, given that  nearly all the content of the game will be community generated.
It's already very fun in its current state. The mechanics are simple, very easy to pick up if you've played any recent isometric action RPGs. The controls are reasonably intuitive, and suit controller based play particularly well (although keyboard and mouse is perfectly viable). Combat is reasonably challenging and satisfying, with slightly more dependence on reflexes than other similar games. There are only a few fundamental puzzle mechanics at the moment- switch operation, pressure pads, key hunts and (interestingly) an autojump mechanic that is based on terrain height. That last mechanic, while seemingly restrictive, actually leads to some interesting puzzle design, and I've already seen it used quite well in some of the player made content.
There's the odd bug or ten still, balance is a bit whacky, and some of the content that does need to be developer created (such as classes and items) is a little sparse at the moment, but this is both a great indie development and a very good quality early access in my opinion.

Finished.  Took my time and stealthed as much as possible, explored (but not enough) and can render my verdict.
PROS: -Beautiful terrain.  Having spent some time in Georgia, CI did at least attempt to convey that feel, at least.  The big town with the wedding church?  Yeah, that exists, almost a perfect match.
-The path you take to accomplish your objective was not laid out for you.  You had to plan your route well.  Not just once did I have to backtrack to accomplish my task because I failed to properly scout the enemy situation or the impassibility of terrain. That's a nice challenge.
-Sound was well-done. With so much taking place at night, sound was important, and saved me a few times.
-Textures of buildings, guns and places was very good.
-Lighting and shadows.  Cryengine is good for these, and CI made good use of it.
-The story.  Some people say there was only the most basic story.  This was true to an extent.  However, what it does do well is hold the whole package together, and keep you enfranchised in what is happening to the people and yourself.  For me, it inspired the desire to keep going and fight more of the good fight.  Had they only cobbled a bunch of missions together, I might not have enjoyed it as much.
-Frequent checkpoints (for reasons which I will detail under cons).
-Finally, the sniping mechanics.  CI has done this to perfection in all Ghost Warrior games now, as well as in a game I wager many have not played,, but should: Enemy Front.  They OWN sniping in the gaming world!
CONS: -Character rendering was awful.  Lydia and virtually every other NPC had a washed out, emotionsless, pastel look to their faces.  Much more detail could have been done...it's Cryengine 4.  Go back and look what Crytek did in Crysis 3 with Cryengine 3!.  Their clothing was only slightly better detailed than the faces.
-Several places my character got stuck in terrain or fell inside the geometry.  Luckily my last checkpoints were recent.
-At great distances, zooming in with the scope sometimes resulted in enemy soldiers disappearing.  Thankfully it was a part-time bug or I would not have gotten my 563m record shot!
-One of the patches took away my ability to repair rifle silencers.  CI being who they have always been though, were super-responsive, and issued a rollback patch within 2 days.
-The savegame bug.  I only mention this because so many had it.  Because of this, I ended every sesssion making a backup copy of the save file and config file.  It turns out, I did not need it.  I never once encountered this bug, thankfully!  But thanks to my fellow gamers making this known, I would have been prepared.
Overall, this game was a blast!  It is fairly unforgiving, and is definately in the more "realism" mode than Sniper Elite 4 (which I also enjoy very much).  Completing my missions did not always feel pre-ordained, and that is a good thing.  The pros outweighed the cons and I think this is a must play!

I understand that this may come off as a very negative review, but I just took what came to my mind and wrote it down. These are the raw feelings I have about the game and I believe I articulated the way the game is in the way I wanted to. State of Decay isn't a bad game, but it's flawed in many significant ways.
I have conflicting feelings about State of Decay. I personally found the combat fairly enjoyable, though it's rather two dimensional. It doesn't take long before you start to see that you've already done most of the quests just a few hours in. Get from Point A to Point B, take what you found at Point B to Point A. Go to Point B and clear zombies and return to Point A. You constantly need to go out of your way to help your survivors because they leave and get attacked by zombies, go missing, or need help killing tougher types of zombies. You also can't cancel a mission once you've started it unless you die or exit and open your game again. Base building falls short, there's a certain amount of squares and you decide what structures are built within the squares. So far, I've found that there's not enough space for all the structures you'd want in any base you may find. Dialogue was a colossal disappointment, most characters seem to only have 2-4 lines of dialogue that are often repeated, making immersion and connection with the survivors rather difficult. You could save a group of survivors from a horde or zombies, and when you attempt to interact with them afterwards all they may say is "Hi", "How's it going?", etc. AI is decent, though survivors often block doorways and you'll have to awkwardly move into them to slowly push them back. Quite a few weapons though they all seem to be similar speed and damage, just different models. This game is a good time waster, but longer sessions may start to burn you out. I've been playing daily since I got it a few days ago and there seems to be just enough to keep me coming back. One of the things that keeps me coming back is the character leveling system, though levels don't really make much of a difference once you get a few levels into your stats, which doesn't take long at all. The feeling of progress is somewhat rewarding, and the way the world quickly becomes familiar makes it oddly seem like home. It crashes sometimes but the game saves often enough to where it doesn't matter much. I quite enjoy State of Decay, despite all the cons I've listed. It's rather simple, allowing for a casual bit of fun every once in a while. Do yourself a favor and play the game in smaller sessions. If you play longer sessions then the flaws of the game become more and more apparent. In shorter sessions I find that I'm able to circumvent the flaws of the game and can enjoy myself with some simple, chaotic zombie killing.
TL;DR: A very flawed game, but simple and can be fun in short sessions. If you play longer sessions then you will get burned out quickly.

Satellite Reign thrusts you into a dystopian world as a competitor to the Dracogenics Corporation, which effectively runs the world. Conversely, you run nothing, quite literally. Your duties are restricted to controlling a squad of 4 agents in a single city, albeit a large one. The city remains firmly in the grip of your opponents no matter what you accomplish, although you'll occasionally receive a congratulatory message when you complete objectives.
The entire game existing in a single large level is an interesting concept for the setting; the city is broken up into the "neutral" streets where you can do as you please as long as it doesn't break the law, and the "hostile" compounds where enemies will actively try to detain or kill you if you're detected. The first stumbling block for me was that the neutral areas are mainly there for aesthetics, very little gameplay actually occurs there for how much of the map they make up.
The bulk of your playtime is in the hostile compounds, several of which can become rather sprawling. Again, the size of the areas feels more to emphasize the scope of the city than to facilitate gameplay. This becomes exceedingly frustrating when your forays into the compounds fail, and you're forced to leave, causing all the guards and cameras to reset. Then you find youself re-treading old ground to get back to where you were in the compound. Usually a small side-quest is available to unlock an alternate solution to the compound, but I still found myself foiled more by AI patrolling erratically at a critical moment, rather than being confused at how to approach a solution.
The 4 agents under your control are forced into seperate Archetypes, with their own skills that help differentiate them (in some cases, the other archetypes can purchase equipment that accomplishes the same thing, such as a cloaking device). In a world full of clones and cybernetic implants however, I was annoyed with how I was unable to modify or reset the skill choices on these characters, as some skills were very underwhelming initially. The speed at which you acquire new skill points is also punishing if you try to salvage the skill choices on one of your agents.
These 4 characters you control for your entire playthrough are severely lacking for aesthetic customization, especially for the genre. There is a single male and female version of each archetype, and no matter what array of armor and cybernetic implants you equip them with, they will look the same as they did when you first launched the game. Their heads can be slightly customized, but this is hidden behind a convoluted system unrelated to appearance.
A good way to give your agents an edge is to improve the quality of their clones; this is a rather involved process that consists of kidnapping people that are superior to your agents (which I feel further trivializes your role as the commander of this super-soldiers) and using them as clone stock. On its face this is an interesting system where you can amass a library of clone stock to tailor your agents, but there is a fatal flaw with the system; whenever your agents are killed, the clone degrades, eventually to the point where the stat bonuses are completely gone and you'll need to kidnap a new person. So a player prone to failure when exploring compounds will find themselves have to kidnap new clones again and again and again.
By the time alternate weapons and equipment upgrades were given to me that would allow me to better tailor the agents to my playstyle, I lost interest in the game entirely. The scope of the massive city is an illusion; the compounds are isolated and seperate entities that will recover from your assaults every time. Even a massive gunfight in the public streets will eventually become a faded memory and you can continue as if nothing happened.
As of writing this review, this game costs 29.99 USD and I cannot reccomend it all for that price.

Despite mostly positive reviews, I have to admit I wasn't too sure about buying the game at first. Most people that reviewed the game negatively, seemed to dislike the apparent long waiting times in matches (and as such long matches) and the general randomness. It put me off a little. I did put the game on my wishlist and I noticed I kept checking it out every day. So what the heck, I took the plunge.
After getting a few games under my belt I can safely say: I do not regret buying it.
The game looks great and plays exactly like a tabletop game should play. Not entirely sure how to explain it, but it has that feel to it. The amount of time you spend waiting for other players is very manageable; I never felt like I wanted to do something else while waiting. Matches take about an hour or so, give or take, which to me is perfect. And the randomness, well.. it's a dice-game.. It seems silly to complain about it (you don't complain about a RL game of Risk, or similar, I'd imagine) and there are plenty of ways to build your character as well as influence the game and other players by your actions. There's luck, and there's bad luck, but I always felt "in control".
The lack of a regular chat system seemed odd at first, and at times I do miss it still, but the preset phrases you can hurl at eachother seem to cover most bases, and I can see the point in that it keeps things friendly. No salt or toxic nerdrage to feast your eyes upon. Being thick-skinned, a mute button would have been enough for me, but we have what we have, and it's fine.
There's the odd quitter here and there, and it's difficult to determine if they quit intentionally or by accident. I've had one game lock up on me after 3 people subsequently dropped. Not sure what happened there, but it seems to be something that's around for a while already. I really hope it's not a too common occurrence; I don't mind losing a game, but getting a big "nope! - you just wasted nearly an hour of your time" simply sucks.
All in all, solid 8,5/10 for the game, well done! If you're on the fence for the same reasons as me, don't hesitate to give the game a try.

This game is pretty well built for a board game and has a ton of interesting features for gameplay! I love the animations and everything seems pretty streamline. I think there are still a few kinks to work out of course, but overall this is a pretty polisdhed product.
Sometimes the game will hiccup, and I noticed multiple sound files would glitch and the right channel would go dead. Other than that, everything ran smooth. This may be due to hardware, but I have a relatively good setup and it should have no issues.
The only cons I can say about this game is that it isn't really friendly to new players. The AI can get sort of ruthless, and you can definitely tell the computer has a plan, and will stick to it till you fail. There was a time where I took over a city, and the bear character attacked me three times in a row. It's possible, except for the fact that I destroyed him the first two times, (thanks to the lucky dice rolls, which is another problem I would like to get into) and on the last, the computer had enough and just killed me.
As mentioned, this game is mostly chance. The only skill that is required of you is map movement, everything else is chance. Whether it be random♥♥♥♥♥spawning of enemies, or the cursed dice doing their thing. I sort of whish it was something more skill based than chance base. Sure, you can enforce strategies into the game, but they are so built on the chance factor (which often seems to be a 75% lodr 25% win ratio most times) that the strategies often fall apart.
TL;DR
Great game, with some minor polishing that needs to be done, and gameplay relies too much on chance.

Republic Commandos is a game I would like to see a modern version of. It's fun FPS gameplay with cool squad mechanics. You lead a squad of elite clone troopers, and your command of them can lead to either victory or defeat. You can order them to act aggressively to wipe out the enemy, or to close in and cover you if you need to heal. You are armed with a multi-purpose blaster that can take the form of an assault rifle (probably the most common mode), sniper rifle, anti-armor, and more. The game makes you feel like an awesome commando as you take out waves of powerful enemies. As for faults, I wish they actually made the squad specializations matter. While you can order members to sniping, or anti-armor stations, any available member will take it up as opposed to your sniper, or whoever. I'd also like to see more precise squad controls. Also more RPG-style perks or upgrades. But these are minor, and more of a wish-list for a sequel. This is a fun game and if you like Star Wars, and FPS then it is for you.

A potentially interesting hack and slash where you can use the included editor to create new content.
Positives
* I like the editablility.
* Graphically the style is nice, although seems to be inconsistent on whether it is supposed to be cartoony or realistic.
* Has single player and can supposedly be played offline (i haven't confirmed).
* Good that levels are short so you don't get stuck being unable to save. Although, would be nice if you could save outside of levels (doesn't seem possible).
* Got better once my character upgraded. Initially it was very tough going. I assume this is tuning that needs to be done as part of the early access.
Negatives
* Game seems very slow. My computer can run Just Cause 2 and Skyrim at high resolution very smoothly and this game is really laggy at the average settings to the point of giving me a headache.
* The controls are not very tight at all. There are long delays while attacking, no indication if you are "selecting" the monster as you try to attack which leads to a lot of misses (or being low level I am suppose to miss a lot, hard to tell), and the jump mechanic could use some work.
* The content is very sparse. They seem to be entirely counting on users creating most of it.
* The UI is bewildering and the style doesn't match the theme of the game at all. Little things like Esc not exiting out of inventory or back up a level (you have hit tab again like TV menus), somethings can only be done in certain situations or at special locations like checking your inventory. Took me a while to figure out that the box with a number and a flashing plus was stat increases but that you have to click on the individual stas to upgrade them.
* Thief doesn't start with a crossbow/bow? Seems wierd if they are going for the guantlet feel. Also, the loot drops seem to be giving me weapons for a fighter (swords, axes). I was only able to get a crossbow from the loot shrine.
* Difficulty ratings are ocassionally wrong, even in the official maps. The Ice pass is definitely not "medium" having beaten several official "extreme" levels.
* Bugs, i think? Somewhat expected with an early access game, but simple things like having a strength of 1+1 (+1 due to item boost) doesn't let you equip a weapon that requires a strength of 2.
Overall not great based on the cost compared to other games at the same price point. That is somewhat expected with an early access game, but the developers keep talking about how playable it is, so ... I can't really recommend the game at this time. Perhaps as it matures it will get better.

Before I can begin I have to say that I can only hesitantly give this a recomendation and only a very situationally.
Emily is away is an interesting and even fascinating concept. In a lot of areas, this game really /is/ amazing. It's a unique outlook with 'branching paths' with a compelling female lead. A number of things are suggested by what the protag and his friend say/don't say and the writing is nearly /perfect/, simulating a real communication between two close friends that are taking very different paths in life.
However, that is also where the game struggles too. Yes, it tells the story on how friend A and B interact with each other, but that's /all/ it does. Regardless of what 'decisions' the player makes, regardless on what 'choices' are made, the ending remains the same and that's a disaster waiting to happen in a game because it essentially takes away the freedom of the player and that's the last thing a game should do.
Sure, other games have locked stories too, and they're excellent, but unlike many games that do that, this game doesn't have some other mechanic saving it.
Xenosaga or Final Fantasy X for example have locked stories and no matter your choices, it delivers you to the same end. However, unlike them, this game doesn't have a gameplay system of choices a player can make to reach their destination.
In short, it has a lot of great things going for it, but it also can leave you feeling hollow and empty. Some of that is from parts of the game's plot (fair enough) but the other is the fact that it honestly would have been better as a book without choices. At least there it strips away the paper thin illusion of choice, leaving a compelling and interesting tale of two friends as they move away from High School and go to College. Even the vast majority of visual novels make it that the choices you make in the novel have an effect in the story, particularly the ending. (Even if it's only two or three endings or a slight variation of the ending.)
So it really ends up up to the player. Do you want to read a compelling story about two friends or do you want to play a game?  If you'd like to read a compelling story, this is it.
If you want to play a game/visual novel? I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

The first impression of the game was really good. I played for a bit and called it a day.
A few days later I started the game up again, just to get a message that several neighbours died. After some googling I found out about that realtime stuff in this game. Basically every time you load the save, it processes what happened while you were 'sleeping' (with diminishing ingame duration, so being away for 1 or 2 real life days make a lot of difference, while being away for 10 real life days gives not much more passed ingame duration)
Which in turn means if I play 1 hour a day for 10 days I get penalized compared to binge playing for 10 hours every 10 days - with the same play time.
Of course, nobody thinks about 'waking' the player character while the hell broke loose. I agree the character needs some beauty sleep, but that's too much.
I like play time to count for something in a game, but not in which portions I do that play time.
Progression through the story does not look feasible as the companions consume food while I'm away and in short play sessions of 30 or 60 minutes a day I have only time for gathering food (which will be consumed tomorrow when I log back in).
Sooner or later I guess everybody will be dead anyway, be it either shortage of food or killed by zombies (which attacked while my companions left me sleeping).
There are a lot of people that seem to like that mechanic (judging from the reviews), but I can't recommend it due to this mechanic.

If you were a fan of the old Syndicate series, and you've been looking for a modern take on the old classics then I think you'd be well served by Satellite Reign.

Fun real-time combat with a goodly number of abilities means that no two fights really play out the same. I really felt that the game opened up about midway through as I had earned enough skill points on each of my four squad members to really approach a broad number of scenarios in interesting and diverse ways. My infiltrator wasn't just an invisible scout, but had grown into a sniper capable of covering my entire squad from an over watch position, or served as deep penetration assassin when needed. With the ability to decide on individual weapons, augmentations, gear, and skills I was able to push my squad progression into the tactical directions I favoured best. The early game suffers a bit in comparison to mid and late game due to a relative dearth of options for your squad skills. Even so, there are still enough options to keep you engaged and interested in figuring out how you'll tackle the next task, and how quickly you'll form a new plan when it doesn't go quite right.

I wish I had pulled this off my 'shelf' and played it earlier, it was a blast from beginning to end. Visuals are nice and cyberpunky, music is adequate and never felt intrusive or distracting. Weapon sound effects became a little annoying as I neared the end of the game as they're more common to hear than the music, and can be constant. The game itself feels very much like a Unity game, that slight unpolished feel that seems to permeate the Unity Engine itself is ever present, but did not keep me from diving in.
Though load times are long -even on an SSD- once you're runnin' around the world there are no more load screens, even between zones. Occasional path finding issues with the AI can be annoying, and rarely AI will fail to take a proper cover position and need some babysitting to get them into position. Annoying, but not frustrating is how I'd describe the bugs. AI becoming stuck in the geometry of the level is quite annoying, and can become frustrating as there can be no way to unstick them at times, and with saving disabled when you're trespassing or in combat, a stuck agent might mean the loss of minutes or hours of play. That being said the buried command to kill an agent (ctrl+shift+K with agent selected) saved me hours of play and only cost me a clone. The base ATM hacking, router placement, and general scouting of each new city quadrant are rather boring mission sets that I did not enjoy repeating upon reaching a new part of the city. I powered through those to reach the real meat and potatoe missions. Those are about my only gripes, playing from start to finish.

If you see this title on sale, and you enjoyed Syndicate or Syndicate Wars, grab it.

Factorio is one of the best automation games I know of. Within minutes of starting, you have several tasks running automatically, which you used to do by hand. In time, you find yourself building conveyor belts bringing incredible amounts of raw materials to rows upon rows of furnaces, robotic arms moving the finished product into an enormous machine that builds them into the many products you need.
There's a catch, though. The locals don't much like the pollution your factory is producing and may attack from time to time. With a few turrets, tanks, and a nuke here and there you won't have much trouble with them though.
That being said, it's important to note that Factorio focusses the building of your factory. Those expecting to fend off wave after wave may not be getting all they want here, though combat is a part of the game it is not at its core. Those looking to build massive fully-autonomous factories, though,
be getting all they want, and more.
Whenever I talk about good examples of progression in games, I always refer to Factorio. It does progression in a unique way; I'm not sure how, but the game pushes you to progress by making you feel like you
the next thing in order to build. Often I play games where you research or unlock new things just because you want something to do, which can end up feeling boring as there's not actually a task you feel truly needs doing. This is rarely an issue in Factorio. You'll sooner catch yourself having been so immersed in chasing the next objective you've forgotten about lunch. And dinner.
If you've ever seen the episode of
in which Hal tries to change a lightbulb, you'll see that Factorio isn't much unlike the process he undergoes. You want to do something simple, but to do that you need a thing. And for that thing, you need those two other things, but before you can do those, you need to build another thing somewhere else, and so on. In this way you're constantly moving forward, expanding and improving your factory.
As for performance, the optimization of the game code is extraordinary. You usually have hundreds of individual items moving about your screen, dozens of drones buzzing back and forth, and if you progress far enough you'll have a train network connecting to other factories far away which each also spitting out hundreds of items each minute. Even with all this, you won't experience the slightest of performance issues. And all of this is synchronized flawlessly over the internet when playing multiplayer. If AAA games optimized their code as well as this game has, I'm sure even the worst among PCs could run almost anything.
Because of the above points, Factorio is a game I always keep coming back to, having played a few hours in Steam, but many many more outside of it. It's especially fun designing a large factory with friends, and as such that's how I usually play the game myself. If you like games like Spacechem, Opus Magnum or Infinifactory, I have no doubt you'll have loads of fun with Factorio as well.

This title was not worth the pre-order. Overall, there's several bugs with the game in various aspects (animations, getting stuck, falling through the world, hitbox detection, invisible enemies) and there are quality of life issues (
)
I do rate the game, overall, recommended however because it has an odd addiction to it that keeps you starting up the game, exploring various points of interests, finding the collectibles, and chasing down achievements. Just know that, until CI Games fixes
, it's an overall mediocre game and there are better titles out there.
It was too predictable and it came across as if a teenager wrote their first short story for English class. I won't give spoilers but the small handful of people responsible for the story of the game could've done a lot better. There were parts (the flashbacks) that could've been developed better instead of just stopping with no conclusion. The actual conclusion of the story was rushed with no real satisfaction of completing the campaign.
I did enjoy, however, some of the dialogue between the characters (again, no spoilers). Some of the antics between the main characters were quite funny, relatable, and gave a genuine laugh.
The sniping aspect of the game - purely finding a spot, scanning targets, adjusting for wind and distance - this part was on point and quite enjoyable. Just about everything else was almost on the horrible side of things.
The vehicle capping out at 80km/h and able to make hairpin turns at full speed and also able to maintain said speed going up hill. Horrible handbrake (even on the vehicle DLC; the buggy. Horrible).
The obvious blocks revealed through scouting while climbing. It looks like I'm climbing legos. While on this point - ladders. Why can't we just continue to hold the down key and step off the ladder? No. We have to "jump" off the last step by pressing the "c" key.
Physics are thrown out the window - falling various (and lethal) distance can be negated simply by sliding against an object be it a wall, mountain, pole, cliff, etc. Need to get down the mountain that's 250 ft high? Slide down the mountain and you won't take a lick of damage. The alternate to this is use the "death from above" game mechanic. If an enemy is 250 below you, don't worry. Just jump and hit him. The game will take over and give you a stealth kill completely ignoring the fact you just jumped 250 ft.
The loading times. Whether you're starting the game up or you're changing zones, the loading times are absolutely unnecessary in today's technology of open world exploration and gaming. This was major as it not only took too long to load during these times but the requirement of loading was just annoying.
There's a huge list of game play issues. At the moment, these are the ones that I found most often repeated and annoying. This barely scratches the surface of all the game play issues I came across, however.
One of the best things about the game (Despite being made with Cryengine. Really CI? Cryengine? Are we in 2007?) is the environment. Graphically speaking it's really nice roaming the mountains of Georgia. The animations among the characters is also respectable.
The one issue I had was, during some of the cinematic cut scenes, there were obvious screen tears. It would explain (potentially) why the game has V-SYNC enabled by default. Again, this is a dated thing and shouldn't have even been an issue to begin with.
If that's even a word, lol. In short, no. Once you beat the the game you can continue to explore the points of interests you may have skipped over but aside from that - there's nothing. There is no repeating a mission with new gear / equipment and there is no "New Game +" feature, either. In all the titles I've played, I can't recall a title that you are not able to replay a mission that's already completed. SGW3 is a tactical, sniping-focused, open-ended, first person shooter that, like its predecessors, put you in control of a sniper that must use stealth, tactics and gadgets to attack enemies from a distance and reach objectives while avoiding detection.
Here's my two cents about it.
It plays with the basic and expected mechanics of a typical tactical shooter, letting the player move around, run, crouch, go prone, hip fire or use iron sights and scopes for precise sniping. The game features a larger array of equipment and weapons when compared to the first two games of this franchise, giving the player a bigger window of customization. Many sniper rifle models are available, as well as assault rifles, shotguns, pistols, knives and bows that help complement your firepower.
There is also a crafting element, that lets the player fabricate ammo, gadgets, silencer repair kits, medkits and other useful items that may be used in the field, using crafting materials looted from enemies and containers throughout the world.
Weapons can be fitted with a variety of attachments, such as scopes, sights, grips, silencers and bipods. Silencers and bipods work in interesting ways in this game: silencers wear out as you use them, and must be repaired with either money or craftable silencer repair kits in order to keep your stealth in check. Bipods add stabilization to your aim as long as you're standing in an appropriate place, making the prone stance really useful.
To help the player recon areas, two functionalities are available: a drone, and the scout mode. With the drone, the player is capable of scanning entire areas, spotting enemies, traps and cameras, without having to infiltrate an outpost. The scout mode works by highlighting any important things in the surroundings, as well as revealing clues to investigations, that usually lead to money pickups or collectibles.
The game comes with a set of skills divided into three playstyles: Sniper, which concerns taking out enemies from a distance, Ghost, related to stealth and infiltration, and Warrior, the basic run 'n' gun playstyle. Each playstyle can be developed separately the more you use them, similar to how Skyrim skill system works. The set of skills is not exactly deep, but it helps enough without making the player overpowered.
Combat-wise, it flows good. Nothing really innovative, but not bad either. Enemies are specialized depending on the weapon they carry, so expect to fight not only machine gun grunts, but also other snipers. While infiltrating outposts, the player is able to subdue enemies with melee attacks and even interrogate them for useful information regarding the surroundings. Dead enemies can be looted for money or parts, as well as moved to prevent other enemies from finding their corpses.
Unlike previous games in the series, SGW3 plays open ended, with a more flexible mission system that lets the player choose when and where to go, as well as what and how to do any action towards an objective. The world is not the largest, but is big enough to make exploration relevant. The world can be traversed on foot, or with vehicles.
Decent. Sometimes not as smart as it should be, but decent enough. Enemies will be found at different states depending on the actions of the player, such as suspicious when a corpse is found, or if a shot is missed in the vicinity, taking cover whenever possible, or alerted, on which the enemy is aware of the player's presence and is now hunting them down. When in alerted state, enemies will take offensive positions and use nearby resources to take the player down, such as mortars.
Alerting one enemy not always determines a whole outpost becomes alerted, and this is a huge improvement to the AI system seem in the previous games.
Haven't seem an absurd amount of bugs in my play time, and the Cry Engine isn't exactly known for their bugs, so I think the game is pretty stable in this aspect. The only bug I experienced and that enforced a restart in order to fix was this:
Generic and predictable, do not expected anything stunning or original.
Landscapes, weapons models, NPCs and details in general are pretty and visually rich, justifying the use of the top tier engine.
Because the game uses the Cry Engine, performance is usually decent, but the game might underperform in some circumstances due to some shady modifications to the engine as it is a pattern CI has been practicing ever since the first installment of the Sniper Ghost Warrior series.
However, it performs good enough to be playable.
Being a fan of the series since the first game came out, I DO recommend it, specially because of the improvements to AI and gameplay, and the package deal contaning both the game and the season pass. Still, might be worth to wait until it goes on sale.
In any case, it is fun, and is worth a try if you come from other games of the series, and/or like sniping and stealth.

Soldats Inconnus--it means 'unkown soldiers'.  I think it a more fitting title for
No, it's not really, is it?
Sure, there are game-like elements to it, puzzles and such, but it is more than that.  It's a testament and homage to all those who served in that Great War.  Some might see it as anti-war in its message, but it is not really.  The reality of war must be taken as it is.  The muted animation quality and atmospheric music begs a tone of pensive study.  The faceless soldiers give the impression that it could be anyone under there, the truly "unknown soldier" of the title.  Lastly, as an American, I find it intriguing that the game ends on an 'open note', only just as the doughboys reach France.  Given the ending, I find it both hopeful and forlorn, as they are too late for so very many people.
As a postscript, I give a hearty thanks to the historians working with the team, as their contributions both within and without make this so much more than a mere puzzle game set in WWI.
Valiant Hearts: The Great War, or Unkown Soldiers:  Memories of the Great War--whatever the title, take this journey, and feel the emotions.  May it let you think.

I love this board game.  Great visuals and lighting effects.  I really enjoy the artwork and unique storyline.  I enjoy the varieties of cards you can collect, along with the attention to detail that was put into each of the animations.  The gaming style has many different strategies, tactics, and angles to think about while you play. While waiting for multiplayer match, the game allows you to play single player game, then alerts you with a popup to join when your match is ready.  You do get to unlock unique items to play in future games (dice with unique bonus symbols for fighting, rings with perks, and badges that give you bonuses to certain character traits starting off) These are unlocked by collecting chests and keys in multiplayer matches.  You do not have to purchase keys to unlock chests like in other games with this feature.  You get to win, collect, and unlock these items for free which is nice.  I did however purchase the DLC expansions because I enjoy the amount of artwork that was put into this game and want to support the developer and see where they go with future titles.
I look forward to seeing more cards and animations added to the game.  The cards themselves  are very entertaining.
The game is very replayable and doesn't get boring quickly. (although, I wish the external movement animations and watching other players battle was a little more interesting)
If you like board games, with a bit of depth, and deck building (per game) I definately recommend this title.

I try to keep my fascination with video games under wraps..it's such a loaded topic it makes religion and politics look positively benign. Some things are just too hot to discuss on social media.
And as much as I love dungeon crawlers and space games, I have to admit they usually don't hold my interest. World of Warcraft was an exception, but after leveling five characters to 80 my heart just wasn't in it any more.
I like to MAKE things, not just play with things other people made..no matter how cool they are. No dungeon crawling fulfills me like painting does, no space battles are as challenging as writing a good song.
With Fight the Dragon that may have changed..
This is a game that you make yourself.
Sure, there are hundreds of levels already made, but you have access to the exact same editor the developers use. Build your dungeon brick by brick. Devise devious traps, puzzles, and mazes. Populate your level with enemies ranging from fire beetles to skeleton archers, each with their own behavior and AI.
Make pools of lava, poison, or mud. Rivers of water and bridges with trapdoors. Gates that open if you find the right key. Pressure plates that trigger walls of fire. NPCs that guide the player along their way.
Then when you finish making your level, you can publish it. Your level will be played and voted on by other Fight the Dragon players around the world.
It's much more fun to make a game than to play a game, and if your kids are into games but you worry that it's not an intellectually stimulating pursuit, you might do well to buy them a copy of Fight the Dragon.
And if you're like me and tend to like the idea of games more than games themselves, buy it for yourself. Spend a few hours in video-game legoland and I'll bet you'll be as excited as I am.
We finally have the keys to the castle!

Its like one of the minigames you can play on garry's mod, but much more fun, with its own community, addons, and it's completely free. You could even say that this could be more fun than Gmod. This is basically what I think is the most entertaining experience you can have for free, and for the time I have played, I have not seen any negative things about this game. There is barely any lag, the graphics are fine, the official levels are very well done, and I think it's the best type of pick up and play. No matter what you like, this game will have something for you.
Some tips if you pick the game up:
-Every class is easy to learn, so if your team needs you to be something else, do it.
-Freindly fire on your other team members  is the least of your worries when there is a giant swarm heading towards your group.
-That does not mean you should be infront of everyone and attempting to be Rambo. Not only will you take alot of team damage but the alien swarm will wreck you immediatly.
-If your gonna be a medic, it may seem against your purpose to leave someone behind, but if that person will drag you with them, heal yourself and run closer to the main group, they may need you more later.
-Killing the aliens is not the purpose of each mission, if you stay behind to kill them, they will swarm you very soon after, and you will be left behind.
-Shotguns and flamethrowers are basically the best weapons when dealing with a swarm.
-Infested team members can be quickly helped by a medic, but try to not use up all your healing on them, just help them enough to be able to survive, and regroup, and once they are, invest what you need to patch them up.
-Being an officer does not make you in charge online, it gives you the gadgets only the officers can use.
-When you are starting out follow the guy who seems to know what he is doing the most, then learn to become him.
-Don't think that running away will ever help. You need to take care of what is chasing you in order to escape, or else it will outrun you and begin to attack, making you move slowly enough to die.
-The mission will always have a point in which the tables turn, and the less abled members of the team will all die. The best thing you can do is regroup with the rest of the team, while the game tests your skills. No casualties in a mission is very rare from what I have seen so far.
-Only type when there is no aliens nearby, never in the middle of a battle.
-Sometimes asking your team members what you should bring can change the result of the mission and reduce casualties. Do it often because theres a big chance a team member knows the mission well enough to give advice on gear.
-Getting the most kills is not important, its actually passing the mission, because it will give you most EXP.
-Download addons cuz they are fun.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is a good game. It's not a GREAT game...but it is a good one. Having played all of the Sniper Ghost Warrior games I can say that the franchise is headed in the right direction here. This is the first time in the series that I FELT like a sniper. The previous games basically put you on rails and once you played it through there was no reason to play it again. The story lines where difficult to follow and were basically an after thought.
SGW3 improves upon almost every aspect of previous SGW titles.
Here is the thing though. To truly enjoy the game and open it's full potential you have to think and act like a Sniper. Using all your tools to solve a tactical problem is the key to this game's treasures. Going from the long distance shooter, to the up close and personal stealth killer, to the all out wielder of destruction and back again to sow confusion in the enemy is overwhelmingly satisfying.
If you try to play it as an FPS...you will be disappointed. If you try to play it like a typical open world shooter i.e. GTA you will be equally dissappointed. Also if you play on normal game mode you may find the game rather unexciting. I would recommend at least hard mode with a heavy suggestion to play on challenge as this will really put you into a situation where you have to play smart....like a sniper.
The story while not ground breaking presents characters with more depth than any other SGW title previous. The characters are more memorable and while the story is a bit far fetched and the writers need to do a little more research and fact checking, it's enough for me to suspend my disbelief and want to progress. But seriously...is John in the Army or the Marines or was he in both? Is his brother in the Marines or the Navy or both? Because I could have sworn John said the army feeds him well in the opening cut scene but he is definetly in the Marines according to the bio and various conversations. I mean little things like that can make or break the story.
The game is fun and satisfying. However it does suffer from a few things. There are some glitches here and there that spoil the fun....such as falling through the game world to my death...hello 1990s gaming. Also while I like the idea of skill unlocking, the skills themselves are not very noticeable or useful.
I enjoy the variety of weapons but the way they are unlocked or rate that they become unlockable is strange. Also the crafting system is a nice touch but somewhat pointless as I can just about purchase what I need with the amount of funds that I loot or earn on missions. A little more customization of weapons would have been nice too.
I am extremely pleased with the open world layout and the climbing ability, however the areas themselves are rather small. There may only be about 500 meters between various mission areas where whole missions take place. The entire play areas may be something the size of a single town or village but will try to sell itself as several different areas. The entire play area is only 2 or 3 square kilometers if even that.
What I wish SGW3 would have: A play area the size of one of the islands in ARMA 3 with sprawling urban areas, destructible structures, more of a civilian populace with characters on a "life cycle". More trap options and gadgets that are valuable but not purchasable. AI that doesn't give up so easy. An enemy heightened state of alert that lasts for hours or even days depending on the severity of your actions. For instance if you are spotted in an area you are not supposed to be in the a search for you is initiated and goes on until you are found and killed or several in game days have passed where security is tightened and more difficult to penetrate. I want to feel like I am being hunted but be able to outsmart my hunters and become the hunter myself.
Also losing sight of AI at 500ish meters is a bit crappy. I want some serious long range kills to happen. But then again shooting 1000ms out is nearly 1/3rd the entire play area.
So ultimately a good game with tons of potential. Really exciting when you play on the more difficult settings.
Needs bigger world with longer ranges. AI that responds to the entire world and your actions in it and not just the few hundred meters around it. Glitches need to be fixed.
I give it a solid 7 out of 10 but only if you play on challenge mode. Otherwise only about a 5 out of 10. Keep it up CI games.

This game is absolutely fantastic. The original was fun, well controlled, interesting and very nice. With a thousand recent remasters that have been incredibly iffy or downright awful (see Marvel Ultimate Alliance and MUV2), this was a definite risk. But alas, Kronos pulls it out. It's simply fantastic, and I'm incredibly pleased to see how they've done.
------------------
Graphics:  7/10
For PS2 age graphics, they've aged incredibly well. My resolution was nice and crisp at 1920x1080, and everything looked really nice. The textures were still pretty okay, but I'm solidly impressed that a game this age managed to be so nicely remastered.
------------------
Gameplay: 9/10
Everything's fast and fluid, and really nicely done. The mechanics have aged really well. Ty himself feels light, but solid, and definitely well done. Failed jumps and the likes never feel like you've been cheated by unfair mechanics, and even still, the whole ordeal is always good fun.
------------------
Story: 5/10
It's an interesting premise, with wildlife conservation themes sprinkled in through the whole thing. The characters and their interactions are all pretty unique and fun. Good stuff overall, but nothing new or groundbreaking.
============
OVERALL: 8/10
============
This game is a refreshing glimpse into the past, and a fantastic remaster in a time of absolute garbage. It's a blast to play this again, and I eagerly encourage anyone interested in old-school 3D action platformers to give this fantastic oldie a playthrough.

If you are looking for a action packed game, well, this game kind of has that, but it is NOT an action game, it is a puzzle game taking place along the German-French lines of WW1 between 1914 and 1917, and do they take you all over those lines. The selling point to Fight the Dragon seems to be that it's the Little Big Planet of Hack n' Slash games. Sadly, if anyone really believes that statement, then they clearly don't understand what LBP is.
The game itself is very bare bones and is very far away from having the complexity of LittleBigPlanet 1, let alone 2. Yes, it's currently in Early Access, but I am not seeing any promises of seeing any real depth being added to the game by the time it reaches 1.0.
The gameplay is shallow at best. Sure, you have 4 classes and several abilities to boot, with both melee and ranged combat, but it's still just the bare minimum of what can be considered gameplay. After the first 5 levels played you WILL have seen 90% of the replay value this game could possibly offer. Hit enemies. Back off a bit to counter their grouping up on you. Hit them some more. Repeat forever. Activate an AoE skill once in a while not out of necessity but just for the sake of changing things up.
So that's the gameplay aspect. But what about the user-created-content? Well, it suffers from two things in particular:
1) The shallow, repetitive gameplay directly affects custom content. Simply put, there's only so little you can do with the creation tools that will make your time worthwhile, and those are mainly cosmetic things like the visual design of your map or the story/dialogue paired with it.
2)There's very few Logic-systems in the game to work with, and this is what separates this game from the likes of LBP. You are handed the tools to make a top-down hack n' slash dungeon and nothing else. You are creating maps for one very specific game. In LBP, you have the ability to create interesting platforming maps, combat, cutscenes and puzzles limitied almost entirely by your own imagination. You can make a map with a working Chess game complete with a functional AI who can Check-Mate you. Fight the Dragon doesn't even remotely come close to having that level of depth.
Now a game isn't bad just because it's not LBP. I simply bring that up because it seems to be somewhat of a slogan for this game, and it's wrong. This game gets a thumbs down because it's shallow. Gameplay becomes boring in a matter of a couple hours and if you're a fan of user-generated-content, you've probably played/used numerous other software that puts this game's Editor to shame already.
For now, this is being uninstalled for me, but I'll follow the developer to see if they have anything substantial up their sleeves. The only possible way I can recommend this game for now, is if you intend your young child or sibling to play it, as they will likely have the attention span required to have real fun with this game, due to simply not having experienced anything better.

I think this was a great game: Solid gameplay, gorgeous graphics within a cyberpunk world, and good value given its lower price tag.
What I really like about this game is that it rightly focuses on strategy and stealth over guns blazing action. I loved the grungy maze-like city layouts that force you to sneak around and enter key locations while avoiding guards, cameras, deadly gas, and large security robots. In some cases, you can blast your way through, but it’s clearly not the best way to play. It’s just what I want in an RPG because I’m not a fan of FPSs. And yes, there are people like me on the planet, so deal with it!
The only negative, at least for me, was the lack of a compelling story. There are no cut scenes to fill in meaningful character development and no inter-character dialog as seen in other turn based RPGs. The story is revealed to the player in snippets as progress is made via mission text and emails hacked from data terminals. I ignored most of it without suffering at all.
Overall, I was happy with this game and recommend it strongly to anyone who likes the combination of beautiful graphics and strategy. If you’re a cyberpunk fan, it’s a must.

Since the co-op patch was installed and I finally had a computer system that could at least run the game at 30fps (apparently a limit thanks to CPU cores and the Unity engine) at 1080p, which is sufficient for this game, I finally finished it.
I wish I had a computer capable of playing this game when I was able to access the alpha and betas. The controls make me swear, the amount of times I have yelled at my units " NO, NO I TOLD YOU TO GO OVER THERE AND START ATTACKING THAT THING FFS" and "NO, RUN BACK OVER THERE" and the bugs I've found where you can clip through walls are, frustrating.
Having said that, there are really satisfying mechanics in this game that I haven't heard anyone I know mention, you can literally play this however you want. You can rock up and smash the doors in, blitz every unit in the area and take the prototypes. You can repeatedly hack into the banks and ATMs and roll around in all the cash you want and black market buy them selectively, or you can be as sneaky as you want, and not kill anyone if you're careful enough.
This game though really comes into its own with co-op, with the intricacies and difficulties of the game in controls there's nothing better than talking on voice comms with someone else as they control at least 2 of the units and you control the other 2.
If you really want, I think you can have up to 4 people controlling each unit individually, and at least with the 2v2 we found that it let us focus on the game in a way we hadn't before. We don't have to worry about micro managing 4 separate units, we can focus on being the sneaky hacker and the explosive support while the other two are the stealth assassin and the backup when it all goes south. Or the distractor and infiltrator by hacking the enemy that can open the doors for you while the rest of the team bring up the rear.
This was a good homage to Syndicate, which I'd played on the Amiga 1200, and it was more satisfying than Syndicate Wars.
The story didn't quite carry the game, but I didn't care. The soundtrack and gameplay was enough.
The game was pretty cheap in the recent sale, and subsequent sales, and it's worth it. I'm glad this was a thing. Though I get the feeling, we're not going to see another, and that's a shame.

Some bumpy progression and a few frustrating glitches, but overall a beautiful and engaging game either solo or with friends.

Satellite Reign is beautifully cyberpunk and every billboard and back alley and corporate stronghold is singing the same song. The music is fitting, but a little loud, so I turn it way down for multiplayer sessions. If you're the sort of player who reads books in a video game, you'll enjoy the story and factions and characters and setting that you find here.

Other reviews have complained about the progression of the gameplay, but it really sat well with me. Early in the game, your team is very weak and you'll depend on stealth to complete missions. You might spend a minute or two huddled behind a dumpster waiting for a guard to leave or an alarm to expire or your energy to recharge. I like that, but not everyone does. By the mid-game, you're seeing tougher enemies, but you have more equipment and character upgrades so you can neutralize a patrol before they call for backup or exfiltrate from an alerted base by using cover and special abilities. It makes me feel stronger, but still tactical. Once you max out your crew, you'll find yourself "infiltrating" compounds by strolling down the middle of the road obliterating combat mechs and elite troopers and blast doors without slowing down. It's a great end-game feel, like a reward for all your careful play earlier.

The transitions between those phases can be rocky, though. I hate having my new demolition charges researched only to realize I don't yet have the cloaking tech/skill I need to use them against turrets the way I planned. There was a long time--maybe two or three hours of play--during which frag grenades could solve all my problems, which felt cheap. The tech unlocks are semi-random, and skills take a while to build, so you'll feel unbalanced sometimes, but when it synchronizes it really feels terrific.

I see a lot of griping about the lack of a tactical pause feature, but there is an unlockable, upgradable slo-mo that consumes in-game resources in exchange for more time to plan. It's a must for me due to my chobo micro, so I'm happy to pay upgrade points and character stamina to keep myself in bullet-time whenever there are bullets about.

Multiplayer is absolutely marvelous. It's laggier than it probably needs to be, and matchmaking seems clumsy, and there are never open servers to join, but having a friend or three along allows mind-blowing sophistication in tactics and planning. My solo play usually consists of my four-man team blobbing around the map and focusing fire to kill enemies, but with an online team I'm posting up in a sniping spot or gathering intel across the map or covering a corridor or rigging a boobytrap and loving it.

The game is not without its glitches. Characters get stuck in cover sometimes, or fail to follow complex orders. The AI is not great, with enemy soldiers doing dumb stuff and player characters behaving bizarrely when they don't have explicit instructions. It can get frustrating, but once you get a feel for it, most of the problems can be avoided or corrected for without having to frag your own dude and respawn him.

Long story short, the game is good, but requires some patience and commitment. Bring some friends along, and it really shines.

Patrick Klepek
an article on why you should play, or at least try, bad games. I won’t rehash what he said, but I do agree with him that there is merit to playing mediocre games. It can make you appreciate what makes great games so good and why that is. Along this line of thinking, I believe that Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is worth your time.
Being the third game in a critically-middling series from a European developer, Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 doesn’t come with the loftiest of expectations but it does come at an interesting time with Sniper Elite 4 and Ghost Recon Wildlands both releasing this year. Now I haven’t played Sniper Elite 4 (didn’t care for 2) and I played Wildlands during the beta and thought that the gameplay and controls were frankly quite poor. I’ll say straight up, I enjoyed SGW3 far more than Wildlands. Funny enough, the best comparison gameplay-wise that I can make to SGW3 is another Ubisoft game, Far Cry. SGW3 feels like the less polished, more tactical cousin of Far Cry 3. This game cherry picks some of the best aspects of Far Cry like being able to attack a mission from multiple angles (stealth, guns blazing) and cuts a lot of the fat from it as well (whole map is open, no climbing towers!). The shooting feels pretty good and sniping was thoroughly satisfying, as it should be.
Now, I’d be remiss to gloss over the issues that SGW3 has, and there are plenty. First off, this game is desperately in need of optimization. My FPS were all over the place and had to turn a lot of settings to low to maintain a somewhat stable 45 FPS. While looking good in spots, the game should be nowhere near as demanding as it is. A sunrise or full moon can make a for a pretty screenshot but the game can also look flat out bad sometime and, most shockingly, in cutscenes. I’m not being hyperbolic, but the cutscenes look straight out of a PS3/360 game, they’re not great. Also, the load times. My god this game has the longest load times I’ve seen in quite some years. Thankfully dying or reloading a checkpoint isn’t too bad, but loading from the main menu or traveling between one of the four zones can be painfully slow.
I don’t want to dogpile here, because I really did have a lot of fun in my 14 hours with SGW3 but there are some serious issues here that until resolved, I would not recommend getting it unless it has a deep discount. A lot of my issues with the game are perfectly fixable and not necessarily design problems, which is good. I would also like to spotlight CI Games for offering a free Season Pass in a time where gamers are getting nickeled and dimed to death. The free Season Pass is very consumer friendly in my eyes and should be supported.
Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is by no means perfect or even a great game, but it is a fun game and one that deserves to be played. I hope that CI Games can work out the fixable issues that are there because there is some great fun to be had in this tactical Far Cry-like game.

Armello is not your average strategy game due to the unique winning conditions and constantly changing board events. In this game you will play as one of the four animal clans seeking to take down the king of Armello who has been corrupted by a evil known as rot, yet there are three other players that also wish to take down the king and steal his throne for themselves. All these players are pushed into one RANDOMLY generated board composed of varying hex tiles that take effect upon the player ( Ex. Moving into a swamp causes you to lose a life while moving into a spirirt circle gives you a life). I personally enjoy the gameplay for there is a hint of cut throat required over multiplayer and in fact many ways to win the game which gives every player a path to take towards victory. The random generation of the board along with the King's Acts that are determined by a player makes no two games alike as players are trying to win the game through their own preffered path. Graphics in the game are rather stunning as the cards actullay have fine detailed art that actually moves upon hvoering over said card. Games can last up to about a hour or more, yet the graphics are thankfully easy on the eyes as you play hours on end. Audio is nothing really to praise nor spit on. The CONS vary in severity to player to player and may effect whether or not you wish to buy this game. Games can last for long hours and demands that you idly wait for your turn as other players take their lengthy turn which can lead you to becoming rather bored after skimming over your cards and planning your next turn if it ever comes. A Multiplayer issue is the ranking system where you maybe a mere level one and end up being paired up with a rank 5 player which seems a bit unfair or poor ranking. I would reccomend this game to those who are fine waiting for their turns over a long lengthy game and are willing to put in time to play a whole game. I give Armello 9/10 Spirit Stones

A no doubt creative project/game with an interesting concept which suffers from horribly boring gameplay.
In it's core, the game is a basic (and by basic I mean REEEEEEEALLY basic) hack'n'slash style platformer. Feeling like a mix of cheap arcade platformers and a cutesy-minecraft graphics version of Diablo.
Fighting comes down to just slashing away, doing the one or other dodge against bigger enemies or occasionally using a special or heavy attack. Every 'class' comes with slight differences, but I didn't really feel any different when playing as Rogue or Fire Mage.
The main selling point of the game is it's 'infinite level content' by means of providing a level editor. However, after playing a few hours, I've already seen and beaten + figured out simple patterns of attack to take down all of the ~dozen enemy types the game has to offer. And here is exactly the issue: Providing players a Level Editro does NOT give you instant 'ininite content'. It just gives you infinite variations of the exact same 15 enemies placed on the same 30 tilesets. If the game would have given me the possibility to pick enemy core animations, then add in my own values and special modifiers, that would have been interesting... but like this? Boring and EXTREMELY repetitive.
Not to mention trivially easy (even when I accidentally entered a high level map with a level 1 mage. Took some more kiting/time, but that's it).
The concept of the dragon arena is nice. And no doubt, the dragon is a heck of a boss. But that alone does not motivate me to grind through the same enemies hours and hours to come just to beat that boss.
Overall, I'm VERY disappointed with the game, even more so because it's not "This is a very early access and lots is to come" but a "It's nearly finished and very playable".
Rating: 2/10
Your money will get you a better hour ratio in ever other game.

Valiant Hearts - runs well (even on Uplay, don't frown),  and offers surprising depth compared to most Ubi games, in the form of collectible items which unlocks  copious amounts of historical information. A good game - would require unique gameplay and controls to be great, but it's on a good way. Be wary - despite its serious content, don't expect much action and combat, because you will be gravely disappointed.
Valiant Hearts is a game that's really hard to classify, and to review. It mixes animation fitting children's books with the horrors of war, simple controls, mild puzzles, and some quick time events while trying to hold up and carry a storyline with multiple protagonists. And not all of these are perfect.
The animation is nice - the presentation is good, it's easy to distinguish certain parts of the gameplay area, and it becomes clear pretty soon that a game has a distinguished art style, which is always a good sign for a unique, good visual experience.
The controls and puzzles work together nicely - the puzzle parts usually make good use of the game's control scheme, but after a while it gets stale. There is a limited version of puzzles you can create with (controller layout) A for grab and operate, RB/LB to send the dog for contextual places (ABXY), and one for throwing the item that you're holding. And that's it. The game has the potential to become extremely boring simply because the gameplay is a single-path sidescroller, and most of the action parts are as intense as getting past a strictly scripted guard.
But the narration saves the day. Without the historical facts on each map, without the unlockable mementos of the era, the game would fall onto its own face. There are many letters, everyday items from the world of WW1 and the countryside, from the soldiers and their families that THAT'S the main reason in my opinion, that people consider this game as good as it is. These help people without the in-depth historical knowledge to appreciate more the simpler graphics, to imagine the mud of the trenches, the freezing cold nights and the problems with communicating with the loved ones. It's needed to make the cute-ish graphics into something that hints the reality of the past.
Technically the game runs well, each episode has around 5 levels, each of them can be completed in maybe 30-45 minutes if really looking around, if needed to restart the level, it can be done in a few minutes - they are pretty short. If one dies ingame, respawns at last checkpoint, if the player exits, the whole level needs to be replayed.  In my playthrough, I've faced two  bugs that forced me to restart the respective levels, but as I said, it's minimal time loss. At least based on my experience, both the game and Uplay was trustworthy and hadn't caused problems besides this little hiccup.
So, after all, I would recommend the game for everyone - at least to check it out because it's a really inclusive game, I think almost everyone could get into it because of it's simplistic control scheme.  But the gameplay is plain without the additional collectibles and the lack of challenge can make it hard to go on - in shorter bursts it's easily approachable for the lovers of more action-filled genres.
