This is the closest you're going to get to a Syndicate/Syndicate Wars sequel. It certainly does borrow extensively from the Syndicate series such as the aesthetic, the four agents, some gameplay mechanics and you'll even hear nods to the franchise which EA buried in the music as they had the same composer. It also surprisingly borrows stealth mechanics from the Commandos games.
You control 4 agents with different classes (Soldier, Support, Hacker & Infiltrator), each of whom possess unique skills. However, based your play style, you might find yourself not utilizing one or two throughout your playthrough. I personally found myself exclusively using the Hacker & Infiltrator during my purely stealth run. A stealth playthrough will unfortunately highlight some of the cracks in the game. Unclear enemy line of sight, AI can be ridiculously stupid & buggy at times such as occassional poor pathfinding, guards escorting my agents into a secure part of a compound instead of out of it or the agents continously stopping for no apparent reason, and guards forgetting that they just spotted me within a matter of seconds. Performance seems to be a bit of an issue as well, the game will occasionally stutter and I've faced some FPS drops on a beast of a machine which can handle way more demanding games. What little story is there is fleshed out through hacking data panels to access logs about the various factions and occasional voiced briefings. The game never really goes out of its way to familiarize you with the world much.
Now that I got the negatives out of the way, let me highlight what the game gets right which fortunately enough is most of it. Let's start with the world, it is gorgeous to look at. The blinding neon lights against perpetual rain along with the synth-heavy soundtrack nail the atmosphere and setting (make sure to buy the OST). As for gameplay, the real time tactical approach definitely keeps you on your toes, as you'll be scurrying from one agent to another, evaluating their situation and issuing commands accordingly. The in-game city is split into 5 sectors each requiring unique credentials to access or you can sneak or blast your way through. There are multiple missions per sector which will help you earn credits, acquire equipment or augmuntation blueprints to research, and to undermine a specific faction's control and security over an area. These missions can be approached in multiple ways from hacking your way through a facility and turning the enemies defenses against them, to tactically dispatching guards in your way or by being a complete ghost. Nothing beats doing some recon on heavily fortified, setting a plan to infilitrate it and then executing said plan without a hitch in one single go. In case one of your agents does die (and they will), the game eliminates the need for quick save/load by implementing a cloning mechanic which allows you to clone your existing agents and deploy them at any point or even have them replaced by new "recruits" whom may possess superior stats.
So if you're looking for an experience similar to Syndicate and Commandos in a cyberpunk setting, then look no further than Satellite Reign. It isn't perfect, but the flaws don't hinder the experience much and can be looked past.

While this game is visually beautiful, that's unfortunately about where the reason to play the game actually ends.
Bad AI? Check.
And by bad, I'm talking functionally broken at a fundamental short bus level. From pathing to not shooting at enemies that are shooting at them, the underlying mechanical decisions made by the developers of this game are inexplicable. The characters won't even attack from behind cover. Click twice? The characters will run (for a couple seconds, then they run out of energy). Click three times, because you're in a hurry? They will start running, then stop, then walk. Seriously.
Enemy AI is even worse, the security forces will take cover... in front of barriers, so you can just shoot them in the back. The enemy security forces will actually deaggro in direct line of sight of a raging gun battle. Enemy security NPCs outside a certain range will remain in idle animations while being gunned down. Honestly, the AI is so bad, it reminds me of TotalBiscuit's review of Day One: Garry's Incident. Yes, it's THAT bad.
Dated game mechanics? Check.
When the devs say they were inspired by Syndicate, they weren't kidding, and the game play is as wooden as you'd expect from a 20 year old game. Don't get me wrong, there's some good mechanics (like how the game is XP and skill based), but even then, the game depends on a "hacked money flow" system (from hacking ATMs), which means that, as I'm typing this, my characters are slowly accruing money with which to buy things. Not that there's much you can do with money to begin with. There's actually pitifully little. And the combat system?
Boring. An 8 year old could have designed better, with little provocation. As stated above, characters don't use cover effectively at all, the clunky way the user interface, the bad AI, and the really limited commands you can give the characters leads to a repetitive series of bland shoot outs, with the characters making seriously toddler stupid level targetting decisions. Worse, it's possible to provoke the police, kite them to a spawn location, and the enhanced healing from the spawn locations will allow your team to tank endless incoming fire, not that the dumb as a box of rocks AI will be able to consistently path security personnel to your position.
Absent Character Customization? Check.
Here I'm talking about the character's appearance. There's precious little in the way of customization. Seriously, in the 21st Century and in a cyberpunk game, you can't even change how the character looks outside of simple color palette swaps. Not that the default appearance is bad. It's just not what I want them to look like.
Underutilization of voice acting? Check.
Don't worry, no one can accuse you of not being a reader after playing this game, because you'll be reading stuff until you're sick of it, because they couldn't be bothered to find a microphone for someone, ANYONE, to read voiceovers for mission logs and quest objectives, or they simply couldn't afford to. It's not a small element, especially since they spent so much time and energy on the visuals, the audio they just completely missed (past the tutorial). It's all just blah blah blah text walls.
Lack of Optimization? Check.
On a rig that can run Saints Row IV on max graphical settings with 60 FPS without any problems, this game crawls. It's a comedy how bad this game is optimized, probably because the devs have no clue how to go about that.
Lack of Support? Check.
The game developer has abandoned this title. Hopefully they are investing their time in other talents, because game development sadly ain't one. :/
What would make it better?
1) The characters utilizing cover intelligently. Popping up to take some shots, then dropping back down.
2) ANY kind of tactical play. Think X-Com, with moving agents to create cross fire opportunities, while others provide covering fire, while NPCs actually respond by falling back, gathering up, and rushing the characters.
3) Being able to move AND SHOOT... at the same time. You know... like people actually can.
4) Implementing Sniper Rifles that doesn't treat them as "just a bigger gun".
5) Any kind of REAL customization. With or without face covering goggles. With or without hoods. Choice of boots, clothes, etc.
6) A better economy than "wait to be rich". No, sure it's a nice basis, but it's boring. No, seriously. Really boring.
7) Find someone that can code AIs above a 2nd grader's intelligence. The combat would be more compelling if they just shouted "Bang bang bang! Bang bang bang! You're dead!", because it'd at least be funny... at least for about 10 minutes. Okay, strike that.
Final Score: 4/10. Meh.
Metacritic gives it a 75. This game deserves half that. It's playable. In the admittedly short period of time I've played it, the game hasn't crashed for inexplicable reasons, blown up, or fell into an sudden death spiral of glitches. So the game, itself, is stable. Sadly, it's just not particularly fun, with the lack of customization, shallow tactical play, coupled with sometimes hilariously bad AI, it's just an uninspired game. It has the slick appearance of a AAA title, with unpolished and clunky mechanics.
Anyhow. No, I can't recommend this game to anyone. Seriously, even at $4.19, it's probably better to just go spend your money on other better games. You're so hungry for a cyberpunk game, with hacking, infiltrating, gun play that you can almost taste it? This game will just disappoint you. It's a cheap Chinese knockoff of a 20 year old game. Do yourself a favor and keep looking.
PS - Just had another of those moments where I'm yelling at my computer "What are you DOING!?" as members of my team run out of cover for no reason whatsoever, so they can get gunned down. One guy gets gunned down, I get him back up, then he liesurely runs in the WRONG direction. Oh, the AI in this game is every kind of stupid. I just had a gunfight with security personnel, and I haven't even bothered to move from where I was standing. Threat level has dropped to nothing.
This game is a bad joke. Seriously.

aside from the shadow bug (fix below) it is a great game!
"aydark  has State of Decay: Year-One Jul 5, 2015 @ 8:10pm
I have flickering shadows as well, on GTX 770 here. For me, it's related to using 16:10 aspect ratio (my monitor is 1920x1200 resolution). It's just one of the bugs related to that aspect ratio. Undead Labs is aware of the issue, but I haven't heard anything about a patch yet.
If this is the same problem for you (that you run 16:10 aspect ratio), then try this workaround (which works 100% of the time for me).
1) Move the camera around until you are looking at one of the glitched shadows (I usually use a large tree or the power lines in town, which shadows show up as zig zags on the road).
2) Open the display options, change the aspect ratio to 16:9
3) Go back to the gameplay and wait a few seconds, the shadows will "reset" and work properly
4) Go back to the display options, change the aspect ratio back to 16:10
5) Go back to the gameplay and the shadows should reset again and be working properly.
Sometimes, I have to try options 2 - 5 two or three times, but it eventually works. Unfortunately, I have to do this every time I start the game up.. but the shadows remain working for the rest of that session at least."

I tend to buy any Zombie game i see, even if it's graphic is worst than minecraft played on 20 fps, even if it's buggy as hell. I know i'm late, but until now i was NEVER happy with any zombie game until i found this one out.
Don't get me wrong: this game is NOT flawless. It is full of bugs, the AI can be wierd sometimes and the Story is a bit "meh".. expecially when you get 20 side quests for each main story mission.
But this is what makes the game great for me. The bugs aren't gamebreaking, at least not for me: You can abuse some to get double resources, and the 'bad' AI allows you to take a 1 v 5 fight with a melee weapon and get out with just a few scratches if you play it smartly .. or you can just take your guns out.
I love the stealth this game offers you, sneaking behind 10 zombies and taking them out one by one feels just good.
3 Different game modes ( one that offers A LOT to do to unlock every possible character and is really challenging and two story modes that are "okay") will make sure that you will play for a while before running out of things to do
I would suggest this game over any other single player zombie game for now, despite the graphics and the AI not being the best.. but maybe this is what makes this game a bit more charming to me. Going back to the 'good old times' where graphic didn't matter and content was everything
Cons: The game FORCES you to play every day. Every 24 hours (in real-life time) your resources will be drained a bit, even if you are not playing! If you plan on taking a break for a few days you must make sure to stock your base with plenty of resources or bad things
happen. But don't worry, if you don't play for 3 days the resources won't be drained anymore. This is just a way to make the game feel more "alive" and letting you worry a bit before logging out with a big "Do i have enough stuff to survive tomorrow?"
TL;DR : Buy it! :D

I have often tried to find a decent PC version of old Pen And Paper games.  I loved playing RPGs as a kid-my older brother would make campaigns for me and my other brother to play, and while I have nobody to play with where I live now the desire to relive the fun is strong.  Card Hunter is the closest game I have found so far to capturing the paper RPG style I am looking for, even with the card game features.  It is fun, and once you start playing it keeps you wanting to play even when you know you should be doing something else.  Best of all, it is free!  I would recomend this to other people looking for an old school RPG experience, especially if you don't have the dosh to by a more complicated game.

Card Hunter has some interesting mechanics worth exploring, all wrapped up in a well-exectued, if well-worn, theme. This is the first game I played blending a card game with a tactical RPG and it does so very well, with your character's deck being based on their gear - which makes it very easy for the RPG fans out there to ease in to the deck-building. Being an RPG fan myself, I can't say that this system does much for the deck-building fans out there, however.
Over all, it's a fun romp and worth a couple hours of your time, if just to check out the systems in play. After all, it's free!
There are a few microtransactions offered, but none are necessary to progress fully through the game. I can't speak to PVP or Co-Op, as I've only played the Campaign.

Keep it mind, it isn't an RPG, there are no real choices or decisions to be made, and there is no multiplayer scene, giving it unfortunately very little replayability other than for enjoyment. As an avid tabletop game player, I really enjoy how League of Geeks have created the feel of a board game in a digital space. Armello offers (at least for me) a good balance between luck and strategy; clever planning can get thrown out the window by bad luck, but good adaptability can salvage a ruined plan. Also, the art and animations are absolutely gorgeous.
Armello is gorgeous  - very slow paced

Armello would be a solid tabletop boardgame. The mechanics are simple, and for the most part are determined by your strategy. There is enough luck to keep it unpredictable, but not enough that you feel you're playing RNG Simulator. So far, games seem to be determined on the last or second to last turns, with no runaway victories or crushing defeats.

Armello is basically a digital board game. It's easy to pick up and play but the gameplay is complex enough for each game to be exciting. (I'm not gonna bother describing the game mechanics because other people already have and I'm lazy! Oops! If you need an in-depth look at how the game plays I recommend finding and watching a Let's Play) The game's aesthetic is gorgeous with beautifully illustrated cards, fun characters and a great soundtrack. The "fantasy w/animal people" setting is strongly realized and despite the fact that there isn't much of an overt story, (it's a board game) there is a great undercurrent of lore, and it's a good world to jump into when you feel like playing a couple of matches.

so this game feeds my need for tactical planing and RNG that a old school pen and paper (like DnD) would give with the bonus of fluffy little critters that are actually cool and fitting to their world.

Sleep is for the weak.
The minutes turn to hours, which turn to days. How long have I been here?
I close my eyes at night but only find endless fields of belts and trains, snaking their way through the fabric of reality. Carrying the materials that move my technology forward. Forever moving forward. Onward and upward. To the stars.
Ah, the stars. I came from there, once. But that life is dead to me now. I couldn't reach it even if I tried.
Turrets perched on the edges of existence, firing endless streams of energy into the abyss. Just because they can.
Killing the natives is only a hobby now. No biological organism could withstand this energy.
Is there even a god that would be willing to claim those horrid creatures as their own?
A belt here. An assembler there. Row after row after agonizing row of inserters. The hum of cooling fans and electric motors fills the air, powered by the coal-fired boilers that coat everything in a uniform layer of smog.
The factory grows endlessly. Ever-increasing complexity, a slave to industrialization. Onward, upward, forwards...
...
There must be no god.
If there was, it would have stopped me by now.
...
I hear a low-resource alarm going off. No doubt a train got stuffed up by an attack party on the northern railway again. I need to go.
~~

The words of the day: simplistic intricacy.
Those two words sum up the whole of what Fight The Dragon (FTD) is all about.  At first glance, the core gameplay appears simple – and it is.  Upon a deeper inspection, however, the intricacies begin to emerge – particularly in its level designer, which I will go into more later.
FTD is essentially Little Big Planet meets a simple overhead hack-‘n’-slash.  A number of community levels and a few tutorial missions await the player within this game.  The interface to select your adventure is easy to use and find what you’re looking for, and there is a search system that allows you to find a level that matches the difficulty you want, whether it’s a favorite of the community, or you can do a direct search for a specific title.
The first order of business is to choose a character class: Fighter, Black Rogue, Fire Lord, and Ice Wizard.  Each of these classes has their own unique abilities and stats, which offers greater variety and opportunities to customize multiple playthroughs.  The appearances of your character can also be customized (to an extent) afterwards at your home base.
While there are many options for combat in this game, the ones that will be used the most are the basic attack and a class-specific special attack (A and B respectively on an XBox controller, which I recommend using).  These moves are all you need if you employ a hit-and-run strategy like I do.  That’s the simple side of it; the more intricate side is that you can also block, dodge, and use another special move as well if you want.  But that feels a bit superfluous sometimes and the majority of your time will be spent just hacking and slashing with your basic moves.
The game also provides ample possibilities for platforming adventures if combat is not where your interests lie.  Climbing, running, and leaping across chasms and lava appears simple enough.  However, doing it *well* takes  a little more attention and skill.  Then try doing it while some skeleton shoots arrows at you or a pyromancer blasts you with fire.  Or do it over lava where you have to think, “Okay, I have to time my sprinting right and aim perfectly or I’m gonna fall into hot burning lava and – dang it, now I’m dead.  Back to the checkpoint.”
After a level, you can donate your unwanted equipment and excess gold to the Loot Shrine, building up enough credit to eventually earn a reward.  The more credit you build up before seeking a reward, the greater the reward.  It's a nice way to reward the people who spend time collecting what is often useless armor or weapons dropped in a level.
But it is with the level editor that this game truly shines and brings to the forefront the reason FTD works so well.  Looking at a custom-designed level, it’s easy to assume that only someone who has played the game long enough and mastered the minute details could create something intricate and amazing.  At least, that’s the mindset I went into the level designer with.
Boy, was I wrong.
Within a matter of hours, I had created a level that involved a good amount of platforming and combat, tested it multiple times, and then released it to the community.  I had only played the game a few hours before to learn the basic buttons and get a feel for the game.  The instructions on how to use different components and how to connect cause-and-effects (i.e. kill this enemy, door opens).  Enemy stats can be modified to vary every time you enter a level.  There are also a lot of different options for what kind of level you want to create.  Various indoor and outdoor biomes are available, and you can mix and match at will.  You can create a massive level before you reach your “building point” limit, and that is half of the fun.
**To see the level I created in my first attempt, look up Necrypt in the level gallery.**
However, there are a few points that should be addressed in terms of what this game does not do so well.
It was an okay-ish FPS.

More Impressions @
(Early Access Impressions)
With random adventures waiting around every corner, Fight the Dragon looks very promising. The aesthetics are rather basic, but the focus is on the adventure and challenges that you’ll face when you go out to level and gear up. The ultimate goal is to go and “Fight the Dragon” (what else?). Whether you’re looking to kill the dragon or just do some damage to him he’s got plenty of health do deal with.
When you go out to adventure, you’ll play random levels as you pick which spot you want to go to on the over-world map (or at least that’s the best way I’ve found to describe it). You can replay levels already completed, but you won’t get a Dragon Scroll for completing them. (They allow you to fight the big jerky dragon.) You’ll get levels created by the developer (3 Sprockets) and those created by other players. You do get to vote for which maps you liked after you’ve either beaten them or been defeated by them. So far I’m in the dark of how I want to vote on some of them due to the content in them. I know that certain aspects of them are good, but if I don’t appreciate them, well… ah who am I kidding, thumbs down! After all, if you don’t like it, you don’t like it. (I like the neutral thumb more.)
The best part of Fight the Dragon for me has to be, hands down, the level editor. I’m enjoying the heck out of the editor and I started by trying to recreate levels from the N64 game Goldeneye. I’ve since stopped doing that since Fight the Dragon doesn’t support multiple levels. Without having ability to create a second floor, my creation of “Not The Facility” has been halted until further progress has been made on the editor. I’m sure that’s something they may add in later. Maybe I’ll be able to make taller maps as well. As of now, you can only effectively make a tall one floor house. As for a beginning setup for crafting your own adventures, it works well enough for making dungeons and outside areas. If you’re willing to work with what you’ve got, there’s plenty of tools at your disposal to make some fun adventures for you and other players. At the very least, I would appreciate the ability to build higher even if I can’t make a second floor.
There has been a few levels that remind me of what I’m not appreciating with some games lately. There’s been a fad with making games super difficult to bring back the “nostalgia of the olden times”. Some of the levels presented include way to many traps and junk that you’ll almost need prescience to know where to go. Can’t anyone remember when you just had a fun adventure and it wasn’t horribly difficult? I remember some games being difficult, but I don’t think many of those devs went out of their way to get your goat.
On a flip-side, you have the ability to follow creators of your choice. It makes it a little easier to find an adventure you’ll probably enjoy more. However, I still recommend going on random adventures since that’s probably where the most fun will be, not knowing what you’re getting yourself into. You may even find yourself on my level. I’ll make more. I’m pretty happy with how the “Tunjair Desert” map turned out. Since I like to be satisfied with what I make, I’ll be taking my time and not rush anything.

Fight the Dragon is a fun little hack n' slash with very basic, Gauntlet-style gameplay. The game is entirely built around player made levels and designed to be played in short bursts, with each level lasting 15 minutes on average. The four available classes are differentiated by each having 4 abilities (in addition to basic attacking), as well as some unique weapon types that are only useable by certain classes.
The lack of combat depth may turn some people off but it comes down to personal preference. The adventure creator is easy to use and offers a lot of freedom, with more content being added on a regular basis. At the time of this writing, they've even begun adding a logic system to the creator as well. The game is great for picking up and running through some adventures in your down time where as making levels can keep you busy for hours on end.
FTD isn't perfect and has it's issues. The entire game's entertainment value relies on the quality of maps and the variety of tools available to those who make the maps. That being said, the devs are very attentive and really seem to care about making the game better and better. They listen to community feedback and continue to polish and add to the game, pushing out great patches on a quite regular basis. Overall I don't see much to complain about. The game is a fun little gem to spend time in and has the potential for a lot of replayability. I look forward to seeing FTD grow and hopefully its community will as well.

Unfortunately, I cannot recommend NGW 3 with the current MSRP. Maybe worth 10 €. I have found many negative aspects in the game.
Negatives:
-Interaction with solid environment/surroundings: 1) You can get stuck in the many strange places in the world, 2) Small obstacles (small deviations/preturberations in rocky environment maybe 20 cm high) can only be jumped over
-Interaction with water (i.e. "swimming") is far from other modern games: character is visually submerged and still apparently swimming above the surface level
-Poor AI and hostile actions under fire. Also, there are many seemingly nice traps and decoys in the game, but poor AI actions inhibits the use of most of these. Therefore, trap and decoy gadgets are mostly useless
-Story is not interesting and is too predictable. Endgame (and story) is ridiculous.
-Vehicle mechanics/dynamics (and the speedometer) is poor and interaction with trees feels like a game published 10 years ago
-Weapon "silencers" and their functionality. In addition, there seems to be a glicth in the LMG ammo count: refilling ammo costs to refill to 999 rounds but you actually have only 250 rounds of ammo in the ammo pouch
-Only very few interesting places to stumble upon in the open-world map. Basically, at least for me, I find no interest to wander around
-Skill tree in general. Also, if you want to conserve at least some difficulty facing enemy snipers, do not pick the skill which grants you the ability to see enemy snipers' line of sights with the drone and/or in recon mode
-Unbalanced in-game economics (used to unlock new gear and to craft ammo/gear/gadgets at the workbench). Currency and crafting material are redundant as you always have enough to buy/craft anything you want
-It doesn't matter where or what level the character aims, in the slow-motion bullet camera the character always aims at the horizon and the bullet leaves the barrel at an angle -> looks ridiculous
-Escape of Lydia: Lydia uses John's voice in interrogation audio
Positives:
+Visuals/graphics are not that bad, thx to CryEngine
+Few side missions where the player acts as a recon sniper and spotter to ground troops
IMHO, SGW 3, trying to be an open-world sniper game, is not as good a sniper game as SGW 2 was (haven't played Sniper Elite 4 yet so can't compare to this new title), and definitely isn't as good an open-world game as Ghost Recon: Wildlands is.
All in all, due to many negative aspects that feel like bugs/glitches and just bad game development, the game feels unfinished and ancient in general -- not a game to be released in 2017.

About This Game
Chaos has erupted throughout the galaxy. As leader of an elite squad of Republic Commandos, your mission is to infiltrate, dominate, and ultimately, annihilate the enemy. Your squad will follow your orders and your lead, working together as a team - instinctively, intelligently, instantly. You are their leader. They are your weapon.

Ok for a single player zombie game. Leaves a lot to be desired though.
The game doesn't offer real base building. Static locations you must choose from that have static "slots" for putting certain buildings like cooking or medical; isn't exactly that exciting in terms of gameplay these days.
What IS fun is looting and running around, managing durability on your car and weapons. Leveling the characters and choosing their specializations.
The lifeline DLC was a disappointment. It's pretty much identical to the regular game, only this dlc puts you in the perspective of an officer in a military outpost rather than the perspective of a civilians point of view. When I first saw the new map I was pretty excited to go running around in it (finally an actual city-map?) but you soon realize that almost 80% of it isn't actually accessable and there are no large building type locations, just more of the same basic small town-type locations identical to the original gameplay.
The biggest problem for me, and why I don't recommend this game, is that its still a fairly horrendous console port. This game is totally unstable and crashes quite often, and I had to figure out that I needed to lock the frames to 60 in order for it not to crash consistently, which is pretty unacceptable these days.
Also the available graphics options are still as horrendous as they were in the original state of decay. There are no individual settings that you can adjust, just 1 graphics slider that goes from low to ultra basically, but you've got no idea what its actually changing from setting to setting which is unacceptable.
Driving around is still glitchy as hell and the game stutters and jitters frequently when driving. It also sounds like the car is bumping into the road or something occasionally when driving. Unacceptable.
Gameplay gets stale and repetitive very quickly.
Like I said, it is an okay single player zombie game to play for a little bit, but other than that, would not recommend.

I was a little wary about buying the game after the latest reviews about how the game was broken due to Games For Windows Live (GFWL).
Running the game for the first time involved a few steps, but I got it running, so leaving here the steps I had to take.
-Setup a Rockstar Social Club (RSC) account and a GFWL account before hand. (if you don't have one yet, if you do, check if you can log in to each one)
-Ran the game the first time, had an error missing GFWL, downloaded and installed the client for GFWL, ran game again, signed in to both RSC and GFWL, it worked. (helps if you set GFWL to auto sign in, or game might restart a couple times before you log in)
-Had a problem with the game not detecting a 3GB RAM vid card, so the graphics were "locked" at 800x600 with all settings set to low, had to go to the Steam entry for the game in your library under properties and launch options, add the commands: -norestrictions -availablevidmem 100
-Game still started in 800x600, but now the graphics options were unlocked and correctly reads 3GB memory, so just set graphics to max and all set!
Of course I can't guarantee this will work for everyone, but did for me.
Have fun!

Great little game so far! At its heart, it's essentially DnD, as all of the adventures you play are made by the community, which all are unique in that you have freedom over the entire layout, theme, loot locations, and even NPC dialog. Even better, you can tag along with friends and adventure together, everyone getting their own loot drops.
You can choose from 4 classes at the moment: Warrior, Fire Lord, Ice Wizard and Black Rogue. You obtain experience and levels and loot as you play through random adventures made by your fellow players and friends. The "item vendor" is actually a "Loot Shrine" that you offer unwanted items to, build up points which slowly fall into higher and higher tiers that grant you better and better items when you "pray" to the loot shrine. On top of that, it's also your loot stash (ie. cross-character).
The ACK (Adventure Construction Kit) is quite easy and effective to work with, already supporting Environment Effects, Time of Day, water/lava/mud, copy/paste (but not undo yet, sadly), with things like music, mutators and map triggers all on the way! The current set of assets isn't overwhelming, but not completely barren either. It also has fledgling "room-over-room" support in the form of some pretty basic bridges, which will hopefully be expanded as time goes on.
In summary, I'm really liking this game so far. Given the fact that the adventures are entirely community made, there's always something new to do, and more loot to find!

A game praying on nostalgia to deliver a Syndicate like experience that turns out to be not a bad game - although with what i felt a lot of potential wasted somewhere between the lines.
First of - I remember somewhat the original Syndicate Wars - enough to feel nostalgic about it but not enough to draw a direct comparison between the two. Might be for the better or worse for a game review but this is how it is.
Satellite Reign is a real time squad based game set in a cyberpunk world of the future. The giant companies control the world and it's up to you and your squad to take the worst offender down. The story is simple and doesn't get much more complicated throughout the game. Most of the text is presented in writing and it's easier to just skim the text for important bits regarding the mission rather than trying to understand the story which seems a bit generic.
Mechanically this is a squad based real time strategy game. You control four members of your squad in a pretty standard set up - soldier/heavy, support/medic, hacker and infiltrator/sniper. Each of those come with a special set of skills you can upgrade with experience gained. Those are pretty cool and useful - some more than other - but generally you do feel like you're making a choice by selecting what to upgrade and it does impact the way you play later on.
Apart from the standard upgradeable skills you get to manage your squad load-out meaning guns, gear and implants. All of these feel pretty varied and provide an impact on the way you take on a mission. Some loud-outs are in fact better suited for certain missions than other - all depending on the mission type and facilities you're breaching, and your preffered game play. The amount of customisation here was pretty cool.
There is also a cloning layer - a place where you take people and by assigning them to your squad members you enhance their abilities - but I found it pretty much useless - didn't understand the concept to well and ignored it entirely. It felt wonky and combined with often dying and loosing the bonuses felt like just too much work for little gain.
Visually it's quite nice. The cyberbpunk atmosphere is there and looks really good. Although seems to be very power hungry. Sure, you can zoom in pretty close and it still lookes good but it's unplayable while zoomed in. So I was completly zoomed out the entire time. The camera for whatever artistic reason is constantly bobbing slightly left and right - didn't make me feel nauseous but I imagine it could make some people. Overall it felt like totally unnecessary thing with no way of turning it off. The graphic in general was looking good - very neon like - and fitting the setting.
The game is divided into four districts - each of follows a familiar assassin creed like structure. You have relay beacons - which when discovered reveal additional missions of which most are somewhat secondary missions but you should complete them in order to get money and experience to equip your squad and level up certain skills in preparation for the final confrontation. Sadly there are only like around five different mission types and although accompanied with large amounts of text boil down to "navigate a complex and enter a certain highlighted door". Sometimes a target you need to kill comes out of it, sometimes you get prototypes you need to carry out of the compound, or escort a certain npc in - or just enter. That's about it - the only difference will be the layout of specific facility and toughness of the enemies.
The main resource in this game is time. It's money actually, but the way you get money is by installing hacking syphons in ATM machines, which give you money over time. Which is very easily exploitable - you just need to wait to get enough time to get prototypes from black marked - which are expensive - and research them - which takes time and money but since you're not limited in any way - the time is all you need.
There is a strange kind of mechanic in the game where you need to die, and you should die in order to get experience and level up quicker. The way it is designed is for when one of your squad members is killed he should be re spawned at the relay beacon and come back to action shortly. It doesn't work that way though - for most of the time - when things get too hairy - it's over. All of your squad members get killed and you can approach the mission again with little or no consequences. But it's worth it as sending your troops for certain death adds experience which is quite valuable. The game is also susceptible to cheesing the hell out of it. Hiding in the corner and killing off one by one enemy - it's hard to tell what will trigger alarm, what will not. Additionally your hacker can hijack enemies and thus add them to your squad - making them natural cannon fodder.
The game has a bit strange paste to it. It's slow at first - you're always under equiped with low tier guns, and no money. The enemies are also a bit hard at first in comparison to your setup. This leads to tackling the first mission very stealthy - luckily the game allows for such approach and you still get experience from doing things without causing mayhem. It gets better over time and things start balancing out and stealth stops being the only viable option.
I'm glad I've stuck through the beginning part as the game picked up somewhere along mid-game and starts getting interesting. The mid and end game is far more interesting as you're much better equipped and have a lot more room for taking different approaches to each mission.
The thing this begs for is an active pause though. It would change the game significantly and i feel for the better. As things stand right now there is no other way than just move your squad as a whole. There is just to little time for any flanking or other clever maneuvering. The slow-down time ability is there for the hacker but it has almost no meaningful impact on the game play.
Overall in the end I found the game to be enjoyable despite a bit repetitive and not giving a lot of control of the action when things get spicy. I have a feeling that making small changes to the game play would make the game much more enjoyable than it is but as it stands it's still worth picking up and trying out yourself.

I really wanted to like this game. I grew up on the original Syndicate and Syndicate Wars, and happily completed them both, so I was really looking forward to something in the same vein. Satellite Reign delivers on the feel and the style... but sadly botches the approach by screwing up the difficulty level.
In Syndicate, even a basic level agent was more than a match for a security guard, but in SR in the first few levels you are embarassingly outgunned and generally weaker than enemies you are facing. Combine that with the random nature of the cover simulator, and your team can be emptying shotguns in to guards at zero range to no effect... if they're even doing that with the non-existent AI.
As such, the first section of the game simply has to be played as a stealth game. Not in the high profile/low profile of the old games either, where you sneak in and the open up suddenly once inside the perimiter, but as pure stealth, sneaking up behind enemies unaware for headshots, as any other approach simply doesn't do enough damage to kill even a single enemy before alarms are sounded and every nearby enemy descends on you.
While annoyingly limiting, this approach does work for the first few small areas... and then you hit your first compound. These are huge sections of the map where there is no low profile option. Being seen there immediately sounds alarms, and you are promply rushed by a dozen guards from all directions, who will either kill your team or escort them off site. When that happens... the compound resets. All the guards that you have patiently spent an hour removing are back, and you have to do it all over again. After the sixth time trying to progress through the first compound after a trivial pathing error scrubbed an hours progress, (because the stealth mechanics suck, enemies home straight in on silenced weapons unless you do a stealth kill, which even with a sniper rifle requires that you be virtually sitting in their lap, and being spotted at all is effectively an instant fail) I gave up in disgust.
The worst part is that you can see that there are so many cool toys potentially available to get round these problems. There are gear and cyberware tabs that are completely empty after hours of play, because all of that stuff is locked behind stupidly hard missions you have to complete with nothing more than the starting gear. This could be a great game... but that greatness is locked behind opening areas that discourage experimentation and force mind numbing levels of repetition until you get everything exactly right in a real time situation.
As I said, I'd really have liked to enjoy this... there's potential in there. But the designers seem to have made a colossal mistake in locking what might be a really good Syndicate successor with free-form gameplay behind a poorly designed out and horribly punishing stealth game.

Just plain great.  I've had this one for a while and it has always been on the back burner, but I finally got to it, and it is worth every second of gameplay.  The puzzles can be occasionally frustrating (but never too difficult), and the controls are a little tough to get used to on the keyboard.  But the game and the story it tells makes everything worthwhile.
The musical choices are simple but perfect - you'll know exactly what I mean during the taxi scene.  The personal stories, learned by reading the diaries and descriptions, are heart-wrenching.  And the art is absolutely perfect - it's serious enough to be an enjoyable side scroller without being silly.  But the simplicity of it all helps keep the player from becoming too distracted to focus on what's important (the stories of the protagonists) while also helping the player focus on all the important details, from the puzzle solutions to the undeniably horrible realities of war.  It creates a great combination of the slow down time punctuated by moments of frenzied confusion that I can only imagine war to be.
Also, like others said, there are a couple tear-jerker moments.  As it should be, because war makes men mad.

Fight the Dragon is a  very nice mini-hack&slash game where you play through several maps that have been created by the community. And I have to say that there are some really nice maps that are fun to play. But there are also maps that aren't thought out so well. But you (and the rest of the community) votes on the map and you can decide to only play maps that have a high community rating. Some people have really interesting ideas for their maps so this game never gets boring.
If you expect a storyline in this game, you won't find any because this is not about long-spanning adventures but more about dungeon-runs that do not take that much time. So, if you have a busy life, it's easy to fit in a FtD session inbetween your busy schedule.
The level editor is also very nice and intuitive. It's really not surprising that the number of maps for this game has exploded.
So, who should buy this game? You should buy this if you like
-Hash and Slash games (like Diablo)
-Looting and equipment management.
-Building your own maps/dungeons and share them
-Multiplayer gaming with your friends
-fighting hordes of monsters with weapons and spells
-solving puzzles (in some maps)
Things you might expect but that are not there:
-Skilltrees. Each class has a fixed set of abilities that unlock at specific levels
-A storyline. But future updates might allow map creaters to link maps to create more epic adventures
-Item trading (but you can drop items ingame for your friends)
-Always a dark atmosphere like in Diablo. Some maps are dark and menacing, but sometimes the overall visual style is a bit too non-threatening. While the graphics are not as spiffy as in Diablo, I think 3sprockets has done a good job with the visuals.
A note for Linux users: There is a thread in the game's forum about systems that are capable of running the game. I'm playing this game just fine with Intel graphics. So check out the thread to see if someone with a similar computer managed to run the game.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

After having completed the game I can say it has it's good qualities. However, those good qualities are shrouded in deficiencies. The shot reticle gets spaztic if you don't position yourself for a CLEAR shot (ie. no foliage, windows, posts, rails.) in close proximity of the aimpoint. Then you fast travel (if you're lucky enough for it to allow FT.) and the glow of the headlights is all you see where the vehicle should be. The machine guns have a bug in the weapons cache. You select the option to top off and the game takes your IGC and shows being full til you exit the cache, then you have maybe 2-3 full mags rather that the (I presume) 999 rounds of ammunition that you just spent around 23,000 IGC on (for the large cap. MG.) The "workbench" (feeble attempt at a crafting system) is mediocre at best. One is better off just mashing the top off option on each item in teh weapon's cache. Load screens are annoyingly long (even with a SSD). after having played the other 2 SGW games in preperation for the release of SGW3 ( and just solely based on the apparent general trend of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥finish game realeases we have experienced as of late)i expected this game to have its issues. but not to the extent that it is for what is supposed to be a "finished product". All in all i will give this game about a 6.5/10 rating. it's really not all that bad if you can manage to look past the bugs and lack of originally promised content. And the story itself does hold some substance. ( though it was kinda transparent/ predictable outcomes) CI has a good idea here but somewhat poorly executed.

I have extremely mixed feelings about Satellite Reign. I guess, I can cautiously - very cautiously - recommend this game, but Satellite Reign has a significant number of flaws. So, what this game can offer?
First of all, there is dense atmosphere of cyberpunk. Action takes place in amazingly beautiful futuristic city: from dirty slums to sterile high-tech streets flooded with neon light... endless streams of cars and crowds of citizens rush through the streets, police and corporate guards are doing their daily patrols, drones and cameras vigilantly search for those who do not fit into the system. Surroundings in Satellite Reign are really well done. Spend a little time, walk the streets, admire the scenery - it is worth it.
There is a huge amount of weapons, implants, gadgets and other "cyberpunk stuff", so player can improve and customize his characters. At the very beginning of the game agents will be equipped only with pistols and light guns, but even first successful missions will bring a decent variety of equipment.
There is a solid stealth system. To avoid patrols, cameras and security systems, player must plan his actions and improvise. Each complex is a labyrinth full of cameras, turrets and guards, and in each case there are two or three possible routs to target. For example, you can go through the main gate, or use a rope, or bribe a guard and enter side door, or sneak through a ventilation shaft. When it comes to skirmish, opponents are trying to be smart: they use cover, call for help and attack agents from flanks.
Unfortunately, there are more than enough flaws in this game too. So:
Storyline is very weak. Game offers tons of text, which is completely useless, as it does not affect anything. You can go through the game completely without reading a single line of briefings.
In my opinion game is very monotonous and this is the main problem. All quests fit in short formula - "go in, hack target, go out". Whatever briefing tells you, goals are always the same. Did you successfully completed your first mission? Well, all other missions will be exactly the same, only the scenery will be replaced and enemies will be more powerful.
As for enemies. During the whole game you will fight with same set of opponents: raw conscript, heavy infantry, commander with shield, drone, robo-dog, stationary turret and jammer. At late stages you will encounter heavy robots, but there are not many of them. That is all. Where are the agents of rival corporations? Looks like there is only four guys in whole city who are smart enough to use sniper rifles, hacking tools and field medicine, and these four guys are... our team. In my opinion enemies are quite boring.
Skirmishes sometimes are looking like Benny Hill Show. Well, enemies are trying to be smart, but they are not, and this causing a tons of funny (or stupid) situations, corporate security acts... very strange, speaking mildly. Soldiers, marching right into poison gas, or unable to find your agent, who hides right under their noses - this is very typical for Satellite Reign. As for final battle... well, "defeat same guy for three times" - this is... ugh!
Economic system is horrible, in fact all you need is time. Just hack a couple of ATM and wait, your money reserve will grow slowly but surely. You do not need to plan your expenses, you always can wait and, well, drink some tea while hacked ATM are providing you with infinite income. There are no choices and no planning, just waiting.
"Huge living city" is not so huge and definitely is not so alive. Cars are aimlessly rolling around in circles and you can not interact with them. Theoretically, there are three factions in game, but it does not affect anything, corporations do not interact with each other, only occasionally you can see how a patrol shoots an unfortunate NPC who accidentally wandered into restricted area. Yes, city looks great. But it is just scenery. City is dead. And do not expect that evening news will tell about bold bank robbery, which your team did yesterday...
Last small drop. City looks great and pretty, but inhabitants of city are... not pretty. I hardly can accept what the characters in this game look like. Soldiers of corporate security are looking excellent in their futuristic armor, but common citizens... they all are clowns or what? I can accept it when it comes to Downtown where all sorts of punks and freaks are living, but inhabitants of high class districts? In my opinion, this clothes are just ridiculous.
Underdone. Unfinished. Unpolished. This is the words that are best suited for Satellite Reign. I really hoped that developers will release a couple of updates (I even agree for DLC), which will expand and enhance the gameplay. Unfortunately, this did not happen, and Satellite Reign is still a raw gem, nothing more.
Well... Satellite Reign is not a bad game, but I can not call it good. It is... average. If you love cyberpunk style - grab this game for cheap at huge sale. Despite incompleteness, Satellite Reign can offer some decent fun, just do not expect much.

Ok. Here's the thing; There ARE moments of greatness in SR, and feelings of great accomplishment when you finally break into the high sec safe, or pull out alive from an intense firefight! However, there are a few issues that, for me, seriously damper the potential that exists in this games execution.
+ you cannot save when you want. ONLY at save stations and it remembers your "checkpoints". So if you get all the way in the base and steal the plans, well you have to get all the way back out again before you can save your progress. If you get caught and things get dicey,....FAIL. Start over. Now, i can appreciate this as a tool to build suspense and challenge....this wouldnt be such a bad thing if perhaps my agents responded to my commands better...however...
+ Controls, can be "finicky" at times (that is an understatement by the way). This comes down to just as much "human error" i suppose, In that perhaps in my moment of panic i click just left a micrometer of an agent instead of right on him, or because my attention is diverted to a sec camera thats about to go off i didt see the barely visible difference between a spent skill and one ready to go....Path finding can be wonky. Sometimes my agents simply just wont respond to a command. They do just stand there and absorb fire without returning fire, which i think is silly. You have to cvommand them to fire back. The game is challenging enough. You really have to babysit these agent and make double sure that your orders are going through. Which wouldnt be suuuuuch a greivous offence...
+ if i could pause the game. This to me is its biggest issue. There is simply too many things for me to handle at once and dealing with frankly subpar AIs and pathfinding and control woes, it just becomes frustrating. You can sink 20 minutes into a perfectly executed mission only to have the game sabatoge you because one of your agents gets stuck and gets caught and then the whole base is on defcon 5, your guys dead in seconds. It can happen, often. Are these situations salvagable? Yeah, and its damn exciting and satisfying when you do manage to pulll off a miracle. But id rather just be able to freaking pause, and issue orders and assess. With the aformentioned issues...this challenge is too great. The stress too high. The frustration outweighs the moments of true glee.
Alone, each of these issues is not a huge problem at all, but all at once, they mount in an extremely aggravating play session. Somewhere in this game, is another game that needs to be made. Better. More polish. The systems really fleshed out. I loved syndicate, and i love love love anything cyber punk, so my heart is in this game, but, it mostly just pisses me off if im not in the most patient of moods and i alt out....

This hurts, because I really wanted to like this game. I really, really did.
Visually, it's nice. The classic rain-slick streets of cyberpunk, the visual distinction between the districts should, in theory, give each a personality, but they all feel rather dull, like a blank canvas. The cyberpunk aesthetic is rarely done right anymore, so that got me in (that and a deep sale discount) and meant I gave the game more of a leash than I probably should have. Unfortunately, that's about the extent of the good.
Everything goes to Hell after the tutorial. Because there's no tactical pause, managing your way through the restricted areas where most of the game's action takes place becomes a tedious process. You have to camp out in a spot out of sight for several minutes to put together a plan of action and execute that plan in real time while simultaneously managing more than one or all four agents, which can take quite a while and can lead to a lot of mistakes that could be avoided by the implementation of pretty much the only common combat mechanic among isometric RPGs. This is presumably a design choice to echo Syndicate, which the game claims at its spiritual predecessor. What it is in reality is a swing, a miss, and a batter hitting himself in the back of the head on his own follow-through. Hard.
That leads me to the combat, which is a complete disaster and where the game decisively falls apart for me. Enemies are bullet sponges to the 'nth degree while your team is made of tissue paper by comparison. The aforementioned lack of tactical pause makes managing firefights untenable; you will frequently be reloading your last save if you get spotted, which means you might've just wasted 45 minutes getting into a place only to get TPK'd on the way out and having to start over from scratch. I had that happen a time or two and eventually gave up, not just on those missions, but on Satellite Reign as a whole.
I'm all for a game being difficult or challenging the player at first to build a sense of progression, but that progression only materializes at the expense of hours of tedium and slogging through poor design choices here. Spend your time and money elsewhere.

Very cool game about a game.  D-n-Desque single and co-op that has a nice interface and unique (at least to me)  game play.  Basically you are playing against the DM on various maps and the goal is to complete 3 missions per scenario.  Each mission is progressively tougher.  It is your team against the DM.  In turn based combat you cast spells, attack, or move about the board to defeat the oponent or achieve specific goals.  You do this by drawing random cards from your deck.  Your deck is built, based upon the type of equipment you are wearing or using.  So a certain shield might give you three cards, two of which are defence and one offence.  A certain sword would give you 5 attacks.  As you get higher in level you are able to use better equipement and get better cards.  This is an excellent, simple, well put together game.  And it's free!  Of course you can make micro-purchases which I have done.  It helps get better equipment and scenarios (free game has a ton, though).  Mostly I made the purchase to support the developers.  An excellent and fun game that is worthy of earning some real coin.  I see some comments regarding a need to pay to progress.  Not true.  I have played solo and with freinds (max 3 per group so far).  We just now, at lvl 9+, decided to purchase items and only as support of devs.  Maybe this need is true at higher levels but even so, considering the time we have into it, I'd say the cost is very reasonable.

Nowadays, modern video games always include classic video game references, such as Mario, Sonic and Zelda, in order to make them more old school and nostalgia to it. But RCR isn't only that but it's also a game that WAS meant for old school fans of video games. It was originally meant to be a remake of GTA III under the title Grand Theftendo but was later changed into a original game in 2007 with the title being changed to Retro City Rampage.
Story focuses on a guy simply named player who was working on a bank heist with the Jester until he time travels to the year 20XX where a young scientist names Doc Choc finds him and helps him get back to his year, 1985, by finding pieces of the time machine which breaks down when you travel
Gameplay does have a GTA feel to it in 8-Bit but also throws in many video game references within the first 4-5 minutes of the game. Theirs also references to classic shows and movies from the 80's. You can also do side jobs in order to make lots of money. And you can even play as famous characters from indie games such as, Super Meat Boy, Steve from Minecraft and Commander Video from the Bit.Trip series.
I say get this game if your a hugh fan of classic games or if you love the GTA series as well. You will be hooked in.

They're still smoothing out the combat (which takes more cues from Gauntlet than modern ARPGs), adding more tilesets and enemies, and developing more classes. But it's a thoroughly pleasant experience for an Early Access game. The dungeon-building is intuitive and well-developed, even at this stage. Updates and regular and substansial, and the developers respond to player feedback. Highly reccomended, especially if, like me, you enjoyed the park builder in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater or the dungeon builder in Neverwinter more than the actual game.

Great game for fans of turn based strategy games done in a single sitting.
Here are my first thoughts after 50 hours.  About 5 hours single player and 45 multiplayer, so I'm definitely focusing on the PvP aspect, though I suppose some might even enjoy single player.
Pros:
+ Great graphics
+ Original and fun gameplay mechanics
+ Pretty good gameplay balance
+ Healthy multiplayer community (rarely more than 30 seconds of queue time)
+ Good loot drop system, especially if you enjoy the Steam marketplace
Cons:
- No replay system (probably the most obvious oversight), especially being a turn-based strategy game)
- No option for a full overhead view, which would be extremely helpful.
- No campaign besides the tutorial
- Very little voice acting
- Technical issues with sound (certain sounds consistently come in crackly, perhaps poor recording?)
- Lots of waiting for your opponent(s) (=overly long matches)
- Some bugs/unexpected behavior with card effects
- RNG + long match time = anti-fun (see below)
I didn't mention RNG itself as a pro or a con, because I think it can go either way depending on the player's taste.  There is too much RNG to bank on being able to pull off a particular strategy each game, but that can be viewed as a good thing since it forces a player to cosider all options at all times.  However, the problem here is that your match usually comes down to a single dice roll (attacking the king), which can be very frustrating at times.  You can outplay your opponents the entire match and go into that dice roll and fail miserably (lose the game), which would be fine with an RNG-type game like this if it weren't for the fact that you spent 45-90 min leading up to it.
IMO, the game should have been made with a slightly smaller board with only 3 players (instead of 4).  This would take the average game down down to something more managable like 30 min.
Despite all of the cons, the fact is that this game a lot of fun, even for an RNG-hater like me.

Armello is an online multiplayer board game (although there's an offline single player option against AI, too) set in the Kingdom of, you guessed it, Armello, ruled by a mad lion king who's infected with Rot. It's your job--as one of eight (twelve with DLC) heroes from one of the four clans--to reclaim Armello by winning the throne, however you choose to do that. You can kill the king with pure strength or healing spirit stones, gain the most prestige in the land to usurp him when the time comes, or become even more corrupted than he is.
The gameplay itself is based predominantly on dice and cards: cards grant you skills or bonuses on the field or in battle, while dice are rolled in battle itself to determine your attacks and defence. Of course, this means that luck--or the RNG--can disadvantage you, even in your starting hand, and the AI can utilize rings and tokens (which modify your character's stats during a game) that you have to unlock. In the couple of games that I've played thus far, I've felt a little as if the AI had more opportunity than I did, but I was still able to win.
My only real complaint would be that, although beautiful (as is the rest of the game's graphics), the maps are fairly similar and feel a little small to me. I'm sure this is to keep the game moving and to force players into conflict, but it's a little annoying when you're trying to get to a certain square and all of your possible movements are blocked or risky to take. The game rules themselves are customizable, but not so much the maps.
I would definitely recommend Armello if you enjoy a mix of strategy-based board games (with a hint of luck thrown in there thanks to dice rolling!). It's a beautiful game with a simple but clear story that wouldn't be out of place in Brian Jacques' Redwall series, and it's entertaining to play.

I do recommend it, but i have issues with the combat. First, the game focuses mostly on production and logistics which usually isn't my cup of tea, but it does a good job and it is definitely fun to build your base/factory and produce all your own items. Now for those expecting standard combat/shooting mechanics, there isn't much to the combat at all. It is frustuarting because the idea of building my own little empire whilst defending against an alien swarm was really appealing. You quickly learn how to easily cheese with turrets, shooting boils down to spacebar to win, and the AI only knows how to run straight into the meat grinder. It really leaves a lot to be deisred.
If the dev's are listening, i can see so much potential in this game regarding how better combat mechanics can really give you a sense of agency, and that you are this solo engineer trying to survive on a hostile alien world by expanding, advancing, claiming territory and basically building your own little empire against an encroaching alien swarm. I REALLY want a combat overhaul sometime in the future that adds standard shooting mechanics: guns having actual bullet projectiles that the player manually aims (instead of the 'spacebar to win' lock on system it is currently), more 'intelligent' and challenging AI that doesn't just swarm you, and more variety in the types of biters. (The name for the aliens) I understand that the game is in early access and that you are focusing on polishing the base game, so i mostly give it a pass. However, i do expect think that this game is of a quality that it DESERVES to see an overhaul to combat; in my opinion there really isn't any reason in 2017 to not expect some of the most basic combat and shooting mechanics, especially out of a game that seems to do everything else fairly well.

YOSE vs. Original: Better graphics, not much else.
SoD either version is a really fun zombie beat-em-up with lots of driving, looting, and fighting. The base building aspects are very simple and contribute little to the game. For the most part, this game is best as a quick-session "let's see if I can't find some goodies and kill some things" game. In fact, playing for more than an hour or so is probably not the best idea, as the game's new things to throw at you become stale after about that long. It uses a mix of real and game time to progress things while you're not playing, meaning it rewards you for playing a little every day instead of long play sessions. Combat is great fun, forcing you to come up with new strategies as the game gets more difficult. Your main enemy is actually scarcity more than it is the monstrous zeds, which are more of an obstacle than anything since you can  never truly win against them.
SoD is not a perfect game at all. Certainly some of the features seem half-baked. There are only two settings to explore, then memorize and master, and the lack of anything new to see can get stale. Your impact on the setting is very limited, and fleeting. The original game's story is kinda meh, Lifeline's is better, and Breakdown doesn't have a story.
However, I have a hard time finding a better game to fill the role that SoD fills, as a simple, short-session, couch sitter.

Best dust simulator I have ever played! It was like I couldn't even see the game behind all the particle effects!
I bought this mainly for the single player, and frankly I don't remember it being this buggy (I first played it on PS3 a few years ago) I mainly got it because it was on sale for like $7 dollars and I had a bit of nostalgia for it.
First the dust/snow is a BIG problem. Half the time I can't see what I'm shooting at because of the all the freaking dust flying around, and I have to get lucky if the cloud breaks up a little bit to shoot the enemy. Worst yet the enemies have impeccable aim, despite you not being able to see a damn thing through the fog of war.
The other half of the time while driving, is not being able to see where you're freaking driving for more than 5 metres away! some of it is luck based, and the other times I have to take my eyes off the road to look at the minimap. I understand that DICE want to show off their physics and environment engines, but you have to draw the line somewhere because it's hindering my ability to even play the game.
It makes it infinitely worse since the checkpoints are bizarre and poorly placed, I have to start whole sequences again because I died for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reasons.
Both the enemy and friendly AI are horribly inconsistent and buggy. In a certain sequence where I had to fight two helicopters, this was a good example of useless AI companions and unfair bugs. My squad mate said to me "I'll cover your six, you focus on the helicopters". The thing is with this games enemy behaviour, the enemy will prioritise you as a threat more than your friend who was MEANT to cover you. Instead an enemy with a shotgun just waltzed up to me and shot me in the back. Apparently my buddy thought it was a better idea to shoot at the sky instead. So I hope you enjoy wiping red jam off your face for 30 seconds over and over again in cover, copping rocket fire, bullets and dust while your friends can wonder freely around.
As for bugs, in the same sequence I was TRYING to shoot down some helicopters with a TOW missle. The first helicopter was pretty easy to take down, but the second one you shoot with a missile it will literally TELEPORT 500 metres away and reset its damage. In this time I try to refocuse on the magical helicopter from another demension, only to get shot in the back because my "highly trained" comrade was watching over me... and I have to start the entire sequence thanks to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ checkpoint.
The point where I quit the game was where I did all the above for about 20 minutes, only to run into the last guy with a rocket launcher. I went to stab him out of reflex, blood actually flew out and I thought I killed him. I motioned to move away and I realised, no I didn't kill him. Instead he freaking stabs me despite my knife registering a hit.
Overall this game was pretty impressive show piece at the time, but the nostalgia has been ruined by bugs, stupid/unfair AI and ♥♥♥♥ING DUST. I played on the highest settings and on normal difficulty. If you really want to pick up this game, get it when it goes on sale. For me however I came in expecting a fun time, instead it left a pretty bad taste in my mouth.

Very heart-touchingly good. This game proves that war story does not have to focus on combats to be good, a rarity among video games about war. Valiant Hearts: The Great War allows you to follow along the side of numerous different characters. The storyline is very well written considering none of the characters through the whole game say a single word. This game relies on its beautiful art style, its carefully chosen soundtrack, and its educational cut scenes to tell its story.
The game is inspired by letters that were written during World War I. You will have the opportunity to be 4 different characters as you aid a German through his journey through the war. This story is about friendships, sacrifice, survival and true dedication. The story will tug at your heartstrings at times, since it does often focus on how the war would tear families apart. However you will also be moved by the acts of heroism from complete strangers that become unlikely allies on your journey.
This game was developed for all sorts of players. Gameplay can be difficult at times since this game is a puzzle solving game. Not all the puzzles are too difficult, but they do offer somewhat of a challenge. I did find myself asking for help on a few occasions due to the level of detail some of these levels have to them. Aside from the difficulty of a select few levels, you will really come to appreciate the creativeness and beautiful scenery illustrated in the story. As you complete the various levels in the game, you are presented with boxes that contain historical information that is optional for players to read further if the topics are of interest.
Overall this is a great game that ties in many different components to attract all sorts of different audiences. The story does not overwhelm you with violence, but a story that allows you to hold onto things such as hope and heroism.  You will have more of a focus on the characters and their experiences rather than the violence associated with the time period, which makes the game suitable for all ages. This game is definitely worth giving it a try. It is most likely not like other games you have experienced before.

Absolutly LOVED this game, both fun and very educational and tells a very emotional story based on actual letters from the Great War. Feels like you're living through a children's book, but one with a very artistic and powerful tone to it that makes the gamer take it seriously. It makes you wander through the destruction and horror that scarred the earth in the years of 1914-1918 which shall remain as one of history's most crucial and pivotal time period. This game is EXTREMELY emotional, and I finished the game crying. A true masterpiece of what educational games should be. If I were a history teacher, I'd have my students play this to learn about the Great War. Like I said, this game is a Masterpiece and shall remain as memorable and heartwarming one. Follows Emile, a grandfather and a father-in-law to a German Soldier (Karl) as he fights in the French Army and endures the horrors of one of greatest conflicts that has forever shocked this world to its deepest core. Loveable characters with simple yet fun gameplay and a story that every gamer must play through. Warning: You will cry playing this game, trust me. If you think the endings to both the Last of Us or the TellTales Walking Dead are sad and emotional. This one tops them both combined.

Valiant Hearts is an absolutely incredible game.  It's the only game I really felt I needed to review.
The story is the sole reason why you need to play this game.  It follows a small group of people, each of which had separate lives at the start, and shows the war through each of their perspectives, how it affected them, and how it caused them to come together. Valiant Hearts does an excellent job at conveying the characters and really makes you feel
for each one.  It spends lots of time showing the horrors of war and all the sacrifices that go with it. Probably the best part about the overall story is that it depicts war not as people vs people, but as a force that craves human death and sacrifice.  It has truly changed my view on war, forever.
The art is absolutely incredible in this game as well.  So while the style is somewhat cartoony, the artists selected the perfect color palette to truly sell the mood that this game is going for and prevent it from being light-hearted.  That's not to say this game is ALL serious though.  There are some small comedic parts that lighten the mood and have some "cartoon physics" in them.  You can also just look at the screenshots if you want to know more about the graphics.  They're great.
Unfortunately, this is Valiant Hearts weakest part.  There's certainly nothing wrong with the gameplay mechanically, but it can get dull and slow at times. The reason for this slow pacing is to keep the atmosphere serious, realistic, and grounded.  While it is a smart move for the atmosphere, the gameplay overall suffers.  I personally am ok with this.  I do think this is a worthy trade.  One nice part of the gameplay is traveling through all the beautiful background environments.  They are all gorgeous and they all help build the mood.  Just know you won't be coming back to this game for the gameplay like you would for a game like Ori and the Blind Forest.
This is another high point for Valiant Hearts! The soundtrack is on par with every moment and can really pull you into the action and drama of the world.  Hard to say anything else here, just know,
If there's one thing that I mentioned in just about every section, it was the mood.  All the various parts of the game build the mood.  Even though it can be rather depressing, its a fantastic experience.  Like I said above, it has completely changed my views.  Perhaps the story might not hit you as hard as it did to me but, this was the first game ever to truly make me cry.  Now I've played some sad games before, but this game, threw me over the edge.  It will forever have a special place in my heart.
This game deserves so much more praise and publicity than it has received. Hopefully they will make a part 2!
