When I first saw Armello, I thought that with the old Disney style animations it would be aimed for a younger audience, and I didn't put much thought to it. I thought it wasn't my kind of game. Then I eventully bit the bullet and bought it.
And damn, this is actually a remarkably good game.
Armello is a board game set in the Kingdom of... well, Armello. You play as one of several animal heroes who are all vying for the throne of the kingdom. The King has gone mad with a disease called the Rot and when he dies, the most prestigous hero will become the next monach... unless someone kills him first.
It's quite clear as you look deeper in that despite the Disney style animation and the colorful graphics, this is a much, much darker game than it seems at first glance. The events that take place in the game, along with the dialogue and info on the cards tells a mucher darker story than what you would expect in the lore.
You can select upto eight heroes, one from each of the four animal clans, being wolf, rat, rabbit and bear with the vanilla game, though one additional DLC grants you four new heroes and there are four more as part of a new Bandit Clan on the way. Each of these heroes has different stats and a unqiue perk to start off with and you can mix and match different rings and amulets to change up how that hero handles in game.
The gameplay itself is easy to learn but is remarkably complex. Four players take turns moving around the board, taking settlements, completing quests, dealing with the King's Guard and Bane NPCs, the perils and of course, the other Heroes themselves. There is a day and night cycle which changes the conditions on the board and makes some Heroes stronger than others. As you play through the game, you can complete quests which allow you to level up your characters stats as you go along.
You have a selection of cards to pull out of three decks, Item, Magic and Trickery, which lets you equip items or you can use them with their varying affects. Such as damaging another character or putting on one of the perils on the board.
All combat and peril solving is done with dice rolls, any cards you have equipped or effects that have been applied to you can alter how much attack or defence you have guarenteed or how many dice you have amongst other things. Dice in the game aren't just RNG either, they are physically rolled much like real dice, although this can be a small pain for lower spec   PCs.
This mix of dice and card based gameplay allows for varied tactics and approaches which often vary depending on who you play as. You can either enhance your character's strengths or remove the weaknesses to balance the character out. Each board is different each time and it offers varying oppitunities to play your game in different ways, and with four different ways to win, each game can be quite different.
Now, the only con I've noticed is one you can't really eliminate with this kind of game with dice and cards. Luck is a big thing. There is a good chance someone is going to get all the good cards at the right time or get through without a scratch and go on to dominate the game. Others might not get anything good at all and fall behind the curve. Since there is no comeback mechanic other than getting lucky, this could leave one player just dominating and another player just left to wonder around the board unable to challenge someone or deciding to quit.
Or those damn card players who get all the attack cards and keep killing you before you get close or slowing you down. It's really frustrating.
Likewise, luck can quickly change the tide of the game quickly and as the game begins to draw to a close you can feel the tension as you try and play your approach and hope your luck holds. It's a little bit annoying but it's also what makes the game catch your attention and keep you invested.
Regardless, tactics and strategy still apply, which can carry you through a game. The games can be quite long though, easily coming upto an hour or more, so keep that in mind.
The game has quite a few things in it, singleplayer and multiplayer is both around, you have a card collection to see all the well drawn and animated cards you have come across in the game. All the games you complete will also give to a chance to get a chest or a key, combining the both together can give you dice you can use in the game itself.
Both singleplayer and multiplayer offer numerous options to change up the standard gameplay, which is a nice touch.
Now, some content you have to buy, though none of it's pay to win and it's not ridculously priced whilst adding additional heroes and new map styles, so it's worth the extra dosh.
All in all, Armello was an unexpected little gem, it's a bit rough around the edges but whetever you are a furry or not, this game is certainly worth your while, with additional content on it's way. It's definitely worth your time.

Early Access Review:
First let me point out that Fight The Dragon is fun and addictive. Once you start getting some better gear and how the game plays, you'll be hooked for hours.
In a nutshell, Fight The Dragon is an isometric ARPG where you hack and slash your way thru bandit camps, dungeons and graveyards. You pick up loot and level up your character. But that's where the twist of the game comes in. These levels you'll go thru are user-created, which means other players like yourself, created them. Level creation is another aspect of the game as you are given the ACK(Adventure Construction Kit) which allows you to design your own level, may it be a pillaged town or a dark and gruesome dungeon. ACK works like a 3D modeling software. There are a lot of tools that you can play around with and you can design the dungeon to your own liking, and I mean a lot, you can put traps, enemies, build rooms, put up decorations, set up puzzles and many more, the sky is the limit. This on the other hand have a downside to it such as other players tend to make troll maps.
The leveling system of the game is the usual as you get experience points from killing mobs and bosses, and the equipment system is typical. On the other hand, they present these systems with a clean and sleek designed hud which is a good touch and a great help to user experience.
You can replay old dungeons if you wanna grind to get better gear and experience as everything follows to your level. and same with new characters.
And with the title, you get to fight The Dragon ofcourse, after you level and gear up, there's a seperate instance where you can go in and fight The Dragon. The Dragon has huge life points but damage carries over even after death. This is a great way to see how much damage you can make and see the improvements of your new gear. As of the moment though, defeating The Dragon has no rewards yet, but this is understood since the game is still in Alpha.
On the side note though, the game feels it lacks sounds as if you turn the music down, you won't really hear anything other than the "thud" that your weapon makes when it hits an enemy, which to my opinion also lacks kick.
Overall, Fight The Dragon is a must have title for fans of the genre and dungeon master sims as well. I personally will follow how the game progresses and hope that it's for the better, With 1418 maps(and counting) and the ACK, you'll be amaze how creative and very imaginative other players can be. You'll surely spend hours with Fight The Dragon.

Can't recommend this at full price. Finished the main story and side quests. Didn't bother with 1/3 of the POI's - bugs prevented me from doing some of them.
PROS
Sniping is fun if you like that sort of thing.
Open world.
Weapons feel 'meaty' and the gunplay (for the most part) is fun.
Combat can be quickly lethal if you get sloppy, so trying to stand in a hail of bullets will end you real quick - as it should be.
At max settings, visuals were average, but not terrible.
CONS
Bugs. Lots of bugs. I won't bother trying to list them here, but if you read the 'bug threads' in the discussion area you'll see what I mean.
The characters were very two dimensional and the story setup gave me no reason to be invested in any of the characters or to care much what happens to them. One female char in particular (let's call her 'cleavage girl'), seemed to have only been inserted into the mix so she could live up to her nickname.
Loads of predictable story 'twists' and overuse of the usual tired 'story twist' tropes.
_Terrible_ dialog + bland voice acting. The banter between characters was cringeworthy. First they hate each other. Seconds later they're best buds/comrades in arms. Moments later they hate each other again. I started to wonder if they were bipolar or something. It feels like the game designers/programmers decided to write the dialog themselves, instead of hiring a writer, or maybe it was not initially written in English and the translation is just bad?
The whole track/analyse game mechanic was interesting, but sadly, they only used it for a few fairly 'samey' things. It had the potential to be a diverse and useful aspect of the game, and it sort of feels like a missed opportunity.
Missions were fairly uniform and became somewhat repetitive. Towards the end of the game I didn't feel motivated to finish off many of the POI's (rescuing hostages etc) as there was little reward for doing so and it felt a bit pointless.
I only bothered to finish the main story to see if my guesses about the ending panned out. I'll avoid spoilers etc, but I will say that the ending was abrupt, unsatisfying, and cheesy as a wine and cheese night, without the wine.
If you like sniper games and this one's on sale for a decent discount, it might be worth grabbing. Otherwise, play Sniper Elite 4 instead, as it's a much more polished title.

Once again, paragon has released a game with great technical ideas and wonderful gameplay... in theory. In reality, you'll spend half the time playing this game figuring out and fixing bugs. Here is a list of the bigger bugs I ran into on my first playthrough.
-Settings can't be opened while connected to the internet, crashes the game.
-Spawning on top of invisible objects, immobile, while enemies kill you.
-Can't use any spell combinations since spacebar doesn't work, have to quickcast all spells.
-Can't change spacebar keybinding, even when offline.
When playing online, you'll often see enemies be randomly invincible or teleport, especially in larger groups. This is because not only are paragon servers a literal garbage bag full of rats, but also the game uses way too much bandwidth for most hosts, and is riddled with bugs. I regularly play 32 person FPS' with no problem, but 3 people in a magicka lobby is apparently two too many.
The game also has a number of glaring issues. The UI in multiplayer needlessly covers 1/4 of the screen across the bottom, and when clicked on, takes up about 1/3rd. This happens almost constantly, when you have 20+ enemies on the screen and are trying to manoeuver around the map casting spells.
It also isn't obvious when you're supposed to be moving forward and when you're supposed to be clearing waves of enemies. The camera movement in general is pretty sloppy, and doesn't prioritize showing enemies or the playable area over showing random background. Often you can be killed by melee enemies hiding under the UI while the top half of the screen is showing background.
You can also tell your character to move while in cutscenes, but it won't start until the scene ends, often resulting in walking off a cliff before you even know where you are.
The cutscenes are well written and voice acted, but were apparently chopped together by a 3 year old with safety scissors, and feel neither smooth nor natural, making them stilted to the point of being unwatchable. I'm really interested in the story and the jokes are great, but I can't handle the 4s wait between each character's line.
Enemies' weaknesses are often very difficult to guess, requiring dying over and over attempting different spells to see what each enemy is weak to, before being able to progess. I beat the game solo without figuring out what a dwarf wizard's weakness is.
The number of small issues that still need to be worked out (but won't, because this dev doesn't fix their work) goes on and on, but at this point in time, the game is too frustrating and bug-riddled to be worth playing, nevermind buying.
Obviously, there won't be any PvP because it requires balance, and you can't balance a game that filled with more bugs than a rotting oak tree. That is why wizard wars died. Hard.
It's a good game if someone wants wizzards. But if this game had a PvP mode would be great. !

State of Decay is a 3rd person open- world, zombie survival game, packed with great rpg elements, exploration and base building. Although some game mechanics are a bit older than nowadays standards, and rather poor optimization efforts, the game still revolutionizes the genre of zombie survival games.
Bringing in aspects that we see from a lot of survival games nowadays like, when your character dies, it's permanent, however instead of just respawning, you will have to use another character in your community, which really brings out the rpg aspects of the game, that you get to go do missions, or supply runs with other characters, which gives the game a flair of diversity.
With a lot of things to do in the game and a relatively big open world, with lots of weapons, characters to find and vehicles, you really can't go wrong with State of Decay. There will be lots of zombie action ahead. Aside from the main game, the YOSE edition also brings with it the Breakdown DLC that makes it technically possible to play forever, and the Lifeline DLC where you play as a military unit attempting to evac assets inside a whole new city. The DLC's that comes along with the YOSE edition, will definitely ensure a good deal of hours more in the game.
Definitely a buy for fans of the zombie open world survival genre, just not the 27,99€ worth, wait for an offer that is at least 50%.

My summary:
BUY IT! Valiant Hearts is a perfect blend of story, diverse gameplay, and puzzle solving.  Rooted in historical events, it is a powerful game that can move you to tears.  You follow a story which separates father and son on two different sides of the war.  Joining them, a US soldier with nothing to live for (save his friend Emile), a French field-medic trying to reach her father, and a loyal dog separated from its owner.  They will all struggle in the war until the end, and no one will ever be the same again.
Pros:
I really want to say my favorite game of all time but I think that would be going too far.  I think it may be my favorite indie-esque 2d game of recent memory, perhaps only with Bastion and To The Moon as competitors.  What I do like about it is it has less gameplay than bastion but more gameplay than To The Moon.  For me, it is the perfect mix of the two, and does both well.
Cons:
In general some of the puzzles are so not-obvious it becomes frustrating but they do provide a neat optional hint system.  The difficulty is also appreciated rather than dumbing them down completely.  Additionally a few elements like the medic revive functions (just mashing buttons in guitar hero fashion) is a bit of a downer to such an exciting game, but it is a very minor component of the game.
Story (9.5/10): Amazing, there are very few video games that can compare.  I have a few minor complaints about it but they aren't worth mentioning and I do not want to spoil the surprises along the way.
Art (9.5/10): Really unique and awesome, my ONLY complaint is that it can become a but blurry and pixelated when some of the sprites zoom in during cinematics.
Sound (10/10): From the mutterings in every language to the music to the narration this couldn't possibly be better.
Gameplay (9/10) Because of a few annoying puzzles that are almost intentionally obscure and the medical revive system which is bashing buttons, I can't give this a perfect score.  But everything else about it is perfect.  Seriously, it feels so good and just when you think a mechanic is getting old, you get put in a tank, car, or are dodging mines or gun fire.

All-in-all... A C- Game.  I had high hopes especially with people Sniper Elite working on the game.  Most of the sniper shots were within 200 meters, and even on the highest difficulty it was more of a point and click shooter then a sniper simulator.  In my opinion, SGW 2 was a better sniping game.
OVERALL SCORE: C-
Sniper Simulation: C-
Story:  B
Game Versitility: B
Crafting: F
Weapon Modifications: F
Purchasing System: F
The open world of SGW3 was nice, and most of the time I could choose my own path through a place, but you had to get too close to do anything.  There were only a few missions (like 3 or 4 of the whole set) where you took a shot over 200 meters.
SNIPING: C-
The only reason this gets any kind of score is there is wind and bullet drop.  SGW3 in♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ed drop adjustments on each scope, but the "clicks" were already figured out for you.  They also gave you a bar at the top that matched the marks on your scope for wind adjustment, so sniping came down to "choose the distance that most closly matched your target, put him in the same spot on your scope as the line on the top of your screen, and pull the trigger".  In SGW2, while I wish there were adjustments, I had to keep a dope chart handy for each rifle.  Much more realistic and challenging if you ask me.
STORY: B
The main story was well written, and the progression was such that game never felt like a complete grind.  The ending was a little cliche and happened too quickly for the long leadup.  I performed all the side missions and never quite understood what (other then XP) they gave me.  I fell the "Most Wanted" line was a waste of time and didn't provide any benefit to the game.
GAME VERSATILITY: B
The game gave you a good since of "attack this any way you want".  The warrior track was a bit of a pain (on the hardest difficulty) but you were given the option in most circumstances.  Every once in a while you were given a mission where you had to perform one of the 3 roles (provide sniper cover, infiltrate w/o being noticed, kill a bad guy and get out without anyone knowing you were there, etc).  The only reason it's not an A is the few and far between 500+ meter shots for sniping.
Crafting: F
The crafting system was a complete joke.  You ran around to points of interest, or found supplies in the middle of missions.  Then when you got back to your hideout, you could use the workbench to craft items.  I was really hoping that by crafting you could mod your weapon, make it more accurate, etc.  Truth is, you couldn't craft anything you couldn't buy, which was easily everything in the game (more on that later).  If you specifically go looking for crafting materials, you're wasting your time.
Weapon Modifications: F
After playing Tom Clancy games, I had high hopes for this, but again they let me down in a big way.  Want to adjust the fire rate on your weapons, or adjust barrel length for velocity? too bad... The following are all the modifications you get:  Ammo type (normal, AP, etc), Magazine size (S/M/L), silencer (Y/N), bipod (Y/N), paint, laiser pointer (Y/N).  Big, HUGE, letdown.
Purchasing System: F
In act 1, I was very hesitent to purchase anything.  By act 2, I had almost enough money to buy out everything in the game.  I never felt like I had to penny pinch, or make any real decision on what to purchase.
Overall, the story is the only thing that saved this game.  It gets a C- because it's one of the few "sniper like" games on the market, and the main story isn't 1/2 bad.  As far as sniping goes, it's a large downgrade from SGW2.

Valiant hearts: The great War... This game will kick your feels HARD. Like really, REALLY HARD.

(Only cons: REQUIRES UPLAY TO PLAY IT EVEN ON STEAM... But it's so worth that this should not stop you at all. On a side note I didn't had any issue with UPLAY at all so it didn't really disturbed me.)

My summary:
BUY IT! Valiant Hearts is a perfect blend of story, diverse gameplay, and puzzle solving.  Rooted in historical events, it is a powerful game that can move you to tears.  You follow a story which separates father and son on two different sides of the war.  Joining them, a US soldier with nothing to live for (save his friend Emile), a French field-medic trying to reach her father, and a loyal dog separated from its owner.  They will all struggle in the war until the end, and no one will ever be the same again.
Pros:
I really want to say my favorite game of all time but I think that would be going too far.  I think it may be my favorite indie-esque 2d game of recent memory, perhaps only with Bastion and To The Moon as competitors.  What I do like about it is it has less gameplay than bastion but more gameplay than To The Moon.  For me, it is the perfect mix of the two, and does both well.
Cons:
In general some of the puzzles are so not-obvious it becomes frustrating but they do provide a neat optional hint system.  The difficulty is also appreciated rather than dumbing them down completely.  Additionally a few elements like the medic revive functions (just mashing buttons in guitar hero fashion) is a bit of a downer to such an exciting game, but it is a very minor component of the game.
Story (9.5/10): Amazing, there are very few video games that can compare.  I have a few minor complaints about it but they aren't worth mentioning and I do not want to spoil the surprises along the way.
Art (9.5/10): Really unique and awesome, my ONLY complaint is that it can become a but blurry and pixelated when some of the sprites zoom in during cinematics.
Sound (10/10): From the mutterings in every language to the music to the narration this couldn't possibly be better.
Gameplay (9/10) Because of a few annoying puzzles that are almost intentionally obscure and the medical revive system which is bashing buttons, I can't give this a perfect score.  But everything else about it is perfect.  Seriously, it feels so good and just when you think a mechanic is getting old, you get put in a tank, car, or are dodging mines or gun fire.
What an absolutely beautiful game. A touching and spectacular story. Great characters. Solid gameplay. A gripping atmosphere. Fantastic dialogue. A great representation of WW1. Where to start? 10/10

I really enjoyed this game.
In short, it's a real time tactics with RPG-style levelling, open world, and ability to play both stealtily or aggressively.
If you want a more detailed description, it's a game where you control four characters with distinct skill sets, plus some potential mind-controlled underlings, and have to undermine a cyberpunk megacorp, mostly by infiltrating into the facilities of the affiliated factions to sabotage, steal technology or earn some dough for research and equipment. You do so either steahily, using cover and steahily takedowns, avoiding cameras, or just break in, using superior firepower and operative abilities and equipment, such as heavy damage dealing and cover wrecking grenades, to overcome enemy groups - you'll still want to use the cover, though, as it provides notable protection, and taking down enemies calling for backup remains essential as that way you'll be dealing not only with nearby guards coming for gunfire noise, but also fresh reinfocements that can easily overcome you. Most of the time, though, you'll likely be mixing the approaches, using the equipment in possession and any found shortcut to avoid larger enemy group, taking on enemies only when caught off guard or confident in own firepower.
It's pretty sad how, it seems, other folks who reviewed it didn't notice the possiblities of character abilities and equipment - it's pretty boring without all the tricks you can pull off. Say, one of characters, the hacker, can hack people, a clear Syndicate Persuadertron homage. This gives you a controllable, perfectly expendable meatshield, but that's not all - enemies unaware of hacking will react to hacked ones as usual, so you can use unarmed civilians as distraction to run past enemy while they're busy escorting out a civvie, or just hack a soldier to access unprotected terminals without alarming nearby guards or to pass trough a restricted door with the rest of operatives. Soldier's hotwiring can be used to block passage by disabling doors, trapping enemies. Infiltrator gets incredible mobility with specific upgrades, able to use wires and airvents without any equipment or augmentations required. And that's just the basic skills, you also get like four implant augmentation slots and from two to five equipment items! Possiblities for creative approaches are pretty great.
Now, visually, it's very impressive, but there's a great price for it as it can be rather slow on some computers. Mine is pretty good and yet I still would ocassionally get under 30 FPS with all the rain and shaders and particles. The world is pretty saturated with effects, really, and while it looks pretty and immersive, it may sometimes feel like somebody forcibly installed the latest ENB mod and toggled on every visual effect possible. Can't complain tho, readability is still great, and even things like game camera bobbing once in a while to imitate drone camera are subtle enough not to provide a distraction. City is well-designed, with each district having a distinct style and feeling convincing. Sound design is good too but soundtrack, while appropriate, may feel a bit repetitive - somewhat disappoint that there were no distinct district music tracts considering atmospheric differences.
Also, gotta warn, the game is bit buggy, with characters getting stuck and a few crashes, but that doesn't seem to be too frequent, so don't worry about it. Though watch out if your computer is weak, as I mentioned it's pretty heavy on the visuals.
So yes, totally worth a try. The freeform missions, the amount of equipment to unlock and the city, it's all top notch with a few minor hiccups. I'm not even sure how some of the folks making all those negative reviews ended up stuck - the tutorial tells you exactly what to do, so I guess they weren't paying attention?

I don't play a lot of board games, card games, or tabletop dice games, so considering that Armello is a mix of all three, that should frighten me. However, I do love the premise of fantistical, swashbuckling, swords-and-magic adventure, and when you add animal characters to the pot it happily brings me back to the days I read Brian Jacques' Redwall novels.
A complete Armello game normally takes about 60-75 minutes, and there are four main ways to win: doing the most "good" before the turns are up is the easiest, while the other three can be much more challenging to accomplish. Over time it may be discouraging to see time-out endings happen the most, but I think a player needs plenty of experience, a plan from the get-go, and modest luck to reliably go for the quicker, decisive wins. I'm not there yet...
The artwork is lovely and so are the landscapes. All of the design resonates charm and liveliness and presents a convincing world with a broad range of characters - but only on the surface. It was a little disappointing to see a lot of this detail come only through the art. There aren't deep backstories of the playable heroes, or lore that permeates throughout the world. Events don't really happen on a timeline or connect to each other very deeply. It's like there's either "good people or bad people", "named character approaches you, you do one of two choices on a quest and that's the last you'll hear of him until you replay". The players write most of the action while fighting, betraying and sabotaging each other, but that story always resets when the game ends and another starts. Basically, don't look for a compelling narrative to be there in stone.
But this takes nothing away from the core mechanics, which are pretty balanced. Each hero specializes at doing something with the three card types, whether it's suiting up in the best equipment, weapons and armor, casting spells and boosting themselves (or crippling others) for a while, or setting up traps and causing havoc to tip the scales in a different direction. Managing gold and magic to do all these things is a tricky task. Anything drastic needs the right cards in your hand and every decision to spend or save them is nerve-wracking and exciting. They're good defense most of the time, but for me they're the reason I keep getting wiped off the face of the earth by lightning when I walk out of tree cover.
I think the biggest issue I have with this game is how easy it is to attack and how hard it is to defend. In most circumstances there's 3 sides of the die that grant strikes but only 1 side that provides a shield, nullifying a single attack; kind of unhelpful if strikes just outnumber everything anyway. So there's a lot of times where two battlers will just pointlessly tear each other to shreds, die, and get sent back to their homes in frustration. The game's tips do point out that combat is costly, which I guess kind of contradicts the thought that things should be settled on the battlefield. However, this ends up justifying the use of cards to do some of the fighting and keep the dice on hold.
Overall, I think I'll get my money's worth out of Armello. It's not an exaggeration that this game sways in the balance of luck all the way up to the final turn and keeps things interesting and unpredictable. Armello is a worthy starting point in a genre I'm no longer unfamiliar with.

Possibly my favourite online board-game of 2016, Armello is easy to pick up, hard to master, generally well-balanced and an absolute blast.

I remember growing up with this game in 2002/2003. Could NOT complete it for the life of me at age 7/8. When I saw this on early access, I knew I had to get it, and finally completed it at age 22. Thank you for bringing my childhood back into my otherwise mundane adult life!

THIS IS A GREAT GAME!
Heck freaking yea I reccomend this! Why you ask? Well let me tell you...
Positives:
+ A classic brought back from the dead! This game is (considered by me and others) a classic from the PS2 era! And you can tell this by the graphics. Even though they have been improving them. but it is still lots of fun, even to this day! :D
+ It's a solid platformer! Nice tight controlls, nothing to horribly hard, and good level design!
+ Quirky characters! From Shazza, to Maurie, to even Ty himself! They all have there own personality and, sometimes they are even funny!
+ Good sound/music! From the didgeridoo's, to hearing the wild animals, the sound is overall pretty good! And they are adding better sounds as it's updated! The music is nice and catchy and sounds very nice!
+ Lots of rangs! Boomerangs to be exact! From the simple Boomerang, to the Flamerang, to the legendary DOOMerang! And you will need these! You might need the Flamerang to melt some ice, or the Zoomerang to hit a button far off. Whatever the case, there are plenty of rangs to choose from!
+ One of the few good Early Access games! Krome Studios have done an AMAZING job with porting this game over from the PS2! They have been fixing LOTS of bugs, improving the camera controls, and improving the graphics and sounds!
+ They have improved this from the PS2 version! They have improved the graphics, camera controls, (they are going to be) improving the pre-rendered cutscenes, as well as adding Steam achivements, Steam Trading Cards, and leaderboards for the time trials!
Mixed:
= May feel familiar to those who have played Super Mario 64 or Crash Bandicoot. Ty shares a lot of similarities with other platformers. But this I consider a good thing because it does it well. But I can see how some would consider this bad.
= Is a collecta-thon. Again this in my eyes, is a good thing because it makes the worlds MUCH more enjoyable and explorable, but if you don't like that then you might not enjoy this game as much.
Negitive:
- Has bugs. These can be expected of Early Access Games. But fortunatly, as I mentioned earlier, Krome has been doing an AMAZING job at fixing and improving the game!
- Everytime you enter a level, it always wants to play the same cutscene with the same dialogue. This is just a minor annoyance as you can skip through it and it does not affect anything negativly but it is still annoying.
Conclusion!
This truly is a great game from the PS2 era! I'm so glad that Krome has ported/HD-ified it on over to the PC! If you like a good platformer, enjoy classic 3D platformers like Super Mario 64, or Crash Bandicoot, then you will enjoy this game!

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a true gem from the past, which has not only been ported to steam for all to enjoy, work and effort is being put in to remaster the game as well to make it better than ever before, thus the reason for early access.
At its core, you have your standard platforming game with an amazing twist, you get to play with some ripper Australian action, staring a boomerang wielding thylacine (Tasmanian Tiger), how much more Australian can you get then that, well there is even a lovable dingo in this cast!
You get a fun and quirky cast of characters who are for or against Ty's cause, and a simple yet entertaining story of our hero trying his hardest to save his family and friends from a deadly fate at the hands of the villainous Boss Cass.
Visually Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is great and getting better with the consistent updates, but it is also important to come in remembering that the original base game is 15 years old.
Gameplay has a vast amount of variety, there is always something new you can do to solve any snags you may run into. Fans of collectable based games will feel right at home, since this game is based around collectable items to help progress story, and also unlock many extras, one such helping you increase your boomerang arsenal to take down the baddies. All in all, the game stays true to being a platformer at heart, and with plenty of lovely Australian scenery to take in. In one level you can be trudging through a dense rainforest, and then the next you could be riding through the wide open outback, or exploring a billabong.
Fans of platforming games such as Rayman, Mario, Sonic, Crash Bandicoot and other iconic characters will love to give this game a go. With the current modest price of 12 dollars, it is a steal given you have plenty of packed to the brim levels, an amazing cast of characters, and most of all a development team that is here to make a game that everyone can love. Not to mention the game has enough content that even kept me busy for over 9 hours of gameplay to get that 100%, and that is with years of experience and knowing exactly how to play from start to finish.

I am very happy to see that Krome Studios has come back to port the original Ty the Tasmanian Tiger. I got so many hours out of this game as a kid on PS2, and I will try and go for 100% this time, so even more hours now as an adult! If you're worried about the Early Access tag, don't be. I was able to run it on my old rig with a gtx 660 at 60 frames constantly (game was designed to run that way anyways, since it could run on a PS2). Whether you're buying for nostalgiac purposes or you're completely new to the series, I recommend this game fully and hope that we'll see Krome Studios more in the future if they choose to port the other games.
Also, this game is best played with an xbox controller or steam controller.

If you like having fun, and like a game that doesn't take itself too serious, play this game!
Retro City Rampage (RCR) originally started as "Grandtheftendo", an unofficial NES port of the first GTA. Later, the author decided to keep the same spirit (retro, 8-bit looks and sounds) while expanding the game way beyond the NES capabilities. Then RCR was born.
It obviously looks and plays like GTA (the first one, with top-down view), but it is a satire of the old (and new?) games, and includes uncountable references to other games and movies and pop-culture and stuff.
It is not a difficult game, although some mini-games are quite hard.
It gives you a smile very often, when you see something unexpected or absurd happening, or when the game throws yet another reference at you.
And it is fun to play!

This episode focuses on motorcycles, as you would expect from a game that revolves around a biker gang. If GTA4 wasn't gritty enough for you, this one's even grittier. Storywise, it's about the same level of grittiness as GTA4, if not more, If you like riding bikes, you'll like this episode; Johnny Klebitz has mastered the delicate art of not flying off his bike when clipping a lamp post at 20 miles an hour. Though he's not as good of a driver as Niko, and you'll definitely notice that if and when you get behind the wheel. There's more content in general, including an exclusive set of weapons to play with, including an autopistol, a sawed-off shotgun, and a grenade launcher. You get all three of these pretty damn early in the game; the sawed-off is Johnny's starter weapon and he can fire it while riding! Worth playing if you want to follow a parallel, equally if not more gritty story to Niko's.
Lost MC! Lost MC!
This episode takes a leap away from GTA4's usual brand of grittiness; it's more colorful, has lots of new fun guns to play with (P90 SMG, advanced sniper rifle, M249 light machine gun, AA-12 shotgun with explosive rounds...), parachutes, upgraded police units, and a whackier tone to compete with its new nemesis, Saints Row 2. This one focuses a bit more on helicopters, so this episode may be good practice for the awful PC controls for the helicopters. Or it may frustrate you a bit. Once you finish the story, you can go back and replay any mission you want. There's a score system for missions this time around, but who cares? I actually find this episode to be more fun than GTA4 just because of all the fun stuff it adds. There's nothing like screwing up everyone's commute in Star Junction with stickybombs and an explosive shotgun. What's that? The police are coming? Pfft. They ain't got♥♥♥♥♥♥on my APC.
You'll have a good time. And as always, mods only increase the fun.

I realized I've sunk over 400 hours into Armello and never bothered to review it... probably because I was too busy playing Armello!
Armello is a digital board game where you quest to improve your hero's stats, with the ultimate goal being to overthrow the king with one of four victories (prestige, combat, spirit stones, or rot). Given that there are decks of cards and dice rolls, there is quite a bit left to chance, but there is also a LOT of strategy involved. The game requires equal amounts of planning several turns ahead and improvising.
Having been playing since the beta (or alpha?), I've benefitted from learning each component of the game as they were gradually implemented, but for a new player it could all possibly be overwhelming. The basics are fairly easy to grasp, but there's a lot of deeper gameplay to master. There's a brief tutorial and also single player bot matches for practicing, but the best way to learn is to dive on in! You're going to lose your first few matches, but stick with it!
If all that hasn't scared you off, then you're going to enjoy it!
See you in Armello!

So I send in the drone, mark everyone and set myself up. But I was surprised to see that unable to see any of them. And she did not load in until I got to about 150-200m. Took a few steps back and she disappeared again. So the number one feature of the game is ruined by these limitations, which really is a shame as the sniping is actually quite fun.
Numerous crashes and relatively low performance for a game that does not have the most stunning graphics out there also does not help its already bad rep.

If you've played and enjoyed (how couldn't you?) Ty the Tasmanian Tiger in the past,
. You wouldn't be looking at reviews if you weren't considering it already.
That said, on to the review for those of you that still aren't so sure. Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was originally released on Gamecube, the original Xbox, and the PlayStation 2. I spent countless hours getting lost in this game as a kid and I was ecstatic to see that they decided to port it over to PC.
At the time of writing this review, the game in still in Early Access. Let me tell you for a fact, it feels far from it. This game is an excellent console to PC port.
The story is pretty accessible, but you have to pay attention to some of the NPCs' dialogue and cutscenes if you want to really follow along. It can be easy to miss. If you accidentally skip a cutscene, you can watch them from the main menu.
The NPCs in this game are amusing and somewhat inept. You might feel compelled to call child protective services on one of them as she keeps losing her children, but thankfully you're there just in time to step in and save the day.
Ty is a 3D platformer. You can do mostly what you'd expect with a game of this genre. You can jump, swim, glide, and climb your way through levels. The movement mechanics are tight, so any issues with falling off or missing a jump is probably your fault, as it should be.
In every level there will be enemies for you to take down, items to collect, and friends to help. Thankfully, you will be growing an arsenal of boomerangs to help you accomplish these tasks with style. I really enjoy the variety of boomerangs to collect. Some are more utilitarian to help you find hidden items, and others can set your enemies on fire or slow down time. There's a 'rang out there for just about everyone.
Once the story is said and done, there's quite a few collectibles to find if you're up for it. They don't take a shocking amount of time to find, but if you don't look closely or consider alternative approaches to finding them then you may find yourself wandering a level for a couple of hours. Some of the levels are
.
For the competitive gamers out there, you can try to climb the leaderboards for each level! I personally haven't looked too far into these, but they appear to be working just fine.
I don't currently have a USB gamepad, so my entire experience with this on PC has been with the keyboard and mouse we've come to know and love. Let me tell you, they feel
.
I have only had a few minor issues with the controls:
The Developers have been hard at work remastering the game to make it feel more at home on modern systems. I played through the game at 2560x1440 (I saw lots of resolutions in the menu too) and its a definite improvement. They're continually releasing graphical improvements while keeping the game minimum-spec friendly.
The story-line cutscene videos are still low-res, but the developers are working on updating those as well. You can stillsee and understand what's going on in the cutscenes though.
The color palettes are bright and varied. I don't like to place much of an emphasis on a game's visuals because there are more important aspects to it. Keep in mind this is a game originally released in 2002. Don't expect Crysis and you'll be fine.
Based on the hardware reports, it looks like the game runs fine on Integrated Intel chips. If you're rocking a laptop without a discrete GPU, you should be good.
I haven't noticed any graphical issues like artifacting or textures not loading.
I would comment on the audio but I don't think there's anything wrong with it and I can't muster much of an imaginary comparison from my past because I'm pretty sure the last time I played this game was over a decade ago (oh my god). It's also worth noting I'm a bit hearing impaired so I don't pick up on much of the audiophile stuff. The game sounds great to me, so that's all I've got.
Like I said before, if you've played Ty in the past and you liked it, you owe it to yourself to pick this game up. It's more than a compulsory nostalgia purchase as the game continued to entertain me while I played through it and collected everything (I didn't 100% it when I played as a kid, 'cause I was stupid).
If you've never heard about Ty the Tasmanian Tiger before today, I hope this review alongside some of the others may have convinced you to try it. It's a great game, developed by people who really care about it (you'll frequently find the Developers in the discussions, responding to feedback, watching the Summer Games Done Quick speed-run).
I'm looking forward to seeing where the developers take this game. I know they have a few more improvements in the pipeline but the game feels like a finished product to me. They did a great job.
The more copies they sell, the more reasons they have to port Ty 2 and Ty 3. Let's make it happen, people!!!

Having owned this game when it first came out on PS2 I was very quick to buy this game once it came out now on steam, and i must say. It's a blast and better than it was when i first played it those many years ago.
I've completed the game to 100%. So and i didn't experience any crashes, missing items or anything. The only thing that i did notice with this game was that a few spots you lost a bit of framerate in. Otherwise, the game is great, controls have been perfectly ported and binded for PC, they've added neat features like being able to fight bosses again without having to restart the game and of course upped the graphics of the game.
It's hard to say wherther this game would fit someone right now with all games these days being much scavange survival, building and First person shooters. But for a nostalgic value or simply if you're someone who enjoys classic platformer games where you collect stuff. This game is gold.
I don't know if you should get it now though, since they do warn you that since they are keeping the game in early access to get feedback on functions that are broken and trying to optimize the game further, there is a chance that save files can be corrupted from updates that are made. And i don't think anyone would like spending hours on maps collecting everything only to have their save file lost and have to restart the game.

If you've never played this game but want to experience classic old platformers in the style of Banjo and Kazooie then get this game the second it's out of early access. It's well worth it.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was one of the first games I've ever played on my old gamecube as a kid. To see it being ported over to the PC is a great thing to see. It may not be as awesome as I remember it, with some levels later in the game that are huge but empty (Ex: Snow worries having a barren mountain to climb and Rex marks the spot has an empty ocean that really doesn't effect anything besides the time it takes to get from point A to point B) and that makes collecting everything a pain. The game still has some solid platforming. If you bought this game in the early 2000s, buy it here. The keyboard controls have been well intergrated so no gamepad is needed.
The graphics (While dated in some parts) still hold up with the cartoony artstyle. And even with the over sized levels in the later stages, the levels are really fun to play and collect items to get new boomerangs. The game's greatest strengh is the Outback setting that's rare to see in games. This give the game an identity The only thing I 100% hate in this game is the characters. Ty is a cardboard cutout of a boy scout and picks one out of the same three lines when finishing a mission, Sly (Not the racoon) is the ultamate edgelord made from the mind of a 13 year old and comes off as annoying, and all the other characters as well as the bosses are completely forgetable.
Overall it is a good game. I'd say the only thing that's holding it back is the developers and being in early access. Fight the Dragon is, in my opinion, one of the coolest game ideas that I have seen, and for the most part it is executed extremely. I originally bought this game in early access and was able to watch it grow, and grow it did.
In FTD you create a character, choosing one of the four classes: Rogue, Fighter, Ice Wizard, or Fire Wizard. The classes themselves each have a unique feel to them and it is fun to check each of them out. There is a decent amount of abilities to choose from for each class and they all seem pretty fun to use. You can customize your character with the in-game models provided or you can download new, unique models from the Steam Workshop.
Where the game truly shines is the ACK - Adventure Creation Kit. This allows anyone to use all of the assets in the game to create their own unique levels. Obviously some adventures turn out better than others, but there is a healthy amount of extremely creative individuals making adventures that are truly astounding. You create everything in your adventure from NPCs and their dialogue to the landscape and buildings. The most creative individuals have weaved some of the coolest stories I've seen in their adventures, and when you complete them you can even follow the creator to be updated whenever they create a new adventure. There are also measures to prevent creators from making adventures that just give you massive amounts of gear or treasure without doing anything, which is a good thing (why exploit a game, the point is to play and have fun)! Writing about it simply doesn't do it justice and it must be seen by your own eyes.
Not everything in FTD is perfect though, in fact one of the largest parts of the game can be quite buggy and frustrating - the combat. You can play the game with a controller or KB/M, but when playing with either I still encounter many enemies that I simply swing at them several times without actually hitting them, even when they're right in front of me. This can lead to some VERY frustrating experiences. On one of my own adventures I created I ran into a bug where it was impossible for me to kill an enemy, and eventually I ended up being pushed off of the map. Reading other reviews it seems I'm not the only one that has had problems with the combat.
Aesthetically the game isn't astounding, but the landscapes can sometimes be very pleasing. The soundtrack again isn't amazing, but there are a decent selection of tracks - you can even choose which will play in your adventure. Even further you can set "triggers" that will cue a certain track when an event happens (the ACK is amazing)!
After logging 50+ hours in the game, and trudging through the frustrating parts I do have to still give it a thumbs up. The developers do pay attention to the community and they try and fix bugs pretty quick. Hopefully they will be able to fix the combat eventually, then this game would be a masterpiece, but for now I have give it an 8/10.
TL;DR Game is really good except for some frustrating combat experience. Creative minds will enjoy making adventures.

This is a good improvement of the first instance of Alien Swarm.
It is a top down shoot them up type of game wich consist of getting from getting to the beginnig of the level to the end alive with objectives on the way(hint: you fight aliens). It also has a good workshop set of improvements and missions for the game.
When starting the game, you get access to a very sober menu, placed on a moving background in a fitting style that isn't obnoxious to the eye and overall pleasing. It has the necesary options, not too much, not too little.  Only down side of it, is that it is a touch to small.
In the options menu you get plenty of tweaks options to make the game fit you and your computer.
Performance wise, pretty nuch any modern laptop will run it. Even low comsumption i3s will run perfect on low, wich doesn't look bad at all.
Gameplay options when launching a game(if you are the host, or play in single player), you'll have choices from level selection, to friendly fire options. There is 9 missions, wich you can choose what section you want to play, on top of that there is DeatMatch, bonus missions, workshop levels, challenges to modify gameplay features and workshop challenges as well. There is 8 characters and 4 classes with their own characteristics, 25 weapons to choose from and 17 side gadget to help you fight against aliens. NONE of the weapons/class/gadjet is useless, you get access to everything via levels exept for characters. The leveling system isn't to slow and you'll get the item you want pretty fast. No transactions, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, not purposly boring level up rate. As always, clear and simple menu.
Gameplay, the interesting part. The game is easy to play and learn, the missions make sense and have a good feel. Aliens don't come in waves(exept for special parts of some missions), and makes the game non-linear. The level design is very good, not narrow, but still makes it easy to find your way. Everything fits well together, and nothing feels oddly placed. Even though the online presence isn't crazy, but finding a game isn't hard at all.

Although there are some things that I encountered in the game that's really frustrating to me:
-Like if you play in multiplayer mode with a slow internet speed or your opponent has slow internet speed, expect some lag(of course, whenever you play multiplayer) that will really make you wait(which was and is really annoying), especially that 1 game takes more than 30 mins of gametime, depending on the players.
-The queue sometimes will really be annoying(for me that is) because it took me like 5-10 mins before I entered a game.
There was a time that I reached the number of stars needed for ranking up, and I saw my new rank on the multiplayer lobby then exited the game. A few hours later, I played Armello again and went to the multiplayer lobby and saw that my rank returned to my previous rank. I restarted the game and saw no change. I hope that it was just a bug, but it really was frustrating to see that.
There are, of course, some good things that I liked in Armello:

-Different ways to win the game
So far, Armello is a great game to play, I bought it 2 weeks ago, so I'm still new with the game. I seldomly, but not always, experience complications with the game.
If you are interested in games that are turn-base, try playing this game, but if you are not interested in these kind of games, you won't really enjoy playing Armello, unless you really persevere in playing the game, maybe you would enjoy it.

I realized I've sunk over 400 hours into Armello and never bothered to review it... probably because I was too busy playing Armello!
Armello is a digital board game where you quest to improve your hero's stats, with the ultimate goal being to overthrow the king with one of four victories (prestige, combat, spirit stones, or rot). Given that there are decks of cards and dice rolls, there is quite a bit left to chance, but there is also a LOT of strategy involved. The game requires equal amounts of planning several turns ahead and improvising.
Having been playing since the beta (or alpha?), I've benefitted from learning each component of the game as they were gradually implemented, but for a new player it could all possibly be overwhelming. The basics are fairly easy to grasp, but there's a lot of deeper gameplay to master. There's a brief tutorial and also single player bot matches for practicing, but the best way to learn is to dive on in! You're going to lose your first few matches, but stick with it!
If all that hasn't scared you off, then you're going to enjoy it!
See you in Armello!

I bought this game on Xbox when it first came out, and I wanted it on PC so I bought it on Steam when they released this edition. This is a really unique take on zombie survival games, as it tasks you with keeping a community alive as you switch people to run missions as. Third person combat to kill zombies, search buildings for items and supplies for your base, and make sure your community members are happy and healthy.
For people who haven't played before the missions can be confusing, as some are story missions that can wait forever and some are time sensitive. This is a bit aggravating when all I want to do is supply my base, but mission control repeatedly reminds me of the same story mission I have on hold.
However, the graphics are the same as far as I can tell, and there isn't a whole lot changed from the original version save for the DLC included in this. I wouldn't recommend this to someone who already owns the full game (DLC included) on Xbox, as it's not worth it in that case unless you're a huge fan of this game (as I am).
One last thing: the game stutters fairly often. I'm using a GTX 1080, playing on ultra settings, and it didn't stutter like this on console. On one occasion, it crashed as I was driving through an empty field, which is more annoying than in most games given characters don't stay where you leave them. Upon restarting, my character had been teleported home without the car loaded up with items, away from the mission I was about to run.
Overall, I'd still recommend this game in general. Techincal issues aside, there's solid gameplay, while the base management and supply logistics are addicting.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger was one of the first games I've ever played on my old gamecube as a kid. To see it being ported over to the PC is a great thing to see. It may not be as awesome as I remember it, with some levels later in the game that are huge but empty (Ex: Snow worries having a barren mountain to climb and Rex marks the spot has an empty ocean that really doesn't effect anything besides the time it takes to get from point A to point B) and that makes collecting everything a pain. The game still has some solid platforming. If you bought this game in the early 2000s, buy it here. The keyboard controls have been well intergrated so no gamepad is needed.
The graphics (While dated in some parts) still hold up with the cartoony artstyle. And even with the over sized levels in the later stages, the levels are really fun to play and collect items to get new boomerangs. The game's greatest strengh is the Outback setting that's rare to see in games. This give the game an identity The only thing I 100% hate in this game is the characters. Ty is a cardboard cutout of a boy scout and picks one out of the same three lines when finishing a mission, Sly (Not the racoon) is the ultamate edgelord made from the mind of a 13 year old and comes off as annoying, and all the other characters as well as the bosses are completely forgetable.
Overall it is a good game. I'd say the only thing that's holding it back is the developers and being in early access. I feel like the developers won't add anything major to the game or provide any real overhalls that can benefit the game at the cost of nostalgia from the fans. Also I'm willing to bet that a lot of Ty fans won't buy this game because it says it's in early access. The game is finished, you can play it from start to finish just as it was in the Ps2, gamecube, and Xbox. It's in early access for patching the game and porting it.
I want you to buy this game, not only to get a good game but to also support the devs so that they can maybe port Ty 2 to PC. And I may be getting ahead of myself here but along with the release of Yooka-Laylee, this can encorage publishers to belive in 3D platformers again and more will appear on Steam.

At first I was impressed, very good visuals, big city divided into sectors, lots of things to do, skills, arguments, gear and weapons to unlock, should be fun!
But after some time I started to see more thing I didn't like, big city but feels dead, lots of mission and thing to do but almost everything feels the same, sneak your way behind guards in the restriced area, get to the door, go inside, go out and repeat. Other than that you have to unlock beacons ~10 in every sector, hack ATMs to get flow of money, hack bank to get 140% of the money from ATM from that sector, look for prototypes or blueprints, research them so you can buy and use them and repeat. All the same all the same.
You can "talk" and bribe some NPCs but this looks like this, you have to find someone, go to location, scan location, find that person, walk to him/ her, click on him and read summary, no talking, no dialogs, no interaction, nothing, you just click on person and that is it.
Another thing is infiltrating restricted area to get to the specific building to steal some blueprints or prototypes when you go inside the building you don't do anything, your men just come out 5s later and you have to sneak you way out to safety. So basically this game is one big, open word sneak game, well almost, if you are caught you can fight and sometimes you must fight and fighting is far from being enjoyable :/ there is not much tactic, you just put your men behind cover and command them to shoot other men behind cover or better yet in the open area because why would anyone want to hide behind cover and live anyway? :) You can have special abilities, grenades, drones etc, but combat itself feels very anemic, spamming bullets, not so much tactical planning like in turn based games.
Your men not always make smart decisions so you have to control them all the time and this is sometimes tedious. Most missions have some simple story and reason why you do this or that, 9 out of 10 you get new gear :) You can only read some mission description in menu, sometimes purchase addition information, or do some small submission to get key to gate or weaken enemies etc but in the end no matter what you will read and how exciting this will sound every mission is the same, sneak in, go in, go out sneak out or fight if you get caught or "talk", bribe or kill NPS somewhere on map.
Every location have a different security system so you have to figure it out and this is fun but it seems like it is the only thing that matter and if do this over and over again it losing its taste and gets more tedious than fun.
And on top of that game can be little glitchy here and there, once when I order my whole squad to move from one location to another one of them decided to run another way and stuck between wall and power generator :) it took me 2-3 min to get him out clicking everywhere, I was considering killing him because I can't teleport him from restricted area. Another time in fighting enemy stuck between wall and concrete barricade and was constantly running so I left poor thing there :)  Or you can run next to guard in restricted area, almost touching him and he can not notice you :D
So yes, it started really well but unfortunately gets less and less shiny after every addition hour

This game is free, and I believe it is worth looking into. It has this somewhat captivating charm for people who enjoy turned based strategy games mixed with dice and cards or who just enjoy a game that somewhat parodies DnD stereotypes. Keep in mind that this game is not a 'traditional' card game, as in you build your deck by buying cards. Instead, you buy items to equip a character. These items add a number of different cards to your deck which you will draw from every so often. Items are found in chests at the end of each battle, bought in shops, or you can spend real cash to purchase loot boxes.
Keep in mind, this is a free to play game so there are pay-to-win aspects. Such as buying the loot chests. Since your campaign and multiplayer(pvp) items transfer over. Though I need to stress that these 'chests' you can buy do not always give good items- the items are so varied in quality and combination in this game that making a setup with what you have can match someone who went out and just bought the majority of their gear through these randomized gamble-boxes.
Pay to win aside, the game has a 'card hunter's club' membership that's just premium, all it does is drop one extra item- and they're not usually any good so far. Then they have the 'costume' shop. Some of the little models are nice, and I would buy a few of them, myself, if I had the cash to spend- if I wasn't already spending it all on other games. Hopefully, they might add a new skin or two in the future that might catch my eye.
So with some of the bad and good out there, I'm going to make a quick Pros and Cons list.
Pros
- Entertaining 'story' one might expect of a parody to what the classic Stereotype of DnD players would be like.
- Many adventures- A ton of them which can be played once, each, daily.
- SO MUCH LOOT; Diablo style loot hunting game. Wide variation and combinations of loot dropped at the end of each battle.
- Combat can be tough and unforgiving, especially if the dice hate you. Or it can all be turned around with one good dice roll.
- Has Co-op. I LOVE co-op turn-based strategy, and this one just feels like it would do good(I have yet to try it, myself.)
- Has multiplayer PvP, seems interesting. I've only played against the bot, though.
Cons
- Pay to Win. Though not as big of a deal as it is in most games. You won't be able to tell if they got it from a bought chest or from playing the game long enough.
- Adventures have a refresh time, three battles each setup. No actual RPG elements aside from fighting, lvling, and equiping things.
- No Co-op lobby, you just start Co-op and invite friends? I have yet to try it.
- 3 classes: Warrior, Cleric, Wizard
- 3 Races: Elf, Dwarf, Human
All in all, for a free game, it is both simple and holds quite a bit of depth with what can be done. I do hope there is an actual table-top version of this. It looks fun. Also, it could do with more classes, maybe. Playing with the same three classes can get kind of old, but it's understandable that there aren't more. Race-wise, it's the rather standarad 3 fantasy races. But, again, more variation would be fun. All-in-all, there's still a lot to do here for such a simple game, and it's somewhat addictive.

This is essentially a pay to win game.
The tutorial is well done and quickly gets you into the game. The loot is varied and interesting. Which makes you want to play more. But as soon as you get into multiplayer, you quickly realize that you need to pay in order to compete. The prices are steep too. Balance is nigh impossible because of how the game is centered around card drops.
Single player campaigns are a grindfest. Campaigns are well made, and the level design is well thought out. They are fun, interesting, varied and challenging. Unfortunately you need to pay to proceed to higher level campaigns. After buying the campaign you still have to grind, pay to grind. There is a 1 day cool down and wait to for all the campaigns too.
This game has so much potential if it do away with the f2p model and just be a proper paid subscription game. After all there is no way you can survive without paying.

The recommendation is based on the alpha stage gameplay.
The Good:
I enjoy the conept of incorporating the gaming community into the actual creation of game content.  This means lots of diversity.  It also constantly improves the idea of a good "map": as one plays different maps from different users, his own taste for a "good" map diversifies and shifts.
What's even better is that, there are quality maps.  Some maps you can tell the designer spent hours on perfecting.  The map creation kit also handles very well-- easy to grasp and almost anyone can build a map. The creation kit is also powerful enough to allow users to create very different environments-- a very elegant blend of simplicity and power.
The game is easy to get into.  Jump into a game, and click on the bad guys. Key bindings are laid out clearly.  The gear is diversified, and your character changes appearance with each piece of equipment equipped. The loot system is balanced in terms of statistics, and it constantly poses questions like, "would you sacrifice LUCK(magic find and crit chance) for damage?"
The bad:
Combat... feels a bit slippery.  Sometimes it feels like youre walking on ice: as you take damage you slide around, and so do your enemies.  Your special abilities are limited.  You have only 4.  Worse, you don't unlock all of them until higher levels.  This makes lower level combat repetitive and at times, monotonous.
There are also certain balancing issues in the game.  As you reach levels 10+, you begin to encounter enemies that can 1 shot you... even with gear deemed rare, extraordinary, and legendary.  (Gear ranks from junk, common, rare, extraordinary, and legendary.)
The downside to incorporating the gaming community into content creation is that there will be inevitably faulty maps that are incompletable or maps that overreward you/ under reward you.  While I understand the developer has taken steps to mitigate such problems, the issues still exist.  I have encountered very hard challenges on maps marked as "easy".
Multiplayer is bare bones.  You can join on players (though, I have NEVER seen more than 2-3 joinable games within the US at any given point in time).  However, you can't trade, share, or give loot.
BOTTOM LINE:
I say hold off on this one.See what else the developer has to offer.  Right now, the game is still rough (of course, its in alpha), and still needs some tweaking.  With the features it has right now, it just isn't worth purchasing for 15 bucks.

I love board games. I play a metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of them. So a game about animals with a cutesy (AMAZING) art style mixed with the bitter taste of medieval RPG politics makes for a sweet spicy blend. I just struggle to really commend it beyond that.
Armello is all about becoming the King or Queen of the land as the former King - as wonderful as he was - is slowly falling into madness due to a particularly painful corruption that's slowly killing him. No matter what happens, this lovable scamp's going to be dead in about 8 days give or take. Your job is to take his place, either through political sway or the incredibly direct route. As for the game itself, it's a matter of going on quests to gain additional stat points which will lead to boosting your chances of victory. Sounds simple enough right? Well, it is, which makes Armello an easy game to pick up and play. But it also leads to one of its failings.
Armello is a game where 80% is decided by luck, not your tactics, but by card draws and dice rolls. "Oh no" you say, player of Armello, "there are plenty of tactics in place to boost your chance for victory!" to which I reply "you are very right, you just need to draw those cards." At the beginning of your turn, you draw up to your hand limit (measured by the stat Wits) from three different decks. Items are all about things that boost your character, whether that's combat, perils, health, etc. Spells range from offensive magic to play on rivals to stat and combat boosts. Trickery cards are all about messing with the flow of the game, creating traps and making political moves. You could get the cards from the Trickery deck that would allow you to create obstacles for your rivals, but you need to draw them. You could instead draw cards that create pacts with others, or offer other abilities which will do you no good. Or you could draw exactly the right cards and just annihilate your hapless foe before they even get a turn. Thankfully there is a balance as more powerful cards are less plentiful and more expensive to play, but nothing says you can't just draw three of these cards in a row and suddenly go from last place to first place.
"Alright," you say "but what does dice have to do with this?" Oh I'm glad you asked. Cards may give you the means to control the game, but dice decide your ultimate fate in Armello. There is a sword, shield, sun, moon, rot, and wyld side to every die. In combat, swords are brought into a total to decide your overall attack, shields mark your defense against an opponent's attack or counter-attack, sun and moon are added to your attack depending on the time of day and count as misses if it's not currently that time of day, and finally wylds and rots are explosive attack dice. If you're playing a normal game of Armello, every wyld will be an attack and then become a free die to instantly reroll to see if you do more damage or take less damage and rots count as misses. If you're corrupt from rot (the local corruption) - and this is harder than you think to do - then rots instead count as attacks that become additional dice and wylds become misses. As you may have noticed, there are only two ways to avoid taking damage from an enemy, rolling enough shields or hoping your opponent rolls enough misses. Dice could say that your hero with seven dice will lose in battle to a hero with two dice because they happen to roll wyld after wyld and suddenly they've rolled eight dice while half of your rolls were misses. Explosive dice also roll over to perils, which are obstacles on the map that you can overcome by - you guessed it - rolling dice to match the correct symbols. Perils however are determined by different stats, there are wits perils and spirit perils, the higher these amounts, the better defense you have.
"Hold on!" you now demand, pointing rapidly, "these aren't set in stone, they can be modified by getting item cards to boost the amount of dice you get or increasing shields and swords without dice!" Alright, notice you just said cards. So, again, let me remind you, what decrees that you will ever get these cards? Luck does. The most strategy that cards and dice give you is the ability to burn cards in battle to give the symbol on the card to one of your dice. Since you refill to your hand limit every turn, there's very little reason to why you shouldn't burn through as much of your hand as you can every turn so there's a better chance of drawing better cards. However, again, you need to draw these cards to give the correct symbols for your dice. So even this strategy is mandated by a level of luck. Really I could go on, but I think you get the point.
Armello is still a good game. I might have ripped it apart for being so luck based, but it's still a game I played over 20 hours of and still enjoy playing. Artistically the game is impressive, and thematically it feels truly alive. Since the game has minimal strategy, games (and turns) are short and intense, befitting of the game's brutal nature, you're invested enough to want victory but still distanced enough to not really care if you lose. It's just a game after all, and in minutes you can start a new one. As I've played Armello, I've discovered strategies on how to best manipulate the game to my advantage, despite all the luck involved. And even now, the developers add new things to the game to increase replayability and balance things out. So I feel like while the game does have its flaws and always will, there are ways to change the game and make it at least a little less luck dependant (ESPECIALLY FOR A ROT VICTORY, HINT HINT).
So I want to stress this again, Armello is a good game and is worth your time and money. If you're a more casual board game player or curious about board gaming at all, then you will love Armello, but if you're someone like me who likes their games with minimal luck then you're either going to need to find another game or adjust. Just like the world of Armello, the game is beautiful and well constructed, but hides an undeniable ugliness that you may not spot right away. Armello is a compelling turn-based board game with a variety of different ways to win. There are always 3 opponents (human or AI controlled) along with a variety of NPCs that hinder or help your progress. Being tasked with returning the kingdom to normal, you can choose to defeat the king in combat, become more corrupt than him by being tainted by the 'rot', gather 4 spirit stones to banish him or become the prestige leader and keep the king alive. The different heroes you play as all have their own talents and skills. Each clan has their own rings and coupled with the trinkets and artifacts you uncover during the game you can have a wildly varied hand. At first it seems easy but there are many things out to get you. You have to face perils, survive enemy players and mobs and get close enough to the king to stop him. I love the aesthetics of this game, it certainly feels and sounds like a fantasy adventure you'd want to be a part of. The animal motif fits the theme and the range of cards and effects makes this a deeply complex game. Definitely one of the best board games on Steam.

A competitor amonst the great platforming mascots, Ty rises once again.
The original was a great fun time of your usual collect-a-thon platforming and world exploring and still holds that today. This is no cheap PC port or cash grab though, no sir. This port, or small remaster if you will, is an example of what PC porting should be. Giving the game a small touch up in small places (such as the shadows being more sharp, some textures showing some polish, ect.) but still keeping what made it great in the first place.
As this is still early acess, there are a few hitches, but they're so far and few between you won't be complaining much. Overall, on my system, the game ran steadily at about 60FPS in most areas, baring the ocassional hint of lag in the more open levels. Again, very minor.
Gameplay is solid as ever, but I don't know about keyboard controls since I used an Xbox controller. There was a slight bug or issue with the camera at times where if I manually moved it with the right analog stick, it'd get stuck like that and not re-center itself. There's no button to re-center the camera either. Only way to correct it was to enter an area where the camera would fix itself back to follow behind Ty automatically. Small issue and didn't really cause any major problems as you could still move the camera around manually until it corrected itself, but it's worth noting.
Each area is unique, wonderfully detailed, and ripe with fun level design. All with memorable Australian-like music and colorful characters. Though if you're short of patience or don't like collecting random items, this may not be the expirence for you. You'll find yourself at many points in the game having to graze over the levels with a fine tooth comb looking for the last opal or cog, but finally finding them is a rewarding feeling, especially for OCD afflicted.
Overall a well made port of a classic platformer that's great for all ages. Hope to see the sequels on Steam soon so I can nab them up as well.
