I find Paint The Town Red to be so much fun I actually have questioned a couple times whether this game has brought out some dark, deep-seated psychotic side in me. This is, without a doubt, the most entertaining beat-em'-up I have ever played. The combination of wacky yet semi-realistic physics, pixelated brutality (in impressive detail for a pixelated game), sheer amount of action taking place all around you at once, the amount of ways to beat the absolute sh*t out of people, and some of the most satisfying blows I have ever delivered unto another person, makes this, as I said, the most fun beat-em-up I have ever played. Allow me to, later on, go into more detail on most of these points.
There are only three levels out right now (Bar, Disco, Prison) as well as a sandbox level, as of this review. However, the developers seem committed to this game, and I am insanely jittery to see new maps being released at some point. Imagine a gym/wrestling ring, city block, mansion, fairground, subway...a bit of Gang Beasts comes to mind when thinking of levels that could be added to this game. And, as those new levels come out, hopefully along with even more weapons, character models, etc., I will be pouring WAY more time into this game than my current 9-10 hours shows, as of this review.
The way the blunt weapons, such as the bat or the baton, smack into your enemies' temples, causing copious and comical amounts of blood to spurt continuously from their face, and then having the next hit warranting their entire face to crumble into chunks as their body crumples to the ground(yes, this actually happens sometimes. I'll explain later), delivers, as I stated, some of the most satisfying combat and victories I have ever seen in ANY type of game.
The game isn't very far from the truth at all when it states you can use pretty much anything not nailed down to take out your opponents. Hell, in the prison levels, you can rip off the shower nozzles and use them as a weapon. YOU CAN THROW APPLES AT PEOPLE. I HAVE KILLED PEOPLE WITH APPLES. I HAVE PUT DENTS IN PEOPLE'S FOREHEADS WITH F***ING APPLES. THINK ABOUT THAT.
The amount of action going on around you for most of the fight, as you work to take out every other living being in whatever building you are dropped into, makes for a constant adrenaline rush as you uncontrollably spout profanities at the various enemies tromping towards you, weapons in hand. You are never safe until every last being is taken out, and, very much like in a real fight, you have to always look behind you to make sure someone is actually dead (even with the signature snare sound that plays whenever someone is dead, you still can miss a few people), or to make sure someone hasn't spotted you and started stalking you with their only goal being to cave your head in until they can use it for eating Ramen.
The physics have multiple chances each brawl to showcase their realism and their wackiness, depending on the scenario. Especially with the "hard hitter" match modifier, kicking people with a full "kick" bar (or whateverthef*** it's called) sends them flying across the map, hitting the roof sometimes (not exaggerating) or getting booted up to a higher floor. In other scenarios, the way some of the weapons bounce off the walls, or the way an enemy will crumple to the ground or fall onto their @ss after a particularly hard hit with a bat, will add to the satisfaction of taking someone out in a more realistic fashion.
The gore in this game is certainly something that I did not see coming, at least not to the extent that it turned out to be. This is strangely one of the most violent games I have ever played. I had no idea until I started beating someone's face in with a tire iron the first time that you can literally TAKE APART someone. Their entire bodies are destructible. Every pixel. And each pixel is colored in to resemble flesh, bone, muscle, or brain. To a pretty accurate degree, given the size of the pixels. You can chop off arms at any area, not just joints (I think), same with legs. You can decapitate people (sometimes VERY cleanly, which will leave you saying "OOOOOOHH SHITBISCUITS" or something at least that's what I would say shut up). You can even curb stomp a f***er until his pixelated brain is showing. This game is brutal in the most comical and satisfying of ways.
Allow me to, off the top of my head, list every weapon in this game. As they come to mind. Beer bottle, cup, cleaver, knife, machete, kitana, pool cue, pool ball (cube), toothbrush shiv, basketball, shower nozzle, frying pan, slab of meat (yes, really), soap (YES, REALLY), money ("I am sad that I lack the talent to make this sh*t up" -Jontron), tire iron, bat, dumbbell, barbell, barbell weights (small and heavy), barbell pole, ham (I'm done), lunch tray, apple, orange, various chairs, nunchaku (hidden), shuriken (hidden), lightsaber (only in sandbox level currently), guitar, shotgun (hidden). Not all of these can be found in each level, however, each level is of decent size and packed with weapons. Imagine more levels with MORE weapons to be found depending on what new levels we get.
Now, before I go to my conclusion, I do need to tell that another part of what makes this game so satisfying is that it is surprisingly difficult at times. Like stated before, if you don't watch your back constantly, a couple blows to your head with most weapons will kill you just as easily as the next guy. Not only that but it can be very easy to get surrounded or in a corner if you don't know your surroundings well. Most of what makes this game difficult are reasons that can be attributed to fighting in real life. Not only this, but there are also "boss"-esque characters in each level, that don't come out to attack you right away. For example, the boxer in the bar level basement, who takes a POUNDING and can take you down with 4-5 punches. Even when it comes to a normal dude, though, a few hits with a bottle, a couple slashes with a machete, etc., and you're down and out, and you have to restart. This game has managed to literally make me jump when I forget to watch my back and I turn around to leave a room and there's a big brolic black dude named Requis ready to skullf**k me.
The game is so addicting, though, that you can't really give a lot of a sh*t if you wanted to. Especially since you have the ability to combat this difficulty with magical powers of blowing people up (yes, really). You have a bar in the top left that charges up as you beat the sh*t out of people, and as of this review, there are three powers you can choose from. The first that gets unlocked is "Shockwave", which releases a ring of kaboom-y juice around you that throws enemies back, across the entire room in some cases. It's good for when you get in a tight situation, but it doesn't do much damage. The second power is "Berzerk", which turns the game into slo-mo, and you have the ability to one-shot MOST enemies with your fists, and see their heads/bodies/wherever you hit them explode into a bloody pulp. This helps if you have a lot of guys following you and you need a break. The final ability is "Smite", which allows you to make a gun shape with your hand, point at people, and have some otherwordly power bring holy, explod-y, bloody death to their entire body at the click of the mouse. This is good for taking out bigger enemies as well as just taking out a large group of people. It's great in general.
In conclusion, this game is hilarious, brutal, satisfying, addicting, and a time-waster all rolled into one. It can also be a very good stress-reliever. I cannot recommend Paint The Town Red enough, and I really hope the devs stick to this game for weeks and weeks to come, adding new stuff to it as often as possible. Delicious things could come to this game in the future.

Star Wars Republic Commando (or as I like to call it also, Band of Clone Bros) is the forgotten and underrated Star Wars video game that everybody that loves the Star Wars franchise should play. The story of the game is based on the 2nd and 3rd movies of the prequel trilogy, where you play as the leader of a Spec Ops squad of 4 Clones of the Galactic Republic who are responsible for performing special missions that occure behind the scenes of the Clone Wars. This is a squad based game, where using your squad team seriously will be your road for victory. The fact that you play as a Clone, fighting along aside with a team of other Clones, breaks the monotony of the usual protagonists of a story of a Star Wars game, which tend to be Jedis, Siths or some random bounty hunter.
I agree, like the vast majority of people who played it, that this is a good game - but not a perfect one. It has one problem that I felt frustrated about: while the enemy was agressive against you, your squad team will be very weak and will lack agressivness, unless you babysit them all the time. Sometimes, they will just get close to an enemy and try killing them by melee (it reminds me of the Warscape Engine BS that is now plaguing the Total War series...), instead of trying to get to cover by their own initiative. Another problem  that I have with the game is the lack of variety with the level designs: the game is divided only by 3 chapters, which are limited equally to 3 areas (first you fight in one planet, then inside a ship, and then again in another planet). A little bit of more effort from the producers of this videogame could have created more variety for you to be present in another scenarios/planets of the Clone Wars. But I believe this problem to be minor, when you compare to the much more positive aspects of the game.
Still, I cannot recommend you buy it at full price (except if your are a Star Wars nerd :P), since it is an old game and it no longer has an active multiplayermode. Buy it only when it´s in promotion.
Like many people claim, this game really needs a sequel - where you play as the same squad team, now part of the forces of the eeeeeeeevil Galactic Empire. It would have been a much better sequel to make instead of the disaster that was Star Wars "BattleFront" EA (THE GAME IS NOT WORTH OF DESERVING OF "BATTELFRONT" ON IT´S TITLE!!!). Unfortunatelly, this game appears to have been forgotten and I don´t think a sequel (or a reboot) will ever be created.

Only 3 options are offered per turn and honestly barely make a difference in the outcome if at all. I didn't want to end up with Emily for a multitude of reasons, yet despite selecting the supportive best friend but not interested dialogue options in the first run, by the final chapter I'd apparently "hooked up" with her off-screen and was now the clingy sad person whose only choices were to either beg to be together or the cold Goodbye that ends the game. I just wanted to be friends??? The second time around, I played the complete jerk and the dialogue remained mostly the same until the last couple of chapters where she hated me and the final chapter lasted for one dismissive line of dialogue. Doesn't give me a lot of hope for the other runs where I can be her friend without leading her on.
There's probably a lot of little nuances I chose not to explore, such as the info boxes for the online buddies in each chapter, and all the secret dps you can unlock, but I'm not sure the whole game is worth it for those tidbits. Then again hey it's free so whatever. Yes it brings back the mems of windows XP days and messenger sounds and emo band/movie dps, but I'm not at all tempted to do another run through to see what the other playthroughs are like, and the first go left me with an overall feeling of "wtf just happened". If you're really bored, it's a good way to waste 15-30 minutes on a quick run with two emotionally stunted individuals (Emily and "yourself"), but otherwise spend your time elsewhere.

I didn't think I would like a digital board game. I'm also allergic to hex tiles. However, Armello is beautifully animated and super fun. I once heard it compared to "what would happen if Disney bought the rights to Game of Thrones" -- while this obviously isn't a completely logical scenario, I think it's a pretty fair comparison. The game is cute, but maintains a mature attitude that makes you take it seriously.
On the sliding scale of skill versus randomness, this game sits somewhere in the middle. You need skill to not screw up, but randomness features pretty heavily in determining the winner. As a skilled player, you won't necessarily win a game against three new players. Lots of fun BS happens at the end of the game; "upsets" are frequent and wins are not locked down until you strike the last blow.
Also an excellent game to multitask on; while you're waiting for people to take their turn, you can do other stuff. Play games 24/7, even when you have stuff to do!

This is going to be really long, as I have just got done beating the game 100% minus the picture frames.
Being the 18 year old guy I am, I grew up in the prime of video games. Jak and Daxter, Grand Theft Auto Vice City, Ty the Tasmanian Tiger, Seek & Destroy, etfc. I played many, many games in my time. But this game personally takes the cake as my all time favorite game from my childhood. Sure, it's outdated. Sure, there isn't much real plot and the gameplay isn't spectacular. But it's still an amazing game nontheless. The uniqueness of playing as a sole surviving Tasmanian Tiger throwing boomerangs in the great Down Under really stands out against games that all seem to involve one thing nowadays; guns and war. This game gives a feeling of actual meaning to your actions, if you watch and listen to the little plot there is. You are trying to save your family from the Dreamtime, where the evil Boss Cass imprisoned them. Every Thunder Egg you collect makes you feel one step closer to acquaring a talisman, which is what is absolutely necessary in the task of freeing your family. Collecting every item is not necessary to beat the game, but it does unlock a nice bonus that I will not spoil. If you're beaten the game 100% on the PS2, Gamecube, or XBOX. And for all the veteren players, there's a VERY special surprise for you after you have beaten the game 100%, too. Trust me, you will LOVE it. The Steam version comes with various new features, such as the ability to replay bosses, map your controls, camera-oriented throwing instead of in front of TY, leaderboard support for time attacks, and the special surprise I mentioned above. Since it is still in Alpha, many things can be added or removed. I personally hope there is some sort of player vs. player time attacks where you can race against each other in real time. Maybe even add in new bosses that can be taken on with two players. This game IS worth the money. I was going to buy a game I had wanted for MONTHS, but then I saw this game on Steam and I HAD to buy it. It is my childhood.
TL;DR - Awesome, fun, amazing source of nostalgia, happiness, childhood memories, new features, awesome secrets
The only cons I can think of are the ocasionally wonky camera angles, and the fact that it crashes often. You can play a full level 100% through, but it will likely crash on the next one.
All in all, I rate this remaster a solid 9.8/10. The only reason it is not a 10/10 is because of the crashes. I can't wait to see the end result of this masterpiece!
P.S. If you DO get it, go to Extras and check out the "HD Test", or something like that. Trust me, you will like it in one way or another.

Fight the Dragon, even in its alpha state, is incredibly loaded and full of potential. The major RPG character archetypes aren't yet introduced as you only have the sword-and-board warrior and a fire mage, with a frost mage currently in development. The dungeon creation is incredibly simple yet powerful, allowing you to create nearly any environment and setup the details such as enemy patrol routes or which combinations of levers open a door.
There are a couple dungeons created by 3 Sprockets, but they're mostly tutorial levels. The gimmick here is the user-created content. Dungeons created can be published and thrown into the pool of user-generated content, randomly chosen for an adventurer. There's filters you can set to get the newest dungeons or the highest-rated dungeons, and you can even set up a list of favorites.
If you're afraid you'll "out-level" a dungeon, don't be. Difficulty and rewards scale with your character so you'll always get enjoyment out of your favorite dungeons. Now, you might say "Hey, if everything levels with me then how do I tell I'm really strong?" Cue the dragon.
The dragon is a premade dungeon (bascially a door and a platform surrounded by lava) for you to head into from your house very early on. The dragon's health is absolutely insane - the chances of defeating him in one go are nearly impossible. It'll likely takes hundreds of attempts across all of your characters. The dragon's health never resets, so eventually you can defeat him, and as you try to your progress is logged. You're ranked against the world and ranked against your previous attempts, so you can see just how far you've come.
I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in a dungeon-crawler. Diablo, Gauntlet, Torchlight - you name it, this game ranks right up there with them, even in it's alpha state.

This game is severely buggy and needs a ton of patches, and the storyline and voice acting are really bad, BUT darn it I haven't seen a game with this much potential since maybe STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl.
I have always liked sniping games, and I like open-world games, and this game does a good job of merging the two genres. The sniping is far better than in games like Far Cry 2/3/4, and the open-world atmosphere means you have a lot more options about what to do and how to do missions than a level-based game like the Sniper Elite series. The sniping is quite good and the different grenades and guns you can get are all fun to use, unlike other games where all the guns feel very similar. I thought the drone would be stupid but it is actually quite fun to use. It is a lot of fun to creep into a mission area, use your drone to find all the enemies, then slowly snipe them one by one. Some of the missions are either boring or short or force you into narrow generic fps levels which aren't fun, but most of the game involves missions where you have to go to a village or base and kill a bunch of dudes any way you want and from any direction you want, and that is where the game really shines.
As I said there are a ton of bugs, like the game's day/night cycle getting reset to midnight every time you die, gadgets disappearing from the menu until you reload a checkpoint, sometimes you get stuck on boxes, etc etc. I really hope CI Games gets on top of these bugs because if they do the game will really be closer to reaching its full potential.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys sniping games. If you can overlook the bugs and the silly storyline and the rather low-budget feel of the open-world, it is really a lot of fun.

(I play on an MSI GE70 2PE Apache Pro laptop - it's a 2,5 year old rather high end laptop, but not a powerful gaming laptop for most of today's games; I guess mostly due to constrained cooling in a laptop.

This game delivers exactly what I expected from it and some more.
I expected a game with exciting sniping and plenty of approaches to every situation.
I didn't realize however that "sniper" is just one of the options you have at any time and you can switch between (by how you play). There is also the "ghost" and "warrior" class - while they are indeed classes in which you can rank up and unlock skills, it should be noted that you are not constrained at all by these classes and they serve only the purpose of unlocking certain skills in that tree which may have just as well been not there for all I care. But that's the strength: the way you play makes you a sniper / ghost or warrior and all 3 those playstyles can be used for every mission and even during a single mission.
The gunplay is great and rewarding, this is true for snipers, but also assault rifles and pistols. The open world is imo interesting enough, with "points of interest" often surprising in terms of what they are exactly (many don't have hostiles, but some do). The driving is very basic but serves its purpose and adds somewhat to the immersion. The crafting feels rather pointless, I'd prefer if it was left out even if it's entirely optional (you can buy everything instead if you want to). The customisation is enjoyable even if objectively it's rather limited. There are some bugs that annoy to varying degrees, but I haven't found any of them to really destroy my experience. Even so, I hope they get fixed soon.
The worst in the game? The story (so far) and the acting. While I enjoy the theme of a seperatist uprising, the 'most wanted' missions etc., the "love story" and/or the way male-female interaction goes is... *deep sigh*... it's very superficial and not very mature. I can add that the animations and modelling for cutscenes is very poor, although it matters little to me relative to the poor lovestory. The developer could have made some easy gains with a good storywriter!
It must be said though that despite this downside, the game is very immersive because the gameplay and environment is so well done. I recommend it to anyone looking for a good stealth/tactical solo FPS.

I have to be honest on this one... Valiant Hearts was not what I thought it was going to be, and not in a good way. Critics seemed to make this game out to be some dark, emotional, and deep experience, when it is far from it. Being a history buff, I was very excited about this game and looking forward to what I heard from critics and the gaming community. Instead, I was dissapointed heavily.
Yes, the game mechanics are simplistic, but that's not what I have a problem with. If the story was as great as people said and what I was hoping for, it wouldn't have been a problem at all. Instead, the game is literally like an oversimplistic comic book for ten year olds. Imagine watching a movie like Saving Private Ryan where the main characters are chasing a bad guy who embodies every stereotype of a comic book villain. That's what you do in this game. The characters freely traverse the German/French front throughout the war, doing whatever they want, even though the majority are conscripted soldiers, and chase a literal comic book villain who flys around on a zeppelin that resembles something from a steampunk mag. It's not deep, it's not emotional, and it's not a realistic potrayal of war. It's childish.
This game had SO much potential, and it was wasted. Utterly wasted. The only interesting thing I could take away from it was all the interesting historical facts that are peppered throughout, and the collectible items you can acquire that give some background on every day soldier life in the time period.
If you're looking for a comic book from the 80's where a motley crew chases down an ultra bad guy with all the attached tropes and sterotypes that you could imagine, this one's for you.

A game which contains several puzzles, a few boss battles and is relatively short (around 7 hours). Valiant Hearts is more like a game that tells you a story, a story about WW1 of course. You have characters from different nations that end up meeting each other for different reasons.
The puzzles aren't complicated and boss fights aren't hard, but they are fun to do. The best part about this game for me is all the knowledge you get from the many facts and curiosities that are given as reward for collecting optional items and such. As someone that loves the subject of wars, specially the 2 world wars that happened, it was a good experience for me since I got to learn about things I didn't know before by playing this game.
The story is good. Before I played this I saw a lot of people saying it was really emotional heavy and I was expecting lots of things to make the players cry or feel bad somehow, but after completing it I must say it isn't that heavy. You'll probably only get the "feels", as they say, by the end.
The only thing that I think is missing from the game is another character with a different perspective from the others (they are all on the allies side), it really bothers me how there's no one having their story told from the German side (Karl doesn't count), specially since that kind of perspective is very often not known by people. I wouldn't say the game tries to deliver the "good guys vs bad guys" crap, but if I was making the game I would add another character.
I rate this game 7/10 and recommend buying it during a sale if you like games that focus on the story and find the history of WW1 interesting.

Insurgency is one of those games that seems to fly under the radar, but has amazing devs and a very dedicated playerbase.

This game is a great lil' FPS that I would classify as "military shooter sim" and the two primary game modes are TvT (team vs team or "deathmatch") and Co-Op (vs AI/bots). TBH, the TvT/PvP in this game was not satisfying to my palette, however, Co-Op vs AI, especially "maximum effort" AI in overwhelming numbers has been some of the most fun gaming I've had in a while. Backed by a fairly strong modding community and a "no-frills" attitude, Insurgency has become my go-to FPS when I need lead slingin', brass kickin', frag handlin' fun on a bun!
My only caveats are spotty server/client relationships that present frustrating problems at times and netcode that can drag a server down when dealing with high latency players. Otherwise, this game performs brilliantly on older tech and buttery smooth on modern (read i5+) hardware at max settings.
Be sure to mod the crap out of this game for maximum pleasure and immersion!

This is the best free turn based strategy game I've ever played.
It has solo, 2-3 player coop and versus. So you can enjoy it however you want.
The best part about the game is the item system. Each character have a deck of cards like attacks, armor, move, block... This deck is made by the items your character has equiped. Each item gives between 3 and 6 cards. But, it's all or nothing. If an item have 5 great cards and an handicap, you have to deal with it. This makes for very unique character building that can be optimized in a lot of ways.
There is also 3 classes and 3 races for characters that all have items that can exclusively be equiped to them.
There is a freaking lot of items in this game and, yep, it's free to play, you can buy more items. But it's not really a problem to me. You will lack some items in the begining but if you play through a good part of the campaign, you'll have a lot of them. If you want to help the devs your options are : timed subscription for an extra item after each fight, buying individual chests with guaranteed high rarity items and new side-missions with guarantee item the first time you complete it. None of those are required to truly enjoy the game. There is also some character reskin you can buy that doesn't affect gameplay at all.
(If you want to buy the missions, the bundle isn't you only option. If you go on the lock mission, you'll be able to unlock it for some paid currency which is a better deal if you don't care about the rest of the bundle.)
The campaing itself it very fun. Each mission is a different challenge with unique opponents. I've yet to complete it. The missions get harder and harder, often requiring you to change your items to match specific opponents. I've started it again with a friend and it still is a blast to play.
But, the story is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't expect anything from that part.

Overall a decent game. I had fun sniping with the gadgets and silencer.
Gameplay
The gameplay itself was nice, except for the many bugs the game has. The movement feels nice, although travelling can get a bit tedious at times. The stealth gameplay does feel nice as well, and it really does make you think about how to approach a mission if you really are trying to go fully stealth on the hardest difficulty. I dont think the game would be as good if you played it on the easier game modes. The rifles themselves are fun to shoot and can allow for a head on firefight game if thats what you're into. Overall the combat feels really nice and is fun when you're carrying out objectives
Story
The story itself was awful. Just completely terrbile. Throughout the entire game the story was just one cliche after another. None of the characters had anything special about them. Sometimes the story's dialogue would completely contradict itself too, with one character saying your orders are to not do something, and the next mission being them assigning you to do exactly that, with no explanation as to why they changed their mind. They even try so hard to make you feel for these characters, where one of theme commits suicide, but they never even try and fully explain why I should care about this person. The story itself completely ruins the game unfortunately.
TL;DR
If you can get past a hilariously terrbile story and just enjoy sniping or stealth killing, then this game is for you. It's fun to play, but the story and the animations and the glitches really really really make it hard to recommend this game. Just like many others here I really wish I could give a mixed rating

If you haven't played Magicka 1, I would highly recommend going back and playing that game instead of this one.  The spellcasting just felt a whole lot smoother than it is in the sequel. Mostly, this is because they added the Focus cooldowns for the Magicks.  Part of what made the first game so awesome was that you got to feel like a god as you slung magick after magick into the hordes of enemies running at you as you hasted yourself to run away and teleported around the map.  With the cooldowns added, you end up in situations where you emergency teleport out of harm's way, but now cannot cast Haste on yourself to keep running.  This really limits what you can do in combat because half the mechanics of the game are based around running back and queueing up your next spell.  It makes Earth based projectile weapons insanely hard to use because you just don't get the chance to charge them up.  I love me some beam weapons, but I hate feeling forced to spam them and shields.   Devs, if you wanted to put a cooldown mechanic in the game, just put it on the quick cast bar and let those of us with fast fingers be rewarded for it.

After playing Magicka 1 I was completely amazed by the game mechanics and the story with its hilarious characters. I almost lost myself in the game because it was so much fun.
Luckily Paradox created Magicka 2 to have me get the kick in the balls I needed, so I can find my way back to reality and the horrible world we are living in.
The first bummer came up right after starting the game: You are now forced to link your steam account to a useless Paradox account, if you are going to play online. I have not been seeing the point of linking or creating an extra account for any game on steam yet, because for me one huge advantage of steam was accessing all your game by using just one single account. But anyway.
So, I started with the campaign and everything felt normal like in Magicka 1, except for the controls that were almost completely changed! For example, the keys for a melee attack or an area cast are now different to Magicka 1. That is probably why the term "Learn to spell again" was added to the game. It was kind of annoying at the beginning getting used to the new controls and I died several times because of it. After a while I finally got the hang of the new controls.
After half an hour in the campaign I realised that there was now a cooldown time for magicks you used. So, I found myself frequently hammering a combination of a certain magick on my keyboard while a horde of enemies was charging towards me, but nothing happened. The cooldown time is a few seconds. Therefore, the fun of throwing some magicks against the endless waves of enemies is almost completely gone. Instead, I often ran in circles to somehow get some distance between me and the foes. But, god have mercy on me, when there was just one enemy with a slowing ability. Needless to say, I died a lot resulting into increasing frustration.
One positive thing I noticed at this point is that one is now forced to find out the weaknesses on the enemies, because the one ultimate spell does not exist any longer.
Besides the gameplay the story of the campaign is boring and way to short. The only reason it took me a few hours to play through it, was the ongoing torture caused by the horrible game mechanics described above. Actually, I felt somehow relieved when I finally played though this pile of garbage.
As a conclusion I can say, that Magicka 2 is definitely more challenging than the first part. For me the necessitation to link your steam account to a Paradox-account defies any explanation. Killing enemies got far more difficult because of the need to find out what spell/element is effective against a certain type and the damn pain-in-the-booty cooldown time of the magicks. The story is almost non-existing, so casual gamers who just want to play through another action-loaded and funny campaign, will be disappointed. I bought the game on sale and still think, it was not worth the money.

A game which contains several puzzles, a few boss battles and is relatively short (around 7 hours). Valiant Hearts is more like a game that tells you a story, a story about WW1 of course. You have characters from different nations that end up meeting each other for different reasons.
The puzzles aren't complicated and boss fights aren't hard, but they are fun to do. The best part about this game for me is all the knowledge you get from the many facts and curiosities that are given as reward for collecting optional items and such. As someone that loves the subject of wars, specially the 2 world wars that happened, it was a good experience for me since I got to learn about things I didn't know before by playing this game.
The story is good. Before I played this I saw a lot of people saying it was really emotional heavy and I was expecting lots of things to make the players cry or feel bad somehow, but after completing it I must say it isn't that heavy. You'll probably only get the "feels", as they say, by the end.
The only thing that I think is missing from the game is another character with a different perspective from the others (they are all on the allies side), it really bothers me how there's no one having their story told from the German side (Karl doesn't count), specially since that kind of perspective is very often not known by people. I wouldn't say the game tries to deliver the "good guys vs bad guys" crap, but if I was making the game I would add another character.
I rate this game 7/10 and recommend buying it during a sale if you like games that focus on the story and find the history of WW1 interesting.

I would usually be inclined to not recommend a game for such a shortcoming, but the story of Valiant Hearts is honestly so moving and thrilling that I cannot help but praise it. More than worth the money.

I followed this game here on steam and had it on my wishlist for a while, then bought it in a sale and installed it right away, but I did not start it.
Why, you ask? Because I was afraid to be disappointed.
I played the original Syndicate in 1997 as a kid and I loved it to bits. I replayed it so often that I knew every map like the back of my hand.
Last weekend, I was forced to cancel all my plans because of a flu and so I said to myself, lets find out if the critics are right about this one.
The game is indeed best described as a spiritual successor to Syndicate. The world, the lore, the style, the music and the tech is much the same. The gameplay is similar but much refined which I want to elaborate.
While many of Syndicate's features can be found in Satellite Reign, their implementation makes for a better gameplay.
The biggest difference between the two is that there is no hard cut between the missions and briefing phases. Syndicate sent you on missions but every time you reached your goals you got to the extraction point and found yourself and your agents in a safe, far away briefing overview. In Satellite Reign, you get your briefing on the go, while your agents are still in the thick of enemy cartel controlled terrain. You can get briefed, buy additional intel, research tech or outfit your agents all while "in mission".
This might seem like a small cosmetic change, but it changes the whole feeling of the pace. While in Syndicate you sometimes escaped into the extraction zone, while being shot at by dozens of gauss guns and it didn't matter, because the next screen was a safe place far away, Satellite Reign keeps you in the game and it feels much more interesting and immersive.
But there is more. There are some key elements that were added to the Syndicate formula that make Satellite Reign even better.
While in Syndicate all your agents were identical and only what equipment you gave them made them take on a certain role, Satellite Reign has introduced classes.
You start with a
which is the tank of your team who also can dish out good peak damage.
You get a
-class agent next, who can scan the environment and augument the whole team.
You have a
next, who can hack terminals, ATMs, and take control of civilians, enemy agents or drones.
And you get the
who can cloak, stealthily kill with a sword and use ziplines without additional tech.
This leads us to
All your agents can be upgraded in Health and Weapon Proficiency, as well as learn to carry more Items.

can learn

So with all these skills there is much more tactics involved, some tactics are slow and safe, some are bold and reckless.
And some are very risky and your agents might die.
In Syndicate if you took your Persuadatron into town, you had an unlimited supply of bodies to fuel your war. Whenever one of your agents died, you lost a bit of money for the cybernetic implants, but after a couple of missions money was plentiful and you did not care about your death toll.
Satellite Reign is similar, but different.
When your agents die, ther is a short countdown during which you can pay money to revive (reclone) them right away or wait till the countdown reaches zero and you can send a fresh clone of the deceased agent in for free.
But it still comes in at a price.
Every individual in Satellite Reign has stats and every agent does as well.
There is a baseline for the stats:
Every time you reclone your agents, they degrade and get worse in one or all of these stats.
It is a good tactic early on to Hijack enemy agents, which have better stats than the average civilian and send them back to cloning. Then clone your Soldier, Support, Hacker and Infiltrator into these bodies with better health, speed and aim.
But when you find a nice individual with +55 health +20% speed and +15% aim, you think twice before you let him die.
This is a nice game mechanic to balance out the free of charge revive and it adds another layer to the immersion where you find yourself thinking in the same perverted way about human bodies like these syndicates do - as just assets to add to your company.
This game is a jewel. I only played it for a weekend and I found myself googling if there will be a sequel or expansion to it, because I already fear that I will play through it too fast.
If you loved Syndicate, you must play this. Don't worry, you won't be disappointed.

First of all, it is VERY buggy. Graphics settings changing by themselves, effects not being displayed, getting damage and/or heal out of nowere (for example, i contantly got damaged while under the Haste effect), weapons not working, terrible sync problems in coop... The list can go on and on. Original Magicka also had bugs, but not as much.
The level disign is bad. Most of the time you will have to fight in very tight spaces, so dodging enemies and strategically choosing spells is not an option - you'll just have to spam with beams and mines. Oh, and usually you cannot go back. Didn't know i'm playing Super Mario.
The number of magicks is way less than in the original, and the number of usefull ones is even smaller. Also, most of the damaging ones are less effective than just spamming with raw elements
Dialogs in the original were short and mostly funny. Here, the dialogs are overly long, and even when they manage to pull of a good joke - they usually spoil it by drowning it in useless blabbery.
There are pretty much no new ideas here, so it looks more like an additional campaign for the first game.
Staffs and melee weapons are mostly useless - and there are very few of those anyway. Different robes don't actually feel different.
Finally, the end boss fight is tied with game's phisics. The problem is - phisics here are really bad.
TL;DR It's pretty much Magicka one, but with everythig done worse than in the original.

It doesn't flinch from showing the horrors of WWI: infantry charges against machine guns, trench and tunnel warfare, and gas attacks on soldiers and civilians. The game incorporates interesting facts about the war too.
But then the main characters go on a wacky chase or you fight a cartoon German villain. The main gameplay is lite-adventure-game usually involving throwing items and flipping switches.
I thought this somehow just worked though. Video games almost never depict "real life", but instead become metaphors of the very thing they are depicting. I would compare the "gameplay" aspects of many games to the singing and dancing in musicals. Why are people suddenly singing a song during a Paris uprising? Because you're watching a musical. Gameplay works the same way: your brain can easily switch from real scenes to surreal scenes.
Not all games get this right, but I think Valiant Hearts did.

Interesting top-down shooter that is free to play for all Steam users, uses the Source Engine 2010.  Based on the movie Aliens.
Alien Swarm is a top-down shooter set at a 60-degree angle. Four players can join a single co-operative game, the aim of which is to progress through science fiction-themed levels while eliminating waves of AI aliens. Players can choose from 40 different pieces of equipment.
The game is class-based, with players choosing from the roles of Officer, Special Weapons, Medic, and Tech. Each class has two selectable characters, with differences in abilities.
Officer =
Grants a passive bonus to damage and damage resistance to nearby allies. He has access to the Vindicator, a class-restricted shotgun with an incendiary grenade launcher and has general all-around abilities. They are also capable of throwing extra amounts of explosive ordnance, and may find class-restricted ammo caches on the field for his Vindicator shotgun. The two playable characters are Sarge and Jaeger.
Special Weapons =
Brings raw damage to the table and starts out with a customized autogun with superior parameters, high magazine capacity, and auto-aiming ability. The Special Weapons gains access to a powerful minigun at a high enough level, and can pick up class-restricted ammo caches on the field. The two playable characters are Wildcat and Wolfe.
Medic=
Is the only class able to equip and deploy temporary healing beacons, and at a high enough level can use a medigun to selectively heal teammates and themselves. The two playable characters are Faith and Bastille.
Tech =
Carries a motion sensor, sets up sentry guns faster, welds doors faster, and is the only class capable of unlocking certain door panels or completing certain objectives by means of a hacking minigame. They also have access to a prototype assault rifle with auto-aiming capabilities and the ability to fire stun grenades. The two playable characters are Crash and Vegas.
The game includes persistent statistics, unlockable equipment, and Steam Achievements.

Each run can be completed within a weekend

Only one save at a time (To be fixed in future patch)

The man on the end of the bar is looking at you funny.
A Japanese crimelord wants you dead.
You've been incarcerated, even after you've pleaded not guilty.
It was self-defense, after all.
Let's paint the town red.
Paint the Town Red is, in a nutshell, a beat 'em up from a first person perspective. It's you and your blocky fists against many other blocky men in an orgy of blood and violence. Voxel violence.
Blows landed will bruise, cut, break, and dismember your enemies, spilling their square blood onto whatever surface is nearby. Anything and everything is a weapon. Bar stools, steak, bottles, afro combs, shuriken, bats, pimp canes... really, the list goes on. Nothing will stand in your way once you unleash your god-like special powers. Stack enough bodies and unleash shockwaves, pop men like balloons using nothing but your fists, and finally, call down the wrath of God and literally smite your enemies, reducing men into lifeless piles of wasted carbon.
The three levels available as of this writing are fun and colorful, bursting with personality and secrets, and they include:
-A biker bar where everyone wants to take a bite out of you
-A Saturday-night beatdown at the local disco
-A maximum security prison where dropping the soap is the least of your worries
There's even a sandbox level to play around with or to learn the finer points of Paint the Town Red.
Do I recommend this? Absolutely. Great for blowing off steam, laughing with the fun physics, or even feeling like the 90's action movie hero you always wanted to be.

Mechanically, this game plays like a cross between Catan and Risk, or Dungeon Dice Monsters. The hex-grid, playing card, and turn-based elements are classics of the board game genre but Armello takes it a step further, cashing in on some of the features only a virtual game can provide, adding Stealth abilities and a Day/Night cycle.
Visually, Armello is a work of art. Alternating between simplistic but well-drawn 2D animation for the in-combat animations and a gorgeously rendered 3D world, Armello flexes its muscles visually while using very little resources to run the game. Transitions are smooth and crisp, there's no clash between the art styles, and the almost-cartoon like stylization gives the game a comfortable charm.
I have not played the single-player experience so I cannot comment on that, but several multiplayer games with friends have been completely unique, well designed, balanced, and of course, incredibly fun each time.

Star Wars Republic Command is a great game but it does have some flaws that might make people think twice about picking it up.
If you're familiar with any of the trailers, you might think that this is some sort of faced paced horror shooter for adults but it really isn't. It's slow paced, there really isn't any horror elements to it, and like the ESRB said its pretty much for teens.
Theres a lot of padding in this game, in the form of making enemies bullet sponges. Some of the common enemies take quite a few clips to kill with the blaster rifle and you only get so much ammo. Its shown that they didn't know how to deal with ammo because the ammo situation is quite speratic with each level.
The AI for the squad is sometimes horrible, but it's expected for a squad based shooting game. Sometimes you have to order squad mates to not do things such as run into a room full of super battle droids via telling them to defend a corner. The personality of the squad, much like other games with, features a serious badass, and playful comic, and some guy in the middle who just follows orders. None of them are that annoying, some of the dialogue from the serious badass can make you cringe because it usually comes off as emo.
At the very end it started to get repititve. If the sequel's gameplay was exactly like this game's gameplay then it wouldn't really do that well.
Great game, well made lots of fun :)

If you like boardgames, or you just want to try a good one here on Steam, I suggest adding Armello to your wishlist.
In Armello you guide one of four heroes on his perilous journey to claim the Throne from the mad king, who's slowly dying. On your path you'll grow your prestige and get stronger completing missions that may also grant you better equipment or a follower. Everything you gain can help you fight off the other heroes, but also obscure creatures and even the king guards when they block your way. It's not easy to explain all the rules and how they can change in just a small paragraph, but don't worry, there is a nice set of small tutorials in-game that will explain everything.
Here is a small list of the things I appreciate about this game, that may help you decide if it's worth your interest:
. different ways to win (you can adapt your strategy as you play)
. a bunch of characters and stats modifiers (lot of combinations to experiment with)
. satisfying dice rolling (you don't really need to buy all those skins)
. multiuse cards (to equip, use or "burn" before dice rolls to mitigate results)
. random missions (to upgrade your stats, get better equipment and find followers)
. rules alteration (game changes if it's day or night and if you are "corrupted" or not)
. prestige points mechanic (if you have the most, the king let you influence the game)
. hand management, area control and stealth mechanics (you get a bit of everything)
. random board generation, great art and nice soundtrack
. well... there is more, but I think you already know if it's something you'd enjoy ;D
I keep coming back for more in Armello: I like trying a different strategy everytime and the fact that developers continue to update the game periodically, sometimes even with new rule-changing elements, definitely keeps my interest high. Unfortunately you can't play it hotseat, but that's because some (stealth) mechanics won't work. Play versus 3 AI with superfast turns, if you're in a hurry, or jump online to test your skills, but keep in mind that every player has to take his turn and you better observe what they are doing while you progam your next move. If you have problems finding opponents online, just keep an eye for special events organized by the LoG devs. Have fun Armellians!

Maybe they'll make a Satellite Reign 2 at some point and remedy these things?  Who knows eh?

As much as I wanted to like this game, the economy just completely killed the game for me. In order to keep you agents with decent equipment you need to research them, which costs a ton of cash, and most of the cash you get in game is through a passive ATM hack. The problem is that even when you're actively pursuing objectives you never have enough money to research the required equipment.
Since the enemies scale with your team's level, I felt outmatched by the enemies before I completed the first area. You have the ability to buy new equipment, but most of it costs 10k-20k and I was getting at most $3 a minute.
The game pauses after any length of inactivity, so there's really no way for you catch up with the curve.
I enjoyed the strategy, but the lack of funds to keep my team going, and what appeared to be RNG equipment drops, just killed my enjoyment of the game.

However it is still a great game. I hope they improve on it some more in a sequel.

"An Imp? A Fiend!" isn't perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but I was surprised by what a solid little platformer this turned out to be. This game can be rather aptly described as a cross between Castlevania and Super Meat Boy, with jumping puzzles spread out between areas where the focus is heavily on exploration. The controls in this game are remarkably responsive, which is a good thing, because there's a few tough rooms where you'll need to use that to your full advantage. The story, to the extent it exists, wasn't great, but it did provide the incentive necessary to play to the end.
While tight controls form the backbone of a good platformer, I'd say just about every other element of this game could have done with a lot more work. Early on, when the flow of the game isn't quite established, it can be difficult to figure out that this game is open-ended, with no set path or order by which is needs to be completed. Boss battles are simple and the rest of the enemies are fish in a barrel, meaning that this is a short, easy game that quickly reaches an unsatisfying conclusion: In one of my least-favorite indie game tropes, this game ends by teasing a sequel that will never come. Still, I finished this one up in just under 3 hours, and I had a decent time, so I would say I got my 99 cents worth.

An Imp? A Fiend! is a precision platformer / adventure game that just doesn't really make it (Imagine an easier Super Meat Boy that plays in a metroidvania game's map, without the metroidvania elements.
It has a lot of promising things in it, but overall lack in game design makes it an unpleasant experience in many parts. Maybe to balance out the problematic map design, the player has 3 hearts, a damage / spike takes down half, and some enemies drop a whole one, and if you'd die, you respawn in  the same room (screen)
The most problematic thing is the hit-recoil. Get hit, and the character will jump up - if a flying enemy descended onto you, you jump up into it, damaging yourself again. Same with wall-mounted spikewalls, a wrong jump can effectively cause a stunlock that takes more than half of max health.
With the forgiving respawn system, the needlessly annoying (but halting only in very few cases) knockback the game is STILL easy, the jumping/traversing the map provides some variety but the enemies are same, and only the "dungeon" parts have some challenging moments, but because of the mentioned stunlock-effect they are less fun as they could be.
All in all: the game works nicely, except from one particularly weak aspect that's still solvable.  If you want to play the game I wouldn't talk you our of it, but neither would I convince you to play it. It's really a truly neutral experience.

A big improvement over the previous game, Shin Samurai Jazz, in basically every respect, but the game itself (level design, specifically).
What stroke me first was how good the game felt to play! The controls are very tight, and both the movement and combat feel very nice! The animation go much better with the moves, and the combat is much clearer in regards to your range and how enemies are affected by the attacks.
The second thing that stroke me, on the negative side, was how the game had 20-30 rooms of meaningless combat/platforming until anything even remotely like an objective was given to the player. And even then, it was very vague. It was filler, like the previous one. And the worst was to come later...
It appears that Blaze Epic likes making the same game over and over again. Usually, that's a bad thing. In this case, things are improving, so it could be worse!
You have the same moveset: double jump, dash, attack. These moves serve both for combat and platforming, which is nice.
The biggest problem with the platforming (aside from how much of it is filler) is that there are spikes in every ♥♥♥♥ing wall. But the infuriating thing are some chandeliers that throw fire at you. In the middle of the platforming sections, of course. And they're indestructible. And the worst thing about them is their random firing time. It makes it impossible to predict when they're going to shoot, so you're just have to pray that they shoot at a convenient time, in the middle to this very precise platforming you have to do...
Later on there's also 1-hit kill lava (for barely touching it, too), which wasn't satisfying at all - the reason being that you have spikes above you, lava below, and a very, very tiny margin for error. Some rooms get frustrating, but it could have been worse.
The game is more or less (mostly less) a metroidvania, in the sense that you have a full map to explore as you feel like. It's a very bad metroivania, though. You have all the abilities from the start. Which makes the exploration rather redundant, doesn't it? Well, too bad. The map is fairly large, and it's all absolute filler.
There isn't a story to speak of. It tries to give you hints of a story, but there is none, since the end
. This could be interesting, but not in this case. It was just a poor excuse for not having a story.
I mentioned about Shin Samurai Jazz that the level design was just about getting keys to unlock doors to unlock other doors, right? Well, it's exactly the same here, if not worse. Worse, because sometimes you have to go to the extremes of each area to open the door you wanted from the beginning, going back and forth, accomplishing absolutely nothing. Same rooms, same enemies, same abilties, etc. etc.
Each area seems different, but it's purely its coating, because every enemy and platforming ends up virtually the same.
The only design to speak of are the Bosses, but even them have a single pattern, and not a very interesting one in any of the cases.
It's almost disrespectful to design levels like this, as silly as this sounds. It's literally about making you go back and forth to unlock doors, filling your time until it's worth any money (because people really like talking about time/money in videogames....).
Even though the controls are pretty good, the game ends up being worthless, because it has no purpose, and so makes the player wander aimlessly back and forth, collecting keys and destroying crystals for no reason...
Because there was some improvement, I'm still hopefull about Blaze Epic's games (Nil Ninjahtic actually looks really good), but it will decline soon, if every game is the same, with the grand purpose of unlocking door and lead into other doors, that lead...

I like that the devs are a highly skilled group that have put together a very high quality product, and I like that they involve themselves with the comunity around their game.

No over inflated price that they'll sometimes put on sale for something reasonable, no knocking a penny off to make you feel like you're getting a better deal than you really are. No drawing you in with a cheap base game that they then barage with DLC and microtransation garbage to bleed your wallet dry. Just $20, and you get everything. Well I'll describe this game as I played it first. Then list some key points. Yeah. That should work.
Anyway. I started the game off absolutely sure I would be useless. I immediately get in there and help out my team in unexpected ways. Everyone has a medkit to heal their teammates so you can immediately become useful.
When I first started the game I found two nice players who greeted me right off the bat. Then I started solving some puzzles. I was amazed at myself. My 6 or so teammates seemed baffled by them yet I figured it out myself. So thats when I realized nobody is truely 100% useless(Unless you try to be useless)
We ended up after beating a mission having a monster battle. The enemy team only had about 3-4 headcrabs. We had 3 bullsquids and a human grunt. Needless to say the enemy team got slaughtered. There was another funny mini game we played later on as well.
So what do I think as key points?
Pros
-Well done and seems pretty solid as a idea.
-You can change your player model and many other neat settings you would not expect with the c key.
-Pretty smooth. In every way.
-Nice community. I don't know if I went to the right place but honestly everyone seemed nice and helpful. What a great bunch of players!
The In Between (Both help and hurt the gameplay)
-Puzzles can be very easy or very difficult. This could make you laugh in some cases or rage in others. If you want a challenge this is good.
-Enemies can be hillariously easy to kill or impossible depending on what your playing. This can lead to some rather unbalanced scenarios. Fun if you like chaos.
-It can be very silly on some missions. You can FEEL the unofficial on a lot of them. Honestly I think it is pretty amazing in many cases. You get to experience some intresting fights and situations you never would otherwise.
Con
-If your a graphics freak you will be annoyed probably. I really don't see this as a big issue. The pros make up for this easily.
I really can't think of another con honestly. Most of them are in between and not completely a con. Honestly I think I should just call the inbetween section pros anyway.
Get this. It is worth it.

Average game, good value for the money, but just short of beeing great.  The friends told me it was like Gauntlet legends so I had my hopes up too high.  The game is missing justa handful of key features of this type of games to make it great.  First, the characters aren't different enough.  The game could use 1 more starting character that different from the others, perhaps a true melee class with a mana shield spell.  I generaly don't play those characters but I know many do.  Also, and this is key, Supers.  Characters need super moves so they can feel empowered and unique from other characters.  The resource for these can be built up in various ways, or found in items hidden in the map to give explorer type players a rewarding experience.   Which brings me to my next point.
The game is split between rewarding exploration and punishing it.  The items hidden on the levels arn't particularly great and the game "features" insta death for walking off the edge.  These elements are contradictory and errodes player agency, and creates a greater sense of a game on rails.   I still enoy it, but it will be difficult to get my friends to play without it offering a truely unique experience for each player. The spells each character has are virtualy a pallet swap difference between them, and the RPG elements aren't nearly deep enough.  Skills are almost exclusivly a numerical bonus rather then having a few key skills which can alter play style.  I would suggest that the blink spell you get for free, should of been a skill you bought with your first tutorial skill point.

Wasn't sure what to expect but Satellite Reign has depth, style, and most importantly is quite a lot of fun.  You control a squad of 4 (sometimes with extra help) and each member has their own skills and progression path.  Soldier, Support, Hacker, and Infiltrator.  Pretty self-explanatory.  You gain XP and level up, using skill points to upgrade specific abilities and passives on each character.  In addition, each character has augment slots for mechanical upgrades and gear slots for all sorts of things... from cloaking devices to drones to grenades.  There are also quite a few varied weapons, which also have available upgrades.
The graphcs are GREAT.  The city is awash in neon and it looks VERY futuristic/cyberpunk.  While you'll likely be playing zoomed out for a beter tactical vantage point- zooming in rewards you with some AMAZINGLY fine detail.  It's a shame that you need to have a panned-out view of everything because the attention to detail up close is amazing.  The gameplay alternates between combat and well-put-together stealth mechanics.  Early on your only option might be to run in and out as quickly as possible on a given target, killing everything possible and running when outnumbered/outgunned.  This quickly changes.... as you gain access to various gear/augments/skills/etc you'll find that the planning of a raid is half the fun.... tactical and strategic options open up exponentially as your toolset expands.  At about 22 hours into the game I've gotten to the point where there are many viable options on a given strike.... but from the list of technology that I have yet to research/buy I can see that I still have a LONG way to go in terms of available tools and options.  Also- at 22 hours I don't know exactly HOW far I am into the game.... but without spoiling anything I DO know that I'm AT MOST at the 25% mark.  It's nice to get good bang-for-your-buck.
This is an open-world game to a degree.  You are in one giant city and while you don't have access to the whole city right off the bat- you CAN, in theory, force your way into parts of the city that you clearly have no business being in yet.  Your map is littered with possible targets and it's up to you to pick which targets to hit and when, balancing the risks versus the rewards of each.  Oh- another neat part of this game: the cloning system.  You pretty much abduct people off the street and clone them to enhance each of your team members.  Your soldier might start out as a black dude.... but you might find a white girl on the street with better stats.  Abduct, clone, and BOOM-  your soldier has had a gender change and has changed ethnicities.  Each time a character dies you can respawn but your stats decrease.  Not your XP-earned skills, but your base stats like health, speed, accuracy, etc.  There is a level where it won't go below, which is essentially a 0% bonus across the board, but it's a neat system and it's fun to troll around for abduction victims.  As you level up your "Hijack" ability you can start abducting soldier, and eventually high-ranking soldiers, giving your team access to better and better stat-buffs.
I expected Satellite Reign to be OK, but it turned out to be REALLY good.  I'm thrilled that it's a really big game, too, as my current rate of play should have me getting at least 70 hours out of this.  At least.  I tend to go through games slowly, taking my time and enjoying the scenery, but I still couldn't imagine someone tearing through this game TOO quickly.... at least not if they want to research all the cool toys and see everything.  I feel I've already gotten my money's worth and I have a lot of game left to play.  Glad I picked this up.

When you meet the villain at the end of the tutorial mission he's an obvious Ubisoft Villain (that is, an edgelord who constantly babbles high-school tier philosophy at you to sound like he's more nuanced than a regular bad guy, see Jackal, Vas, Apollyon, the villain from Dying Light) but it's jarringly haphazard and forced. And the good stuff, with some caveats.  Most of these will be compared to the other big sniper game, Sniper Elite.
RANGE.  ♥♥♥♥ING.  RANGE.  This was what killed Sniper Elite for me, the way even the more open maps of SE4 were designed to force fights at 50-150 meters, which is practically phone booth range for sniping.    SGW3's sniping tends to be longer range, but the story missions still tend to constraint you to closer range.  I guess I understand why, a silenced rifle at 700 meters would obviate most of the challenge of a lot of these scenarios.  Also, ballistics isn't as challenging at SE4.  The magic elevation dial means even extreme-range shots are pretty easy to make even on the hardest difficulty setting.  Damage model isn't as good either of course, though enemies aren't as ironman resilient as SE4's bulletproof Nazis who can take a .30-06 to the chest and keep running like it's nothing.
AI.  AI isn't perfect, but it's much better at staying alive than SE4's bullet sponges.  SE4 enemies seemed designed to be shot and would repeatedly stick their heads out of cover even when bullets were bouncing off the wall literally inches from their stupid heads.  In that regard SGW3's enemies are miles ahead.  They actually take cover and they don't expose themselves.
However, they seem less adept on the offensive side.  SE4's enemies were pretty bad at counter-sniper tactics as well but occasionally you could provoke them into doing something semi-dangerous for you.  Maybe I just haven't gotten far enough for them to competently attack me.  We'll see.
Lethality is extremely high on both sides.  On the highest difficulty which is the only one you should play, one or two bullets is all it takes.  This makes the stealth and sniping much more important and going loud is very risky.  It's a good thing.
Overall compared to SE4 I'd say this game has the edge when it comes to feeling like a sniper game and providing a satisfying experience on that front.  SE4 wins on polish, but it often feels more like a gruesome shooting gallery and the knife-fight ranges kill the feel of sniping.
If you like sniping and you can get it on a discount you probably won't hate it.
edit:  also, fake gun names ruins any gunwanking you might do.  weapons are still obviously recognizable but the names are changed.  M1911 becomes M1984, etc.

Card Hunter is a deeply enjoyable game. It's a fusion of traditional Dungeons & Dragons tabletop and Magic: the Gathering style card game presented in a charming aesthetic that mimics classic D&D boards. The mechanics, while odd at first are quick to learn and work very well. There's a full suite of some 30 multi-mission adventures on offer, along with fleshed-out PvP that's accessible basically right off the bat in a competitive state.
Oh, and all of this is free. Not bad, right?
BUT - and this is a very big BUT - the amount of RNG involved in the gameplay is absolutely through the roof. Each character you control draws every move (up to and including actual moving) from an unseen, randomly shuffled deck of cards. The only guaranteed draw is the basic movement card which is always given to you at the start of each round. Absolutely everything else from attacks to healing spells to self debuff cards is completely random.
It is maddening and sadly all too common for my fighter (big chap who hits things with a sword/club/lightsaber) to go several rounds in a row without drawing a single attack card, and then draw a single kind of crap one before going another round without. For a class that's supposed to be up close and personal at all times this is downright deadly, especially since in the campaign adventures monsters seem to have an incredibly strong chance of drawing their most potent attack more or less every turn. This also applies to the priest (healing and buff/debuff support) and mage (killing things from far away), who are also both often caught without anything useful in their hands in the heat of the action.
Don't get me wrong, Card Hunter *is* a good game. The positives definitely outweigh the negatives by a fair margin. But I cannot stress enough that it can sometimes be an incredibly frustrating experience because so much of it is left down to the whims of RNJesus. The only thing you have complete control over is the positioning of your characters. Play it, but be very aware of that fact because it WILL bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥♥with alarming frequency.

I rate the game Battlefield: Bad Company 2 4/5. Good. If the singleplayer campaign had been better I would have been able to say this game was truly excellent but...
Let's face it. The single player campaign is short, linear, full of bad dialogue, boring, shallow characters (except for maybe your squad's sergeant), and even worse music. However, the visuals are amazing (and extremely well optimized so they run very fast) and the multiplayer capabilities of this game are excellent.
Indeed, although this game is about five years old the multiplayer modes are alive and kicking with lots of players who, while highly upgraded and ranked-up with access to far better equipment than any new player will initially have, surprisingly do not seem to be hacking or cheating so far as I can tell. Just be sure to use the server browser function the game comes with to find an active server (many active servers are packed to the gills with players too, even at all hours of the day).
Good things (where to begin?):
+Wonderful (and in places almost photo-realistic looking) graphics which run very, very fast on modern computers. The graphics have very few readily apparent graphical glitches. This game has particularly fantastic dust and smoke effects. With so much detail though it can be very difficult to see enemies due to their camo and all the smoke and dust which usually permeates many battlefields.
+Multiplayer matches are often large (or at least feel large if they are not actually huge) and open with lots of indoor and outdoor areas throughout. You often will find yourself running into and out of buildings.
+Most structures are almost fully destructable. If you fire a rocket at any random building a big wall of that building will come tumbling down or be blasted away. The buildings do tend to fall apart in a predictable manner allowing you to hide behind certain pieces of rubble which you know will never come down but for the most part any given building can take damage and be reduced to ruination. In this way, the replayability of multiplayer matches is greatly enhanced as what goes on can radically alter the often quasi-urban environments of the multiplayer battles.
+Though the gore in this game is very low (unrealistically low) with no torn limbs or pools of blood, the extremely destructible environments and smoke and blowing dust make up for it and come together to create a very tense action experience. You cannot simply hide behind a random wall and feel safe. Any wall can easily be destroyed with you along with it.
+The amazingly realistic, excellently echoing cacaphonous sound effects add to the tension even further. I heard just a single sound glitch where a machine gun firing sound would continue even while I was reloading for a particular weapon but it was not extremely annoying.
+The vehicles are extremely detailed as well and easy to quickly learn how to use. I wish there was a way to invite anyone nearby to come to the vehicle but you can enter the secondary position of any vehicle on your team that is being driven if you can catch up with it without getting run over you in the process. Real world weapons and vehicles are used throughout with their names being, if not perfectly correct in all cases, very close to what they are actually called in real life (thus potentially giving you a little tiny bit of an education in military hardware along with your fun).
+The maps are varied and matches are fun even if your team loses the battle. You are graded after each battle and experience is assigned depending on your individual performance.
+As with most multiplayer games, while Bad Company 2's multiplayer can become repetitive it usually takes about an hour or two to start to feel that way, making it a great "little" game to play once in a while when you don't feel like playing something more involved which has a detailed plot and so forth.
+This game can be gotten during steam sales for an absurdly low price (like as low as 5 dollars or something when it's 75% off).
Mediocre things:
+/-The initial difficulty of the multiplayer matches (in any mode) can be very off-putting because most other people who still play this game have already upgraded their characters' skills and unlocked all the more advanced weaponry. As a result, initially you will be lucky to get 6 kills per match (and matches can last an hour or more). This can be frustrating. True, advanced players should be rewarded for having played the game a lot but the multiplayer matches are ruthlessly unforgiving toward new players. The online community is at least moderately helpful though not extremely talkative. Initially it may seem like players are cheating but if you look at all the skills and other weapons that can be unlocked it will become apparent that most people probably aren't really cheating.
+/-Enemy AI is excellent when fighting in close quarters (they throw grenades properly, flank, call for reinforcements, change positions, do just about everything except retreat (except in situations wherein it is specifically scripted that they should do so). But the AI cannot put up organized resistance on any kind of large scale. As a result, fights in the main campaign are usually fairly close-range affairs. While the game tries hard to make you feel as though you are in a huge battle the single player campaign merely simulates this. You need to play multiplayer if you want to participate in battles which are actually huge.
+/-It might be nice if some player on each side (the most experienced perhaps) was designated as a commander for that match and had some sort of controls or additional ability to direct other players to use certain tactics. Despite the constant automatic (and helpful) radio chatter (helpful unless you are playing on the russian side and then everything is spoken in russian), matches are often very uncoordinated, particularly if players don't know each other and aren't specifically trying to speak with each other using microphones. I really wouldn't mind following some more experienced player's orders and tactical suggestions if doing so would help me maybe get more kills and level up more easily. In multiplayer, battles can almost feel like disorganized mob fights but the game does a good job trying to hide the fact that this is what is essentially happening during most matches by automatically giving you waypoints and clear visual objectives to move toward. But then battlefields should feel confusing and chaotic to be realistic after all.
Bad things:
-Short single-player campaign with bad dialogue, boring characters, bad music and a stupid, unsatisfying standard videogame ending. The singleplayer mode does have several difficulty levels but as the singleplayer campaign has only 1 possible ending it seems pointless to play through it over again. I was really expecting a more witty experience with better dialogue than this.
-Occasional graphical glitch where the screen disturbingly flickers on my GTX 780 but panning my view quickly up and down makes the glitch vanish.
-I might be wrong but it seems like this game could have had more mods or DLCs and could have encouraged more modding. I wish there was a future war Terminator Humans versus Skynet version of the multiplayer for this game or a DLC along those lines. Instead they seem to have an add-on about Vietnam which I've heard is great too but I like me some sci-fi and laser guns once in a while also and this game engine would be able to simulate a Terminator battlefield wonderfully.
-The marking of team mates versus enemies could be easier. Instead of a small colored diamond above each person's head the people on your team should be highlighted or glowing or something while the enemies should not be highlighted at all.
-I wish the groin area of the soldier on the main menu of this game was not on fire. He looks like he might have had a bad day at a venereal disease clinic.
