Pros:
*Early game melee
*Initial immersion factor
*Voice Acting + Quantity of characters
*Weapon variety
*Driving is decent
*Fun gameplay loop of loot, build, loot, build.
Cons:
*Significant level of low polish, including numerous launch/crash/freeze hangups in Breakdown.
*Low fidelity graphics feel like Cryengine 3 permanently set to low settings. Most jarring sin is vegetation, grass, ground textures and LOD distance even on Ultra + SweetFX mods.
*Breakdown being a recycling DLC was a poor idea to feign a difficulty mode, and takes too long to reach meaningful heights. You'll easily put 4-8 hours into the same map before you reach Level 5 or 6, when the game actually becomes difficult and harrowing.
*Dead open world
*No real sense of mid or end game
*No meta events or map control or dynamic weather or anything of the sort.
*Doesn't bring you down to earth. Your own personal hunger, sickness, health, morale, or all those traits the game showcases (poet, builder, musician, etc) mean absolutely nothing. NPC's do not interact with each other much at all.
I originally bought State of Decay on the 360 and enjoyed it for what it was then. The original PC port actually turned out to be a bit more stable than this combined release, but more on that later. Ultimately you might be asking: What is YOSE? Why should this game interest me, there are a million zombie sims out there.
To start with the positives, the gameplay loop in Decay is rewarding. You find or start a small community in one of a few predetermined "start options" you can roam around on the map and find. From there you need to loot buildings of various size and complexity to find rucksacks full of either food, ammo, supplies, or some forth income that is illuding me at the moment. This is your base building and maintenance currency which you use to construct/upgrade tiers of modules like sleeping room (more survivors) medical bay (faster health regen on chars you're not using) and so on and so forth. Killing zombies is mostly rewarding at the earlier levels with a pretty immersive melee engine, but is -- to me -- murked completely at higher levels when you become a crowd controller similar to Dead Rising.
You can equip 2h saws and spin to win, you can one hit kill enemies with fast light handed weapons and chain combo, etc. I found the combat most immersive when dodging, hitting, and running while managing stamina to be the most fun. At higher level characters, which is easy enough to do in one or two in game days, you become a killing machine. Janky animations, but meaty impact helps to level out the combat. Ranged is awful, I have nothing else to say there.
Zombies tend to spawn around you in a shell, out of view, rather than say roaming the map in swarms or migrating. The lack of any established a-life tends to bring down immersion since you can clear a house, go to the top floor, come back down and it's full of zombies again. This happens a lot.
Because of this, base attacks are predetermined "horde" events that spawn out of thin air and rush your defenses. This is fun, at first, but as you tier up you won't even notice or care as your snipers will make swift work of things.
There is not much of a mid or end game to speak of. There are no dynamic events, military incursions, zombie migrations, roaming survivor bands like you just fighting and looting, special weather or sickness events, etc. The big world is really static and tends to have a small center of gravity -- you. Enemies spawn when you're there, stuff is raided when you're around, "Defense" missions for outposts only happen when you can help, etc. The game uses missions and gametokens (cryengine stuff) to feign a sense of dynamics. In reality, the game stays put until it can pull your hair to do something close by.
Breakdown Endgame is just getting in an RV, reloading the entire map and it adds mutators to enemy count/strength/ and loot amount/scarcity. That's it. Ultimately, SoD is a decent looters beat em' up with a faint semblance of an open world. It is worth it on sale for $10 or below, but it isn't going to be the diehard zombie sandbox you were hoping for. It is too detached from itself, too player centered, too easy and has a strange dichotomy between corny Dead Rising combat and struggle-to-survive (implied, anyway) basebuilding.

An update of Alien Swarm with various improvements, new items, and additional campaigns. It can be played in single-player mode (with bots as companions) if you don't feel like playing online. It's fun but also suitable for more casual gamers -- the learning curve is not steep, each individual mission is short, and you can start at any mission instead of having to start a game from beginning of a campaign. Strongly recommended.

Revival of an excellent CO-OP game released for free by Valve long ago, of which multiplayer slowly died due to its lack of content. (I wasn't able to play it much due to hardware issues I had before.)
Alien Swarm: Reactive Drop alleviated the issues of the predecessor suffered; from minor to major tweaks, 8-player lobby for added action and twice the fun, additional campaigns created by talented community whose affection for the original game was significant despite the flaws and steam workshop support for sharing more community created contents with ease.
Controls are easy to get used to, you can customize the way you like and combat is very basic as you can evade enemies and only kill when you have to but that those not mean its not fun when slaughtering tens of bugs swarming at your team.
Missions are also straightforward and simple, your team has to follow the direction of arrow marker indicated on minimap and make your way to each objectives and extract safely. However, as some maps require Tech class to proceed with objects, teamwork and coordination is crucial and covering each other's back is essential. Playing solo or harder difficulty settings are possible but it requires far more strategy than the normal gameplay.
There are total of 4 classes with 2 possible 'marine' to choose from, each marine offers a variety of perk and benefits but does not discriminate one another from their roles.
Multiplayer functions and connectibility is fluid and they work well most at thd time, any players can host a game and play with friends/players worldwide without portforwarding or any sort because game already seems to do it. Game runs in Source Engine just like L4D which shares many similar aspects of the game like helpful gameplay tips popping up the first time you play and you are able to make use of multiplayer lobbies/dedicated servers (server browsers are available for joining one)/steam group servers just the way you do in L4D.

and
. It could be hard for new players at first but this is only temporary as you will get used to gameplay sooner or later and there are many friendly players out there helping new players.

It's not the realistic sniping game people were maybe hoping it out to be but it can be fun. However the gameplay mechanics don't match the aspirations that perhaps went into trying to make the engine and open world into the first AAA style ghost warrior game. The gameplay feels rather last gen and the graphics, while ok and often atmospheric are not certainly on par with most modern titles. They are better than attempts from the developer in the past and this is clearly their best attempt to date but it's not a game in my humble opinion that gives you that ultimate sniper feeling either. Nothing here feels polished enough from gameplay to sniper mechanics to graphics to storytelling. As a non realistic sniper/shooter/stealth game it definitely can be fun though if you adjust your expectations. There are multiple bugs and problems though least of which is the draw distance for enemies that disappear after 400 meters and reset their locations and behavior. Needles to say if anyone is expecting to snipe from 800 meters an accurate shot, this is a glaring problem. It maybe is due to design, because the game is not exactly running very smoothly either and perhaps the draw distance was lowered to allow for better frame rates, who knows. In any case a slider should be in place to let the player decide a performance/draw distance ratio based on their hardware. Story is very basic and lackluster but setting and atmosphere is great! It's an ok game in it's own category and there certainly are decent moments to be had despite the general mediocrity. Maybe wait for price to go down before picking up? I give this one a 5/10 as an overall experience at it's current state. While SE4 is far from perfect either, it clearly is the stronger sniping title from these two, however it's unfair comparison because they are designed to be such different from each other by setting alone. If there was a button to have mixed opinion that's what I would choose but as steam does only have recommended or not recommended, I cautiously do not recommend.

People always compare this game to Magicka. They shouldn't. While this game did get inspiration from Magicka, the game is really different. They aren't even in the same genre. Nine Parchments is a twin stick shooter, where you chose your "weapon" (spell), they have separate ammo and recharge. Combining beam works similarly, but no other mechanic is similar enough to compare this game to Magicka.
Overall the atmosphere is a bit Trine-y, music is obviously a lot like Trine, and the looks are as amazing as you would expect. This shouldn't be a surprise, because the game is within the Trine universe, from same developer team. This also means humor isn't like in Magicka (why would it be), it's like in Trine. I don't know why anyone expected the humor to be like in Magicka... But some people did.
Single player isn't as fun as cooping, but that should be expected.

The good:
It looks amazing. I love these kinds of games. I love the spell interaction. I like that you can damage your teammates and are shouting at each other to pay attention to what you're doing. The spells are fun. I had fun directing a 'beam' spell from an enemy into another enemy. Or see my fireballs bounce of a shield and hit my friend right in the face.
But it's just missing everything that makes something a good / memorable game.
You play random level after random level (level 8 might just as well have been level 3) following some  idiotic story.
There are no puzzles, no exploration, no hidden areas. The ones that are hidden give a chest.. with 61 xp. or a hat you've found 2 times before.
Items you find are either hats (that dont do anything) or staffs, that g ive a small bonus to something. whooptydoo.
All unlockable characters are basically the same, they can use the same spells only the skill tree is different.
But unless you play it really hardcore in a group (which you probably wont cuz it's just not fun playing it again over and over) I didnt think the skill tree had a huge impact on my character. It's just 10 percent bonus to this etc.
You can't even properly customize your character because each time you unlock a new spell, you can choose out of 3 randomly selected spells.
No loot system, no challenge and no story means I don't see myself playing it again.
The spell selection is annoying to play on a controller. You have to cycle through 9 spells and you really need the correct one at a specific time.
You only have one save slot
I really wanted to like the game. It really had potential.. and it looks amazing. But all the qualities that make a game good are just missing here.
Might be fun to pick up 4 copies for 20-40 euros in total and play it with 4 friends
20 euros for 7.5 hours is not good money imo.

Great game. But be very aware, the optimization for the game is very bad and even some good systems might have problems maxing out all the settings. If you look past the horrible optimization you'll get a fun game that'll last you a very long time with it's awesome mod community. You get two stories for the price of one and there both great. You'll play as a night club bouncer and a biker. Two completely different life styles and there both intresting to be apart of. TLAD is more serious and TBOGT is more like a fun action movie with plenty of humor. The TLAD was great but you'll have more fun with TBOGT, the missions are more fun and the story and characters are more memorable. As always with GTA Rockstar North packs the game full of humor in it's radio that lots of Americans or atleast western people will get. With lots of jokes poking at western society, from the far left to the far right, celebrities the media and everything else that's wrong with the world we live in. All of the jokes are just great with the TV feature it gives them an opportunity to put more humor and parodies. Believe it or not you'll find yourself sitting down watching fake TV. It's a real good distraction from other stuff and the Republican Space Rangers is so spot on it's almost scary. Now the combat, the shooting in the game is great, you shoot someone and you actually feel just from the way NPC's react when getting shot. The game doesn't have the largest weapon arsonal but it's full of real guns that you'd expect to be used by either criminals or law enforcement. standard rifles, shot guns and pistols. Usual stuff, even fun weapons that'll really mess up someones day like an RPG. As for the hand to hand combat, it's not that great. You'd expect with the fighting motion capture being done by someone who's done martial arts it'd be faster and more responsive. But when you counter someone in a fight it's so cool and very satifying. Turn kicks, round house kicks, spining back fists are just some very awesome counter attacks you'll see. Just a shame we didn't atleast get something more responsive like Sleeping Dogs. The driving in this game is not that great, the cars and motorcycles won't turn for anything and when it do turn cars do this weird lean thing. It's not realistic and those that say it is are too young and never actually driven a real car before. So yeah driving not that great. The city in the game is so cool. It's almost a dream of mine to see New York City in person so I'll just use this. Because Liberty City looks just like what I think New York City look like. Though to be honest I feel like they shouldn't of even bothered with putting and area based off New Jersey. They should of just focused on working on Liberty City and maybe ad some of Liberty State. Alderny is still fun and cool place to check out non the less but I still would of liked to see more work put in to just Liberty. Multiplayer is almost dead but you'll still see some people playing and with mods. Some are nice and just want to mind their own business or use the trainer for everyone to have fun and some are just plain out rude and mad with power so look out for that. The games mod community is very strong. When you get it remember to install a trainer you won't regret it. Last but not least at all. The video editor. It's great and with the right skills you can really make something great out of it. It comes with lots of options to make a very well done movie using GTA. You can film in both singleplayer and multiplay just incase anything crazy happens that you want to be filmed. Only problem is the camera can't go too far away from the player so if that becomes a problem just install mod to fix that. This is a must buy for anyone that likes games like these.

After scanning some of the other reviews you might notice that the negative ones often mention not getting the cards they wanted when they needed them. These are people who don't know how to survive rounds of "not the cards I wanted right now" and those who do. I also suspect that many are just bad at deck building.
If you don't like the luck of the draw AND dice rolls in your rpg's look elsewhere.  On the other hand I will say that although really bad luck may lose the occasional match in the long run the better deck builder and tacttician will win most of the time.
if I have a complaint it's that in the PVE portion some creatures are immune (or nearly so) to certain attacks. This means that before going in to a battle I need to know what I'm fighting and reequip accordingly. Fighting slimes with bashing weapons is a waste and stabbing weapons are next to useless against skeletons(for example).  So if you go into a battle  not properly equipped your warrior (in particular) can become useless. An interesting mechanic on paper. But in practice it came down to constantly reequipping my characters (which got old) or worse not knowing exactly what I'm fighting making the resulting battle much harder than it needed to be.
Nevertheless as you get to higher levels a lot of possible tactical options open up. I haven't really tried any of the higher lever stuff in pvp yet but based on lower lever trials I can see smart players trying all kinds of unusual tactics.
In summary a fun little card game with tactical elements mixed in. Which has it's advantageds over games like Hearthstone where all you do is play cards. On the other hand it's also a little less of both. Not quite as complex as classic deck building card games. And the rpg elements are also very sparse.
The game is not P2W and considering that it's free I give it a 9/10. If I had to compare it to all similar games regardless of cost I'd probaly call it a 7/10 game.

A game with a cool setting, awesome toys but a bit rough around the edges.  If you can look past the bugs and the difficulty spike in the middle, it definitely a gem in the rough.
Pros:
- Cool Cyberpunk world with lots of beautiful scenery
- Lots of toys (augments, gear and weapons) to outfit your troops with.
- Pulling off a mission with either stealth or brute force feels awesome!
Cons:
- Bugs.  I'm particularly sick of having my guys get randomly stuck in walls. :(
- UX problems: there are times when you issue orders and they just don't take.  Very annoying as things can go downhill quickly on a mission.
- Braindead AI, particularly for your guys.  They will stand around getting shot even though they have their guns out.  Won't take cover even when it's right in front of them.  Will shoot at a wall instead of the enemy.  You get used to when you have babysit them, but it's annoying that you have to do it at all.
- Big diffculty spike in the middle of the game: right about after you clear the first area, the missions get much harder (see tips below for dealing with that).
- "Going loud" in the early to mid game will probably get your team killed.  Later in the game once you have outfitted yourself with all the cool toys, you can easily mow down lots of enemies.  Thus the game actually gets easier later on as you can survive the mission when you screw up sneaking around.
Tips:
- Always do the bank mission ASAP and then hack all of the ATMs.  Half (or more) of the strength of your team is the gear you have, so more money = stronger team.
- After you clear the first area and have access to the next two, go to both and do the bank missions plus ATMs.  Then use your new found money to gear up as the mission will be much harder now.
- Abuse the stealth instant skill, especially with the infiltrator.  It's easy to get behind a patrol using the cloak and then murder them all before they can respond.
- Grenades are powerful.  Make sure to equip them and use them on groups of enemies.  Grenades do lots damage, blow up cover and knock down enemies.
- Plasma and laser weapons are the way to go.  They're stats might not look much better than bullet weapons, but shields and armor are harder to remove than regular health, so you need weapons that have bonuses against those.
- Heavy weapons are mostly meh.  The exception being the rocket launcher and the plasma canon.  These are basically "guns" that shoot "grenades" :)

What a beautiful game. And the story itself was beautifully told. I really got attached to each of the characters. The mechanics were very well done, though I did have a small hang up with Emile's digging the first time I had to use it. So much has already been written on
that it seems almost redundant to add yet another glowing review admiring all the things this game does so well. Situated in the First World War,
is at heart a 2D side-scrolling adventure game with quite some puzzles added into the mix. While the gameplay itself is top-notch on its own (controlling the different characters is a breeze and solving the puzzles offers a decent but surely not too steep challenge), the true genius of the game lies in the way the story conveys all the emotions that can be linked to a catastrophic event such as the First World War.
The story tells in a gripping way the effect of the ware on four characters: a French soldier Emile, a German soldier Karl (the son-in-law of Emile, which offers a lot of possibilities for the story-writers), an American volunteer Freddie who gets befriended with Emile and a Belgian nurse, Anna, who tries to help and comfort as many wounded a possible, without looking if they are friend or foe. The game surely is not "heroic" in any sense: it's not the (often false) heroism of the war that stands in the spotlight, but rather the life of different "ordinary" people who try to survive amidst the carnage. If there is one theme that stands out, it's that of human compassion even in such horrible circumstances: not only does the nurse tend to all soldiers she meets, the familial relationship between Emile and Karl puts the French-German conflict in a completely different light. The unexpected but true friendship between Emile and Freddie offers yet another layer of interaction. Furthermore, on several occasions there are situations in which soldiers of the different armies help each other out rather than blindly slaughtering their enemies. You even get a dog as a companion, who helps out on many occasions and is often the key to solving a puzzle.
The story is told both during the actual gameplay and in different scenes between the chapters and portions of the game, and it turns out to be a true rollercoaster of emotions with a gripping, desolate end. It is rare for a game to move the player into tears, but
managed to do so on more than one occasion. I truly felt emotionally shattered once the game had ended. Ubisoft Montpellier also went to great pains to provide a lot of historical background on the First World War, and it manages to do so without giving the impression one is playing a mainly educational game. It was a very smart move to introduce "collectibles" throughout the game, which add a lot of information about daily life during the war and which can be picked up during actual gameplay. Together with the diaries of the protagonists and the historical facts which unlock when the game progresses, one gets a ton of interesting information.
There really is no reason not to try and probably love this game. I know that it is a Ubisoft game and that it forces to use Uplay, but believe me: the quality, also from a technical point of view of this game is miles above the big budget games Ubisoft have released over the past years. The only downside is that there are no Steam achievements, which could have been a very fine addition - the Uplay achievements, though well done by themselves, are no match for the real stuff. Be sure to use a controller for this game; the controls are nigh-perfect and very intuitive.
In every other department the game shines as well: graphically it does a very good job at conveying the often bleak atmosphere of the front - using a cartoonish comic-book style was a risk, but it pays off very well in the end. The sound department is even better, with a wonderful soundtrack and exactly the right background sounds at the right moment.

It's hard for me to recommend Armello. While it is undoubtedly very beautiful, the gameplay suffers from several issues, which are only reinforced by quite lengthy matches (it's unlikely that you'll finish in less than an hour, perhaps even longer).
The main gripe I have with it is that victory is largely based around luck. Nearly every step of the way you'll enounter it - from card draw to combat to exploring dungeons to whether the damn guard is blocking the path to your next quest. To quests themselves actually - when you finally reach it, you have the option to take the risk and potentially win a reward - an item, a companion or a spirit stone needed for one of the victory conditions. However, if you fail the dice roll, you'll receive a penalty instead.
Sometimes you get lucky and the penalty is harmless. Sometimes it's awful. Sometimes you'll be lucky and get the item, other times you will fail despite having damn good odds. It can be very frustrating that way.
Every turn you'll encounter situations like these. To me, eventually, that was a deal breaker. Matches became frustrating chore.
Oh, and speaking of a chore. For some god forsaken reason you have to unlock most of starting items (you can customize your "loadout") by playing the game a lot. It's at least 10 games for each clan to unlock all of their respective items (with last ones arguably being the best across the board, with some exceptions). 4 clans times 10 games times 60 to 90 minutes per match (you can do this in bot matches, though those quickly become boring as hell). I mean at the time of writing I haven't even clocked enough hours in the game to unlock everything, and I'm long done with it.
The game also lacks any sort of meaningful communication system, instead opting for Hearthstone-esque chat bubbles. Why would you want to play a board game without being able to talk to the other players I cannot imagine. Due to this, the only form of diplomacy is possible between parties using external software. Teaming up against others is fairly popular in those cases.
It's actually astonishing that there are tools in the game to help others (healing items can be used on others, some cards help both caster and castee when used), but no real way to arrange that outside of being in a party.
It's not a bad game all in all. Picking it up on sale with a group of friends is probably worth it if you like what this game has to offer. Alone, I would give it a pass.
Though you might want to buy it just to take a good look at the gorgeous art alone.

Usually, I'm not really interested in computer-tabletop games. Because it makes me feel like I'm playing a game about playing a game. And any kind of tabletop game would make me want to play it in real life around a table with good friends or family, instead of with complete strangers; as I would imagine that it would feel kinda creepy, sitting around a table with strangers, silently, playing a game.
And that's really what makes the game fall short for me. I could see this game being a great game with my friends at my house. But if we were to play a game online, I think I'd prefer playing another game.
Now, it might seem like I am completely bashing this game. Which I'm not, the game is absolutely beautiful! I love the artwork. And the gameplay feels balanced and challenging.
So why the thumbs down? Well, for starters, I really had to think it over for a while. And in order to decide on that, I have to go on my gut-feeling if the negatives are game-breakers. And sadly yes, yes it is. If I wanted a RPG, I'd want something with animations and controls, instead of dices and cards. And if dices and cards are offered, I'd want to play that with my friends, at my house... Which I can't... So that's why this game gets a thumbs down.

Great game. But be very aware, the optimization for the game is very bad and even some good systems might have problems maxing out all the settings. You'll play as a night club bouncer and a biker. Two completely different life styles and there both intresting to be apart of. TLAD is more serious and TBOGT is more like a fun action movie with plenty of humor. The TLAD was great but you'll have more fun with TBOGT, the missions are more fun and the story and characters are more memorable. As always with GTA Rockstar North packs the game full of humor in it's radio that lots of Americans or atleast western people will get. The driving in this game is not that great, the cars and motorcycles won't turn for anything and when it do turn cars do this weird lean thing. It's not realistic and those that say it is are too young and never actually driven a real car before. So yeah driving not that great. The city in the game is so cool. It's almost a dream of mine to see New York City in person so I'll just use this. Because Liberty City looks just like what I think New York City look like. Though to be honest I feel like they shouldn't of even bothered with putting and area based off New Jersey. They should of just focused on working on Liberty City and maybe ad some of Liberty State. Alderny is still fun and cool place to check out non the less but I still would of liked to see more work put in to just Liberty. Multiplayer is almost dead but you'll still see some people playing and with mods. Some are nice and just want to mind their own business or use the trainer for everyone to have fun and some are just plain out rude and mad with power so look out for that. The games mod community is very strong. When you get it remember to install a trainer you won't regret it. Last but not least at all. The video editor. It's great and with the right skills you can really make something great out of it. It comes with lots of options to make a very well done movie using GTA. Remove that, and you're left with a game that's probably a mixture of enjoyable and completely baffling.

When the game starts, it's funny. The intro manages to both parody AND lampshade the Megaman 2 intro, and pretty much 90% of the intro level is a parody of the beginning of The Dark Knight Rises, and a well done one at that. All in all, this is one of those games that, while i'm glad i bought it, if only to learn about it, i honestly would've been♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if i had bought it at full price. It's not nearly as good as the trailers make it out to be. I'd reccomend leaving it be.

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.

At the time of writing this I have played Factorio for 160 hours.
The game is a master piece. But admittedly most of the game mechanics have probably come from minecraft mods like tekkit or FTB. For an indie game it's spectacular because it makes you think and gameplay is addictive once you get past the first few hours of "what the f%$& am I doing..."
The game revolves around hoarding resources and using said resources to expand your production line and feed your research. You accumilate more and more resources which feed machines that produce more advanced items and so on and so forth. Alien attacks are in waves, so you will learn to build a wall and turrets around your base. If you're really clever you will build a production line of ammo which constantly feed those turrets.
Surviving on highest difficulty is a lot of fun if you play co-op in a team environment to manage a base and try keep things together. (Hint use voip eg: mumble) Your base can get quickly over run if you don't plan early and think big. In saying that you probably need to do at least 2 play throughs to actually understand the game mechanics. My first game was a disaster and most people who play this will probably tell you the same.
The game includes a story mode which is more or less like a tutorial. I highly recommend playing that just to learn the game mechanics. This alone could have been masively expanded because it feels very incomplete. The real fun and games is when you play co-op multiplayer against hard ai. This is where your real skill and team work is tested.
The only gripe I have is that the research system is a little weird in that you feed actual objects into research which get turned into research vials, which then feed into research domes to gain research points.... Fair enough the game needed a research tree but I think personally the devs could have come up with a more imaginitive way of researching. Watching resources go into thin air just for research almost seems like research was a hack and not really thought out in this game. I personally think research should have been based off electricity (ie build larger research domes that consume more energy) and finding runes and artefacts around the map...
If you love building steam trains, this game is for you. Just this feature alone is a lot of fun but be warned, train networks can get complex very quickly. I still don't completely understand how the whole train system works.
The game does feel a little incomplete but you get that with most indie games. I feel like the research tree and some of the more advanced tech could be more extensive. The end game condition is a little simplistic considering how huge the game can get. The top down 2D graphics are deliberately retro but in this case it's a good thing. Also the game has some serious networking bugs which has been a bit of a problem with co-op games. (Nov 2017)
Overall I highly recommend Factorio. Especially if you like strategy games or games like simcity.

Remember one of the penultimate fight sequences in Kill Bill Vol 1 where Uma Thurman is surrounded by "The Crazy 88" Yakuza swordsmen and proceeds to defeat them in a long and extraordinarily bloody sequence? Have you ever wanted to play a game where you felt that tremendous sense of "One Against All" in a way that felt equally thrilling and brutal as that scene?
Meet Paint The Town Red.
The setup is very simple: Enter an area with a large amount of individuals (presently a bar, a nightclub and a prison), find a weapon (or don't) and proceed to kill everyone. Kill enough enemies and you unlock the first tier of a special "power". Don't use that power and kill more and you advance to a more powerful tier, continuing on to the third respectively.
It's an astonishingly simple setup which is just too good to deny. Smashing a chair over someone's head before running across the room to grab a bottle, which I throw into the face of one of two individuals surrounding me. With a large group in pursuit, I run into a supply room and grab a guitar and come out swinging - taking down several individuals before I activate my power, sending the large group of seven flying across the tables and chairs that litter the bloodsoaked floor.
Aesthetically it's just ludicrously appealing, seeing pixelated seas of blood bathe entire rooms in seconds after you stab a mob boss in the face and then punch his bodyguard across the room. Watching the faces of tougher enemies fall apart, gushing blood before they eventually fall after repeated pummelings with objects.
There could do to be more content in the game, e.g: weapons (and I'd love to see a cinema level), but what is supplied here at the minute is more than enough to keep you playing for hours.
Paint The Town Red is sheer, all out war. It's a hell of an experience that grabbed me straight from that Kill Bill feeling I got the moment I started fighting someone, all the way to being cornered in a room with a tire iron while furiously smacking at everyone around me.
Stick on some smooth jazz or some beatdown hardcore and get swinging.
PAINT THE TOWN RED!

I have a love/hate relationship with this game. But I can't in good conscience recommend it.
The Good: The game mechanics are well thought out, the characters and their abilities are also very balanced. Playing a game, you feel like you always have a chance to win it, even if there are setbacks. There is enough strategy to keep your brain in it, and enough luck that it doesn't get repetitive. Basically, the game itself is awesome.
The Bad: It crashes. A lot. There have been days where I've had four games crash in a single day, due to reasons like someone quitting the game - more often than not, that locks up the game for all of the other players. This wouldn't be that bad, if it didn't happen afte you'd already invested 45 minutes into a multiplayer match. Don't take my word for it - go to the discusson forums and the Bug section. It's the same problem, hundreds of times. Every time, they ask for bug reports, but there's no solution. When I have reached out to the developers for assistance myself, they've said the same thing, asked for bug reports and game logs, which I've provided, on numerous occasions. Then nothing happens. The issues are never fixed.
Even this wouldn't be that bad, except that they keep releasing DLC. It's like they're building additions onto a house with no foundation. Also, they're parting out cosmetics like they're trying to turn this $20 game into a $60 release. I get that no one has to buy extra dice or seasons, but it's infuriating that they seem to have the development time to push this stuff out, but not fix the very serious game breaking bugs that have been in here since the very beginning.
I have about 250 hours in this game, so obviously there is a lot to enjoy. But I don't recommend you buy it until you start seeing posts here about these issues being resolved. It's absolutely infuriating, because this could be a truly great game, and instead it's something I come back to every few weeks, hoping will be better, and it never is.

I have to give it to the developer, they made an eye-catching name for this game. When I saw it was called, "An Imp? A Fiend!" then I was going, "Okay, I have to see what this is about." I am a huge Metroidvania fan, so hearing it had those elements was enough to convince me to get it. I traded a game I had no interest in for this one, and I just blindstreamed it for some friends over the past few days.
Long story short: fun game with a lot of flaws. Long story long: read below.
Let's start with my favorite part about An Imp? A Fiend! The controls are glorious. You can double jump, dash on the ground or in midair, and attacking lets you "hover" if you keep hitting the button. This makes your character (who has no name as far as I know) feel light as air, yet completely responsive to your inputs. It was so enjoyable to run through the areas simply because of how smooth and reliable your protagonist controls. Major props here.
Now for some splits. One thing I find interesting is that there are no power-ups at all. Five areas exist, each with a dungeon, and you can tackle them in any order. Sure, I would call some more difficult than others, especially ones with tricky platforming sections. But you never get more than three hearts for life, and you never get any kind of items besides keys. This means you have complete freedom on where you want to go, and in some ways, I like this subversion to the genre.
Then we come across a serious flaw. This game has no maps. None. You had better hope you remember which generic path leads to which generic town, because it is very easy to get turned around if you don't. A lot of tunnels and corridors look the same, to the point that I sometimes wondered if I had somehow looped to go back the way I came from. There are no warp points, which also sucks because these rooms get tedious. You can only stay excited about spike-filled rooms that are easy to wall-jump around for so long. Oooh, what's that, a third screen with a wimpy dragon, rabbit thing, and annoying bird? How dangerous... no, the word I want is unnecessary.
Speaking of which, let's talk about the game's difficulty. I found some platforming rooms to be challenging, and most of the time, I felt it was my fault that I died rather than the game being cheap on me. That's a good thing. I will also note that you respawn in the same room that you die in. I personally like this, because there's nothing as dull as running back from a checkpoint to die in the exact same way as before. Some people might not like that, but I do, so there's that.
What is pretty lousy is the bosses. The bosses are absurdly easy and stupidly tedious. They all have very basic patterns that are jokes to get around. But since they have tons of HP, you are going to be wailing on them for a long time with pretty much no chance of you dying if you can play platformers better than a mushroom could. I personally would not want insanely difficult bosses, but there's pretty much no satisfaction to creaming these losers.
Oh, and one other complaint I have? Death by juggling. You do not get much in the way of invincibility frames. If you land on spikes or a sawblade wrong (and there are a LOT of sawblades, fiends must get them in bulk at HellCo), you will get flung up just enough to land on them again, and again, and then probably die. It didn't happen to the point that I wanted to toss my controller or anything, but it was annoying when it came up.
So, on a complete change of topic, how about the music? It's pretty average. The town theme is nice, the dungeon theme is okay, the outdoor sections are shrug-worthy, and the boss theme is so bland it makes crickets chirping sound like fine opera. The graphics are not bad. I could tell what things were most of the time, barring bizarre monsters. Your sprite is kind of cute. Kind of. I still don't know if this guy is really a kid or not, because he looks like an adult from his sprite. Oh well.
I did not go into this game expecting a lot of plot. You know what I got? A fair amount of plot... that was completely nonsensical. One of my friends commented that it made less sense than Evangelion, and frankly, I agree with him. It's so bad that it's actually pretty funny. I had a great time laughing about some of the conversations that took place. That being said, the grammar could use some work. "Lets" and "Let's" are two different things, but that error cropped up a ton. At least the spelling seemed fairly good, though it didn't help decipher the jargon that was the "plot."
This game has no trading cards. Boo hoo for those who get games just for cards. I personally don't care. Heck, the game's so short that most people probably wouldn't naturally get them all anyway. No achievements either, but I don't really think they're necessary, either. I guess some generic ones could be added for beating dungeons and the game. I also don't see a reason that they're needed. No complaints here about them not being present.
All in all, there are a lot of problems in An Imp? A Fiend! That doesn't change the fact that I really liked playing it. The controls just make this game, and there are so few games I will say that about. It was the right length in my mind, with three hours or so meaning it is entertaining for a while, but does not overstay its welcome. If you can get it in a bundle or for cheap, go for it. Otherwise, I'd wait, since it's really nowhere near perfect. Do give it a try if you like the genre, at the very least.

Like the other Larry Stover productions, it's a short but sweet pixel-platformer guaranteed to soothe the frazzled nerves of any world-wearied neoretro enthusiast.
has the most appealing graphics and sound of any game that he's made so far (
is the most recent as of this writing).  It also offers the greatest freedom of movement -- the titular imp/fiend can not only wall-cling, but can jump, double-jump and dash before resting upon a solid surface.  Coupled with the fact that you do not have to defeat all enemies to proceed, this potential air time makes the game pretty easy when compared to the
games, and for this reason I prefer their slightly more restricted movesets.  The later dungeons up the ante considerably, though, and all of the dungeons have a fine flow to them.  Flow is highly important; it is what allows the harried ego to sleep, and the reptile mind to come out and revel in those simple, twitchy pleasures that to it hold an almost spiritual power.  Thereafter the ego can resurface, recalibrated and calm.  Flow is a large part of what makes simple games like this such a life-affirming pleasure!
I do think that the hub-world (or "overworld" if that is appropriate) can be a bit of a drag in spots, and that the skeletal story is interesting enough to merit more exposition, but these quibbles pale in light of the fact that
is a pocketful of platforming miracles for the cost of a pecan log.

This game has such an interesting problem. Well, a few.
First, the positives:
1. The controls, they work well. The jump and dash are nice, the attack is serviceable.
2. The platfroming design is good, everything feels fair and there's a good degree of challenge to it, but not too high.
3. Plenty of content here for a $2 game, I played it through to the end in an hour and a half and felt like that was satisfactory.
But the big problem:
It's too easy. This could easily be solved, too.
A: Make the game checkpoint-based instead of "respawn on the same screen when you die". That way the life system actually means something.
B: Make the game one or two touch death. I think it'd be reasonable for most points in the game, though a few spots would need rebalancing, probably.
It's frustrating when the game poses almost no challenge at all because of weird design decisions.
The game also is nonlinear in the sense that you can do any dungeon in any order, but not really a metroidvania, and the backtracking the game forces you to do is kind of irritating. In one zone you have to run around between houses getting a key for the next in each until you get the last one, and that's a looot of backtracking. In others you have to go find an item, take it to another place or use it to find another item, then go back and find the dungeon. And each dungeon, after you clear it, you have to go back through, though the locked door system means that usually isn't too far to go back, not as much work as getting to the end in the first place to be sure. So there's a lot of unnecessary backtracking, definitely.
A few other gripes; the torches that fire at you are a bit cheap, especially in the awful, awful boss fight based around them, where the boss is completely static and you just have to dodge torches firing at you. A few other bosses kind of suck, too; some are pathetically easy to the point that they pose no threat, some don't give you time to react to their attacks and get in cheap shots. The final boss is a bit too tanky, but he does give you mobs to heal off of, at least.
Overall, I wish I could like this game more than I do but it has problems; still, for $2 it's a worthwhile purchase, and if you can get it cheaper that's fine too (got this from a bundle of this dev's games, actually).

I am always looking for a good games to play with your friends on the couch, or maybe even online in co-op. That's one of my favorite things in gaming, when you can share your experience and happiness with someone else, these feelings are really special and non-comparable to a single player experience.
I used to play a lot of video games with my girlfriend recently, sitting on the couch, laughing a lot and screaming at each other, when other person was fooling around. And these moments are just brilliant and, definitely, unforgettable.
So, when I saw Nine Parchments announcement trailer, I was hyped about this one a lot! I really enjoyed the trailer and I already knew from the beginning, that this game will be boring to play it solo. Then I shut it down after 10 minutes and was waiting for my girl to come over to my place. My girlfriend didn't even know about a new game, so she was pretty much excited when I told her that I have an activity for us on this evening. We started to play that game and first 30-40 minutes were pain in the аss, because we were getting into it, especially my gf, trying to understand how everything works. Another problem for here was to realize, that this game has a friendly fire mode and you should be really careful with your spells casting around your teammates.
Basically, the whole gameplay idea is all about casting spells of different schools, killing enemies which are protected with magic as well. That means, that if the big fat boar has a fire shield, then its pointless to throw fireballs at him. The best tactic was to freeze him up with my ice beam, while my bae was shocking him with her electric spells. So now, imagine, how fun can it be, when you are running around small narrow area, surrounded with dozens of enemies, with different magic school shields, trying your best to survive in that madness.
At the start of the game, you have only 3 spells to cast and the more you play, progress through the game and level up, you gain an opportunity to choose another spells. At this moment, after 4 hours of non stop gameplay, we already have 6 spells on your action wheel, for a different situations, which we need to use efficiently, working as a team. Plus, every level you can upgrade your skills, adding points at the tree skill, to make them more powerful and effective.
You can find staffs and hats through the game, I still dont know anything about the hats and I am not quite sure either they are just cosmetic or they can change your hero stats, but staffs thing are much more interesting. Staffs are used to start trials to unlock new characters with new abilities and stats. The trick is that these staffs and trial enters located at some random places all over the levels and you have to find them by yourself and I missed already one staff, which makes me sad, especially knowing that fact, that we don't rush through the game and try to explore every single piece of the map.
After few levels, you end up with a boss fight and we really enjoyed them all. We defeated three bosses at the moment I am writing the review, the only concern that I have, that only one of them was a bit difficult, other two were pretty much doable and we nailed them quickly. What I really liked during these fights - bosses were unique and with their own mechanics and visual differences, so you can be sure, that devs never wanted to copy paste enemies in Nine Parchments.
Cherry on the top of the pie is graphics. It's really beautiful and colourful, after four hours of gaming I have already seen already dozens of different landscapes with amazing and breathtaking sceneries. So, that part didn't let me down as well, it works really well with animation and professionally designed environment.
Just don't let the mixed reviews on Steam fool yourself - all these reviews were made during the first hour of gameplay and players weren't able to save their game progress during multiplayer coop game, which was fixed in hours.
So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:
+ Love coop gaming
+ Want to play something, where team play really matters, and you need to coordinate with your friends, not just auto-play
+ Enjoy beautiful games with a well design levels and brilliant graphics
+ Used to play Magicka games before and want to play something better and much more improved
+ Eager to play the game with interesting mechanics
+ Just want to spend a really great time with someone you love/care. I literally, lost count of the hours, playing this game, 4 hours went like 4 minutes to me, super addicting and absolutely amazingly fun!
You better avoid if you:
- A tilted person. Playing this game with someone in coop means that you will die sometimes because of a Friendly Fire mode and some of the skills have a bouncing effect, which can also hurt you and your teammates, so if you are easy triggered one, better move on to the next one
- Were never in love with this cute games, with cartoonish graphics, cheesy visual style and all these magician fairy tales and prefer something more bloody and gore
- A solo person, seriously this game is completely dull playing it alone.
Enjoy!

Do you like Trine ? Magicka ? Magic ? Fantasy adventures ? Casting spells ? Having fun alone or with friends ? If so, Nine Parchments is a game for you.
Nine Parchments is a spell-casting blast'em up adventure to play alone or co-op up to 4 players that offers 4 difficulty levels : easy, normal, hard and hardcore (in which it's game over if every party member dies). Starting easy, it gets quite challenging even if you're familiar with that kind of game.
The gameplay is rather intuitive : movement, melee attack on right click, cast spell on left click, spell slots and spell selection (key binding can be personalized of course). The game is divided into several diversified levels ; in a Trine spirit, there are hidden chests and enchanted quills to find. By progressing, you'll be able to unlock new spells for your character and use your skills points wisely, as in an RPG. There are also staves with unique stats and hats to collect. The combats are funnily chaotic : you can kill your entire team because you misplaced a skill or even die by falling off the cliff by misjudging the blink distance. Basically you aim with your cursor and cast one of your learned spells, each one having its own mana gauge, which makes the combats interesting and dynamic.
In total, there are 8 characters, each possessing 4 different skins and 3 starting spells. In the beginning, you can choose between two unlocked characters : Cornelius Crownsteed (starting with Ice Beam, Small Fireball and Death Circle) and Gislan of Alcyon (starting with Small Life Circle, Lightning Spray and Death Beam). Up to you to unlock the rest of the characters with quests and achievements. For example, Cornelius's third skin - Cornelius the Forester - starts the game with Fire Beam, Frost Spray and Death Bolt instead.
About the story : after the attack on the Astral Academy, some students will seize the opportunity to go after the Nine Parchments and learn more spells illicitly : gather your party and embark on a magical adventure to confront hundreds of various enemies and to discover 49 spells. The story itself is quite simple but sufficient, because you play that kind of game mostly for its gameplay.
Nine Parchments feels like the gift Frozenbyte's fans deserve : a great and challenging co-op game reminding of the Trine series, with a beautiful and astonishing art style, a fantastic soundtrack, lots of spells and hours of fun, for it doesn't get boring to replay the campaign with a new character.

There's a lot to unfold here.  Each character levels up through a skill tree and there is much loot to dive into.  Sure, the waves and waves of enemies can be a bit of drag late game, but it's simple controls and easy interface for spell selection help this sucker go a long way. Chaotic, fun and light-hearted spell-shooting mayhem. The element based spell system is quick to learn and use in mid-combat. It still manages to provide depth and surprise you even after long while of playing.
The art design is stunning! Simply breathtaking. Beautiful vistas full of details from level to level. Beautiful characters with great voice acting. The writing is clever and fun without feeling forced, which is often a problem with humorous games.
Nine Parchments is great, addicting fun when played alone but really shines when played together with a friend. Or friends, if you have several! There were some problems with the multiplayer, but as we were playing on the publishing day, I'm sure they are temporary. But you might want to wait a bit with the epic quest with your friends.
The controls are slick on both gamepad and keyboard & mouse. There are some small problems (as the annoying proceude of opening the inventory with TAB, but closing it with ESC), but nothing serious. Take note: you need to connect the gamepad while on the main menu.
There are some areas that could be improved. The loot from the chests could be more interesting from the current hats or experience points . Why not magic rings or other apparel that give you boosts? Or one-use bottles to fill your mana?
I could have used some instructions for some parts of the game. For example the 3 skill trees: it took me long to notice there are more than one. There are instructions on the loading screens, but they go by so quick!
Technically impressive game. I don't have the best rig (Intel i3 @ 3.30 GHz / GTX 670) and still the resolution and framerate are great.
Oh well, one parchment left to find. Wish me luck!

THIS GAME IS AMAZING
You know how when sometimes you play a classic game you are kinda worried because you know deep down that the game was probably only amazing to you because of nostalgia and/or your childish imagination?
Well Ty isnt like that.
The game design of Ty the tazmanian tiger held up so well that as I was playing it again on PC for the millionth time, I felt it was still an interesting, amazing, fresh expierence. The level design, the music, the voice acting, the overall atmosphere of this game is phenomenal.
The story of this game is a simple 3D platformer story, where ty's parents are sent to an alternate world and ty needs to rescue them by collecting 5 tallismans. Overall very simple, but this simple story allows for the gameplay to really shine as it was meant to. Imagine banjo kazooie, mixed with basic mario platforming from sunshine, combined with a unique take on fast paced ranged combat. THAT is Ty the tazmanian tiger, and its brought together really well. The rangs within the game allow for the player to challenge combat in whatever way they deem right. The game doesnt hold your hand either, and I still had challenges with obtaining some of the thunder eggs. The level design is mixed between open levels, where you can go anywhere. And linear levels, where the goal is to get thunder eggs as you go through the level. These mix really well with each other and allow the player to never get bored since all levels are unique. The water levels in general are amazing in this game, and allow for a "taste" of what an open world ty game would be like. The platforming it solid and smooth, allowing for brilliant maneuvers to be done that get the player where they want to go.
Now in terms of bad things for the game, there are some glitches here and there, but thats to be expected of an early access title and it never BROKE the game so I forgot about them. In terms of story, it could have been more fleshed out, but this is a 3D platformer from the early 2000's and the gameplay makes you forget all about that. The character of Sly within the game felt kinda....eh now that I think about it. He implys certain things within his dialouge that is never actually fleshed out, which, if done correctly, could have been AMAZING. However these kinda story problems are fixed with later installments in the series such as ty 2 and ty 3, which I can say had some of the more interesting, serious stories of any 3D platformer i've played. This is ty 1 however so that can be annoying to anyone who nitpicks that stuff. Controls are being improved constantly and I've had the liberty to play this with the xbox one controller, the steam controller, and mouse and keyboard. The xbox controller is the most standard and probably the best one to use as of right now if you're not accustomed to the steam controller. IF YOU ARE however, the steam controller is the way to go as it allows precise aiming during Ty View. Keyboard and mouse is also ok, but that has some bugs that are still getting fixed.
Honestly this game is worth the money JUST for the investment. Ty 2, was better than Ty 1, and I for one really want this game to succed to down the road I get 2, 3, and Ty 5. However on its own, I believe this game is an amazing title for any PC owner that wants change from their regular games, and wants to play a 3D platformer on PC.

What really stands out, and I mean
stands out in this game is the storytelling.
Valiant Hearts follows four different personas with interwoven stories throughout the course of World War 1, "The Great War". You quickly become attached to the characters - a French farmer serving in the French army, his German son-in-law in the German military, a US soldier and a Belgian student serving as a medic - and feel involved in their and their families' fates, which lets you be a witness of the gruesome war in a way no documentary can convey.
The game depicts the war in an authentic, accurate and thus very cruel way, not hesitating to show the suffering of women and children - war doesn't stop where the battlefield ends. Still, there are many moments of joy and humanity to be found within the tragic, war-torn story -
If you enjoyed Telltale's The Walking Dead you'll most likely love this game - same goes if you're interested in history, of course.
The game comes with 2D-optics, so there's not much to say about high fidelity graphics, but the game has a really nice art design. The drawn, sort of cute graphics stand in stark contrast to the the terrible, all to real horror that was World War 1, but somehow that doesn't hinder you from identifying with the characters of the game - quite the contrary, actually.
When I finished the game, it seriously send a shiver down my spine.
Valiant Hearts really shows the potential of the medium videogame. There aren't many other games that left me as impressed as this one.

If you've ever played the card game Android: Netrunner and want a real-time, singleplayer (or co-op) version of it where you play as the runners, here you go.
This is not a stealth game like Commandos or Shadow Tactics, if you try to stealth through everything you're going to get frustrated. This is a game about staying hidden until the right moment and getting your squad into position before taking out the generator with a grenade from your cloaked infiltrator so that your soldier and support can zipline in from a nearby rooftop while the cameras are down and security is tied up at the generator, then hacking into the commander's mind and opening fire on his minions while your soldier lays down a hail of plasma and your support unleashes nanobots to heal and the distraction ties up the garrison long enough for your hacker to steal the important files AND for your infiltrator to hit the bank vault and walk out with a money sack.
And it's good at that.

A stealth RTS with 4 (and at times more) units that have their own skills that focuses on get-in-hit-target-get-out gameplay. I've never played the Syndicate game that people keep comparing Satellite Reign to, but as someone who's played tabletop RPGs, Satellite Reign to me is essentially Shadowrunning: The Game. No, it's not Shadowrun because there's no magic, the story isn't anything special, and it's not turn-based, but it's hard not to compare SR to SR when you case a joint and bribe a janitor for information before you sneak in to assassinate some wage slave that upset a rival corp to get some creds to buy new ware.
+ Gets the cyberpunk feel down perfectly. From the terminal memos, to the megacorporation subterfuge, to the rain, to the clothing, to the neon.
+ Excellent gameplay. Difficult but fair. Mechanically sound. Works no matter how you decide to play it.
+ Open world. Not all games can pull off an open world setting, but it fits like a glove for Satellite Reign, and SR wears it well. Choose what missions you do, if you do them, and how you do them. Is this a sneaking mission? Is stealth optional? You decide!
+ Death penalties are small. The only downside of dying is clone degradation, but you can easily grab new clone stock.
+ Lots of customization for characters.
+ Multiplayer support for up to 4 people. Part of the difficulty is controlling four different agents, and being able to micro them at a high enough level is made easier if you play with friends.
+ Music and sound are good. Nothing outstanding and nothing poor. Music hits the right tension moments, and sound design works.
- Unpolished in the sense that the game occasionally bugs out. Usually for me, characters just get stuck inside objects along walls. It's frustrating to be seven minutes into a sneaking mission and then someone gets spotted because they clipped through a pipe, and the only way out is death. Multiplayer is occasionally buggy in various ways, like lag during a gunfight. There are some other bugs as well. I can't judge this too harshly because this game was developed by five people, but it's still a negative.
- Game mechanics a little bit unintuitive. Dead guard bodies don't alert anyone, disappearing guards don't cause alerts, smashing drones with a katanta makes a loud noise over your speakers but nobody else hears it or notices, drones will immediately start shooting at you, but guards will investigate the drone's gunshot noises instead of what the drone is shooting at, you can't cloak if you've been spotted, and other such nitpicks.
- Unoptimised. You might experience poor performance even on decent machines.
- Very minimal story. The comparison to Shadowrun is most evident here: you're a group of runners on one long shadowrun, and that's pretty much it. There's a few snippets of story here and there, but they don't matter and I was not compelled to care.
? Strange AI behavior that both does and does not make sense and may or may not be intentional. More funny than anything else, but I felt it was worth a mention. One time I hardwired a door to a corporation compound open, and the city patrol went inside. The compound guards thought the patrol were intruders and a gunfight ensued. This happened at another compound later, and the city guard didn't know they were doing anything wrong. Another time, a guard investigated a dead civilian body after my agents fled the scene and thought a nearby bystander was responsible. Yet another time, I was going through the district scanner, and the door closed behind me while my agents were being scanned. The civilians in the scanner queue started walking around the closed door and went into a secure area where they were immediately gunned down.
? The game is repetitive because it focuses on one particular game mode: get-in-hit-target-get-out. This isn't in the Con section because the game doesn't get boring because each compound is unique and has different approaches. There's probably not a lot of replayability because part of the appeal of this type of game is finding the weak spots in security. Once you've figured out a way in, it will work most of the time. You could think of some ways to handicap yourself, such as no murders, but the game won't enforce it.
? Long up-front loading time, but no loading time during the game. I'll take this one as "mostly positive."
. A very solid game with a lot of game to it, but a bit homogeneous and rough around the edges. I look forward to possible mission packs that offer new locations or better story, or a sequel.
Edit: having finished the game 100% and played with friends, I have to commend the game (again) on allowing either the sneaky approach, or the "stealth is optional" approach. It's not often enough that games allow both to be equally effective. Of note, this does add a fair bit of replayability to the game. I also felt like the last mission in the game was a lot more polished, with better music and a better integration of story into gameplay. A great capstone to the experience, and makes me excited for 5 Lives Studios' future work.

Pros
+Stunning graphics, as usual. They made the Trine trilogy after all.
+Nice optimization. 4k and highest setting with a constant 60 fps on my GTX 1080ti i7 6700k. Also 4k 60fps on Xbox one X and 1080p 60 fps on PS4 pro.
+HUD is concise, without that cluncky element combination of which in the Magicka, everything feels smooth and right.
+I really like some of the music during fight scenes, which,  brings the old feeling when I was playing Trine.
+Just like any other similar wizard game, you have to choose spells with corresponding element to fight various type of enemies, there are a bunch of spells, characters and equipments to unlock. Each character has their own 3 skill trees.
+Combat is both interesting and satisfying. Each spell uses its own MP gauge, so you have to time your attack and plan your move accordingly.
+Control. Besides your normal WASD movement, you use the mouse to aim(like a twin-stick shooter) and a blink button for you to dash through hazard and enemy spells. The blink can possess various properties due to the wand you are waving. Movement feels comfortable except me keeping plunging off a cliff from time to time.
+You can play it solo, but there is more fun in local co-op with friends and online mode.
+Lovely characters and Amadeus the Wizard from Trine trilogy.
Cons/Neutral
-There is not much of a story in the game for now and I only have the last piece of parchment to find.
~You can only use 1 character for one run from the beginning to the end. But I would be more than glad to replay this game several times within different characters.

Factorio is a game of excessive labour - think of it as a model railway you have to build over a long, drawn-out process, assembling all you need to, buying the pieces you don't have, slotting everything together to form a fantastical and rejuvenating experience for your train to go on.
The soul of Factorio exists in the feeling of accomplishment you get when you align everything as perfectly as you can, and all the components to automate that thing that once took you a good ten minutes of waiting to craft suddenly is pumped out on a timely manner, to be absconded onto a train's caboose and rolled to some far-off production line, deposited into another machine or safety box, to be used in another process far beyond your tiny human hands. It can be messy, intricate, chaotic, organised - Factorio is guaranteed a game that will give you the feeling of "What shall I do next?" after you've finished the production for science vials, and leave you hungry for more. I recommend this game highly, especially if you have multiple friends - to either compete against in organising a factory that can produce the most, or to work with one another, and have a mad dash to the finish together. Even as a solo experience, I can heartily recommend the game to those whom need to have that itch of watching pieces of a jigsaw puzzle slot together, for I can assure you, Factorio delivers an experience akin to it in spades.

Aside from the odd server which has unexperienced players in it, Sven Co-op is a thrilling, intense and highly cutomizable mod for the original Half Life game, all bundled together into a free to play standalone. With no freemium purchases or microtransactions, you get the whole package in this bundle.
Mods are built into Sven Co-op to allow Roleplays, Labyrinths, Quests and much, much more on multiple servers. With Sven Co-op having a proactive community and the ability to make a standard Half-Life Vanilla server yourself, one can not get bored. I would recommend inviting all of your friends who love the Half Life series over to Sven and playing on your own server with them, nothing as hectic as 'partially' co-ordinated strikes against zombies, whilst only having crowbars. The interesting bit behind Sven Co-op however is the customization, with you able to change the colour of your 'avatar', which ranges from the models Sven Co-op has, the female versions of Gordon, Gordon himself, Barney, alternative skins, a Jill Valentine 'Half Life' style skin, Robots, Marines [Including Shephard from Opposing Force] and even Ivan the Space Biker! [The original Gordon].
With Sven Co-op allowing you to download extras, such as the campaigns for Blue Shift and Opposing Force respectively, you will not feel a sense of repetition in the campaign and when you're all done, you can go back to the Mod-built servers.
Overall Sven Co-op I recommend for anybody who wants a pure free-to-play game, wants to reminisce the old days of gaming or has wanted Half Life [1] to be Co-op. There is something in Sven to please everyone, ignore the negatives that people say, it is as easy to leave a server or mute the players and proceed on. The positives are only found by actually searching, I was unlucky as I automatically connected to a Russian Mod/RP Server, where everyone was screaming Russian over the microphone. I simply disconnected and joined a Vanilla server manually, from there on, it was easy going.
On a rating of 1 to 10, I would give Sven Co-op a 9.5/10, as it is the best it can be, the only downsides are.. You guessed it! The lack of 'Instructions' when you start up the game and the small amount of 'bugs' that are present, but are generally NOT gamebraking: I do not play this on a 'Gaming Rig', I play this on my Laptop and this game runs very smoothly for a £200 Laptop. With the developers quite pro-active themselves, the bugs are not around for quite long before they get patched.
Sven Co-op in my eyes, is one of the best mods on the Half Life series and does not require anything at all, not even the base game to play. I would recommend this to anyone who asks me about Sven Co-op.

Satellite Reign is a cyberpunk-themed RPG, in which you control 4 different characters at once.
Most of the game is either based on stealth or combat, depending on your preference. The vast majority of the missions can be done either way.
Not really. To me, for a game to be open-world, the world actually needs something to do in it. Satellite Reign has more of a hub with certain areas in which you do missions.
The core of the game is to do missions in each area to aquire items, which make your characters stronger. Some of these items are weapons, some are stat upgrades, others give your characters new abilities.
Other than that, there's no reason to remain in a district after every mission has been completed.
I highly recommend you to play this game together with at least one friend. Team communication is very important, so be sure to use a VoIP service when you play.
Singleplayer is possible, but controlling 4 characters (or more) at once is just incredibly difficult. Even controlling two at once is sometimes hard.
Absolutely! After a tough battle or an intense stealth section, you feel quite the reward, simply for beating the mission.
I played the game for about 28 hours from start to finish together with a friend and we really had a blast while we played.
As for replayability, there is not really that much of a reason to play it more than once.
Sure, you could do an "all stealth" or "all loud" run if you want, but the XP and skill system doesn't force you to make any choices.
The only
you have is which skills to get first.
It's a bit of a mixed bag. In general, I'd call it stable.
Multiplayer over internet works fine, but Multiplayer over LAN does not work at all.
The game itself doesn't crash and can be minimized without problem.
However, sometimes the characters in-game start to glitch out. Once (in 28 hours of gameplay), my character got stuck and died.
At times, characters are slow to respond to commands, especially if they choose to reload after switching targets, or if they have to put their gun away.
All in all, I would say these can be annoying when they happen, but it's not frequent enough to really spoil the fun.
This is the only major downside. If you have a very weak CPU, then the game doesn't perform well at all (State: Jan 2017).
As far as I could read from forum entries, the developers vowed to improve the performance. If you have a very weak CPU, don't expect top performance.
All in all, Satellite Reign is 20-30 hours worth of multiplayer fun. If you have a friend to play with, give it a shot!

It reminds me not only of Syndicate, but a bit of Shadowrun for SEGA with its open world and the remake of the SNES version of Shadowrun, which for me, is fantastic. Everything that I felt left out of the Shadowrun remake seemed to complete in here.
The controls are slightly clunky however it's hardly a sticking point at all. The ability to take group cover or make from place to place discretely is quite well done and logical, and is no-more worse than some of the route paths I find on games such as XCOM to be frank.
The story is great. I love the factions. I particularly enjoy how the factions recognise each other as enemies if members from different Corps. intrude on another Corps. area. It makes me feel like it's not just Players and Enemies, its Players, and Enemies, and the Enemies of my Enemies, which really allows for some creative gameplay when trying to do certain missions.
My only wish (which I hope the modding community gets a hold of this game and implements something like this... or the Game Developers) is for a bit more lore and backstory in the game for immersion (not to say there wasn't any, just I felt the gameplay could have incorporated it a bit more, basically, some storytelling), maybe some NPCs to converse and interact with, and more personal side-tracks such as visiting bars for jobs, raiding homes, moving into to full on entering buildings and corporate headquarters (instead of their grounds) and running around inside hacking and stealing (kind of linking back to SEGA's Shadowrun).
All in all, it’s a great game. 9 out of 10 from me, and I hope 5 Lives goes on to develop this amazing game and can't wait to see what else they can come up with in the future!
