EDIT: The game is now out of early access, but I will keep all mentions of it still being in EA below as it makes no difference to the final review and still reflects the same opinions I have.
Full Review:
Ty oh Ty... Where do I begin...
So this game was made by a company called Krome Studios and was originally released on the PS2, Xbox and the GameCube and was quite popular for the company being relatively unknown at that point. I personally started playing on the PS2 when I was just a young lad, and is one of the games I remember most about my childhood, it just pressed all the right buttons for me. Anyway to the actual review.
Gameplay:
So this game has been completely remade in HD... well kinda. Right now most of the game is in HD though Krome Studio are still releasing updates with new up-res textures. The game though at this stage is still far better looking than the orignal counterpart.
So the gameplay, is it worth it as a whole, 100% yes. You play as TY and start with 1 boomerang which turns into 2 after the tutorial area. Boomerangs are the main premise of the game and all attacks revolve around them. As you continue playing the game, you will unlock more by just playing the game, though even more, and much better ones can be obtained by collecting cogs in each of the areas.
Collectibles:
So in each area, there are a multitude of collectibles which can be obtained by searching (some of them can only be gotten with other rangs which you will get later in the game, so going back into old area's definitely happens). The main collectibles are Cogs, Opals and Bilbies. The other collectible are paintings which are invisible in crates unless found accidentally and can only be seen through the use of another rang later in the game. This means overall, there are a lot of collectibles to be found and its actually very fun looking for them all, though missing one opal is pretty annoying and can take a while to find.
Performance:
So because this game is in early access, this means performance issues are going to be a thing, especially with lower end rigs, I personally don't have any type of problem performance wise though I know some people have stutters and slight freezes now and then. In general if you love the TY series, please remember that this game is in early access and is bound to be a bit weird now and then; just bear with it, the devs on this game are working very hard to bring the best TY experience to desktop.
Music:
Sexy riffs, a real outback feel mixed with the didgeridoo makes this games soundtrack so memorable and one of the best parts of the game.
Drawbacks:
So now onto the bad things, which surprisingly, there is not a lot of stuff in this category. As I have said above, this game is in early access and is bound to have some weird quirks, and all depends on your rig. Saying this though, some people have reported weird V-Sync issues and stutter, though if you go on the forum and tell the devs what the problem is, they will gladly help and have been for a while now. Another drawback is that the game is quite a lot shorter than I once thought it was (100% will keep you going for a while however). This also might be the case because I played it a lot as a child, so I know the what is where ect.
Final Thoughts:
Is this game worth it after all this... YES!!! If you love TY, then just buy the game, I promise you will not regret it!

I wasn't expecting this game to leave me emotionally devastated but then I didn't have many expectations going into this game. I saw a pretty looking game on sale and thought why not.
Valiant Hearts: The Great War™ / Soldats Inconnus : Mémoires de la Grande Guerre™ follows four characters, Emile, Freddie, Anna and Karl and their hardships throughout World War One. Karl is a German asked to leave France after the outbreak of World War One and is conscripted into the war. Emile is his French father-in-law who is also conscripted into the war. Freddie is an American who joins voluntarily after an incident in his past. Anna is a girl from Belgium looking for her father. This game deals with the grimness of war and hardships much more than I originally thought. The puzzles flow together nicely and I never was lost as to where to go. All the characters play similarly, Emile can dig his way through dirt, Anna has a healing mini-game and Freddie is tasked with driving the tanks. Besides that it is all the same. The other puzzle element was the dog. The dog added a whole other area to play with. The dog is able to access different areas, distract guards and hold things for you.
The story tells us the progression of each character and their motives/feelings with it. Emile is never proud of the things he does as he believes in peace. Anna may be looking for her father but that doesn’t stop her from healing everyone on her way. Karl just wants the war to end to return to his wife and son. The beautiful narration from Dave Pettitt makes the story flow together and helps set the scene. Emile’s (James Barriscale) monologues are also a lovely addition. I felt the accent was genuine and I felt it matched the character perfectly. On the topic of sound the music was thoroughly enjoyable and I felt that it always was relevant and accurate. The art style conveyed lovely bright colours and dark grim colours to back the story at the same time. I felt each character looked interesting and the attention to detail was nice. The relationships between the characters were beautifully crafted and it made me personally care about their relationships and in turn their characters. I felt thoroughly connected to each character, even Karl who gets the least screen time as it were. At one point when one of the characters was in danger I genuinely wanted to help him. The game tells us just how close many of these soldiers were to dying and how they watched many die around them. It helps us to realise just what they went through. In most areas the game also gives you lots of accurate historical facts for you to see in more detail the events the game goes over.

This game is definitely an amazingly crafted game, it is fun and interesting and a bit of an emotional roller-coaster. It was a game where I left it devastated and yet fulfilled. Through tears I whole heartedly recommend you to try this game if you even slightly think you will enjoy this game.

After playing this for a couple of hours this afternoon all I can really say is I was a little underwhelmed with the single player experience.
if you've ever played Magicka before and you've got friends ready to join you for a spell in the wizarding arts Nine Parchments should be a [fireball] blast.
As this game is from the same folks that brought us Trine, a team with a strong pedigree when it comes to delivering fun indie experiences with a strong visual flair, there was probably a certain degree of expectation - at least when it comes to presentation. Thankfully Frozenbyte do deliver on this front creating a lush fantasy world very reminiscent Trine 3 with it's 3D world and attention to little details in the environment.
Unfortunately if you were hoping for brain teasing puzzles or original, innovative gameplay then you maybe a little disappointed. This does just look and feel like another installment of Magicka. Though with this being on console aswell the spellcasting is a lot simpler. You are not typing combinations of letters to cast instead you just cycle through the spells you acquire along your journey.
You do have a nice variety of magic at your disposal. And as you would expect certain elemental types are better suited against certain monsters and this does all give rise to some nice combos. And there is a strong RPG thread running throughout the game allowing to spec your character however you like with certain hats and staves altering you build.
Though there is a definite downside to all this customization in that you only have access to 2 of the 8 characters at the start of the game - even when you're playing in 4 player co-op. To unlock the other wizards and the various skins/outfits available to them you have to play through the game. Whilst this does give the game replayability it would have been nice to have at least half the cast of characters available from the start.
as you might expect this game wasn't really meant to be played on your own. And it does really start to shine when you are playing in multiplayer. And for the very same reason Magicka was and always will be a riot to play - Friendly Fire. Yes, the biggest risk to your character is not the enemies but your friends as spells go awry missing the monsters competely and hitting your colleagues square in the back.
To sum up if you are looking play this on your own then I'd maybe give it a miss. But if you have friends to play with in local co-op or if you can persuade some people to pick it up now (or maybe on sale) then this should make for a fun few hours of entertainment.

Factorio truly is a "you versus the world" game.  You can start with nothing but your bare hands and work your way towards a sprawling strip mining operation capable of manufacturing a rocket able to go into space!
The game mechanics are simple enough to understand.  It is usually just a matter of working your way up the tech tree and exploiting additional resources as they become available to you.  Logistics management skills are a must.  Should yo use a giant network of conveyor belts to ship your iron ore across a continent to your furnaces? Or should you use tons of worker drones to lug all of your goods around the world from one factory to the next?  The choice is yours.
The game has changed a bit since it first started.  I would say the changes have been justified and helped move the game along at a reliable pace.  Building your first self sustaining loop can be rewarding.  Aliens attacking your base at the wrong time (or location) can make you scream at times if you forgot defenses.  Running over aliens in a tank that you made yourself....priceless.
I feel that some communication between you and your homeworld or an unknown entity could add some extra life to the game.  But, all in all, it is a wonderful sandbox that I have enjoyed for many hours.

Factorio, which is tied with Prison Architect as one of the best "early access" games in Steam's storied history, is a game about a guy who is stranded on an alien planet, whose goal is to rebuild is spaceship and escape the planet. You accomplish this goal in the only way you know how: by automating everything. Have you ever played Minecraft and gotten to that point where you are tired of digging and thought to yourself "Isn't there a better way to do this?" Factorio is the answer to that question. Every stage of building the rocket can be automated, starting at the mining of the materials, to the automation of the intermediate materials, to the automation of the final products, and straight into forming a rocket.
This game is one of the best automation game on Steam right now, and this game is the pinnacle of how the early access system should be used for a game. Even though it is still in an Alpha state according to the developers, it is one of the most polished Alpha's on Steam right now. Updates are added routinely to fix bugs, with large content updates that add huge features to the game coming at regular intervals. This game serves as a perfect example of how early access games should be: games that can be updated with features using regular content updates that change and improve the game. Even though it is only in an Alpha state, this game is entirely worth the money. Just be prepared to lose a lot of hours to this game, but you will have a ton of fun doing it.

State of Decay is a 3rd person zombie survival game. The pros of it include the exploration, community building, and overall atmosphere aspects. The game is aging graphically and technically, but it still holds up to other similar games, in some cases still beating them. I enjoy all the different characters despite their shallow backstories, and how you can mold them into the survivor you want through the rpg elements; shooting, cardio, fighting, etc. The music is awesome too.
The con of this version and the game at this time is that it's not optimized very well at all. For instance, I have Windows 10 64-bit, a GTX 1070, and a FX-8350. The stuttering is completely unavoidable when driving fast through the countryside to new areas, the shadows were a flickering mad mess, and also upon startup, the resolution natively wouldn't accept 1440p. I'm competent with making games run how I want, so I figured out the screen fix, (make a user.cfg file in main game folder) figured out the shadows by removing them completely, (courtesy of a modder from nexus mods) but the other little optimization problems I had to live with.
So the game is one of my favorites, and the issues don't kill playing it, but I know it also could be smoothed over better than this too. I give it a 7/10, mostly out of having so much experience and fun playing it at launch, but if I'm being honest, I was disappointed in how this version ran for me. It is what it is; a solid entry in the zombie survival series, at the cost of performance and quirks at the technical level.

In all honesty, this is the way to experience GTA4.  While the base game takes on a dark and all-too-serious mood (as does The Lost and Damned), The Ballad of Gay Tony strives to bring back some of the madcap energy of Vice City and San Andreas.  Many of the missions are completely off the wall, in the best way possible.  Most of the supporting cast are in the vein of the crazies you may have worked for in VC and SA.  And it may just be me, but the city seems more bright and colorful in TBoGT, as opposed to the washed-out look of the base game and TLAD.
The Lost and Damned is worth a play, tho.  While not as high-energy as TBoGT, it sports some interesting features and a solid story.  The changes to motorcycle driving are very welcome, as is the ability to call for (and cruise with) backup.  Cruising in formation with Liberty Rock Radio in the background is a soulful experience.
But TBoGT takes the cake.  More supercars, skydiving, a rocket-spitting attack helicopter and a tank make for a great after-story sandbox of urban chaos.  And then you get to use all of those in multiplayer.
If you wanna get ready for the PC release of GTAV, The Ballad of Gay Tony is the way to go.

I love Insurgency.
Somehow I managed to convince my flatmates to team up with me, and our weekly clan trainings are so much fun and frustration and excitement and freaking out over amazing clutches.
It's an easy game to pick up if you're somewhat familiar with FPS mechanics, but the skill ceiling is crazy high. Especially if you get into higher level competitive matches with experienced players, e.g. through playing PUGs. That's when a dedicated team that communicates well and knows the maps is crucial.
Movement, guns, recoil and the maps feel so solid, it's easy to lose yourself in the game. The tension is real when you're the last one of your team standing, trying to sneak around the opponent to capture a control point and save the day.
One major downside of the game is the implementation of the competitive mode - or rather lack thereof. It was in Beta for a while but then got scrapped; now there will never be proper ranked matches with timeout penalties for leaving. Also you can't queue for a game with a team, which means there will be a lot of switching sides and fighting autobalance when you want to play with friends.
The community is small but dedicated, which means an good percentage of players you'll encounter are very good at the game. There is a certain level of toxicity going on at times, but much less than in other competitive games like Rocket League or CS:GO.
Absolutely recommended.

As of writing this review I have just finished the final mission, credits rolling etc.
In a nutshell, if you have the patience and skill for micro-managing 4 individual characters with a variety of skill-sets in real-time, I think you will enjoy this game. Obvious comparison being the Syndicate series, which this is supposed to be the spirtual successor.
It is a little flat in terms of presenting its story, which amounts to major developments when you move from one district to the next with a little audio snippet from your Handler, but other than that you get most of your story from blocks of text relating to the mission objectives, or the assorted terminals scattered across each district. It does round up nicely, if somewhat very abruptly with a nice piece of music playing which adds some nice atmosphere.
While not completely flawless, and somewhat slow (as if viewing a video at 3/4 speed, though this might have something to do with my PC) it is a very well put together game. I only had a couple of moments where it glitched out, mostly where 2 of my Agents would either stand still regardless of input, or get stuck in the world geometry, and I mean only 2, during my last 2 hours or so of gameplay, though some mechanics did require some key spamming to get the desired effect sometimes throughout my playtime.
Gameplay can be somewhat repetitive, as for each district you generally have the same set of objectives to complete in order to continue your long standing goal, but the thing that offsets this is that because of the mechanics and set-up for said objectives, it feels different each time. A good example is the Bank. Each district has a large branch of the Cities major corporate bank, which you can go and smash open for a lump sum of cash, and increase the amount of money you get over time from the hacked ATM's which scatter the City. While the same objective exists in each block of the city, they each have different defenses and physical layout, prompting you to approach each objective in a different way.
The shootouts your agents get into can often feel frantic and overwhelming at times, and more so as the game progresses and you meet more impressive enemies. Careful positioning and use of your Agents abilities will see you survive these encounters, or alternatively, just run away, as the Enemies do seem to suffer from short-term memory loss now and again.
That said, with regards to the Stealth aspect, its is very hit and miss. While the enemies you encounter tend to follow the Sight/Sound rules much like Splinter Cell for example, if you do wind up in a colossal shoot-out for which you are not prepared, breaking line of sight and moving a good 50 metres away from the hot-spot seems to cause the AI to think "No problem anymore, back to patrol." which does seem odd, considering that there is now a massive whole in that gate which I blew open with a grenade not 5 seconds ago.
All in all, while Stealth is certainly viable with assorted EMP gear/Sound Suppression/Cloaking equipment and silencers for your weapons, take the advice of Gabriel Angelos, "Walk softly, and carry a big gun.", because if your luck is anything like mine, you may need it.
With regards to the 4 Agents under your control, you have your Soldier, Support, Hacker and Infiltrator. Each has their own skill set up, with both passive and active ablities relating to the role they are designed to fill.
Each agent can be equipped in various ways with the variety of gear, weaponry and augmentations that you will pick up over the course of the game, new items of which will require researching before you can mass produce them for your Agents, because while you can equip your shiny new weapon or augment immidiately onto an Agent, should they be killed in combat, you will permanently lose it. So I thorougly recommend researching anything new that you may want sooner rather than later.
While certainly nothing to get excited about, the visuals of the game to make for an impressive display, even with the almost over-powering presence of neon lighting all over the place, but this can be addressed simply by turning off the bloom.
The sounds and music of the game are a joy to listen too. Gun fire and explosions feel just right, with a satisfying weight to them. The music is very atmospheric for the most part, each of the 4 districts having its own ambient track, both when wandering the streets and getting into trouble.
Overall, I would recommend this game, though I would advise to buying it on sale along with the soundtrack.

Syndicate returns. Game has some bugs, and control issues at times, but nothing you cannot get used to.
Outstanding game for such a small dev team (5 people afaik). The city is gorgeous, and while individual assets repeat, the overall layout never looks identical. The story is mostly conveyed trough data logs, however they are written really well. It is fun reading them.
The game's style and aesthetics are really spot on. The whole world presents itself as a blend of Shadowrun and Syndicate.
Gameplay wise, you have to struggle a bit to get the hang. It can be frustrating at times, especially at the start. Once you figured out how stuff works and how to avoid getting into certain-death situations, the gameplay starts to shine. There is some tactical Commandos gameplay there, where you approach with stealth and hit & run. Though if you are strong enough, and♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, all out guns blazing secnarios are just as likely to lead to success. Given that you know what you are doing. It can get quite hectic at times, and a fast and precise mouse-hand should be part of your skillset if you favor brute force.
In terms of character development you have a limited but quite nicely paced progression. Limited in a way that you do not have extensive skill trees or extremely exotic abilities. The classes stay mainly inside their intented function. However, breaking into compounds to gain new equipment is a big part of the game, giving you another layer of development through gear, ranging from sniper rifles to flamethrowers or grenades. A third layer of development is the bionic augmentation.
To me, this game is a gem. A bit unpolished around the edges, but with a vibrant soul and a great atmosphere.

Open world game
Very good gameplay (with minor UI flaws)
Tons of ways to do each infiltration (from 4 squad team blowing everything to sending one cloacked man trough the venting)
Immersive environment
Good cyberpunk ambiance (really like shadowrun. You do not have spell, but you have mind control, drones and hacking)
The only negative point I found is the lack of scenario and NPC to talk.

While I did recommend the game, please bear in mind that the game is pretty glitchy: character falling through the floor, character getting stuck in a wall, important NPC not spawning, etc. I encountered all of them in my playthrough. That said, I really enjoy the concept of the game though, so I can bear those stuff just fine.
Another thing to note is that I used total stealth on my playthrough, so that may give a different experience than people who just shoot stuff.
Anyway, as I've said, I really enjoyed the game. The whole game design seems to be well thought out. The game takes place in a GTA-like open world where you can choose which mission to do first. Afterward you carefully inspect the mission location so you know the best way to tackle the mission. Do you go through the front door? Do you put sniper in a high place? Do you enter the vent and shut down the electricity? Do you sent in an agent via zipline to so he can open a backdoor for the rest of your squad? Each mission/location have a different weak point.
And on almost every mission, the map layout seems to be carefully thought to support multiple strategies. If you notice a vent or a zipline, you can be sure that it would lead to a strategic location. If you find a nice, hidden pathway, you can be sure that it would take you closer to the mission goal.
The RPG aspect is surprisingly handled pretty well too. In the early game only a specific squad member can use a specific pathway, so you must combine all their power to reach your goal. As the game progress, that pathway can then be used by everyone and you will feel stronger because of that. But even as you get stronger, the game throws more type of obstacle at you so the game never felt too easy. Late in the game maybe your whole squad can turn invisible, but that's not really useful when you need to escort a normal person into a building.
The stealth seems to be a bit wonky because you're never sure why guard can suddenly detect you. But all you need to do is play super safely to avoid those guards.
All in all, the game totally satisfy me, and I wish to play more of the same game!

Aside from the odd server which has unexperienced players in it, Sven Co-op is a thrilling, intense and highly cutomizable mod for the original Half Life game, all bundled together into a free to play standalone. With no freemium purchases or microtransactions, you get the whole package in this bundle.
Mods are built into Sven Co-op to allow Roleplays, Labyrinths, Quests and much, much more on multiple servers. With Sven Co-op having a proactive community and the ability to make a standard Half-Life Vanilla server yourself, one can not get bored. I would recommend inviting all of your friends who love the Half Life series over to Sven and playing on your own server with them, nothing as hectic as 'partially' co-ordinated strikes against zombies, whilst only having crowbars. The interesting bit behind Sven Co-op however is the customization, with you able to change the colour of your 'avatar', which ranges from the models Sven Co-op has, the female versions of Gordon, Gordon himself, Barney, alternative skins, a Jill Valentine 'Half Life' style skin, Robots, Marines [Including Shephard from Opposing Force] and even Ivan the Space Biker! [The original Gordon].
With Sven Co-op allowing you to download extras, such as the campaigns for Blue Shift and Opposing Force respectively, you will not feel a sense of repetition in the campaign and when you're all done, you can go back to the Mod-built servers.
Overall Sven Co-op I recommend for anybody who wants a pure free-to-play game, wants to reminisce the old days of gaming or has wanted Half Life [1] to be Co-op. There is something in Sven to please everyone, ignore the negatives that people say, it is as easy to leave a server or mute the players and proceed on. The positives are only found by actually searching, I was unlucky as I automatically connected to a Russian Mod/RP Server, where everyone was screaming Russian over the microphone. I simply disconnected and joined a Vanilla server manually, from there on, it was easy going.
On a rating of 1 to 10, I would give Sven Co-op a 9.5/10, as it is the best it can be, the only downsides are.. You guessed it! The lack of 'Instructions' when you start up the game and the small amount of 'bugs' that are present, but are generally NOT gamebraking: I do not play this on a 'Gaming Rig', I play this on my Laptop and this game runs very smoothly for a £200 Laptop. With the developers quite pro-active themselves, the bugs are not around for quite long before they get patched.
Sven Co-op in my eyes, is one of the best mods on the Half Life series and does not require anything at all, not even the base game to play. I would recommend this to anyone who asks me about Sven Co-op.

I had high hopes for this game, but it doesn't quite live up to them. At least, not yet. Aside from the big issues that everyone and their dog has written and ranted about, there's a few other issues I haven't seen mentioned yet that irk me more than the commonly mentioned stuff.
First, I'll repeat what most others say about this game: It's not polished, it has some stability problems, and it's not quite 'done' yet. Some places where there are missing textures, really low res textures, odd mechanics, and occasional bugs (permafalling next to a box? wtf?) can make play less fun and generally distract from the game. Personally, I'm playing this to shoot people in the head from distances, so I don't really care that much about the graphics problems. I've got around 24 H of play time in right now, and I've only had a few CTD's, I think 6 so far. Luckily, the auto save has prevented me from losing too much actual mission time, so no biggie there.
The parts of the game that irk me the most are realism issues. To start out with, the 'night vision goggles' are basically a green lense. They don't actually enhance what you can see at night. If you go into a room and shoot the lights out, and it's really, truely pitch black, the night vision goggles (NVS) just puts a slight green hue on the pitch blackness. It basically does nothing. Modern NVS uses an IR illuminator, so in pitch black, you can actually see fairly well using the NVS.
The second issue I have that's actually fairly huge is despawning. If you find a terrorist camp at a point of interest, then go up an adjacent hill to snipe the terrorists from a longer range, they are very likely to despawn once you're more than 200m away. This is, I'm assuming, a mechanic to reduce lag. Having to render 200 terrorists across a huge map, even when they're several KM away, is a waste of resources. But, the easy fix here is to just put a flag on these guys. Once they're tagged, they won't respawn unless you really, truely, leave the area.
Another issue I have is with ammo. Yes, .50BMG rounds are heavy. So ar .338 rounds. And 7.62 rounds. But, why can I only carry 2 clips of ammo? I can lug a .50 rifle around with 80 rounds, but a 7.62 rifle, with smaller, lighter rounds, I can only carry 20 rounds? Come on. Give me the option to at least increasey the number of clips I carry.
While on the note of ammo... I've got a 7.62 sniper rifle, and a 7.62 combat rifle, but the ammo isn't interchangeable? I understand this makes sense from a balance point of view, but... Well, actually, it kind of doesn't.
The third large issue I have is with pickups. I went on a mission with 4 silencer repair kits, I can carry 5 total. I looted a dead sniper and found another silencer repair kit, but I still only had 4 of them in my inventory? I also have an issue with one of the guns, the one that is belt feed. Game shows you can carry 1,000 rounds of ammuntion. If I buy, craft, or get more via a combination of those two, every time I leave my hideout, my total ammo pool gets set to 250. I had 397, and was using another 7.62 combat rifle, and swtiched, and when I left my hideout and went back, I only had 250. Big bug, there...
Some people are complaining about long load times. I'm running my game off a dual SSD setup in RAID 0, and my map load time is between 40 and 60 seconds. I actually timed it a few times using a stop watch. I don't mind, especially seeing how infrequently I switch maps.
Things I do like: It's actually fun to play. The guns are varied, and as much as I'm annoyed at having to choose between my favorite gun and 20 rounds of ammo, or a gun I like less, but has 80 rounds, it is a challenge and can lead to unexpected things.
The thermal imaging system works really well, it's not perfect, but it does help a ton in low light areas, or where you have difficulty seeing the difference between a terrorist and the background. It's possible to switch between thermal imaging and no enhanced imaging while in your scope, which is handy in some situations. The 'not perfect' part is minor, but if a dude leans up against a wall for 5 minutes then walks away, in reality, you'd still see some residual heat on the wall where he was leaning, this doesn't happen in game.
I like the upgrade system. I especially like that if you buy a scope, say the NATO 6/12 zoom scope, for example, for one gun, it also is available for any other NATO sniper rifle. This makes it worthwhile to buy scopes early on, as opposed to larger clips, which are only unlocked for that specific gun. I would have liked more customize options for the secondary weapons, and the two bows never really seemed to work with my play style, but the sidearms are nice.
I thought, before playing for the first time, but after watching youtube previews, that I would absolutely hate the drone. Luckily, that's not the case. The drone isn't a gimmic, it's functional, and slightly broken. The drone is the easiest way to tag enemies, and sometimes, it's nice to send it in to places to get a view, even if it's just going to get shot to bits, but it works. The 'broken' part of it is the battery. If your battery runs out, you can fly it back to yourself (or recall it), and launch it again right away, and the battery will be back to 100%. A balance issue, partly, but this is single player anyway... It would have been more realistic, and I would give it more points, if you could only carry a specific number of replacement batteries. It would also be nice to have a second, more powerful drone, that could do more of an overwatch thing. It would have a much larger battery, you'd just launch it, position it, and leave it. If you needed to get an eye view during a mission, it would still be there, you'd just grab your computer and have an instant overview of the field without having to relaunch or recover or whatever. Oh well, I'm not a dev, just a gamer...
Last thing I like is the open maps. There are several world maps, and they're large, but not overly so. We aren't looking at GTA V's map, here, but they are interesting. But, as much as I like open world maps, there is one thing that bothers me about the mapping: They aren't persistant. If you clear out a point of interest without a specific relic, then close and reaload the game, that POI comes back with it's loot, and enemies that spawn there will respawn. At least so far. Exploring is nice when you get tired of the missions.
In the end, I was hoping for SE4 with modern technology and weapons, but it's not quite that. It's close, but not there. Maybe SGW:4 will be more of the good stuff, with less of the bad stuff. Or, maybe there will be some patches in the future that fix some of the more annoying bugs, glitches, and problems. Only time will tell.

I've seen fixes that helped improve performance for some by 20 frames, and then when I try it it does nothing to the performance. But overall, you're getting a very solid package with EFLC.
TLaD:
This expansion in my opinion has the stronger story of the two, but the weaker world. You are "Johnny the Jew" part of a biker gang that has been on the fall since its peak in the 60s. The leader of your bike gang begins to go crazy with power, and starts a war with the AoD (Angels of Death), and as you can imagine, chaos ensues. I'm going to leave the story off from that since as I said it really is quite the ride, and if you liked GTA 4's story you'll really enjoy TLaD as Rockstar really managed to combine the stories quite well with several crossovers from Niko. This was the first game in a long time that I sat down and beat the story in one sitting, it really is that good in my opinion.
However, if you DON'T like GTA 4's focus on story and grim approach, TLaD probably isn't for you. Now, that's not to say if you didn't like Niko's story you won't like Johnny's, as they are quite different, but Johnny's story is still very grim compared to other GTA stories (not to say it doesn't have its share of laugh out loud moments and some absurdity thrown in there).
But if you're expecting this to bring the insanity of GTA:SA combined with a ton of unique side missions, TLaD is not for you. The only notable side missions include a new race mode with bikes and you now have the option to hit oppenents with bats to throw them off course, and a "gang wars" side mission which is cool on paper, with X-COM style mechanics in the sense that the more you use a gang memeber with out them dying the better they become in battle, but when they die that's it, they're dead and you have to start all over again with a new memeber. But the AI is just not good enough to make it worth your time, and often my team mates would die from a bomb I threw at a car that my team mates are trying to ram, no matter how hard I try to get them to get away. Also there are only like 5 scenarios that just repeat through out the 25 side missions, and only a few lines of dialogue that the characters just repeat over and over again. You do get some guns from doing it, but if you've already beaten the story, chances are you have a ton of ammo for these guns already.
Overall I give TLaD a 8/10:
Pros:
Great Story
Great mechanics
Some fun new toys
Overall solid expereince
Great Voice Acting
Cons:
World feels lacking
Grainy filter makes the game look ugly and even more washed out
TBoGT:
This expansion without a shadow of a doubt is one that every fan of the GTA series should play. The story, while not as strong as TLaD, wraps up many, if not all lose ends from GTA 4 and TLaD. The world is great fun with loads of side missions that will keep you busy for hours and hours. And you get some fantastic toys that brings back some of that absurdity many loved from GTA:SA.
You are Luis Lopez, a former criminal who was involved with a lot of drug dealing in Northern Algonquin, but has since moved to Downtown Algonquin and changed his life around. He's now making a lot more money, works night clubs, and is the body guard of Tony Prince (Gay Tony) a once big shot going through a mid-life crisis, threatened by the closing of his night clubs under a new law in Liberty City, and he owes money to just about every major gang in Liberty City...I think you see where this is going. So through a 6-8 hours long story you'll go from blowing up cranes, highjacking trains, and riding planes. It truly is a fun time with some of the best missions in the GTA 4 trilogy. Also, the start of this expansion is in my opinion the best of the series.
TBoGT also has a fantastic world, and in my opinion is more engaging than even GTA 4's. You have fight night matches, an awesome racing mode that has you jump out of a helicopter, land in a boat, then drive to a car, and race in the cars which also have nitrous, it really is fun. On top of that you have club managment which is...so-so it's rather boring as you just watch over the crowd for a few minutes but every time you do it you get a mission from some celeberity at the end of your shift, this ranges from simply escorting them from paparazzi to spraying people down with a fire truck, it feels very familiar to the wackiness in Saints Row 2, which is definitly not a bad thing. You also get base jumping side missions, which are really fun. You'll be jumping out of helicopters, off of buildings, and off of motorcycles mid-air, and it feels very similar to GTA:SA. And finally, you get some "Drug War" missions, which are very similar to the "Gang Wars" from TLaD, the only difference being they got rid of the X-COM mechanics and instead of just killing everyone, you normally have a goal to steal the "product" and cash and get it to a safe location without it blowing up or you dying. It's fun for the first few times, but just like the gang wars  it's really just like 5 scenarios repeated and the dialogue begins repeating.
TBoGT will pretty much appeal to anyone that has liked a GTA game in the past, and in my opinion that's fantastic.
Overall I give TBoGT a 10/10. Must play.
The overall package is fantastic, and well worth your money. Rockstar did it again.
PC PERFORMANCE:
Yeah, so I'm going to be frank here, if you don't have a decent PC in TODAY standards, you may want to consider getting this on console. Now-a-days the game is so cheap on both platforms it's worth getting the PC version anyways just to mess around with mods, even if the game doesn't run so hot for you. But on my 660 and i5-3470 rig this game runs very poor, especially for its age and the visuals. The frame-drops in the game are just really strange, I've gone from 140fps in one second to 30 in the next, it's just all over the place, and I STRONGLY reccomend putting V-sync on to stop this, even though V-sync locks the fps at 55...seriously what the heck were you thinking Rockstar? Oh yeah, and the benchmark is pointless, unlike other games like Metro: LL where the benchmark pushes your PC to the limit and you'll never encounter that heavy of a load in game, the benchmark is really easy on your PC and I get almost double the fps average in the benchmark than I do in game...
There are some fixes out there that are worth a try but I couldn't find one that worked for me. Also if you have more than 2GB of Vram the game won't let you change the settings (there are some fixes to this, just google it). And on top of it all, this game uses not ONE, not TWO, but THREE DRM services...including GFWL...yeah.
So the PC port is pretty abysmal I must say, and I hope Rockstar treats the PC version of GTA V with more care (they better, considering how long we've waited). That being said, if you have the PC to run it well, this is WAY better looking than the console version, especially now that the shadows actually look like shadows and not blobs! And there are some cool PC exclusive features like your own radio station that plays your own songs, some improved animations, and the ability to save video clips and edit them together. Also, if you're like me and had a XBL account GFWL isn't all bad, as you can still get into private chats with people using the XB1 and 360, so that's sorta neat.

This review will contain a lot of spoilers because I don't want to spoil anything so keep that in mind.
Alright, so I started playing this game back in 2013 (3 years ago) only for a "Team Fortress 2" hat. I am sure most of you did the same. xD But recently I started playing "Alien Swarm" again and I had a great time. That was maybe a week ago. Back then I had only 5 achievements (less than 10%) and now I have all of them (100%). Took me about 50 hours so I sure played this game for a while. My point is that I can tell you what the good and the bad is.
There is a grindy achievement that requires you to kill 100K aliens. There is a legit way to do this without cheating.
Some achievements require you to play with a friend or two so better find some. Overall it's not hard to get 100% achievements (if you're an achievement hunter like me :P).
So in "Alien Swarm" you have a great variety of weapons and stuff. This is a third person game.
There are a few mission to complete and I found all of them fun. You can create a server too.
However, there are a few glitches that you will probably notice. But they aren't that bad and the game is still playable so nothing to worry about. Yea, I've played a game where it was hard to complete it because it was barely playable due to the number of glitches it had. xD
You can select what character you want to play as. There are a few characters. Each has unique stats.
You can play in offline practice mode to train your skills. I don't remember doing so, though. Multiplayer is more fun.
I've read a review on Steam where a guy had written that they think for each 1 euro/dollar you pay you should recieve at least 1 hour worth of gameplay. I have to agree with that. There are games worth 10 or even more euros and you can beat them in a couple of hours. Not worth it, right? But this game, on the other hand, is quite the opposite. As I mentioned earlier it took me around 50 hours to get all achievements (i.e. beat the game as I consider a game beaten when I do so). What I am trying to say is that this game is free. Absolutely free! So you can try it and if you don't like it, simply uninstall forever and be happy. Try it. If you like shooter games you will most certainly like it.

If Recommending this is the only way to make my Friends see it and play it, and bolster its failing playerbase, so be it. It can run on a toaster, it's fun, it's free, and it has a TF2 Hat. Also, Achievements that actually do something.

This game is the spiritual successor to a game that I used to play on the commodore Amiga. That game was Syndicate, by Bullfrog. Basically, you control 4 agents with distinct specialties and make them work together to do missions in a futuristic city, in the style of Blade Runner. You can split up the agents, or keep them grouped together.  One agent can hotwire the doors to get the other agents into a facility, one can take control of robotic equipment.  One uses a cloaking device and can sneak around. One can slow down time so your team can move faster in battle. It's a run and gun or stealth action game, depending on the missions you do.  Your agents get upgrades in equipment and weaponry, and you unlock different sections of the city as you move through the story.  I am not quite finished with the game yet, but am finding this game very entertaining, and from a game developer's standpoint, a very impressive example of the Unity Game Engine. Not one crash yet, and I am many hours in. I would definitely recommend for people who like 3/4 view action RPGs.

This game makes for a cool nostalgia trip and is an excellent microcosim of the human experience.  It's flaw is in pretending to be an interactive medium.  Unfortunatley this is a short story or perhaps short film forced to try to be a game.
The gameplay is limited to choosing from three choices how to respond.  It is after making the first choice that the game reveals its first sin; rather than just having the choice pop up and dialogue continue in an attempt to be interactive you have to bang random keys to simulate typing it yourself.  Furthermore, the Telltale-style "Emily will remember that" pop ups mislead you into thinking you have any actual choice in the story.  Bear in mind I play and enjoy those types of games, and even some excellent text-only games like Choice of Robots, so I know that especially in repeat playthroughs there is a sense of looking behind the curtain, but this doesn't even offer the choices those games have.  Worse yet, before the end of the game it no longer offers even the illusion of choice.
I hate to have to say this, since for the first ten minutes or so I was playing this seemed like a cool idea, but even for free and with the low investment of time needed to finish the game once, I cannot say this is worth anybody's time to play.

If you are an older gamer like myself, you want two things:  To relive old games you loved with ruby-coloured glasses, and to chuckle at parody games and reliving "those were the days" moments in your head, either recalling difficulty, or when you first started up an NES console.  This game, is for people like myself who have been desiring something to scratch the itches I had mentioned earlier.  A nifty, retro-reference laced game, I have found references from the early 80s through 2000s, I've enjoyed gameplay I have longed for since the first Grand Theft Auto, while indulging in gameplay that is remarkably easier to control.  Between the subtle and blatant nods to influences of the past, with gameplay to tickle your nostalgia bone (GUNGAMUNGA!  Or whatever that phrase was for the satire of the followers of Sun Yun Moon used by DMA Designs,) or to entice the player who loved the original GTAs and Death Rally who wanted their funny bone tweaked, but no desire to grind the skills once more on game systems who's control is nearly as much an enemy as the opponents programmed in.

Admittedly, I love the Retro Gaming Trend. But I also love free roam sandbox shooters. This game delivers on both. The game actually plays better than GTA 1 and 2, effectively improving on the original. Plus it also pays homage to other classic 8-bit games of the NES era along with other current games in the Retro Genre.  All in all, good game. Check it out.

This is probably the best digital boardgame I've played. And, yes, it includes digital versions of actual board games. I originally Kickstarted it way back when, and it remains one of the very, very, few games that I do not regret Kickstarting.
Things I love most about Armello:
1 - The visual design---especially character design---is phenomenal. At one glance, even if you're not familiar with the game, you can guess how a character plays. Thane (wolf with sword) is an offensive combat character. Barnaby (bunny with giant hammer and armor) focuses on equipment and combat. Elyssia (who is the best design character of all IMO) is a builder. The king's a lion, and his guards are faithful dogs. All the playable characters ooze personalities, kind of like a dark fairy tale Overwatch. This is actually the reason why I Kickstarted it.
2 - Just like how games like Hearthstone does things that CCGs not played on a computer can't do, Armello does the same with boardgames. Things that would be too tedious to keep track of or involve secrecy that's impossible in tabletop play can happen easily here. Some people view that as a bad thing because it means that hotseat Armello will never happen (the devs confirmed this). I find that a plus because with Armello as a hotseat / physical game it means it's slightly easier to choose a board game when I'm playing with friends.
3 - It's just a really good board game. I'm not a super board game geek (case in point, I don't even have a Boardgamegeek account) but I've played my fair share of games. And Armello is definitely in the top 10 of my favorite games. Maybe even top 5. The mechanics are interesting and mostly balanced (yes even that stupid bear with his spells). And it makes me say "mmm this is clever" both on plays and mechanics quite often.
Biggest problems with this game are game length and NMA (no more action, essentially game ending bugs). It takes an hour or two to play a game with 3 human opponents, and while you can do things offturn things do get slow. I often multitask while playing, which I like but may or may not be a plus for you. The NMA bugs are annoying, especially given the game length, but I've only gotten them in 1/10 games in the past and haven't seen any since a few months ago (after the War chest update). The devs clearly love the game and update it pretty often with bugfixes and new content, so I'm pretty happy.

Honestly? This is a fantastic board game if you go deep into it, but it's important to remember the role luck plays. You're not going to win every game even playing optimally, but the feeling of managing a victory is more than worth the slog, at least for me.

A beautifully designed, highly polished and all-around impressive game of mild/average difficulty combining environment/physics puzzling with cutscene-ish time-based trials having you endure the hardships of World War 1 through the perspectives of characters of different sex, age, race and species (persons and a medical/rescue dog).
The game has great art, great music, highly varied levels and gameplay executions (as much as is possible within this theatre of war anyway) and generally feels very thoughtful. There is a brief encyclopedia updating itself throughout the game giving info on the places you're finding yourself in and there are collectibles that are actually interesting to seek out because they relate to specific situations, behaviors or events of the time - for example bullet/artillery casings turned into other tools or decorative items by soldiers out of boredom, logistical necessity or in an attempt to keep the mind occupied when hunkered down in the trenches (I can't always be bothered with the brainless collectibles in other games; I might actually replay this one at some point just for those).
The story has you switch between characters rather frequently, each having their own abilities of sorts and reasons to join the war (willingly or unwillingly) in some form or another until the individual lines of at least parts of them converge into one. This was done rather well, and has you wonder how everyone is holding up when not playing them, even though at times it can feel a little artifical how by the unlikeliest of circumstances and against all odds they still find each other again in a conflict as chaotic and brutal as this one consuming lives left and right regardless of ambitions and hopes.
The story itself has some emotionally striking moments but otherwise left little impression to me. That's no real issue though since this game is more about the people and their imminent struggles within this time period which all works well enough as it happens. Even so I could've lived without the first half or so of the game having you chase down some evil German general criss-crossing Europe in his Zeppelin because that was just too much a cliché for my taste. There is a genius scientist of sorts too, fortunately not a mad one. If you can forgive these stereotypes you still have a beautifully designed and emotionally engaging experience that can be called bold for presenting things in such a rather unique, thoughtful manner and tackling a war that might be criminally underrepresented in games.

Card Hunter is one of the best co-op turn-based strategy games in existence. Enough said there.
Given there's no true pay to win or catchup mechanisms, however, PvP tends to be won by the guy who's been around the longest. Since this PvP is what most would consider the endgame, this means that the game eats itself as it ages.
Attempts have been made at making the game more evangelical. Leagues, particularly limited format ones, are incredible, and maps you create can be added to the game in the Mauve Manticore dungeons, which are finally firing once per month like they stated when they first devised the idea. Further, Aloyzo's Arsenal allows players to submit custom items which can be added to the game.
The issue here is that none of their evangelical work gets to the heart of the problem, which is that their loot design denies new players the ability to try entire categories of strategies - burst mage and vampire priest being the worst offenders - for their first months of playtime. And if a set of ranked maps favors these old-player builds for that month, well, Card Hunter likely has lower new player retention that month.
Basically, the game needs to ensure that there's no exclusivity. Stay to win is almost as bad as pay to win.
Still, play the PvE. It's incredible, and you'll have a blast.

TL;DR I would not recommend CardHunter. The game mechanics are interesting and fun but it is pay-to-not having to grind and you are playing an RPG without story or immersion or atmosphere.
It is such a shame that a really great idea for mechanics is wasted because of greediness (asking money for content and loot) and laziness (no story, animations, atmosphere).
PROs:
- Game mechanics are unique and interesting. It is basically a puzzle game (which gear to equip for which battle) meet tactical combat a la XCOM.
- The whole "meta" aspect - you play someone who is playing a game - is funny (for about 15 minutes).
CONs:
- The devs ask you every 5 seconds for real money. Big portions of the game are only available when paying for it. Image that in The Witcher you are being asked to pay 4 Euros to enter this dungeoun. The game really is all about loot (cards). Every single action a character can perform - even to walk - comes from cards which come from equipment. Loot is everything, levels are nothing. Now, you can grind your way to victory over countless hours or simply pay cash to get loot. At the same time, the  price per month is about the same as for a triple A MMORPG, WTH?
- Multiplayer is very asymmetrical, players do not get even chances because single player loot is used.

I uninstalled State of Decay and asked for my money back last night.
Hopefully they give it, despite spending 10 hours in.
Problem is, you need 10 hours or so to fully experience the game to determine if its good. There are quite a few mechanical bugs and problems that severely detract from fun and ability to play the game effectively.
1: Doing stuff, especially later in the game requires 1-2 more party members. Getting a party member requires 100 influence, which degrades over play so you have to constantly do stuff to get influence.
Problem is, those party members will often randomly and suddenly run off when you trigger some event even if its a conversation and walkthrough of a survivor site.
-So you can spend 100-200 influence, clear two houses with them and then they leave.
Despite the fact all the event that you triggered does is do some dialogue and a walkthrough another settlement.
2: You don't have a personal stash, its always community, so even when you find badass stuff and you need to store it; you have to pay a large amount of influence to take your stuff back out.
Combined with the many ways the game wastes influence, it hurts.
3: Combat is slow, you can't attack things on a ledge right next to you, your characters (even with max cardio stats) will become tired and sluggish after running 50 yards.
This means, if you get attacked, that you can't fight anything off because everyones a wussy; unless you eat a snack thing.
It just feels WRONG with how tired your survivors get and how fast that occurs. Considering the body adapts rapidly, you'd think Cardio stat increases would yield a VERY visible increase in stamina. It doesn't.
4: The above problems with influence and party members screwing off randomly causes you to often not want to take the risk of wasting influence.
This means that more often than not you find yourself in situations where you actually need them, dont have them, and either loose HP/get sick/DIE.
5: Unless you're playing the game constantly, you lose so much influence that you spend a 1-2 hours just bulding influence back up to even take out party members/guns and ammo from stash that you yourself put in.
This causes you to lose opportunities to do missions and help people because you're trying to get influence to get stuff and help so you wont die, which risks death of others.
6: Characters use weapons oddly. Even with max melee skills, your character will swing a "polearm" which is a 3 foot stick with a blade the size of your head on it like it weighs 50 pounds.
---
This game is a fantastic idea. It really is a good idea, and was fun for a bit; but after playing a significant amount of it a ton of horrible and glaring problems made me rage quit and actually ask for my money back.
I wouldn't recommend this to anyone.
The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing is, all that needs to be done to fix the game is cause your party to stay with you after closing and reopening the game and having them NOT ♥♥♥♥ off when you start events or things like that. That one small change would make everything else better. You wouldn't need to spend so much time getting back influence, you wouldn't have as many issues with danger, spending influence seems less horrible,  and the combat mechanics are less infuriating when you have help.
----
Which would mean that if State of Decay 2 comes out and is actually co-op; all of those problems largely cease. They could just have 2 be a near mirror image of one in a new area and story and it would be fine; because the game wouldn't make your party dissapear if that party is other people.
--------
If you go to the Nexus and download a bunch of mods, you can fix some glaring and nonsensical problems and game mechanics, which is sad. A lot of the♥♥♥♥♥♥wrong with SoD shouldn't have made it past QA. Which leads me to believe they didn't do a QA.

I have more than I can even use, having purchased almost everything that is unlocked as soon as it is available.

Paint the Town Red is a game I've come to know and love on Steam. Despite making it's debut through Greenlight, where nobody really knew it much, it's a game that has definitely found an audience who enjoy it's brutal combat and fast gameplay. Short story;
I first played this game before it got on Steam, where the developers had released a demo. The setting was a small bar (similar to the bar level we have in the game now) and I was enjoying my time drinking with fellow patrons. My phone rumbles and apparently 'I've been made.' Cue every goon within a mile radius, in and out of the bar jumping down my throat, attempting to do me in.
It was great and the combat was incredibly engaging. Improvised combat in a small area with multiple enemies is pretty frantic, and the game's physics were astounding. The game is centered around melee fighting, but you can throw weapons at enemies. The bar was being sieged endlessly by♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bikers, and they only stopped coming when I finally dropped dead.
The credits mentioned the game was soon hitting Steam Greenlight, and I knew it had to be upvoted. It had so much potential. When I eventually seen it on Steam and it hit it's
Good news is, it's even better. Frequent updates have seen us fighting in a Disco Club, and a Jail (with a hidden shotgun inside if you can find it), along with the larger, updated bar. There's even a Sandbox level to mess about on. There are tons of weapons to choose from and the physics are even better. You can literally beat someone's head in until their skull starts to show, and every enemy has a full rendered skeleton. Combat is just as good as it was before. Bad guy coming at you with a bottle? Slice their arm off! Kick them while they're down! You also have special abilities to use (which, although aren't the most realistic of abilites, they are damn cool) to gain an edge in the brawl. Basically, the level only ends when you batter the crap out of everyone else, or you end up on the list of 'people who have had the crap battered out of them.'
To my delight, the devs have been going at a steady pace with updates including additional content. As well as having added a new♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥map, with a range of new weapons, an Arena mode has also been added, where you must fight your way through up to 10 waves as quickly as possible. Multiplayer has also been added! And even better, a Level Editor has been included! Now you can create your own scenarios and fufill all your brawling fantasies, without the scars and jail sentences! I was also highly anticipation Steam Workshop support, and now that's been added too, allowing users to share their created levels. So far, it's been great!
To end the review I would just have to say that PTTR is definitely worth your time if the idea of a mass pub brawl sounds like your ideal Friday night. Even if it isn't your kind of thing.
9/10.

After eleven months, and over 600 hours played I felt it was time to voice my amazement at this absolute gem of a game. Armed only with some iron (presumably left over from a crash) and some coal-fired equipment, your goal is to launch a rocket.  How you get there is completely up to you.  The level of control you have is nothing short of mind-blowing.  Want a sprawling mass of belts moving product all over?  You can do that.  Efficient lines of product moving in just-in-time sync? Also possible.   A minimalistic factory, creating minimal pollution?  Check.  Trains?  Don't get me started on trains.  I can watch 30 trains all moving to specific schedules with no attention needed for hours.
Of course, all this industry breeds pollution, the natives tend to get restless, and will send groups to attack your factory.  Factorio does include a basic RTS aspect, but unless you're caught completely unprepared is not much of a threat.  Rightfully so, this game is all about problem solving (usually self-created), logistics, and automation.
However, the real gem here is the development company behind the game.  Quite simply, you do not see this level of detail and attention.   In all my hours played, I have run across exactly three bugs (two were related to the initial 0.15 experimental launch, and were patched THAT DAY, the third is a rare train pathing issue which is fixed for 0.16).  This is one of the most optimized games I have run across, and is only getting better.  The developers are extremely active and engaging with the community, and seem to genuinely care about the quality of their product.  Visiting their official forums you can see this in every area,  especially the bug forums: where every single bug is tracked until resolved (even if it turns out to be a feature).  Weekly development blogs are a real insight into the development process.
TLDR.  I like trains.  Buy this game.

The game is a side-scrolling, platform puzzle game with views into WW 1 through the lives of 4 characters you play in the game.  And when I mean "views" -- literally!  At the start of many levels there is a "Facts" page that can come up where it shows you ala a press photo or something and a paragraph of what's going on in WW1 at the stage of the game you're playing.  So while you're playing a game, it gives you the background of what's going on.  Also there are a number of hidden items that you can collect on each mission (over 100 in all) that then shows you a blurb about that item from that period in history.  It really sets the stage and atmosphere for the game.
I wasn't expecting such an engaging story from this!
for different viewpoints of the story.  You play the game as four different people, not counting the helpful dog that you run across who assists your characters and you can give him commands too.

I just love that "moving pencil sketch" look in the game, and they all move smoothly and comically.
Fabulous.  The game is NOT narrated with speaking playable characters, but they do have voices.  The voices just give a hint of what they're saying, in the accent of the character, and adds to the charm.  The narrators they do have in between missions are great.
The NPCs in the game that you meet communicate with unintelligible words, but it is made clear through pop up boxes or icons in speech balloons.  It's done very well, and conveys the meaning perfectly.  Great.
Each mission there can be 3 to 8 items that you can find in out of the way, hidden spots.  And each gives you a little paragraph of history.  Loved it.

This is because you can essentially grind past that either by switching over to multiplayer for a handful of games for better item drops, or repeat previous adventures for  gold to buy better items. The game has been losing players steadily and is currently only at 25% of its average players online at a given time compared to what it had when it released, only 6 months go, in July 2015. (per steamcharts).  Having that large of a drop over that short of a time should be an indication of the game's longevity.

The random number generator style of card play can be frustrating.  Selling items is a joke as there is no difference in gp value for a level 1 item, or a level 18 item. It also seems the developers are not interested in keeping players by ignoring any criticisms that have been made. There are plenty of ways to incentivise purchases but pay to progress, and pay to win for multiplayer, are the least player friendly ways to go about it.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 (SGW3).
The first two games in this series had been hit or miss. The original was entertaining but underdeveloped. The second was a step in the right direction with greater scripting to the missions and rework to the ballistics system.
I had hoped the third would be the penultimate vision of the Ghost Warrior franchise. Unfortunately, it is not.
SGW3 fails for me on several levels. As a long range and PRS shooter in my spare time, the key phrase in SGW3, "sniper" is woefully inaccurate. Distances feel far shorter than they displayed. The weapon models themselves are of decent detail but I don't understand the developers reasoning of putting so much junk (dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥ on all the weapons and attachments.
Many of the weapon models and the majority of the optics suffer from this too. From zip ties and elastic bands to pencils taped to the sides, the developers have tried way too hard to make their models look unique; I wouldn't have half the crap they do on my rifles.
Next lets look some minor details, the ammunition. SGW3 boasts a lot of different calibres with a diverse number of types ranging from "sniper bullets" to luring, explosive tips and armour piercing. I'm willing to suspend disbelief for some of the more sci-fi types but the models for the ammunition would cause anyone who has actually seen a real bullet to have an aneursym. The "sniper bullets" feature solid turned projectiles that look ridiculous which look like they are ribbed for your target's displeasure and what I can only call "speed holes". If any of the developers even bothered to search for "match grade ammunition" or hell, "sniper bullets" they might have been able to identify that projectiles are simple.
The armour piercing ammunition look like scaled down 105mm or 120mm tank ammunition even down to the paint scheme. Ridiculous. I was half expecting the bullet game to show the whole damn bullet (case and projectile) flying through the air.
The bullet cam shows nothing amazing especially those familiar with the Sniper Elite series. I disabled the bullet cam after the first dozen or so shots because it only seeks to disrupt your ability to realign on a second target quickly.
We have multiple rifles using the same "7.62" ammunition which I can normally forgive but there are too many other issues that have gotten on my nerves with this game to ignore. .300 Win Magnum, 7.62x51mm and 7.62x54r are all different natures of ammunition. The only commonality is that 7.62x51mm and .300 Win Magnum can be loaded with the same actual projectile but even this is uncommon.
One more on the shooting side of things because terminology goes a long way. If you "salvage" an enemy sniper's rifle, you can recieve "Bullet heads". Bullet heads? You mean projectiles right? These may not seem like much, but if you can't even nail down the simple things, how can they even make a successfuly game out of this? Well I wouldn't worry because they didn't.
The setting of the game at first seemed interesting. I've always held a big interest in European conflicts and the Russian invasion of Georia in 2008 was one I followed closely. The game world is gorgeous but it feels so dead. There are no enemies outside of predetermined locations and even when you do find some, they are hardly a challenge. Their AI is poor and will gladly stand in the open, asking no one in particular why their mate's head just exploded.
There is little variety in the side missions and most do not identify as a mission until you're already on top of it. Meaning any chance at stealth is already out the window as you're forced to mag dump your AK just to get to cover.
The characters are a string of tropes and cliches. Conversations sound like they were written by someone who hasn't held a real conversation in five years. Characters' motivations are are fickle as hell. I can get ANYONE in Georgia to help me just by repeating these three magical words.
One bloke plays a game of Russian roulette for the life of a prisoner, himself and you and knowing the chamber is loaded, just blows his brains out like it was a given. This guy was on the screen for all of like thirty seconds after being alluded to being the key to everything. I still don't understand what I achieved through doing so.
One of the reviews I read on here before I took the plunge said the story was great. Great? Were we playing the same game? And if you can't guess who the mystery sniper is in the first five minutes, uppercut yourself.
The only saving grace is that the game does look pretty but it is an empty shell I cannot recommend anyone buying this game at full price if at all.

I was excited for this game and hoped it would be good, and when I finally got it in the steam sale I couldn't wait to play it. Unfortunately, it was far below my expectations. It's rare a game makes a bad enough impression in a short enough time for me to refund it, but this game pulled it off.
TL:DR at the start: Game sux, I refunded it.
Longer Review:
At first the game seemed fun, like a sandboxy commandos-esque awesomefest. I love cyberpunk in general and cyberpunk games with RPG bits especially, so it had already found a way into my heart. The tutorial made the game seem good, everything worked and I didn't see any of the bugs or control issues people reported in the early access. And then the game proper started and it♥♥♥♥♥♥itself.
This was my experience: I attempted to sneak into a location, some corporate warehouse whatever. On my first attempt, I slipped past the cameras, and herded my agents/cats into a corner to wait for a patrol to pass. As it did, it left one man behind, and I thought "Perfect! Stealth kill time, I'll pick them off one by one". Then I hit the stealth kill command, and my agent spun around three times and unloaded a clip into the box beside her, alerting every guard in the world to my location. I was swarmed and reloaded a save.
Then came strike two: Loading a save puts you back at a checkpoint anyway! To me at least, this game seems like one rife with experimentation; all stealth games are. Yet if my experimenting leads to failure and I die or reload, I just get sent back to the start of the level anyway? That sounds insufferably annoying.
After I made my way back, came strike three: I shot out a camera. I did not realize that this was, in fact, the greatest crime that would be committed within a century of my purchasing of this game. I had been warned that shooting out cameras would attract attention, I'll admit. I had not been warned "attention" meant nuclear countermeasures. Every guard in the level swarmed me. Dropships sent in elite troops. The Future Navy Seals sent in every man they had, plus some kind of terminator/rambo hybrid armed with a minigun shooting rockets. Even employees of the rival company of the facility I was infiltrating showed up to stop me. Finally, they all just decided "♥♥♥♥ it" and glassed the entire city to stop my heinous rampage of destroying 1 camera. I felt this was slightly excessive. Exaggeration aside, the level of response to this, and I assume every violation of stealth, was insane. I enjoy playing stealth games through my mistakes, but it feels incredibly intimidating knowing one ♥♥♥♥up with call down the entire wrath of the world's militaries.
Finally, after receiving another sound thrashing, and beginning to question whether this $6 was worth it, the game decided to answer me with a fourth strike. Along the way to try again, I stood next to the door to a restricted area. I did not enter it: I was standing in the street. I don't know if a camera spotted me through the wall, or if the guards are just that paranoid, and I don't care anymore. All I know is, despite doing nothing and standing in the middle of the street, and alert was sounded, and for the third time in an hour every guard in the entire level began swarming my position.
I closed the game, saw I had played 111 minutes thus far, and took it as I sign that the universe wanted me to refund it. So I did.

This is more than Syndicate.
The environment with rain and neon, the music and the darkness, it all adds to an excellent Cyberpunk themed, Blade Runner inspired setting.
The gameplay is not easy, but with time you start getting the hang of it. I'm not a big fun of stealth so I usually just go guns blazing with the help of some mind controlled enemies.
The variety of equipment and abilities also helps to diversify the missions you'll have to accomplish to progress in-game.
The developers have continuously supported the game, they added multiplayer co-op and even slow motion to help those more accustomed with turned based games.

If you remember playing and enjoying Syndicate Wars from way back, then stop reading and buy this game now - Satellite Reign is the spiritual successor to Syndicate Wars. I backed this game after the Kickstarter ended and I have no regrets, it delivers what was promised and feels like a worthy successor.
Game play consists of controlling 4 agents in real time, in a cyberpunk open-world setting. You break into different compounds to steal/assassinate using stealth or brute force. Rob banks and hack ATMs for money and use it to research and buy better gear. As you complete more missions, your agents level up and gain more abilities as well, in preparation for a final showdown with the mysterious CEO of the Dracogenics corporation.
+ The game has a great traditional, Cyberpunk atmosphere. Bladerunner-esque neon visuals are colourful eye-candy.
+ The futuristic soundtrack fits the game perfectly.
+ Stealthily sneaking into a compound, hacking your target and then slipping out undetected past guards and security cameras is tense and great fun. Even when it all goes pear-shaped you can still fight your way out or run away.
+ The map design is excellent - with dark, cluttered alleyways and brightly lit, heavily guarded compounds. The city feels organic.
+ The world feels like a sandbox where you can mess about with different guns and explosives. Silenced sniper rifles, cloaking devices, sound dampened grenades or augmented armour/shields with mini guns and rocket launchers? You decide.
+ A new co-op/multiplayer mode has been added, if you are into that sort of thing
+ There is a long, initial load time, but once you are in the game, there are no loading screens at all which is very convenient and easy to take for granted.
- This game was developed by a studio of just 5 devs on a small budget. They had to make smart choices about what to focus on during development so some areas of the game are a bit rough around the edges.
- AI for the security guards can occasionally be a bit wonky and exploitable.
- Rare bugs include agents getting stuck in the environment and one instance of an agent falling through the floor. Simply reload a savegame to work around this.
- Lacks the extra polish that a bigger studio with a bigger budget could achieve: no cinematic cutscenes, brief tutorial, lacking background environmental sounds. Much of the story is revealed through reading emails and data logs. Something that would have made this game an instant classic is some kind of extra strategic layer - heres to hoping for Satellite Reign 2.
- Breaking and entering compounds gets a little bit samey after a while, although the final confrontation adds a small twist.
- Very CPU intensive for a top-down isometric game. Don't be surprised if you can't get 60fps with your latest high-end graphics card.
This is a very ambitious game for a 5-man studio. It is tremendously fun to play and succeeds in what it set out to achieve: to be a spiritual successor to Syndicate Wars. In the end, it is limited simply by manpower and budget. I sincerely hope 5Lives Studios continue to make further games.
