I remember playing this game all the time when I was a kid. It felt so nostalgic to play this in 2016. But I ain't gonna lie, I mainly got this in hopes that they will also add the 2nd and 3rd game to the PC. Can't wait for that happen!
Anyway, about this game. It is a bit of an old game, but older games normally tend to be fun, if not more fun than games from today. The story is rather simple, and though many know the story already, I will avoid spoilers. You play, as the title says, a tasmanian tiger named Ty. Ty explores many different terrains and weather in search for thunder eggs, golden cogs, opals, his bilby friends, and most importantly, talismans.
Gameplay: The game offers about 4-6 hours of gameplay. You are given many different levels to explore, take what is available in each level, and progress. The difficulty of the game is rather easy, in all honesty, the most likely thing that will kill you is the stuff on water slides and fall damage. Most the bosses are rather easy to beat, but that doesn't say the bosses aren't a battle to forget.
Characters: This game does have some memorable characters with some interesting personalities. Ty himself, in my opinion, didn't seem to be the most interesting character in my mind, but I will remember him only because he was the character you played as the whole time.
Controls: I understand they are still working on improving the PC version of this game, but the controls at the moment are really sloppy. The camera oftenly got stuck, the sensitivity for me was pretty low, even after I turned it up, and movement, espacially around corners, felt real awkward and oftenly costed me while fighting or sliding. I have only used the keyboard and mouse. I can't say for controller.
Graphics: Obviously, for an old game, this game kind of lacks textures and effects. But I will say that the lighting (for at its time of release) is really not bad. Though obviously, you should never judge a game by its graphics. 2D or 3D
Price: For 4-6 hours of gameplay, some replayability, and maybe a few memorable moments and characters. The price of 12 dollars isn't to bad. But if it ever is on sale, highly consider it.
Rating: For people who played this back when it first released, it will be a trip down nostalgia lane. For people who are new to the game, it will prove to be a good experiance. For a price of 12 dollars, and all that I said above, I think it is a fair 6/10
Make sure to support Krome Studios to help them improve this game and hopefully get Ty The Tasmanian Tiger 2 & 3 moved to PC!

First Impression Review!
Hello everyone, after spending 15 hours in this game, I would like to give some insight from a total newbie for the other newbies who are planning to buy this game...
First things first!
If you are thinking to buy this game and If you like FPS games.. Just dont think anymore and buy it. The price is so reasonable and worth it...
I played mostly Co-op (only 2 games in Multiplayer) and I can say,
- The community is much more friendly compared to other online shooters as I've seen.
- People dont flame you when you fail, or have a brain fart.
- Communication between players a really low, but I consider that as another side of a hardcore realistic shooter game. You dont talk much with your comrades while in the heat of battle.
- Game is not easy but it is not as hard as people says. You get used to it easily.
- There is a workshop and a lot of mods, but for me it is a big plus that I've never said that "If only this was like this.." for anything. So no mod is necessary to play it smooth and comfy (totally personal opinion)
- Graphics are good.. or a tick or two over from good.. But there are better ones I know.
- Game is optimised very nicely, I dont understand why people complain it that much, I can play it on max settings on my 5 year old gaming laptop, on an external monitor.
- Game is very challenging, It is a plus If you like this kind of game.
- Yes I know I've said it is not hard but I've said very challenging.. what does that mean?.. This means.. you cant get lazy at any second.. No.
- I really like the AI level of the bots. They are not idiots (As opposed to the teammate bots you get in solo mode)
now lets get to the not so likeable part:
- I tried multiplayer only 2 matches. I got pawned. I believe that is because I am a total noob for that, dont have any idea about most of the maps and tactics.
- Community in multiplayer looks like a little bit more toxic but I cant say it for sure because I didnt spent too much time in there.
- My only fear is game becomes boring after you learn all the maps because Co-op mode is static. The good thing is, there are a lot of map choices, a lot of modes even for co-op so, If it gets boring, It will get after a long while and with this price tag, this game worth it.
As I've said,
I didnt spent too much time in, %99 played co-op, just trying to learn the game. These are my first impressions. I say, If you are interested a little more slow paced, tactical, unforgiven but exiting FPS shooter. You buy this, and try it out.

Insurgency is a rich and deep tactical FPS with a heavy focus on teamwork and tactics. Developed by New World Interactive and released in 2014. After a few years in the process of improvement, it’s one of the current best FPS in the market. The price is too attractive, towards the quality that the game presents. This FPS is a mix of the two of the better online tactical shooters: Counter-Strike and Red Orchestra.
The game seems too normal where there are two teams, the classic push/conquest/objective style game types, and guns. However, there is more than seems be. Insurgency is mechanically different of others popular known FPS games.
If you usually play COD or BF and enjoy these styles, then Insurgency isn't for you. It's a game for those who like difficulty. The sights, the aim, the recoil, everything is heavier.
People that start play this game will said Insurgency is bad or strange, I guess. The recoil is totally different than CS:GO. Anyway, CS:GO is more popular but in these terms, I think Insurgency is more realistic. The game is really realistic and unpredictable how bullets can kill an enemy with one shot through a wall, and it makes matches a challenge. If you stand staying in one place for too long, that's can be a problem, forget that. After a while, you'll realise that Insurgency have entirely different gameplay mechanics than COD or BF.
The controls are solid and the game offers to you one of the most intense firefight games I have played. They're intensified through really good audio and visual effects, that make a spetacular environment around you.
Insurgency is a truly tactical FPS. The teamplay here is more important than in any FPS. Don't think about running through the open countryside. If you want to win, you need to be tactical, otherwise, you'll be quickly discovered.
Graphically talking, Insurgency is appealing, particularly the detail put into the guns is extremely well done.
Instead of having reinforcement pools like BF, Insurgency uses spawn waves to regulate gameplay flow. It can sounds weird, but it works extremely well in practice.
The game offers a nice customization to your weapons, everything is unlocked, so that there is no level up.
The maps are amazing, sort of based in places like Israel and that. Insurgency removed the massive maps and endless walking that features Arma, e.g., delivering a fast-paced, intelligent FPS game unlike anything in the market. It's an amazing game in almost every way I can think of. Don't expect kill cam, no crosshairs, no radar, no medic or healing. No enemy damage notification. Totally hardcore.
The game offers a several game modes to chose from and they're well-made, too. You can play on solo (with bots, against bots), and it's the same game modes as Co-Op (with people vs. bots), some of which are: Hunt (prettty much kill a certain number of people and blow up a cache), Survival (cap points to gain the in-game currency which you buy weapons with; however this in-game currency is different to the in-game currency is CS:GO), and so on. There is a timer between spawns, but it goes fairly quick, so don't worry. You can spectating your friends that is still entertaining.
On multiplayer there is all the gamemodes like Firefight and Ambush, which are preetty much king of the hill but harder and protecting a vip until he reaches a certain point. Sometimes, this game really forces you to trust your instincts and your teammates due to the lack of information.
Recommended that you have a mic on the ready because the VOIP is pretty crucial in communication. It's somewhat positional audio so it's easier to tell who is talking just by the direction of the voice; but beware, enemies can hear you too if you are too close to them, positional audio is just that. It will also help when flanking, calling it out so you don't get murdered by your own team when you come around a corner.
All in All Insurgency is a really good Tactical Game!

I have no illusions about how I'd survive in a zombie apocalypse. I'm not the fastest, the most prepared, the most agile, or the most sensible. The uncertainty of such a dangerous, nomadic lifestyle, where vital resources could simply not exist wherever you choose to go; I find it demotivating, a response that would prove deadly. But, in spite of this, I've always had a fascination with zombie survival games (i.e. not the arcadey shmups like Resident Evil 4 or Bulletstorm). There's something about that delicate balance between horror, stealth, action based combat, strategic base building, economic management, and curshingly bleak drama to be found in a deadly, crumbling world, all wrapped up in an emergent, player-driven story. It's a heady 7-ball juggling act that many attempt but few do well. Often the game can only juggle one or two at a time. Often, some balls are just dropped altogether.
Make no bones about it, State of Decay is brilliant. I've played my share of zombie survival games, and just about every single one of them has left me slightly unfulfilled, thinking about the potential the genre has to be great. And, when I do, State of Decay is the game I keep asking for.
With the exception of perhaps the drama, State of Decay juggles all the balls with aplomb. You are an ordinary person, on holiday with a friend, when zombies strike. After a small tutorial, you're then basically free to explore the massive area, looting resources, building outposts that net you resources, finding people to help (or do missions for), or just to walk around killing zombies. You can approach the zombies as stealthily as you want, either by sneaking up to them and smashing their brains on nearby objects, shoot at them with the firearms of your choice, by just running away, or any combination in between. Zombies will naturally spawn in various locations, and there are no progammed jump scares, so the horror is completely organic.
You also are only human, so after enought time and exertion, your character will become fatigued, which lowers maximum fatiue. That's when you have to return to base to rest. You can then talk to another NPC to take them out on a mission, or even convince them to join you on a scavenging hunt. The base can be upgraded using scavenged materials, which affords a variety of benefits. Bases have running costs too, so the scavenged materials must address these needs. Plus, killing zombies affords benefits to your base, as it naturally should; the fewer zombies around, the less damage they'll do to the base and its morale.
On top of all this, there is a story, and missions for you to complete. So there is drama, although not all of it emergent. It's a delicate balance between story-driven purpose and sandboxed fun. There's plenty of reward for exploring and doing your own thing, but at the same time, you don't feel like it's all pointless.
As the big red thumbs down indicates, after such glowing sentiments, there is a big ugly "but" coming. BUT, as much as State of Decay expertly realises some high ambitions, and as much as it is the game I keep asking for, I'm not sure if it's the game I want to play. The problem is that surviving in State of Decay feels a little bit too like the real thing (obviously I don't mean "the real thing" literally!).
First and foremost, there's State of Decay's most controversial feature: real time passing changes things in game. Remember when I talked about the running costs of bases? They subtract from your base's total every 24 hours IRL. It's also not the only thing that changes IRL. I came back to a game I had stopped playing, and found that several of my people were either dead or missing, which is potentially a big problem. Bases also chew up building materials like nothing else, which is essential for various upgrades.
This ties into my second gripe, which is that resources are more or less finite. Once a place is looted, it doesn't magically spawn new resources. With certain upgrades, it's possible to convert certain resources into others (e.g. food into fuel, by a process of making biodiesel), but other resources (such as building materials) cannot be manufactured or converted at all. So, it is possible to arrive at a situation, after many hours of play, where you no longer have access to any building materials. Plus, when a base can't cover its running cost in materials, this causes a very large hit to the morale, which can cause people to run away, so refusing to collect them until you need them is not a good option either.
The people are finite too: once you run out, that's it. The game doesn't generate any people procedurally, and once your last person dies, that's game over. It accumulates to a rather off-putting thought: that the time you spent slacking off and exploring, or the hours spent making mistakes and trying to learn the various mechanics could cost you the game down the road. I don't think the game is that unforgiving in the end, but the thought is discouraging nonetheless.
That kind of pressure can really work well in a roguelike game (e.g. Invisible Inc -- great game, by the way!), but State of Decay is too long, and doesn't have enough procedural generation to work on that level. While the economy of zombies is very much dynamic, and makes the world feel alive and dangerous, the missions are exactly the same every time you attempt them.
So, despite the obvious brilliance of State of Decay, it's a tough title to recommend. I appreciate more as a piece of art than a game, and not because the graphics are especially pretty. It's that hardcore ideal that I hold zombie games up to, conveying both the intoxicating freedom and the unforgiving hopelessness of surviving in a zombie apocalypse. The problem is that it conveys it too well. I'm hoping that anyone who actually reads all of this will not be discouraged from buying and trying this game. Most gamers just want a game they can be entertained by, and on that basis alone, I can't really recommend State of Decay. But if, like me, you can appreciate an innovative, indie take on a tough formula, even if it can be unpleasant to play, I wholeheartedly recommend trying it out.

Whenever I attempt to describe State of Decay to people who have never played the game, I find myself describing the game I want State of Decay to be--and the game that Undead Labs attempted to craft--more than the game that State of Decay actually is. State of Decay wants to be many games--chief among them the first video game to properly capture the community survival elements of a Dawn of the Dead film in mechanical terms (as opposed to the narrative terms of Telltale's The Walking Dead)--and, at its best moments, it creates a sense of community, tension, and character agency matched by few of its peers. But for each moment of spontaneous, unscripted story wonder that State of Decay generates, it is also one glitch, bug, or broken feature away from drawing you completely out of its experience.
- Creates legitimate sense of community among your group of survivors
-  Permadeath adds tangible tension to every outing
- Building up base & team feels like a less pessimistic George Romero film
- Omnipresent bugs ranging from humorous to game-breaking
- Controls lack finesse for more hectic action sequences
- Multiple modes of play fail to meaningfully feed back into one another
- World lacks distinct sense of place
In my opinion, I give this a 6 out of 10.

A few bugs (e.g. ombies suddenly teleporting through closed doors), but they aren't enough to distract me from what is a thoroughly enjoyable game.
Other reviews have drawn parallels with the Walking Dead. I can see why. but don't expect this game to be as strongly character-driven as that. Each character does have unique characteristics and traits, but they don't seem to have much actual impact on my tactics or weapons loadout. So long as you're a bit cautious (i.e. don't dive into a horde with just a crowbar to hand and expect to walk away - although it can be done) you can manage to deal with most situations using any character. There are exceptions like the military being more receptive to characters with a military background.
DLC - Breakdown is more of a sandbox version focussing solely on survival.
Lifeline is focussed on a different, more urban map where you play as the military who end up cut off from supply and reinforcement, so you need to balance progress against survival with dwindling loadout of the chunky weapons you start off with. Different enough to add a lot of additional gameplay and enjoyment.
Definitely worth a play.

👍 The asthetic — overall art style looks and plays really nice
👍 The controls — tight, though unforgiving
👍 The longevity — the campaign doesn't overstay its welcome, and the added arcade mode can provide many hours on top for the fans
👍 The concept — fun mechanics make for an addicting experience of retrying "just one more time" to get things right
👎 The level design and overall approach to difficulty — this is the game's main problem, and it's especially annoying in the first half of the game since the levels are way too long and new mechanics and traps are constantly being introduced to you at the END of a level (rather than the start) which usually leads to you dying to the new trap before properly learning how it works and forcing you to grind out the entire level again until you get it. Dying to challenging levels and unique traps is fun. Having to spend 3 minutes over and over again just to get to the hard part isn't. This is exacerbated by the developers' will to troll you - the most glaring example being adding a sudden triple machine gun trap at the end of a "sawtooth traps only" stage.
👎 The story — pretty uninspired, though I didn't really expect an award winning novel inside the game so I really can't blame it for that.
[-] The music — though thematically appropriate, it really gets on the nerves after a short while since it's constantly looping and it also makes some levels quite harder (the buttons)
I'd suggest you get it during a sale or in a bundle.

Combat and danger altimately come down to rolling a handful (or bucket full) of dice, and there's something satisfying in seeing a few dice hit the "succeed and roll again" result several times in one test.
You will at some points get destroyed by RNGesus, but overall the game balances out, and has enough for the price to keep you entertained. For me it's not going to be one I'll play obsessively, but I will keep coming back for a bit more fun. Would definitely recommend.

One of the more redeeming qualities is the new open world where you can traverse through on foot or in vehicles. Finally breaking away from the constraints of a linear world, it is nice to move freely and move at the pace you think is best. What plagues the game constantly are the bugs, inconsistent frame rate and poor graphics.
Honestly, whether it's enemies appearing in a room before your eyes or the game practically chugging through certain segments as I swing the camera around, it's hard to just write these off. What is enjoyable is why we are here in the first place, which is shooting sniper rifles. Whether its turning the dial on the scope to account for wind or patiently waiting for the right moment to strike, the game makes you feel authentic and deadly. What is surprising is the amount of times the game forces you to use other guns and unfortunately, they aren't designed well. The bullets don't do much as the AI just runs at you or just stands in the open at times. Overall, I'm left with a lot of mixed feelings. I love setting up my shot, waiting for the right time to pull the trigger and then executing my plan while other times I don't get how a well known game in 2017 could look this unpolished. Here's the breakdown:
Pros
+Sniping feels authentic
+The attention to detail when setting up shots and firing is great
+ Wildlife in the woods
+open world is MUCH better than the past two games linear design
+ Bullet cam actually much better
+ Driveable cars
Cons
-Graphics are really washed out and subpar
- Civs dont react to you or gun shots at all
-Writing and Story are nothing to be excited
-Plain Open world
- No Online multiplayer

Paint The Town Red
First-person Brawler
South East Games
South East Games
is a first-person brawler game developed and published by South East Games. It is currently available in Early Access, and the developers are fixing bugs and adding new things almost every week.
The game is seen from a first-person perspective, and it looks fairly good: the blocky characters that you fight are nicely varied and feature different facial animations, the blood that spills from their wounds really paints the whole level red, and the level design is well done, with hidden weapons and such that reward your exploration. There are a couple of animations bugs, like beheaded enemies that are still alive, or doors that glitch out of existence, but it performs really well and I haven't found anything annoying.
Your goal is simple:
. You can use your fists, your kick (which makes your enemies fly in the air), or you can pick up almost everything that you find in the levels, from chairs and beer bottles, to baseball bats and katanas and guitars, as well as a shotgun (the only firearm currently available). The weapons are powerful but break down after a couple of hits.
There is also a Power Meter, which grants you three different special moves: a Shockwave (which makes every enemy near you fly away), Berserk Mode (which gives you a one-hit kill for every punch you throw), and Smite (you point your finger at an enemy and he blows up). This helps turning this already violent game in probably one of the bloodiest I've ever played, making every game session engaging and rewarding.
Unfortunately, the game lacks a lot of variety, and after a while you will get a bit bored of it. But after one or two days, it will be just as exciting as the first time.
Excluding the mini-bosses that you find in each level, every enemy goes down with a couple of hits from the weapons you find, so they aren't that hard to kill. However, when there is a mob of people that puts you in a corner, they easily overpower and destroy you, making everything a bit more frustrating than it could have been.
The sound effects are spot on, and every hit from punches and weapons gives you an adrenaline rush. The music from Kevin McLeod fits the game very well, and even though the tracks aren't all that memorable, they are very fun to listen to while playing.
The game now has three levels (a bar, a disco floor, and a prison) and a Sandbox Mode to try out different weapons and attacks. There are also some modifiers that you can use (like giving every enemy a machete, or giving you unlimited power) to spice things up a bit and making the whole experience fun every time.
Overall, this is a very good game to play when you have thirty minutes of free time or when you are upset: it is rewarding, it is fun and it doesn't last long. I strongly recommend supporting this game, especially because the developers are constantly fixing the bugs and adding new features to satisfy the fans. I can't wait to see what they will give us next.

Maybe not. I'll try to keep it spoil free as much as possible.
First, Is this a bad game?
Answer: No, not at all. This was an experience that was relatable in many ways.
Is this a good game?
Well, no because the game offers the illusion of choice when in reality it's just trying to tell a set story with only 2 possible outcomes.
What makes it good?
It's an interactive love story, plane and simple, and it does a good job pacing it out and establishing what's going on through simple messages in an IM format.
What makes it bad?
Again, the fact that you're offered the illusion of choice when in reality it doesn't matter what you choose, it's still going to end in a set way.
Final Words: Ultimately there's nothing wrong with the game as it's a functional, narrated experience. I just wouldn't recommend it to anyone looking to make a difference in the game's narration. I suppose this would be the spoiler bit where it's kinda like Far Cry 2 where you're damned if you do and damned if you don't.
Final Score: 6 out of 10, The game wouldn't let me choose any other score.

Emily is Away is an incredibly intense 3D action/stealth platformer with challenging boss fights, a genius combat system and extremely beautiful graphics. It takes place in post-apocalyptic future where disease has turned most of the mankind in hungry, brutal and mindless zombies. You are a survivor looking for someplace where you can feel safe.
But for real, Emily is Away is a love story. You are a young adult in love with Emily, your best friend. In the game, you get to talk to her via chat. Whenever she says something, you can reply with one of 3 things given. This game has a sad tone to it, as you also get to witness the main character hiding his feelings and his love interest going down an arguably sh*tty path.
The game is very short and doesn't offer a lot. To fellow completionists: The game gives achievements for finding secrets.  Even without using a guide, this game is only ~40 minutes to get 100% in. Penarium is a pure platformer. No exploration, no shooting. Only moving and jumping.
What else is there? A self-contained level whose borders you can cross to find yourself on the other side, and traps. Tons of traps that cycle during the duration of the level. Machine-guns, homing missiles, bubble-gum to make the platforms sticky while a see-saw journeys across… The goal of the game is to collect items that spawn in the level while avoiding different sets of traps. Simple, and yet effective.
This game is exactly what I was looking for. I am quite sick of the ‘muscle memory’ platformers where you have to learn by heart at which point of the level you jump, the perfect trajectory to land between spikes, and so on. Penarium focuses on the moment-to-moment frantic experience. Quick skills are required instead of a good finger memory, and it is rather telling that less than 20% of the players completed the 1st world. Penarium is very difficult, and as it sports a “sadistic circus” theme, you would have to be a masochist to like it.
And yet I never found its difficulty to cross the “unfair” invisible line. The hitbox of the character is actually smaller than he looks. The movements are perfect, with double-jump and responsive controls without either the sliding momentum or the input delay that harm many platformers. The traps are more or less hard to avoid, but all can be predictable or give the player visual cues. But yeah, quick thinking and fast reflexes are mandatory. Oh, and I really appreciate that there is no timer adding an external pressure to the action. It is possible to either rush through the traps, or time them carefully.
So despite the high difficulty, moving like a madman and surviving amongst the chaos is exhilarating. It is fun. It does not feel like the game is punishing the player, because the action is constant and the threats come from everywhere while still being manageable. And the variety/movement of traps help make the game not feel repetitive. It can be finished in a few hours, and this type of game is not enjoyable if it gets much longer than that. To extend the fun, there is an endless mode with permanent progression.
To conclude, I was surprised to love this simple game so much more than the other hardcore platformers. I think it’s due to the good maneuverability, the difficult yet manageable design, and most of all the dynamic traps that require quick skills and provide a lot of fun by getting rid of the ‘muscle memory’ level design that usually goes with that kind of platformers.

Emile, the french man that will do anythig for his wife and country.

Game runs extremely well for me, constant 60fps with an i7 and 1070 max settings. On the hardest difficulty, when you die from basically one shot, the game is very enjoyable. However the franchise seems to have moved away from sniping to accomdate this "warrior" and "ghost" playstyle. In the first and second game you could get kills at 500m+. In SGW3 the game has been designed to decide when and where you can snipe from. Most enemy settlements are surrounded by terrain to prevent long shots. Even in areas where there is nothing between you and the enemy the game doesnt bother to render them in at around the 400m mark - even though some scopes can be set to 600m. This may be to accomodate the poorer hardware on the consoles but for the fact there isnt even an option to increase draw distance on PC is pretty dissapointing when you consider that the sniping system is actually really enjoyable.
If you are looking for a pure sniping experience I wouldnt recommend this game in particular. The reason I have given this a thumbs up is because some of the infiltration missions in the game are genuinly enjoyable and tense. I bought the game after reading good reviews about it and its sequel on GamingOnLinux, because I loved Raiden and to support a day 1 Linux game!
I finished it with my girlfriend 2 days ago.
She dislikes playing video games in general, especially ones that seem to take forever (to her), but enjoyed playing this one. She was on auto-fire, using the keyboard, so not having to worry about much and we were able to play together. The levels were not super long so she never felt stuck in something.
Playing as a ghost on level 5 was a good way for her to train (I have the card) ;) Let it be known that she joined after I had got to the 8th stage and got the plane mostly upgraded, so not starting on the beginning with the super weak base plane...
I showed her SFR and she looked forward to playing it if I were to buy it which I may.
As for me, I usually dislike grinding, but I enjoyed this game quite a bit. I finished it but will keep going after all achievements which I usually don't do, because it's feasible and fun enough. Having said that I do dislike the fact that the game is blocked until you have enough medals, ie enough achievements... It'll prevent bad players or people that just don't want to grind medals to move forward. I also dislike the fact that we have less missions than on Android, even though the 9th says that more should be coming after us.
The story is never explained, it would have been nicer to get a little more, or nothing at all, I don't get the point of what we get. The game also needs a way to remove upgrades, it's too boring to get all medals in the first stage after the plane is maxed out, but I also don't want to keep doing the same stage over and over before doing anything else.
The game is not for colorblind people, as sometimes it's a bit difficult to know what is coming at you, especially under clouds ;)
The game is also not very long, only 9 stages, each one being fairly short. Without grinding/going for medals, it would not take very long, and that's kind of a cheap way to build a game.
Overall, for a low price, I had a lot of fun, and was happy to share it with a non gamer. I will look at getting the sequel!

Yes, this game looks really pretty and if you just want to play it casually to have a bit of fun, that is, not trying to go for 100% completition, you will like it. However behind this pretty facade there are many problems lurking. And since this is a re-release of a game from 2004 this means that for over a decade the developers would have had time to fix all those issues but did not. Hence my negative rating.
The issues:
- The ship is slow, like really, really slow. In some levels it is simply impossible to travel along the rows of incoming enemies before at least some of them have left the screen again. This is not about avoiding enemy fire, its simply about being able to kill all enemies which proves impossible even with a fully upgraded ship. Such a design error could have been caught with only little playtesting before the release. This shows plain lazyness on the part of the developers.
- Related to above: No indication of the path the enemies will take. It is not possible to know in advance if an enemy is going to fly straight through the screen or if he will loop around a bit. This gameplay by trial and error belongs to the era of crappy SNES games, a real, genuine difficulty that requires skill would be much more appreciated.
- As with all bullet hell games, some enemies will fire pretty patterns of bullets. Your job is of course to skillfully navigate through it. Unfortunately this proves often impossible as there is simply not enough space between the salvos. I suspect that it is because the hitboxes of the ship and the bullets are slightly larger than they appear on screen. This means that either you get lucky by coincidentally being where the shot wont be or you lose your "untouchable" medal for that level. Again: lazyness because it would have been trivial to avoid this mistage
- Sudden Player death syndrome: Sometimes you suddenly die. No reason at all, your ship just goes boom. No bullet on screen, no enemies... I suspect a bug in the engine which does not correctly draw some enemies or bullets. Occasionally the engine will also lag, meaning that you will suddenly find your ship at a completely different position on screen.
- No mouse support: Yes, officially you can enable the mouse. Except moving the ship with the mouse reduces its speed by 80%. Again shoddy, design or programming is to blame for that. A simple sensitivity scaling would have been enough. This forces everyone to play with the arrow key (I am not even going to dignify the gamepad option here, this is not a console game!) which are extremely inaccurate.
I have written this after having reviewed Sky Force Reloaded, the successor of Sky Force Anniversary, many of the complaints are still present in "Reloaded". This really shows that there are fundamental issues with how the devs (do not) handle bugs and errors.

Insurgency is quite different from most other first person shooters. There is this sense of realism that other games don't quite capture. Insurgency does a great job when it comes to damage, from explosions to bullets. It's not like other games where you can get shot 7 times in the chest with an assault rifle. In this game, 1 or 2 shots with most guns would do the trick. Speaking of guns, there are interesting ways to customize them based on your role in the game. Although it does run on the source engine, the graphics aren't bad, as well as the look of the guns and animations are nice. To add to the realism, there's no kill feed (unless you're in specific servers). This is a great part of the game, as you need to be confident in your shots to truly know that you've killed your target. This factor adds a lot to the suspense of a close game, or even gameplay in general. Probably one of my favorite parts of the game is the ammunition display. There barely is one. Unless you are shooting a revolver or bolt action rifle, you have no clue how many rounds you have. It simply shows how many magazines you have remaining. This leaves the player to have to either guess or understand how much ammunition they have. The Sound of the guns is really nice, and the other sound effects such as explosions, bullets whizzing past your head, and getting shot even sound pretty accurate. The game itself requires tactical precision and coordination, especially in modes such as skirmish or competitive. The gameplay is enjoyable and usually competitive, with a mostly great community to play along with you. Speaking of community comes my final point. The community is a good one, with many workshop items available, from sound packs, different weapons, and character skins. I highly recommend that anyone looking to buy should totally purchase this game.

A fantastic game with excellent music and endearing squad humour. In my opinion it has also aged well.
You are Delta 38, leader of the 4-man Delta Team who are clone troopers with advanced equipment and medical implants, as well as more personality to help with creative thinking.
The gameplay mostly revolves around ordering your squad members into positions, which also tells them what weapons to use. Best of all your squad will actually do what you tell them to, even if it gets them taken out. Makes you wonder how Fallout 4 still can't fix companions standing in doorways!
Know that the first area (Geonosis) is the least fun, so stick with it. As you progress the game (slowly) gives you more options, as in there will be more positions than you have squad members, so you will have to make quick decisions while under fire. The pacing gets faster as well, both from more dangerous enemies and more heavy weapons available, but also thanks to good storytelling and use of the loud, epic music this game has.
There are good mods to fix common graphical issues/crashes and allow higher resolutions (I played it in 4K).
Unfortunately it ends on a cliffhanger as it sets up for a sequel that never came.
But yay, Wookie life-debts for everybody!

Very brief mention - this is a REVIEW. I hope people get the common ♥♥♥♥ing sense to write REVIEWS on these pages instead of little stories or cooking recipes. It and anybody who does that are completely pathetic.
Now, moving on...
I was a veteran of this game on the Xbox 360 - when I say veteran, I mean I recognize the sounds of each gun being shot from afar, even the suppressed weapons. I got lots of enjoyment out of it, and I couldn't help but "upgrade" to the PC version. I upgraded for several reasons:
1) I felt that more people played the PC version, since that's the target console of the series.
2) I was sure that the graphics would be improved on the PC.
3) I would be able to browse servers instead of just doing a mandatory quick match on the 360.
Within about half an hour I got all three of those points addressed.
1) There are FAR more people on the PC version as opposed to the Xbox 360. There aren't tons of full servers, but there are still a rather stunning number of people with taste in terms of Battlefield games.
2) The graphics. Holy CRAP. 60 fps without tweaking a single setting. Overwhelming lighting effects. Much larger and more detailed levels.
3) Server browsing is just as useful as I suspected it would be. There is a glitch, however, where when you start up the game and go under server browsing, there's an empty list - don't fret; the fix is to simply press "Search", and they all load in.
Now, in terms of gameplay; it's perfectly balanced and hectic gameplay that rewards players of all playstyles, both infantry and vehicular. It stays basic without falling to the crap that Battlefield 3 and Battlefield 4 brought to the table; there's none of that "lengthy reload on an empty magazine" BS; there's no suppression; you don't wake up from a nap after getting revived, only to get shot again; there's no vehicle healing or crippling; no crazy weapon attachments...
None of that crap is present here. If you want more of that, don't buy this game.
The singleplayer took a shot to the head in comparison to its predecessor (an Xbox 360/PS3 exclusive; I wish it were on the PC, too :,C), in the regard to how boring it was, and how fast you'll shoot through it. There's a video on YouTube (it should still be up) of somebody beating the campaign in just slightly over THREE HOURS. Enemies die in one or two shots, which renders all challenge moot, everything is scripted and hideously linear, and there's little to no point playing it. The four main characters just become dreadfully unlikable in the campaign; again, in stark opposition to the first game. With the sole exception of Battlefield: Bad Company (1), all BF games' strengths are in their multiplayer.
So do I recommend this game? YES. ABSOLUTELY. It was phenomonal on the Xbox 360, and it's equally as nice on the PC. It has better ease-of-access when it comes to finding matches, better graphics, and is just completely mindblowing.
And, of course, it has a massive Vietnam War expansion/conversion...

If you enjoy board games (not Monopoly or Risk, but real board games), you'll enjoy Armello. It reminds me a bit of a simplified Mage Knight (board game) or Runebound. It's addictive good fun, so long as you don't mind random elements like card draws and dice rolls. If you go into the game appreciating it for what it is, and not expecting every element to be skill based, you'll have a blast. I don't think it's fare to give the game negative reviews simply because you didn't know what it was going into it.
While there are random elements to the game you have no control over, there is still a large amount of strategy and skill. From hex movement and board control, to skillful usage of card playing and 'burning' cards in combat, to equipping your character before and during the game... there is a lot to it.
The animated 2D art is absolutely fantastic - the cards and the (too few) cut scenes are beautiful, the 3D board itself is fairly meh. The character designs are great (I'm especially fond of River's design and Sana's design), and their implimentation in 3D is the best aspect of the 3D elements of the game.
I would recommend the game to anyone that enjoys colourful art, doesn't mind spending an hour or an hour and a half playing a game based roughly 50/50 on skill and chance, and that likes board games.

Correct me if I am wrong, but the ADHD children of this age are not the target audience of this game. Based on the negative reviews shown to me, these are the kinds of people making a lot of the bad reviews. They seem hastily written by semi-illiterates used to the numerous, and very often poorly made, free games on Steam.
You can't really blame them for their opinions, though. It's a bit like how children who are used to eating only tasty fast food will prefer fast food over a nutritious, healthy meal. The problem is that they will always prefer this. They're used to a yearly CoD release with pretty graphics and mindless shooting, not puzzles, exploration and cooperation. This is why a game like Sven Co-op will never get the recognition that it deserves; poorly made but easier alternatives. Teaching yourself to digest something real requires motivation, of which said people have none, since there is a steady supply of junk always ready on their plates.
I'd call this a blessing in disguise, however. By not compromising with modern audiences, the developers have managed to stay true to the spirit of a now 17 year old game. They haven't sold out their game, and I am personally grateful for that. You see, this keeps away the stupid - the average 2016 consumer of video games - which keeps the game in its normal state, since nothing has to be dumbed down for a quick buck. For instance, I love that on every server I've played on, people are still capable of assisting each other. Firefights, puzzles and healing each other all comes naturally. This is not possible on an average server in a game like Team Fortress 2, and feels very unique to Sven Coop.
It's too bad that today, it seems you either have to make a great game that a few people might really like, or a horrible, generic piece of fast food that everyone will want to consume. It's truly fantastic to see the game finally reach Steam though. A group of people idealistic and interested enough to stick by a Half-Life 1 mod for 17 years is something very special. Someone like that is capable of great things, Sven-Coop being a prime example. They deserve a great deal of thanks for this mod. I am so glad to be playing it again after all these years.
I recommend this game to any patient lover of the fluid gameplay that the Half-Life 1 engine provides. The amazing and original map design also deserves mention. You will know how much of an understatement this when you play the game. Map series like ‘sc_tetris’, ‘They’ and good old ‘Toonrun’ spring to mind. I highly recommend that you try these, if you decide to test out the game.

Writing this for the Steam Nomination badge, so it isn't going to be a super in-depth review. But I seriously recommend Factorio, there is nothing quite like it. Try the demo, and if you like that, you'll probably not miss your $20.
The way I'd describe Factorio is that it is a puzzle or designing game with a mixture of city or RTS basebuilding mechanics and some tower defense type mechanics (optional). You have a set of tools that work in certain ways and you use those tools to design factory layouts that contribute to your factory's overall efficiency, or to make your factory look aesthetically pleasing. Or both. That's where the "puzzle" part comes in - you'll be asking yourself how you can arrange things to be more efficient and beautiful.
And that rabbit hole goes DEEP. Here's a rough example, there is an achievement for "finishing/winning" in 8 hours. The world record is finishing in about 2 hours. I have 500 hours of gameplay time, and I have not managed to be efficient enough to finish in 8 hours. Don't think I even have the "win in 15 hours" achievement. There is so much room for learning how to be more efficient and so many ways to layout your machines.
And if vanilla isn't complex enough, there is a healthy selection of mods. A set of 2 in particular (Bob's mods and Angel's mods) takes the vanilla complexity and doubles it. Or maybe triples or quadruples it, I don't know, I've only peeked at them. I can say that if Bobs/Angels was the base game, most people would probably be scared away before buying. :P
It isn't for those looking for a story, or those who need an endgame goal and want to "finish" the game. It's more about the journey, in that the fun part is figuring out designs/layout with all the various tools given to the player. And if you like a good puzzle and like building your RTS bases to be visually appealing, Factorio offers the deepest of that kind of gameplay. Nothing else quite compares in terms of the massive scale of Factorio.

I don't normally write reviews, but I felt I needed to write this one because the game design is so bad it's unforgivable.
I downloaded this game and tried to jump into playing it with another friend. We failed a simple mission a few times because we made some dumb mistakes, but the majority of the 10 times we died were due to small aliens that attached themselves to us and sucked our health away. I'm sure there was a way to kill them, (i can't imagine anyone putting a small hard to hit enemy that always kills you a few seconds after it touches you) but the game never had any prompt on screen to tell you how to prevent them from killing you. No helpful button presses, no information on how to deal with it. Just instant death if the smallest enemy in the game touched you.
Combine that with some average graphics and badly lit levels that were supposed to be "atmospheric" but just made it impossible to see, and there wasn't much reason to play beyond the first few failures. I'm guessing they also have a flashlight that allows you to see in the direction you're looking, but there wasn't any information on how to turn that on either. So combined with how easily you die, you also have enemies that are near impossible to see because sections of the level are simply dark.
Maybe I missed it, but a simple tutorial for the first time you entered a game would have gone a long way to making the game enjoyable. Maybe a simple menu that directed you to some helpful tips, or a message that popped up on screen when you died the same way. Anything that would have given me any knowledge of how to not keep dying from the same minor enemy would have kept me playing past the first few games.
I'm sure that this game could be fun, but the lack of feedback and information as you're playing makes it a game I can't reccomend.

Sky Force Anniversary is an amazingly inclusive shmup. I mean that because it has a steady progression system, and everyone no matter their skill level is always progressing to the next upgrade. Yeah, it is a little slow going at first, but once you add missiles the game gets a lot more fun.
It helps that the aesthetics are beautiful and recall shmups from the past while updating the graphics to a nearly stunning realization of old school and new school. The newly patched warmer colors make the game shine at its most potent. I play a lot of shmups, and while I'm not the best at them, I do enjoy the progression systems, the mentality of the gameplay, and the challenge they pose on different levels.
There are hard challenges to complete for every stage if you feel the need to go above and beyond the call. Each stage as its proper look and feel, and the bosses are fun. I find the upgrades and guns fairly straightforward. There is no real innovation here, but it's a great shmup to introduce people to the genre for sure, and it's throwbacks to old school design are welcome along with the splendid visual presentation.

is a 2D platformer with a very simple premise, surviving in an arena full of deadly traps, all designed to murder you in the most horrible ways. It is one of those games that made me go “Just one more”, despite the many times I fell victim to the treacherous traps.
You play as Willy, a boy who’s been bored of working every single day of his life in his father’s farm and who is craving for an adventure. Then, one day, a circus arrives in town and Willy feels an uncontrollable urge to be part of it. And so, lured by a mysterious man he is trapped inside a wagon and thrown into the circus floor. Willy must now beat every circus challenge in order to be free, he has to become the ultimate champion of Penarium.
The game features three different modes, multiplayer, campaign and arcade. I didn’t try multiplayer so I’m just going to skip that one. Campaign mode is divided into three different arenas, each arena having ten different challenges. Upon completing an arena, you’ll be able to play it on Arcade mode. Arcade mode is basically survival mode, you must survive for as long as possible while destroying barrels that spawn throughout the arena, while also collecting coins that you can then use to buy upgrades. Every 5 barrels you destroy, the traps will change. Both on Arcade and Campaign mode, the traps don’t have a specific order, they are random so you don’t know what to expect and must adapt everytime the traps change.
The traps itself are pretty diverse ranging from heat-seeking missiles, tesla coils, bees and various others. The game slowly introduces you to new types of traps, progressively increasing the difficulty.
The gameplay is pretty simple, each arena is composed of several platforms and you have to stay on top of those, if you fall you will die. On the other hand, when there is not some type of trap blocking your way, you can transition from one edge of the arena to the other and so do missiles, bullets, etc. This allows for some tricky manoeuvering while trying to complete each different challenge. Challenges require you to do various different things such as, pressing buttons in a predetermined order, destroying barrels or blowing up balloons.
You’ll probably die a lot in Penarium. It takes some trial and error in order to figure out how each trap works and how you can avoid it. That said, the game has a very lovely pixel art style and the cutscenes particularly are pretty well realized. The narrator also has a very cool voice and the music overall is very fitting for the the whole circus/fair theme.
Penarium was a blast to play. Despite the somewhat short length of the campaign, depending on how good you are, the Arcade mode is also pretty fun and allows for some replayability. The game is charming and pretty, extremely fun to play and there’s a huge amount of satisfaction everytime you beat one of those though levels. I avidly recommend it to every single fan of platformers!

This game has many bugs that went unfixed despite being made aware by many steam users- one of which prevented me from finishing this game for a while. If you don't think your computer is capable of running this game at 60 fps, I don't recommend buying it. But if you have a quality computer and some money burning a hole in your pocket, I deeply recommend Valiant Hearts: The Great War
It's difficult, in my opinion, to find a war game that is mostly unbiased or handles historic themes (accurate or not) with even a semblance of class. Despite the gore, this is a game I would feel comfortable letting a young teen play. The messages are deep and plentiful. The game succeeds at telling the story of war without extreme amounts of demonization. It shows that the soldiers, officers, workers, women and children of war all share a common goal.. to live happily. People in all walks of life are shown struggling in a system that leaves little choice for comfort or morality.
Valiant Hearts is filled with mostly puzzles that require finding the correct order of events or time-based. They are slightly challanging, but far from difficult. Although I think the method of telling stories out of timely order is strange, by the end of the game you feel connected to the characters and have come to understand how they all came together. The collectables are all actually very interesting... I found myself wanting them simply for the sake of knowledge. God knows I didn't want them for the ubisort achievements...
You are presented with characters, and once you become attatched to them, you desire to learn about their world. I never enjoyed history back in school... But now, I "know" people who have experienced the war, and feel inspired to understand their actions and emotions.
Valiant Hearts: The Great War is an emotional journey that I encourage you to take.

Valiant Hearts is an emotional, well crafted puzzler adventure game set in World War 1. There are point and click puzzles, dodging games, a rhythm game while doing first aid, puzzles involving swapping between your character and your dog (who can fit in fox holes, distract soldiers, fetch items and pull levers), and actual historical facts mixed into a solid plot. You play as four different people and a war dog. You'll be digging trenches, ducking mortars, escaping from behind enemy lines, impersonating officers, blowing up a zepplin, pulling wounded men from piles of bodies just to see them shot down, and taking cover from machine gun nests behind those same piles of bodies. Despite the stylized cartoon art, the game manages to connect on an emotional level, at least it did for me.
The simple mechanics are used in interesting ways. In my favorite segment you are driving an escape car and must dodge mortar fire, TNT barrels, road blocks, strafing machine guns, grenades and ramming attacks by the giant tank chasing you long enough that its driver gets impatient and opens the hatch to throw nades (leaving it open for YOU to throw a grenade into the tank). AND you do all this synchronized to beautiful classical music! (Flight of the Bumble Bee.) The music in this game is wonderful.
The main downside is UPlay, but it didn't get in my way much. Opening in Steam directly opened the game and UPlay was minimized.
There is genuine emotion in this game, you can tell the developers cared and treated World War 1 with as much respect as they could in a video game about it. They included artifacts with detailed descriptions for you to find, letters from soldiers you may read, they based levels on actual events in the Great War, and short factual write ups on aspects of the war for each level. One of those write ups includes the fact that chlorine gas bombs killed men by burning when exposed to water, so the insides of unprotected soldier's lungs burned and blistered until they died in agony, and one of the remedies the men came up with was breathing through urine soaked rags. Horrible stuff but this developer didn't shy from it, war is hell.
It's a perfect game for history buffs, indie and adventure gamers, and people who love dogs. It has some moderate challenge, but isn't a hardcore type of game, I finished it in 6 hours and my reflexes aren't great.
8/10

On the other hand, the project may have been more than the devs could chew. The game blatantly markets itself as a parody of retro gaming, for better and for worse. Some kids grew up with hundreds of other mascot platformers. I, along with many others, had TY the Tasmanian Tiger as my entry into 3D platforming games. Aside from my nostalgia, the game has remained competent if nothing else. Time has been generous to TY by how a once oversaturated market of 3D platformers feels refreshing nowadays by its scarcity.
However, let's be honest about TY: You won't find anything groundbreaking if you've played plenty of Collect-A-Thons before, and if you haven't played TY since the GC days then you'll probably find a lot more problems than you would as a kid.
It's the style (both artistic and musical) are what transform the mediocrity of TY's substance into a platforming zen-like experience. Nothing brutal for challenge, yet nothing too dull to bore you. That is what might interest new players who are curious to give the game a try.
True to their word, KROME studios has managed to launch two Ty games so far with all content available since launch with performance boosts and quality-of-life fix-ups to make these games fit for the PC. The main difference between the console versions and the PC is the performance boost and "remastered" (not remake) visuals. Wide-screen support (no black-bar boxes), improved textures, shadows and other visual details and the 60 FPS change are what the PC port offers, and if this system of bringing old games to Steam for modern audiences has shown anything that even finished games can be done better on PC as a result of an early-access system with competent developers.
TY 2 is currently available on Early Access with the same plan of a few months of polish and optimization to bring it up to par with TY 1, and Ty 3 will also follow this plan once Ty 2 is complete. It’s a shame there is no bundle option to buy all three as of right now for fans to make the most of these games while in development, but hopefully with the launch of Ty 3 there will be a series sale to help bring Ty back from obscurity with a new fanbase borne from the goodwill of these ports.
As another Collect-A-Thon, TY derives a lot more from what worked in the past rather than innovate the genre. This works to the game's favor as it avoids forcing you to play everything. You explore nine levels from various locals to collect a general collectable for progress. Each level contains 8 Thundereggs--5 are level-specific objectives, one time-trial challenge, one collect 300 Objects goal and collect 5 caged friends--and you'll need 17 to advance to next area of the HUB.
The benefit of this system that Mario 64 capitalized on was if you don't happen to like one type of side-objective you can avoid doing them so long as you collect enough tokens for progression. (You only need to collect 5 or 6 in each stage to get by.) This is especially useful if you hate collecting 300 Opals in some of the more larger areas that can result in wandering aimlessly for a meaningless reward.
Another reward for exploration outside of the Thundereggs are Golden Cogs. Collecting 17 of them will reward the player with a non-essential boomerang to your arsenal, which tends to be combat-focused. Some of which are so absurdly over-powered they become amusing distractions to break up the monotony of fire, ice and shock boomerangs such as the Kaboomerang.
However, if you are the type of person who enjoys going for 100%, however, Ty suffers the genre’s issue for scavenging for the last remaining collectable that Yooka Laylee has addressed. It’s difficult to suggest the amount of content available in games like this but if you go as a completionist you'll get a dozen hours minimum. If you go for only the Thundereggs as well as the Golden Cogs to progress the storyline, then you'll get 7 to 10 hours worth of content.
After playing Ty 1 and Ty 2, which I never had the chance to play the sequels, it’s a shame how these games squander the potential for more skilled gameplay of TY 1 for a unique platformer experience. It’s easy to dismiss this issue because these games were intended for a younger audience; however, if the appeal of complexity behind Minecraft and survival games shows anything kids enjoy overcoming adversity in games that treats them with respect as an adult rather than being treated as children.
The biggest disappointment of TY is the rang-system. Similar to the issues I found in TY 4, the variety of rangs are either superfluous in combat as visual differences or the essential rangs are used in one or two instances with no complexity or ingenuity beyond their limited scope. Shock rangs can only work on generators; fire rangs can only burn ice and wood; ice rangs can be used to freeze fire or the water. This last one showcases the potential of a unique tool as it can be thrown on water to create infinite platforms, and this mechanic is used ONCE in the entire game. Had they utilized all the rangs for unique platforming challenges and obstacles, the variety in Ty 1 (as well as Ty 2) would improve the overall experience to make Ty a more versatile character.
Instead of exploring the possibilities of Ty’s boomerangs, the game rather stays within the scope of his mobile abilities for basic platforming, gliding and swimming challenges. On top of these limited challenges, the game also adds a “spirit” form that serves no purpose in the puzzles or challenges other than making combat even more simple to overcome, which could have utilized Ty’s arsenal to a greater effect than making a needless mechanic that will rarely ever seen any usage by the player. Ty 2 also weirdly stuck with this idea with the BunYips, the Australian equivalent of those mini Metal Gears from MGSV (D-Walker) with their own abilities to expand upon Ty’s arsenal, sometimes to the detriment of the platformer focused gameplay of the original.
Exploring these ideas is not for the personal clout of an arm-chair critic, rather to illustrate how if KROME studios wants to bring back this series they’ll have to adapt these games in the future with the expectations of their audience. Whether they are kids or adults, the potential of Ty to engage with audiences has always been apparent in Ty 1 but never seized its opportunity to stand out in future sequels; instead, the focus has been on how to remove more of its platforming roots with each game when the focus should be on expanding them with the mechanics they have already established. As I mentioned in Ty 4, the possibilities of the rang-system for more creative means of exploration and skill-level has always been the one misused opportunity of Ty, and I think if KROME wants to step-up their game they will have to examine the strengths of each game they are revitalizing to learn from their legacy’s mistakes and to create new ideas for a sequel.

This review is not about Uplay. This review is not about Ubisoft. This review is about the game.
If there was any game from Ubisoft that would counter the argument laid out by Roger Ebert of the Chicago Sun Times, it would be this game. Not only is it art, it's reality. It's history.
This game must be played by all. This game requires you to stop being stubborn/ignorant/childish and accept the realities of this world. War, no matter how it's played out on TV, the news, movies, books, or history can truly reflect it's dehumanizing nature. Pitting people against each other for some imaginary maluable lines that were created by the powerful hundreds/thousands of years ago to keep people in check.
This game is about emotion. It's about puzzles. It's not too hard, yet it's not too simple. If you want to find everything it'll require much more dedication and time from you. If you just want to play the story it'll take about 8-10 hours.
I was always wondering what everyone was talking about with the emotions. And then the end hits you. Even if you can't keep the story straight, or who each character is and what each character does. Once the ending hits, it doesn't matter. You see the reality of war and the toll it has on real, living, breathing people who have friends, family, children, brothers, and sisters.
If you read this far into my review, you're probably not going to be one of those people who is an ignorant Call of Duty player.
I implore you, even if you don't care about finding objects (which I enjoyed because it provided insight into what life was like back then -- each object is something that soldiers used on the field), buy this game, and more importantly finish it. If you really rush, it can easily be completed in five hours. Two weeks max if you put your mind to it and say, 30 minutes every other day.

Ubisoft developed a kind and wise puzzle adventure game which gives you an opportunity to live through the war and look at it from 4 points in a few hours. Maybe it is not perfect, but still touching. The plot, the beautiful soundtrack, all those characters... This is the story about people. About love. Friendship. Honor. Life.
"..Our time on Earth is brief.."
This Is One Masterpiece You can't refuse, trust me. I'ts now In My top 10 Of All time.Buy It And Be Blown away,Atmosphere,story,and game play.

I had a lot of fun with this game.  More than I expected actually.  It just plays so differently from anything I have played in a long time and it really hit the spot for me.  It is pretty similar to the original Syndicate games, if you are familiar with those.  You control 4 agents which can be cloned, gain skills and enhance themselves with cyber and gear.  The story takes place in a single, large city, with various districts that unlock as you complete missions.  Missions can be completed in different ways, based on the path you take, your agents skills and any special perks you unlocked (like convincing someone to open the front door for example).  Gameplay is full real-time, which honestly isn't ideal for me, but doesn't knock the game down that much.  A pause feature would definitely have been a plus.  I often found myself splitting up my agents, having my stealthy and hacking specialists opening the way for the more combat focused partners.  It can definitely be a bit challenging controlling all 4 at once, all doing different things.  Other than that, no real complaints, other than a couple of minor bugs which didn't stop me from finishing the game and are probably fixed by now.

You are compromised! Enemies spotted your Soldier trying to hardwire an automatic door, and are rushing to cover while firing assault rifles wildly. Your Support and Hacker are caught flat-footed in the open, leaving you to order them into cover to return fire. You activate your Hacker's attack drones to give you an edge, and watch in glee as quad-rotor robots fly up to blast your attackers with energy bolts of sapphire death.
Now the alarm status has gone up. The pressured guards radio for backup, alarm klaxons blare throughout the compound, and you hear rushed combat chatter and the sound of cargo doors sliding open. Your Infiltrator spots another group of much tougher guards on the approach and, desperate to buy time, you have her take a sniper shot.
Their officer is knocked on his♥♥♥♥♥by a kinetic impactor round, stunning him. While his fellows sprint to cover and start returning fire, your Soldier has now managed to open the door -- but now you realize that your Infiltrator is too far away to rejoin the group in time. You frantically order your Hacker and Support through, to cover your Soldier from the other end while he locks the door behind him to deter pursuit, even though they've taken quite a few scratches themselves from the brief firefight.
But by now, you've been made. The alert goes up even further as your corporate mercenary enemies realize they're dealing with individuals who are heavily armed and extremely dangerous. Desperate to protect company secrets, they authorize the use of extreme force, and soon you hear the sound of a bipedal mechanized unit stomping towards you from the other end of the base.
Will you get your Infiltrator to safety in time? Perhaps you could have her zipline over open space and use her cloaking device, bringing her close enough to stealthily pick off a few enemies with melee assassination strikes. Did you bring enough firepower to deal with this operation, though? Should you hide and wait for a more opportune time? Do you exhaust your supply of frag grenades to blast a way to your objective? What are you going to do about your Support operative's low health???
Choices. Satellite Reign is all about choices, and making them under extreme duress, because this is a tactical squad-based RPG that does not have a mid-battle pause button. The closest you will ever get is time dilation (slowdown), and that's from one of your Support operative's skills, so you'd better keep his Energy level high enough to use it! What I love about this game is that everything can go to hell in the blink of an eye, so now you actually HAVE to be smart and plan your movements carefully. You are up against superior numbers, and sometimes superior firepower. This game rewards you for being quick to think and quicker to act, and punishes you for getting caught with your agents out of cover or for having no backup plan.
Satellite Reign now has multiplayer co-op that is in open beta (as of the date of this review), which allows different players to take control of any number of the four agents available for play in a given game session. This gives it some solid extra replayability, I think.
Is the game worth it to buy? Well, it will likely take you around 30 hours to beat, less if you already know what you're doing. I think that the rewards from playing smart and successfully passing the tests of quick planning and execution that the game throws at you are well worth it; in fact, some of the best experiences in any tactical game I've played since the new XCOM: Enemy Unknown series. Satellite Reign can get a little repetitive late-game, though, I'll admit, and stealth is a little... too powerful, especially once you can afford to get every agent a cloaking device. But yes, I'd say Satellite Reign is very worth it, with or without a sale discount.

Ah, WATERSHIP SMACKDOWN. Play it solo and it's like a relaxing game of furry chess. Play it in mulltiplayer, up your chances of getting neato dice skins even if you lose the match! I call that win-win.
I'm probably a weirdo, but I really enjoyed playing single player matches against the AI when I was beginning, just to figure out all the systems and such. Once I got a handle on things, I went multiplayer and saw how to really put the screws to my fellow players. Sometimes I even win!
The variety of characters also keeps the game from getting stale. Right now I'm really enjoying carrying around ridiculously huge hands of cards as Mercurio--but some months ago, I enjoyed being the undefeatable wolf fighter Thane. Lotsa different tactics here.
The devs do a lot to keep it fresh, too--I haven't yet paid for any DLC (though I plan to--Hello, Sargon.), but new cards, systems, and character chat have all been added for free--and those changes are enough to keep me coming back.
Do I have to mention that it's one of the best looking games around? The beautifully painted animated cards are great, the UI is lush, and battles look way cooler than rolling dice has any right to be.
It's not a fast-paced game (although if you're quick on the draw--or roll--you can help make it be!), but its atmosphere and variety are worth signing up for.

On the surface, Armello is what the boardgaming community classify as an ameritrash. There's nothing wrong with that. Some of my absolute favourite game is an ameritrash, it just means that the game favour theme and the experience resulted in said theme and a good amount of randomness over a thinky robust mechanic commonly found in a eurogame.
Not that Armello is lacking in the gameplay departement. I personally think it's quite fun. There are several characters you can choose from with unique abilities and stats that play very differently to each other. During the course of the game you explore the land to finish a quest, improve yourself with various power and weapon, harass your opponent, or work toward a victory.
The rounds are finite and it's a race against the others. Every single move counts and a mistake can set you back significantly. There are multiple path to victory that's a little bit confusing at first but once you fully understood it you'll soon realize that being the strongest in the land may help, but it's not necessary to win.
As you can see in the screenshot and video, the visual are amazing. it may not have the best fidelity, but the work the art department did was quality. You might miss it in the screenshot or video, but some of the cards are animated. A little touch that makes the already beautiful game more pleasing in to play. That is if you're into art.
A downside of the game, much like any other game in ameritrash category is the randomness. Sometime you love the dice, sometime you wish nobody invented one. The game can overstay our welcome sometime, dragging for quite a while if nobody plays well.
All in all, despite the downside, I'm still in the opinion that the game is worth your money and your time. A thumbs up!

Armello is a visually beautiful, tightly designed, quick-to-play adventure. I tend to play by myself, but multiplayer is functional and offers a bit of a different experience. I love this game.
It's rare to find a game that packs so much, narratively and in terms of interesting mechanics, into a 90-minute session. All of Armello's characters are quite different from each other, and there's a lot of variety in how you set up your character to start. Once the game begins, though, it's time to be flexible, because with dice fights and card draws, you've got to enjoy rolling with the punches. I disagree with the reviewer who said that everything is determined in the first few turns -- things can, and do, change suddenly. If you want to set things up perfectly and then have them go exactly according to plan, you'll be thwarted.
Armello is well worth the money, and so is the expansion. It's fun, thrilling, sometimes heartbreaking, and just technically really well done. The studio crossed their t's and it shows, and I hope they continue expanding it in the future. I would definitely throw down cash for an RPG set in the same world.

Have you ever felt your life is boring, have you ever wanted some big change? Willy, the farmer's overweight kid, wanted. Farmer's work wasn't exciting at all for him, so when he met a suspicious guy with a mask who offered him a ride in his wagon, he wanted to have an amazing journey for a day. But, oh boy, he was stupid. The masked guy locked up Willy until they arrived to the sadistic circus, Penarium. And now it's up to you - can you survive in control of Willy?
Penarium is a platformer with priority on difficulty and simple controls - all you can do is running and (double) jumping. You are thrown into the circus arena where you have to do specific tasks (break barrels, burst balloons or push buttons in specific order) while dodging deadly traps. There are no lives nor checkpoints, you just have to do your best or... try again.
What I've really liked on Penarium is the whole pixelart graphics style with cool animation work. There isn't much environment variety (only 3 circus arenas) but there is fair amount of traps that can make every level a little different (well, from what I've seen, only the order of traps is random, but that's still something if you're dying often). Also, the game has pretty good soundtrack with circus melodies that can extend your hate towards circus and clowns, especially because of the overall higher difficulty the game has.
I've already broached the subject of length with low amount of environment variety and, well, that's the biggest downside of Penarium. There are only 30 levels (challenges) that can be done in pretty short time, depending on your skill and experience with platformers. To those who want more, there is an arcade mode where you also collect coins to get bonuses for that mode. If you have a friend to play with, there are also co-op and versus modes. But I guess that's not enough to those who expect some sort of main campaign with stable unlocking of game's content.
Penarium is a nice difficult platformer, with polished design and fluid gameplay. If you don't mind its shorter length, or you want another game to play with a friend on local multiplayer, it's definitely worth buying.
