-It's a good idea to get really familiar with one class, its nice to work with people who specialize as a medic or tech as they really make a huge difference in how a mission can go. Support is great but you only need so much. As a support I personally usually cover the back with the minigun while the soldier leads the pack. the medic and tech stay int he middle as they are the softest.
and last but not least
-Watch your friendly fire!!
Anyway best of luck in your hunt. I'll see you out there sometime Space Marine!!

Didn't know what to expect when I got this game, but was totally smitten by its premise. Set in a dystopian future where the city is run by greedy, unscrupulous, amoral megacorporations. You emerge as a rival corporation set to bringing down the big bad megecorp that has the monopoly on Immortality.
You start off small and you need to build up your resources by infiltrating and stealing from other rival corporations. Weapons, Cybernetic implants, Money, Gear are all up for grabs as you build up to prepare for the final showdown.
It is an open-world environment where you extend your will through your four agents. Each are a different class with their own special functions to help you go about waging corporate espionage. Most jobs have more than a few ways of going about, from guns blazing thru the front door to softly softly approach via zipline. You can customise the weapons, gear and implants to further whichever playstyle mix you choose. I say mix because you're going to need to be able to switch between going Loud and Quiet when things don't go your way.
It takes a bit of getting used to for figuring our stealth and combat. There aren't any visual representation for line of sight so you'll have to be patient to get the feel for what the enemies can see and which cover will hide you from them. Otherwise knowing directional cover, using flanks, silent takedowns, agent abilities are keys to waging effective corporate warfare.
Game is not without its imperfections however. AI can sometimes do stupid things at times. An Infiltrator with silenced sniper rifles screwing with patrols till they are all picked off without sounding alarm for backup is an example of the limitations of the AI. Your agents and enemies sometimes get stuck in the environment on rare occasions, forcing a suicide for affected agent. When alerted, enemies seem to develope eyes on the back of their heads to catch your agents going the other way while ignoring the big obvious distraction you've set up.
But overall this game should keep you entertained for at least 40 hours depending on pace. But if you want a teamplay element added to the mix or you find it too hard to manage 4 agents all at once in realtime, there is a co op feature where you can have up to 3 other friends control an agent each, tho i find it easier just playing with one other player and just controlling 2 agents.

the game is supposed to be a spiritual successor to the PS1 game Syndicate and Syndicate Wars and i feel this game is that. It's a 3rd person, Isometric, cover based shooter, in where your team of humans, over the course of the game, end up turning into cyborgs and where you go from ballistic ammo to lasers to plasma weapons.
The game plays very well in regards to commands and path finding, i've come across a few issues where my team thought that running through a poisoned area into a locked a door was a faster method than going around the building but over all, pretty solid.
The team is split up into 4 members: the solider, the support, the hacker, and the infiltrator. The solider can carry heavy weapons, has the most hp and gets skills of doing more damage, taking less damage, and getting aggro. the support can scan the world showing where wires lead (so you can disable doors or cameras), scan civilian and enemy stats, locate targets for missions, etc. He is also the medic and has skills to raise the party's HP, Energy, and regens for both. The Hacker can hack into doors and cameras allowing your team to get into areas, can hack ATMs for you to get money, and can hijack (mind control) civilians and baddies alike (as well as drones). he also gets skills to summon a few drones of his own. The Infiltrator is your melee/sniper, he can access high to reach places and has a personal cloaking device.
The game is an open world game where after doing missions, you can buy upgrades for your team but for every successful mission, the baddies also improve their gear. It's because of this, i find the game to suffer a bit though, because the game doesn't stop. If you're in enemy territory, the alarms get raised and an infinite amount of baddies spawn thus making running and gunning a really bad idea. as (for all, most) missions require you to run into these territories and infiltrate a building, the sniper (with this cloaking) turns into the most over powered class of the game...really fast. most missions are normally him running through the area while the rest of the team hide somewhere.
Combat is real time and if you turned on the option of pause (default to D key....) time slows down enough for you to issue specif orders to your team. however, they also give you the assassinate ability which allows you to one shot anyone making the starting pistol the best weapon of the game. The weapons you get are all highly fun to use, but as stated earlier, if you're going to run in guns blazing, expect to die.
Overall, i'd easily give this game an 8.5 - 9. it has some issues but is still pretty solid

This is an incredible game that the author never bothered to write a manual for, and left out too much in the tutorial.  You must read the manual guide first.
I played the original Syndicate all the way through around the time it came out.  This is a worthy and much improved successor.  It adds a lot of elements that the original game didn't have, and has much better gameplay and a lot more depth.  Also, the fan provided steam controller profile works well, this is a good game for a steam controller.
The combat feels great, and so does the preparation and stealth.  It isn't too easy like the original Syndicate.  In the original, you could just stand there with miniguns and kill all comers without much thought or difficulty if you did a little bit of prepositioning.  This one requires a little more thought and tactical awareness, and makes stealth effective, while still leaving Rambo style invasions viable.  It reminds me of Deus Ex, in that there are many ways to do the same objective, which I love.
The load time when you first start the game is really slow, but don't let it put you off.  The way the game is designed you shouldn't need to load the game unless you just started it up, even if you die, so it isn't really a problem during play sessions.  The game will not punish you significantly for dying as long as you do not use prototypes in combat.  The cloning decay mechanic on death is quite gradual, and does not go below 0.  The tutorial left me thinking that I had to load or I would be kneecapped - but that is totally unecessary.
READ THE GUIDE WITH THE FANMADE MANUAL FIRST!
Read the guide that is a fanmade manual for the game before you start.  The tutorial misses important gameplay elements and is a bit buggy, sometimes repeating parts when you load unnecessarily.  Retreating to the beacons lowers your alert level more quickly, and the game needs to tell the user this, but does not.  It's really important.
10/10

Bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s! All of them!
How could they!? HOW COULD THEY!?
Willy’s just a poor and chubby farmer boy who’s just bored so he joined this big and fun looking Circus … only to find out … to find out …!
Read on if you want to know what this game’s all about.
The game’s about the hero, the legend, the man himself … Willy!
Just a lil’, poor and chubby farmer boy who’s just bored out of his mind. He’s living all alone with his father since Willy’s his only child. One of these days there appears something magnificent.
A Circus! Seeing all the fun he could had Willy decides to approach the Circus and is greeted by the Director which offers him a position in his Circus and invites him to a wagon. Right after Willy boards said wagon they take off leaving his poor and old father behind and Willy’s now supposed to entertain the crowd in the
Oh and it’s a sadistic one.
You’re supposed to entertain the crowd Kiddo. So that means dance! Dance Willy, dance! Or die!
Both are fine since that’s what the crowd wants to see!
Well, well, well … The game takes place inside a circus, duh. Not just a circus … the circus extravaganza PENARIUM! And the crowd goes wild! That’s probably because someone died again. Oh well onto the actual gameplay!
You start of inside a cage and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a Director gives you orders. That can be to smash 20 Barrels or to fetch his Body Lot- errr I mean his
. Ultimately that would sound rather boring so why not put up some Death-Traps? Yup. You’re supposed to do a bunch of tasks while avoiding those pesky traps in order to survive. Sounds more interesting doesn’t it?
And the game’s full of those darn traps let me tell you that.
There’s a machine moving on the top of the screen and dropping a big ball every now and then in order to kill you, or there’s another one shooting icicles trying to give you a
, oh and hey also pierce through the stage so beware of the pointy bits!
Hell there’s even a giant Death Laser moving around the map relatively fast in order to annihilate you! And for what!? Just to entertain some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s … Sigh.
But the one trap that annoys me the most are those birds … God I hate those birds. They’re just flying around grabbing those barrels you have to smash. So that means you have to chase them, while avoiding all the other traps and death of course.
But the Director wouldn’t be the Director if he’d only tell you to smash some barrels no.
You also have to step on some buttons in the right order to survive the stage. And if you fail to do so then you can start all over again. However … if you manage to survive a bunch of stages you’ll be rewarded! Yes rewarded! You get ballons! I mean which child doesn’t like ballons?
To be specific …
Yup everything in this Circus is to entertain the crowd. You have to collect the ballons in a specific order and in timely fashion or else you’re not gonna see tomorrow.
The only thing that you can do in this game is run and jump.
Here’s the good news. You can jump out of the screen, unless there’s a trap set up, so you will end up on the opposite side of the level. Neat ain’t it?
Alright and here’s the bad news. All those traps can do exactly the same. Be it rockets, giant balls, lasers or whatever. You all are allowed to do that which at the end of the day will save your behind more often then it would kill you, let me tell you that.
Quite charming. Really shows Willy from his best side!
Let’s be serious for a while. The art style’s well chosen. Here’s the thing. The game’s pretty harsh and needless to say sadistic. Playing such a game in 3D would be a lot … how do I put it .. well worse and more serious. Choosing this art style though makes it very clear that it’s not be taken serious. It’s meant to be fun. I mean not dying is fun right? And listening to a big ol’ ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a Director with the mouth of an idiot is fun as well right?
Well the character’s are looking good and so do the stages. Oh and the traps yes of course. They look good. They look even better when you survive them!
I don’t know about you but this art style gives the game a very unique personality and to be quite honest with you it’s thanks to that, that I do enjoy the game tremendously!
The music manages to stay in the background. Which isn’t always a good thing but this time it is.
The sound effects on the other hand like the explosions … Well you hear them. That’s a good thing. Even better is that they do actually sound nice.
Overall it’s quite fitting and it’s also thanks to the music that there’s no pressure on you. It somehow manages to put one into this comical and dark mood at times, also thanks to the dialogues, so you end up enjoying every death.
The real charm is in the dialogues though. I found myself looking forward to what the Director had to say this time. I mean when he told me I had to go and fetch his Body Lotion ... yes it's body Lotion and not dark magic voodoo potions of death or whatever! Anyway I really enjoyed those dialogues.
It's stuff like that, which make a game rather unique and fun. I mean there's not really that much text but the tiny bit of text truly makes a difference.

Penarium is a pleasant surprise. Bursting with personality, this arena-based arcade game is simple to look at, but a ton of fun to play.
Seriously, you need to check this one out!

Welcome to the crazy Circus: Penarium. The game is a platformer, where you try to survive different levels that increase in difficulty as the circus throws more and more traps and obstacles at you. The platforming gets pretty hard fast. Check out my first impressions video here:
Lovely game. Graet spooky circus vibe. Simple but addictive gameplay. Couldn't get enough of it. Some of the levels are hard but fair. Can't not play. Recommended!

In Penarium you play as a boy named Willy. When you decide to join the circus you quickly find out that this is no normal circus as you are thrust into an arena where your life is always at risk.
Penarium includes two different game modes.
The campaign teaches you the mechanics of the game and provides different challenges that you must complete. The campaign is kind of short since it will probably only take around 3-4 hours to complete.
The arcade mode lets you try to survive as long as possible while collecting/smashing barrels. You can collect coins that you use to purchase upgrades to help you on future attempts. The objective of the arcade mode is to survive as long as possible while smashing as many barrels as possible.
Overall I had fun with Penarium. Outside of the theme though Penarium is not a highly original platformer. The game doesn't really add any new mechanics and will feel familiar to people who play a lot of platformers.
Difficulty wise I would say that Penarium is medium-hard to hard. You will die a lot but the game is not as difficult as some of the other "hard" platformers.
If you like hard platformers and you think the theme/concept is interesting I think you would like Penarium and you should pick it up.
Note: I received a free review copy of Penarium.

This game is very challenging, and a LOT of fun. I got the 50 deaths achievement within 40 minutes of play, but never once felt frustrated or that the game was unfair. The gameplay is deceptively simple: all you do is jump between platforms. However, the different level goals, and the absurd amount of continuously changing trap combinations, force you to keep an eye on the entire screen and always keep you on your toes.
The campaign appears to be somewhat short, i seem to be over halfway through it within an hour of play, though your mileage may vary. Personally i feel that i got my money's worth, but you may want to keep that in mind. There is also an endless survival mode and a local multiplayer mode which further extend the game.
I love everything about the game so far, from the gameplay, to the art, to the music, to the setting, and definitely recommend it.
Fun game, nice art, great music and lots of fun playing the story line.

You know that face you make when your playing an extremely difficult game and your trying to concentrate as hard as possible to not die? Well that's what Penarium does to me. Penarium is a rage-inducingly difficult platformer survival game where you will always feel determined to be able to complete the next level how ever many deaths it takes.
In penarium you control a boy called Willy. He strives to become a top circus performer. His wish comes true when a travelling circus man comes and introduces himself to him. However it's not as he expected. Willy is sent to entertain a crowd of bloodthirsty sadistic people. His goal is to survive in increasingly difficult circus stadiums while being attacked by various different traps. Definitely not an easy task.
That is the main premise of Penarium. You are basically in a small arena that is filled with various traps. You can jump across platforms to avoid these traps. Within these rooms you have different tasks to complete. This can be something as simple as collecting barrels or something difficult like having to stay in a moving spotlight for the allocated amount of time. There was a suprising amount of variety in these different tasks and I didn't find myself getting bored of them at all. My favourite of the tasks was basically a "simon says" where you have to copy the pattern of pressed buttons in the correct order.
While doing these tasks the traps will change frequently giving you different things to avoid. This keeps the gameplay a challenge and means you can't learn the patterns to make it too easy. The traps you are given are semi-random as well as the patterns they move in. Some levels have a scripted set of traps and others are completely random. There is also a fantastic variety in the types of traps. Each are unique in their own way. They include traps like homing missiles, electric cannons, moving lasers and birds that fly away with the barrels. They each require very different strategies to avoid them and so change up the gameplay for you constantly.
Penarium has 3 different gamemodes. Within the campaign mode you get all of these different modes that I described above. They are organized into levels of increasing difficulty. There isn't a huge of levels in the game being only 30 levels total. However with the insane difficulty that I mentioned earlier they will take a long time to complete each. I estimate i've probably spent around 4 hours on the campaign so far and gotten to level 23.
It then has the arcade mode. This is a pure survival mode. It uses the barrel gamemode. You have to collect as many barrels  as possible. It is unlimited and completely random. Attached to this gamemode is a leaderboard so that you can compete against your friends to collect the most barrels possible. This is a nice additional feature because the gamemode would be incomplete without it.
The final gamemode is multiplayer. This is split into 2 submodes which are versus and co-op. This is probably where I had my most fun playing. In versus mode you compete with the other player to click each button that spawns first. You also have the added ability to jump on the other persons head and knock them out for a short period. I had a huge amount of fun in this mode. Then you have co-op. In this mode each of you has a different button to press and you have to stand on them at the same time. Again it is a survival mode and you have to try and do it for as long as possible. There is also a leaderboard attached to this. Unfortunately multiplayer is only local though and can only be enjoyed by a maximum of two people. I would have liked to at least see online multiplayer implemented.
Within the arcade mode you also have a store. This can be used to purchase upgrades that can be used to help you survive longer. I haven't had much of a chance to test this but I thought it was worth mentioning. However i'm not a big fan of this system and would prefer just a straight up survival with no additional benefits.
Penarium itself also has a certain charm to it. The graphics style is designed in a striking pixel art fashion which I absolutely adore. Arenas could very easily be bland and static but they have so much variety to them graphically. The backgrounds are even full of activity and animations that make the world seem very much alive. Penariums cutscenes also have a wonderful charm to them. The voiceover is mesmerizingly good and really sets you in the mood of the game. A wonderful circus soundtrack also helps to build this atmosphere. The only issue I do have with the soundrack is that it can get very repetitive after a while because it doesn't have enough variety.
Overall if you love difficult games and are a fan of platformers then Penarium is definitely a game for you. The developer has gone all out to create an experience full of variety and a beatifully styled world with a unique charm to it. However if you don't like difficult games then you can safely avoid Penarium as it definitely isn't a game for you. But if you do I think the price of £6.99 is more than reasonable for the insane amount of fun you will get.
Disclaimer: I was provided with a free early review key by the developer to make this review.

is an arena arcade game developed by Self Made Miracle and published by Team17 Digital Ltd.
The story is about a boy who joins a circus, only to be part of life-threatening games. That's pretty much it. Because the story is basically non-existent, I'm not gonna take it into account.
The game is nothing special: the 16-bit look is charming at first, but there isn't much variety in the levels to make anything stand out. Sometimes you might struggle recognising some threats that appear.
The game features 3 arenas with 10 levels each, as well as 4 game modes. In the Campaign, you complete levels to get money to unlock new features and to play locally or online with friends and other players.
Going into this game, you have to ask yourself one question: are you willing to play some really hard challenges in which there is something constantly trying to kill you, just to unlock more content? If so, you will have fun like I did playing the game. All you can do is jump around, avoid threats and pick up objects.
I had more fun playing locally with a friend than playing the solo campaign, so I strongly recommend having a friend by your side when playing.
The challenges are increasingly harder and harder, to a point of extreme frustration. If you enjoy getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by sometimes unfair threats, then you will have fun with the game's singleplayer.
The sound effects are of very little importance, and the soundtrack, while fun at first, quickly started getting on my nerves for its repetitiveness.
Most of the lasting appeal of the game comes from its multiplayer components: every achievement is pretty easy to unlock, and the campaign will last for about an hour.
Overall, if you like arena games or are looking for something to play with a buddy, I recommend this. Beware, however, of its high difficulty spikes and sometimes unfair challenges.

Ty the Tasmanian Tiger is a wonder of the past. So many games these days promise nostalgia but fail to deliver a fun or genuine experience, but Ty delivers on almost all fronts. This is largely due to it's 2002 roots, a much different age in gaming. I grew up playing Ty (and its subsequent sequels) and still fondly remember it. When I heard that it was being ressurected, I couldn't believe it.
This port delivers, despite still being in Early Access. It stands up beyond nostalgia- offering a bright, fun and engrossing experience. Despite it releasing only a day or two ago, I couldn't help but play through and complete the entire game. However, the length of the game might be the title's biggest downfall; To complete the game at 100% (Which does NOT include the hidden art) it took me between 9 and 10 hours. While my playtime might have been influenced by prior knowledge, it's important to keep in mind.
But for the price of about $9 to $12 it delivers a worthy experience. Make sure you have a gamepad before playing and enjoy the delightfully corny Australian experience Ty delivers.
I look forward to the ports of the two subsequent 3D Ty games, and wish the best to the developers with bringing this classic mascot platformer franchise back.

Having played this for a long time on console, now almost exclusively a PC gamer, this remains a must have for the collection. While it has less in the way of RPG-like elements that made San Andreas so extremely replayable, the physics featured in this game are the pinnacle of the entire series. You can easily see how this began the trend towards realistic reactions for npcs, which were perfected later in Red Dead Redemption, LA Noire, and Max Payne. Even the new GTAV lacks the exaggerated nature of impact as experienced here, and it has the best car damage features out of any GTA game.
I do think San Andreas has the better gameplay, overall -- territory warfare and how you would be left alone if going against other criminals made for a fun experience that can't be beat -- but it's hard to go back to the days when characters only fall flat no matter what, not after playing with IV's engine. The worst part of this game is how the police seem to roam every five feet, and you can't get away with anything you do unless absolutely silent (even in the expansions where you are part of a crew, expecting to be left alone if only attacking rivals and not hurting unaffiliated innocents), but there is an active modding community where you can find ways of reducing the number of cops and their constant interference... if you're like me, and playing The Lost and the Damned, for example, where you want to go after all rival gangs for an immersive experience without constant police harrassment, I'd highly suggest some sort of mod to address this issue if you get a kick out that, because the cheat system in IV pretty much sucks to have to use.
Also, pro tip: turn your phone to sleep mode. I think we all kind of know that particular annoyance, of course. Otherwise, with the cover system, gritty look and feel, amazing physics, and killer soundtrack to back it up, this game is just as good today as anything else out there.

In a time where the 3D Collect-a-thon seems to be at its least visible, this game is like a shining beacon of nostalgia for me. I remember playing this back on the gamecube when it first came out and absolutely loving it. Playing through it now, I can see a few issues that I may not have noticed back when I was younger but overall this is still one of my favorite platformer games I've played. I have to say I am kind of surprised how well this game holds up, but its music, art, and gameplay all manage to still captivate me. The music especially so. Once I heard the first level's theme I was instantly transported back in time to when I first played this game. On the negative side, there are a few slow downs and audio desyncs here and there, but I would attribute that to it being an early access game. Hopefully by the time the game is fully out these issues will be fixed. As well, there are a few relics of its time that still cling to this port such as low res cutscenes and an occasionally wonky camera. As well, this game can be a bit on the easy side. Overall however, the pros vastly outweigh the minor cons that I pointed out. This is one of my favorites of the 3D Collect-a-thon subgenre and if anyone has been wanting for such a game this is absolutely one I would have no issue reccommending. With some work for optimization, I can easily see this game as an 4/5. It's not perfect by any stretch, and the challenge mostly comes from collecting everything 100%. Regardless, I have been missing these types of games for a long time now and I'm really glad to see one of my favorites coming back on PC.

Ok, lets get this straight to avoid any confusion.  This game has nothing to do with roleplaying games, but what it does have a lot to do with is classic fantasy boardgames, like talisman, dungeon, or heroquest.  Unfortunately this is marred by the whole having to pay to unlock certain features and bonuses, and in the pvp section this really does show as to who pays and who's here just for fun.
There are a few stereotypes which immediately feel out of place, especially as this isn't 1986 and games like this are far more mainstream these days, so the depiction of everyone who plays this as a nerd hurts more than helps.
Ok, on to the game itself, past the cringe-worthy imagery.  What I will say here is that everything that follows is why I gave it a  positive thumb waving.
They have for the most part, got themselves a really good package here, with board based tile movement and card based combat.  You fight all of the fantasy stereotypes of goblins, orcs and other such things.  The combat is resolved by using cards for each adventurer that you have until you find you can't use any more, due to running out, or just not having the right card at the right time, like in the video where the guy says 'I cast a lightning bolt!' etc.  At the end of every round the adventurers and remaining monsters get to draw new cards.  This can be a little difficult to catch when the game uses the terms 'rounds' and 'turns' applying htem to what they want.
Movement can only take place if you have movement cards, and I don't see any indicator to show when you're arriving at the end of the round.  So tactics like waiting for the monsters to move and expend their cards for movement/attack before you make your decisions aren't really possible.  If you do try to estimate that, then you could end up in a poor position, as if you have over two cards per adventurer left at the end of the turn, then you have to discard them until you have the sacred number of 2 for some reason.
The amount of money you gain is determined by how much treasure detritis you find after each battle, which usually comes in quite low amounts, so most of the time you will depend on the other treasure items you find to equip your adventurers.
I would recommend this game, but only if you want a very superficial experience and aren't looking for anything with more depth than your 12 year old brother might be looking for in a fantasy board game.   Maybe good for an hour on the weekend with your favourite intoxicant/food-snack while still wearing your p.js perhaps.

I don't know where to start with this game. Apparently there's no intro-- I start a new game, the scene opens and I'm standing by water being attacked by zombies. Not even time to get my bearings, adjust to the physics of the game, make any necessary changes, or even process a storyline. Following this my main character acts completely nonchalant about what's going on, apparently unbothered by either the zombies attacking him or, if he's unaware they're zombies, the fact that he just murdered three people.
The controls are not good. The movement feels awkward, turns are awkward, the camera is also awkward. I suspect gunplay would not be particularly fun in this game and the melee (at least at the start) is mindless mashing.
Following the very abrupt introduction (i.e. appearing with no context or character/story build-up whatsoever), I make my way to a nearby ranger cabin and am greeted by someone who acts like I know exactly what's happening. Here, take these supplies and head back out to secure the area! And I, seeming to lack interest in the background of this situation, unable to express shock or horror at the unfolding situation, agree to do this with no particular need to question this man.
I head back out to explore the area, climbing a water tower to assess different points of interest. This is pretty cool and finally begins to ground me a bit. I manage to access the menu system (which, for some unknown reason, does not default to the Escape key but instead picks a random button on my mouse) and am fairly bombarded with information. It's not an excessive amount of stuff-- it seems they struck a good balance between depth and accessibility-- but it's still a lot to take in at once and with no real tutorial. I manage to access game controls and can finally fix the y-axis reverse and change some of the hotkeys.
Following this I begin to explore and seek out quest locations. However, my minimap is not 'locked' but changes as my facing changes-- again, I can't comprehend why this was done. So I have a difficult time orienting myself in the pursuit of static locations. I also realize that the movement isn't getting much better, even after adjusting the camera sensitivity.
I find a few cabins, beat down some deadites, and enter to see what appear to be items strewn all over. Yet the cabin is described as empty and there's nothing to loot. I noticed the same thing in the ranger station-- lots of goods lying around that can't be picked up. I find this strange and an immersion breaker.
A few minutes later I realize that I am already bored and have no real interest in trying to adapt to the game's clunky controls, no real sense of world immersion (largely due to the horrible 'plop you in with no context'), and am getting no enjoyment whatsoever from the combat. I log out after about twenty minutes for the second time since I picked the game up, recalling that I had tried once to play, didn't enjoy it, but wanted to give it another chance.
Now I know it's not a fluke. The game as a whole might be fun, and it might have been more acceptable before I got into the Fallout series, but at this point I just can't comprehend some fo the developer decisions or the lacklustre beginning-- which is generally among the most important parts of a game and should be polished quite a bit before release.
Scoring this game would be difficult because I haven't given the breadth of it much of a chance. So I will say 5/10, but if you can get past the issues I've outlined here, or really, really love zombies, the system seems interesting enough to warrant a 7.

I do recommend this game.  Some people apparently find the combat system to be "clunky" but seems just fine to me.  Enjoyed base building, little missions, world, etc.
Lots of caveats though!
This game has a ridiculous amount of bugs.  Nothing seemed to be fixed from the non YOSE versions.  Not too bad if you always keep an eye out for them.  Zombies WILL randomly go through walls and doors.  Sometimes it will just be "cosmetic", as in you can see them but they can't see you or hit you.  Sometimes they will just flat out run through things.  You may also accidentally run through walls or closed doors when you least expect it.  Most annoying thing is when the gates in Lifeline no longer exist for the zombies.  It seems you can reset the issue by running down and opening and closing the gates.  But kind of disappointing when a whole horde of zombies just phases through your closed gate.
If you alt tab to look at anything else on your computer, you will be stuck in a non full sized game window.  You have to exit the game fully and re enter to fix this.
Be careful driving.  Sometimes hitting even small objects with your vehicle at relatively low speeds can make it fly through the air and crash.  If a vehicle is upside down, it will automatically explode after a minute or so, no exceptions.  So if you have sacks in it, you'll want to rapidly unload them or lose everything.
Your NPC allies tend to be incredibly stupid.  They don't seem to use silencers, so if they go with you to fight, be aware that they will use melee weapons only, even if their life is in danger.  They also will sometimes suicide, so if they say "clear out, I've got these guys!", listen to them and clear out.  They may use an incendiary or explosive.  I've had my vehicle blown up by an NPC doing this next to me, which basically killed me too.  They may also freeze, not fighting the zombies or doing anything else.  I've had refugees do this as well as a fellow soldier on base.  For the refugees, I was able to push them outside, then push them all the way to base with a car, then inside.  They remained frozen until picked up by helovac.
All this being said, this is one of the few games I've played through many times and am still playing!  Hoping all these issues disappear with SoD 2, when they use the Unreal engine instead of the Cry something or other engine.  Assuming it was named "Cry" because when you play a game with it, most of the time you just want to cry due to the poor quality.

Overall:  Yes, recommended.  It has a story line that is above-average, game-play is above-average, graphics are above-average (considering when made).  Everything is essentially above-average.  It needs a bit of work, but still worth buying, especially on sale.
Pros:
Story - A bit fast-paced at times, without much explanation for the "why", but it's not the worst.  Immerses the player adequately.
Playable Characters - Each character seems unique and has their own personality.  I believe there are over 100+ characters/NPC's in game.  Characters/NPC's will bicker between each other and do small missions (i.e. scavenging) on their own.  A nice touch.  Makes the base camp feel like the NPC's are contributing without you having to do everything.  They also defend the base on their own.
Game-play - needs some polish, but it's still enjoyable.  Melee (blunt, edged, heavy weapons, etc.), gun-fighting (all types of pistols, rifles, SMGs, shotguns and sniper rifles), and vehicles (cars, trucks, SUVs) sum up the way to kill zombies.
3rd person perspective only - pro or con based on your taste.  Works great while outside.
Base-building - definitely one of the best characteristics.  Build up the infirmary, food storage, tower, workshop, etc. to provide various benefits for your group.
RGP-like - can level up various skills.  Not very intricate/complex, but enjoyable.
Weapons degrade over time and need to be repaired.
Scavenging - fun to scavenge.  Grab a survivor to watch your back though, especially at night, and hop in a car (more cargo space than your backpack).
Radio - can call in scavengers to help bring back supplies, back-up (SWAT), artillery, new home base relocation, etc.  Of course, you have to complete missions to unlock many of these.
2 other DLC's that are included in YOSE which change things up a bit.
Cons:
3rd person only - pro or con.  Can be problematic when entering buildings and small rooms.  Cannot see threats until the character is fully in the room due to 3rd person.
-Driving - one area that really needs a patch.  It...just...doesn't....feel right...the turning and handling is a bit strange; also, accelerating and decelerating does a weird zoom in & out which distorts vision - hard to drive and recon the area b/c of it.
-Closing Doors - ugh, an area that is very annoying.  Sometimes you'll close them without a problem, other times you have to maneuver the character a bit before you can close doors (time consuming) - not good when being chased by a zombie horde.
-NPC's / AI - weird glitches occasionally such as:  will stop accompanying you for no reason - happened twice to me; when escorting AI to destination, they've stopped moving just outside the objective (I had to physically push them into the objective to complete the mission - happened twice).  Companions like to block doorways - not game breaking, just an annoyance, you can roll through them or even push them out of the way.  They also like to spazz out and take their time when loading into vehicles - again, not game breaking, just needs a patch.

I purchased expecting a mostly modern take on the old Syndicate game. I was not disappointed. Great graphics and depth to the upgrading of your agents. Plot line is pretty basic. Gameplay is a bit overwhelming at first but the complication is very rewarding later when you find that you need to try different strategy. Easily one of the more entertaining games in my library.
This game does require a fair amount of thinking how to approach a scenario. And, to up the risk/reward, there is no pause, so your strategy has to be workable in realtime AND account for changes. With the limited resources you have at hand, you are supposed to build, upgrade and automate a factory.
There's tons to do here. You have a lot of technologies to research, all of which unlock more crafting items, machines and upgrades. The eventual goal is to build a rocket, which is the main win condition.
Doing all of this takes some time, but it's challenging and satisfying. A lot of your time will go in figuring out the logistics. Optimisation and proper organisation is key here, and it's incredibly rewarding. Oh, and you've got to keep the ever-evolving aliens at bay. They're drawn to pollution, so it's wise to keep that in check.
There's just far too much to do in this game. I've spent 30 hours and I'm nowhere close to researching half the available technologies. It's a great time sink.
For being an early-access title, it's an incredibly stable game. No bugs faced, yet. The game plays smoothly. It doesn't show signs of an early-access title, that's for sure.
It's also in constant development (as is expected). The developers are active and they post once every week on their blog. The community is really nice, too. So my initial statement for this game is a bit harsh, maybe too harsh. SFA is a visually polished vertical shmup that plays similarly to the 1942 series or the Raiden series. The closest game I can compare this to visually is Sine Mora. It may perhaps be the best looking 2.5D shmup ever - I never see clearly defined "polygon lines", the water looks excellent, and there are nice fog and glowing effects. I've never seen any other shmup have 8x anti-aliasing. The limited 2D character art is another story, which is even more low budget in apperance compared to the original Pokemon anime.
SFA starts at a very slow pace with the player only having the ability to move and shoot a pea shooter. Now imagine playing 1942/3 or Raiden, and instead of maximizing your damage output and ability to use bombs with in the first or second level, having to slowly unlock the mechanics of the game via in-game currency. Not a terrible idea - if implented properly, and allows the player to adapt to new mechanics instead of having to use everything in your arsenal to barely survive level one. The problem in Sky Force Anniversary is the cost of these ship upgrades, which essentially requires the player to farm for the currency of stars dropped from enemies and destructables. This is made worse that after the first time you use some of the upgrades: the shield, the laser, and the screen clearing mega-bomb, will deplete after level completion (or death/restart) and require more stars to refill them. You need to grind for stars to unlock the mechanics of this game so you can grind for stars to use said mechanics.
Grinding is made worse by the medal requirement of future levels. In order to proceed further in the game, you need to complete challenges in previous levels which unlocks medals. This generally requires killing 70% of enemies, killing 100% of enemies, rescuing "humans", and not taking a hit. This would all be easy if you had the upgrades, but you don't, so you often have to replay these levels to get these medals - surviving the level is easy, getting the medals often require level memorization, hence, more repating. Worse, further levels require more medals than you can obtain from the previous levels, meaning you have to COMPLETE ALL THE MEDALS from a previous level, which FINALLY UNLOCKS A SLIGHTLY HARDER DIFFICULTY WITH MORE MEDALS (which are usually the same, or require collecting a percentage of stars). Why they couldn't allow the higher difficulties to be unlocked from the beggining is beyond me and will force the player to play the same level even more times in order to play the same levels again with slightly more durable and more frequently shooting enemies.
I was willing to put up with some of this until I reached level 5, which introduces an EMP ball that chases you the entire level. Get hit by it, and you can move, but not do anything else. This effectively eliminates the strategy of standing still or shooting single file to kill a tough enemy (which the level is full of) with your weak weapons. This would be an interesting mechanic if there was a way to destroy said EMP, or if it stopped attacking you at certain intervals, like Death from Gauntlet (2014).

I really don't like this game, and I'm usually quite fond of a bit of arcade inspired shoot-em-up action. It's not that the production quality is lacking in any way, as the whole thing is quite well put together in terms of design and basic gameplay. But I would much rather play a game like CounterAttack, Blue Revolver or Wolflame (just to name a few of the top of my head If I were to have a quick glance at my Steam library and maybe my wishlist I could probably name at least half a dozen titles which are superior in almost every aspect).  All of which offer a much more fun, arcade like experience instead of the tedious 'grind-fest' that this title offers.
If your gaming experience is anything like mine you will grind the first 2 levels until you have enough basic firepower to tackle the next few grind the next few levels, especially the downright annoying level 5. I think perhaps they were going for some kind of bonus level where the players weapons were taken out by an EMP, and you have to collect as many stars as possible without getting shot down. Upgrade everything to maximum power and then just blitz the remaining 4 levels, as well as 100% completing the first 5 on all the three difficulty levels.
And the names they have chosen to call their difficulty levels also annoyed me a little too.
are a little misleading. Compared to other examples of the genre I would rate them
. With the only real difference in difficulty that I could detect being enemies taking more damage to kill and shooting slightly more frequently on higher difficulty levels.
The game requires you to earn medals for things like 100% kills, rescues, etc. in order to progress. And they are all quite attainable, even on the "insane" difficulty. The only reason I have not yet collected all of them is that I really can't be bothered seeing all the same 9 levels all over and over, and over again without the game offering any real challenge:).
It's not that I didn't enjoy playing this game, it's just that there are so many better examples of the genre out there that I cannot possibly recommend it to fans of the genre, especially not hardcore arcade shoot-em-up freaks. But if you're more of a casual gamer who finds most shoot-em-ups to be several orders of magnitude too hard for you then you should probably check this out, as despite everything I said about it it is a moderately fun game.
But then there are so many more things that annoyed me at least a little, far too many to mention but most notably how you don't get to keep any of your (sometimes expensive) powerups upon completing a level, or the ridiculous amount of firepower required to destroy the lighthouses and patrol boats found in the early levels.
Overall I couldn't possibly give it more than 7.3/10 (which for those of you who are unfamiliar with my reviewing style is just 0.2 shy of recommended)

This game parodies just about anything and everything from the 80s and 90s: from video games, tv shows, movies -- I'm talking everything from TMNT, Metal Gear, Mario, Back to the Future, Duck Hunt, River City Ransom, The Three Stooges, Die Hard, Skate or Die -- and even freaking Saved By The Bell! And these are merely the things I can remember from the last couple of times I've played! Plus, the first couple of Story Missions are so jam-packed with references that I'm almost positive I've missed a few.
This entire game was made completely by one guy (save for the AMAZING 8-bit soundtrack, by various artists), and it took FOREVER to release, but it's finally out, and worth the price of admission.
Imagine if Rockstar made GTA while they were still DMA Design and you might have a good idea of what this game is. Who needs fancy graphics anyway?

Penarium is an arcade platform game set in a circus where you have to complete a given challenge without being killed by a trap or falling off the bottom of the level.
The traps appear in the level one or two at a time, and include homing missiles, spiky moving walls, machine guns, deadly bouncing balls and more. Some are quite inventive and are more about making life difficult rather than killing you - check out the thieving bird.
There are three modes: campaign mode, arcade mode and local two-player mode.
The campaign mode is a set of 30 prescribed levels with a dark little story about how a child (who looks straight out of The Far Side) is kidnapped and forced to perform for his freedom by the mysterious masked Director.
This mode offers three different arenas, each split into 10 levels. Each level has one goal - destroy 20 barrels, collect 35 balloons in order, press 20 buttons in the order specified etc. Every 5 things you do triggers a new set of traps to replace the old - which are (sometimes) chosen at random.
Watch Campaign Mode gameplay in this video:
The arcade mode allows you to pick one of the three arenas, and you get an endless version of the level where you have to destroy as many barrels as you can, with worldwide leaderboards. Again, every 5 barrels you smash triggers new traps. One death and it's all over.
You can collect coins in arcade mode that allow you to buy power-up cards at the shop on the map screen. These power-ups can be played during future arcade mode runs to give you a temporary one-off buff, such as flight, coin magnet and invincibility when standing still.
The cards don't seem hugely useful since you have to buy them before you start the run and drop into the arena (one at a time) as a reward for smashing a certain number of barrels. It would be better if you had the choice of playing the perfect card at the perfect moment, eg play the invincibility-while-standing-still when you couldn't otherwise escape the sweeping vertical laser.
Penarium is unexpectedly not that difficult. None of the traps are unfair or overpowered - in fact, some of them (such as the water) are easily ignored and could do with toughening up. There's never more than two types of trap active at once, and sometimes only one, even late in the game. This means you'll be able to get through the campaign very quickly.
I haven't played the local multiplayer, but should cause plenty of excellent swearing. Both competitive & co-op require the players to hold down randomly appearing buttons for a few seconds each - in competitive, there's one button to fight over, in co-op both players get their own button. There's only partial collision - you can't bump the other player off a platform, but you can stun them by landing on them.
I'd like both arcade mode and multiplayer to offer different challenges instead of just barrel-smashing (arcade) and button-pressing (multiplayer). A little customisation would go a long way here.
To get the most out of Penarium you'll need to learn to love the beat-the-high-score arcade mode and hopefully get some couch multiplayer action going. Campaign mode won't keep you for long, but in general the game never makes you wait to get back in the action, has a very replayable arcade concept (perfect for quick coffee-break blasts) and best of all, contains NO CLOWNS.
Thanks to Self Made Miracle for the preview copy.

Insurgency is a game that puts you in a situation similar to real anti-terrorism IRL. Though the graphics aren't phenominal, they definitely poses what i would call: "fits the situation"
Pros
1) Gameplay
If you ever played Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, most people know that the game isn't what really counter-terrorism looks like, in fact, it's actually a competitive shooting game with a skin of counter-terrorism. If you want to take a real feeling of counter-terrorism, Insurgency is, as how we say it in China, "not your second choice". Insurgency offers a realistic gameplay, from gun customizing, to role dividing. This game shines in co-operative, each player must be good at their role and help others in order to win, for example, The Breacher must be able to lead the charge when ready, Support must be able to give firepower support when ready, sniper must be able to pick off lethal targets. If you play this game like CS, where one could win by just going Rambo style, you will not win this. The Game makes it so that you can only choose a certain role, so that your team must be able to co-operate real well. The map designs are pretty well made, each place is designed that you are never safe from the enemy. The Game also makes it that you can't tell where your enemy is unless you spotted them in the first place, just like in real life. Even the callouts that the AIs make when they're shot, reloading, and being firesurpressed not only makes the feeling more realistic, but gives the game a theme of anti-war.
2) Graphics
Though as I said, the graphics aren't the best, they fit well for the game. The graphics are designed in a way that though not good, it's more realistic. The fact is, better graphics doesn't mean realistic, the graphics in this game nailed that point. When in real life combat, you will not have a good view on anything except you, your teammates, and your gun. The environment is made figgy so that you have to have a sharp eye to spot the enemy. Heck, even the environment motion is designed that anything that moves makes you think it's an enemy.
3) Price
When Speaking of Games, price is also important. You can't expect me to give a positive review on a game that sells way over it's price. This game's price is decent, though i would say buying it during sales would be better, but hey, you don't get a lot of games that do this well in putting realistic in it and selling at a low, decent price. So if you could, maybe do the developers a favor, and buy it at its original price. But if you can't afford, wait until sales, which it would drop to an amazing price.

I really, REALLY wanted to like Satellite Reign more than I did, but it's so riddled with problems and flaws that overtake it's positive points.
- Unresponsive units that take forever to do orders, have terrible pathfinding and are in general absolutely stupid. They'd be much, much easier to use if the game wasn't realitime, which it is, sadly. Units will disobey your orders, break formation "just because", will not shoot back if they are shot at first, etc.
- Terrible performance
- Horrible U.I, that is cluttered and obscures actually useful information
- Broken stealth mechanics- enemy sightlines are not accurately shown to the player, guards behave in mysterious and weird ways and will often glitch themselves in an attempt to find you, and their reasoning is brain dead stupid (huh, these 4 glowing cyborgs just broke into our secret military installation? better kindly escort them out considering none of them are currently armed! Oh, some are carrying weapon/gear prototypes? Better let them just keep those!).
- Lots of loading
- Droning music that sounds good at first but quickly gets old when it turns out they loop forever
- Repetitive gameplay and missions that drag down the open ended nature of the game. ALWAYS break into this bright glowing green door.
- Micromanaging the units is way too tough for what they want you to do. Coordination is key, but your units move too fast and combat happens so quick that you have no time to react.
- You deal a pitiful amount of damage early on, which means stealth or bust. It's only until the midgame, 10 or so hours in that you can begin to go in guns blazing, and even then enemies send hordes and hordes after you, endlessly respawning. Apparently one soldier with a machine gun can easily take down one of your dudes early game, which is just... pathetic, really. I'm not asking to mow down tons of soldiers easily, but I am asking to at least stand a chance against one.
-No quicksaving.
- The awful, just.. TERRIBLE controls. To say the game feels unresponsive is giving it too much credit. It is a chore to get your units to do anything at all.
Just go play Syndicate instead.
Now, despite this, I did clock 11 or so hours into the game before I gave up. You may say... why? Well, because it's a fun game. If you can look past all of these flaws, you'll adore the game for sure. I enjoyed myself, but these flaws got me to stop playing.
This game needs to either run a LOT smoother or be turn based to even be worth considering.  Hell, I wouldn't even play a turn based game that was this poorly optomized.

Pros:
Story - A bit fast-paced at times, without much explanation for the "why", but it's not the worst.  Immerses the player adequately.
Playable Characters - Each character seems unique and has their own personality.  I believe there are over 100+ characters/NPC's in game.  Characters/NPC's will bicker between each other and do small missions (i.e. scavenging) on their own.  A nice touch.  Makes the base camp feel like the NPC's are contributing without you having to do everything.  They also defend the base on their own.
Game-play - needs some polish, but it's still enjoyable.  Melee (blunt, edged, heavy weapons, etc.), gun-fighting (all types of pistols, rifles, SMGs, shotguns and sniper rifles), and vehicles (cars, trucks, SUVs) sum up the way to kill zombies.
3rd person perspective only - pro or con based on your taste.  Works great while outside.
Base-building - definitely one of the best characteristics.  Build up the infirmary, food storage, tower, workshop, etc. to provide various benefits for your group.
RGP-like - can level up various skills.  Not very intricate/complex, but enjoyable.
Weapons degrade over time and need to be repaired.
Scavenging - fun to scavenge.  Grab a survivor to watch your back though, especially at night, and hop in a car (more cargo space than your backpack).
Radio - can call in scavengers to help bring back supplies, back-up (SWAT), artillery, new home base relocation, etc.  Of course, you have to complete missions to unlock many of these.
2 other DLC's that are included in YOSE which change things up a bit.
Cons:

State of Decay is one of the best zombie games out there. If you like slaying hordes of zombies, building bases, awesome meele attack animations, nice cars, characters with personality, horror and lots of fun this is the game just for you!
Firstly I would like to point out, that the game is very beautiful, the animations are amazing and lifelike.
Your journey takes place in Trumbull Valley, which is a rather large open world filled with lots of zombies. Your mission is to escape the Valley, while you try to survive and gather as many followers as possible. A great difference with this game and other games in the same genre is, that when a follower/character dies it stay death. At first I was really shocked as I lost a character in the beginning of the game, and was sitting back with mixed feelings, because I already felt that I bonded with the character. So you have to be careful, when you are exploring. Loosing a character might affect the way that your game plays out in the end.
The two DLCs are fun as well. The Breakdown DLC is almost the same as the originally game, tho there is no main mission line. Your mission here is to fix a truck to move on to the next level (same map but increased difficulty), you begin at level 1 and it goes all the way to level 99. So if you love grinding and killing millions of zombies this DLC will fall right in your taste!
The Lifeline DLC is in another map, where you this time follow the millitary aspect of the zombie apocalypse. Your mission is to survive wave after wave of zombies that attack your base while you are extracting civillians and VIPs. This DLC has different endings, which depends on the choices that you make during the game.
Overall I would like to say, the sounds are very realistic, nice voice actors, the visual is damn neat. Only con I would like to add is, that the main mission line is very short and it could have been a lot longer. Maybe we will see that in State of Decay 2? I am very excited!
So should you buy this game? 28 euro is a cheap price for a game of this size! If you like the aspects of roaming from GTA, crafting from Minecraft and zombies from The Walking Dead, this is just the game for you!
Be aware, when you rush out excited to smash some zombie skulls be careful, this is not like Left 4 Death, you can't just take 20 zombies on you and beat them by meele. Max is 3, more than that you'll get overrrun if you are alone fighting with meele!

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
A huge world of community-made adventures! A tight single-player 2D platforming action-RPG at heart, Below Kryll is a vast, online, continuous world composed of player made adventures. Everything you play, even the tutorial and story-mode themselves was created in-game. - Highly Recommended!

It says early access, but it's nothing like alot of the early access junk we see; in it's current state, it's completely playable, and very enjoyable at that. All of the main gameplay features are intact, the small but often updates add new styles and slightly new content to help bolster the creativity of levels!

I think it might be best to start this review with the following message: If you at all enjoy action platformers and/or games which focus upon player-created content then Below Kryll is absolutely worth the asking price.
I have easily spent several dozen hours on Below Kryll (most of which is from before its Steam launch) and even after having spent this much time with the game it is difficult for me to find much in the way of fault with it. The game has a neat, unique look to it and Mitsu, the main character, animates particularly well without prioritizing animation over input. The music and general sound effects are also well-made, though there is not at this time too much in the way of track variety.
Gameplay and exploration are the parts where Below Kryll really shines. Mitsu has quite a bit of momentum to his movement to the point that the controls take a bit of getting used to and they might initially feel overly slippery when trying to do more precise platforming. However, abilities such as an air dash and kunai throwing (which completely stops Mitsu's momentum) as well as a few other tricks allow you to both move quickly and precisely.
Speaking of tricks, Mitsu has quite a few of them as experience is gained from completing areas and new abilities are unlocked along the way. In addition to dashing both in the air and on the ground as well as throwing kunai to stun enemies (not to mention several other skills), Mitsu can jump and slide off of certain walls, grind rails, perform a downward diving attack, and even chain together multiple dashes and jumps by killing enemies in the air; the playerbase has also found quite a few creative ways to utilize Mitsu's varied skillset and maps generally do a good job of both teaching and incorporating these skills, such as using the downward thrust to slightly extend the horizontal movement of a jump to create a 'long jump'.
This extensive skillset is particularly important largely because of just how much freedom it gives players when creating areas. If it is not already apparent, the vast majority of the content in Below Kryll is created by the playerbase and incorporated into a giant interconnected metroidvania-style grid with each area being a single rectangle on the grid. As Mitsu's skillset is so varied and flexible, areas which focus upon combat, platforming, and/or puzzle solving are all equally viable and can range anywhere in difficulty from trivial to insanely hard
As for the creation side of things itself, it is handled well and making a new area is simply and intuitive. Upon reaching an unclaimed rectangle on the grid, players can pay some gold to reserve it and start building. Which enemies, traps, and objects can be placed in a room are determined by just where on the map you are placing your room as more dangerous or tricky objects and enemies are reserved for deeper floors. Otherwise, creating an area is largely a matter of  clicking and dragging to clear or create terrain and to place objects and logic gates.
Lastly, there are a lot of little touches in Below Kryll which serve to give it the polish which many similar games lack. Reviving at the most recent checkpoint after dying requires the press of a single button and is otherwise instantaneous; players can even reset the stage completely or warp back to a checkpoint without dying at any time. If a stage has pits, players can quickly toggle between treating them as death pits or as paths to a new area. Although players cannot yet directly interact with each other, there are chatrooms and players can see the shadows of each other in real time when moving through the same area.
All of this adds up to a game which is not only a unique and interesting concept, but one which is executed very well in practice; as the content is primarily community-made not all of it is great and there are some parts of the game, such as the main storyline, which are still being worked on, but Below Kryll excels in all the most crucial areas and is simply a joy to both play and to create in.

Just don't expect to much tactical approach here.
Fun weapons, nice pacing of ammunition drops (so you really need to switch between weapons) and good one-liners. Retro City Rampage is a unique sort of indie game. It was originally an attempt to remake GTA3 for the NES console, and became it`s own project that was ported to the PC. The influences from that game are very clear, as are the other games the author sought to parody.
The game from intro screen to gameplay is pure NES. It replicates many of the problems that programmers had creating for that system, and in a lot of ways moves past them. The gameplay is modern, it runs at a very nice framerate and in general reminds me a lot of GTA2 in some odd way.
It is also riddled with references, it shoots them out almost as much as a bodily function. So if you like loaded action packed indie games that don`t take themselves seriously, I can`t recommend this game any more.

Retro Old school, new school, it has it all. If you love the NES you will love this game!

I dunno.  It's kind of tiring.  The fundamental game is really well built and is fun to play, but over time it just doesn't feel enjoyable.
This is strange since Retro City Rampage is full of unique content, and the game always keeps you doing different things.  The story mode is just an excuse to string you along from one referential set piece to the next, but what's interesting is that many references take the form of one-off gameplay homages rather than merely verbal shout-outs; I think that's rather novel—interacting with references to interactive things where the reference is the kind of interacting you do.  I don't think I've seen that before, and here is an entire game made out of it.  Also, it's rather remarkable to note how flexible the basic mechanics are as they reproduce the mechanics of other games without actually changing.
So this is a hugely impressive game in one regard, but I don't very much like playing it.  You should definitely try it sometime, though.

3 hours (and 4 maps) into the game, and it's exactly as i remember it!
This is one of my favourite games growing up, and i'm so glad that it's finally made it's way to the PC. If you ever enjoyed Ty on the older consoles, this is certainly something you should pick up.
First off, as stated, 4 worlds in so far. Zero bugs found (some dodgy camera work if walking through a narrow walkway / door. But that's easily sorted by tilting the camera.
Judging by the achievements, it seems as though the game is incomplete. As i have 4 maps complete, currently sat at 42% game completion. So this feels like there are only 9 available levels so far (10% per level), plus 10% for the home world. I could be wrong. But this is my observations so far.
Regardless if the game is currently only half complete, if you enjoyed it 14 years ago, chances are you will enjoy it today!
Worth noting, i used an XBox controller to play the game, so i have no experience or recommendation regarding keyboard and mouse use.
Also, the game maintained a solid 60FPS throughout gameplay, however. i have a fairly powerful machine, so results could vary drastically
Having completed the game, i can confirm that it i was incorrect about the game being incomplete. Every level is there, i just remembered the game being a lot bigger.
Bugs! throughout the entire game, i only experienced 3 bugs, and only 2 of them have any effect on your gameplay/
Bug 1: Opals missing, found them in trees. Leaving the level and loading it back up placed the opals back where they should be. This only happened once, on the map "Lyre Lyre pants on fire"
Bug 2: graphical glitch in the sky on "Rex Marks the Spot". Hardly anything to cry about
Bug 3: The "Free Boat Battle" mission on "Rex Marks the Spot" cannot be completed, the NPC just repeats the quest line over and over instead of giving you the thunder Egg.
Hopefully these bugs will be fixed, but other than that. an awesome game, All the nostalgia. I hope older N64 and PS1 / PS2 get ported over. This has reminded me how amazing video games can be, with very little in the way of story, graphics or big budgets
100% recommend!

For those who want a short, snappy review:
This almost beats Masters of Orion 3 as my most regrettable gaming purchase.
I love Syndicate. I long ago lost track of how many weekends I spent on my SNES, happily using the Persuadatron to mind control drones, and later I did pretty much the exact same thing with Syndicate Returns on the Playstation (never did find the Graviton Gun). I was utterly delighted when I found out a game billed  as a spiritual successor had been released and as soon as I could, I snagged a copy.
And now I kinda really, really wish I hadn't.
The game is supposed to be set up so you can go through in two different ways - guns blazing, old school cyborg killing machines slaughtering everything or stealthy, in and out before anyone ever knows you were there. I decided to try the stealthy approach (the game actually encourages this, you get more experience for your goon squad by sneaking into places. Hell, there's a string of achievements for doing it!) but good god it is AWFUL.
One of the main rules about making games is that the player should always be involved - you should always have something important happening for him/her to react to. There really shouldn't be a point where the player has so little to do they think 'why am I playing this?' Well, if you try and go stealth, that's exactly the question you'll be asking yourself as you sit there waiting for the various guards to sloooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooowly make their way somewhere else. I have a book here. To read while I wait for the AI pathfinding to decide to move the NPC guards away from the place I need to go. At no point in a video game should the person playing feel the need to pick up a book to keep entertained while waiting.
I suppose I should give a few points for actually setting up random pathing for NPC's instead of just having them patrol the same route for all eternity though. It even spawns different NPC's every time you load. The developers were obviously trying to keep things from getting too dull and to give the game some replayability (the various weapons and items you can aquire are randomised as well, or so I've been told). I just wish the NPC's didn't also seem to have randomly determined sight and hearing as well - sometimes the guards can't see you if you are stood right in the open twenty feet down the road directly in front of them and sometimes they can see you from off the screen and through the wall you are trying to hide behind.
I don't think I'd be too bothered about all of the above save for one thing - the save system is completely awful and probably the worst I can think of. You need to be near relay beacons to save. Okay, save points. There are plenty of them, and you can warp directly to them. That's not so bad, right?
Well, you can only warp to them if you A. have all your team alive, B. not under attack or C. not trespassing. Whenever you go into a mission area, you are most likely going to be trespassing. See where I'm going with this? (Here's a hint: go reread the bit about randomised NPC's, I'll wait here. Done? great!) You want to sneak into somewhere, you can't quicksave, so you can't chop it up into managable little bits, you need to do the entire section in one go. Trial and error time, right? Oh, wait, no, because the NPC's change where they are everytime you reload! It pretty much comes down to pure luck, and that's a slow and miserable way to do things.
There's also the obvious problem of not being able to save if you need to leave suddenly or whatever - you can't pick this up for a quick five minute session, set aside an hour or so or just don't bother.
What else? well, the graphics aren't utterly terrible. They aren't amazing, and the way the camera pans slowly from side to side doesn't help. At all. It's actually giving me a headache. It does look all retrofuturey cyberpunkish but it just looks utterly washed out. It's raining, of course - pretty sure there's a rulebook somewhere that states any game in a dystopian future is only allowed to have scenes set in the rain at night.
All told, for anyone who wants a game like Syndicate, you could always snag an emulator from somewhere and play the actual SNES version instead.
Edit: Okay, like ten minutes after I type the review and I'm back, I need to add this in: There literally are psychic guards in the game. I just spotted one who couldn't have seen my team at any point suddenly stop patrolling, turn around and run right over to where everyone was hidden and only then stop and turn on the 'Gosh, these people aren't supposed to be here!' orange flashlight of doom. This wasn't 'oh, I got a bit too close and he spotted me', this was 'he suddenly knew where we were from across the compound while my team was hiding behind a wall that was itself behind a second bigger wall'.

I have waited so long for a Syndicate Wars successor to come out and this one nails it! Research cyber augmentations, weapons, and gear to enhance your clones and deploy them around the open city with the goal of penetrating enemy corporations strongholds to steal more weapons, gear, and aug plans. You can hack ATMs to slowly siphon money from them, bribe researchers on the street to work for you and guards to give you information or forget your crimes, and hardwire doors shut so that enemies can't get through. They even kept a type of "indoctrinator" mechanic from Syndicate Wars, only they call it "Hijacking".
All in all, I would highly recommend this game, especially with a friend. With each player having two runners the game feels very well balanced.
I hope the devs continue developing this game and in the process continue raising the bar on coop tactical combat.

The classes are unique and balanced, and as your characters grow you go from feeling like you have no power to completely over powered (which is incredibly awesome when you're wiping out a wave of troopers responding to an alarm and blowing up giant turrets).
Another interesting component, I picked this up with my friend that played Syndicate Wars back in the day.  Slowly, our other friends that enjoy cyberpunk and Shadow Run, would watch our stream and start buying the game.  We're about 5 people deep now, and each person's game (you can drop in drop out) has a different progression of technology.  In mine, we have fully augmented bodies, in my friends we have high powered machine pistols and plasma rifles.
If you liked anyone of these games this is for you: X-Com, Syndicate, Alien Swarm, Shadow Run, basically any tactical game.
The only con I've found so far on the game is in the UI department.  But that's been pretty easy to navigate once you understand the nuances.

(Story Complete) Satellite Reign is a squad based RTS where you take 4 opratives into enemy headquarters to steal sensitive intel, weapon prototypes, kill targets, or help informants escape. I went into this game thinking I would like it and came away loving it.
The highlights to Satellite Reign
- Atmosphere : The story takes a backseat but neo-future artstyle and sound design are great.
- Infiltrator & Sniper : The best two classes of your squad by far. Stealth ops is generally the course of action. These two classes are much more useful than Soldier or Support.
- Infiltrator Hacking : Making enemies kill enemies.
- Enemy Patrol AI : Satellite Reign does a great job of balancing the predictability of enemy patrol routes & reinforcements.
The low points of Satellite Reign
- Cover system : the cover points on the map are great in the beginning of the game and sketchy/missing in the reamining areas. You can find yourself stuck in walls at times.
- Soldier & Support : The game will keep reinforments coming if you are alerted so a full on attack never feels like a viable option. Support has some great abilities but nothing the feels like you care if he is on the mission or not.
- Headquarter resource respawn : clearing an area just is see the cameras and turrets respawn is not fun.

Everyone loves a party game - take some frenemies, a whole bunch of dice, and a competitive setting, and let the salty, salty blood flow. Games like Talisman, for example, or your pick of most all physical board games. Enter Armello, another game to scratch that itch. And I for one think it does that admirably.
The gameplay mechanics are a bit complex, but easy to understand after a few games or playing the in-game tutorial settings. The game itself is thoroughly enjoyable, and I've personally enjoyed every game I've played insofar.
That said, this brand of multiplayer isn't for everyone. Those who aren't on speaking terms with Lady Luck need not apply, nor those who don't enjoy losing to a fluke of RNG. As with most of this sort of game, the catch is in the chaos.
The game's graphics are superb, and all the art is well-illustrated (more or less). The art style is something to behold, and all the animations are fluid. Even the rolls of the dice are something else. All the card arts are animated, as well.
In summary, if you like chaotic games of chance, Armello is for you. Go on, pick it up.
And as a footnote: If you really like this game, you can turn a profit off of it. Yes, you read that right. After every match you get a chest or a key which I'm told is worth around $0.25. Mind, I personally use them to try for dice skins, but perhaps you're not so into cosmetics.

BASIC INFO
This game is old and runs great for everyone and has stunning graphics for back then. If you like call of duty, but love star wars also, get this game. YOUR TEAM
You lead delta squad that consists of 3 people- dev, fixer, and... forgot his name... You command them to do stuff, make them your ♥♥♥♥♥. Battle droids were hard to take down, usually in pairs of two or gaurded by some droids. Second map enemies (MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS)- some weird lizard people that looked like enraged zoibergs, usually easy to take down. Can carry shotguns or be agile with knives. Some weird flying droid thing that zaps you, sometimes gaurded by lizard things, can be taken down with one hit. They explode and suicide kill you. Third map- (AS I SAID, SPOILER ALERT HERE ALSO)- same as the second map.
Not a lot of enemy types but who cares?
GRAPHICS
Not much too say, it looks great and runs great. The pictures will tell you how it looks. Run it at 60 fps with absolutely any computer; get if you can't run pretty much any game.
STORY
The story is dull now, but for back then the story is an A+. (SPOILER ALERT)- first map you blow up a droid factory, second map you save a hijacted ship, third map you rescue wookies from kashhykk.
OVERALL
If you like star wars battlefront, like call of duty, or love the animated series, this game is right for you.
