Below Kryll is an amazing game.
It plays very much like Super House of Dead Ninjas, but what makes it truly unique is what lies beyond the first few tutorial levels : a whole world made by the players themselves !
Featuring a very easy-to-use and friendly level editor, Below Kryll allows you to go crazy and make any kind of level you want. A complicated adventure with a twisted plot, spanning across several levels ? Yep. A torture chamber filled with deadly traps ? Why not ! A pixel art gallery that you visit on a moving platform as player-made music plays ? Definitely !
The game feels rewarding both as a player and as a creator, as several good ideas were used.
As you complete levels and gather the shurikens scattered around them, your character will level up and unlock new moves (sword attacks, flying tricks...) and you will be granted access to deeper levels.
When you create a level, people can play through it, apply tags to it from a list, and leave a comment. And you, the creator, get trophy points that you can spend to buy new things to use in your levels.
All in all, it's a very addicting and creative game that you can explore in various ways depending on your mood.
Greatly recommended ! :)

Honest review after about 2.5 hours of gameplay. The gameplay is fine, unless you are overly critical about the lack of innovation, or the graphics being "out of date", you will enjoy it. The game does suffer from optimization issues , no doubt. Read more below. I will go very much into depth with my experience.
Now, what's wrong with it?
As of release, there is very poor optimization, resulting in low FPS, and really bad lag spikes at least in my experience. If you have a newer rig, at least I assume, you will be fine. I was getting lag spikes every time I scoped in on Medium settings. During Gun fights is where it was worst. You know, the place you don't want lag issues.
One other thing I dislike, is the lack of settings to mess with. You cannot adjust your FOV (Without going into the config file), And you can't set a draw distance. For me, the game had to render every time I scoped in, resulting in bad lag spikes. Which is not ideal for a sniper game. These settings are easy to look past, just really annoying I can't optimize my gameplay experience with missing settings like anti aliasing etc.
This is another one of those that I don't really care about, but feel it's worth putting in here anyway. The voice acting. At least in some characters, seem a little bad in my opinion. Not Far Cry 2 bad, they do breathe. But for you critics, there you have it.
Feel free to skip past this if you want, it's my personal horror story with the game. So I was playing for about an hour and a half, and I was in a mission. I got myself into a gunfight, and my game decides to freeze. I could still hear background audio (Someone talking over a loudspeaker), but it all froze. I waited and it did not close the app, so I had to force shutdown my PC. When I powered it back on, my PC was super slow. How odd. I shut it off again, the proper way this time, And the same. So I did it again. What I ended up having to do was restore my PC from a restore point before I installed the game. It's the only instance I've ever heard of this happening, so I wouldn't worry about it.
Up until this point I've told you all bad things about the game. What's good about it?
Well, it's great. It's SGW, open-world, with weapon and equipment customizations, a skill system with three different trees, and plenty of side quests and activities to excel in all of these. From what I've played, The main story is pretty good as well. I won't spoil any of it, but you can do that yourself with a quick YouTube search. I enjoyed it so far.
So if the game is good, why did I give it a negative rating?
The only reason I give it a negative rating is because of the optimization issues AT LAUNCH. If you are reading this months after, I would read a couple more recent reviews. So no, I wouldn't recommend this game at the moment, but give them a couple of months, or maybe even weeks. I would definitely recommend you give it a try then.

Overall Rating: 4.4/5
Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 has come from a series not many are familiar with and those who are, either enjoy it regardless of the series' shortcomings, or they steer clear in all. In many ways I can see why people don't like this game, but for their first title with a better budget you gotta hand it to CI Games that this is their best game they've created in a long time.
Story: 8
This is the hardest rating for me because the story in this game is actually pretty decent, in many ways it can pose to be realistic. Yeah the voice acting at times can be sub par, but its been awhile since I've paid attention to every bit and have been kept interested. John and Robert North make good characters especially in the Prolouge when they are giving one another sh*t, I know brothers that do that but would die for one another. The characters throughout aren't forgetful as they have a decent story either directly or indirectly related to John and they always have a good enough line to keep that character interesting enough. In terms of 23 S being more of a para military with futuristic tech it is fine for me and having a little out of this world idea is welcomed, kinda like what Sledge Hammer games did with COD: Advanced Warfare and Kevin Spacey was a ballsy badass CEO of the paramilitary contractor company ATLAS. Yes its done before and the store of a relative gone Rogue in combat, hell even Russian enemies in many games. The thing is games continue to evolve but there is only so much gameplay and story telling to do different before someone complains its a "copycat"! Overall the Campaign is very enjoyable.
Graphics/Sound: 7.5
Taking a look around the world CI Games created it's not as breathtaking as BF1 or even a COD Campaign but what it is, its an open world game not too small and not too large and its filled with enough content to keep you busy. There are a few gripes I have and they are just a few. Others than textures being a little hazy, my biggest issue is the unlively skybox and the carboard cutout border which surrounds you. Each time I look in the distance I feel like I'm playing an early COD and as far as the skybox I understand that in nature the sky may not always have a noticeable flow in wind but with none at all it just seems a little dead. In terms of sound that game has enough life from the open world to keep things from feeling if you were in a vaccum of space. And the music being foreign to me is a nice touch, every time a rap song comes on it reminds me of GTA VI. The weapons sound just fine, but just to nitpick (and it may just be a bug) I have to turn on the radio then off then on again to get the sound to work. While sniping and the bullet cam plays through it never sounds as if my silencer is even on my weapon.
Gameplay 9.5
I love open world games but at the same time I like to play a games story and enjoy that and move on to the next campaign. I enjoy military type games and this being an open world action with very nice and sometimes subtle RPG Elements the game is refreshing. Some games I feel as if skills are a burden or there are too many to even understand. in SGW3 you have three tiers of skill sets and each has their own three tires of abilities to upgrade from. Each skill set has their own skill point and you don't share spendable skill pints with all three so its a very simplified system but yet rewarding. Cusomization is a nice touch from modifying your weapons to crafting your own ammunation to medpacks from resources found in the world again it is not over bearing. One of my favorite features in the game is the mirror's edge like climbing experience especially when you need to get to a higher ground and you wanna melt your enemies face off. Please do yourself a favor. Sniper Rifle with Armored Piercing rounds and a Headshot followed by a bullet cam.

While I hated GTA4, Episodes was actually WAY better.
The controls, driving, and some of the visuals are still crap, as well as the car limit and being infected with GFWL, but there were actually some improvements in a few areas.
Both extra campaigns each added some new and improved weapons, which added to the fun factor.
The Lost and Damned was focused around being a biker, and as a result made the game a lot more interesting. The choppers are some of the better handing vehicles in the game, and there was almost always at least one around, and so you never had to drive one of those 4 wheeled icy marshmellows commonly known as 'cars' in GTA4 unless you REALLY wanted to.
In addition to having your trusty gang deliver a bike to you whenever you wanted, you could also call them for backup, either just for fun, or to help you out on a difficult mission. Successfully completing missions leveled your gang members up, actually making them even more useful.
Lost was definitely the most enjoyable version of GTA4 for me. Probably because it felt a little more like Saints Row.
The Ballad of Gay Tony wasn't quite as good as Lost, mostly because you were back to reliance on cars for most of your traveling and didn't have the option of backup whenever you wanted. But it DID have the explosive shotgun.
And dancing. Don't ask me why the dancing was so fun. Maybe because the rest of the gameplay was so meh.
Getting a dance-off going at the Hercules was probably the best part of the episode.
Each episode was around 10 hours for mostly the story missions, but they felt a lot more fun overall. While you still got calls to hang out every so often, it wasn't nearly as bad as GTA4.
There also weren't as many difficult missions as there were in GTA4, and there were much more plentiful checkpoints in the ones that were difficult.
While Episodes still shares a lot of problems with GTA4, if you REALLY want to play a GTA4 game, I'd recommend just playing Episodes from Liberty City. There will be a few plot holes, but who's playing a GTA game for plot?

A game with tons of potential let down by some truly sloppy UI design.  There's a delay on seemingly every action, and when the game is real-time and some actions demand good timing... it's an inexcusable flaw.  If you can't get snappy, precise timing on actions, then don't make the game real-time!  The amount of time it takes your apparently developmentally disabled units to respond to an order given and then execute it is absolutely absurd, particularly for important actions like silent assassinations.
I also ran into an issue where, after loading a game, the game forgot I had completed the tutorial earlier and started spamming the screen with the tutorial pop-ups... and there's no way of clearing those out of the way.  It's very clear that, for all its strengths, Satellite Reign is held together with duct tape and spit.
As far as actual gameplay goes, it's quite fun.  It's just a huge problem when you develop a real-time game and then design such ludicrous delays on so many actions.  The game probably would've been fantastic as a turn-based game, but as a real-time game I'm going to have to recommend people give it a pass.
The absurd delay on units executing your commands and doing simple things like sprinting, apparently refusing to return fire even when you have their weapons out, and just general idiotic behavior by both player characters and NPCs (who don't seem to give one whit that their colleagues' corpses are strewn all about the alleyway they're patrolling around) just... PROs:

+ Art: Well done cyberpunk art direction. The game world is accented with plenty of neon to break up the urban dystopia.
CONs:
-Annoying, unskippable tutorial that seems intent on shoving blinking boxes in your face.
-Clunky, unsatisfying combat. Picture a smooth, flowing river. Now picture a dude trying to take a♥♥♥♥♥♥after sex. It's the latter one.
-Lame auto-scaling enemies ensure you are almost always out-gunned if you want to "go loud".
-Tedious, grindy missions.
Short story long?

Ok, I loved Syndicate and Syndicate Wars when I was little. Seriously, LOVED.
I read about this game being THE remake Syndicate deserved (rather than that FPS, although cool but totally out of context). I approached it thinking "yeah sure, let's keep the refund option ready".
Ho boy was I wrong.
The game IS Syndicate on steroids! An open-world game with massive customization for your agents, an interesting gameplay and massive options for real-time strategy. Hack through consoles, cut wires connected to cameras and gates, hide your sniper, lure guards, acquire scientists, clones and prototypes and fight the opponent corporations!
PRO
- I mean, it's SYNDICATE.
- deep and addictive gameplay
- massive customization
- cyberpunk atmosphere well portrayed
CON
- horrible, horrible optimization... be ready to run it at 30 FPS even on ninja computers
- sometimes the controls and the visuals are a bit confusing
- definitely overwhelming during the first hour
So far I'm loving it. If you loved Syndicate as I did as a kid and if you've waited for a sequel all this time... wait no more and get it ASAP.

Everyone loves a party game - take some frenemies, a whole bunch of dice, and a competitive setting, and let the salty, salty blood flow. Games like Talisman, for example, or your pick of most all physical board games. Enter Armello, another game to scratch that itch. And I for one think it does that admirably.
The gameplay mechanics are a bit complex, but easy to understand after a few games or playing the in-game tutorial settings. The game itself is thoroughly enjoyable, and I've personally enjoyed every game I've played insofar.
That said, this brand of multiplayer isn't for everyone. Those who aren't on speaking terms with Lady Luck need not apply, nor those who don't enjoy losing to a fluke of RNG. As with most of this sort of game, the catch is in the chaos.
The game's graphics are superb, and all the art is well-illustrated (more or less). The art style is something to behold, and all the animations are fluid. Even the rolls of the dice are something else. All the card arts are animated, as well.
In summary, if you like chaotic games of chance, Armello is for you. Go on, pick it up.
And as a footnote: If you really like this game, you can turn a profit off of it. Yes, you read that right. After every match you get a chest or a key which I'm told is worth around $0.25. Mind, I personally use them to try for dice skins, but perhaps you're not so into cosmetics.

I'm only just over a quarter-of-an-hour into this, but already it's a winner for me. As a big fan of the Sky Force game on the iPad, the main limiting factor was having to pilot your ship by touching the screen. It works - but only so far. When the levels get frantic - busy with incoming fire and enemies swirling around you, your own hand gets in the way of the action. As a consequence, it marred an otherwise cracking game.
Now on the PC and paired up with an XBox One controller, the game plays as it always should have done. Vibrant, detailed and super smooth graphics are a treat to look at. The action is pure arcade retro from the 80's and the instant vibe of classic titles such as 1942 and 1943 comes flooding back.
I have this super-scaled up to 4K and it looks stunning. The sound affects and music are pure old skool too and perfectly match the gameplay involved. This is a scrolling shooter to simply jump in and enjoy. No planning, no long-term strategy or weapons selection - just apply your hard earned stars to upgrading your ships(s) as you see fit and off you go.
The genius in Sky Force is the constant battle with yourself to pick your preferred reward. Do you play a level to rescue all the human hostages? Or do you go for destroying 100% of the enemies? There's even a reward for making it through an entire level unscathed. Whichever path you chose adds more depth to the game than simply firing up the screen.
Each level is littered with small scale enemies, through to fixed emplacements, intermediate bosses and final boss fights. As such, it's a varied, engrossing and intense scrolling shooter that firmly places it's emphasis on fun.
9/10 - highly, highly recommended.

Well there's a game I never thought I'd see again. Suppose I'll give my opions on everything then.
Well as far as the HD part goes, I really can't argue with it. It's a very pretty game in comparison to the old versions. I love the water texture personally and the shadows are actually really well done. The controls for Ty's movement are actually really nice. Something about the feel "faster" for lack of a better word, but I actually really like it. Preformance wise, I was really happy. For the most part my fps stayed at 60 but occasionally dropped to 30 or 40 for seemingly no reason. It was never really an issue though as it never went below 30 and even when it did go that low it very quickly went back up. I probably wouldn't even have noticed only for the steam fps counter.
Starting up the game's story, the cutscenes look the same as the old versions which takes away from the HD part of game completely. For some reason I can't move the camera when Ty is mid-air for some reason. I'm able to do that in the old versions so I really can't understand why I can't do it here. The last negative thing I would say here is only annoying more than anything. Whenever I get an item like a thunder egg or golden cog, the tune for getting them plays along with the main music of the stage. In the old version the music stopped to let the tune play and then resumed. As I said it's just annoying, not game breaking by any means. Also I did notice that it really doesn't like alt-tab at all which can be very annoying if I want to do something else while the game is running.
There's also a few things I noticed that I wouldn't even call complaints and I honestly don't care if they ever get fixed I just want to point them out really. Let’s state the most obvious flaw with Valiant Hearts prior to me actually talking about the game itself.
This is a Ubisoft game. Meaning you are forced to use their 3rd party DRM, Uplay.
Take that as you will, I just feel that it is important to mention when it comes matters such as this as many people deal with many issues in Uplay.
The art style in Valiant Hearts is that of a comic book.
In itself, this is no issue at all, it’s perfectly fine. However, graphically the game is unimpressive to say the least.
Countless times I’ve witnessed the camera zooming-in slightly on a certain part of the scene, only to be distracted by the incredibly jaggy lines of objects or general area on the screen which I’ve stumbled upon.
I understand that some would consider this a minor and petty complaint, but as I see it, it is still important to mention as it can completely pull you out of the game while trying to get immersed with the story telling the game tries to offer you.
The puzzles are a weakness of Valiant Hearts. They’re no-brainers, yet at times illogical. They easily break the pacing of the game and disconnect you from its narrative.
You follow our unlikely heroes’ unlikely story through unlikely puzzles.
Most of the time the game is divided to the gameplay (mainly puzzle-solving) and the story. Both of which are the most important, main components of Valiant Hearts as an adventure-story-driven-puzzle game.
Valiant Hearts is incapable of balancing these two pieces, and fails in combining them so they could add up to make this an enjoyable game.
The story is emotional, tear-jerking, and as mentioned – unlikely. All which make it stronger together as a whole.
It’s incredible to think that it’s based on a true story connected through letter from the War.
The unlikelihood of the events of Valiant Hearts are what makes the art style fitting and not just a mean of presenting the irony and contrast in showing the grim, dark, horrific reality of war through a  softly painted world with the aesthetics of a children’s comic book.
It’s also worth noting that throughout the game you are provided with little bits and pieces of information regarding the War. These are very much worth reading through. They are not given to you for nothing and they’re not forced as you can access them through the menu.
All in all, in the end, after crying for a while, you don’t remember the puzzles. You’re only left with this one, final image from the last scene, and the beautiful, mesmerizing, heartbreaking soundtrack playing in the background.
And that’s what makes this experience so goddamn worth it.

Some people are complaining that they can't support a company who re-releases a game a year after it was made just to fix some graphics and bugs. A "Paid for patch". But that's not what this is, its their own version of a "Game of the year edition".
Games and companies have done this for years. A Prime example would be bethesda with fallout and skyrim. they've always re-released their games as special editions with all the dlc included. they didn't even improve the graphics, it was just a straight up re-release. And worst of all, they charged the price of a full 60 dollar game.
This is half that with a really decent amount of content. I'd say it at least rivals fallout 3, maybe rivaling skyrim.
One thing to note is the game can get a bit grindy at times. I often find myself just going back and forth between my base and town gathering one or two types of resources because they're used so heavily. only to get on a few days later to find all of that resource completely drained. There are things you can make and do in game to ease this and i've just not made it that far but it's still a small gripe
The other issue i have with this game is that it tends to expect alot of foreknowledge of you as far as the way things work. I had no idea you could recruit neighbors if you had enough trust with them and talked to the right people. Nothing in game seemed to tell me this (granted i could have missed it. The tip dialogue seems to be either really short and specific, or very long and vague). I ended up watching a youtube series and saw someone able to do this. Which is somethign at the time i had wish i had known.
The main thing is it rarely tells you how things work. It doesn't explain outposts. It doesn't explain recurting members or how you become friends with people (so that you can take control of them). it doesn't explain how much time you have left for missions in any way other than hearing "some of these things are running out of time here" over the radio. Which, when you have 20 "things" on the map, it makes it hard to descern what exactly they want you to do.
One last major dissapointment is the lack of co-op or really any mutiplayer aspects. This game just screams, two friends riding in a car bashing heads in and would benefit GREATLY from something like that. I have however heard the sequal (which was announced last year) will contain multiplayer (as far as i'm aware) so we'll have to wait untill then!
Overall, a super fun game, some mechanical issues but nothing that can't be solved with a bit of research on the wiki. I've had to do that for many a game before so seeing it here is not unprecedented. I'd definintely suggest this if you're a fan of the zombie survival management game.

I have extremely mixed feelings about this game. I put a good amount of time in the "original" version and then went on to get this one while I had major discounts on YOSE. Yeah, you read that right - major
. Here is why I'm conflicted, but ended up not recommending it.
The original state of decay (no longer being sold as of YOSE release) was a game that was quite unique. A third person survival game with base defence, the need to gather resources which are actively used each "day", perma-death, social problems (such as people becoming suicidal or overly problematic anger problems), cars, and rpg elements such as the ability to specialize in certain weapons such as: blunt, edged, pistols, shotguns, etc. I honestly cannot find another game like it, though I wish I could. (This is NOT like Dead State). All in all, quite the good game!
However, with all good things there are bad. In this case, it's the company itself. When they released YOSE, I supported them due to their explainations. They (undead labs) partnered up with Microsoft and, instead of releasing patches to fix and add things, they decided to re-release the game which was a year old. People who owned the original
. This sparked a lot of controversy, but I was willing to overlook the issues and even defended them on massive thread wars. But, the more I played it, the more I realized what was wrong.
They claimed to have fixed the bugs. They claimed that they would support this version. They claimed a lot, but delivered very, very little. The only difference between YOSE and the original is a combat knife (if you are unarmed) which is useless, a few new weapons, all the car models do not look the same and that's.... pretty much it. Those bugs they squished? Nope. Still there - pretty much all of them. This includes such wonderful bugs as: getting stuck on curbs, having cars randomly twist spin into the air and land on their roofs causing them to explode, fps spike jitters (fps drops down really, really low), characters not responding to commands and continuing to do their last command such as run forward instead of turning around (not fun when you threw an explosive and your character auto runs into it while you're holding the back button), and more. They. Were. Not. Fixed. They even said that they fixed the keyboard and mouse controls - my friend got motion sick from the speed differences as it moves choppy one second and smooth the next.
Speaking of keyboard controls, if you use a mouse and keyboard one of the "specializations" is completely, utterly and totally
!!!!!!! If you put points into Rifles (as in hunting rifles) and you use a mouse and keyboard, you have wasted your specialization and you cannot unspec. What the specialization does is that it increases the "snap headshot" area and range. It has no effect on damage, recoil, range or anything else. It doesn't tell you what the "snap" is, so I looked it up and found out that it
only works if you use a controller. The reason for this is because it is literally aim assist that auto-snaps to zeds heads. It does not work with M&K, nor are there any other perks for using it.
To make matters worse, this version was hardly supported as well. Instead, they decided to work on their next money maker - State of Decay 2, which I will most likely only purchase on an extreme sale, if at all. Even their leadboards, which sparked controversy as well in a different way, were (I don't actually know if they are still) messed up. Example: My score got reset 3 times when I was going to get into first place. I was on level 13 breakdown (the endless mode, before it was "updated") and it claimed I had killed literally 0 zombies. Zero's acrossed the board, while on the lifeline dlc "Undead Chris" had saved over 10,000 civilians with the next person down (in 2nd place) being approximately 30.
To close this somewhat confusing review, I guess I would summerize it as this. Is it a fun game? Yeah, I'm still putting time into it on and off as I already own it. Would I say that it was well made? The concept of the game and even it's playability (if you ignore the bugs) is quite good and enjoyable for someone like me. However, would I recommend the game to people? No, not unless it's on a mega-sale such as the Christmas or Summer sales. Do NOT purchase this game at full price if you intend to get it, and keep in mind that it will not get any more support.
Oh, that leaderboard controversy I mentioned? The store page for State of Decay (the original version) stated something along the lines of "Play with your friends!" so people purchased the game thinking there was co-op. There is not, there never was intention and it was mistaken. This was before you could apply for refunds on steam, and people didn't want it if there was no co-op as it stated there was. Turns out, according to one of their people, that it meant with the LEADERBOARDS, NOT other players. So you could play AGAINST THEIR SCORE, but NOT with them. That was the controversy.
Not bad for a 10-year-old game, but there are MUCH better (and longer) shooters out there. Nothing to write home about.

As a clone trooper commander (voiced by Temuera Morrison himself), you command three fellow commando’s during the Clone Wars. It’s a fresh breath of air not to play as a Jedi, but at the same time it just doesn’t feel like Star Wars without a blue or red lightsaber popping up, even though there is an epic score (Vode An!).
Because the game focuses more on tactical combat there are no single iconic enemies to fight, just waves after waves of nameless flying Geonosians and battle droids. You’ll mow these generic enemies down with ease, but on occasion there are great tactical moments where you will need to advance from cover to cover under enemy fire.
There are some caveats though. Most irritating are the flying droids that will zap you to death within seconds, making an otherwise welcome solo-mission frustratingly difficult. The ending seems rushed and unfinished, which is not helped by the game’s short length (8 hours). The healing system is archaic and time consuming, but sometimes this adds to the tactical combat: you let your squad mates heal one at a time while the other two cover them; rinse, repeat.
Republic Commando’s missions never really rise above that grunt work. It helps that one of the commando’s really stands out (he’s probably descended from KOTOR’s Carth Onasi and a forefather of Mass Effect’s Kaidan), but the game misses its one opportunity to get you emotionally invested because of the rushed epilogue.
Republic Commando’s well worth a single play through for all the things it has done right though.

I really wanted to be able to write a positive review and recommend this game, but I just can't. It has fantastic artwork, and *some* fun game mechanics, but its flaws in sum are crippling, and in the end cause more frustration than enjoyment. The game suffers from a combination of excessive luck, snowball effect, and too long average game sessions accordingly. Far too often, within the first 2-3 turns, it's already obvious which one or two players will actually have a chance at winning, while the other two or three players got screwed by RNG. This would be OK, in a game that takes an average of 30 minutes. But to have zero chance of winning over half the time due to bad luck just ten minutes into a one-hour game is just not my idea of fun or enjoyable. For this game to be what it could be, they need to find a way to drastically cut down on the snowball effect, or give players more control over their fate. One idea I can think of is to add a deck-building component, where players can choose which cards will be available to them, so as to be more likely to draw cards that work together and help a specific build; think MTG.

Never having been a strategy/board game player, I had my doubts about Armello and was almost certain I would hate myself for spending even 15 dollars on this. But I promised myself that was the last game three games ago, it's 4am and I still want more.
Even for a huge strategy idiot like myself, the game is relatively simple to catch on to, and as you come to understand how everything works and the various ways to victory, the plotting and scheming is suddenly intense – there can only be one winner. Despite competitive gameplay and false diplomacies (Mecurio, I thought we were friends but I knew I couldn't trust a damn RAT), the developers have done a good job keeping players friendly to each other, with the only form of communication you can send to another player being prefixed character dialogues. Contrary to many complaints of the game being buggy and unplayable, I have yet to run into a single issue. Game works like a charm and doesn't even require much to run it.
Unlike usual strategy titles that require hours of commitment each game, a round of Armello takes only slightly over an hour. Except you're not going to only be playing one round.

My play time for this game is disgusting...  If you enjoy optimizing things, complexity, maddening complexity and potentially destroying an indiginous species then this game is for you.  Though you should really be spending your time programming instead of playing a game.
Part by part
The demands on your computer can be high if you go for some crazy goal beyond the base game but a recently purchased cheap off the shelf PC is good enough to enjoy it.
Graphics: The graphics are reasonable and will be improved before the final release but that's nearly insignificant and no idea what will be considered beautifully polished by the end.  It might get too noisy with flashy graphics.
Combat: The "enemy" AI might benefit from some intelligence if you like the war game but is mostly a swarm you to death type of mechanism.  You can go the game mostly leaving eachother alone or play a boring pacifist version where you have to strike first if you want to fight.  The usual interaction in my experience is turtle away from them rarely interacting until you come out of your shell in complete domination or an incessant struggle to keep your walls together and try to develop passed them before you run out of local resources.
Value: A typical playthrough for myself is about 40 hours so you definitely get your money's worth assuming you play to the end goal at least one time...
Audio: I don't have a comment on the audio... I'm not sure if they fixed the music being too inconsistently loud.  Used to have long moments of silence followed by a building up to extreme volume in some of the ambient music.  I've turned down in the audio controls... There're enough visual cues that I play while listening to music from my own library with the game muted.
Gameplay: Tetris' cool progeny.  The goal is to assemble complicated products from their ingredients ultimately building and launching a rocket.  You can make some things by hand but eventually need to automate the process with machines that make other items and more machines.  This ends up being a fun mess of deciding where to place mines and machines.  Conveyor belts and mechanical arms to move items between belts and factories (assembling machines).
The other heavy gameplay element is resource management, deciding whether to spend raw materials to research a new weapon/turret, improve a current one, build a few more turrets, make yourself some armor or automate a section of your factory better.  This is quite a task early on in the game when surrounded by hostile enemies and not being certain if, when and where they'll attack from versus automating the factory now so you have even more defenses ready in a few minutes.  Later in the game it is more about optimizing your production so you aren't running out of certain intermediate products, keeping the power on, figuring out how to manage a minor chemical industry.  All alongside combat which you can decide the intensity of yourself with the initial start-up settings and how you manage the pollution your factory generates.
Then there are numerous systems and features to play with...
Setting up networks of trains to transport your resources and products around
Setting up networks of drones to fly items around (easier than trains)
Precision control of factory with logic circuit networks
Assembling powered armor and modules you need to customize it for speed or war or rapid large-scale factory building
Setting up a sustained nuclear power plant and/or supply of nuclear weapons (no more difficulty with enemies or large forests)
Speaking of forests... running around setting large forest fires is fun at least once
Fire is well behaved in this game (it spreads)
Multiplayer has come a long way and is capable of supporting tens and hundreds of people if you have the computer and internet for it.
Modding is supported and like most games adds tons of added features.
Ability to launch orbital weapons into space and at least one can be automated to attack enemies
Expanded industries and more complicated recipes (maddening complexity mentioned)
Added vehicles and units to control
If you're on the fence or looking at the fence, buy it at your earliest convenience / ownership of assumed still? 20 dollars.

Magicka 2 is the sequel to the much loved Magicka (This was sort of obvious). Although Magicka 2 has significantly improved gameplay mechanics over the first game, it feels as though its heart and soul has been partially removed in the process.
Magicka is all about wizards and spells and the wacky world they inhabit. While the spell casting is better than ever with the inclusion of a hot bar for quick casting of complicated spells and significant improvements to overall movement / control, the story / plot / writing is significantly worse than the original. The original game while being almost unbearably buggy and in a constant state of not quite fixed was super fun, incredibly challenging and had amazing writing, funny and memorable moments everywhere. The original had references to movies, characters, games, everything and was constantly trying to be funny. Magicka 2 isnt... it is not bad, and it isnt un-funny it just doesnt even remotely compare to the first experience (which may be part of the reason you are considering buying this game).
The game is also sadly too easy and too short. While the first Magicka was challenging and almost impossible to beat in some situations, Magicka 2 manages to be easily completable solo and takes almost no time at all to do so. The game is built upon replayability though so I guess they expect you to constantly replay the same campaign... however with aforementioned lack of the charm that kept me coming back for more of the first game, I sadly do not see the chances of that being high.
Now with all that negativity in comparison to the first game done, I want to stress that the game is enjoyable and fun and should be purchased if you plan on playing it with friends. Solo mode however is not very fun and the writing and enemy variety doesnt justify multiple playthroughs even with unlockables.
Totally worth a play if you already own it and have not managed to get to it yet.

This game is terribly dull - not a single puzzle can be considered fun and some like the button QTEs are overly simplistic and annoying. The puzzles are very, very brainless, consisting of mostly QTEs, fetch quests, and reaction puzzles. Any puzzle you are unable to solve is probably due to bad game design; for instance, there was one puzzle in Chapter 3 where you needed to create a diamond shaped object, I handed in a square and was denied, and only the diamond is accepted. The characters' individual 'powers' make little sense, because apparently only the old grandpa with the big ladle can dig through mud but the muscular soldier cannot pick up a shovel and do the same, or why does one character has a pair of pliers that never breaks while all the others can only pick up one use pliers to force the problems unto the player instead of presenting interesting puzzles. This necessity for detailed solutions shows how lack of attention to details game designers gave it. Thankfully the game is very forgiving with checkpoints, and frequent deaths due to unfair situations can be forgiven. Simple and forgiving however, makes a good game for children.
The collectibles contribute absolutely nothing to the story, and I feel they are just added to pretend that there is a replay element when there really is not. If you need a game that has a lot of padding to distract your children, tell them they have to collect all the collectibles and remember some of the factoids to get a present. Sometimes, these trinkets you collect are immersion breaking too - why would you bend down and collect a small trinket amidst gunfire, or running to save someone crying for help? For a 'completionist' run one would have to ignore all logic in situation and try to search for places that these meaningless items are hidden, why such an option is added is puzzling. All it is, I think, is useless padding to make the game seem longer.
The story, love it or hate it, is completely devastated by poor game design. Emotions sessions are padded with boring puzzles that breaks up continuity, and doing the same old chores simply makes one feel frustrated, but not frustrated in the way the story wants you to feel. Bugs and the distraction of collectibles aside, the lack of attention to scenes, characters and puzzle design is especially disruptive to immersion because that makes up the bulk of the game. There is a part where your character is supposed to pick up the pliers from the floor at the midst of battle, if you press the action button but miss the sweet-spot you have to stand on to prompt the action, your character will scratch his chin and think - all in the midst of heavy gunfire - like he does during other puzzling moments. Why was this overlooked? How could this have been overlooked? This constant immersion breaking experience is probably the worst sin this game has committed. I tried killing the dog, throwing grenade at people, but the world seems to ignore it and never had I gotten a gameover screen other than getting the character you control killed. You can't kill anything in this game. Drive the tank in chapter 3 and do the logical thing and fire the cannon at the German soldiers - guess what - nothing happens. Good games send anti-war messages by forcing the player to make painful decisions that would not have been necessary if it was not because of war, and make players regret the decisions they make, make them feel pain for the people they killed and the buildings they destroyed. Turning everyone invincible to the devastating elements of war and battle, or making the characters unable to pick up weapons and gun down enemies to save their own lives when it makes perfect sense to do so, is not the way to deliver the message.
The narrative in this game is so atrocious that the game feels like an afterthought than an integral part of the plot. It seems like the developers were thinking, how do we make this game an arbitrary length long so that it can justify the price tag, instead of thinking of how the game-play can help to complement the story. There is so much wrong with the narrative that I don't think the game should have been made in the first place. It was a very disturbing experience for me, but probably not in the way the developers wanted. I wrote this review concurrently while playing the game, not because I wanted to write a review, but I felt the need for a rant every time the game breaks me out of the immersion. As for the story, I think it is good, the message is good, but it is honestly nothing exceptional and I would have rewritten some parts of the ending just to knit together some game-play elements and the story to better create that devastating sensation felt from the quote uttered at the end "War makes men mad". The game has a message, but it is as though the developers did not understand that message themselves at all. Chapter 4 is probably the best chapter, but the whole game could have been condensed into a much shorter experience to make Chapter 4 feel more impactful - because a bored man can't feel any other emotions, he just feels bored.
I applaud the team for trying to do a non-FPS war game, but as the game stands now it should have just been at most a graphic novel and not a stealth-puzzle game. The puzzle style can work, because there are parts where the interactive elements of the game actually contributes to the narrative, such as the final battle in Chapter 4. Having a good plot is important, but having little to no game-play elements to support that plot almost makes this title a non-game. The experience feels toned down and censored, prepared for mass consumption but cannot be considered a breakthrough because of the extremely poor narrative. Valiant effort, but still not enough effort.

I have extremely mixed feelings about this game. I put a good amount of time in the "original" version and then went on to get this one while I had major discounts on YOSE. Yeah, you read that right - major
. Here is why I'm conflicted, but ended up not recommending it.
The original state of decay (no longer being sold as of YOSE release) was a game that was quite unique. A third person survival game with base defence, the need to gather resources which are actively used each "day", perma-death, social problems (such as people becoming suicidal or overly problematic anger problems), cars, and rpg elements such as the ability to specialize in certain weapons such as: blunt, edged, pistols, shotguns, etc. I honestly cannot find another game like it, though I wish I could. (This is NOT like Dead State). All in all, quite the good game!
However, with all good things there are bad. In this case, it's the company itself. When they released YOSE, I supported them due to their explainations. They (undead labs) partnered up with Microsoft and, instead of releasing patches to fix and add things, they decided to re-release the game which was a year old. People who owned the original
. This sparked a lot of controversy, but I was willing to overlook the issues and even defended them on massive thread wars. But, the more I played it, the more I realized what was wrong.
They claimed to have fixed the bugs. They claimed that they would support this version. They claimed a lot, but delivered very, very little. The only difference between YOSE and the original is a combat knife (if you are unarmed) which is useless, a few new weapons, all the car models do not look the same and that's.... pretty much it. Those bugs they squished? Nope. Still there - pretty much all of them. This includes such wonderful bugs as: getting stuck on curbs, having cars randomly twist spin into the air and land on their roofs causing them to explode, fps spike jitters (fps drops down really, really low), characters not responding to commands and continuing to do their last command such as run forward instead of turning around (not fun when you threw an explosive and your character auto runs into it while you're holding the back button), and more. They. Were. Not. Fixed. They even said that they fixed the keyboard and mouse controls - my friend got motion sick from the speed differences as it moves choppy one second and smooth the next.
Speaking of keyboard controls, if you use a mouse and keyboard one of the "specializations" is completely, utterly and totally
!!!!!!! If you put points into Rifles (as in hunting rifles) and you use a mouse and keyboard, you have wasted your specialization and you cannot unspec. What the specialization does is that it increases the "snap headshot" area and range. It has no effect on damage, recoil, range or anything else. It doesn't tell you what the "snap" is, so I looked it up and found out that it
only works if you use a controller. The reason for this is because it is literally aim assist that auto-snaps to zeds heads. It does not work with M&K, nor are there any other perks for using it.
To make matters worse, this version was hardly supported as well. Instead, they decided to work on their next money maker - State of Decay 2, which I will most likely only purchase on an extreme sale, if at all. Even their leadboards, which sparked controversy as well in a different way, were (I don't actually know if they are still) messed up. Example: My score got reset 3 times when I was going to get into first place. I was on level 13 breakdown (the endless mode, before it was "updated") and it claimed I had killed literally 0 zombies. Zero's acrossed the board, while on the lifeline dlc "Undead Chris" had saved over 10,000 civilians with the next person down (in 2nd place) being approximately 30.
To close this somewhat confusing review, I guess I would summerize it as this. Is it a fun game? Yeah, I'm still putting time into it on and off as I already own it. Would I say that it was well made? The concept of the game and even it's playability (if you ignore the bugs) is quite good and enjoyable for someone like me. However, would I recommend the game to people? No, not unless it's on a mega-sale such as the Christmas or Summer sales. Do NOT purchase this game at full price if you intend to get it, and keep in mind that it will not get any more support.
Oh, that leaderboard controversy I mentioned? The store page for State of Decay (the original version) stated something along the lines of "Play with your friends!" so people purchased the game thinking there was co-op. There is not, there never was intention and it was mistaken. This was before you could apply for refunds on steam, and people didn't want it if there was no co-op as it stated there was. Turns out, according to one of their people, that it meant with the LEADERBOARDS, NOT other players. So you could play AGAINST THEIR SCORE, but NOT with them. That was the controversy.

Sniper Ghost Warrior 3 is what I like to call a "Double A" game. It almost feels "Triple A", but there are a few issues here and there that stop it from achieving that. Although overall, it's quite a satisfying experience.
I would have to say if you are a fan of the Far Cry series, then you will probably enjoy this. It shares a lot of similarities.
The core gameplay has you scout a location before infiltrating it. You can use a flying drone, or just look at enemies through your scope for a while to tag them permanently with white markers. After you have done so, you can either find a small place to lie your sniper down, and take enemies out that way. Or, go in close and personal with a silenced weapon, and take out enemies from behind. Or go loud with assault rifles and grenades.
I'll start off by describing the sniper mechanics. When you look at an enemy with your crosshair, their distance will appear at the top of your scope. You need to adjust your scope physically according to that. As well as taking into account wind distance and speed. It's a very satisfying feeling to land headshots on enemies after you've calculated it all. Well, as long as you've disabled "red dot aim assist". I'm not sure if it's just normal difficulty that defaults this option ON, but I'd recommend turning it off no matter what.
What does this option do? Well now when you press SHIFT (the button that makes you hold your breath to steady your aim, and slows time down a little bit), you get an extra little dot next to your crosshair. This dot takes wind and distance into account for you, and shows you exactly where you should shoot your bullet in order to hit your target.
It completely takes away the fun and whole point of strategic sniping. It's good that there's an option to disable it.
You also can use different types of bullets. Explosives, tagging bullets or ones that are just meant to make noise and lure an enemy somewhere.
The game has a decent climbing system in place. You can scale buildings and rocks if you find a grabable ledge. When you hold CTRL you'll get this sort of weird vision mode like every other game has had for the past few years. This will highlight items in the environment and ledges you can grab. It's pretty fun to climb stuff, actually.
If you'd prefer, you can go into the base and take on everyone at close range. Pop a silencer on a pistol, shoot guys in the back, backstab, and then move and hide their bodies. It's just as viable as sniping, which is great. You also have the option to interrogate enemies from behind. This will prompt them to give you a bit of a tip. They might tell you "there's a ladder on the side of the building you can use" or "there's an underground sewer pipe". It's a nice touch.
If something goes wrong and the enemies detect you, you can also go loud. Nothing special about it. Just shoot dudes and take cover.
Although one thing worth mentioning is that even on normal difficulty, the game is relatively challenging. Enemies can kill you pretty quickly. You have 3 chunks of health on your HP bar. The first one regenerates over time if you haven't lost it completely. The other two however, you need to heal through medical supplies. Using adrenaline only heals one chunk, but allows you to run while using it. It's good if you're taking fire and running away.
Pills heal 2 chunks, but you can only use while walking.
The medkit fully heals you but you need to stay stationary. All of this is a nice little bonus and indicator of the freedom the game gives you when it comes to choices.
Also, depending on your playstyle, you will earn points for the corresponding tree.
Let's say you perform a lot of melee and close-up kills. Then you will gain skill points for the tree that allows you to crawl faster, or auto-loot enemies when you melee kill them. It's a nice way to give you a feeling of progression for the way you play.
Now onto the open-world aspects of the game. I personally am not a huge fan when games go open-world when they don't really need to. Especially when the worlds are a bit lifeless. In this case, it is a bit lifeless, but luckily the driving is actually pretty solid, and the distances are short. You will also unlock fast-travel points as you travel that you can teleport to in the future. You can also explore the map for collectibles and crafting materials, but I didn't really feel motivated to. The option is there for those who would enjoy it though.
Speaking of crafting, as you loot bodies and open chests, you can gather crafting materials to create bullet types, or tools. You don't get too many, or too little. It's basically just enough to always have what you want, but keep you from wasting things.
And finally, the story. It's alright. That's it, really. It's a bit generic, with forgettable characters, but it's there to give you a slight motivation within the world to do what you do. Although it's definitely not what kept me playing the game. Some of the characters are voiced pretty well, while others sound very amateur. I can say the same for some character models. Some are nicely detailed and look great, while others look a bit plastic. It's a very strange mix.
Overall, the game has its problems, but I'm actually having a lot of fun playing through. Planning your next move and then carrying it out feels really satisfying. The full price might be a big hefty, so perhaps wait for a sale. If you've played Far Cry, that's probably the best comparison I can give. If you, like me, enjoyed infiltrating bases in different ways, I think you'll have a lot of fun with this one. Recommended!

Armello is a strategic and turn-based board game which feels to me like a mix between Endless Legend, Heroes III and competetive boardgames -
.
The game takes place in a fantasy universe inhabitated by animals with humanoid characteristics. Upon launching a game you'll be able to pick from an arry of different heroes - each one of them having special strenghts and traits depending on their "animal clan" (There are rats, wolves, bears and rabbits). The map is open to exploration and consists of tiles.
You'll then spawn on the map and from there on you have only one goal - to defeat the other players and to kill/replace the dying and insane king. You can archieve this by different means, there are four ways to win the game - by killing the king in direct combat, by banishing him through the use of "spirit stones", by waiting for him to die while having the most prestigue/influence in the realm or by becoming more corrupted than the king - and slaying him in close combat. The entire game is round based and lasts up to 10 rounds (~19turns).
Every player starts with a set of cards, some of them being useable skills and some being items. They can be equipped/used by investing spellpoints or coins, thus adding a tactical approach to the game. Items will influence the combat against other heroes and NPCs and you'll have to consider how you want to use them. There are also tiles with perils, dungeons, poison swamps and mountains, all of them having different effects on the characters.
The combat system is heavily RNG-based but also contains tactical influences to some extend. Upon starting a fight each side will throw a certain amount of dices, the symbols will determin the effect (either defense, offense or nothing). The outcome of the fight will determin if damage was taken. You can burn cards to influence the outcome of a duel. If a hero dies he'll respawn on his starting field.
Lastly I found the graphics of Armello and it's music to be beautifully made, and I really enjoyed the combat animations and the attention to detail which was put into the game! If you like competetive boardgames and (maybe) have some friends to play with you'll surely have lots of fun for a long term playing. Playing offline is fun as well, but certainly shorter lasting than the multiplayer!

I’m very much in doubt on whether to recommend this or not but this is my first impressions. I really want to like it and will give it some more time.
The things that’s been bothering me:
There’s an odd pace of perceived speed in the game but maybe it’s just because of the way I’ve played so far. Walking around the district, reading stories, learning how things work, etc. takes a long time. Then when combat comes it seems very high paced and its over almost before it has begun. Aparently you can slow the game down by upgrading a skill of one of the agents but it seems odd that this mechanic is locked for newbies.
Combat, well, maybe I’m crap but every time I’ve been in an all out firefight with all my agents I’ve lost big time. Despite using cover, moving around to better cover, I just keep dying. This feels very unsatisfying that my supposedly tough agents dies at the first sign of danger. This is of course at the start of the game without any upgrades, so they’ll get better but I really should be able to handle the enemies at my current level.
With combat being impossible, I’ve been forced to playing the stealth game making the game feel even slower. Don’t get me wrong, the stealth game is quite fun and works well, but progression just takes too long. This also means that I’m pretty much only using my hacker and the world scan ability of the support. The rest are just tag alongs.
Then there are some minor issues that keeps bothering me. Somethings the UI isn’t as intuitive as I would like and some help messages aren’t really helpful enough. Sometimes a tutorial message pops up but if I’m in the middle of moving an agent the message disappears without me getting a chance to read it, leaving me wondering and frustrated about what I’m supposed to do next. That’s terrible design, right there.
Finally, the sounds of the city seems oddly missing. The music is good and sounds following your actions are good, but you’re in a big and oddly quiet city. I’m really missing some ambience sounds. I’d also like that the NPC’s had some more to their lives than randomly wander in circles. Maybe I’ll see it with more play but in a modern game I would expect people to go about their business and having a daily routine.
The good:
The game feels and looks good, and is a good successor to the Syndicate of old. The graphics are in most cases beautiful, the theme grim and dark as it should be. The story is as you would expect if you’ve played Syndicate (this is a good thing) and there seems to be a lot of side quests you can do.
The agents are responsive and mostly good in their pathfinding around the map. The cover mechanics works good (except in those cases where cameras can see though it). Sneaking in and hacking the different terminals is a lot of fun.
I supported the Kickstarter and was thrilled to see Syndicate revived. I tried it a few times during beta but in the end, I wanted to wait until it was finished. Now that I’ve finally picked it up again I’m still unsure about it. It feels right and good but there are still some polish to do before it becomes great.

This is genuinely one of the best games I've ever played. In fact, "play" isn't the right word for it.... "live" perhaps.
You can't really just play it for a couple of hours and then leave it.
You play it for 18 hours a day for a week straight and then wonder why you're hungry.
Your whole life becomes factorio while playing it, and that's not entirely a bad thing -- there's ALWAYS about 10 things to do.
I need A
But to get A I need B and C
I'm making B but if i do D and E I can make B faster
To get C i need E, F and G
The list continues infinitely, I can't begin to imagine how many times I've lost my train of thought being about 20-deep in distractions.
Yes, it's incredibly time consuming to play it to its best, but seriously, it's the most rewarding experience to improve all the automation, making it more efficient to help yourself later on down the line.
And finally, as long as you figure out robots, this game features the single best inventory management system in any sandbox-like game I've ever played. Gone are the times of Minecraft when I would blindly dump items in random chests to free some space, to never find them again. With Factorio bots, AI does that for you! It's the most joyful experience to come back to main base after an excursion and watch hundreds of flying bots effortlessly manage your entire inventory perfectly.
I cannot recommend this game enough. It's an absolute steal at even 3x the price.

This is one of those games that really makes me wish there were a "meh" option instead of just thumbs up and thumbs down.
As vertical scrolling shmups go, the game is fun for awhile.  However, the game has way too much grinding in it, and that was when I started getting really bored.  You must play the same levels over and over and over again in order to advance to further levels.  It is not that you need to increase your skill in any way.  The enemies on later levels just cannot be killed until you upgrade all your weapons, and it takes so long to get the upgrades.  As I progressed through the game I did not feel as if I were ever getting any better at the game.  I would have preffered to have to play the same level 20 times because my skill was not good enough at first, but I slowly got better.  Instead, I had to play the same level 20 times to get one more upgrade point on my health, shields, and lasers.  Then I needed to play the level another 20 times to upgrade other things.  Proceed to the next level.  Repeat.
It is too bad the grind got so tedious, becuase otherwise the game probably would have maintained being fun.  Perhaps in a future patch they could make upgrades cost less, so that you at least do not have to grind as much.  As it currently is, if you can get the game for $1 or so I guess it is worth it.

This game is terribly dull - not a single puzzle can be considered fun and some like the button QTEs are overly simplistic and annoying. The puzzles are very, very brainless, consisting of mostly QTEs, fetch quests, and reaction puzzles. Any puzzle you are unable to solve is probably due to bad game design; for instance, there was one puzzle in Chapter 3 where you needed to create a diamond shaped object, I handed in a square and was denied, and only the diamond is accepted. The characters' individual 'powers' make little sense, because apparently only the old grandpa with the big ladle can dig through mud but the muscular soldier cannot pick up a shovel and do the same, or why does one character has a pair of pliers that never breaks while all the others can only pick up one use pliers to force the problems unto the player instead of presenting interesting puzzles. This necessity for detailed solutions shows how lack of attention to details game designers gave it. Thankfully the game is very forgiving with checkpoints, and frequent deaths due to unfair situations can be forgiven. Simple and forgiving however, makes a good game for children.
The collectibles contribute absolutely nothing to the story, and I feel they are just added to pretend that there is a replay element when there really is not. If you need a game that has a lot of padding to distract your children, tell them they have to collect all the collectibles and remember some of the factoids to get a present. Sometimes, these trinkets you collect are immersion breaking too - why would you bend down and collect a small trinket amidst gunfire, or running to save someone crying for help? For a 'completionist' run one would have to ignore all logic in situation and try to search for places that these meaningless items are hidden, why such an option is added is puzzling. All it is, I think, is useless padding to make the game seem longer.
The story, love it or hate it, is completely devastated by poor game design. Emotions sessions are padded with boring puzzles that breaks up continuity, and doing the same old chores simply makes one feel frustrated, but not frustrated in the way the story wants you to feel. Bugs and the distraction of collectibles aside, the lack of attention to scenes, characters and puzzle design is especially disruptive to immersion because that makes up the bulk of the game. There is a part where your character is supposed to pick up the pliers from the floor at the midst of battle, if you press the action button but miss the sweet-spot you have to stand on to prompt the action, your character will scratch his chin and think - all in the midst of heavy gunfire - like he does during other puzzling moments. Why was this overlooked? How could this have been overlooked? This constant immersion breaking experience is probably the worst sin this game has committed. I tried killing the dog, throwing grenade at people, but the world seems to ignore it and never had I gotten a gameover screen other than getting the character you control killed. You can't kill anything in this game. Drive the tank in chapter 3 and do the logical thing and fire the cannon at the German soldiers - guess what - nothing happens. Good games send anti-war messages by forcing the player to make painful decisions that would not have been necessary if it was not because of war, and make players regret the decisions they make, make them feel pain for the people they killed and the buildings they destroyed. Turning everyone invincible to the devastating elements of war and battle, or making the characters unable to pick up weapons and gun down enemies to save their own lives when it makes perfect sense to do so, is not the way to deliver the message.
The narrative in this game is so atrocious that the game feels like an afterthought than an integral part of the plot. It seems like the developers were thinking, how do we make this game an arbitrary length long so that it can justify the price tag, instead of thinking of how the game-play can help to complement the story. There is so much wrong with the narrative that I don't think the game should have been made in the first place. It was a very disturbing experience for me, but probably not in the way the developers wanted. I wrote this review concurrently while playing the game, not because I wanted to write a review, but I felt the need for a rant every time the game breaks me out of the immersion. As for the story, I think it is good, the message is good, but it is honestly nothing exceptional and I would have rewritten some parts of the ending just to knit together some game-play elements and the story to better create that devastating sensation felt from the quote uttered at the end "War makes men mad". The game has a message, but it is as though the developers did not understand that message themselves at all. Chapter 4 is probably the best chapter, but the whole game could have been condensed into a much shorter experience to make Chapter 4 feel more impactful - because a bored man can't feel any other emotions, he just feels bored.
I applaud the team for trying to do a non-FPS war game, but as the game stands now it should have just been at most a graphic novel and not a stealth-puzzle game. The puzzle style can work, because there are parts where the interactive elements of the game actually contributes to the narrative, such as the final battle in Chapter 4. Having a good plot is important, but having little to no game-play elements to support that plot almost makes this title a non-game. The experience feels toned down and censored, prepared for mass consumption but cannot be considered a breakthrough because of the extremely poor narrative. Valiant effort, but still not enough effort.

If you wanted to play just one definitive Magicka game, then definitely go and pick up the original Magicka (1) it is better in all the meaningful ways, if you want to play them all though, you can surely pick up Magicka 2.
So how is this game on it's own (with extreme self-control not to mention Magicka 1 at any point, except for just now, and now and now and now....)? Well it's actually really really fun.
The graphics look lovely and lively. Most of the levels look absulutely stunning beautiful albeit each feeling really short, but the load times in turn are pretty much instant.
You have your cool magickal element combining mechanics which are really unique and unlike anything in the other games. This brings with it the quirkiness and fun part of the game where you can experiment limitlessly and panick like hell in the pinch situations where in the end it turns out the main damage source that killed you was actually YOU (it gives nice statistics to mourn at after you've died).
So all in all a good game, with really well done last boss fight. It felt different and really majestic as a last battle should be. The only overall caveats would be an extremely weak storyline, short campaign length, uninspired level basis (here you have your complimentary *dungeon*, also your *forest* and your *castle*...) and as it seems it is with all the games nowadays - the huge and unneede overuse of pop culture references.
And now the question everyone is interested about: how does it stack up to Magicka 1? Well, after playing both of them back to back it is safe to say Magicka 2 feels nothing more than an add-on. It's short, it's unmemorable and does not feel as well crafted as the original Magicka. Well yes, it's  a lot more refined at the techical side: it's gorgeous and crisp with it's antialiased graphics and all, the movement, and interactions feel a lot more smooth, you don't seem to be able to break the main game rules as easily so it's alot more refined of a game.
The main casting mechanics are pretty much the same with minor tweaks here and there. Nothing even worth mentioning, except maybe being able to move while casting. And some magicks have different cast sequences and most of them have now done bye bye.
What *is* missing is the cool and intricate story of Magicka 1, this one falls more into clishe *meh* category.
And to add to that the pop culture reference "jokes". Please tell me again, why do we need this sh*** in every single game nowadays? It's bad BAD BAAAAD. Where original Magicka had, ahem, *original* jokes to tell when talking to townsfolk or really subtle hints at pop culture, now we have full on frontal assault on pop references. (SPOILER alert, do we really need it on this POS part?) It's really screwed-up like oh you know Game of Thrones, here IT'S John Snow, He knows nothing, HAHAHAHA. Oh you know, there's also Hunger Games, let's have a girl puke out something about birds and revolutions. Bleigh..
The real saving grace is though the last level - after all the uninspiring (though beautifully crafted) ones this still hits the same spot but really nicely leads to the grandiose finale. I could argue it's even beter than the last battle in the original one. It's abolutely completely different than that one, for sure but really well done.
At the time of writing Magicka 2 is still plagued by tons of bugs though. The most annoying one: it doesn't seem to be able to save the game settings: every single time it forgot the full 1080p resolution and went to some weird boxed one, or reset to windowed mode for no real reason. Also had a few crashed straight to desktop, and at one launch the mouse was clicking at an offset from the cursor.
So to sum things up: was it the sequel we were all hoping for? Not really. But if after completing the original Magicka you find yourself craving for more, you probably should/could pick up Magicka 2, cause it actually *is* a nice game.

I just got this game yesterday and it is already so fun. It has lots of elements on how a real zombie apocalypse would play out. If someone dies they are dead for good and the game saves all the time so you cant reset to where they are alive (I learned that the hard way).
I do have some complaints, mainly that the controls are a bit clunky and the graphics could be better but overall a great game.
I also love how the ultimate weapon in this game are cars. If you have a car you can last for forever and when you get out the zombies know that they have an opening and take full control over it. The car's horn helped me clear out many of the infestations and save many survivors. A little tip to anyone looking to buy this game... NEVER GO OFF ROAD WITH A CAR YOU WILL CRASH AND DIE! ALSO NEVER DO A MISSION WITHOUT A CAR BECAUSE THEY ARE EVERYWHERE! A car can take out basically every zombie I have come across so far. If they weren't so overpowered I would be more in fear of the hordes of zombies around every corner.
It is still possible to die a lot even with a car and I love how nothing lasts forever in this game including survivors and have lost 2 of the 8 starting survivors already. It happened when I went off road while trying to rescue Jacob. I never got to know the character that died yet still felt sad and regretted my choice. Everything is life or death in this game and that makes it all the more fun.
I would say this game is part The Walking Dead and part Dead Rising. The Walking Dead because you get to love the characters and truly feel bad when they die, and part Dead Rising because it is all out good times and chaos whenever you play.
I also love how many things you have to take into account when managing your survivors and base. If you focus on one thing and not the other you will die a painful death. You truly need to manage every little thing about your character to survive. The clunky controls make it a little bit harder to get out of sticky situations but I still love the game none the less.
If you aren't at least interested after all this who are you and what have you done to your personality. There is truly something everyone can love in this game. I haven't had the game crash on me yet like others have said and it runs well on my computer. I love this game and think you will to no matter what your preferences are.

Armello is a nice looking game, though that's where the positive notes end. I've played about 5 or 6 games I think, and they've all been dreadfully slow paced and most times quite dull. The supposed intrigue between players doesn't really happen, and in my experience there really aren't any big incentives to interact with them at all, except maybe kill them if they venture too close to your settlements. The game is easiest won by grinding, amassing gear and waiting for the king to get to about 3 health, then move in for the kill. Gathering stones is not gonna win you the game unless you get extremely lucky with stone spawning, since moving around the board takes forever and will probably see you perish to the many dangers along the way. I've not tried for a rot victory, but it seems underwhelmning since you're probably going to be weak health wise due to attrition (fellow players have gone for Rot victory about 3 times and not succeded once).
All in all a pretty game, but I would rather play another boardgame irl. This is a slow affair with little few tactical options that loses it's novelty very fast. After the first session of Armello, I found myself constantly alt-tabbing and reading the news instead.

My childhood favorite game. I was so glad when I heard they were porting this game to PC and re-doing the textures. It's exactly how I remember it, except for some new great looking textures. The game itself is a fun lighthearted 3D platformer, lots to do, great level variation and fun platforming. Each level is completely different and offers some brilliant music along with interesting strange characters.There is a sense of accomplishement from collecting the little collectibles hidden in the map, you can obtain multiple new boomerangs from these collectibles. The game looks beautiful with so many colors and interesting enviroments. The voice acting is not the best, but what can you really expect from a 15 year old game with a reasonably low budget. I have noticed a few issues here and there. In the very first cutscene the audio gets really out of sync with the video towards the end of it. Sometimes the camera will just lose Ty completely, but only for a couple of seconds, this usually happens when getting out of the water. I haven't really noticed too many techincal issues other than a very few amount of frame drops, and they weren't too big either.
I would absolutely reccomend picking this game up, and if its your first time playing it, I envy you.
In its current state, I would give this game a 9.5/10. Other than a few minor techincal issues, there is nothing wrong with this game.
EDIT: I have to give a whole lot of respect to the devs who are trying to pin down every single issue that people are having, good on you Krome Studios.
EDIT 2: There have been many subtle upgrades since my last update, they have really enhanced the performance and made it look much better. Easily a 10/10 now.
EDIT 3: All previous issues mentioned have been completely fixed, the game now runs like an absolute dream. Absolutely fantastic work Krome, onto Ty 2!

Satellite Reign is in a paradoxical state of being a disappointing game despite being pretty good. Its extensive potential is sadly (once again) limited by an indie development which didn’t allow squeezing more quality because of a tight budget and so another great opportunity goes away just partially explored. Its gameplay mechanics feel unpolished and incomplete at times while the need of more production value is visible at every corner. Despite being flawed, Satellite Reign stays strong with its liberty of action reinforced by great level design and in depth mechanics which allow the players to approach the game in their own unique style.
The strains of indie development might stop Satellite Reign from achieving the greatness it deserves, but surely don’t stop it from being a cyberpunk delight that the fans of this setting are going to consume despite its problems.
Pros:
+ Amazing neon cyberpunkish style graphics
+ Great level design
+ Suitable music
+ In depth character progression and research system
+ Plenty of tactical options
+ Interesting game mechanics
+ UI design
Cons:
- Repetitive missions
- Problematic combat system
- Sluggish controls
- Performance problems
- The story needs way more development
- The city feels lifeless
- Lots of bugs
