Every overall gameplay element - combat, stealth, hacking, world traversal, hardwiring, character management - fits into every other element with near-perfect fluidity. For maximum effectiveness, you'll be asked to combine various elements at various times, on short notice and under pressure. I suppose it might be possible to set up a near-total stealth run, but the game is much better when you're smoothly blending stealth, combat, and just plain-ol' running away as fast as you can.
Oh - and remember that world scan ability, because you're going to need it to figure out how the world is wired up.
And it's seriously entertaining.
Every infiltration turns into a realtime, high speed tactical puzzle with multiple solutions - including subverting the fast tempo and taking a super-cautious route. The amount of thought and care put into creating a large number of viable options for each problem is very noticeable, and highly impressive. The game is great at making you feel smart; There's a special satisfaction to scanning over a target area with the camera, and finding a really sneaky way to get in.
Of course, there are also the pulse-quickening moments where you suddenly realize that you've kicked the hornet's nest, and the way you came in is NOT going to be the way out.
If there were some way to Frankenstein this with the recent "Shadowrun" offerings, you would probably have the ultimate cyberpunk RPG. Just by itself, Satellite Reign is 100% top-shelf, and a must play.

Valiant heart is one of the most original and unique game I have played in the last few years. The gameplay is nothing exceptional, a few puzzles here and there, some challenging, but most of them pretty straightforward. However, what this game does well is the narrative. You follow the story of a handful of characters during the World War I, most of them soldiers. The game succeeds in portraying the sacrifices of the normal soldiers who fought in the front lines as well as some heartbreaking stories of their families' struggles. The art in this game is another thing that really stands out, and I personally never thought that it would fit a game about war, I was very wrong. They managed to pull off a great narrative off the back of this very neat and simple 2D art-style.

is a game that left me wanting - not wanting for more, but wanting after what it could have been. As a fan of story-driven games and the emotional engagement the medium can provide, I was excited for this game. It promised an emotional story of the normal human lives caught up in one of the most horrific tragedies in human history. Also, it is rare to see a game set in the first World War and I wanted to see if Ubisoft could do the period justice. Sadly, this game failed on both of these counts.
is full of conflicting ideas and design decisions that undermine its message and squander the potential of its setting. The puzzles (the game's core mechanic) are often obtuse and silly, frequently breaking the pacing of the game's storytelling and trivializing the gravitas of the surrounding events. The art direction, while enjoyable in its own right, feels as if it reduces the expressiveness of its characters (who only talk in mumbles instead of real words) and the potential emotional impact of its narrative. As far as the narrative itself goes, the plot acts a WWI sightseeing tour, trying to cram in as many locations and battles as it can while rarely settling on each long enough to give them context or meaning.
I quite appreciated that the game goes to great efforts to show the contributions of all the countries and people groups that participated in the war, including some I learned about for the first time. It features characters from many different nationalities, including a German immigrant in what appeared to be an attempt to humanize the German side of the conflict. This becomes instantly undermined, however, when the game chooses to create a cartoonishly evil German villain of ridiculous propportions. When the game could have easily used the conflict itself as an antagonistic force and a means of driving its plot, it instead resorts to cliches and lazy writing, painting the Great War as a battle between good and evil.
Despite its many flaws, there were a few things I found enjoyable about the game.
provides a lot of historical facts and trivia through its collectible system and in-game menus. A lot of this information was interesting and helped contextualize what was happening in the game. There are some rather charming sequences where you are forced drive vehicles while avoiding obstacles in time to classical music. While the game ended well and had a couple of final levels  that were effective at depicting the horrors and tragedy of war, it was largely too little, too late to make up for the rest of the experience.
If you're really intent on playing this game, be warned that it requires you to install Uplay. I would also recommend playing with a controller. I started playing on my PC with a keyboard and mouse, but the controls felt somewhat awkward, so I completed the game on my Xbox One (hence my low play time).
is by no means a terrible game; it's just a game that could have been so much more.

Armello is a nice looking game, though that's where the positive notes end. I've played about 5 or 6 games I think, and they've all been dreadfully slow paced and most times quite dull. The supposed intrigue between players doesn't really happen, and in my experience there really aren't any big incentives to interact with them at all, except maybe kill them if they venture too close to your settlements. The game is easiest won by grinding, amassing gear and waiting for the king to get to about 3 health, then move in for the kill. Gathering stones is not gonna win you the game unless you get extremely lucky with stone spawning, since moving around the board takes forever and will probably see you perish to the many dangers along the way. I've not tried for a rot victory, but it seems underwhelmning since you're probably going to be weak health wise due to attrition (fellow players have gone for Rot victory about 3 times and not succeded once).
All in all a pretty game, but I would rather play another boardgame irl. This is a slow affair with little few tactical options that loses it's novelty very fast. After the first session of Armello, I found myself constantly alt-tabbing and reading the news instead.

Previously:
The game is a work of genius. Balance, gameplay mechanics, the climactic struggle of heroes and various win condtions, artwork and thematic elements make this game an epic fairy tale with each play. I am amazed by it's simple play and deep strategy. While turn-based there are some real time aspects and tough decisions to be made, and all the intrigue of any adventure novel. Sadly, while the game excels in solo mode, mactchmaking seems to be at times problematic. Groups of friends are able to search and it appears that some are throwing games in favor each other. They have offered a chest or key drop for every game I have played since Art of Treason was released however, which is a really great bonus and incentive. These contain dice skins, many with effects, that are used throughout the game.
The game is casual not competitive as a number of heroes are available by paid DLC.
I can not recommend the game at this time due to the Bandit Clan Kickstarter issue. As I have been able to read it appears that this content was promised exclusive to backers but is now being sold. This sounds like a breach of contract. I think that the developers should not have to have a court tell them to do the right thing. I am not a Bandit backer and I do not need content promised as exclusive, it appears, to those who did. And because of this, I have no plans to buy it. I hope that someone can correct me if I am wrong on this issue. You may comment on my profile page to alert me of this.
It's a great game, the Bandit issue is my only reservation.

A childhood favorite of mine that looks better than ever now! Couple of things I've noticed right off the bat are significant FPS drops just from running around in Two Up, as well as the background music not cutting out when I collect a cog or free a bilby like it did in the original release. Additionally, sometimes the dialogue is out of sync with the animations.
Also, controlling the camera is very difficult sometimes, as it feels like the accelleration is cranked way up proportionally to how I move the analog stick. I have the PS2 release with me and have compared, and it was like that in the original, but an option to adjust camera sensitivity would be nice.
Finally, the mouse cursor does not dissappear when I am in-game and using the gamepad, and it appears that I cannot tab out easily.
Still, these are just little things I've noticed so far, and since it is in Early Access, I figured I should chime in with those issues to make sure that they get fixed and help make this every bit as good as I remember it being!
Moving on to the positives, the HD looks amazing, especially for such an older game, and the reflections are a sight to behold on the highest settings, Controls are tight and responsive, except for that little camera nitpick previously, and Ty controls beautifully. I can't wait to complete this game all over again, especially since my old PS2 copy is nearly worn out!
I've not ventured past Two Up so far, so I'll be sure to edit this review with any other points of interest I come across.
*EDIT* Okay, so I just finished Ship Rex, and I'm a little baffled by a few musical changes. For one, when I obtained the Zoomerang, it played an... odd, foreboding sort of jingle, as opposed to the carnival prize-ish sound of the original game. Secondly, when I raced Rex, the original music seems to have been replaced by a more vocal track. Those are the only two I have noticed, but I'm wondering why they were changed?
Nothing much else to note other than the horrible lag, and occasionally the camera seems to get caught on objects in the world, such as the gate in Rainbow Cliffs.

There are four goals per stage, per difficulty level. They are: don't take damage... rescue all the guys... kill all the doods... kill most'a dem doods. As you achieve the goals, you unlock new stages of the game and new difficulty levels for previous stages.

I would really like to see a selectable difficulty level on the game.  Easy mode, Normal Mode, Ultra-Hard Mode, etc...  Spawning is an issue in my book.  Whenever you get detected, the waves of enemies keeps spawning and spawning and spawning getting progressively harder with each wave.  Once you're discovered you're pretty much screwed if you think you can stand and fight.  You HAVE to run and hope to find a spot to evade detection which seems very hard to do. First, I am terrible at writing. Most of my reviews are not very well written, so don't expect J.R.R. Tolkinesk embelishments.
I have been playing this game since it came out quite some time ago and have lavishly enjoyed playing it! I have a fondness of games with animals in them and this is no exception. In fact, it has been a joy to engage in this fun little computerized board game.
I really like the "Disney" quality animation with the charaters and the beautiful set up of the "board" landscape. It is very intuitive and you can easily learn the game play very quickly! Especially when you start it with playing the "Prologue" which helps teach you the movements and plays from the point of each of the four main characters.
To sum Armello up, it's exactly what I mentioned above; a board game. Not a RPG like The Elder Scrolls games or World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy game series, eventhough it has some RPG-like game play. The character you play is a computer animated game peice you play. It moves a certain amount of board spaces and interacts with whatever is in that board space it lands in.
Addition, like a boardgame, it is random. It gives you a random set of cards and a random set of plays and no two plays are alike. You have dice that you roll for your battles or for removing "Perils" that you enter into. The cards, also, give you some leverage if you have the right cards in your hand. The type of cards that you recieve are by chance and you can never tell what types (in the three tiers that you can select) of cards you will be given when you pick them. If you get to challenge the King you have three types of victories you can perform. They are "Battle,""Spirit," and "Rot." There is one more type of victory you can obtain without challenging the King and that is a "Prestige" victory. As far as I have played this game, a Prestige victory is the easiest to obtain, while the Rot victory is the hardest.
With that, the game is awesome a lot of fun to play. The AI of the "Heros" that you don't play is (in my opinion) astounding. They act as if they are run by an individual person because their moves are so unpredictable. They can attack or choose what to do as if they had a true mind and conciousness of their own!
The board's artwork is stunningly gorgious and the changes of the day and seasons are nice additions.
The UI is, also, very intuitive and can easily be manuvered.
So far, I have not found a "con" I can think of that I can even mention against Armello.
For those with families, the game is definitely very family friendly. No blood or gore in the game at all. Which is a nice reprieve from games that do.
All in all I find this game a real treasure and hope that the company can make it even better and, hopefully they can create a sequil. The game creators have been working very hard to add new features to the game. The DLC "The Usurpers" is out now and is actully a fine add-on to the game with four new characters to choose to play as well as some additional items.
This game will definitely end up a classic!

is a prime example of how to do a proper shoot ‘em up! It’s not a super frantic, reflex driven, seizure inducing affair you find in some bullet hell shooters, rather it’s more subtle, focusing on precision & perfection.
This precision & perfection reminded me more of the older school shooters like
, where placement, timing & learning the waves were key. In
, it is implemented by several gameplay mechanics including medals for completing the level untouched & collecting 100% of the stars, or 100% civilian rescues. These offer a greater challenge than simply completing the level alive, & only when all  challenges are complete will you be able to unlock the next difficulty tier
. Each of the nine levels progressively unlocks as you earn more medals, with your high score being persistent between play throughs as a total of all your highest individual level scores.
progression system really hit the sweet spot for me, offering good replayablity, while gradually unlocking more content & without any grind or difficulty spike to discourage you. You can purchase & unlock more power-ups & with those in hand you can go back to replay earlier levels on harder difficulties or to complete medals you may have missed. The frustration factor is also removed as you get to keep any stars you have earned up to your death, so even attempting a harder level & loosing can help you advance. Dying can also be rewarding ..
.. well for your friends anyway, who can rescue you on the same level
.
I also enjoyed the rescue mechanic, which forces you to remain stationary on screen for a cooldown timer before you pick-up the civilian. It creates some interesting situations where you are challenged by the need to keep killing or disengaging & rescuing first. There is also rarer VIPs to look out for to rescue & the rare card drops to collect which offering permanent boosted effects.
Boss fights were fun & fairly challenging in the earlier stages, but eventually they become a non-issue once you are equipped by a few power-ups for the battle. I never played the 2004 original to compare versions, but this release looks modern & runs well. 3D Graphics are sharp, they have depth & beautiful effects not to mention a decent soundtrack. The level of control you have with directing your ship using the analog stick is excellent, allowing you to pull off very delicate moves, or move at speed with ease. Hitbox around ship is also very precise allowing for some tight escapes at times.
Two player local coop is offered, but regrettably I cannot you offer my views on this as
seems to have issues identifying/mapping two wireless Xbox Controllers
. This makes attempting to play with a friend on the couch a bit difficult
, which is a shame since this is perfect for such an occasion! Another issue I experienced was the lack of controller support when using Steam In-Home Streaming. The game would run but was unable to find the Xbox Controller. Had to install locally to get it to work. There is also no button remapping in-game. When you press 'Play' in Steam, you need to hold down ALT to bring up menu to edit. Should really be in-game in my opinion.
Hope to see these issues addressed in the future. It would also be fantastic to see online two player coop offered for the times you don’t have a friend over or where you’re other friends who play the game are in another country.
For some ongoing competition, there is a weekly tournament you can enter which consists of level of increasingly difficult, randomly generated enemies to kill. You can compete against your friends and the world through separate leader boards. Once the tournament is over the scores are wiped. It’s a good distraction when you are stuck & wanting to try something different, but could benefit from an expanded roster. By this I mean different challenges other than just score based such as longest distance runs, no weapon or power-up runs, power-up only runs! Also, multiple challenges per week, records of wins/medals, highest world rank, how many entered, ability to unlock runs/sequences to play outside tournament etc. Something more enticing to keep players coming back regularly.
is a top quality shoot ‘em up that ticks all the boxes for me. It’s a fine example of great replayablity & finely tuned difficulty scaling that encourages instead of discourages. There are longer term collectables & challenges, plus good competition with friends with online leader boards, friend rescues & weekly tournaments.
Highly recommended!

I've been gaming as an adult since the PS1 and Win98.   I have my favorites like we all do.  But few games really grab me anymore, maybe its age I don't know. I feel lucky to have discovered gaming when I did, each new title was a completly new ride, everywhere you turned gaming was a trip to the unknown.    For me that has pretty much ended, there just isn't much new or fresh,
Valiant Hearts has renewed my faith,  i'm so glad I stumbled on what is in my top 5 games I have played this year, just excellent...what a cool game.    In this age of hyper realistic graphics, the cartoon approach I normally just skip right over,  if you're like me and tempted to do the same thing....dont....the mood and atmosphere they are able to create with such simple side scroll gameplay and graphics is (at least for me) completely refreshing and unique.  This game oozes atmosphere.   I found myself stopping many times just to enjoy the scene and watch all that was going on in the  background.  The animation is adorable while at the same time perfectly effective at getting the point across.  Same to the the gibberish dialogue...in perfect accent.. which is wonderful.  The music is great as well.
I found myself drawn in to the story, the characters and of course the time period.  If you don't know much about WW1 the game does a great job of educating on the basics and will link you to more information if you are interested. I do know a fair amount about WW1, and thought the way it is presented in Valiant Hearts is wonderful and full of tension and weight while still being fun to play... to me that is a feat...the designers should be applauded.   I even got attached to the dog.  I thought the puzzles were well balanced and  just difficult enough to require some thought and a few tries to get through them.   Highly recommended, and appears to be an overlooked gem.

If the fondest of memories aren't what's behind your decision to just flat out buy this, like if you've legitimately NEVER heard of Ty the Tasmanian Tiger at all because you weren't born yet—
Let me tell you Right here and now: (jeez I made the game sound older than it really is)
This game defined a generation's worth of adolescence, and it shaped those people into great people because it was made by a great team of people. I like to think that Ty was a great role model for me when I was younger.
I had nothing BUT Ty, and we hung out together all the time; even warranting further playthoughs because I had the time. No one understood why I loved Ty so much, and some people are just now hearing about him. I personally think it's rather shameful. As with a LOT of underrated games that I enjoy to the fullest, Ty was one of them. But little did I realize that he was more popular than I led myself to believe, as with how I see all these people here on Steam who do, in fact, love him. They love Krome Studios for holding onto the rights to Ty for so long, and with such little funds behind them. But later last year, they pushed out a fourth installmen to this series, and by golly, did people throw ther money at Krome. And with that money, they re-released this first indstallment, in HD.
And again, by golly...<3
It's all here—the core mechanics from the original release for Gamecube, PS2, and XBOX. Every level is the same, the overworld is the same. Every thing at all is the same, but that's DEFINITELY not a bad thing, as it's what the fans loved from before, and still do, and will forever.
-------
For new players, read here:
The gameplay is by NO means lackluster, while it may be simple. It really is an easy 3D platformer with its own collection of...collectibles for you to find. A lot of them are really out in plain sight, but with a lot of those that are in plain sight, you'll sometimes need to get a certain 'rang' in order to gain access to it and grab it. And all of these collectibles help you out in the main game as well. You'll see~
The game—assuming you're new—would probably last you about 5 or 6 or even 7 hours alone, and FULL completion can take you as long as you'd like it to.
I won't say anything about the story, because if you're one of those who is just now learning how loved this series is, it's best to let you experience it for yourself, completely blind, if you're up for it.
Yes, this is Early Access right now, and there are minor—I repeat, MINOR—errors in the game. No real bugs, or anything truly game-breaking, as the game has only needed to be rewritten in every regard. And as with Early Access, you would encounter these should you purchase the game, and your interest turns to adoration (though you might not appreciate the game as much as all of us prior fans do.) But Krome is VERY responsive ALL over the place: Facebook, Twitter, in the Steam discussions... Everywhere. None of your input will be missed, whether it be helpful input from this Early Access period, or just admiration for this game and how amazing in every way it is.
I agree—the price is a bit much if you're just jumping onto the bandwagon, and also assuming you have neither of the games that would give you a small discout; and even with the early access discount, too. But again, going back to how I started this off:
Us fans will GLADLY give Krome our money in hopes that they regain financial stability to become as great as they were before, and it's just so cool that they're still here<3

AHHHHHHH OMG TY ON PC YES YES YES YES YES.
Okay, now that that's out of the way...
Playing this game maxed out at 1440p with a controller, I have little to complain about. First and foremost, the performance needs to be addressed. It is by no means at a solid 60FPS all the time, and I wouldn't expect it to be at this point in development. There seems to be an inconsistent V-sync cap. Sometimes when the framerate dips below 60, it will cap it to 30FPS, and other times it doesn't. Bearing in mind that this game was designed for 6th-gen consoles, it is more than playable in this state.
Visually, there's some bugs here and there, some clipping textures in the HUD, some shaders gone awry (for example, the heatwaves coming from torches at the end of Walk in the Park). Some textures have been remastered and look gorgeous at a high resolution. Others still have that pixelated "Minecraft" effect to them. Shadow maps could do with being a bit sharper. Overall, the graphical quality is inconsistent, but I'm sure the devs will address this in future updates.
Keyboard controls are a cumbersome mess, but I would recommend playing this game with a controller anyway. If the devs fix keyboard and mouse controls in the future then I'd be interested in trying it out, but this isn't a game that demands accuracy so it's not a big deal.
Sound design is a little glitchy too, just minor things I've noticed here and there. At least once, ambient background noise drowned out some dialogue. When you collect items and a jingle plays, it doesn't fade out the level music, so you just get this audible mess in your headphones. Regardless, this game's soundtrack is utterly fantastic.
The FMV cutscenes look HORRIBLE. Completely unchanged from the console days, there's just a pixelated mess all over your screen whenever one plays. In-game cutscenes are a little odd sometimes too, since the animations for the characters are 30FPS, but the world they're in is running at 60FPS.
Okay, now that I've nitpicked over every little thing I've not enjoyed so far, let me just finish up by saying that this game is fantastic, a relatively unknown platformer from the sixth gen of consoles that I've been hoping for years will come to PC. It's finally happened, and for the first Early Access build, I'm really rather impressed. I'm very excited to see what this game will become as more polish is added.

Nullify, AOE sheild + dry off, Arcane. Now, no nullify, your sheild is broken with little to no effort, and it seems they want to force you to use Arcane. Magicka 2 builds up disruption, this ancient spell which makes people drop magicks at will as better than Vortex, if I had Vortex, I would've beaten the final boss without trying. They removed freedom, and nerfed what you have.
In short, if you want more magicka 1, turn around. If you are new, play magicka 1. Screw this game where the only way to win is to spam revive because you just got one hit by the final boss.

Basically when it comes to these sniper games, you have either Sniper Elite, or Sniper GW. One is set in WW2, and one is set in a modern war, so you basically choose a time period when buying these games.
Sniper GW lacks the spectacle of Sniper Elite. In GW3, peoples head either have holes, or they pop open like a pinata. In Elite, it plays a Mortal Kombat Xray clip as you shatter skulls and spines, or pop hearts, stomachs and even testicles.
Elite has the sense of satisfaction of landing a long distance shot with a WW2 sniper, while GW3, well of course you can land that shot, you're using high-tech modern weaponry.
Elite has a variety of difficulty choices, so you can have dumb AI, but immersive sniping, or the other way around. You can choose what effects sniper shots, like wind and gravity. GW has has 3 difficulties and only change HUD and AI
On a technical level, Sniper GW3 is bad. It is a mess. Inconsistant framerate, freezing for about 2 minutes, abysmal load times (i actually thought my game froze as it showed one of those pre-mission quotes, it took that long, hell, it may have actually froze). Jerky mouse movements, no head bob options (in a game that causes severe nausea), no FOV option, etc.
Gameplay? I could only play the prologue, because I felt sick by the end of it due to tech issues and bad design decisions. Specifically; the recon drone (with only one propelling blade - and it functions like it only has one too). a)  it is extremely hard to maneuver, it rolls about very easily. b)  hitting the tattered curtains of the domed facility in the prologue causes the drone to fly backward and spin, like it hit a steel pole, c) it is also very hard to aim, despite using a mouse, it has a momentum to the aiming, so it carries itself away from the intended point. this made tagging the 6 enemies extremely difficult, and when i did complete it, my drone had, not once, but twice, tagged enemies through a very solid building. these 3 issues only increased the nausea the framerate and fov were causing.
Otherwise, the sniping works as intended - line up the guide circle on enemy head and shoot.
Oh, and enemies detected me through a wall
Story; i stopped playing after the prologue, but the prologue was garbage.
Your characters are infiltrating a Cold War weapons testing facility (the WMD kind), and are informed by the pilot that there is a bioweapon in the facility, but have no idea how dangerous it is, and if it is still a viable WMD. Naturally, I thought my character was going to investigate what it was before acting on it. NOPE, your handler comes on the radio and says: "You have to blow that whole♥♥♥♥♥♥up." What? Possibly releasing a biological weapon into our immediate atmosphere. Thankfully Mr. Worst Villian Ever (because he doesnt actually kill the protagonist, leaving it to russian-roulette fate) comes along and captures you before you can press the Boom button. (Also, they enter and exit a BIOLOGICAL WEAPONS TESTING FACILITY WITHOUT A HAZMAT SUIT AND WANT TO BLOW UP A CONTAINER OF THE STUFF, SURELY CONTAMINATING THEMSELVES AND ANYONE NEARBY WITH A POSSIBLY LETHAL VIRUS)

I provided a "thumbs up" to this game, mostly because there is no conflicted mode on steam. This isn't a bad game, but it has enough flaws and problems that make sure its also not an excellent one.
Video:
Text:
As expected the varied mix in quality is the biggest flaw of the title, and this is evident in all locations and mechanics throughout the game, like the developers decided to focus on a few core mechanics, cut-scenes and goals and tried to bridge the rest as half an afterthought and half a desperate attempt to catch up.
The best examples I have of this are Animations and textures. While the animations for character movement, combat and interactions that are central to the game are excellent, other animations (such as facial ones in cutscenes) look very dated by comparison. the VO Work of the main cast is competent, if not amazing - but the VO work for random areas of the game like radio chatter and the like sounds like a group of 8th graders pretending to be " IGOR THE DESTROYER, Comrade."
This again, is not a "Good/Bad" - every part of this game has excellence and mediocrity in spades, nothing is ever truly terrible, but compared to where it shines, the mediocre stands out even more. Neither is it saying that a specific mechanic is truly bad... its always "parts of it". Part of the gun-play is great (sniping), part is meh (pistols), part of the world is amazing (artstyle and setting) part is meh (grass textures for example).
Part of the AI is great (responsive on high difficulty) part is terrible (Triangulation Ai, ever heard of it?).
As i mention in the video, the game takes two steps forward, and one step back - making sure that the game is never bad, but also keeping it away from great. Flawed with excellent parts is the best way i can sum it up.
So overall a tough sell at the full price, but also not one to ignore completely.

This game is superb.  Stellar.  Fantastic.
Saying it is like Syndicate is accurate, only it is much, much better.  And I LOVED Syndicate.
Sandbox cyberpunk city, a crew of different skilled runners, a plehtora of facilities to infiltrate.  All at your own pace.
Want to crash the gate with all four agents, plasma guns a blazing?  Do it.
Want to send in one stealthed agent with proxy hacker to kill the cameras and sneak in and out?  Easily done.
Want to send your soldier to the front gate with a laser mini-gun, creating a distraction so your hacker can slide behind the firing guards so he can put a syphon on an ATM?  No sweat.
How about hijacking a pedestrian and making him assassinate that target so your crew can be on the other side of town scouting out the next heist?  Totally doable.
The sheer number of options available for mission competion in this game is amazing.  I've left agents deep in enemy lines so I could watch guard movements and plan the next attack for hours, all while executing a bank job on the other side of town with my other three agents.  You can do whatever you want, dang near however you want.  Every facility has multiple ins and outs, every camera and door can be taken out in multiple ways, and every carefully planned job can go to crap in a moment.  The game just feels so right, give me a crew, give me augments and weps and gear, and set me loose on a cyberpunk city.  So beautiful.
54 hours in and I have not beat it yet.  Still so much to do.  You can spend two hours just planning a job if you want.  I've spent who knows how many of those hours just hijacking people for cloning to increase the stats of my agents, finding the perfect person, then figuring out how to hack them in the middle of that base.  Do I go in after them sneakily?  Or hack a cop and make him attack the gate and hope the guy I want comes out?  Such open ended sandboxian (may have just coined a new phrase) shadowrunning has never been seen before.
The game offers you a palet of masterful levels, a team of highly customizable agents (towards the end the combo of ways you can complete tasks given the various gear and augments you have makes the game open itself up more and more as you go), a great ambient sound track fitting of the genre, and the freedom to do as you please.  One of the best shadowrun-esque games ever made, and one of the top sandbox tactics games I have ever played.
Now back to figuring out how to smuggle a scientist deep into a heavily guarded corporate facility so he can hack their targeting systems and leave the Eternals with a permanent debuff to accuracy against my crew.  This game rocks.

Was skeptical about getting this game about 5 months back, but then the steam summer sale came by and I decided to try it out, not many board like games come to interest for me. This one changed that, but this review isn't going to be a thumbs up for a handful of reasons.
Pros:
The game has a good tutorial on showing the mechanics of the game. (Compared to others I've played)
It has various victory conditions which keeps it from being a dull (kill everyone else) game.
Characters with different stats and equipment that can change the flow of the match in a single turn.
And many others.
They did not implement an actual chat system into the game. This is actually good because I'm sure you all know how kids online act when they can't get their way in a game. Instead, the chat in-game is by pre-set commands that can be used to praise a player for a good move or to warn players etc etc.
Cons:
When learning the game from a few AI matches, the AI doesn't seem overall challenging, they don't set many traps or use cards to boost themselves sometimes.
Online matches will never be fun unless your playing with friends you know or they fix the current issue. For some reason online skirmishes allow you to invite your friends to fill slots if need be. This is what really breaks the game. In my case I had a 3V1 match because one player had 10+ Prestige, the other 2 players played most of their trap cards on me and prevented me from getting to quests by sitting near each other near it, but let the 10+ prestige player wonder about getting to dungeons to boost themselves. So the match ended with the prestige leader winning by favor of help.
The game is good, but can be better with a few simple fixes, until then I can't give this
game a good review because online matches is pretty much what this game is all about.

I have fully enjoyed my time playing this game thus far and, for a sound investment of $0, it's one of my cheaper experiences. The combat flows extraordinarily well and is pretty easy to understand.
However, this game does come with some notable flaws: Card draw and deck size. There are a few cantrips scattered throughout what I've seen so far, some even going so far as to allow you to take another action after drawing the card. These lack of cantrips can seriously drag a game on or even completly screw an attempt over. You can continue to draw only movement cards, or armor cards, or block cards. This gets highly frustrating, especially when it happens two, three, or even four rounds in a row. Being able to opt into slimming your deck size down might help this a little bit. Perhaps this is handled later on down the line and I just haven't gotten to it.
On the other hand, it does have some great mechanics. Your choice of cards (or, rather, items which have cards attached to them) plays out as a big "Risk vs. Reward" when comparing cards from a single tier. Do you want an armor that has three "Armor 1. Keep."s, or one that has one "Armor 1. Keep.", one "Armor 2. Roll 4+", and one "Armor 2. Keep. Roll 4+"? Further, the usage of monster groups that use a card pool is a very clever idea that I for one would never have considered; it helps to balance out combat between 3 player characters and many more enemies without bogging down combat by making groups move at once.
Overall, it's an awesome game. Highly recommend it.

Throughout the course of the game the player is given the option of changing his/her avatars in tandem with whatever was popular at the time. Their friends also show progression by choosing new icons, biographies, and away messages.
In the protagonists' senior year of high school in 2002, they use a chat client to talk with "emilyluv", "emerly", or Emily. They discuss high school and a fellow student, Brad, who keeps sending Emily messages. They also talk about a party that a classmate Travis is throwing that evening, which they may or may not go to, depending on player choices. Then they say goodbye as Emily logs off.
In their first year of college (2003), the player talks to Emily again, who has gotten together with Brad or Travis (depending on if the player chose to go to the party or not), though she hints that the relationship has become rocky. The character congratulates her, and shifts to other questions, such as their classes. They say goodbye, as Emily yet again logs off.
In their second year of college (2004), the player learns that Emily has broken up with Brad/Travis, explained by Emily as "growing apart", and the character is given the option of consoling her. At this point, Emily either asks why they didn't come to Travis's party in 2002 or why they didn't kiss her if they did attend, depending on the player choices. They both wonder what could have been, and Emily immediately asks if she can come to visit. Most of the time, they will agree for Emily to come, and the player will subsequently cancel their plans with Emma, a friend of the player. The player, alternatively can choose to not allow Emily to come. Emily signs off.
In their third year of college (2005), the player again talks to Emily, who wants to talk things over about her previous visit. If the character doesn't set boundaries and Emily visits, it turns out that Emily and the character ended up hooking up, and Emily feels like she was taken advantage of when she was vulnerable. If the character does set boundaries and they don't hook up, Emily asks if the character had feelings for her when she visited and why they didn't make a move. Alternatively, if you choose to not let Emily visit, she will ask you about your new friends. The conversation is awkward and distant, with Emily eventually leaving due to her discomfort, feeling too weird to continue.
In their final year of college (2006), Emily and the character have clearly grown apart. Emily comments how her life is better now; she started dating Brad/Travis again and is involved in other things. The player themselves have lost their friend Emma, in some cases because of Emily. As the conversation comes to an uncomfortable and cold finish, the character begins to revise sentences asking if the two will ever be the same - deleting earnest questions and asking about the weather or other mundane affairs instead. Despite the protagonist's obvious feelings for Emily, she obviously no longer cares, and as a result, they say goodbye. For the first time, the player character is the one who leaves the conversation, logging off.

Satellite Reign is a small scale RTS set in a cyber punk universe. Imagine a modern XCOM game with a cyber punk setting and real time combat. There are some interesting mechanics and it's very pretty world. As you can see I haven't played a ton of Satellite Reign just yet and I really hope I can play a lot more in the future.
Sadly, at this point I won't be playing any further unless there is some major improvement to stability. While I have liked what I've seen so far the game is very poorly optimized. Most of the video settings had very little effect on how well the game ran for me. The most effective were resolution and bloom. Yes this is fairly typical but I had almost no improvement from disabling ssao or shadows completely and almost no effect from dropping the image quality or anti-aliasing.
To be honest, things were fine in the beginning. I was getting between 40 to 60 fps even though I exceeded the recommended specs for the game. The problem came later when going into areas loaded with NPCs and traffic. Suddenly I was getting 12fps. There is a setting for civilian population but again that had almost no effect on the framerate for me. All in all I hope that I can come back to Satellite Reign some day (and I'll update this review if I do) but right now I just can't stand the poor performance.

Overall I can recommend this game, it is very fun to play for the most part. Yet there are some issues with it, which to some extent are ruining gameplay.
The major flaw of the game for me is economy. You get small amounts of credits from hacked ATMs in real time, which means you have to wait to buy toys you want. For most part of the game it is not a problem, because you are waiting by doing missions and you also get bigger amounts of one time money from them. The issue appears in the end game, when you run out of almost all the missions and you are left with only the hardest. Most likely it is not a problem for a stealth player, but if like me you like to go guns blazing, then it is tremendously important to have the best gear and team setup available. Sadly such team setup is incredibly expensive. I would love to have all the things I want exactly in this moment of my playthrough, where I will be doing last missions, but I don't have the money for it, so I have to wait till I get it, or replay older missions for very small amounts of money (which is basically pure boring grinding). There are still many toys I could get for my agents, but I am far from having money to get them. On the other hand I could just wait for the money by doing nothing at all instead of grinding, but the issue here is that the game pauses itself automatically after some time of player inactivity, which is most likely a protection against exploiting hacked ATMs mechanic.
Therefore I ended up in a situation where I almost completely lost my motivation to finish the game, which for me is a sign of either bad game design or unfinished game. In case of Satellite Reign it is the latter. It can clearly be seen in both, item variety and item balancing. In short there are plenty useless items in the game, like for example implants version 1 - why have v.1 when you can get better version 2 later? It is clear waste of money. Another example is there are three splash damage end game weapons: plasma, laser and explosive. They work in the same way (like a rocket launcher) and the difference lies in their shield/armor/health damages, where plasma has slightly bigger damage against armor, laser has slightly bigger damage against both shields/health and explosive has balanced damage on all defenses. It is like this with every weapon type in the game, but in case of weapons with splash damage the explosive seems to be the best (at least in my opinion), where I cannot say the same thing about miniguns, because energy miniguns are much better, with probably laser being the best. Balancing is only one thing as I said earlier, another is variety and there is zero variety in end game plasma, laser, explosive splash damage weapons, because they work in exact same way. It is literally copy-paste, same issue with miniguns.
To summarize this is still a very fun game to play even with its flaws, but it really could use more work and it would also be great to see more content being added to it.

Like it was made by a bunch of close friends, joking about. Not anymore. Now, it was a good campaign. Although the only entertaining joke I got was 2 people who wanted to mary horses. Might have just been the same guy, actually. But, now that's all humour, what about the gameplay? Turds compared to magicka 1. It was no longer this, play-your-way game. But this thing where the players have next to no tools. Where, rain can make many wizards near useless. And others shake in their boots. Before, there was a way to work around rain. Nullify, AOE sheild + dry off, Arcane. Now, no nullify, your sheild is broken with little to no effort, and it seems they want to force you to use Arcane. If you couldn't use Arcane, you couldn't play in this game. Meanwhile, in Magicka 1, you could cast many spells and magicks without even needing it. Magicka 2 builds up disruption, this ancient spell which makes people drop magicks at will as better than Vortex, if I had Vortex, I would've beaten the final boss without trying. In short, if you want more magicka 1, turn around. If you are new, play magicka 1. Screw this game where the only way to win is to spam revive because you just got one hit by the final boss.

Graphics 100%
Audio 100%
Gameplay 80%
Replayability 70%
Value for money 100%
Total 90%
I picked up this game at random, always trying new Shoot'em ups/bullet hells. This game is not really a bullet hell before you encounter the bosses though.
The first thing that struck me, was the very nice graphics. And that is really important in games like this, or else it would  boring quick. The enemies and backdrop are animated nicely, using colors as it should be. Along with tight controls (only tried keyboard) did make a good first impression. The music, sound and speech is spot on: Fitting, and no way annoying after playing for several hours.
I discovered however, that the gameplay was not up to par with the rest. Instead of creating a proper ammount of levels, the game is locked down by goals instead. You end up doing the same maps over and over again. This is because you have to get a certain ammount of total goals, before the next level is unlocked. And they are all the same on each map, except for one: Kill 70%, 100%, Rescue all the pilots and don't get hit a single time. To help out getting further, you permanently upgrade your plane, so each map becomes easier each time. I feel this is a bad choice of extending the game. The bonus level after you kill the boss, however, is a much better designed level. A few of these, and the game didn't have to rely on doing maps over and over to progress. The last level actually pulls up the score a bit.
Another thing that puzzled me, was the lack of help for the keyboard controls. After a while, you unlock one-shot mechanics (shield, laser etc) and they have to be fired manually. But the game doesn't tell you which keys. And it goes without saying that I haven't found a way to rebind the keys either.  For the record: you can pilot the plane with arrow keys, and wasd. The specials are fired with 1, 2 and 3. Since the main guns and missiles are autofired, I thought perhaps the one shots fired automatically too. But it didn't. So a little ingame-help would have been nice.
So how long do I think I will play this game? Well, the review was written after 2 nights of a total of 6 hours of gameplay. I have beaten the main boss and the boss on level 9. But I haven't unlocked all the goals or the steam achivements. I feel I might go back to play a little bit more. But the goals are pretty non-inspiring, so I doubt it will be a game I play for more than 10-20 hours. Might fire it up from time to time though.
So, the final question, was it worth my time and money? I will say absolutely. The game is a very solid shoot'em up, despite the choice of progression system. Perhaps this is how PC-arcade games have to be made, to compensate for the lack of quarters.

Valiant Hearts is a gem.
It wasn't wildly promoted as some of the studios predecessors, but it is as lighthearted and beautiful at it is deep in it's message.
A must buy if you like to play story driven games.
Story:
You follow 4 intertwining stories of people affected by the the first world war as you travel through historical events common during that time. I admit that it got me thinking about how war changes people, and the ending was really something. it's really the strong suit of the game, makes you not only experience war from a different perspective as it makes you feel for the characters. Ubisoft's storytelling at it's best. 9/10
Gameplay:
The gameplay itself is quite rewarding, For starters, you're not exploding everything in sight. This is not the typical war game. you have some puzzles to make in each chapter, mostly based in exploring your suroundings. and as you do that, you get a folder of information, historical facts and even photos that depict the many aspects revolving around WWI, you end up learning, or rememebering some things in the way. 8/10
Graphics:
The art though seemingly simple and some may even say childish suited the game, don't be fooled by the goofy looks of the characters though. 7/10

You beauty! What a wonderful nostalgic feeling it is to replay my very first and favourite Playstation 2 game on PC in High Definition, such a really great port too!
Running silky smooth with no lag or errors or anything, the controls feel tighter and more responsive than ever, little tweaks have been made to make it a really great experience, the colours are bright, sharp, and the whole game looks and plays amazingly.
Ty, for those unaware, is a 3D action platformer, in the vein of Spyro the Dragon or Banjo Kazooie (although I always thought it would be as if Crash Bandicoot was made into a 3D open world platformer, judging by the style, enemies, location) Whilst platformers were more abundant than hydrogen back in 2002, its so fresh and awesome to see a classic platformer like this getting a facelift and being released on PC in 2016. I absolutely loved this game when it came out and having played it for an hour this evening, straight on launch, my rose tinted spectacles were not needed. The game is amazing, fun, slightly silly but genuinely exciting. Its easy enough for newcomers to platforming won't have too much of a challenge at first, but enough so that veterans will have a great time searching every huge level for every single shiny thing to collect. I really love the plinky plonky sound collecting opals makes, and just enjoying the feeling of running around on the beach in ship rex, its like liquid nostalgia is dripping through my PC.
As for other thoughts, I would be interested to see antialiasing turned on (rather than being forced by my graphics card) as when I first booted the game up, there wasn't any. Perhaps a few more options considering it is running on PC? (The game had a hard time deciding which of my multiple monitors to run on at first) it would be cool to alter a lot more in depth settings the game has to offer. I'm assuming it being early access the textures will be upgraded? Like on the boomerang start menu, it is very low textured, the same with some parts of some levels. At the moment it feels like its a 1:1 port of the PS2, lets aim to make Ty feel comfortable in 2016, yeah?
Thank you for bringing Ty out of retirement and back into the real world again, its been too long. I had a glint of hope supporting Ty 4 on PC would reinitialize the franchise, so glad to see it paid off!

This game has been in development for years and in my honest opinon, the game does not reflect this. I believe a much smaller team of around 10 people could have achieved what this game has in the same time frame.
To start off the game is still very buggy and with simple things such as key bindings not working properly. I had to redo the prologue because i was stuck in a car and the exit button just would not work. Also for the whole game I was unable to pick up bodies from enimies I had just killed which meant I was constantly alerting other players when they saw them so I had to take them out quickly too. Pros:
-The sniping is fun, i had to turn the bullet cam off after the first few missions though as i found it more satisfying seeing the bullet hit the target from where you shot but this is totally optional.
-Open World
-Love the scope animations for changing the distance and the zeroing.
Cons:
-Bugs
-Repetitive
-Boring storyline, (Ending Sucked)
-Zeroing didn't seem to have much of an effect. I could scope in on most NPC's and when holding my breath still hit them at most distances.
-Missions are confined to an area of the map which means you rarely get over the 250m mark. Shame for a sniper game when you are wanting to make them insane long shots.
I feel as though they have been heavily inspired by Far Cry 3/4. It certainly feels like FarCry but it is no way near as good.

"Oh My God, I'm a Jerk" Simulator 2015.
Ironic, I suppose, that the gameplay is built around a nostalgic recreation of online communication, but it only really allows
communication. Maybe this is an intentional commentary on how terrible teenagers are at things like emotional honesty. Maybe they are simply doomed to screw it up.
I can respect an interactive story that sacrifices player agency to preserve an intended message. The game is an artistic expression; I'd say the creator's message is of utmost importance. The delivery, however, feels frustratingly heavy-handed.
I'm not unhappy because the scenario is "unwinnable" (indeed, the attitude that it
be "winnable" is problematic). Rather, I'm annoyed because I made choices thinking they were honest, straightforward, and kind ones, and the player character
ended up hurting Emily. Sure, that happens in real life, too - but here it felt like I selected something innocuous and the player character went off and did something stupid off-screen, beyond my control. This only served to alienate me from them.
But let's not forget that Emily is supposed to be her own person, with her own take on things. Let's not neglect to give her character agency just because she's the NPC. If she were a real person, we would respect her right to be upset, or dissatisfied, or uncertain of what she wanted, right? We would respect her right to change her mind, wouldn't we?
Wouldn't we?

I'm recommending this game because it's free -- if it were a paid game, the review would be different. But as it's free, I'd definitely give it a quick go, just to experience the story once through.
That being said, this is a story game that can truly only be experienced once. After that, you'll find yourself hating not only Emily, but also the game (I'm sorry, devs).
I recognize that at 1.5 hours, I haven't finished the "full game" -- but I have completed the story of the game three different times. As someone who loves player-choice games, I thought this game would be perfect for me.
Alas, such is not the case.
Emily is Away is a player-choice, button pressing game. Your interaction with Emily changes depending on what you choose, and the gimmick works and is good -- I enjoyed it tremendously and it deeply reminded me of my AIM life. You can play as whomever you want, as your character's gender is never even mentioned, and I appreciated that as well.
What I didn't appreciate was the identical dialogue and the "losing" in the game.
Let me explain.
There never is a positive outcome of the game at all. Ever. Not only that, but the majority of the "you lose" dialogue cycles -- so you don't even get to hear how much you screwed up in an interesting way.
Every option ever directs you to another failure. If you hang out with her, she's mad. If you asked to be her friend, she's mad. If you don't hang out with her, she's mad. There's no way to win, making this game one with no replay value and... kind of just depressing and heartbreaking. There's no way to win. I understand things happen eventually, and sometimes there's no way to win, but at times, it feels like she's just mad at your choices for no other reason than for you, as a player, to no longer be her friend. That's it. Completely out of your control. It's ridiculous.
That being said, I guess it's worth a single playthrough. But no more.
Games succeed when they make you feel that YOU screwed up, and that's why the outcome is bad.
Games fail when they make you feel that there is no right way to play, and the outcome is bad because the writers and devs hate you.
Unfortunately, this game falls into the latter category.

ORIGINAL REVIEW / TL;DR:
Best zombie game on the market. All it needs is co-op, and we're getting that with State of Decay 2.
NEW REVIEW:
I didn't expect this to become the top review, so I'm rewriting this review...
First off, many of the negative reviews for this game are those who bought SoD before YOSE came out. I agree with these negative reviewers that this is a sham deal on the publisher's part making people pay for a repackaging of the game. YOSE is essentially SoD with all the DLCs and improved graphics, so if I had bought SoD before YOSE came out, I'd be upset too.
State of Decay is certainly a different type of zombie game, as it is one that you can play at your own pace and unlike many other zombie games you actually work to try to form a civilization out of the apocalypse. I haven't played every single zombie game, but I've played ones like L4D, CoD Zombies, The Walking Dead, DayZ, 7 Days to Die. SoD is definitely my favorite out of these because it couples an open world with characters that have personalities that can grow onto you. So I guess you could call this game a cross between the Walking Dead and DayZ.
Another thing that makes this game more interesting is character death. Once a character dies in a playthrough, they stay dead for good. This has resulted in me deleting my save at one point because my best character got killed in an attack. It certainly changes the dynamic of the game, and even the characters who remain alive address the death of a character.
The game is very well developed mechanically. I never ran into any game breaking glitches during my first playthrough, if any glitches at all, honestly. The game is good on this aspect, although the game still has a bit to be desired in the graphics department. I don't mind that seeing as this game is about two years old and never saw a physical release until YOSE released on Xbox One.
Now for actual gameplay:
In short, the game is fun to play. Melee combat (which is the majority of what you'll be doing in SoD) flows very smoothly, with fluid hacking, slashing, and swinging animations. It doesn't look like you're swinging at air when you're trying to fight off zombies. Shooting is also a lot of fun. The reload times are pretty realistic (meaning they're not very fast). This can make or break the game for you, depending on who you are, but I personally love it. You also can't spray everywhere with automatic weapons and hit your targets like you can in other shooters. I think the devs did a great job overall with combat.
Driving is okay, I wish the vehicles were a bit faster/more durable than they are. Also on vehicles, they can't be modded with things like bullbars, armor, etc. Although the driving in game isn't great, it isn't unbearable either. It works well for what it is, and running over a horde of zombies is always a blast.
Scavenging is also a lot of fun. Essentially, you comb through buildings, landmarks, etc. for supplies to bring back to your settlement. The types of supplies vary (food, medicine, ammo, etc.) When you find supplies, you can only carry one rucksack-full at a time, so it's always best to bring a vehicle with you and possible other people from your settlement to scavenge with you. Supplies also don't respawn in the buildings you scavenge as far as I know, so you can play at your own pace as long as you can find supplies. I'm sure anyone can finish the game before they run out of places to loot so this isn't really a problem.
The single complaint I have about this game is that there's no multiplayer, but that doesn't really stop me from having a lot of fun with this game. It has so much replay value. Co-op will be coming in SoD 2, though.
I barely scratched the surface of this game while writing this, there is so much more to this game than what I went over. It is certainly worth full price in my mind, so give it a go. Definitely buy it if you see it on sale, though. You won't regret it. 9.5/10.

Magicka 2 is not quite as strong as its predecessor, but it is a Magicka game nonetheless.
Let's get the bad stuff out of the way first.
(-) The innovative charm has worn off a tad and the over-hype didn't help.
(-) The game doesn't have as much content as the first one.
(-) Balancing the spell strength was something that many players resented,
since a lot of the fun in Magicka resulted from having a spell system, too powerfull to handle,
that few people knew how to use. Players were their own worst threat, which was funny.
However, once people figured out the most effective spells, players turned out to be just overpowered.
(+) Since most Magicka 2 players are veterans, it was a logical decision to balance the difficulty and keep the game interesting.
Despite these shortcomings, the distinct Magicka-ness is still there.
What Magicka was always good at, was juggling elements (pun intended) that make the game feel childish, yet adventurous and epic at the same time.
(+) A unique game mechanic that allowed for both jovial and explosive experiments as well as serious and challenging gameplay.
(+) Additional functions, such as the 4 instant-spell-slots, and spell reactions, like the poison element, the automatic spell prisms and the beam annihilation (especially this one).
(+) Another epic story, filled with the shenanigans, fitting for this universe.
(+) A unique final wizard battle, with a clever mechanic, that extended beyond “shoot it dead“
(an improvement from the trivial “Corporealize“ concept, already present in the first game).
In conclusion, not the novelty the first game presented, but a solid sequel for any Magicka enthusiast.

You'll die, but that doesn't mean the end of the game. You'll restart on your clan base again and the only thing you'll lose is prestige, which is a very important stat to win the game.

Like Civilization and Kerbal Space Program before it, Factorio has a unique ability to timewarp players hours into the future unbeknownst to them.  You've got to keep a real close look at a clock if you're going to play this game anywhere close to bedtime.
There's also more to improve on your base setup in Factorio.  Whether it's expanding into more land by wiping out biter nests and placing turrets to hold territory, building more mining outposts to increase the flow of resources, tweaking your rail setup, tweaking your factory, adding more assembly lines for materials and parts, fixing the flow of items through your base, or even looking up other players' blueprints online, there's always something more to do in Factorio.
It's a gigantic resource optimization and logistics game.  It's the eternal struggle of buying more dip because you ran out and you still have chips left, and then later buying more chips when those run out and you still have dip, ad infinitum.  And like Minecraft, once you get bored of the base game, there are several widely played mods that change everything (such as Sea Block) and essentially give you another game to learn afresh.
Factorio will certainly appeal to anyone who likes strategic/thinking/puzzle games, and especially to any engineers out there (software/hardware/otherwise).  To give you an idea of how deep the rabbit-hole you can go: Factorio is Turing-complete.

"Oh My God, I'm a Jerk" Simulator 2015.
Ironic, I suppose, that the gameplay is built around a nostalgic recreation of online communication, but it only really allows
communication. Maybe this is an intentional commentary on how terrible teenagers are at things like emotional honesty. Maybe they are simply doomed to screw it up.
I can respect an interactive story that sacrifices player agency to preserve an intended message. The game is an artistic expression; I'd say the creator's message is of utmost importance. The delivery, however, feels frustratingly heavy-handed.
I'm not unhappy because the scenario is "unwinnable" (indeed, the attitude that it
be "winnable" is problematic). Rather, I'm annoyed because I made choices thinking they were honest, straightforward, and kind ones, and the player character
ended up hurting Emily. Sure, that happens in real life, too - but here it felt like I selected something innocuous and the player character went off and did something stupid off-screen, beyond my control. This only served to alienate me from them.
But let's not forget that Emily is supposed to be her own person, with her own take on things. Let's not neglect to give her character agency just because she's the NPC. If she were a real person, we would respect her right to be upset, or dissatisfied, or uncertain of what she wanted, right? We would respect her right to change her mind, wouldn't we?
Wouldn't we?

I'm recommending this game because it's free -- if it were a paid game, the review would be different. But as it's free, I'd definitely give it a quick go, just to experience the story once through.
That being said, this is a story game that can truly only be experienced once. After that, you'll find yourself hating not only Emily, but also the game (I'm sorry, devs).
I recognize that at 1.5 hours, I haven't finished the "full game" -- but I have completed the story of the game three different times. As someone who loves player-choice games, I thought this game would be perfect for me.
Alas, such is not the case.
Emily is Away is a player-choice, button pressing game. Your interaction with Emily changes depending on what you choose, and the gimmick works and is good -- I enjoyed it tremendously and it deeply reminded me of my AIM life. You can play as whomever you want, as your character's gender is never even mentioned, and I appreciated that as well.
What I didn't appreciate was the identical dialogue and the "losing" in the game.
Let me explain.
There never is a positive outcome of the game at all. Ever. Not only that, but the majority of the "you lose" dialogue cycles -- so you don't even get to hear how much you screwed up in an interesting way.
Every option ever directs you to another failure. If you hang out with her, she's mad. If you asked to be her friend, she's mad. If you don't hang out with her, she's mad. There's no way to win, making this game one with no replay value and... kind of just depressing and heartbreaking. There's no way to win. I understand things happen eventually, and sometimes there's no way to win, but at times, it feels like she's just mad at your choices for no other reason than for you, as a player, to no longer be her friend. That's it. Completely out of your control. It's ridiculous.
That being said, I guess it's worth a single playthrough. But no more.
Games succeed when they make you feel that YOU screwed up, and that's why the outcome is bad.
Games fail when they make you feel that there is no right way to play, and the outcome is bad because the writers and devs hate you.
Unfortunately, this game falls into the latter category.
I made the wrong choice and the game forced me to feel. This game's good if you're into that sorta thing.

(This is not exactly a negative review, but more of a "Meh" review. This game can be nice for you, and i liked it for quite a while. But if you don't like losing in a game, even if you did very well... then this is not a game for you... and so is Mario Kart. Also, I am not talking about every aspect of the game, just about something that has been bothering me)
The fact that each player takes their turn one after the other ruins some of the fun for me. At the beginning of the game it is decided who gets to play their turn first each day/night, for the rest of the game. To me, being first gives you quite a list of advantages that outweights the advantages someone might have, that is last.
Here are a couple of scenarios where this bothers me:
(Note that to win the game, all you can really do is trying to shift the chances to your favor)
- You can win the game by having the most prestige of all players. If there is a tie, the person that got this amount of prestige first, wins. Being first to take your turn generally gives you a better chance at getting this prestige first, giving you a better chance at winning like this in general.
- You can win the game by collecting enough spirit-stones and then entering the castle. Spirit-stones will spawn each night in one of the stone-circles. The first person to take the stone gets and keeps the stone, no matter what. If the game decides that you are first overall, you have a better chance at grabbing a spirit stone, since noone else can take their turn before you do.
- The two other ways to win the game need you to kill the king. This is where it doesn't bother me just as much, but it still bothers me. Getting into the castle and killing the king is hard, but once you are inside the caste, it is always possible to kill the king. If you go inside the castle and fail to kill the king, maybe even lowering his health, this leaves a gap that everyone else can use to easily get inside the castle. First off: Being first gives you the chance to kill the king first. And it is ALWAYS possible to do so, even if not very plausible. Second off: If the first person fails to kill the king, the second person now has a good chance at entering the castle. So if you are last, you need to wait for the your turn to use this gap. Given that it takes a full day or night until they can actually enter the castle, you can only really use the gap, if someone else kills the person that's trying to get inside the castle... which can definitely happen. It's just the idea that the odds are against you there that bothers me, but it's not a big problem overall, which is why it doesn't bother me that much.
Overall, Armello is really not a game that you should play with the intend to win. The odds can be against you really badly, which wouldn't bother me if a game wouldn't last ~1hour!

Truly the best World War I game I've ever played. Granted its one of the only WWI game I played, but as someone who have played many war base game ranging from FPS to RTS, this easily blow  all of them out of water in terms of story.
Story:
Valiant Hearts follow around Emile, Karl, Freddie, and Anna through the war. You watch as all their stories line up together and they must help one another to survive. The fact that they tell this story with virtually no dialog is amazing. The characters simply grunt and show speech bubbles with a picture in them to get their point across. Even with the this cartoonish way of communication and in the art style, the game nail the style and atmosphere of this time period. Honestly I wish I could speak more about each character story but I don't want to spoil any part of it. Also it was nice to see that they added a historical fact tab so that you could get some real facts on WWI. Always nice when a game include little bits of facts over whatever time period they're covering.
Gameplay:
The gameplay involve moving one of the control characters throughout a 2D map to find items or tools to help you to complete task or solve a puzzle. The player actions is generally limited to throwing and pulling levers, but there are some characters with special abilities or tools. These special abilities generally have a slightly different play style to give you some uniqueness between each character. Such as Emile being able to dig through certain areas or Anna doing button prompting mini game. Nothing ground breaking, but the puzzles are enough to keep you entertained and can even stump you sometime.
Final Comments:
I know WWI is a hard era to make a game for since so much of it was static trench warfare. Most people don't want to play a game where you spend half the game in a trench and the other half running through a kill-zone while you get riddled with machine gun fire and artillery barrage.  But Valiant Hearts use this to it advantage by focus on the individuals force to deal with these horrors. You become attached to these characters, and don't want to see bad things happen to them. This attachment motivate you to keep playing to see how this war will end for them. Also I like how they just don't straight up demonize one side as the "bad guy" but rather show that at the end of the day, it was just a bunch of people fighting to stay alive and get back home.
I would easily trade in many of the Call of Duty, Battlefield, and other war games campaign stories for this one. I found great pleasure in the game and even greater in the story it told.

Plus there's a few good mods for the game. Definitely pick this one up.
Classic FPS shooter in the Star Wars Universe, NICE!

Republic Commando is a pretty unique game... well for Star Wars, but nevermind that. It's refreshing to see a Star Wars story that doesn't care about light/dark side schenanigans. You never pick up a lightsaber, you never listen to sage jedi wisdom, you never even hear a single jedi voice. Rather, it takes the standard 4-man tactical blah blah blah and puts it IN SPAAAAAACE.
However, Republic Commando does one unforgivable thing that pisses me off to no end: It throws infinitely respawning enemies against you while giving you limited ammunition. You're suppose to tactically flank these enemy spawners and draw fire as a squadmate goes to disarm it. However, the game seems to forget about this premise by the second half of the game. There's a specific part late in the game where there are several of these enemy spawners at the top of a stairwell, with no other path foward. The only thing you can do is just brute force your way through it. Then the near exact same scenario is repeated again. It's like moving a truck by repeatedly punching it, hoping it moves far enough before your fist breaks. I could forgive the game if this just happened once or twice, but the second half of the game is FILLED with these sort of scenarios.
The game is definitely interesting enough to bring you through to the end. However, it was an experience that I stopped enjoying about halfway through. However, the parts without said enemy spawners were fun and possibly worth the price of admission.

I'm not easy to please and came in expecting disappointment. Judging from all the hate you'd think the game is a buggy mess with serious performance issues and lackluster gameplay. That's not my experience from two hours play (Hard difficulty), but maybe it gets awful later
Keep in mind that SGW3 is discounted in price compared to AAA games. This doesn't excuse problems but is worth considering over AAA priced games like Sniper Elite 4. I've played all the recent AAA shooters and am comparing this to them
Performance: it hasn't dropped below 60 @ 1440p High/Very High on my gtx 1070 + 6600k. Many complained the initial loading time was around five minutes. On my hard drive it was less than two. Remember how long GTA and Doom load even on SSDs? It only loads once after the prologue so even five minutes isn't bad
Controls & options: not good enough. No FOV, motion blur, or toggle iron sights (rather than holding down). Settings are limited but not a serious hinderance
Graphics: colors are a bit saturated making environments pretty. Graphical fidelity is below AAA but not bad
Gunplay: it's the best recent sniping game period. I'd describe it as a good version of Ghost Recon Wildlands or MGS5. Sniper Elite 4 is terrible by comparison (and let's be real, gunplay in SE4 is bad). You can actually see where your shots land (unlike SE4) and the wind feels realistic (albeit a bit wonky). In SE4 you're almost forced to use the aiming assistance whereas here I feel like actually have control over where shots land
I've enjoyed using all the guns so far, except the sights on the second unlocked pistol. The AK47 has a nice kick. Silencers have a limited life (much longer than MGS5) but can be repaired in field. There's other various gadgets that I haven't yet used. Enemy gun variety is lacking
The drone flies much better than GRW by moving around instead of being a static platform. Multiple mods can be attached at once unlike GRW. Tagging is less precise though and you will want to rebind the keys
AI isn't good. They're very accurate and appear to alert immediately and precisely when the player is spotted. Not good
Setting: I was impressed by some of the setpieces - the best example being the dome in the prologue. Most aren't too interesting though, like copy paste buildings and drab rocks. I can see it getting boring
Story: I expected the worst but thankfully it's decent and the intro short. Nothing to complain about if you know what to expect. Cutscenes look dated
Crafting, Leveling, Upgrades: Crafting is composed of finding parts (explosive, mechanical, electronic) and combining into different ammos and gadgets. There's three perk trees which level independently. Perks aren't very interesting - kinda like GRW. All enemies drop money which can purchase items and ammo, I haven't found a need to craft them yet. Guns unlock through missions or picking up on the ground. Gun upgrades are good
Bugs: I've encountered one bug - the mouse doesn't appear in menu or map. It works but is invisible. Haven't seen this reported and it may be due to my two controllers and gameboard also plugged in. Oh well
Recommended so far if you like sniping games. Lacking in some areas but when compared to SE4 the gunplay and immersion is no comparison and it's less expensive
