SGW3 takes Call of Duty, Modern Warfare's "All Ghillied Up" and makes it into its own little game.
You play as Marine, John North, older brother to Robert North. Your mission is to take down a secret group known as "23 Society", a terrorist organization that manipulates captured soldiers and uses genetic mutations to turn them into "Ghosts" otherwise known as Super Soldiers.
Your brother Robert is captured during a failed raid on a Russian Forward Operating Base, and you're tasked with taking down 23 Society, while also finding his whereabouts.
SGW3 allows for a multitude of different methods to approach the game. Stealth being the main benefactor to the game, but also allowing for non-lethal and "Guns Blazing". The sniping is crisp but it's nothing we haven't seen before, the weapon models are some of the best i've seen yet in an FPS, and the drone spotting, allowing for complete stealth add to the complete immersion.
SGW3 takes place in Russia. The terrain is foresty with beautiful waterfalls scaping the land, and as you head north, a frozen tundra of death and dispair, allowing for a diverse terrain to play in.
Depending on your rig, the graphics played on high or very high settings look amazing. The detail done to the environment is perfect and are not CPU or GPU intensive in the slightest.
I believe SGW3 is a great time waster of a stealth FPS but it's real problem is that its not innovative or new. There's plenty of other games made just like this and although this game takes the cake on how it does stealth FPS, it can get boring as the missions seem like the same thing over and over. The story is quite bland with no real context or background, and the cliche love interest seems to sprout in this title. Albeit the predecessor being a glitchy, laggy, hell haven, this game has not yet had one bug that i've encountered. The weapon customization is somewhat minimal to the extent of changing scopes, sights, and magazine size, but that's not a large factor in my rating of the game.
Best advice i can give is either to wait on buying the game as $50.00 USD seems quite steep for such a short game, or to go the route i took and buy it off a third party website. ($28.00 USD on CDKEYS . COM).

If you want a pretty game that's a charming diversion you can (possibly) play with friends, you might like it.
If you like board games, but don't care too much about balance or attention to design details, you might like it.
If you like the idea that there's an absolute limit to the number of turns possible in one game, you might like it.
I do not fit into any of these categories, so I find it horribly frustrating. I gave it SO MANY chances to keep me interested (hence a played time that I now find rather depressing), but I've finally realized that this will never be a game that I'm happy to be playing.
(Also regarding that played time: Many of those hours were spent trying to obtain random dice drops, yet another supremely annoying feature that I now despise. Believe me when I tell you that those were not hours of enjoyment, but rather hours of tedium spent trying to obtain something that I'm not even sure why I ever wanted in the first place.)
The game will never be balanced, as there are a couple of ridiculously overpowered paths you can take that may not absolutely guarantee victory, but they will definitely boost your chances. This is a problem to such an extent that some players will quit a multiplayer game if someone else takes the overpowered hero(es) before they get a chance to grab the one they want.
The luck factor doesn't bother me as much as it does some people, but it is pretty strong, so if you hate games that are often decided by random events, you'll want to steer well clear of this one.
One of the worst design problems is the "rich get richer" effect that plagues so many games created by amateur developers. What may start out as a small gap in power will invariably spiral out of control as the more powerful character just gets more and more bonuses while the one who suffered a bit of bad luck at first will simply never catch up. If you happen to be that unlucky player, the rest of the game becomes a demoralizing torture session.
The game was fine for a while, I suppose, and I'm glad I got to play it and see what it's like. But at this point, I'm just so sick of it all, it hard to imagine ever wanting to play it again. Maybe I can recoup the cost of the game by selling all these stupid dice.

A custom feature now exists that provides a great deal of control over the victory conditions! Games can now be as long or as short as you want, and some of the more contentious mechanics can be modified or disabled outright.
Very well done, and kudos to the developers! This removes one of my main issues with the game, and changes my review from a "don't buy" to a "buy". I'm still a bit peeved that the prologue sets up a grand universe that's really just a neat board game, but now that it can be customized, I'm less bothered about it.
The original review remains below, unaltered.
This game is beautiful, and perhaps that's actually some of the problem. You play through the prologue, and you get this very slick, almost Civilization-esque board game laid out for you piece by piece, with a very fleshed out and stylish world. Very nice.
But then, you go to play a game, and you find out that no, there's no story, and in addition, a single game cannot be any longer than 9 rounds. One of the mechanics is that whoever has the most influence points when the 9th round is over automatically wins (barring the occasional edge case). 9 rounds goes by in a hurry, and the game is over much faster if any of the other victory mechanics are achieved.
It feels like they missed the boat here. I personally can't recommend this game due to violated expectations. The talk of "role playing" in the game's description? Almost deceptive.
If you go into it knowing that all you're getting is a board game, with the story being a paper thin framing device, then you may be able to enjoy Armello. Otherwise, you may end up disappointed. Decide accordingly.
+ Beautiful and atmospheric. You can tell a lot of love went into this title.
+ There's nothing wrong with short games per se; it's great way to kill an hour or so with some friends.
- Cap of 9 rounds per game, and this cannot be modified by the player. Certain rare game actions will cause this to be extended, but this is rare.
- Games end too quickly
- More luck than skill based
- Any strategy you'd like to play (perhaps trading off a character's strenghts and weaknesses) is stuck behind an inane achievement-based unlockable system.
* Realizing that the grand story laid out in the prologue never goes anywhere - it's just a way to frame the tutorial. There is no campaign.
* Realizing that the biggest annoyance with this game (the 9 round limit) could be trivially patched out, giving a lot more replay value, and the developers won't do it.
Too short, too expensive. Armello is like an ice cream sundae from a very fancy restaurant - looks beautiful on the plate, tastes amazing, but at the end, you're left wanting for more, and wondering why you paid what you did.

This game is fantastic in almost everyway, particular emphasis on ALMOST, as there is one particular part about it that you should consider before getting this game.
But before I do that, let us discuss what is great about this game, which is a lot. For starters, the gameplay in general is nothing short of amazing and gritty. The gunplay between the various different types of weapons (really attachments to one gun that all do different stuff but w/e) is satisfying. Most battles are often ripe with tension thanks to the more or less competant AI.
The game also has a squad system. Wherever you go, you have about three other clones with you to help you out in battle. Like the enemy AI, they can hold their own fine. I especially like how they sometimes go into weird fighting animations with other enemies that they never lose. You can command these troopers to do certain stuff, like blow open doors, hack open doors, take up sniping positions, heal themselves, etc. This provides some level of strategy, though it's usually obvious what you want to do when you do it due to conveinient placement.
Now, if any of your members (including yourself) ends up biting the dust, then you or another member can help them back up. Overall, the system works well enough, and  I reccommend you learn it fast.
Normally, something like this would be good, but the game continues to impress with its characters and story. Just in case none of you know, this game takes place throughout the Clone Wars of the Prequel Films. It centers on Delta Squad, a four-man squad of elite clone troopers, who are genetically modified soldiers. Essentially ten-year trained badasses. However, the different types of personalities between the four all make sense. Boss, the clone you play as, is more or less uptight, but compassionate and caring for his men. Fixer is by-the-book, standard soldier guy. Sev is dark and overall creepy, but you grow to love the guy due to his wisecracking remarks with his fellow squadmates as well as his ruthless combat skills. Finally, there's Scorch, who is hilarious in every way. Throughout the story, you grow to care about them and what they go through, something you wouldn't normally expect from a game focusing on emotionless military badasses.
The story itself is grand, if short (clocks in around 6-7 hours at most.) You get lead through planets like Kashyyk, an abandoned ship, and Geonosis.
Overall, the game is amazing... except for one thing.

I had fun with this game, but I can't recommend it due to a number of issues.
The story:
The storyline is extremely bland and forgettable. The story takes place in a cookie-cutter American zombie apocalypse universe. No suprises here. The characters and dialogue are just as bland as the setting. In all fairness, the storyline in Lifeline is actually somewhat interesting. It's still not great, but it actually has some suspense and drama to carry it forward.
The voice acting:
It seems like the minor survivors are voiced by 2, maybe 3 actors in total. I was regularly saving survivors with the same voice as Marcus. You'll hear the same lines of dialogue over and over again. Many of the character models are recycled too, it seems.
The gameplay:
The combat is pretty fun. Popping zombie skulls open with a well-placed bullet is always fun - can't really go wrong with that. The melee combat isn't too bad either. It's all pretty simple, but I don't really have any big complaints.
Mechanics:
Base management is simple and boring. There's no real strategy or depth to it. It feels really lazy, and it's a big missed opportunity to add some much-needed depth to the game. Base defense is buggy and obnoxious.
My biggest complaint about the game is inventory management. There are several different types of painkillers that do the exact same thing but take up separate precious inventory slots. Weapons occupy backpack slots, whether or not you're holding them in your hands. The trunks and truckbeds in this game are the size of a suitcase apparently. A small pistol takes up the same amount of space as a grenade launcher. There's a weight system, but it only really exists to punish you for carrying the wrong combinations of items - it's not something you really care about, it's just an annoyance. You'll find yourself making constant trips back to base to drop off loot. I feel like I spent most of the game tediously managing my inventory and running loot back to my base.
Summary:
Driving around running over zombies is pretty fun. And there are lots of different guns to shoot zombies with, which is fun. But unfortunately the game suffers from a depressing lack of depth and polish.

Although it lies merely a 100 years in the past, I have the feeling that WWI is far less present on our historical consciousness today, than it probably should. At least in my mind it became more or less overshadowed by historical events that occured later in the 20th century. This might be justified, by saying, that WWII, the cold war period, aso. have more immediate (or at least more obvious) relevance for the politics and societies of our time.
But there is something about WWI, that feels different, when you start imagine how people, who  grew up during this time, may have experienced it. I try to imagine, how it would feel, if the world as I know it would suddenly turn into a depressing nightmare of fear and violence. A nightmare that would physically last for years, if you somehow manage to survive meat grinders like the western front, and psychologically last the rest of your life.
Now I am writing this immediately after I finished Valiant Hearts. So if the idea behind this game was to spark historical interest and to give one a glimpse of how this hell that was Europe during its second decade felt like, it served its purpose for me.
Especially towards the end the game has its great moments, when the player lets the main character commit an action, that feels natural because of the immediate involvement, but would be at least morally controversial from a more distanced standpoint. This is something that I feel is the strength of games as a cultural technique and justifies them as a medium of art. This kind of immediate involvement is hardly reached by movies or writing.
Although history is an important element of the game and short paragraphs with historical facts pop up now and then, it does not feel like a gamified history lesson. An interesting decision was, to have hundreds of collectible litte objects, that represent day-to-day life of the period, spread throughout the game. Objects, that get explained by a sentence or two, as soon as the player finds them.
There are also some elements of the game, that I dislike. From an entertainment perspective it is highly repetetive in the things that the player is required to do. Puzzles througout the game consist of the same recurring elements and are probably for most players no challenge at all.
Of course historical adequacy was sacrificed for a more streamlined story telling in the artificial, abstract and graphic-novel-like world of the game. The story itself is hardly worth mentioning and serves basically the purpose to get the player from one famous battle field to the next. Also I find the character design to be very flat and stereotypical and although one of the playable characters is fighting in the forces of the German Kaiserreich, the Germans are reduced to their role as super-villians.
Despite its repetetiveness I enjoyed the game a lot and I keep it in mind as an example of video games, that have an educational and maybe even a certain artistic value.

Oooh yeah! Sniper Ghost Warrior 3; here we go!
So I have played around halfway of the main campaign through, if you are to believe the numbers of missions. Or more saying that I have pushed quite hard through the main missions, as I personally was very curious about the storyline. Thus I can mostly speak of the main missions and very few extra things.
First of all, I find this game beautiful. I play on "High" settings on 1080p with no drops to FPS, using a GTX 970 STrix and a 4700k CPU. The optimization that had some issues in the Beta have been resolved quite well.
Some people have trouble with the loading times into the game (Personally it takes 15-20 sec for loading in the game and 5-10 sec to jump between maps). I do however appreciate the priority of making a long loading, so the game feels alot more fluent when playing it and that you do not have to load in at the middle of everything (Which is the same for e.g. GTA V)
Secondly, the gameplay is awesome. One chooses between around 15 sniper rifles, 10 secondary weapons (AR, shotguns or the infamous bow) and a sidearm of pistols or revolvers. Overall are the weapons of same kind quite alike, though still having a somewhat unique edge. The main difference are the weapons kinds (shotty, AR, bow, pistol, revolver) and the two categories of snipers: .50 cals and.... Not-.50 cals? (main difference: .50 cal explodes heads like a pumpkin hit by a train, killing everything in one hit. Non-.50 cal have suppressors, funky bullets and gadgets to play around with).
The feel of shooting are amazing. Scoring a good shot are really awarding and depending on if you have bulletcam enabled or not, either seeing the head explode in a thousand pieces or following the bullet for a couple of seconds before ripping a head of.... Huhuhuhuhu, that gives the chills!
The game can be played both stealthy and loud, but it tends to be a lot more forgiving and easy for the stealthy approach. While you can mown through an army with a shotgun (which makes you feel like a BEAST), it can go bad very fast and does usually work only when in a pinch.
On the neutral side, the story are quite generic and has by now not many surprises - But it quite catching and suits the characters pretty well. But I guess that it is quite limited of how much story a one-man-army can have.
Also, there has been a few bugs when playing the game - However, nothing gamebreaking at all. Mostly it is about weird movement of not being able to climb small steps on rocks and a single time where I got stuck between two cliffs and had to fast travel out of it. However there has also been times where liberating an outpost has been impossible, due to some hidden unknown enemies, it would seem. Again, nothing gamebreaking but quite annoying.
On the worse side, comes the choosing of elements in the game; like camouflaging and equipment.
Which quite limited, you can pick different weapons and upgrade them over time. You start with a basic rifle, then unlock and buy the improved parts (e.g. extended mag or bipod). This goes only one way, which feels.. Weird for a game that want to let me do what I want?
You can use camouflage on your weapon, but it does not affect you or your gameplay. And most of the times you won't see it, as you are looking through a scope anyway.. Then why have it?

I must say, I really do enjoy this game.
The visual style is, of course, stunning, with the nice blend between the cartoon animated characters in the fight screens and the 3d models in the world emphasizing the uniqueness of each character, and the backgrounds being quite easy on the eyes as well.
The battle system is very quite enjoyable as well, with a nice random element in the dice rolling that is curbed by the card burning mechanic, in which you can sacrifice a card from your hand in order to get a precise dice roll. For example, if you burn a card with a shield symbol, you will lose the card, and one of your dice will become a guaranteed block.
The reason I'm giving it a negative review, however, is the fact that player interaction in this game is completly crippled. All conversation is limited to a range of preset emotes, just like in Hearthstone. While that may work in a card game like Hearthstone, where only limited messages need to be sent across to the other player, in a strategy game such as this, free chat is vital. There are basic emotes such as "Let's form a truce." and "Let's attack X character.", but these emotes completly simplify and dehuminize the message. You can't ask to form a truce personally, negotiating terms such as "I'll get rid of your bounty if you form a truce with me." And endeer yourself to the partner in the truce, therefor making them less likely to break it, you can't play any psychological power games with the other players, you can't even ask someone to move from your quest tile, as you'd rather not fight them. In strategy games free chat is a vital element, and removing it like this makes you draw no disctinction between the players and AI, and makes it impossible to form relationships. All and all this game is still very very enjoyable just because of it's mechanics and style, however I could not recomend it to anyone who's looking for an in depth tactical expirience, unless the developers decide to add free chat as a house rule, then I could recomend this game to everyone.

Disclaimer: I had a very positive attitude toward the game after participating in the open beta weekend.
The short version of this review is that the game is not for everyone, but it certainly delivers on quite a few points, which to some players may seem quite contrary to what they expect, or even want.
--
I will start off by just listing some of the key features of the game, this is not meant to be an analysis or a conclusion, merely an account of what is in the game, for you to make your own decisions.
The sniping mechanics are nothing phenomenal, quite similar to the Sniper Elite franchise, with wind and distance determining the exact location your bullet will hit. An added (and phenomenal) mechanic on top of this is the ability to adjust your sights, so you can zero for different ranges. This has already been a stable in Arma for quite a while.
There are various bullets you can load your rifle with. They each have their own use, with some being perhaps a little too niche, at least for my playstyle. There is a bullet which always strikes the centre of your scope's aim, one which can strike through thin walls and obstacles (for example, to strike into the engine of a vehicle, or to kill a target when you can't get a perfectly clear shot). Another bullet is explosive, for detonating the fuel tanks on vehicles, and interacting with trees (?) - although I have only seen the tree interaction in the prologue.
Enemies are hardy if you do not get clean shots off, especially if you're at short range with an assault rifle. You will likely end up using more ammunition than you ever really expected, considering how easily the opponents drop to your sniper rifle.
Ammunition is a very precious resource in the game, with harsh limitations (in the beginning) on how much you can bring with you out into the field. The early missions provide you with perhaps some 18 possible targets (in each mission), and assuming that you do not have some way of getting a larger ammunition pool with you, you have around 25 sniper rifle cartridges. You can carry more ammunition later on, if you do not care for the micro management, or you can decide to use smaller magazines for your weapon, and continue with the tight ammunition limitations.
Finally, enemies are fairly competent, and can sometimes turn up where you least expect them to, when you least expect them to. They will not hesitate to gun you down, and even on the medium difficulty setting, their shots - when they connect - will hurt. If you are sniping from a concealed position, the enemy may try to use mortar fire to flush you out. Mortars are fairly effective, and a single well-placed shell will kill you. Enemies will stay in cover for a long time, if you spook them, and they have no reasonable way to fight back. You cannot expect to defeat an entire outpost from a single location, every time. (Although there are definitely cases where such a strategy is possible, perhaps even preferable.)
--
Now, to alleviate some fears or confirm some. This section is about graphics, animations, general feel, performance, and bugs.
The graphics are not overly stunning, but there is an attention to detail that cannot be denied. This attention comes best to light when you take a moment to consider just how varied the colours in a scene often are - especially if you have a good bit of sun and the right angle. Like reality, the game has moments when it looks bleak, boring, and wet, but like reality as well, it has moments where everything looks gorgeous and incredible, where you can see the myriad of colours in the vegetation, and the red brick of that wall, along with the green moss that is slowly growing from the ground.
(Anecdote) Oh, and my favourite piece of detail that I have spotted yet. I heard the sound of a jet plane overhead, and I spun around, looking for the source. I didn't expect to find anything, but much to my delight I saw two fighter jets passing low over the scenery, just adding that little extra flair.
NPC animations are nothing incredible, though they have a certain quirkiness that some may find endearing. First person animations are often stiff, and may have some jagged-ness. I play slowly, deliberately, and patiently, and I do not experience particular problems with slow or jagged animations, although I certainly notice that there is a potential problem here. If you desire everything to be absolutely smooth and sync together perfectly (in the style of Dishonored), then this game does not provide that experience.
The game has run an unapologetic 60fps at 1920x1200 resolution, high settings on my machine. My machine has a GTX 1080, an i7-4790k at stock speeds, and 32GB RAM. I cannot begin to guess how the game fares on lower machines, and I have not tested the game at higher settings, yet.
I have encountered two bugs thus far.
The first bug was me getting stuck between a stack of wooden planks and a wall, endlessly falling. This solved itself after 30-40 seconds, and I could jump out. I was listening to some of the story exposition over the radio as this happened, so I didn't mind the wait too much. (I think I could have fast travelled out of this, if worst came to worst)
The second bug was dying during a mission, I loaded my 'last checkpoint' and ended up at the entrance to the mission area, although I had already completed the mission objective, and I could just step out and I got the mission complete screen. I cleared the area afterwards, and found no sign of the enemies I had killed on my way in originally.

Let me state right off I only give this game a moderate recommendation. I would've scored it higher except for several factors:
1. The checkpoint process is too long and unbalanced
2. The re-spawning of areas and outposts that were previously cleared and defeated.
This is a very large game wiith lots to do and without a quick save (F5) function and (F9) quick load the constant re-doing of an area is too redundant and disappointing.
Yes, I know, you can complete the regular missions and side-quests fairly well without respawn but then you have a game that is too short. If this is all you play for then you are missing the sand-box potential of the game. The developers have wasted a significant importnat factor here.
Now for why I give this game a recommendation:
1. Good graphics, ambient sounds, and terrain detail and variety.
2. Nice use of the drone to scout and mark
3. Weapons quite good and they sound accurate.
4. Variety of cartridges, grenades, bombs, etc. to use
5. Fast travel and custom travel (light blue road direction) availability.
6. Fairly decent dirt buggy to ride.
7. Lots of items to retrieve.
8. Choice of game play skill level
I could go on but you get the idea.
Some other things that were annoying but I could live with:
1. Redundant and too long opening music.
2. Long load times for missions or to start the game.
3. The silly and/or vulgar language from enemies and heroes.
4. Somewhat silly or stupid story.
5. I couldn't get the hang of how to fully utilize the workbench
6. Some graphical and/or getting stuck in area glitches
When the price is about $15 or lower trhen I'd say purchase the game and maybe you'll feel like you got your monies worth.

I might end up one of the few people giving this a "not recommended" while not at all bothered by the uplay aspect.  I won't be saying it was a bad game but one that did not meet expectations.
In brief I would describe this game as a somewhat moving World War I story spoiled by tedious puzzle sequences.  Some of the puzzles are fine but others you'll likely be looking up walkthroughs for the solutions.
The story is told through a number of different characters, with voiced narration breaking up each segment with a historical overview of the events as they happened.  The characters once in game speak barely a word of any language, using pictures in speech bubbles to convey their messages.  Occasionally this lessened the atmosphere; real language (as dialogue) could have increased the emotional impact on the player, and characters would not have had to communicate in such simplified messages.
While it was disappointing that some of the enemies were overly stereotyped and one-dimensional, the devs did a good job of showing the humanity on both sides of the conflict.  Many of the people in this war did not want to go out and kill others but the circumstances of their time forced them to.  You see this in characters helping out others in need when they could, like a nurse giving aid to a fallen enemy.
Probably the most appealing part of this game is its art, in graphic and sound design.  The background of machine gun fire and artillery bombardment give you a sense of the pure dread these people went through.  You will experience the Great War as a muddy and bloody mess.  At one stage I had to take cover from machine gun fire behind a pile of dead soldiers!
In the end, I feel the story was able to draw some emotions from me but the sometimes frustrating puzzles dampened the experience too much.  I expected a bit more depth overall given how highly it had been rated by critics.

My experience in Magicka 2 vs Magicka 1.
I'll start it off with the first time I played Magicka 1. The moment I started to grasp the concept of regular combinations, element combinations, and the special spell combinations, thats when I begun to experiment on so many spells (be it regular spells or the special combination spells, or both), and found it absolutely fun at how I can play the game differently each time and would still enjoy it nonetheless.
Thats when I absolutely fell in-love with Magicka. It promised a sort of freedom to your utilization of these spells. And the better you got at utilizing regular combos or utilizing multiple special combination spells, the more satisfying the gameplay was.
People tend to have different opinions and first impressions with this game, so I'm going to state my opinion and hope people would understand that I, as a person writing this review, do not present the entire community who plays magicka.
As I have loved Magicka, I got excited with Magicka 2. It promised something a bit new. Movement while casting a spell, and I thought "This is amazing! Just with this Magicka would be even more fun!"... I didn't pre-order. I waited about a year because I had other stuff to do. And when I was finally free, I took the chance and bought this game.
The campaign was never spoiled to me. I never knew the story progression. And I certainly didn't look up all the available magicks, whether old or new in Magicka 2.
So I got in here. Bought the game without hesitation, downloaded it, load it up, and played for hours.
It was hard! I loved it! I was doing it alone as single player, so naturally, it was difficult progressing. And I just wanted to finish the campaign so that I can make a new game and search all the spells. And then join public games.
-Now this is the part where the disappointment comes in-
As the game ended, and I finally opened up my web browser to search for all the spells.
I was shocked to know that so few spells were actually in the game.
The old ones that I loved and even the old ones that I rarely used (but still used nonetheless) weren't there anymore.
Magicka was more about weapons and dodging, and thinking of clever use with the upgraded regular spells.
(Absorption aura is awesome, I'll give them that. but I now have to use more than one element multiple times just so I could be immunite to it. And  you can only ever be immune to just 1 element. And that got me sad.)
The madness and chaos of using spells like Thunderstorm, Meteor shower, Vortex, Conflagaration, Phoenix, Invisibility, and even the meager Rain spell... was nowhere to be found. (I used to do Rain spell + Blizzard spell back in Magicka 1. I loved freezing my enemies)
It might be found in the other modes. I don't know, I have not checked.
But this wasn't the magicka I know.. The idea of making incredible combos and whatnot were slightly there.
But the larger special combination-spell combos (Like Rain + Blizzard) were gone.
And I couldn't help but feel, for the first time in the entirety of my Magicka gameplay experience... feel disappointed.
(Again, this is just my point of view)
Magicka is much more crazy now with some few added spells and new upgraded-regular elemental spells.
But I think the lack of... Chaos... that the old spells gave... made Magicka lose a bit of its charm.
I will still play Magicka 2. It is fun, there is no doubt about it.
But I can only wish and hope.. That one day a dlc campaign will be added. And all the old spells added into the game, as well..
A man can dream, right? A man can dream.
I just wanted to get this off my chest.
Because it just saddens me on how I miss my old spells.
Well, that's all I've got for you folks. Time to jump back into it...
Happy spell-ing! XD

Alright, I’m going to be upfront, I did not really enjoy this game, but I want to be constructive with this review. Starfighter Origins plays like an alpha to me. There are some interesting elements, but I feel like the game hasn’t been fleshed out completely and I ran into several buggy spots while playing.
The first issue I had was with the controls themselves. I tried this game using both the controller and the keyboard. With the controller, only half the controls worked initially. After a quick reset, the main ship controls worked, but other functions, like the match speed function, still didn’t work. As for the keyboard controls, the given controls spread players fairly far across the keyboard with buttons programed across the board. Luckily, the game does offer players the option to rebind these keys, however the first time I attempted this every key defaulted to pause. Again, the second time the key rebinding worked, but it was an issue.
As for the game play itself, the UI is built into the design of the ship, which is fine and fits with the aesthetic of the game, but the UI changes between the different kinds of ships, small shifts in where information is and what it looks like. This wasn’t a huge issue, but in the tutorial the layout of the UI is explained for a specific ship and so it could be a little disconcerting to quickly adjust to a different UI. Additionally, some of the information displayed seemed extraneous to the game (i.e. there were numbers and bars that did not seem to have a bearing on the ship), and some of the information didn’t feel particularly useful (like the speed of the ship, which you didn’t really notice a huge change in when floating through space). That being said, there were elements that I liked; in particular, I liked the radar, which was able to show not only the direction of targets in the 2D plane, but also where targets were in the 3D plane, which was helpful in pinpointing tiny targets in a large space. Also, I liked the targeting screen which game the player a sonar view of the playing field making it easier to find and target enemies in the space. However, I would prefer that the scanning view was the normal view out of the windscreen because even though I think the game had some beautiful scenery, since the game focuses on targeting enemies and fighting, I think the focus should have been on optimizing finding targets, which were hard to spot.
As for the mechanics, the firing and targeting seemed to work fine, but the match speed function slowed the craft to zero. The firing was simple, although in the heat of battle it felt a little slow. Also, when in battle, it felt difficult to follow what was happening in battle. I was almost constantly barrel rolling the ship attempting to find my targets.
Final note, the game crashed 4 times while I was trying to play. Three of the crashes were on the pirate battle simulator and all of them  came up as fatal errors. Overall the game was buggy and like I said, just needs fleshing out.

Light on gameplay and heavy with heart, Valiant Hearts: The Great War provides an interesting, albeit flawed, way to interactively learn about the people, places, and events in WW1. It does not take itself too seriously but does a fine job of treading the line of making the horrors of war both approachable and unknowable except by those who lived it.
The game primarily follows Emile, a farmer; Freddie, an American bent on revenge; and Walt, a war dog. Their tales create a fantastic, interwoven story arc that will also encompass Anna, a nurse; Karl, an exiled German soldier and brother-in-law to Emile; and Emile's family. Major historical events will shape the outcome and little details on a soldier's day-to-day life (discovered through trinkets scattered through the levels) bring a sense of realism the cartoonish style attempts to negate.
Like I stated before, the gameplay is sparse and mostly involves dodging incoming fire and solving puzzles. That really is it. Nothing spectacular in any way.
Play this game for the story and historical retelling. It really is worth the money and reminds us--even if it's just little bit--of how awful the world can and could be. But, more importantly, it reminds us that the human spirit can endure and grow from the muddy trenches and scarred faces of those who survive catastrophe.

When you see all these positive reviews and have discovered that in the all time list of top rated steam games it is only second to (the equally brilliant) Portal 2 you may wonder if a huge hype is going on, but Factorio really is that great!
It is not a game of fantastic stories or beautiful graphics or impressive action.
Instead the setting is simple: You are stranded on an alien planet and your objective is to get a satellite into orbit and call for help while fending of aliens, who are not happy at all about your not so environmentally friendly activities.
The way to building the satellite is long. You have to mine, craft, and build up a factory that will produce what you need piece by piece but things are getting real fun, when you start to automate things and try to draw your picture of the game. More often than not you will build parts of a production chain, see that they don't work as flawless as you imagened and redesign them again and again until satisfied and it is not unheard of that people who wanted to "just finish something up" in the evenig end up still "finishing up things" far into the next morning.
Factorio needs a bit of time to get into but if you can muster this patience, you will probably not be disapointed.

Emily is Away is a wildly simplistic game; you chose a screen name and a profile picture, then go chat up your best friend Emily on an old-school Windows OS. The whole thing takes about thirty minutes to play through in entirety, but holds a surprising amount of emotion, combining the nostalgia of the game's format with the all-too-familiar nostalgia of remembering how things used to be before complications (like college) got in the way. After the 28 minutes I spent playing the game for the first time, I felt much more emotionally invested in Emily and her relationship with my character than I expected when I started, so much so that I teared up a little at the end. I'm about to go dive right back in for my second playthrough - the decisions offered in-game feel varied and important enough to make replayability high with this one.
TL;DR: It's free, short, packs a surprising and familiar emotional punch, and will make you remember the good ol' days before Windows XP.

It's a kind of engaging story, though the simple mobile game "Seen" for Android basically did it better, while retaining the same approach.
Obviously, a game for free is a game for free - you cant expect tons of content. And "Emily is Away" doesn't offer you that ton of content. With its multiple branches and endings, it certainly has replay value, and can keep you playing for an hour or two, but it lacks in
choices. After several playthroughs with vastly different choices, the actual story always stays linear and on the same track, no matter how hard you try to derail it by being destructive or nice to the deuteragonist Emily. The visuals are simple but nice, the sounds and ambience are very intriguing and a superb throwback to the earlier times of computers and the internet. The given options in a simple text adventure to imply actual emotion (like bits of text being deleted and rewritten by your protagonist, while youre typic the message) are used well.
All in all, I do recommend it. Its a nice little creative indie game. And with it being free, and taking up barely any disk space at all, its definitely worthy of being in your library.

Story Time~
-------------
Paint The Town Red
Club Beatdown, 11:32 PM
After finishing the fight I started, I exit from the bathroom completely caked in the blood of my fallen enemies. My next target, the Boss. I grab a glass bottle on the way up the stairs to his office, breaking it on the wall. I stand outside his door, waiting for the opportune moment to strike...
Finally I kick the door open, driving the shards of glass into the throat of one of the Boss's guards, letting his lifeless body drop to the ground. Having nothing but the neck of a bottle, I drop my now broken weapon, and await the Boss's retaliation. His remaining three guards circle around me, and the Boss slowly rises from his chair. He turns to the Katana hanging above him, taking hold of the fine weapon and slowly unsheathing it, basking in it's glory.
"So, you've finally come for me..." The Boss says, looking into the deep silver steel of his blade. "I do hope you've said your farewells, because you won't be leaving this place alive."
I stare to the back of his head, waiting eagerly for him to turn and face me. Finally he does, his blade readied in front of him, and I make my reply - "Bring it, ♥♥♥♥face."
His three guards come in to strike. I manage to block the incoming attacks of two of them, however the guard behind me is able to kick me in the lower back, dropping me into a kneeling position. The Boss swings his Katana downward, but I roll to my left just in time, and he does nothing but tear a hole in his fancy rug. I swiftly recover from my roll and tackle one of the guards onto a chair. His friends are quick to react, however I am quicker. I kick one of them in the stomach, which caused him to stumble into the other guard.
I reach over and break a wine glass I grabbed from the table, and I jam the shattered neck of the glass into the pinned guard's eye socket. At this time the Boss has recovered and he makes his next swing, to which I jump off of the chair and over the table, landing next to the door from which I entered. With the remaining two guards and the Boss quickly giving chase, I make my way downstairs and into the storeroom directly below the Boss's office.
I grab a chair and smash one of the guards in the face with it as he rounds the corner, knocking him unconscious. As the Boss and other guard round the corner, I step on the downed guard's throat which collapses his wind pipe, then I throw the remains of the chair at the Boss. I run out of the other side of the storeroom and into the lobby, quickly making my way back to the staircase and up into the Bosses office again. I grab a Ninja Star laying on the Boss's desk and I hurl it down the stairs at the incoming threat, successfully nailing the last guard in the jugular vein, ensuring his demise.
Now, inside the Boss's office, just he and I remain. I grab a bottle of Vodka and smash it on the Boss's desk, and we quickly exchange swings towards each other. Each is met with a dodge, until the Boss gets a lucky swing at me, slicing me in the lower back. He taunts my carelessness and takes another swipe, and I am left with no choice but to retreat. I roll out of the way of his incoming attack, and make my way back down the stairs. With the Boss right on my heels, I have no choice but to go through the storeroom once again, when I find something I hadn't expected to...
One of the civilians I had recently fought with in the Bathroom area had survived, and he was armed with a baseball bat! Knowing I can't run with my wound, and facing the Boss unarmed would be suicide, I grab a glass plate and smash it over the civilian's head, prying the bat from his hands. The Boss stands back now that I wield an actual weapon, and I finish off the civilian with a single blow to the head.
Now the tables have turned, and I am no longer at such a disadvantage! Now, there we are... Alone in the storeroom, staring each other down, knowing that despite what happens next one of us isn't leaving this room alive.
The Boss and I charge each other and he swings for my head, I slide under his attach and hit him in the stomach with the butt of the baseball bat, temporarily stunning him. As he recuperates, I take one more well placed swing, hitting him in the jaw. The Boss falls to the ground, dropping his Katana at his side. As he goes to reach for it, I smash his hand with the bat, and grab the Katana before he can make another move.
Now I stand over the Boss, his Katana in my hands, and I mutter the last word he'll ever hear...
"Sayonara."
I swing the Katana downward, splitting his head in two, like a hot knife to butter. There I stand, victorious, over the corpses of my fallen enemies. I have won this day.

As a huge fan of the Space Combat Sim Genre, I had high hopes for this game and seeing where this game took it's inspiration from I admit I allowed myself to get a bit excited. However, what I was forced to endure for my First Impressions review quickly dispelled any vestige of hope or excitement.
The options menus are a broken mess, some even requiring a loading screen? Also there is no menu for audio adjustments and the buttons to select an inverted Y axis do not seem to function at all. Also, in spite of the Developer's claim for HOTAS support, the game refused to recognize my joystick and only allowed me to use the controller... where I'm sorry but right stick for maneuvering and left stick for throttle? To me that seems exceptionally backwards.
The game itself is buggy and tedious. It requires you to slog through the tutorial missions before it will even unlock the campaign. Once you finally get there, IF you manage to get the campaign to load, you will be met with more tedium and broken missions.
There is a good game here, but it is buried under layers of inadequate controls, menus, and bugs both game breaking and non. Do not buy until the game is HEAVILY patched. See my First Impressions Review above for more information.

First Impression Gameplay:
I really wanted to enjoy this, and at some points I did, but I think the game currently falls a bit flat.
Right away, you are forced to play through training missions, being locked out of the campaign until you complete all 4.  The training missions are a bit boring and really could have been implimented in the first mission of the actual campaign.
I can tell they put a lot of effort into making nice cutscenes, but the voice actor sounds like he is talking from the bottom of a well (echo and reverb are set extremely high).  Also, the loading of the cutscences seems excessive.  Loading happens between the beginning and end of each cutscene, and the game has 2 cut scences per mission.  Having 4 load sequences per mission is a tad bit excessive.  Perhaps the mission end and next mission begining cut scences could be combined together?
As far as actual gameplay, I played with an Xbox control (as was recommended by the dev), and for the most part controls were okay.  I say okay, because it is very very difficult to hit enemies with your base lazor at range.  Maybe it's just because I'm not used to controler joysticks as much as a mouse/keyboard, but I really struggled.  Also, why not have mouse/keyboard support?
Mission-wise, things are a bit dull:
-First mission you fly around for about 10 minutes in formation and fight only 1 guy the entire time.
-Second mission, you fly around in formation for another 10 minutes before arriveing at a wreck and getting called back to your ship.  Seriously that is it.  No combat, no real involvment at all from the player.

For those looking for an actual review..
MULTIPLAYER:
For me, and quite a few people it seems, this is the best battlefield released to date. It's the most fun and most well made addition to the series and I think it's down to the simplicity of it's loadout system, as well as the great team and game play, and of course the destruction that every one loves.
When you jump onto Battlefield 4, I feel its too complex for its own good. way to many class options and quite a few flawed items that became over powered (Especially a lot of the DLC weapons and gadgets that they released) BC2 gives you a good selection of guns and perk options without going overboard. There are one or two things I would maybe change (Magnum rounds and the shotty slug rounds) but everyhting else works well.
The maps are really awesome, some better on different modes than others, and some you can only play on certain modes, a bit weird really. But they're all pretty awesome. rush and conquest are the main game modes available, along with squad deathmatch and squad rush, but just stick with rush and conquest.
The general gameplay is standard battlefield fare, just awesome. Stuff's blowing up all over the place, soldiers are shouting their heads off about snipers blowing their mates head off, bullets are wizzing past and it combines to make probably, in my opinion, the most cinematic war experience ever made for a multiplayer game. Some people will be craving jet gameplay and the more varied vehicles that BF3 and BF4 have, but the ones available are all you need. Unfortunatley though there are no jets, for those that didn't know.
And the audio... it's the best ( And make sure you go into the audio settings and turn on war tapes)
SINGLEPLAYER:
Decent for one playthrough I guess, played it on the 360 back in the day once and never really went back to it apart for achievements, but it's not the worst campaign ever. Not big, open free roam areas like BC1 had in the singleplayer which is a shame, but the characters and action are interesting enough to keep you interested.
So overall:
Multiplayer 9.5/10
Singleplayer 7/10
Audio 11/10
The audio's so good...
Buy it while it's cheap people.

(Last week,one of my friends excitedly told me that he had found a game named Alien Swarm:Reactive Drop,which is the remake version of Alien Swarm.And I was also really impressed after downloading this game and having a brief game experience.What I have to say is that this game can be the biggest surprise to me in this month,since I love Alien Swarm and have been keeping my eyes on its latest news.)
Therefore,I am here writing something to share my excitement with the ones who are hesitating and wondering whether they should download this game and help them to make a decision.OK,now let's talk about the game's differences compared with its older versions.
-----------------------------------
Contents added:
·Versus mode - The weapons which were used to fight against swarms only are now allowed to point at humans.This mode can bring you another kind of joy,especially when you're playing with your friends.
·Several new guns - The newly coming guns are  wonderful except the last one,there's nothing between it and the medic gun we got before.
·Single player mode - It enables you to finish a campaigh without other players' assistance,since you can have several assistants controlled by the computer.
·Workshop available - Players can get maps and mods made by other players from the workshop directly.As is known to all, the workshop provides a wonderful platform for players to share or get self-made extra game contents.From the reviews about Alien Swarm can we see that there are many people who want a workshop for this game.
-----------------------------------
Other improvements:
·More players online - That is to say,we don't have to join a laggy server as we used to.Because there are much more choices now.
·Better game optimization - In other words,the waiting time for start has been shortened and unexpected incidents are less likely to happen.Also,the game just operates more steadily.
·Other details - For instance,the lines painted by players on the map are now divided into 4 colors to show who has painted them,the characters are now allowed to jump in Death Match,and so on.
-----------------------------------
Having discussed the advantages of this game,I hope that a general impression about this game is built in your minds.Because I'm going to show you the shortages of this game to leave you a deeper impression as well as point out the problems to help the producer improve this game.

·The unreasonableness of the lines' colors - It bothers you when you are represented by the color of blue.Because there are many maps using light blue and dark blue to show the boarders (or a better word to describe),which makes blue lines almost invisible.

automacally healing the others can get themselves killed when they are being attacked too.

Summary: Co-operative top-down shooter game available for free. An epic bug hunt featuring a unique blend of co-op play and squad-level tactics.

As long as you connect to servers with a good ping you will have no connection issues. A lot of people complaining about these issues are only connecting to public games rather than dedicated servers. Often "crashes" are in fact the host leaving. Bots can be a bit of a pain, however there are fixes to make them "smarter" but really you either want to team up in MP, or go for it solo. Any player worth his salt should be able to complete Landing Bay on Hard by themselves ;D With easily 4 times the content (including campaigns, weapons and game modes) of its predecessor, ASRD is a huge success in revamping AS. Steam workshop has been added for ASRD making it even easier to add extra content than ever before, no more searching for mods then replacing steamaps files The graphics still look fresh. Sure, they aren't top end, but neither is my PC, however my computer runs smooth, the game runs smooth, and it looks ALOT better than a lot of games around.

Now, don't get me wrong, the game is fun but it doesn't fit here.
First of, the game itself is your run-of-the-mill trivia quiz setting. You are presented with a fact and then say whether it is true or not. From a gaming perspective the game isn't made well as a majority (+- 70% ? didn't check for sure) of the answers are yes.
The game consists of 3 modes, 1 of which requires DLC and as such won't be described.
Campaign mode: runs through every question in the game once, gets to 200 i believe/ Once you finish it and start again, they're in the exact same order making easier than it should, especially sisnce there is no "difficulty" scaling. Doesn't matter how many you get righ or wrong, it just keeps going till the end and then gives you % of correct answers.
Quick Play:
10 "questions" of the same nature. the same ones as in campaign but now selected randomly, you get all 10 right, you complete it. Once you get something wrong you fail.
Now, the game wasn't that bad since the aim of these type of games is education mixed with fun, and I did learn a bit, I guess.
My problem is that the game is payed. These types of games are quite numerous on the mobile market and are free (and to be frank, more enjoyable than this one).
So, to sum it up, if you are to pay money for this, I recommend against doing so and get one of the many free games of this type on your phone.

It's a basic true or false game, it will present you with statements and you are to determine if they are true or false. The number of different statements are limited to 200, I think, which isn't a very large amount, but it's not too few either. The game might be fun to play with children if they can speak English or with friends who like trivia, or maybe you can play it serveral times and learn all the trivia yourself to become the life of every party you go to?
However, it has easily obtained achievements (or through a little bit of grinding) and some of them are a must if you like to collect achievements or are an AC/DC fan. I would recommend to buy it at a sale, unless you're a hardcore AC/DC fan that needs that particular achievement right away.

While the title entices with interesting mechanics and ideas - especially for those of us who fondly look back on titles such as wing commander and freelancer - there are an insurmountable number of issues with this title that hamper it.
Video:
Text:
Before anything else we need to look at the control options and control scheme. While the game support full key rebindings it lacks a functional mouse movement support so while you can rebind you keys to your mouse buttons... moving your mouse doesn't actually do anything, and if that wasn't bad enough the default binding only work on the xbox controller.
Moving on further, the games issues in terms of controls also translate to movement and interaction with the world, with physics being wonky, animations being non-existent and various targeting, aiming and particle effects causing more problems than they solve.
Lastly, while the flying feels good and the game has quite a bit of replayable content, there is a distinct cal of polish moving on into the campaign as well with mission failing to update objectives and thus not being finish able.
While an interesting idea, the game has to many mechanical issues, to many design choice frustrations and a complete lack of any polish you might expect.

Emily is away is a really interesting experience, unlike anything I've played before. It is basically a visual novel that you play through an instant messenger, talking to a friend from high school as you both progress to college, one conversation a year, where you can make choices that will later affect how your relationship with this friend, Emily, develops.
This game is beautiful in more than one way. The closer you get to the end, the more weight you feel from the distance that builds up between you and Em, depending on the choices you make, you might find yourself living a
.
This game had what was perhaps one of the hardest video game moments I've ever played, and on a free-to-play, 30 minutes experience. I'll probably be playing this again to see what other endings there are, and how differently things might develop.
This game tells the story in a really interesting way, everything through the instant messenger app, where all information you find of the world can only come from your chat with Emily, or from the profile descriptions all the characters might right for themselves. However, the way you have to pick what you want to say, and then actually keep typing a bunch of whatever until the text is all written by the computer, and then you just press enter to send the preprepared message. This makes the game feel more realistic, in a way, but it also get's kind of annoying later, since what you actually type has no effect in what appears written, which breaks the suspension of disbelief a little.
Overall, this was a really worth it little game to play, and as visual novels go, this is perhaps one that I've had the most interest in playing, and would recommend (not a big fan of vn's over here).

Unironically the best game on the Goldsrc Engine in my opinion, if only because it's a recreation of the unbeatable and timeless Quake by id Software.
I strongly recommend giving this game a shot, even if its predecessor to which it's trying to imitate is vastly superior, DMC is still worth a visit. The classic gameplay is solid, the maps are beautiful depictions of decrepit castles and facilities that are fun to get lost wandering through, and the barebones playerbase of random people who found this simply from it being bundled with Counter-Strike is sure enough going to ensure an interesting encounter every time you play.
Though only a handful of servers remain, there's still plenty of fun to be had. Even if you can't find any human opponents, several servers still feature computer-controlled bots that are surprisingly challenging at times given the situation.
Is this worth $4.99? Probably not (unless you're like me and this kind of thing fascinates you), you could get Quake 1 for that same price, but should DMC be overlooked? Not at all, it's a lovely recreation of an already perfect game on a more accessible and readily available engine with a higher chance of meeting a human opponent than the original due to how it's easier to set up on a modern system.
I give this game a 9.5/10, with the 0.5 being docked for how clunky rocket-jumping can be at times. I can't tell you how difficult it is to rocket-jump up the mid area in dm3 here compared to the original Quake, it just doesn't work the same.

I was really excited for this game, really. I thought we'd finally get that realistic long range-shooting game we'd been waiting for for so long.
It pains me to say that this is not it. I wans't even able to go trhough the third main mission, because of the frustration.
And my biggest isue with this game is pretty simple: NO SHOOTING RANGE.
As thos of you that played the previous installments already know, SGW has a wind mechanic and a bullet drop mechanic.
The bullet drop is quite easy to compensate for with the zeroing options (quite the same for all the scopes I've tried, but whatever), but the wind will still blow your bullets sideways. This wouldn't be a problem if you had a place to train a bit, to learn how to use your rifle/scope, to fiddle with the adjustments. But NO! Nothing. In a game where every single bullet counts (you have to craft those at a workbench), there is no way to train with your guns.
Meaning that, unless you play on Normal difficulty (with that immersion breaking red dot to indicate the POI), THERE IS NO WAY TO LEARN HOW TO HANDLE THE WIND.
The wind may not be a problem at close ranges, but it's very annoying when you have to shoot at 300m and you have absolutely NO IDEA where the bullet will drift. Thus resulting in you having to guess and pray you guessed right.
The game suffers from alot of other flaws, some minor, some bigger, but this is what bothers me the most. Clearly this game was thought as an arcade shooter, and the harder difficulties were but an afterthought. The shooting mechanics are solid and immersive, but you have no way to actually train and learn how to face the longest shots. Remember thos 800m shots in SGW 2? Well, good luck trying to nail one of those with a 14 m/s wind with absolutely no training.
So, unless you're okay with having the game hold your hand with that red dot, I'd say this is not the sniping game you want.

My review chronicle of gameplay so far.
"**" prefix = I think you might want to know this more than the other, lesser review points.
(After 2.1 hours of play)
Military ninja simulator 2017.  Great graphics, smooth controls, nice customization (weapons), **sounds are good (not great), story narration is a bit elementary, high fun factor if you enjoy: hunting sims, Dying Light, Ghost Recon, or stealth games.  I haven't encountered manny game-breaking bugs (or many bugs in general, for that matter (see below)). I recommend it. It's fun.
(After 3 hours of play)
10 years ago (this fall) Crysis 1 came out.  10 years already.  I've seen the comparisons of this game to games like Ghost Recon Wildlands, it's different enough to justify a look.  I also saw a comparison to Call of Duty?  Uh, lol.  No.  Call of duty? I guess the guns look about as good as Call of Duty makes, but... where in call of duty can I escape hit-scan, insta-travel bullets(?), large open sandboxes to explore, stealh mechanics, and sniper-elite-like bullet time?  Sniper 3 can, if you're smart, allow you to go full throttle on the guns and run and gun, but if you like taking out bad guys without raising an alarm, this game is more like metal gear solid than anything like Call of Duty.  No, the closet game to this would be the game engine and interactive freedom of Crysis 1, a much more hardcore and modern Sniper Elite, and a little of that Far Cry ability to go faster than your own good. The ballistics are simulated well, and some of the hits are more gory than Max Payne 3, which is nice.  When I played Crysis 1, I remember wishing that it was less linar and with more of a Grand Theft Auto, 'sitting' open-world feel, with pedestrians.  Sniper 3 is fufilling my wish from back then.
(After 6 hours of play)
I've gotten comfortable with the controls to the point where I'm choosing riskier courses of action with confidence.  Being able to verticall scale buildings like in Dying Light is very satisfying, especially when the purpose of it is to go to the top of the building and snipe someone.  It feels like almost a ninja-like game since I'm always sticking to shadows and waiting for the right time to make my moves; my moves are often 100% effective, and trying to interrogate everyone is fun.  Urban-rock climbing mechanics allow you to vertically scale buildings like assassin's creed, and getting to the top to snipe makes it feel like you're James Bond or Jason Bourne.
**Issue discovered: move your in-game mouse cursor off the screen if you use a controller because if you don't, and a menu item rests under your cursor, the cursor will hover-select, making your controller selection bounce back to the cursor.  Moving the cursor off screen fixes this.
(A few minutes later)
I stopped to write my last chunk of the review at 6 hours beacuse I had just taken out my target and was feeling like I was on top of the world, but shortly thereafter, I returned, became a cowboy moron and got myself killed.
**Here is something that I don't quite get: when I die, as far as I can tell, instead of returning you to a recent game save, this game appears to plop you down in some alternate dimension than the path you were just on.  For example, before I dide, the alarm was raised but the bad guy was dead and I was exfiltrating.  Upon death, I return to the bad guy still dead, but many of the minions I killed brought back to life!  It didn't return me to any previous point, but instead put me into an alternate relatity (time and location) from anywhere I had been.  I'm not complaining so much as just confused.  That's a very weird choice for the devs to have made.  Since I died, it's not so bad as it is strange.  Like I wake up in a slightly alternate universe where things went a little better than the one I just woke up from.
(After 7 hours of play)
Never had this much fun adjusting for wind and distance with my scope.
(After 11 hours of play)
**I'm starting to wonder if the shots during bullet time are directly connected to shots that do not go into bullet time, or if the bullet time ones are hit-scans.  I say that because it seems like when I press the trigger, it immediately will go into the kill cam and follow the bullet.  Furthermore, sometimes the enemy will be squatting when I take the shot, but when the bullet arrives (during the kill cam) it'll hit the enemy while he's standing.  I'll mark that down as something I don't really care for, but it's not game breaking... Just kind of immersion breaking.
(After 12 hours of play)
**The game did just experience its first crash.  Granted, I had rebooted my PC just prior to starting, and right before the crash the game also experienced its first excessively long load time. Restarted the game and it works fine.
(After 13 hours of play)
** Another annoyance I've encountered is when moving bodies, if I attempt throwing the corpse into a location where the game doesn't appear to like (like narrow rooms/dump piles with lots of clutter) when you 'drop' the enemy, they'll magically fall way back around the area you picked them up at.  Not the biggest complaint, but added to some of my others, is kind of annoying.
(After 17 hours of play)
Went to boot up and the game loaded all the way into a game, then crashed before I could take control of my character.  Just re-checked the files in Steam, everything okay.

The character from the resistance you first meet for a side ops for example really could do with some more texture detail and that is nitpicking. It could also do with windows smashing when you sniper through them, twice I shot an NPC that was stood behind a window and it looked like the bullet magically passed through......
The game does have some erratic FPS but never below 60 at least for me on a gtx MSI 1080 (2 but sli is not supported yet) i7 5960x, 64g DDR4, Win 10 64bit. I have been trying to create the stutters that others have been reporting including in and out of scope and cant seem to replicate them, the FPS fluctuates between 70 – 110 on Max settings at 1080p. I do experience the odd jerk but that is not reflected in FPS, so it could be the scene loading, I have installed on an SSD.
Yes they are terrible even installed on an SSD, once you are in the game world its fine, not fast but fine, but the initial game load on my SSD takes around 50 seconds.
The sound on a whole is great but it does require attention, some sounds do not reflect the environment you are currently in, for example reverb when reverb is not needed.
There does seem to be a lot of cut and paste models which is a pity really but not as bad as lets say Far Cry games.
From the short time I have spent with the game so far the cut scenes seem to be of a lower resolution, I did not notice it at first during the prologue, but you do notice it when you first meet Lydia or whatever her name is.
Load times, this really needs to be addressed, also we could do with some more graphical options on PC, motion blur for one, that is a personal preference. Like I first mentioned I am only 100 mins into the game so this brief overview may change.

I am a big fan of these silly clumsy beat 'em up party games like Bomb Squad and Gang Beasts. So I have high hopes for Aiball. It's an open market with a lot of interesting opportunities.
Right now if you get the game you get what you pay for. The developers make no false promises here, they say that only basic content is accessible. It is even noted as early access. I actually really appreciate that they would price the game reasonably, for $1.99 I have no ill feelings about not being able to do much.
In Aiball you control a cute little claymation figure and clumsily try to play soccer. Everything is moveable from the ball, to the flags, to the seats, to even the goals. It was pretty funny dragging goals around. There are three modes with one map each. There is the soccer mode with the map in the screenshots, a king of the hill mode and a sandbox mode.
The king of the hill map is a bland (read: everything is grey) mountainside with boxes falling down. I have no idea what to do and it is pretty hard to get up the mountain. The sandbox mode is even more lame with an empty black space with two boxes that can be moved around with crappy physics. Don't get me wrong, I'm not hating. I totally get the game is in early access and I'm sure more will be added later. Just want the users to be aware that the soccer mode is really the only interesting mode at present.
There seems to be some keymapping and joystick support which is cool but I cannot figure out how to get additional players to move. So while I recommend the game and its potential I would probably tell users to wait to buy it until additional player controls are sorted out. It was amusing to play alone but would be way more with friends. If I could get the controls working this would be really funny for a group of four friends and definitely worth the $1.99 fee (and maybe more).
@Devs, feel free to comment on this review if y'all get the additional character support figured out and I'd be happy to amend this review.

Most of the time, there won't be anybody on any servers. And there may only be up to 3-4 servers online.
If you have any buddies that you want to play some retro shooter games with then you should all buy this and play together, as I mentioned before, the online community for this game is quite dead, but it is still entertaining to play with friends over the internet or through LAN. Overall, I recommend this game, and I think that you should give it a chance, even if it is a bit outdated.

This game remains my #1 favorite squad shooter that I've ever played.
While that may come from a personal bias of being a huge Star Wars nerd, I still stand by it.
Republic Commando puts you in the duraplast boots of RC-1138 "Boss", head of a Republic Commando squad set in the Clone Wars. At the head of your squad, Fixer, Sev, and Scorch, you take part in infiltration, recovery, and recon missions that would make your average Mando Clone end up as a crumbled pile in the corner.
You come across said crumbled piles, several times.
You will face overwhelming forces. You will get outgunned and outnumbered. You'll get rushed. You'll face shields and giant droids. While not necessarily hard, the game isn't exactly easy, either.
Keep in mind, as the game description says, the multiplayer servers are shut down now. This is now a single-player game, but it's still a really good one that has a very strong feeling into what the Clone War was like when Jedi aren't hogging the spotlight.

I just finished this game and I actually enjoyed it quite a bit. I'm a fan of point-and-click adventure games and if someone were to tell me this is a game that came out in 1998, I would believe you as it feels right at home there. Like adventure games of that era, you've got funny and obscure solutions to problems and even a handful of minigames thrown in (with a surprisingly chibi style in a few of them). As it has been noted by others, for some reason the game does not start with a setup menu or even has a good one in-game. HIGHLY recommended to run "settings" in the captain morgane steam folder (common standard being steam/steamapps/common/captainmorgane) and you can then adjust it for higher qualitiy and widescreen mode.
I found the acting to be very good. None of the performances took me out of the atmosphere and all of the accents felt like they belong there. The music was excellent and I enjoyed all of the soundtrack even if it was a bit repetetive. Like the games of the 90's, though, that was fairly common and since it is caribbean themed and light it doesn't get annoying.
Other than a few minor bugs here and there, this was an adventure game worth playing if you're into adventure games. Since Monkey Island always has a soft spot in my heart, any pirate-themed adventure game set in the caribbean will spark my interest. :)
TL;DR - Good adventure game for anyone looking for a pirate style point-and-click adventure. Bad game for FPS players who need to kill stuff.
Long adventure, nice story line, if you can get around the sometimes clunky point-to-move navigation this is a very nice adventure. Recommended!
