Plus sides. I love the concept, and the voice actors are nice.  and it has enough guns and melee weapons that you have several choices for each character.   Unfortunately that cant make up for its down sides.

This game is the best at its genre...
There is no zombie survival with community management game out there that can even begin to compare to this game's brilliance. Sure, its a little rough on the edges with a few bugs and performance issues but then again, what game out there doesn't have these issues?
Maybe the biggest sin Microsoft commited was releasing YOSE with a 36€ tag (when i purchased it) even for owners of the original State of Decay. Needless to say that this didn't sit well with users and they got allot of flak because of this.
I myself owned the original SoD and i still got the YOSE because i loved this game to death and i still do. I'm not gonna say i bought this game with a smile on my face but imho it was worth it. On to the review, shall we?
State of Decay YOSE Story mode:
The game itself has been graphically improved and smoother combat/shooting mechanics have been implemented as well as better driving. The use of vehicle storage is now usable in Story mode, making scavenging less of a chore.
Story mode remains pretty much the same and will give you easilly 12+ hours of fun scavenging and zed slaying.
State of Decay YOSE Breakdown mode:
Breakdown has made a turn for the best since a new (and final) update has been implemented, raising the BD levels to 100, each run getting harder and harder and introducing beefed up enemies such as Fatalnauts which are Juggernauts that will instantly kill a character if they get a hold him/her regardless of remaining HP. Later levels of Breakdown will put your skill and wits to the test. Lots of new heroes are available including a very good bonus survivor that you can use in Story mode, Breakdown and Lifeline DLCs by selecting Bonus Survivor in your radio (default key ALT). Lifeline Heroes are also available in Breakdown by completing specific challenges ingame.
State of Decay YOSE Lifeline mode:
Take command of a military unit complete with a base and survive zombie sieges in this urban setting of State of Decay. You have a mission to find and extract key personnel in the hopes of finding a cure for the zombie virus outbreak. Build up your base of operations, establish contact with the higher ups and gain access to Drone Strikes, Flaming Barrages, Drone Recon, Artillery Strikes and Heavy Supply Drops in order to survive the ever increasing Zombie Sieges that come from the city itself. This mode is a 2 in 1 since after you complete the main story you can just stay and attempt to survive as many Sieges as you can. You can also scoot on over to a Danger Zone and attempt to survive alone or with backup. Danger Zones provide the most fun since zombies are constantly spawning and WILL overwhelm you if you are not quick in dispatching them.
Now like i said before, the game is not perfect and has some performance issues and some bugs. Zombies waltzing through locked doors and climbing over large rolls of barbed wire kinda make you go WTF.
Pros:
-Endless hours of fun, especially with Breakdown mode.
-Graphically stunning and the attention to detail is pretty good (This isnt a AAA title but still amazing for what it is)
-Combat mechanics are VERY easy to learn and master. Combat is satisfying when you find combo preference.
-Literarly over 100 different melee weapons and firearms each with their distinctive look, detail and impact
-Over 50 different Survivors each with their own traits and quirks, Heroes being the most usefull and powerful.
-Large open world that you can explore, scavenge and drive in
Cons:
-Performance issues such as FPS drop when driving certain vehicles and fighting in certain areas.
-Annoying bugs such as zombies clipping through locked doors like they were open and climbing walls full of barbed wire (Whats the point of having walls again?)
-NPCs will block each other sometimes in doorways... luckilly they will unstuck after a few seconds.
-Inability to choose a Melee mastery and a Firearm mastery separatelly... Luckilly mods will fix this.
-Physics can sometimes work against you when driving a car full of resources and you have the gall to drive over a small stone, making your car lift itself in the air and do a 4 flip stunt before landing wheels up and spitting you on the ground, exploding on your face and destroying those 6 crates Materials you were lucky enough to get... DAMN YOU SMALL STONE!!!!.
-Lack of Multiplayer... Everything in this game just SCREAMS for at least 2 player coop, making it an amazing experience.
Verdict: This is an amazing game that is worth the 28€ current price for NEW USERS. Owners of the original State of Decay should buy this game ONLY if you loved the first one and want a better experience from it. If this was a "meh" game to you, then i do NOT recomend it for ORIGINAL SoD OWNERS that did NOT enjoy the original.

The Good:
- Endless hours of fun.
- Incredibly terrifying moments when you truly believe that all is lost and there's no point in going on. (Which leads to one of the best achievements involving 1 grenade and many zombies *no spoilers*).
- This is a fantastic game for virtual hoarders. (I've spent more time in cars than on foot, hooning around the map picking up rucksacks just to keep my influence in check *Influence is actually a currency in the game which you will need to build or use just about anything*).
- A huge modding community which enables you to change the game to suit your own personal play style. (This is a must for any good apocolyptic sandbox).
- Awesone game play.
- Decent sound effects and music throughout.
The Bad:
- Yes, the graphics are outdated, even with the YOSE version (Year-One Survival Edition).
- Lilly: Your Personal Assistant to "The End Of The World". She's an annoying woman. Does this sound familiar to all you SOD Veterans? "Sounds like they're in a bad spot, maybe you should lend them a hand". Yes, the character audio gets old VERY quickly. But thankfully to the Modding Community, you can shut her up.. PERMANENTLY.
- Soul crushingly repetitive quests. Go here, fetch this, kill that and save this person from themself. Again, gets very old.. very quickly.
- There are many elements to this game which fell short upon release, but again.. thanks the modding community, a lot of this game has been improved. More inventory slots in vehicles and the ability to slow down (control) behaviour of the zombies is a nice touch.
The Horrible:
- Lilly. You all know what I'm talking about. She sure as hell doesn't have to keep reminding me that time is short on EVERY single BLOODY mission. I'll get to it ALRIGHT?! It definitely makes freedom hard to bare when you're being constantly verbally carpet bombed by an incredibly up beat woman, who realistically does SFA towards helping humanity during the apocolypse.
State Of Decay 2 has been confirmed:
Is there anything they should incorporate to improve on the original game? Yes. Many things. Here are some of the main things that need to be improved:
- Graphics, obviously.
- Sound (character or otherwise). This includes and is not limited to character dialogue.
- Music.
- More quests. (And a lot more variety).
- More vehicles. (Modding them would be great. Let us go all "Dawn Of The Dead" on the apocolypse, heavy plated shuttle busses for everyone!). Oh, and for the record.. there's a big difference between putting 6 rucksacks and 6 stacks of cofee in the back of a vehicle. I'd change the storage slots to a "Weight Limit". It makes more sense.
- A lot more base customisation. There's no need to go Fallout 4 on the game, but at least give us some nice choices.
- Weapon customisation. (And more melee weapons. Firearms too if they can.)
- A larger playable area. The original mad from SOD is incredibly small compared to other modern sandboxes. Think: Day Z, on a much grander scale. Show us what Trumbull Valley really looks like.
- A wider variety of buildings.
- Possibly destructible environments as well.
- And if the developers see fit to release a similar DLC like BD, go a bit harder on the density of zombies. I loved games like Dyling Light that made you really work to get where you needed to get to early on in the game. This made for an excellent challenge and a superb gaming experience all round.
And most importantly.. Co-Operative play. MUST HAVE!
Yes, I have much love for the Zombie Apocolypse. Many say it's being done to death. The truth is.. you can never have TOO MANY zombies. Bring on the end of the world.
I'm really looking forward to SOD 2, and I'm hoping that Undead Labs knock one out of the ball park with it. Come on guys, don't dissapoint us! (No pressure)..
Final thought: Would I recommend this game to anyone? You bet I would. 8/10 for State Of Decay - YOSE.

Morphite is an Indie FPS game about a woman called Myrah who explores planets to get resources for her father’s shop. One day, when she is exploring a planet, she encounters a strange object called Morphite. After getting some use from the Morphite, soldiers appear, prompting Myrah to go back to her ship and tell her father. Of course, he doesn’t believe her, so Myrah goes to explore what these soldiers are actually up to.
While the story isn’t all that groundbreaking, the pacing is good and there are moments when the game can get very interesting, if not a bit cliche. The voice acting is well done, bringing some life into the characters throughout the plot.
The gameplay is, at most, decent. It’s your standard FPS but with a specific mechanic that makes playing the game easier: an aim lock-on. If you don’t like aiming at the center of the screen, you can right click to Lock-on an enemy close enough and is on screen. There are over 5 of different guns to choose from, and over 5 tools. Each have a lot of upgrades to chose from. For the guns, you have the Plasma Gun (Very first gun you get in the game), Charged Lazer, Missile Launcher, Auto Rifle, and more. For the Tools, you get the Scanner (you use this to scan plants, animals, and other things for mostly Chunks.), Beacon (you use this to call your Drop-pod to your location, if it can), Ion Grenades (you use these for a boss battle or two, but they’re mostly used to destroy cracks in walls.), Puggles (he has unlimited uses, and he can be an ally for a battle if you summon him. He attacks enemies and helps.), and much more. There are a bunch of enemies in the game, which makes exploring different planets interesting and usually fun. For the guns, you need Ammo, right? If you’re out of Ammo for a gun, it will refill very slowly to a certain number. For the Plasma Gun, if you run out of Ammo, it start to refill slowly until it’s to 5. For the Charged Lazer/Missile Launcher, they can only go up to 1 when refilling. If you want more Ammo than just 5 total every time, some enemies might drop Ammo for your weapons. There are also objects that drop Ammo and other resources, when destroyed. Not only are the guns for shooting, they’re also for unlocking doors or activating objects as well. It’s kind of like Stories: The Path of Destinies where in order to unlock doors blocking paths you can take, you need to have a type of sword for a type of door. That’s what the door are like in Morphite, but instead of using swords, you use guns. Some doors needs the Plasma Gun to shoot at it in order to open. Some doors need the Charger Lazer in order to unlock. Some doors need Missile Lancher. etc.
If you’re not in a planet, you are in the ship. In the ship, you can travel to Star Systems. Each Star System has a planet, and a Station where you can refuel your ship, get upgrades for Myrah at a Conversion Chamber in the Station, get upgrades for the ship, accept side-quests, and break some objects for Ammo. If you are at a Star System and want to go to another one, it will use up fuel. You can get fuel at the stations, or just wait for a bit for the your ship’s fuel to fill up. If you’re in a planet, the ship’s fuel fills up while you’re there, which makes going from one play to another not all that tedious to do. It’s a bit annoying that you have to A) Wait for your fuel to fill up, or B) Buying fuel every single time you go into a Star System. What makes the ship moments interesting is that there can be a random event that can happen. Like there’s an event when you have a choice to trade and buy materials from a ship, or there’s a meteor dodging minigame where you have to dodge meteors in order to not take damage, and much more. While it doesn’t really make up the annoyance on traveling from point A to B, it’s cool they’re there.
But there are two problems I have with this game: the game needs some more polishing, and scrolling through your weapons/tools can get tedious.
Let’s start with the polishing. There were moments where I encountered frustrating bugs. For example, when I got out of a Conversion Chamber in the middle of a planet, I kept on walking to the left for no reason. When I pressed D, I walked right, and when I stopped pressing D, Myrah starts to continue walking left. This bug was fixed when I finished the planet and went back into the ship. Another example is one time when I was exploring a planet I’ve haven’t been to, I just started randomly shooting even though I wasn’t left clicking, and when I ran out of ammo, I couldn’t shoot anymore even though I had 2 ammo when it was refilling. This bugs was fixed when I went back into the ship. I found places where I can clip into objects, like big rocks. And there are moments where Checkpoints resets cutscene spaces. Like I started this cutscene, did this, did that, got the thing I needed, went here, and made it to a Checkpoint. I started the boss, died, and I did the boss again. When battling, I accidently went back to the place where the cutscene is, and it started the unskippable cutscene again while the boss was attacking in the background. For the scrolling being tedious: the order the weapons/tools are in don’t make sense. It would be easy to scroll through the weapons to find the weapon/tool you want, but it’s just a mess. You can press F to select what tool you want, which makes selecting weapons easier, but I just wish scrolling weapons would be easier.
As for the graphics, it’s quite hard to not be reminded of No Man’s Sky. They share strong similarities when it comes to the look of both games. Humans looks like humans, soldiers look like soldiers, robots look like robots, and the monsters look like monsters. The level designs in planets are very detailed and look nice for the most part. While I’ve played indie games that look better, the look of the game is nicely done.
For the soundtrack, it’s not all that good. While the soundtrack does fit the game for the most part, it’s quite forgettable. There are some songs that are quite decent, but for the most part, the soundtrack is just forgettable. The voice acting for characters is very well done, but the music at times is way too loud, which makes it hard to hear what the characters are saying (but there are Subtitles, which is good.) The sound effects do their job well is all I can say about that.
Over and all, Morphite is a very decent indie FPS that has a decent story with good pacing, nice graphics, and while a bit unpolished, the game is fun for the most part. If you like Indie games and FPS games, this is for you. If you want to play a game that has a catchy soundtrack, this isn’t for you. While this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea, I think people who enjoy FPS in general would find this entertaining. It’s not a great Indie game, but it’s not bad.
Mostly Recommended!

I’ve played fifteen hours of Morphite and have really enjoyed it so far. Some people compare it to No Man’s Sky (to the point that Youtube sticks a NMS icon on all Morphite Let’s Play), and to Metroid.
I can’t say anything about Metroid because I have no clue what it is. Maybe because there’s platforming?
Morphite has a fun, cute and effective main story that’s voice acted. I’m about 35% through the main quest (the game tells you that). It spans 15 hand-crafted planets, allowing for interesting puzzles. You can’t really rush through the main quest because your gear will be totally underpowered.
You need money to upgrade your ship, minerals to upgrade your tools and weapons, and scans (plants, minerals, fossils, tech, animals) to upgrade your suit. A bit like in Zelda games, upgrading your suit and acquiring new tools opens new areas, so take notes of where you’ve found locked or unreachable things.
There’s no free flight in Morphite. Click on a solar system, click Go, watch the two seconds warp animation and you’re there. Click on a specific planet or station, click Go, and watch the two seconds landing animation. We live in the future, autopilot exists.
There are however minigames in the form of space encounters. Sometimes you’ll man a turret to shoot at hostiles, sometimes you’ll navigate through a ridiculously dense asteroid field, but that’s the closest to flying you’ll get. There’s only one ship but you can (need to) upgrade it.
There are thousands of procedural planets, which you’ll want to visit for their resources, weird life forms, landscapes, villages, shops, and (usually silly) side quests. You won’t get a bajillion square miles of perlin height maps. Instead you’ll visit a couple of caves, fight in a tiny but dense forest, jump over one toxic river, find your way to the top of one platformingly nasty rock, etc.. Quality and variety before quantity. I’ve landed on 50 planets and I’m still discovering new things (first lava river last night!).
Oh, and there’s no inventory! Well, you do carry tools, weapons, scans, minerals, quest items, but they all show in their own list and stack infinitely. No weight, no slots, no encumbrance.
I haven’t finished the game so maybe I’ll get bored, maybe the end will suck, maybe I’ll encounter a game-breaking bug. I’ll write an update if that happens.
=====  UPDATE  =====
I've finished the game.  My recommendation is a bit more tepid, now.  The second half of the game is visibly less polished than the first and makes little annoyances more annoying.
* The checkpoint system is supposed to autosave your progress through the main quest, but it's really weirdly done: say you die or quit the game between talking to a quest giver and finishing a quest.  Next time you load, the quest giver will still deliver their dialog as if you never started the quest, but they won't give you the item you need. The item isn't in your inventory or on the floor where you died either; in fact it's been magically teleported to where you were supposed to bring it.  This is utterly confusing and caused me to believe I had been struck by a game-breaking bugs.
* You're going to see through walls, walk through missing colliders and fall through the level.  It reminded me of Daggerfall.
So I consider this game as a very good Beta.  It's fun, it's feature-complete, but it needs a few bug fixes and a layer of polish to avoid useless confusion.

I play games for the journey sometimes more than the goal. If I was to judge this game solely by that criteria it would probably be a neutral for me. Metroidvania games are popular because they have an open ended journey and it's usually a lot of challenge and discovery getting to your goal. We start off the game with a clear precise goal. To get into the castle of the big bad evil that has put your sister in some kind of coma with his evil powers. Okay, I'm down with that. So with my trusty sword and a bit of magic I head off on the journey of reaching that primary goal.
Now the first thing that's a little strange to me is that this game is terribly linear. You really only go forward. There are a few inaccessible areas that you can backtrack to for completion but really once you reach the castle there's no reason to explore any of the other places ever again. Though I don't mind the single minded straightforwardness of the objective. There was perhaps a missed opportunity but that's okay.
Second is there's a lot of platforming elements, which in and of itself isn't bad but it's a bit difficult to distinguish a hole that might lead somewhere and one that just sends you to your death. Sometimes one must learn by dying, again perfectly acceptable.
Our character grows stronger and develops his powers to eventually take on the master of the castle. I found the balance to be decent and the game does reward you with adequate prize for finding the hidden puzzles all around the island. I did encounter a few bugs. One major in a boss battle but nothing game breaking. It took me roughly 3 hours and some change to complete.
The biggest issue I have with this game is it's BS ending.
*SPOILER ALERT*
Now I'm all for "it was all a dream" games where you find out your actions really had no effect on the outcome. Usually there's significant character growth that happens to compensate for lack of change. However, Hald, our protagonist, doesn't grow in any meaningful way throughout the game that can justify it being all a dream.
Then the ending shows us the reality of the situation that alludes to serious issues that the developer glosses over in a super short scene and leaves it at that. So you have no growth, no sense of accomplishment and the realization that you have been put in a situation that your character can't change. Yeah, not only did the ending leave me a bit confused as to what was going on but what it alludes to was some really dark themes.
Now I'm not saying you can't make any kind of game you want but when you introduce implied issues such as incest and♥♥♥♥♥♥as a developer you should really flesh out your game to just not end on a note that goes "everything you just did, it was all a dream" and then wake up to that reality. It cheapens your game and the player experience. And from what I've read there's no other ending. So we're left with a whole bunch of questions that won't be answered and nothing gets resolved. Even if there was a sequel I don't think I'd want to play it. The way the first one ends was frustrating enough.

I don't remember how I heard about this game, but I had this game on my wishlist for months and kept forgetting about it until I was 50 cents short of a trading card during a winter sale purchase. It's not much, but doesn't really claim to be more than what it is, either. I played this while waiting for another game to download in the background.
Pros:
+ Tight controls (Not the tightest, but still tight enough to where most of your mistakes are your fault)
+ Costs less than a soda when it's on sale
+ Trading Cards and Achievements
+ Great controller support with rumble
+ Visuals and audio are mostly consistent and make the game really feel like a SNES game
Cons:
- Requires administrative privileges (Why??? This killed any desire I had to keep this on my living room steambox. Means I can't play it without a keyboard attached to my living room PC.)
- A little too linear for what claims to be a metroidvania
- Magic is useless beyond shooting at a switch or teleporting; while I didn't spec into it, your magic pool is so small and regenerates so slowly that it just ends up being quicker to rely on melee
- The writing is almost embarrasing at times
Mixed:
~ Story is weak/forgettable, felt like the twist ending was shoehorned in and could have been more impactful by having the world you explore, equipment you gain, and enemies you fight tie in with it somehow
~ Level design goes from linear to labrynthine without warning and makes the last level arduous
~ The skills you learn, while nothing new, serve mainly to progress the story, don't add anything to the other mechanics, and doesn't give much of an incentive to go back and explore areas you've already been to.
~ The most expensive equipment you can buy ended up being underwhelming and not worth the time it took exploring to find enough coins to buy it with, but it's still entirely possible to play to the end without them without much trouble
All in all, it's genuinely not that bad. It's not without its flaws, but for the price of admission ($0.59 at a 90% discount) it's a fun action platformer. I hope the developer learns from this game and improves on the next game he makes in this genre (if he ever does).

A quite short but very well-packed Metroidvania.
You won't have any trouble to know where you should go, as the game is very linear, even if you can still explore a little to find weapons, armors, items and puzzle pieces, sometimes after defeating a powerful foe. Yes, the storyline is short, and the scenario quite anecdotal. But you won't be disappointed with the action/plateform part of the game, which works perfectly, with a good dodge system and some epic boss battles, including a challenging one (who didn't lose against Scylla?).
The game's not very difficult to beat however, since there are a lot of save points, which is perfectly fine to me.
The pixel-art graphics are good (especially when you play in windowed mode), depicting the classical environments you can expect from a Castlevanai-like, but the soundtrack really is the biggest surprise of the game, with some true audio gems inside (the moutain's theme).
So yeah, Inexistence can't pretend to equal its model, but is good enough to keep you hooked for a few hours, and even make you go back to it from time to time.

Got this game when it was a whopping 90% off (that's 60 cents, no joke). I can certainly see why it was so heavily discounted. Honestly, it's a very underwhelming title -- while not totally horrible, it's definitely nowhere near the full price, but it does have its positive points.
First, the good: It's got pretty good soundtrack and a pretty nice visual aesthetic. Control is pretty solid on the keyboard. The game handles well and doesn't rely on particularly frustrating platforming. Also the fact that the game over screen doesn't waste your time (no cinematics or drama; you can go back to the last save point mere seconds from when you drop dead) is thoughtful.
But then, the bad...
First off, this game is painfully short. I nearly 100%'d the game on hard mode, one playthrough, in just a few hours. And that counts excess time spent grinding. There's only a small handfull of areas to explore, and there's not much freedom of exploration to be found. There's a few side paths to get to treasure, and the last area does branch out somewhat but in that area, you have to hit most of the branches in a set order anyway. Don't be fooled by the description as there is not much content, and they use the word "many" overly liberally. Two difficulty levels is not "many". 10 Steam achievements doesn't generally count as "many", in comparison to other titles. And I'm sure 10 pieces of collectable equipment (not counting the two you start with) and three obtainable skills (not counting the two you start with) don't sound particularly impressive, either.
Secondly, the game has some embarassing bugs. One of which will infuriate completionists. There's a bug in the game that sometimes makes some treasure chests and/or puzzle pieces start out pre-opened/collected by the time you get to them late in the game, and you don't get the credit for them, which makes your savefile permanently unable to attain that achievement (forcing you to start over if you want the achievement). This bug has been known for at least a month, judging by a skim reading of the Steam community, and still has not been patched at the time of this writing. Additionally, one of the bosses has projectiles that don't even move when launched and just sit there for the duration of the fight. Finally, using alt+tab to switch in and out of the game in fullscreen mode messes up your aspect ratio if your native aspect ratio is 4:3 and not widescreen, causing the game to lose its letterbox effect and stretch the image unnaturally.
It just doesn't feel like much effort or thought was put into this game at all, aside from the visual design. In turn it winds up being very forgettable. Since I got it for so cheap I'm not particularly incensed at the cost, and I'd say it's worth the 60 cents it's on sale for (as of this writing). I wouldn't pay the full price for it though, personally, at least on gameplay merit alone.
Still, though, it's a start. The developer might have some potential here on future works, but he needs to think bigger if he wants to put down any real opening price on future works. If you're reading this, Mr. Brassaud, then my advice to you is this: Up the ante. Go all in. Invest more time and effort into your next project. It will show. I wish you the best of luck in future projects.

Perfect game for anyone who loves building a team of kick♥♥♥♥♥zombie survivalists as well as feel immersed within a zombie apocalypse.
I was thoroughly impressed with the amount of fixes that were made on this version of the game. I love the additions to the loyal fans and love how modding has progressed within the game.
During the campaign, you look at the survival of 3 main characters. Marcus, Ed, and Maya. You find them stranded at the very start of the game. You are invited to join another enclave of survivors who are in the same position. As you progress you are introduced to new characters and the military's involvement within this apocalypse. You are constantly bombarded with quests that will allow you to help your community prosper as well as the characters you favour most but make no mistake the dead are still there.
If that was too laid back and easy for you then the first edition of DLC will help you get that difficulty increase you desire. Unlike in the story, during 'Breakdown' you start off as one character with the forever loved radio girl, Lily Ritter. You are tasked with finding an enclave to take shelter in and help them thrive. While you are collecting resources and battling the dead you will be looking for an RV. A large vehicle which you can fit up to 7 survivors on to progress to the next level. As you increase in level, so does the difficulty. Introducing fewer resources for you to take home. More deadly special zombies which will tear your characters up one by one and faster zombies to make sure you are always on your toes.
If that's too grindy for you and you'd like to play a story with a bit more then 2nd edition of DLC is perfect for you. Looking at the military's involvement far from the home that you are used to in the Campaign and Breakdown. In this post-apocalyptic city, you will battle your way through hordes of zeds to extract VIP's from the area in all hopes to defeat the virus. You will also be tasked on the side if you wish, to help civilians still trapped within the city before it goes up in flames.
I put a lot of hours into the original game during my time on the Xbox 360 and I can happily say that the game runs perfectly on both platforms. I don't think I could find a more perfect game when looking at survival a zombie apocalypse.
I recommend highly to anyone looking for a challenging experience into the survival of the undead.

This is a solid shooter.
Republic commando was released in early 2005 for the original Xbox, less than a year from the launch of the 360. A novel was released a few months prior. I played the game and read the novel within a month of its release, and so I'm fairly biased.
Graphics: The graphics have held up suprisingly well. The game's style seemed very gritty and realistic when I first played it, but now seems mildly cartoonish. I'm not sure if it is just the way games were back then, or if my memory is colored from the way this game compared to other star wars games of that generation, which seemed more clean and colorful. Either way, the cartoonishness makes it hold up better than other games of that time, the character models especially are a great study.
The hud in particular stands out for mention. Each member of your squad is both color and number coordinated: Green, Yellow, Red, 40, 62, 07. When your crosshairs sweep a member of your squad, your hud lights up with that unit's color along several bands, and the number above the health and status indicator blinks as well.
Also, your visor will get splattered with rain and blood, and wipe itself off.
Sound: The music in this game is absolutely fantastic, especially when compared to the other Star Wars games i've played, which tend to barely derrivate from the original movie scores. The game's main theme is an original choral peice in "Mandalorian" the language used by the ancestors and trainers of the Clones. The games composer seems to have originated the language for the track. The score is well mixed from the movie scores, and coordinated occasionally to smart decicions by the player. The voice acting involves both the work of the actor who played Jango Fett, several sound alikes, and a few unique voices.
Gameplay: The gameplay is the meat of it. You play as a squad leader in a squad of 4, through linear FPS levels set in the Star Wars universe.
Combat: You have shields and a health bar, as does each of your squadmates, just like in the first Halo. Also like Halo, your enemies can take quite a few punches before dying; one super battle droid in this game can wipe out your squad if you are not there to throw an EMP grenade or launch anti armor at it. Whenever you or one of your squadmates goes down, its up to whoever is still up to come and recussitate him. If all go down, obviously, it's game over. There are frequent health stations throughout each level, and you may order a squadmate (whose health is visible in your hud) to the station as well as heal yourself.
Tactical Shooter: You have a limited number of commands to give to your squad, obviously intended to work well with an Xbox controller. You have a 4 basic movement commands, such as form up and move to attack position, and a concentrate fire command. Besides these, your commands are restriced to specific selectable actions. The enviorment contains turrets, places to plant a bomb or mine, places to hack, positions from which to snipe, throw grenades, or launch anti armor from,  and doors where you can breach and clear. These are all indicated by an icon, and when you aim your redicule at one your hud will show a hologram of a soldier in that position. You can do many of these your yourself, or give an order for one of your squat to get in that position. This is the extent of the tactical side of the squad mechanics.
An example of this in action; you may see a place to hack into a console (the objective), and two positions to snipe from nearby. You order a squadmate to hack the console, and the two others to each of the sniping positions, while you dance around in between, monitering the situation, and providing grenades where needed. It's not very intricate, but I found it thoroughly enjoyable.
Weapons: You have 4 basic guns; a pistol, and a rifle with both a sniper and an anti armor attachment. You may also choose one weapon that you run across to take with you at a time. These range from rocket launchers to shotguns. Melee is an option, with a wrist blade and rife butts, and there are a few different grenade types.
Multiplayer: I've never really played multiplayer, I imagine the servers are currently dead. The largest thing lacking in this game is  co-op of any kind: co-op is perfect for a squad based shooter, it's sad that it couldn't be added.
Story: There isn't much of a story. After a brief prologue, you land on Geonosis, the first of three 'campaigns' the game is comprised of, the other two being an 'abandoned' republic ship, and the prelude to the battle of Kashyyyk. The game ends with a cliff hanger setting up for a sequal that has yet to be realized. There isn't that much lore either, it's no KOTOR, it's mostly about the gameplay and setting.
Characters: The three squad mates are simple cookie cutter characters: the sniper psycho, the wise cracking demo guy, the austere by the book electronics guy. They weren't much, but their personalities did add alot to the game's downtime, and made you feel anxious when each one went down.
Recommendation: This is a game explicitly designed for Star Wars fans. It's one of the best things lucasarts has done, and if you love that era of expanded universe games, then this is a must play. It's an easy to grasp squad based shooter with a 10-15 hour campaign and not a single Jedi slicing things up.
Note: A major issue for some AMD cards will cause the game to crash if 'bumpmaping' is enabled in the options, but this is fixable via a mod.
Note: The lead programmer for this game, Brett Douville, has a series of archived streams entitled "An Oral History of Star Wars: Republic Commando" available on youtube, which are an excellent watch for fans of the game.
Rule 39 out of 10

I am legitimately confused at why this game is so highly recommended in the Star Wars library. Seriously? What's so special about Republic Commando? The story was complete wank, first off. Everything was just one battlefield to another with no special connection. They try to tie them in with some "mystery" arc, but I never believed it, as they'd drop all sorts of ideas minutes after you'd hear them.
The characters are all pretty stereotypical war game types: Boss is the Leader, Scorch is the Joker, Fixer is the... Fixer. However, I'll give it to Sev for being my favorite character. You'd figure in the middle of the war with all those millions of clones there'd be at least one who loved killing things, and that's really why I appreciate Sev so much. He's got some of the best lines in this game. But, in the contrast, Scorch has some of the WORST. He comes off as such forced humor, I'd constantly sigh a contemptuous breath every time he'd utter another snarky comment about the situation. And he has a limited number of dialogue options, so I'd hear those bloody jokes over and over and OVER again, till I wanted to strangle Scorch with my bare hands.
On top of all this, the gameplay is hardly anything to brag about. It feels like the game was trying to be something of a Strategy game combined with an FPS years before Mass Effect came out and really solidified that type of game, and RC's attempt is just really... sloppy. The Strategy elements are simple and once you give your teammates something to do, the battle is pretty much in your favor. NEVER let them be idle, because the AI in this game is horrific, and the game itself is suscepticle to numerous glitches that'd often have me restart from my last save to make sure Fixer got in the bloody turret.
The FPS gameplay in this is also totally off. The machine gun should- and again, for emphasis, should- be a moderate gun, but it's the weakest in your arsenal. Your pistol does more damage than it. I'm not kidding. Whenever I'd spray a Super Battle Droid with my machine gun, it felt about as effective and satisfying as spraying them with a water gun. There were parts I started to have fun in this constant, repetive shooting and running exercise, when I'd plan a bunch of traps for the enemies, but remember how bad the AI is? The enemies would just stand there, telepathically knowing all the traps I had cleverly laid down, putting all my work to shame, and putting me back into the monotony of shooting, commanding, covering, and running.
The environments themselves lack a lot of vivid color. They're all greys and darker colors so it has this very muddy-like feel about it. For what it's worth, I'll give the game one other credit besides Sev. The windshield wiper. If you know anyone who's played it or if you've played it yourself- EVERYONE remembers the windshield wiper. It's a cute, humorous little thing. I liked it. But, seriously, though, that ending? I won't spoil anything, but it literally felt like the game had run out of ideas and just decided to end where it was, even though there was a story somewhere that needed to be finished, so they shoved in a couple BS lines (delivered by Yoda, of all people), and the game just... ends. I felt unsatisfied, bored, and ultimately angry with this Star Wars game. I really can't see a reason why other people like this one, but I'll always remember the windshield wiper. Forever. Everything else is just crap.

I read books, ladies and gentlemen.
Don't get too scared, though; I only do it sometimes.
But when I do, I like to read books about games, so long as they are accepted as cannon in their respective universes. I happened upon one written by Karen Traviss, named Order 66. I was interested, so I read it. It was, unexpectedly, one of the most depressing books I have read: but that isn't the point. The point is it contains a story that includes and expands upon the one in this game. And it doesn't conflict with this story either.
What you have just read, if you read this far, is not a review of this game. If you want a review of the game, find one that says the game is perfect and was far beyond its time when it was released, and you have an accurate review. This is one of my favorite Star Wars games ever. I'm trying to think of something wrong with it, and I can't. It's great.

After giving this game very, very little of my time I'm going to go ahead and put it down and get a refund. Why do I want my fifty-nine cents back?
- Sounds are ridiculous. Every time you jump it sounds like somebody banging on a very large, very cheap drum.
- 'Combat' consists of stringing together a whole two button presses...one shortly after the other...and firing a magical projectile in a straight line.
- The levelling up system consists of a point dump that seems worthless to do anything but pour into strength, both from what I've seen and what others have stated.
- Uninspired level and monster design right off the bat. Small, green haired, two-footed things that looked suspiciously like reworked goombas, plants with yoshi-shaped heads that spit fire and don't even turn when you jump behind them, and pit-dwelling hopping critters with big eyes and pincers.
- A Legend of Zelda reference. Seriously. The shop-keeper is named Sahasrahla and even is an old man who helps the hero.
These simple sins alone take away and detract from the entire experience. The game isn't fun, it isn't challenging that I can tell, and it sure as hell isn't original given the monster designs plug off of goombas and petey pirahnas and the first helpful NPC you meet is named after a LoZ character.

Morphite feels like a well-rounded early access game. Solid gameplay, everything works, even some voice acting, but with fixes required. However, that said, the price is right for the game, and while I would love to see improvements made I am enjoying my time. The game is pretty much a zen-like experience, and even the combat could be removed simply in favour of puzzles and environmental platforming challenges.
The one thing that does bug me is that it appears like there are only a few models for plants and animals, and these are recycled endlessly, to the point where it is essential to scan everything just to see if you already have it. Even within "species" the variants (strong, weak, diseased, rare) all appear to be identical. I have not determined if there is an upgrade that allows you to see without scanning whether something is new, but better visual feedback here would be appreciated.
And no, I will not comment on whether or not this is a No Man's Sky killer, as I have not played NMS.
Positives
- Interesting art style
- Exploration
- Shoot everything that does and doesn't move
- Interesting story
- Very casual experience
Negatives
- Some of the procedural generation results in very strange clipping and texture errors
- Have fallen through the floor on more than one occasion
- Minimap is nearly useless
- Planets and space stations quickly feel samey
- Colour palette could be more varied on the planets, and especially on the space stations
- Plant and animal variation limited

Morphite is an enjoyable casual game that offers a bit of adventure & exploration.
I created this review near the game’s initial release so please keep in mind that things can be fixed or changed since the point of this review. Also, since the game is still quite new I'll try to omit any bugs from this review and rather focus on the points that I enjoy or dislike about this game.
First, The Cons:
- Resources seem a bit low to obtain for the potential upgrades needed, the game is already quite casual and the pace of gathering resources is already low so expect it to take a while to upgrade your ship, suit, and weapons.
- There’s no run button… You don’t move that slow and you can later upgrade your movement speed with resources, but there’s no run button.
- Not enough interaction within space stations. It would be nice if I could destroy computers or plants for resources. Or have some kind of consequence like hostile station visors if you shoot them or take the resources from that room. I don’t have any sense of ‘new’ or unexpected when visiting them unlike planets.
- I noticed the same 'pattern' for a few planets, the same slopes, the same layout segments. It's not overwhelming but noticeable enough for some maps to feel 'visited'
- Scanning things can get annoying for being a major aspect of the game. Tiny bugs are sometimes almost impossible regardless of scanner upgrades.
Pro's
- Simple graphics that doesn't look ugly
- Plenty of content, mineral harvesting, exploration, missions, storyline, side quests, space interactions, player, ship, weapons, etc upgrades.
- There are plenty of planets to explore and each new visit leaves me enjoying the visit with a 'new' enough experience.
- Additional weapons are unlocked with a 'Metroid' feel behind it which kicked up some nice nostalgia for me.
- Creatures and AI interactions are nice in that anything could be hostile, fearful, or careless with the players presence.
- There's nothing to ruin my playing experience. No hunger bars, no nagging messages, no stamina  meters, no small inventory space, no survival gauges, just a nice Casual / Exploration game that was designed with the intent of being ENJOYED.
- Why couldn't NNS be more like this game.
Overall, it's not a bad game for the price, but there is plenty of rrom for improvement & bug fixes.
So far it's an ok game. It needs to be improved on many regards, but I like it overall.

NOTE: A Key for this game was providedee by the Publisher. No other consideration was offered, requested, or expected. My opinions are my own, and are offered here so that the Consumer may make an informed decision.
Going into a $15 game that seems as ambitious as the claims in the description are, I braced myself for the pain of NMS with degraded visuals.
I'm happy to report that the game manages to hit its marks and goes on to offer more if you really want it. Fifteen handcrafted worlds and innumerable others await the intrepid explorer, with lots of varied flora and fauna to scan before you kill it dead. Your little android buddy, Kitcat, is possessed of the sort of sense of humor one finds in a friendly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing forum, Myrah has a dream that she stretches to realize, and her mentor is a dark ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Go figure.
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely. It does have the odd bug, but I have yet to discover anything gamebreaking. There's no crafting, for a wonder, and the soundtrack is quite tasty. Unlike other (not as fun) games of late, it even seems that they took some time and effort with the voice direction.
Imagine, if you will, Mass Effect: Andromeda and No Man's Sky, with the things that made those games terrible either avoided (facial animations, implied Multiplayer), or done properly (voice acting, procedural generation), less the ridiculous crafting. What use there is for resources is handled by simplifying it to an extreme degree. Gone is the requirement for our hero to be not only starship pilot and explorer, but carpenter, metalworker, weaver and every-damned-thing-else under the sun.
The result was made by a small team, better than the two games I mentioned above, for an eighth of the price at release (less if you get it during the intro sale). For the type of game it is, I find myself genuinely thankful that I don't have to tell her to eat every ten minutes, drink every other minute, or anything else. Not having to babysit a woman grown is a breath of fresh air. Gone is the infant of your average survival game, and in its place we have a polished experience that can show AAA how its done on a budget of less than half a billion dollars.

Hawks Tactical is not a typical RPG Maker game. It is more a tactical strategy game. Battles are played on a map full of enemies, where each turn, each of your units may move, attack, and use one or two skills, the goal being to wipe out all the opponent's units. The game lasts about seven hours total.
There is a storyline, but beyond the initial premise, it mostly serves to lead in to the next battle. There are decisions to be made at some points, which lead the story along multiple paths, with multiple endings possible, but these are few in number.
There is very little exploration, and the tactical battles are the primary focus. These battles can last anywhere from ten minutes to an hour. They may look difficult, but if you know what you're doing at all, they are easy to beat.
Battles provide you with money, which can be spent in stores to buy weapons, armour, and skill enhancements. These stores, however, appear at unpredictable points in the game, and may not be there when needed. Occasional treasure chests provide items which are useless, as far as I could tell.

What a little gem this game is. You play as a leader of a 4 man squad of commandos during the clone wars. You take on 3 campaigns, the first is on Genosis where the Star wars film episode 2 ends. The second campaign is on a ghost ship and the final part takes place on a Wooky planet as you spearhead an invasion.
The gameplay is a bog standard shooter for the most part with your usual affair of weapons: Assault rifle, sniper rifle and so on. The game does have unique weapons for each level but they are all pretty unremarkable. The game does boast tactical decisions however, Place a soldier on a turret ? sniper position or just hold their ground? the choices are rather basic which is an interesting comparison to the actual games difficulty which at times can be downright punishing.
While this all sounds fairly samey its the characters interactions and music really add another level of immersion and epic moments. The Ai is rather good as well seeking you out to destroy you and punishing you for mistakes. However there is one enemy that doesn’t really fit with the rest of the game, its a flying enemy with an overpowered laser that will always damage or kill members of your team, it seems a little imbalanced and you will always sigh as soon as these guys show up. Your team mates in comparison do a good job to an extent. sometimes they freeze and refuse to move. The worst is when they are flanked and they just get malled rather then retreat or reposition. As a whole the game is fun, i find the ending campaign wasn’t as interesting as the previous two in my opinion and the finale was a complete yawn, same enemies same corridors and a boring final resolution that disappoints.
It seems like the developers really wanted to give another approach to the Star Wars universe and for the most part they succeeded the game is fun and when the maps open up for a big skirmish it really clicks. A few nagging points and the lacklustre final section of the campaign as well as maps at times being a little repetitive holds the game back. Overall : Good but not great.

Fire damage is
here, being the fire traps in the Arena game mode.
More destructable objects is confirmed, first example being tables.
EDIT: The new bodytypes are Muscular and armored. With Tank Top Prisoners and the Buff Boss being Muscular, and the Riot Helm guards being armored.
Paint the Town Red is a medium-paced bar fighting game with a large variety of weapons and enemies now and here to come. It still needs a bit of optimization, but the devs assure us that the game will be optimized as the game progresses (And updates.)
The enemies are completely destructible. You could dissolve someone if you have enough time and the weapon doesn't break. All the voxels on the enemies have different properties, with bone being the strongest natural voxel and skin being the weakest. (You will be able to damage Riot Helmets later on, but those aren't natural.) Additional fact, is that if a enemy's brain is damaged in anyway, they will instantly die, if they don't, its a bug.
The weapons range from messy steaks and urinal cakes, to Katanas and Shotguns. All of them have different durability, damage, throw damage, voxel damage, and maybe even a unique trait, such as being able to instantly stun someone if you hit them in the head area with Soap or a Urinal cake.
(You do not need to directly aim for the mouth to stun the enemy, and you can stun a enemy with any blunt weapon if you hit them in the face, though it is random.)
The combat is quite intense as it is mostly melee combat, you can do overhead and right side swings and normal attacks. You can also kick of which knockback power and damage depends on how full the bar is. Full means a guaranteed knockdown. (Knockback has not been implemented yet.) Throwing damage, speed and range also depend on the bar level. But if you sit ontop of the bar throwing mugs at people, you aren't playing the game right.
Extending on the Combat subject, if you damage a enemy enough, they will go into a enraged mode dealing extra damage, having extra speed and attack speed.
If you are having problems with FPS, look at the low performance section of the "Common Issues" thread I linked above. Otherwise, the game runs quite well when you select the appropriate options for your machine. (In game options.)
I rate PTTR (Paint the Town Red.) 9/10.
Positives:
-Fun Combat.
-Great Mechanics.
-Active Developers.
-Very Friendly Community.
-Relatively fast updates when they're not working on bigger things. (1-2 Monthly big updates, weekly small updates.)
Small Negatives.
-Still needs a bit of optimization. (The Disco Dancefloor.)
-A bit of bugs, not necessarily gamebreaking, but immersion breaking.
-Rare crashes.
This is most of the information I've gathered so far. Thank you for reading this review.

CORRECTION: in an earlier version of this review, the game was stated as free. This is not true, it 98¥. The review has been corrected.
A minimal-effort my-first-project phone app that made its way to Steam to fund the developer's lunch money.
It's squares, circles, rectangles, and triangles galore. Shapes have been put together to make a pig, and monkey, and a panda. If you looked at this game with a kid's junior high school computer class project, you would never know which one made it to Steam. The music sucks, too. It's just a repetition of a few notes played in an endless loop.
I've given this game a higher rating than Sakura Clicker because the chartacters move. Somehow, the developer knew enough code to make the animals wink; that's more action than what you see in Sakura Clicker.
It's a simple and straightforward concept. A statement is made, and you decide if the statement is true or false. Click on your guess and find out if it's true or false. That's it. There's nothing else to it.
It's worth mentioning that there are two modes of gameplay as of this writing, quick mode and campaign mode. However, there is very little difference between the two. Quick mode gives you 20 statements to verify, and if you miss one, it's game over. It's the survival mode of the game. The other mode is campaign mode. If you miss, you're fine; you get all the statements in the library. It's a surefire way to get all the questions you can be given. I call it, "practice mode" and the quick mode the main game.
As the graphics suggest, it feels and plays like a junior high student's computer class project. It's a simple concept that doesn't require much thought into it. This kind of game has been aroun since the dawn of man, when the sphinx asked Oedipus a riddle. It's a short, lazy trivia game.
For a simple game, it has its moments, The facts are interesting, and there are times where I unsure about the correct answer. This comes from a man, who was his school's academic team star. They're the kind of facts that no one would know, unless you hear it in a trivia game before. While they're pointless, the facts are neat for about 10 minutes. And, that's more than what I can say about Sakura Clicker.
And here is where I justify why I give this hackneyed game two stars. The gameplay is simple and repetitive, and the game is way too short, even though it's less that a dollar. No one should have to pay for extra statements. If this is actually a trial version in disguise, then shame on them. No one should pay for a trial version. At least freemium has the option of playing the game for free, the pay isn't necessary. The one big plus about this game is that the badges are easy to obtain via campaign mode, and I don't have to waste my time grinding to get them. There are only a few and now I can tell all three of my friends that I have completed a Steam game 100%. Hooray, I feel accomplished!

There's also other modes, but you need the DLC for that.
It would be a fun little game to play and learn interesting facts with for 30 minutes or so... if it weren't for one glaring problem.
Not all of the questions are correct.
There are many times where I got fed the wrong information from the game by telling me that something isn't right when it actually is or vice versa, which makes me paranoid as to what's true and what's false.
The game's free to play, but I don't reccomend it unless you're an achievement hunter.  Just get 12 particular questions correct, and you'll get an easy 100% completion, no DLC needed.  For the rest of you, look elsewhere for trivial knowledge.
Some interesting facts fo sure.

Rebellion are a company that've brought us some pretty great games over the years such as Alien versus Predator 2000, Rogue Trooper, and the Sniper Elite series; we'll just forget that Rogue Warrior ever happened, that chip also falls on Bethesda's shoulders. For those unaware, the Sniper Elite games are World War II based, hyper-realistic first-person shooter titles that, surprise, revolve around sniping. Played on the right difficulty, the player is tasked with aiming with such precision that a mere slight whisper of wind can put their bullet trajectory off. In 2013, Rebellion decided to cash in on the zombie craze, and in doing so they brought us the first installment of Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army.
If there's anything that Wolfenstein has taught the gaming community over the last two decades, it's that killing Nazis in any form is just thoroughly satisfying. Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army has stepped in and managed to make mangling hordes of undead fascists all the more delightful with the series' signature bullet cam, which is triggered randomly upon landing a bullet in an enemy. Seeing Nazi skulls and eye sockets shatter in close up, slo-mo is not only just enjoyable when it's against a "living" AI, but it's all the more gruesomely fun when it's against a zombie AI.
So what's going on here is that it's the end of World War II, and Hitler is realizing that he's losing the war. Determined to completely destroy the world, he unleashes "Plan Z", which as it turns out is the resurrection of all Wehrmacht's fallen soldiers. That's pretty much as far as the story goes in this release, though it is further elaborated on in the Zombie Army Trilogy. Nevertheless, OSS operative and sniper Karl Faireburne, veteran Red Army infantryman Boris Medvedev, Wehrmacht Captain Hermann Wolff, and German occultist Efram Schwaiger are here to save the day. Although if you're playing the single player campaign, you're forced to only play as Karl.
The game is spread out across five chapters, each that last about an hour a piece depending on your skill. Every map shows a war-torn Germany in the throes of Nazi warfare. Propaganda litters the walls, Nazi banners are present everywhere. There are also dismembered bodies hanging from street lamps, obvious suicides huddled into corners, blood-drawn pentagrams and swastikas everywhere, and tons of blood and gore splatter all over the place. Most levels also feature fog effects, whether it be low to the ground or encompassing the map. The lighting looks absolutely phenomenal, and it really causes the visuals to pop out and be exceptionally striking. Accompanying the aesthetics is a slightly out of place soundtrack that is reminiscent of the 1980's, and while it doesn't suit the time period of the game, it's a decent listen.
Now, Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is one intense game. It's extremely easy to get overrun by zombies if you don't have patience or take your time; rushing into any part of the map is an incredibly bad idea. You will constantly be questioning yourself, and discovering new tactics to take on the small amount of different enemy types. Should you use your sniper rifle here? What about your pistol there? Should you stick to the beaten path, or do you want to explore to try and find Nazi gold and bottles of blood? Venturing off the trail almost always results in more enemies appearing, do you have enough ammo for that? You're constantly thinking tactically, as ammo conservation is pretty concerning; if you run out, you're dead as weapon and ammo pick ups outside of safe-houses is rare.
Your enjoyment of this title will rely very heavily on how good and consistent you are with headshots. Unlike many other zombie shooter games, this one keeps Sniper Elite's signature realism, and in doing so you must aim for the head. If you hit a zombie in the body, it will fall down for a few moments and resurrect, costing you precious ammo to strike it down again. With that said, the enemies can die without headshots, but you will find yourself both starved for ammunition and almost always overrun if that route is taken. Headshots can be very tricky, due to the exaggerated shambling of the foes; their heads are constantly moving, and if you're on stairs you might as well forget about it.
As far as mechanics go, pretty much everything from the main Sniper Elite games make an appearance. You can carry three guns with you, one sniper rifle, one shotgun OR automatic weapon, and one pistol. At any time you can also have up to two of each throwable, such as a landmine, dynamite, and grenades. You don't have a health bar, but more than a handful of hits on even the easiest difficulty and you're back to your last checkpoint; which thankfully are placed in generous locations. You can even make your character hold his breath while aiming with a sniper rifle in order to slightly slow down time, though it can only be done if his heart rate is low enough.
Much like Left 4 Dead, Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is truly built for co-op play with up to three other people. Though the game is still a blast during the solo campaign, it doesn't have a big replay factor unless you have some buddies that you can play with. Sadly, online play is dead now, so I can only suggest purchasing this iteration of the game if you want to experience the original solo game; even then I say to consider waiting for at least a 75% discount, especially given the age of the title. There are also a handful of problems that cause the game to feel a little clunky at times; the reach of the enemies is just a little too long for their models, grenades are practically useless due to being unable to control their throw distance, to loot bodies you have to stop and press a key, and the bodies disappear quicker than you can loot them.
Despite its very few grievous flaws, Sniper Elite: Nazi Zombie Army is a breathtaking experience. I found myself holding my breath at times, when I was aiming down the scope of my sniper rifle trying to land an important shot. I even uttered the words "oh no, please, no" when a bulky, gun-toting Nazi soldier came into play. The game is incredibly immersive, and even though it's tough at the beginning, once you get your headshots down and learn how to deal with each of the five or six enemy types, it becomes a little bit easier. It does take a lot of inspiration from Left 4 Dead, such as safe-houses and siege moments, but it's a much more exhilarating, gore-soaked event. If you have friends to play with, or don't mind a single player experience, grab this one on a 75% discount. Otherwise, look into grabbing Zombie Army Trilogy instead.

The No Man's Sky killer? Not quite.
In this review a want to adress 2 different subjects, one is the game as itself, and the other is the title "NMS done right" as put by many other reviewers... i have been too long chasing this fabled "NMS done right" and i have always come out empty handed... this is no exception, this is NOT like No Man's Sky AT ALL. (to read about this, skip to the bottom of my review)
Morphite is an exploration/platformer/puzzle game. It has many common elements with the Metroid Prime series, down the female character, we have then some dungeon crawling with passive and agressive wildlife, we shoot things to get health/ammo/etc, and we scan different creatures. We can get different upgrades for our scanners/suit/weapon, upgrades that will allow us to resist new enviroments, open new paths and such, standard metroid content here.
-Graphics are all made of big polygons and bright colors, i'm not going to complain here as it's only an artistic choice, you may like it or not, but it's not the game's fault.
Music feels aproppiated, no complains here either.
-Controls are a little "off" specially when trying to guess where are you going to land as we have many small platforms sections that might get a little frustrating, but a little practice you will get better. The scanner range (at least the initial one) is so small that you have to be face to face with your target, making scanning hostile animals a little dangerous.
-The story seems alright if something generic, and i didn't care much for the "young and reckless" protagonist... the cat it's kind of funny i guess as he seems to voice my own thought many times.
All in all, Morphite it's ok. Maybe a bit "poor man's Metroid Prime" i guess.
An 8/10 seems an alright rating for me.
Now, as a NMS killer...
The opening of the game hints a lot about NMS... the ships, the space stations, the space traveling setting, even the drop pods look the same, and this about as similar as they get.
-You can't fly your ship, just pick a solar system, and then planets/space stations from a menu, the ship will get you there and drop you off in a escape pod.
-The planets are not planets, they are just walled and closed areas, with platforms, switches to press, creatures to kill, and loot to get, it's all pretty linear and completely different from the planets from NMS
Those might be only two points, but by themselves they destroy any hope to compare both games, except to people blinded for their hate for NMS, who will end up claiming that Super Mario Galaxy was NMS done right. Morphite is not a bad game but it's nothing like No Man's Sky and i wasted more money on my quest to find my holy grail...
Just played Morphite for an hour, but i'm not petty enough to refund it, even if i won't touch it ever again. Morphite is a good game, but if you are looking for "NMS done right" keep looking as this is not.

First Impressions vid/casual review:
TLDR: Mechanically similar to Metroid Prime while still containing some roguelite elements and vast exploration along the lines promised in No Man's Sky, Morphite manages to inject a considerable amount of personality with its low-poly graphic style and voice acted cutscenes. Morphite is casual, relaxing, fairly well crafted, lightly story oriented, but a bit buggy and rough with some questionable UI choices. In conclusion:  a soothing time waster in small chunks for those that have the space exploration bug.

Having squadmates in a game has always been an issue. Often times they are faceless henchmen who are barely more powerful than the enemies that you are fighting and you feel like you have to babysit them through battle. Even fully fleshed-out, three-dimensional characters can feel like a burden when the game design makes the player the only entirely competent piece on the board. There should never be any question as to the usefulness of your comrades in battle. This has been handled poorly for so long that I wondered if anyone would ever get it right.
Republic Commando knocks it out of the park beautifully and simply; I can't recall the last time I regarded any sets of NPC squadmates as equals--not even Garrus, no matter how much I loved him. Sev, Fixer, Scorch--they started out as archetypes but ended up as characters as their personalities became fleshed out. The characters were simple, yes, but not boring. Never boring. Upon the first encounter and exposition I fully expected to be playing as and alongside cliches. The regimented leader, the tech-savvy stickler for protocol, the assassin, and the immature one that loves explosions. But over time they were shown to be a tight-knit group that not only serves together but grew up together, that loves each other, relies on each other. This was conveyed entirely by listening to the inter-squad interaction. They may be identical in physical appearance, but they more than just the biological equivalents of the droids they fight.
In battle, you and your squadmates' health gets decimated from taking even light weapons fire, turning the act of making progress in most of the levels into a near impossiblilty without the support of your squad. The number of times they revived me was much greater than the number of times I revived them. Most times they revived each other--sometimes without any imput needed on my part. Bacta stations are numerous, but every single one is needed. There are no encounters in which you come out unscathed. You are fighting against a simple but deadly enemy and you are not a bullet-absorbing badass. You and your squad are all human and none of you are going to survive without the others.
Your DC-17 rifle is only moderately effective against most enemies and the ammunition for the attachments runs dry quickly. There needs to be as many guns in play on your side as possible in order to make any kind of stand against even moderately-sized groups of foes. But you are the only member of the group that has limited ammo; the others can keep firing that sniper rifle and grenade launcher for hours without leaving the same spot while you are limited to a mere handful of rounds even at full capacity.
That is a brilliant aspect of its design.
The player is the only member of the group that requires ammunition pickups in order to stay in the fight, and the scarcity and ineffectiveness of the standard weapon make it so that you need to rely on your squadmates' support in battle even more. This isn't to say you as the player aren't effective in battle. This means that in a firefight your role isn't to be on the front lines. Your role is to lead. Yes, sometimes your squadmates will revive the downed members without your direct command, but only after battle is done. If one goes down (I'm looking at you, Fixer) in the middle of a firefight and Sev and Scorch have their hands full, it's up to you to take control of the situation. The entire design drives home the point that one commando acting on his own is nothing compared to when they act as a unit. You learn to rely on them as they save your life and help you do what you could never do alone.
While short and by no means perfect, Republic Commando is to be commended for succeeding in an aspect of design where few (if any) have done before. No game with squad-based combat developed after Republic Commando has an excuse as to why they still make such misdirected approaches to squad-based combat. This game is not only a gem, it is an unsung feat of elegance.
Now excuse me while I wipe the lust-induced slobber off my keyboard.

Magicka 2. You can see an unpleasant amount of negative reviews. And yes, they've got a great point. Magicka 2 feels like an expansion to Magicka. People compare these two a lot. And I mean A LOT. Yes, the campaign is fairly short and there are quite harder enemies.
But, you mostly can't see them mentioning to use the new mechanics. The enemies are hard, yes, however if you use the new movement system to your advantage, they become much easier. It is hard to get used to, don't be mislead, but once you get the hang of it, you fly (not literally). People dislike the fact that now you can't SPAM. Yes, literally. You cannot spam the same op spell combo for the whole game. You have to differ your attacks. And people hate it. Enemies have elemental resistances which, in my opinion, is a great thing. You now have to use different combinations and A-S-S (lightning-death-death) or A-R-S-E (lightning-cold-death-shield) are not the way to go the whole campaign. And the thing about magicks having a global cooldown? Meh. I don't mind.
In conclusion people got so used to Magicka, they cannot accept the new mechanics. And look at how much time most people that reviwed negatively have put in the game! Less than me! (and I don't have much) It is a matter of adaptation. If you adapt to this game, you will love it (especially if you are new to the Magicka "franchise"). But if you can't adapt to this new thing, then you won't enjoy it. And you won't find out until you have bought the game (lols). I really recommend you adapt to this system. And if you do, I can almost guarantee you will enjoy the game :-)

I was excited for this game when I first looked at it, it had good reviews and it looked like a cool metroidvania-esque game. So when I sat down to play I was looking forward to the hours of fun I'd get from the game. Two hours later I finished the game disappointed in almost every way. So lets go over the good and the bad:
The good
-controls work well enough
-art is rather good
-gameplay is enjoyable
The bad
-The game is insultingly short, you can beat it in 2 hours if you feel like grinding or less if you don't.
-There is almost no story in the first place. Seriously all the story for this game could probably fit in about 10 pages in a notebook.
-The story is bad. Really bad. Like, feels like it was written by a 3rd grader bad. What's going on? Who knows and who cares. I didn't get 100% of everything because I didn't even realize the game was about to end (see complaint #1)
-The gameplay gets old. Sure its enjoyable but only because you can finish the game before you realize its getting boring. By the time I'd been really getting the hang of the game and its mechanics it had ended (again see complaint #1)
-The replay value is low. There isn't much to do in this game, unless you want to speed run this game you aren't going to really want to play it again.
In short don't buy this game, I don't know why its got such good reviews, but it isn't really worth whatever their asking. If you have to have the game (which why would you) get it on sale when you won't regret the decision.

This a great game for any fan of the post apocalyptic survival genre. The game puts you in charge of several survivors as they struggle through a zombie outbreak (Explained in the story mode).
You get to manage the survivors home, and its different upgrades, which all add something different to the survivors (Kitchen/training room/ sniping tower, etc). You can control each and every survivor that is in your group as long as you befriend them (which can be done easily) and then use them to scavenge or go out on a killing spree against zombies.
The story mode is decent enough to be played through a couple times, it explains why the outbreak happens and introduces the main characters. But where the game really shines is in the "Breakdown" mode, where you start on level 1 with just one survivor and your goal is to find a van and "move on" to the next level. While searching for the van you come across other survivors you can help and have them eventually join your group. Now this is a fun mode in itself, but add a couple of simple to instal mods and Breakdown suddenly turns 100 times more fun and enjoyable.
The game does have a few issues, like zombies spawning out of nowhere and getting you potentially killed at higher levels, but you learn to manage it (as you should be using survivors with Ninja-sneak perk anyway).
Overall its a really fun game that I'd recommend to any zombie/survivor fan.

This game is great, but there are a few bad choices in game design, which all revolve around one simple skill, multitasking.
It's an inherent rule that you cannot use 2 elements of opposite types when using magic, and it is infuriating to fight more than 1 element you must fight against, and it is incredibly hard when at least 2 of them are opposites.
The other issue, is that enemies just LOVE to group around you, and chip off health at an alarming rate, making it so that you're forced to spam death and AOE every second, which is bad game design. It's even worse in multiplayer, where colateral damage leaves only 1 person alive who's forced to revive someone before they die.
If anyone has reached the final boss, you know that you must fight against the flying knives which set you on fire, and drain your quick action slots (which you should never do unless the area is really easy), and then you have to fight a golem which has both physical and cold elements, making it impossible to protect yourself against one side without being exposed. What's even worse is that it is impossible to move the little energy balls around when you do disable Lok, and you have to do it FOUR TIMES.
Now, a few things are wrong with Lok, the first being that you shouldn't have to fight multiple elements, and the second being that you don't actually fight Lok herself, but rather her golem.
I would've just had a regular 1v1 fight with her, where you do no damage, but as the fight progresses you disable each of her beams, until she runs out of options. That would be good game design, but no. Paradox wanted to be original, and built one of the most infuriating bosses I have ever encountered.
I still recommend the game, for being an original concept and pretty fun to screw around, and the jokes are hilarious at times. But the actual combat is very much sided against the player, and difficulty is very random even when you go to the menu to swap your gear out for something better suited for your current situation.
