Two good expansions in a pack for a low price, Main storyline lasts about 12 hours per expansion, Plus several side missions. However, If you're buying this for the Multiplayer, Don't bother, Nobody plays it, Buy the original GTA IV for multiplayer.

I can't stress enough how fantastic this game is.  The freedom is amazing, the city richly detailed, and the realism absolutely astonishing for its genre.  With the graphics turned up, it looks beautiful, and immersion is quick and easy.
Building on the original GTA IV, the EFLC stand-alone expansion adds two shorter story modes with two new playable characters.  In "The Lost and The Damned", the grit is turned up to 11 as players get a look into a criminally involved biker gang.  For the other expansion, "The Ballad of Gay Tony", the dark, grungy atmosphere is gone entirely, replaced with the lively pace and bright colors of the nightclub scene.
The Lost and The Damned puts players in the shoes of a veteran of the biker gang lifestyle.  Faced with developing rifts in the gang and an erupting war with rivals, the player has to ride hard and fight harder to keep things hanging together.  There are a few new weapons to play with, along with a fleet of new vehicles that share a theme of being very old or very dirty.  Of course, there are also bikes... lots and lots of bikes.  From the player character's custom chopper to the random rides parked on the street or driven by other bikers, there is a huge variety of two-wheeled machines here.  Story-wise, this expansion is about as serious and dark as the original game, perhaps even more so.  I wouldn't play it more than once, but I'm not sorry I did.
The Ballad of Gay Tony is where this game really shines, and it's worth purchasing just for this expansion.  The player has it all in this one, taking the role of a night club baron's bodyguard who finds himself dragged into all kinds of trouble and has to use his skill and toughness to come out alive.  All the depressing motifs and perpetual desaturation of GTA IV are a thing of the past as the player runs free with exotic weapons and exciting new vehicles.  The characters are funnier and the missions are better than in both previous stories, with the exception of a notable few like GTA IV's "Three Leaf Clover" bank heist.  In addition, the most irritating features of IV, such as the nagging girlfriends or constant hangout calls, are gone.  Everything that has changed has been for the best.  At the top of my personal list are the new APC (with its powerful cannon), AA-12 shotgun (with optional explosive rounds that destroy cars), and Buzzard attack helicopter (based on the AH-6 "Little Bird" and just as capable).
If you enjoyed any previous GTA game, or you just like driving cars and blowing things up, this one is for you.

At the time of me writing this review, I would not suggest this game. I'm a bit over 4 hours into the game, only to have deal with multiple bugs that have soft locked me.
Now, I got this game right when it came out due to being excited for the sequel to Boot Hill Heroes, and after sinking dozens of hours into that game, I was really happy to dive into Bounties. While I ended up getting soft locked in the first 30-ish minutes of the game, with another 30+ minutes to figure out something screwed up in the files and I had to verify them, I reported it on the forums but couldn't reproduce the bug.
My second time? I've gotten further in the game to the Mines, and shortly after fighting the first boss enemy there and picking up what I can only assume was a key item, the game soft locked when I moved over towards the elevator by the camp at the mines. I had to alt + tab out of the game to manually close it due to the game becoming softlocked.
Keep in mind that steam says I have 4.3 hours into the game. But easily an hour, or even longer of it, is due to me trying to deal with bugs that happened. I know that players are supposed to report bugs they come across, which I have, but when you keep getting ones that soft lock the game and prevent you from moving forward, it's hard to want to continue to play the game.
In the current state I would not recommend playing Boot Hill Bounties, due to it feeling like more testing was needed before going public for the game. I paid for the game the moment it came out, partally due to it being on sale the moment it came out due to being a new release, but I am second guessing myself at this point.
Maybe after this game has recieved numerous updates after others have played further into it and helped report bugs and the like I'll give it another chance, but at its current state I can not play a game that keeps giving me this many issues.

Honestly it hurts me to write a review for this game and giving it the 'Not Recommended' tag. I loved the first game after I had been introduced to it by my boyfriend, it had that old school RPG charm and when we were made aware of this game I was excited to see what was coming next.
Right now in the game's current state? A buggy mess is what we have so far or at least thats what it seems like to me. Not even two hours into the game and we both had ended up running into multiple issues (Him not being able to end a battle at all until he re-verfied the files and myself somehow breaking a sequence just from not talking to an NPC).
Today we decided to give it another go and sure enough we began noticing graphical glitches and hell he even softlocked at one point. The game at its core is much like the first in the Boot Hill series but right now I just can not recommend anyone actually purchase this game until some of this stuff is fixed further. Glitching out in the opening scenes and areas is a little much in my opinion.
In terms of the games actual game play, if you have played Boot Hill Heroes you will be able to jump into this one right away. The battles feel very similar with a slightly upgraded way to how vantages and hats work and the music is still very well done. I do have to get more into the games story to let you know how well it was handled on that aspect but at this time I don't think I'll be going back to it until some of the mentioned issues have been touched upon and fixed.
Please take this as a warning for right now; buy it at your own risk. The developer is still working on it which is good but it feels like they still have a lot of work they need to do on this game to make it as good as the first one.
I will add, once things have been fixed more who knows maybe I will change my mind, but right now as it stands, I can't tell people they should play this.

I grew up playing Gun.Smoke and Dragon Warrior on the NES, and gazing at the picture of the first Mother game that appeared in Nintendo Power (before anyone had even heard of Earthbound). Decades later, and my love for cowboy games and JRPGs hasn't died at all. The Boot Hill series blends the wild west with a fantastic SNES JRPG vibe in a way that feels incredibly fresh and makes me feel like a kid again.
Since I was a huge fan of Boot Hill Heroes, I offered to help with the testing for Bounties. I received the game for free in order to test it. My only regret is that I never got a chance to buy it for myself, because I've had more fun with this game than any RPG I've played in years. I would gladly pay full price for it. You'll love it, especially if you played the first game in the series. (This game is MUCH better than the first one, though.)
The jump in quality from Boot Hill Heroes to Bounties is surprisingly staggering, from the much-more-detailed 2D graphics, to the neat little twists in everything from the battles to the optional sidequests and the dialogue. There were many times when I thought to myself, "I've never seen an RPG do that before." I was also extremely happy to see that Kid, the formerly silent protagonist, now talks! You can really connect with him more this way,
The battle system, although rather unconventional, was easy for me to pick up since I played the first game twice. If you've played Boot Hill Heroes, you know the drill. Knowing when to launch an attack, when to cancel, and when to trigger the proper "vantage." If it's your first experience with the Boot Hill series, the game does a fine job of explaining the battle system, and it does this (for the most part) without breaking character.
And with farming, weapon-modding, cooking, riddles... Even outside of battle, there's still a ton to do.
The story proceeds in a quasi-linear fashion. Unlike the first game, all of the bounties are available for pursuit in any order, but each bounty's arc must be resolved before moving on to another, with side quests unlocked each step of the way. Even after the credits roll, there's a completionist challenge (that I still have yet to complete) with the promise of something BIG if you finish the full list of stuff to do. I can't say what that is, but what I can say for sure is that you'll get your money's worth here. See if you've got what it takes to complete the checklist... Good luck!

Disclaimer: I did receive an advance copy for Youtube coverage and assembling a guide for the game.
This is the sequel to 2014's Boot Hill Heroes, which is a wild-west themed JRPG with an old school art design reminiscent of Earthbound, and loads of charm.  The first game itself was a very good Indie RPG in general with the one downfall of being rather short.  This one remedies that problem and loads it up with even more content.  Most of the downfalls of the first game have been addressed and the outcome is a stellar experience all around.
To explain, this does pick up where the first game ended, and you may be a little in the dark about the various characters if you are coming in fresh.  This game does feature data carry over where you can import your items and levels, to encourage you to come in after playing the first game.  To summarize what happened there, the Saints-Little Gang framed the Chepakwik Indian Tribe for destroying the town of Ashwood in an attempt to incite a war between the tribe and the settlers.  Their exact motive was unknown, and the first game ended with you defeating one member of the Gang, and then hearing the story of how their leader was arrested 10 years prior to the start of the game.  Your objective here is to round up the gang members who are up to no good and find evidence to clear the Chepakwik before a war breaks out.
So one of the big changes you get right out from the gate is the non-linear gameplay.  Once you return to the hub town, you are free to go after any of the members of the gang, provided you can find them.  This will affect your equipment, what side quests you can take, what recipes you can learn, and other sorts of minutia that are important to the world building experience.  In doing so, you learn about past events related to the characters themselves and the world they live in, and also allowing you to see first hand what kind of chaos this gang has unleashed.  Additionally, the way hats in the game has also changed.  The first game featured them as a tool for learning moves for combat, but now they function more along the lines of a job system, sometimes teaching you new moves for the hat itself, giving you abilities to be used with other hats, and also exceeding the 4 move limit from the first game.  Beyond just this, there are many new moves that open up different strategies for fighting your opponents, meaning that you don't necessary have to grind to win, provided you look at what hats are available and adjust your strategy for whatever obstacle is in your way.
As for graphics, everything has been touched up from the first game, with portraits being added for many of the important characters, allowing you to see the smaller details of their characters.  The playable characters themselves both change on map as well in portrait as you change their hats around.  Cities have been re-designed to be more stream-lined and everything is just better.  You will re-visit some of the locations from the first game, but there are also many other places to go, many of them having something unique to set them apart from the other areas.  Seeing as you're playing as a farmer, it is nice to actually be able to use your farm to generate materials for some of the new systems in the game.
In terms of gameplay, there is both good news and bad news.  The first is that the battle system itself still carries over a lot of the weaknesses it possessed from the first game, with an all-or-nothing aspect where you either dodge a move in its entirety or you take the hit in its entirety.  This is bad when the shot is going to kill you from full health, which is a threat periodically throughout the game.  However, the good news is that there are new systems in place that can make your life a little easier.  Should you go down, Doc Valentine can now treat your wounds, meaning you don't have to go to town and shell out a fortune.  If you need money, Rosy can use the food you collect to make dishes to sell, or just to eat to obtain some buffs for a few fights.  And finally, when it comes to combat, Moon Dancer can augment your equipment with numerous effects to inflict statuses, boost your damage, or help you hit evasive enemies.  Additionally, with the new hats in the game come new abilities to help speed up battles by allowing you to break enemy stances, turn normal moves into AOE, or other effects.  Most of the things from the first game are still intact, but everything is bigger.  And should you find the game too easy or tough, you can change the difficulty at any time to better suit your experience.
Overall, I have been waiting for this game to come out since I finished the first one, and I am impressed with what I've found so far.  It occupies a niche of its own, and I recommend it to anyone interested in wild west themed gaming environments or those just looking for a fun JRPG to sink some time into.  It truly is a unique experience and I am looking forward to whatever Experimental Gamer puts out next.

Earthbound is a game with a legacy that has enriched ‘90s kids and inspired classics such as Undertale, LISA and Citizens of the Earth as well as Pony Island and OneShot. While seemingly unrelated, subversion, of gameplay and of storytelling, combined with deadpan comedy of modern tropes of RPGs has always made these titles special to make up for their simplicity. Along with different themes, tones and comedy, each interpretation never feels like a copy; instead, each game feels like a game based around what aspects resonated with each creator who had played Earthbound.
Boot Hill Bounties is another Earthbound-inspired title that challenges what you might expect by taking a more straight-faced approach. As someone who had not heard of the original, it was not confusing to start with the sequel, yet the gameplay is largely the same except with more time with a full-party. Gameplay largely borrows from Chrono-Trigger’s turn-based combat with its own ideas how to make standard JRPG battles more diverse. Linearity is replaced with branching paths; and instead of a story relying on spectacle and lore, there is a surprising richness behind every character, friend or foe, involving a pulpy adventure in a loosely historically accurate Wild West. While BHB may not be revolutionary, it is a game that will leave you with fond memories as it rides off into the sunset.
Saying that the gameplay is largely uninspired would be unfair, but it’s easy to see why when you compare it to Undertale’s non-combat system and LISA’s status-heavy combat. The gameplay borrows various elements from Chrono-Trigger’s battle-system; Earthbound’s pre-battle, status-effects and anti-grinding elements; and Harvest Moon’s progression system for skills like farming. On top of these features, BHB also creates its own unique battles that feel more like puzzles such as a sniper shootout with destructible cover or a security door that must be disarmed in a fight. Moments like these, though sparse and sometimes frustrating, are the best gameplay elements BHB has to offer.
The problem with the rest of BHB’s gameplay is how simple it is. Combat doesn’t suffer as much because you can always ramp up the challenge by switching to Hard where tactics are a requirement. Synergy between companions’ skills (Vantages) makes up the gameplay where party members rely on buffs, status effects, etc. to get through as a team. Every encounter, even if it’s standard JRPG combat, always feels impactful as different hats reward players with new strategies to accumulate on top of standard leveling up. These progression systems benefit the game because it rewards variety.
Outside of combat, however, is where the gameplay’s shallowness begins to show. Map design and side-quests are actually the highlights as every area offers activities to break up combat like riddles or mini-games like a food contest. However, skills (farming, weapon buffing, cooking, etc.) are simply meters increasing the number of options to do the same thing. Guessing with reagents to find weapon-buff combinations is more often a crapshoot unless you know the recipes from NPCs. Doctoring is simply a stat-removal skill to sap away money unless you invest into it at campfires. Lastly, if you were expecting BHB to be a JRPG mixed with Stardew Valley/Harvest Moon, then farming will disappoint you the most; it’s simply farming for extra resources to sell. Items also seem oddly placed where you may get the best gear early on, making money a commodity with no usage except for increasing these progression ranks.
None of these elements ruins the gameplay, but they feel like features simply there for the sake of variety without thinking of how to best integrate them. At worst, it can showcase a lack of extra polish that could have improved sections like Little Creed’s apparatus, yet none of these features are mandatory. (The game itself is highly polished with relatively few technical issues, which all have been addressed.) It seems odd to add extra things when the game is not lacking on content; it took me twenty-one hours to complete 66% of the game—most of it was completionist rewards for an end-game reward, which you can complete post-game, but there were a fair number of side-quests incomplete. The only reason these extra features bother me is that it takes away the real star of Boot Hill Bounties, the storytelling.
Storytelling has never been a large focus in Earthbound-inspired games much like the original. The comedy, the weirdness of its spectacles, and in some games like LISA and Undertale, the lore, have all supplemented what threadbare narratives they have had. (The one exception being Mother 3.) None of these statements are to say games with lore have bad stories; it’s simply a different way to tell them. In contrast to other titles, Boot Hill Bounties has not only the pulpiest of stories inspired by Spaghetti Westerns but it also has the strongest sense of storytelling because of its emphasis on plot.
This effect is largely the result of how much BHB emphasizes character development for every main character as vignettes behind every branching path. To tie everything together, the set-up is simple: Hunt down the remaining members of a gang during an impending war between the Indians and Settlers. Similar to games like Shadowrun Dragonfall, the plot begins on a set-path before allowing players to choose different junctions to focus on both the protagonists and antagonists. (Choices, however, seem superficial as they don’t appear to impact the outcome.) Each path tells its own story to completion which allows all of them to have a nice sense of pace and purpose. It also not only ties the plot together with relevant details but also give motives behind the antagonists that flesh them out to be real characters than simple bad guys. This is BHB’s greatest strength, characters.
Fans of Mother 3 will truly enjoy this game because of how character driven it is. The adultness of the world is handled surprisingly well with the kiddie visuals and perspectives as the game explores themes of war, racism, violence, religious institutions, and other matters that fit the Western times. It always borders the line of tasteful portrayals mixed in with creative fictions like the Mexican nationalists waging a war in the U.S. and Mexico because they are abandoned, “We are men without country, unbound by laws or customs.” These result in some well-executed gut punches later on that truly surprise you because the narrative builds up to them striking at the right moment. Even without playing the original, the sense of growth of every character feels like a complete story-arc that only suffers from the fact that the game goes out with a taste of what’s to come as its final act.
Unlike the original which was marred by the fact that the game ended as soon as you rounded the whole posy, the sequel does a better job ending to set-up the third game. Some may not like cliffhangers but if a game can resolve its plot to let another game take up the reigns, then the role of that story fulfilled its purpose. Boot Hill Bounties manages to end at the right time, though it may feel anticlimactic depending on what order you took as it doesn’t have a final boss or an ultimate challenge. That is obviously the purpose of the third game, but it is a hard truth when it may take years to see it.
The people that I believe will truly appreciate BHB are not only fans of Earthbound but also their families. While some aspects may be questionable for younger audiences, the fact that you can play this game with others lets the legend live on beyond the hearts of Earthbound fans such as their children who can share that memory with the same passion.

What a wondrous creation. Where to begin? I think this game became so much more than it meant to be, which is great, but alas time goes on, and so many people have moved on to bigger and badder titles. However, just to be clear, as of my writing, this game -->STILL HAS A MULTIPLAYER PRESENCE<-- In fact, it was a bit bigger than I expected, with multiple servers still available to play on. Vietnam is a bit worse off though...
Anyways, moving along to the good stuff.
Bad Co. 2 had a pretty nice engine and look. Frostbite 2 was great, and the destructibility of environment items was amazing at the time, it felt rather new and exciting. The attention to detail was fantastic as well, the scenes typically felt as if they were alive instead of some dull backdrop to your gunplay. The maps, both in SP and MP, looked rather stunning. In multiplayer, the levolution was creative, and often times very exciting to experience.
Oh, gunplay! Did it feel joyous? Well there were some flaws, as per usual, but BC2 certainly made up for those. It was nice, at least. There were (and still are) several occasions upon which I would 'trade' lives with an opponent. That's alright though. Weapons at least fire bullets. It was a ton of fun to have to deal with bullet drop, and watch people play terribly because they came from a hitscan game. There was a nice selection of weapons to choose from in each class, and several weapons that were usable in all kits! Classes felt great in multiplayer if you ask me. Giving LMGs and medic items to a support class felt ingenious, whilst having engineers stealth via suppressed weapons and blow things up, assault characters drop ammo kits and provide grenade launcher support (with different types of rounds), and recon players call in mortar strikes, throw radar mines, and... snipe. It felt a little more balanced and well rounded, albeit the fact that the occasional wall of recon players seemed indestructible.
Single player had it's side of followers as well, and for good reason. The story seemed well cared for, and it was structured well. There was enough variety in the levels and combat experience in each mission, that I didn't feel like I was playing one never-ending unchanging campaign. I also got really attached to the characters, as I'm sure many people did. Each personality was fleshed out, detailed, and lovable. It was all of the squad members put together, with a kickass story, and a variety of gameplay options that made this the game we still love 6 years later
This is all I've got on this one for now, I've left out a ton that others loved about the game, but add to it! You know what you loved about BC2!

Alien Swarm is a unique game especially for that of the magnificent Source engine, as it is viewed through a top down perspective. This kind of game play style isn't experimented with or even used that much in most games, so making an entire game with this formula is quite the achievement on it's own right. The game play revolves around classes that have specific roles on the battlefield. These classes include officer, an all around class with added bonuses for the team. The special weapons, a class that uses a variety of unique and powerful weaponry to blast through the enemy. The medic, a class that is there to look out for the team with their healing capabilities. And the technical specialist, who acts as an engineer of sorts who can build structures and deal with other machinery on the map. There is also a varied amount of weapons and gear to unlock and have fun with for each class. Teamwork is a very important aspect of this game, without it you probably wont get to far before the alien bugs come for your blood. The aliens themselves have good diversity as well, with different battle styles that you will have to adapt to quickly to survive the alien threat. This is a blast with friends and if you and a friend or two are wanting a good co-op experience this is definitely a great choice.

If you're into survival in general and Zombies in particular this is a game for you. With three different playstyles; Storydriven (State of Decay), level based (State of Decay: Breakdown) where you can reset the game to reach a higher difficulty in the next level, and last but not least the Military perspective (State of Decay: Lifeline) on a City map specific for that story.
The story told as well as the game in general emphasizes the building of a community of survivors and the teamwork required. Despite it being a Single-Player game only, they succeed quite well in portraying the everyday struggle of a (albeit fictional) Zombie Apocalypse.
However it does get repetitive, the narrative could have been expanded upon. Especially in Breakdown this becomes obvious, but if you aren't annoyed by that one issue you're free to enjoy the game on higher and higher levels of difficulty with each new level you reach. I have noticed some glitches related to the graphics, specifically the lighting and shadows which is unrelated to the game functionality and I do not know if this is a problem on my system only or a general issue with the game. It is only noticeable in the early morning hours of each 24 hr cycle so I think it's a minor issue.
In Lifeline you get all the cool Military Hardware so desired in the other two versions of the game. Based on a story where a team of soldiers find themselves isolated in a City full of Zombies, their only support being Helicopter supply drops hence the name of the title; Lifeline. Once the storyline is completed you are given the option to continue playing and save as many civilians that you can find (still alive) or end the story and the game to finalize your score.
Overall a very enjoyable game. It's a shame there is no Multiplayer mode, though.

This amazingly unique and gory game is like Hotline Miami in first person. It uses voxel gore that's procedurally generated for extreme "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I just, like, scalped a guy." The game's enemies have layers, an outer one with textures and faces, an inner muscle layer of blocks, the skeleton and their head has a brain inside. The game is... Extremely brutal. It's a bar fight simulator, essentially, but it will soon branch out into a prison riot level and maybe even more varied things after that. You can grab basic weapons Dead Rising style, such as weak chairs, bottles, plates or mugs. You can go into some hidden-ish areas and find more formidable weapons, such as the kitchen of the biker bar and kill the chefs to take their meat cleavers and knives, break open the safe of the biker gang leader and take his spare tire iron, steal the band's mic stand or even take a katana from the owner of the Yakuza controlled disco club. As it is, this game is worth the 10 schmeckles but there's one good thing that you won't notice unless you get to the community hub ASAP. These guys made Probably Archery, a funish YouTuber bait game made for a game jam. Imagine that game, 3 times more complete, and the devs gave it weekly updates. Since its extremely recent release, the devs have given the game a few updates and are active with the community, responding on the subreddit (reddit*com/r/paintthetownred), and in the community hub. They talk about their future plans, development, bug reports and suggestions from players. It's clear a lot of care and work went into this game, even in its very unfinished state. In the interest of honesty, take the following opinion lightly because I am easily swayed. I've been burned before on early access games (Starforge, *hopefully not* Medieval Engineers, and I don't remember if Signal Ops or Redshirt were Early Access but you get the idea) and I preorder games a lot, some of which come back to bite me (GTA V, Batman Arkham Origins, Watch_Dogs) but this game is being made by the most trustworthy developers I've ever seen since Godd Howard unveiled Fallout 4. Which is a short time, but these guys are comparable to Bethesda and the amazing looking job the did with Fallout 4 and whatever that doesn't matter here. These devs are communicative, which is a rare trait these days and I would give them 10 dollars for the first level of this game, let alone the other one and the upcoming sandbox and prison riot levels.
PROS:
Amazingly fun, yet simple gameplay. Melee features jabs/stabs with fists/objects, or powerful sideswiping attacks. You can throw your fists and you can throw objects. Devs plan to add very rare guns later on, it's not a gun based game.
Incredible gore system, imagine if the Minecraft world you've most destroyed was a person's face.
Responsive and trustworthy developers.
Ingame idiot proof gif maker, automatically records the last 15-10ish seconds of gameplay and can make a gif in the folder of your choice.
A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush and there's 2 levels about to be released, consider it an investment.
On that note, the price is fair for what you get if you're easily entertained by bashing a man's skull in with a tire iron (I know I am), otherwise there's gonna be more content for you /r/patientgamers who want more bashing for their buck.
CONS:
Poorly optimized game. I won't pretend to know how games are made, but it seems like the lighting is the culprit. Maybe. I don't know, I don't even know if the game is optimized well or poorly. I do know, however, that the game is reported as lagging for a ton of people and my 4.5/10 system (BF4 all low settings at 1080p gets me 50ish smoothish fps) can't handle this without 1/4 resolution textures (because the 1/8 resolution smallest size ones are awful), lowest settings and 1368x768 resolution. Then I get 60ish fps, very spikey and the dance floor of the disco is a 10-20 zone.
That is quite literally my only fault with the game and I don't mind the lower resolutioon, the game is stylistically ugly anyway. Overall 10/10 for me, it's one of my favorite games and you should get it.

Let me start by saying I hardly ever write reviews, for video games, products, or really anything, so excuse the poor formatting. This game had been on my wishlist for quite some time, and after seeing it on sale I finally decided to pick it up and check it out. The first thing that struck me was the delivery of the game, very pleasing and it made me feel involved. Then I was sucked in by the voice acting and visual aspects of the game. The dialog choices really made me feel like I had a choice, and I was actually out in that damn forrest. I have not played a game in some time that made me "feel". It made me want to go volunteer and run away and live a different life. It made me mad, and worried for the characters. If there is a thing as a video game novel, this game would take the cake for me. Before this I tried Vanishing of Ethan Carter and couldn't quite get into it so I was afraid of what this game might be, but all my fears were put to ease with Firewatch and honestly gave this type of game a new life for me.
However, with all good must come bad right? You are absolutely right. My total in game time is 3 hours. Just three, and I finished it, while I have heard and read about its replayability I have zero desire to do anything again. It is sort of like those books where you choose your fate by going to certain pages, I don't want to change my fate. A game that sucked me into this emotional rollercoaster just seemed to end way too soon. I did get the game on sale, so I felt my money was well spent, however I am glad I did not pay full price for the game as I feel it would have swayed my judgement due to the short playtime.
All in all I would recommend this game, if it is on sale. It was a lot of fun and I have not stopped thinking/talking about it to my friends, but that same talking about it comes with a warning. A warning that this game is very short. I wasn't looking for a 50+ hours of gametime game, but if I can finish it in 3 hours it feels a little like a college project that blew up, in fact even Stardew Valley lasted longer. It may sound like I am bashing the game, but I truly loved it, just wish there was more of it!

+ Includes co-operative play, which enhances the entertainment value massively
+ Bullet time and X-ray features are excellently employed, look fantastic, and the frequency can be scaled up or down as the user prefers
+ Points system encourages taking risks with difficult and long-range shots; often does well to increase the feeling of satisfaction earned when eliminating a difficult sniper
+ Loot and cover mechanics are minimalist and practical
+ Gunplay and hit mechanics are all top-notch; everything connects well and feels appropriate
+ The game's atmosphere is absolutely palpable; this is largely enhanced by the shrill screams of the enemy mobs and the dark theme music pervading throughout
+ Levels are well-designed and objectives are clearly marked; one is not likely to get lost while moving about
+ Quality audio design
+ Lighting plays well against the walls, and generally looks excellent in terms of quality
+ Environmental textures are quite detailed; overall visual presentation is adequate
- Plot is nonchalantly presented and woefully underdeveloped
- Characters are as bland as smooth stones; no lines, no reactions, nothing
- Game shows an over-reliance on wave mechanics; gets frustrating and predictable in a hurry
- Realistic lighting is often sacrificed for atmosphere; that is, while the lighting mechanics themselves are done quite well, the colors and tones of the lighting feel extremely out of place and unrealistic
- There is really only one boss, and it is encountered more than once; boss fights are bland and uninspired
- Bodies will, more often than not, disappear a bit too quickly to loot to one's satisfaction or requirements
- Precious little in the way of collectibles and in-game lore; does not lend to a high replay value, save for co-operative play with friends
Do not recommend for single player. It might be fun in coop but in single, it's just boredom.

Man, what can I say about a game getting made 100% correctly? A lot actually but I'll keep it brief. Kids today play Battlefield, CoD, and other multiplayer FPS' thinking that it is a great FPS. Well I am sad to say they are incorrect. Most people today don't understand a TRUE FPS expierence. SW:RC is a great FPS at it's core and it's shell. Opening with a few awesome cutscenes that give enough back story for you to understand what is going on, but doesn't over do it.
The Experience:
Republic Commando gives you the power of a Special Forces unit of Clone Troopers, called "Delta Squad". You are their leader, Delta 38, and as their leader you can issue commands to your team. These commands can be setting traps, rigging explosives, slicing (hacking) terminals, mounting heavy machine guns/rocket pods, targeting certain enemies, reviving team mates, and much more. The gun play is amazing and the weaponry has actual recoil if you spray, this is probably why Storm Troopers in the earlier (really later) movies can't hit anything for it is a harder thing to do at distance.
The Weapons:
Holy Star Wars, you want a game where you actually feel like a Clone Trooper? This is it then. Your main weapon consists of a DC-17m Interchangable Weapon System, as you prgress you can pick up attachments for your weapon, incuding a Snipers attachment and an Anti-Armour rocket launcher attachment. Other weapons include the DC-15s Sidearm Blaster, a rechargable infinite ammo energy pistol that you will be using a lot more often than not*, and MANY pickups from dead enemy. This can range far and wide. Shotgun? Why not? Submachine guns? Ok! WOOKIE BOWCASTER!? OH YEAH! But that's just a layer of the cake.
*Quick note: The DC-15s is a great blaster, you will be using it to mainly conserve ammo, as it is scarce for your other weapons later in the game. You are an Elite Unit in the middle of nowhere sometimes so the DC-15s and enemy weapons will be your primaries depending on where you go! Holy crud a game that understands that your advanced weapon doesn't just have ammo laying around an old school slaver camp where shotguns are used.
The A.I.:
Your teammates are EXTREMELY qualified to be your TEAM MATES! They kill things, but it's a challenge enough to where if you don't fire you will be overwhelmed. All 4 people in the team MUST be in the fight. If only ONE goes down it could mean the end of your team. They also have great animations for up close enemies. Each enemy type has a different hand to hand combat scenario for your team mates, which your teammates will win. These are a must watch for a first time player, as they are bada**. Although the AI is not perfect (i.e. crouched right NEXT to the enemy staring at him every now and again) they get the job done better than any other AI I have ever seen. They interact with you and how you fire, giving you compliments as you succeed in awesome. You can set them up in ambush postions or just to take cover. The BEST thing in my opinion though is when you are firing, if they are going to walk in front of you THEY ACTUALLY CROUCH WALK UNDER YOUR FIRE SO YOU CAN KEEP A BLASTIN' AWAY! It's AWESOME!
The Enemies:
Apart from the easy regular driods (and main enemies as they differ level to level) you are going to have a challenge. Some enemies require you to take cover as they will end you and your team in seconds. These enemies can come from no where and are often enough to keep you on your toes, but rare enough to where you aren't thinking they are a cheap cop out for lengthy play time.
Twists and Turns:
Sorry but I do not give away spoilers ;D, but I will say there are moments where you will go "Well . . . sh**".
Conclusion:
This game isn't perfect as it hasn't aged well. Some weapons consist of Polygon. However this is something you can expect from a game that is up to a decade old, yet still provides a great experience. With compontent AI, awesome gunplay, a great leadership orders mechanic, and great voice acting? This gets a 10/10. For only $2.99 right now (as of 5/2/2015) it is a MUST pick up!
May the Force be with you, and happy hunting!

I read mixed reviews, and I honestly don't understand the negative reviews.
The application is crazy light weight on size.
When you first launch, and mind you the application must be launched before your steam game of choice, it prompts with a guide on how to access the options, what icons mean, etc.
If you want the 100fps feature, you will need to go into settings and simply pick 100fps, as the default is set to 30fps.
If you want to use a USB headset, simply select it from the Microphone settings once you enable Microphone audio under the Sounds options. It even shows feedback live as you talk and allows you to even decrease your mic audio level when it records.
If you want to add your own logo, as say you want to upload lets play recordings to YouTube -yes, it does that just fine and will even allow transparency so your logo can be noticed but see-through enough to not block out vital visuals of the game recording.

About the zombies: there are a few types that you will encounter million times in every mission: normal walkers, snipers, suicide bombers, minigunners and skeletons. Ofcourse he appeared twice - why make 2 bosses when you can reuse the first one? Guns - every weapon feels the same, there's no point in choosing any other weapon (except shotguns). It's colourful, it's vibrant, it's a ton of fun. If you like retro platformers with a modern edge, a bit like Shovel Knight, you'll like Joylancer. The platforming is functional, the rev mechanic is fun, the spritework is the highlight of the game. I want to recommend this game, I really do.
The thing keeping Joylancceer back is the soundtrack. This is some of the most grating chiptune music I have ever heard. The meldodies clash with the chords to produce some horrendous sounds, the likes I've only heard in Hilltop Zone, with that godawful harmonica sound. Thankfully you can replace the soundtrack with songs from your own music library with an in-game feature, except it only accepts .ogg formats.
This has the potential to be up there among great retro-throwback platformers, but it's held back by some poor sound design. The UX isn't the greatest, with unintuitive choices made for menu navigation. When you enter your name the first time you boot it up, you can't use your keyboard, you have to enter each letter via a list you scroll through with the arrow keys. On a gamepad, You select with Square or X depending on if you're using a DS3/DS4 or an Xbox Controller, and Cross or A will act as the "back" button.
If the above could be addressed, I'd rate the game higher, but as is, I think Joylancer needs a little more time in the oven.

Simply put: This game is pretty damn good.
I've been on the hunt for good platformers to play and luckily, stumbled upon this early access gem.
Aesthetics - While the gaming market is saturated with titles that attempt to capture the retro game art style (most done poorly), Joylancer manages to pull off the style well. The sprite work looks very nice, especially with the bosses and Joy, herself. Sprite animations are great as well. The color palette used for the game looks good and can be changed in the options menu.
Gameplay - As I mentioned before, a lot of games are now trying to use the retro aesthetic and most of those games, in my experience, are pretty awful gameplay-wise. I was skeptical at first, so I downloaded the demo. After playing the demo for a bit, I decided to get buy the complete game (Well, as complete as the game is currently in early access).
You control the character, Joy, who wields a drill lance. In order to use it properly, you need to power up the drill by charging it. When I first started playing, I found myself annoyed with the idea of having to constantly stop and charge my drill to dish out the most damage during every fight. This changes very quickly though, as there are plenty of gems spread all throughout the stages that charge your drill and every enemy you defeat drops those same gems. Each stage promotes exploration, as you can drill through parts of buildings and into the ground to find hidden pathways. Some times, these hidden areas can lead to items that you can use to customize your play style and significantly improve combat. I want to mention that the game controls pretty well, in general.
Speaking of combat mechanics, they are very fluid, brawls are chaotic in the best kind of way and beating up on enemies is so satisfying. You have your basic uncharged attacks that don't deal too much damage, but are still helpful. Your attacks can be done on the ground or in the air. As you charge your drill, your character gets a boost in running speed, jumping height/distance and combo ability. Being max charged can result in beautiful things. Find yourself locked in a fight with a group of foes twice your size? No problem. You can dash in and drill right into them. Occasionally, enemies will get a little ambitious and attempt to block or clash into your attack with their own. This can result in a brief power struggle that requires tapping buttons, which isn't difficult to press through. Winning the struggle, will result in you pulling off a cool finishing move such as grabbing the enemy, propelling yourself into the air and pile driving them into the ground. This is just one of the few finishers that I've seen and my favorite so far. These attacks can also damage other enemies that get caught in the crossfire. Fighting is damn fun.
At the moment, I've only been playing single player mode and it's been pretty awesome. I can imagine multiplayer being awesome as well.
Music - If I had to complain about one thing, it would be the game's music. Regularly, I enjoy chiptunes, but they need to redo the game's soundtrack. It's really bad and you're better off muting it while you play. Hopefully, with this game still in early access, they improve on it.
Controller Support - I had no problems with it. I actually use a PS4 controller to play this game and it works fine for me.
As mentioned previously, This game is in early access, so it's obviously not 100% complete or perfect by any means. There are still things that need to be improved on (Clearly, the music) and I'm sure in time, they will be (I hope! There hasn't been any recent updates on the game). This game being as fun as it is already, still has plenty of potential to get better. I downloaded the game for $10.00, which I feel is a good price point for what you get. I've paid significantly more for AAA games that were significantly worse to play. If you can pick it up during a sale, that's even better.
So, do yourself a favor and play this game. It's a good time.

Geonosis is the squad’s first actually deployment and to survive it I actually had to rely on the support of my AI squad mates. The operation turned out to be an odyssey of ever increasingly difficult military objectives to be completed with little assistance other than your three brothers. And brothers they were, the sense of connection was made strong with well written characters and superb voice acting. Before completing Geonosis I had already developed a sense of attachment for my squad and their quirks.
I won’t spoil anymore plot but I can attest that by the end I was left feeling a little less complete knowing I won’t be going on any more dangerous missions with my squad.
*Game play*
- Shooting is pretty good, some weapons feel rather weak but there is a use for every weapon
- Squad tactics, not complicated, but not necessarily simple. Some segments of the game require proper squad placement.
- The atmosphere was unexpected for a Starwars game. More mature, but not edgy, it would make for a good movie theme.
- **Multiplayer is down is idk how that would have gone.
*Final Impressions*
Great experience in the Starwars setting, that did not overstay its welcome (about 8 hours to complete).

Well worth the cheap price, and if you want to play multiplayer even now that GameSpy is dead, you can get GameRanger.

The game starts you off in a post apocalyptic world where you can do anything you want, whenever you want. Regardless of how good the port is (and it's really good), the developer's interaction and openness with the community is above and beyond expectations. The first two hours of Firewatch were very excellent. Then it kind of slowly and awkwardly slides its way off-stage with one of the most unsatisfying endings I've ever played.
It's a shame that a game so laugh-out-loud funny, so emotional, and so well-crafted has to end with such a sad whimper of an ending. Why.
Imagine if you were playing Uncharted or something and you're being hit with the usual story flags: hints at the ancient civilation, signs of a curse, and then Drake discovers that it was all some elaborate prank some dude pulled off. Everyone packs their stuff up and goes home. The game ends.
What I'm getting at is that Firewatch has incredibly minimal payoff for everything it expertly builds up, Reflecting on it now, there's a defining moment in the game
where the story begins its gradual descent from everything it worked towards.
Is the point of the story that
Maybe so. But this could easily be told in a way that doesn't make you feel like you've just wasted four hours.
Here's another wonderful kicker. None of your choices matter.
I have absolute faith that Campo Santo will learn from their mistakes with this title with In The Valley of Gods, because *most of* Firewatch was a wonderful and emotional experience. But if you believe that the most important part of a story is the ending, stay far away from Firewatch.

Deathmatch Classic is Valve's praise on Quake. It's basically Quake rerendered in the GoldSource (Basically still the Quake engine) engine. It adds in a few half life textures, and the open source and infinite maps possibility, but overall, it's just Quake. Very fun and addictive. I definitely prefer HL DM Source though. The community, kind of isn't there, but you can probably find a server with 5-10 people on there at the right times.

Deathmatch Classic is Valve’s first game in their “Classic” series which consists of games that are either an homage or just related to the game Quake in one way or another, why? I’m still not sure, but I can only assume it’s because Valve loves Quake.
The game takes all your favorite Quake deathmatch arenas and puts them into source, while still replicating all of the weapons from Quake and having the same placement around the maps for players to pick up and use.
Just like Half-Life you can select your model to use while playing, and of course it’s all Half-Life characters. So what is this game then? Is it a Half-Life and Quake crossover? Well not really, because there’s nothing in the game that even says Quake or shows the Quake emblem and all the powerups such as Quad damage are replaced with the lambda. It’s just Quake Multiplayer reformed into Half-Life.
So Valve made an online deathmatch shooter focused multiplayer game, even though they just replicated Quake and treated it like a tribute, they didn’t even bother to fix the problems it already suffered from previously
All the weapons are incredibly unbalanced to where it’s just Rocket Launcher: The Game, really. They didn’t change any of the weapons from Quake at all.
In Quake’s singleplayer the regular shotgun is made to do a set amount of damage to enemies who have a set amount of health, so that’d be around 2 or 3 hits for your basic enemies because their health is built around what weapons you can obtain and when. But this game still gives you 100 health so therefore the regular shotgun is like throwing pebbles at your enemies and the rocket launcher can and will kill people in two shots.
They didn’t even think about the fact that your weapons get better the further you progress in Quake, and that it would be a stupid idea to just randomly scatter them through the maps to where when you get the best weapon (The Rocket Launcher), you’re set for the rest of the game. I am 100% aware this is already a flaw in Quake’s multiplayer already, but it still plays into this game and that doesn’t make it okay.
This game overall just feels lazily put together so Valve can feel like they made their own rendition of Quake, the game can be fun but the horribly balanced weapons will be your worst complaint.
The game’s $4.99, but I would just buy Half-Life, Day of Defeat, or even Ricochet. But this is still good to have if you already own all of Valve’s other Gold Source games.

Alien Swarm is a free top-down cooperative shooter where you will have to pass a small campaign of 7 levels of shooting down cute aliens who look like cousins to headcrabs from Half-Life franchise. It's a remake of Unreal Tournament 2004 mod with same name, I sure remember playing that one once.
The thing is, this game is strictly multiplayer. You can't beat it in single-player. Well, I mean, you can surely force yourself to, but it's not designed for this, hard and doesn't reveal full potential. Game has practice mode with bots, but only through the first two levels. Otherwise, you better find three more marines like you. Thankfully, public multiplayer is active enough, can find at least one game running.
And yea, it's focused on teamwork by using loadouts. Got to balance between general and specialization and then not to shoot each other during gameplay. While campaign is short, it grows in difficulty non-stop, so there will be a challenge to a good team. Can always increase difficulty.
It's just a shame that it doesn't fit to lesser player count. I mean, would be nice to have it like in Left 4 Dead, where all spots are always filled with bots and players just take their place, and thus can always expect a support. Because when you play it with just one friend, it's hard to balance between firepower and special stuff. Almost always one tech, almost always one medic or you will die. But hey, not designed for that after all. It sure can be tough with just friend even on easy, sometimes.
Oh, there is no microtransaction. Valve didn't bother to profit from this in anyway, it's just that some devs that Valve hired were original creators of Alien Swarm mod for Unreal, I heard. It got modding support, but no Steam Workshop. And uses leveling system with which you can unlock new items as a way to prolong the life.
But eh. For free, it's pretty nice team game. But could use better music. Like most games.

"Let's be like Halo" said every first person shooter developer of the early 2000's. Recharging shields protecting a non-recharging health meter, all weapons are fired from the hip with no form of aiming besides a centralized targetting reticle, got your melee attack that's always at the ready, easy-to-use grenades that are always at the ready, linear paths to objectives that take you through numerous firefights along the way, and you watch all of this from behind a combat visor.
Fortunately for Republic Commando, I love Halo. Plus, RC tends to add some nifty features to the mix, such as the tactical aspect of commanding your squad (although the main tactic seems to be "tell squad to snipe, step away from keyboard"). It also does a pretty good job of giving the characters personalities. They seem real, as opposed to just monotonous drones like Halo marines.
Well worth the cheap price, and if you want to play multiplayer even now that GameSpy is dead, you can get GameRanger.

If Heisenberg had been a computer science teacher instead of a chemist, Factorio would have been his blue tinted digital crack.
The learning curve is practically non-existent, but youll never master it.  No matter how hard you try, you'll never be as efficient as you want, and the environment you're playing in will always throw in some nuance that has to be considered and compromised around.
You'll want to finish the game once, to see what happens. Then you'll want to try it again, to see if you could do it better.  Then you'll want to change the scenario, or join friends, or maybe just try and be a little faster.
Just one more minute, one more batch of plastics, one more conveyor line, one more train.  It becomes a mantra, a feedback loop in your head - Just one more...
And then, when you think you're all out of "just one mores" and that your physical health is shot, you're living in a cardboard box with a laptop and a severe case of scurvy and ready to pack it in, the devs will release an update with an amazing sounding new feature that you just have to try out on a clean save first....
